visits.text: You'll reach the Rocca di Asolo via the lanes that climb from Piazza Maggiore, about 20 minutes on foot. The view from the ramparts embraces the Veneto hills that poet Carducci called 'the city of a hundred horizons.' Open weekends, check weekday hours.

The 'city of a hundred horizons' deserves its reputation: from the Rocca, the gaze slides over hills covered with vines and campanili. Caterina Cornaro, exiled Queen of Cyprus, chose Asolo for her court in 1489 - understandably. Plan 2h for the old town.

Experience Asolo, known as the 'City of a Hundred Horizons' and the 'Pearl of the Province of Treviso'. This picture-perfect town in the Dolomite foothills has attracted artists, writers, and royalty for centuries with its beauty and cultural richness.

Explore the historic center with its elegant palazzos, ancient castle, and stunning views across vine-covered hills. The atmospheric streets and squares reveal why this has been a haven for creative spirits throughout history.

activities.text: You'll stroll on Asolo's Piazza Maggiore before climbing to the Rocca. Thursday morning markets are an opportunity to see producers from neighboring hills sell their products. Arrive hungry: the market cured meats deserve a tasting.

Soak in the countless horizons visible from various viewpoints around the town - each turn reveals new panoramas of hills, vineyards, and distant mountains that have inspired generations of artists and poets.

places.name: Bassano Del Grappa

visits.text: Palladio designed larger bridges, but none has the lightness of Bassano's Ponte degli Alpini. The wooden structure, based on the master's plans from 1568-69, has been destroyed and rebuilt several times, notably by the Alpini during the Great War. It doesn't look like a monument.

Behind the postcard image of the bridge, Bassano del Grappa hides a heavy military chapter: the Monte Grappa overlooking the town was a World War I battlefield. Two ossuaries at the summit contain the remains of thousands of Italian and Austrian soldiers. A sober and necessary visit.

The Bassanesi call it 'the city of grappa.' The Grapperia Nardini, founded in 1779, has been installed at the foot of the Ponte degli Alpini since its creation. It's a way to understand why the town became the world reference for this spirit.

Ponte degli Alpini (Ponte Vecchio) - The covered wooden bridge spanning the Brenta is the symbol of Bassano del Grappa. Palladio designed its reconstruction in 1567, on a bridge existing since the Middle Ages. The wooden structure, destroyed several times by floods and wars, has always been rebuilt identically, most recently in 1948 by Alpine troops after its destruction in February 1945. It bears their name for this reason and was declared a national monument in 2019. The bridge connects the two banks where the Brenta narrows, with a direct view of Monte Grappa and the Prealps. The town changed its name from 'Bassano Veneto' to 'Bassano del Grappa' after World War I to honor the soldiers who fell on the mountain.

Museo degli Alpini - Installed in the vaulted stone cellars at the bridge's foot, this small museum preserves uniforms, weapons, documents and photographs tracing the history of the Alpini—the Italian army's mountain troops—since their creation in 1872. The battles of Monte Grappa (1917-1918) occupy a central place: this is where the front line held during the Austrian offensive of the Strafexpedition and the 1918 offensives, just a few kilometers from town.

Castello degli Ezzelini - The ruins of this medieval fortress constitute Bassano's oldest point, dominating the center from the northern hill. The Bolzonella tower, called 'di Ser Ivano', dates from the Middle Ages and served as an independent watchtower. Giuseppe Verdi's first opera, Oberto conte di San Bonifacio, is set within these walls—proof that the castle still fed the imagination in the 19th century. In summer, the open-air theater inside the ramparts hosts the OperaEstate festival.

Palazzo Sturm - This 18th-century Rococo palace, built on the Brenta downstream from the bridge, offers from its courtyard the best viewpoint of the Ponte degli Alpini and the mountains. The interior hosts temporary modern art exhibitions. The outdoor terrace is the best place to photograph the entire bridge with the snowy massif in the background.

activities.text: You'll cross the Ponte degli Alpini to reach the Grapperia Nardini, founded in 1779 and considered the oldest in Italy still operating. Tasting is at the counter, standing, like the Bassanesi. No reservation needed.

The alcohol of grappa perfumes the cellars and lanes near the bridge. At the Grapperia Nardini, the house serves its Mezzo e Mezzo - half grappa half herbal liqueur - in a crystal glass at the bistro counter. You rarely stay for just one glass.

Visit and tasting at Nardini distillery - Bortolo Nardini founded Italy's first grappa distillery in 1779, at the northern entrance to the Ponte Vecchio, where it still stands today. The guided tour of the historic cellars traces two centuries of distillation: copper stills, maceration jars, production line. The tasting includes the famous Mezzoemezzo, the house aperitif based on rhubarb and citrus, and Tagliatella, a ruby liqueur from a secret late-18th-century recipe.

Poli Museo della Grappa - On the other side of the bridge, the Poli distillery museum traces the history of marc brandy from its medieval origins to modern techniques. The visit ends in the exhibition room with tasting and shop. The Poli distillery, founded in Bassano in 1898, is today among Veneto's most renowned.

Stroll along Viale dei Martiri - This panoramic avenue running along the old town's northern ramparts offers an open view of Monte Grappa massif and the Prealps. Its name comes from a September 1944 episode: in reprisal for a resistance action, the Germans hanged 31 partisans from the avenue's trees. An individualized memorial honors each victim.

visits.text: The South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology houses Ötzi, the Iceman discovered in 1991 at 3,210 m—killed by an arrow around 3300 BC at approximately age 46, he is one of the most studied human beings in the world. The museum occupies a 1912 building (former bank) right in the pedestrian heart. Closed Mondays, allow 1 hour.

Piazza Walther is a strange homage to a medieval poet in a bilingual city: Walther von der Vogelweide (c. 1170-1230), statue erected in 1889, watches over the square. The adjacent Gothic cathedral, completed in 1519, is distinguished by its green, white, and yellow diamond-patterned roof—bombed in 1943, meticulously restored. Free visit.

An ordinary medieval castle would have saints and martyrs. Runkelstein Castle (13th century), perched on its rocky spur above the Talvera, is covered with entirely secular frescoes—jousts, hunts, courtly love scenes, not a single martyr. Free shuttle from Piazza Walther every 30 minutes or so. Closed Mondays.

The South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano is housed in a 1912 building (former bank) and has sheltered Ötzi the Iceman since 1998, discovered on September 19, 1991 at 3,210 meters altitude in the Ötztal Alps by German hikers Helmut and Erika Simon. The mummy is preserved in a cold chamber at -6°C and 100% humidity, visible through a small window. Ötzi lived around 3200 BC (Chalcolithic, Copper Age): he was about 45 years old, stood 1.60 m tall, and weighed 50 kg. He was murdered by an arrow with a flint tip piercing his left shoulder blade (discovered by X-ray). His body bore 50 tattoos, probably for medicinal purposes, and he was equipped with a copper ax, bow, arrows, and clothing made of goat, deer, and bear skin. The museum attracts about 260,000 visitors per year.

Piazza Walther is the heart of Bolzano, an elegant 19th-century square where stands the statue of medieval Germanic poet Walther von der Vogelweide (c. 1170-1230), one of the most important authors of minnelieder of the Middle Ages. The Gothic cathedral (Duomo Maria Assunta), begun in the 14th century, is distinguished by its multicolored tile roof and richly decorated tower. The adjacent chapel of San Giovanni preserves a complete cycle of Giotto-school frescoes, one of the oldest in the region.

Via dei Portici (Arcade Street) is Bolzano's main medieval artery, lined with arcades, some dating back to the 13th century. This pedestrian street, characteristic of Tyrolean architecture, houses craft shops, galleries, and cafés. At the northern end, Piazza delle Erbe hosts a morning market where South Tyrolean apples are displayed (the region is Europe's leading producer) along with Speck Alto Adige IGP, the cold-smoked and air-dried ham that defines local gastronomy.
Cable car ascent to Soprabolzano to admire the Dolomites panorama
Discovery of the Renon plateau and its natural earth pyramids
Visit of Bolzano's old center: Piazza Walther, Duomo, Piazza delle Erbe
Discovery of Roncolo Castle and visit of a wine cellar with tasting
Self-guided visit of the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology

activities.text: Walk Via dei Portici and its medieval arcades to Piazza delle Erbe, where the daily market animates the stalls around the Neptune fountain. Best before 10 AM. A good hour of wandering among cafés, Speck stands, and South Tyrolean cheeses.

If you extend your evening, the osterie on Via Argentieri serve Lagrein, a red grape unique to South Tyrol—thick, slightly bitter, perfect with Speck. The city center's enotèche also offer Schiava and Gewürztraminer by the glass, no reservation.
Scenic route along Lake Garda toward Bolzano
Round-trip excursion from Bolzano to Merano

The Renon cable car, rebuilt in 2009 by the Leitner company with 3S technology, departs steps away from Bolzano's train station. In 12 minutes, its cabins climb from 274 to 1,227 meters altitude over a length of 4,500 meters. It replaced a rack railway inaugurated in 1907, deemed too slow (1h40 journey). At the summit, a small historic narrow-gauge train takes over to cross the plateau and reach the Renon earth pyramids, also called fairy chimneys.

The Renon earth pyramids are clay columns formed from glacial moraines, each topped with a protective rock block that slows erosion. They can reach several tens of meters in height. Three main groups punctuate the plateau, the most impressive being in the Rivellone valley. A trail with wooden boardwalks winds through the forest to offer several viewpoints over these natural formations. From the plateau, the panorama extends over the Dolomites and the Bolzano basin.

visits.text: Piazza del Kuerc (14th century) with its Torre della Bajona—whose bell sounded the alarm for the entire County during invasions—forms Bormio's dense historic center. Spot the dragon-shaped corbels beneath the Kuerc's gutter. Off-season (June or September), Via Roma is quiet and its shops accessible.

At Bormio, Cassiodorus, secretary to King Theodoric, recommended these waters as early as the 6th century. The Bagni Vecchi occupy natural caves a few kilometers from the center with water between 38 and 43°C flowing from the Ortles massif. Panoramic views over the valley from the outdoor pool. Reserve in high season.

Bormio deserves the detour beyond skiing: in Palazzo de Simoni (17th century, built on the foundations of a medieval castle), the Civic Museum of Bormio traces the history of the 'Magnifica Terra'. On the carved wooden portal, look for the De Simoni coat of arms: a monkey holding a branch and an eagle. Open in summer.

Stroll through Bormio's historic center—the 'Magnifica Terra'—and its Piazza Cavour surrounded by noble palaces with painted facades. The first mentions of Bormio date back to a letter from Cassiodorus; in the Middle Ages, the town was the seat of an autonomous county covering the present territories of Valfurva, Valdidentro, and Livigno. The name Bormio probably derives from the Gaulish 'bormo,' meaning thermal spring. The Bajona Tower and the old Via Roma testify to Lombard medieval architecture. Bormio will be one of the Alpine sites for the Milano-Cortina 2026 Olympics for alpine skiing.

Take time for a soak at the Bagni Vecchi, perched 3 km above the center on the Stelvio road. These thermal baths have been known since pre-Roman antiquity: a bas-relief discovered during the demolition of a local church represents a water god and is dated between the 5th and 1st century BC. Pliny the Elder reportedly mentioned the springs in his writings. Nine natural springs emerge between 1,280 and 1,421 meters altitude at temperatures of 37 to 43°C. The Grotte di San Martino, a natural Turkish bath carved into the rock, is one of the oldest springs; an infinity pool overlooks the entire valley.

activities.text: Walk the historic center from Piazza Kuerc northward: Via Roma, Via Alberti, the Quadrilatero degli Alberti and its medieval portals. A peaceful hour in preserved lanes, with the first slopes of the Ortles visible as soon as you look up.

If the Bagni Vecchi strain the budget (paid entry), the free thermal springs of Bormio offer a no-cost option: follow the Stelvio road 2 km from the center, park at the bridge over the Frodolfo, walk upriver 200 m. Water shoes recommended.

Ski Bormio's slopes in winter—the domain extends 50 km between 1,225 m and 3,000 m altitude on the flanks of Monte Vallecetta. The Stelvio piste, inaugurated in 1982, hosted the World Alpine Ski Championships in 1985 and 2005; it's part of the World Cup circuit each December. In summer, hike or mountain bike in Stelvio National Park, the largest of Italy's Alpine national parks, created in 1935.

Excursion to Stelvio Pass (Passo dello Stelvio, 2,757 m): the second-highest paved mountain pass in the Alps, it connects Bormio to Bolzano through a succession of 48 hairpin turns on the Lombard side. In summer the pass is open to road traffic and hikers; the summit glacier enables year-round skiing. In cycling, the Stelvio is one of the legendary climbs of the Giro d'Italia.

places.name: Bormio Lx

visits.text: Morning walk through Bormio's medieval centre. The town predates the Romans and still has a compact old quarter with stone arcades, frescoed churches, and the 13th-century Torre delle Ore. It feels genuinely lived-in - not a ski-resort museum. The Kuerc civic tower on Piazza Cavour has been the town's meeting point since the Middle Ages.

activities.text: 🍽️ LUNCH - Ristorante Kuerc in Bormio's old town centre. Valtellina cuisine done right: pizzoccheri (buckwheat pasta with potatoes, cabbage and Bitto cheese), sciatt (crispy fried cheese fritters), and bresaola from the valley. Unpretentious, local, and exactly what you want after three hours of hairpins.

🍽️ DINNER - Ristorante Salone dei Balli at QC Grand Hotel Bagni Nuovi. Traditional Valtellina cuisine in a grand Art Nouveau ballroom with over 100 local wines on the list. The venison with polenta taragna and wild berries is the standout. Reserve when you check in - only hotel guests can dine here.

🏨 NIGHT - QC Grand Hotel Bagni Nuovi. Art Nouveau palace from 1836, now a 5-star thermal spa hotel in the Stelvio National Park. Over 30 thermal treatments: outdoor infinity pools facing the mountains, saunas carved into rock, hot tubs fed by natural springs.

Half-day hike in the Stelvio National Park. The Valle dei Forni trail leads to the Forni Glacier viewpoint - one of the largest valley glaciers in Italy. The path is moderate (about 2h round trip from Rifugio Forni) and rewards with close-up views of crevasses and icefalls. The rifugio serves simple but solid mountain food if you want lunch up there.

🍽️ LUNCH - Rifugio Forni if you hiked, or Osteria Belvedere at the hotel if you stayed. The Belvedere does rustic Alpine dinner food (fondue, raclette, grilled meats) with a terrace view over the valley.

Afternoon soak in the QC Terme outdoor thermal pools. After the hike, this is non-negotiable. The pools are staggered at different temperatures, and the views of the Ortler massif from the infinity pool are absurd. Stay until sunset - the light on the peaks turns gold then pink.

🍽️ DINNER - Enoteca Guanella in Bormio centre. Smaller, more intimate than the hotel restaurant. Strong local wine selection (Valtellina Sfursat is the region's top red - similar to an Amarone but from Nebbiolo). The tasting plates of local cheeses and cured meats are a meal in themselves.
🏨 NIGHT - QC Grand Hotel Bagni Nuovi (second night). Try the 'emotional path' - a circuit of hot, cold, steam and salt rooms. Best done before dinner.

visits.text: The water color is unreal: pale emerald against white rocks of the Croda del Becco. Lake Braies (Pragser Wildsee), at 1,496 meters in the Pustertal, is one of the most photographed lakes in the Dolomites. Arrive before 8am in summer: access is regulated and charged after.

Lake Braies is too famous for its own good - and yet the north shore of the lake, beyond the chalet-hotel, stays quiet even in high season. The lake circuit on foot takes 1h30 for 3.5 km. Swimming is discouraged: the water stays icy year-round.

activities.text: You'll rent one of the wooden rowboats from the Pragser Wildsee Hütte dock to approach the vertical walls of the Croda del Becco. Rental lasts 30 to 45 minutes. Arrive before 9am: boats go quickly in high season.

visits.text: You'll cross the Brenner Pass via the A22 Autostrada at 1,374 meters, without really noticing: it's one of the busiest Alpine crossings in Europe, invisible behind highway ramps. Stop to see the two customs posts side by side, witnesses to Schengen's recent history.

A strategic passage since Roman times, the Brennero was the route of medieval armies and 1943 convoys. The border has been erased since Schengen, but traces of the customs post are still visible. The small chapel on the Italian side is worth a five-minute stop.

activities.text: You'll pause at Brennero to observe the Munich-Verona axis that concentrates one of the densest truck traffics in the Alps. The cafeteria on the Italian side, just after the border sign, is authentic in its own way.

visits.text: Bressanone has everything of a fine compact medieval capital: cathedral, cloister, episcopal palace, and cobbled lanes, all within a twenty-minute walking tour. The town is mentioned as early as 901 as an episcopal seat, making it the oldest city in Tyrol. Arrive early, before tour buses.

The smell of Speck, ham smoked and dried in the South Tyrolean Alpine wind, fills the artisan butcher shops in the center. The ochre-yellow arcades of the Portici Maggiori create a typically Mediterranean play of light. Enter a Weinstube for a Speck platter and a glass of local Lagrein.

Bressanone locals will direct you to the Augustinian abbey of Novacella, 3 km north, for its white wines and 12th-century cloister. The tasting cellar is open in the afternoon. Take the bike path along the Isarco to get there in 15 minutes.

Bressanone's Piazza del Duomo gathers in a single glance the Gothic Duomo and its famous cloister with medieval frescoes, the Palazzo dei Principi-Vescovi with its arcades over the moat, and Via Portici Maggiori lined with 16th-17th century façades. Episcopal capital since the Middle Ages, Bressanone was the favorite resort of Habsburg nobility in the 19th century. Free cloister visit; the Palazzo keeps museum hours.

The Augustinian canons of Novacella are not modest: the fountain in the inner courtyard of Novacella Abbey depicts the seven wonders of Antiquity, with an eighth niche reserved for the abbey itself. Founded in the 12th century, it also produces Sylvaner and Kerner in the northernmost vineyards of South Tyrol. 3km from Bressanone, guided tour €15.

activities.text: You'll cross the Portici Maggiori to Bressanone cathedral and its well-preserved Romanesque cloister. The cloister visit takes 30 minutes and is often quieter than the nave. The neighboring Palazzo Vescovile completes the visit.

If abbey wines interest you, Novacella produces Sylvaner and Kerner from high altitude recognized throughout northern Italy. Tasting at the monastery cellar on weekday afternoons. Reservations recommended in July and August.

Walk to Novacella Abbey from Piazza del Duomo along the Isarco river heading north: 3km each way, easy marked trail, 45 minutes. You'll arrive among the abbey's vineyards for a tasting in the cellar—the estate's dry white wines are among South Tyrol's most acclaimed.

visits.text: You'll climb to the Castello di Brunico, built in the 13th century by the Bishop of Bressanone, which dominates the town from the hill above the shopping center. The view over the Valle della Rienza is clear in tramontane weather. Fifteen-minute walk from the center.

The MMM Ripa, one of Reinhold Messner's six mountain museums, has been installed in the Castello di Brunico since 2011. It's dedicated to mountain peoples of the world: Tuareg, Tibetans, Maasai. 'Ripa' means 'mountain man' in Tibetan. Open May to October, check hours.

Built in 1250 by Bishop Bruno von Kirchberg to watch over the Puster Valley, Brunico Castle now houses the Messner Mountain Museum Ripa—'Ripa' meaning 'mountain man' in Tibetan. Reinhold Messner has gathered objects and stories from Sherpas, Tibetans, Tuareg and Maasai. Open spring to fall (roughly mid-May to November), closed Tuesdays.

Brunico's center unfolds along Via Centrale and its bourgeois houses with painted façades, punctuated by old portals. The atmosphere swings between Austrian Tyrol and Northern Italy—two menus, two flags, two languages on the signs. A quarter-hour pedestrian stroll covers it; stop for Speck and local products.

activities.text: If the weather is good, the Plan de Corones (Kronplatz) is accessible by cable car from Brunico and offers one of the broadest panoramas of the Dolomites, at 2,275 meters. The platform alone justifies the trip. Check hours: variable by season.

Walk down from Brunico Castle toward the center via the castle path: views over the Rienza valley and the Dolomite slopes. At the bottom, Via Centrale leads you naturally to Piazza del Municipio and its cafés for a well-earned break.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Traverse, 16 days: Grisons to Trieste
Grand Dolomites Tour: Braies, Cortina and the Mountain Passes

visits.text: The region's finest trail: the Viel del Pan from the Col dei Rossi station (2,382 m) runs along a balcony beneath the walls of the Marmolada for 2 to 3 hours with continuous glacier views, no technical difficulty. One of the great classics of the Dolomites, accessible to all hikers.

The only glaciated summit of the Dolomites, the Marmolada (3,343 m) reads on the horizon from Canazei: the road to Lago di Fedaia 8 km away leads to the foot of the north face and the cable car departure—covered separately tomorrow. A quick orientation from the center suffices before heading up.

Canazei in summer has this rare quality: the Dolomites are in every angle of view from the terrace of the smallest café, the village keeps its human scale and Ladin animation. In summer, scent of larch resin and terraces open from 8 AM. Artisan markets and evening events in July-August; check the local program.

The best thing you'll do in the Dolomites might be the Viel del Pan trail. From the Col dei Rossi cable car station (2,382m), this ridge path balconies above the Marmolada, following the cliff to Lago Fedaia—permanent view of the glacier, immense horizon, no technical difficulty. Allow 2 to 3 hours one-way descending to Canazei.

Canazei's center stretches along the bottom of a valley ringed by blonde rocks, with the baroque church as landmark and local-product shops along the main street. In summer, scent of larch resin and outdoor terraces from 8 a.m.; from any café, you can make out the silhouette of the Sella and Marmolada at the end of the valley. Allow 30 minutes to stroll.

The Marmolada, roof of the Dolomites at 3,343m, is approached from Lago di Fedaia 8km east of Canazei, then by cable car. The Marmolada glacier has been retreating for decades; in July 2022, a serac collapse killed several climbers. Access to the glacier is now discouraged in warm periods; the panorama from the upper station remains exceptional.

activities.text: Leave early from Canazei for the Sella Ronda loop by car: four passes (Pordoi, Campolongo, Gardena, Sella) between 1,875 and 2,244 m, Dolomite panoramas at each descent. Allow 3 to 4 hours with stops. In July-August, traffic can be heavy at peak hours.

If you have two extra days, the Alta Via 2 of the Dolomites passes through Canazei between Bressanone and Feltre: the section around the Pordoi is accessible without advanced technical equipment. Book refuges online from July; the best places go in a few hours.

Leave early from Canazei for the Sella Ronda loop by car: four passes (Pordoi, Campolongo, Gardena, Sella) between 1,875m and 2,244m, Dolomite panoramas at every descent. Allow 3 to 4 hours with stops. In summer, traffic can be heavy at peak hours on the passes.

If you have two extra days, the Alta Via 2 of the Dolomites starts in Bressanone and ends in Feltre—Canazei is just a central stage. The section around Pordoi is accessible without advanced technical equipment. Refuges book online; from July, the best spots go in a few hours.

visits.text: Drive to the Cinque Torri (Five Towers) - a cluster of Dolomite rock pillars that look like a giant's abandoned chess pieces. The short hike from the Averau chairlift (30 minutes) takes you to World War I trenches and open-air fortifications carved into the rock at 2,300 m, with interpretive panels. The contrast of war remnants and pristine mountain scenery is sobering and stays with you.

activities.text: 🍽️ LUNCH - Rifugio Averau, at the top of the Cinque Torri chairlift. Mountain rifugio cooking at its best: canederli (bread dumplings in broth), speck, polenta with deer ragù. The terrace faces the Marmolada glacier. Simple, hearty, and the views do half the work.

visits.text: First capital of the Lombard duchy in Italy, Cividale del Friuli was founded by Julius Caesar under the name Forum Iulii - which gave the Friuli region its name. The mid-8th century Tempietto Longobardo, UNESCO-listed in 2011, is the best-preserved Lombard monument in Europe.

The Tempietto Longobardo is one of the most intact works of the Lombard world: stuccos, frescoes, and 8th-century mosaics in a room barely larger than a chapel. Morning light streams through a small east-facing window. Come at 9am for this grazing light on the stuccos.

Cividale's Ipogeo Celtico, a network of underground galleries whose origins remain debated, descends several meters beneath the old town. The humidity and smell of stone recall that Cividale's soil has layers. Guided tour only, reservation at the tourist office.

activities.text: You'll cross the Ponte del Diavolo, a medieval bridge over the Natisone, to reach the east bank with views of the cliff and ramparts. Legend says the devil built it for a soul. At night, the bridge is beautifully lit.

Known for its Lombard Tempietto, Cividale also hides remarkable Friulian gastronomy: its centro storico osterie serve boreto alla graisana, white fish stew with vinegar and garlic. A local dish little known outside Friuli, ask the owner.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Traverse, 16 days: Grisons to Trieste

visits.text: Gothic and Baroque on the same façade: Como Cathedral, begun in 1396 and completed in the 18th century, is one of the few buildings in Italy to pull off this marriage. The two statues flanking the main portal depict Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger—the two great Latin scholars born on the shores of this lake. Guided tour recommended for the Flemish tapestries in the nave.

Como has been 'la città della seta' since the 15th century—the world capital of luxury silk. The Silk Museum exhibits period looms and the complete production chain: the great fashion houses have their finest scarves woven here. Two informative hours, 20-minute walk from the cathedral.

Alessandro Volta was born in Como in 1745—and the city remembers him with the Tempio Voltiano on the lakeshore, dedicated to the inventor of the battery. Just 400 m away, the Casa del Fascio (1936) is a masterpiece of Rationalist architecture by Giuseppe Terragni, studied in architecture schools worldwide. Free entry to the gardens of neighboring Villa Olmo.

Como's Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta is considered the last great Gothic cathedral built in Italy: construction began in 1396, ten years after the Milan Duomo, following a design by Lorenzo degli Spazzi, and wasn't completed until 1770 with the addition of the Baroque dome. The building measures 87 meters long and rises 75 meters high. Its façade, created between 1447 and 1489, features an unusual detail: two statues of Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger flank the main portal, honoring the two scholars born in Como. Inside, the 16th and 17th-century tapestries and paintings by Bernardino Luini—a pupil of Leonardo da Vinci—deserve close attention.

Adjacent to the cathedral, the Broletto is Como's former town hall, built in the 13th century. Its façade in gray and white stripes with a medieval tower is one of the best-preserved examples of Lombard communal architecture. The cathedral-Broletto ensemble forms a rare testament to seven centuries of civic and religious life in the same square.

The Como-Brunate funicular, inaugurated on November 11, 1894, climbs in 7 minutes over approximately 1,100 meters with a maximum gradient of 55%. It reaches Brunate at 715 meters altitude, a village nicknamed the "Balcony of the Alps" because, on clear days, you can make out Mont Rose and the Apennines. Brunate was a favored destination for Milan's bourgeoisie during the Belle Époque: its Art Nouveau and neo-Gothic villas are still clearly visible. Alessandro Volta lived here during his childhood.

Villa Carlotta in Tremezzo was built in 1690 by Marquis Giorgio Clerici in a natural hollow between the lake and mountains. In 1801, it passed to Gian Battista Sommariva, former director of the Cisalpine Republic, who assembled works by Canova, Thorvaldsen, and Hayez, making it one of the leading centers of Neoclassical art in Italy. In 1843, Princess Marianne of Nassau purchased it as a wedding gift for her daughter Charlotte of Prussia on her marriage to Georg II of Saxe-Meiningen—hence the name Carlotta. Since 1927, a royal decree has entrusted its management to the Ente Villa Carlotta.

Villa Carlotta's botanical garden covers 7 hectares and shelters 150 varieties of azaleas and rhododendrons that bloom in spring. The park includes a fern valley, a bamboo grove with black bamboo, and a series of terraces with lake views. Georg II of Saxe-Meiningen, passionate about botany, significantly enriched the plant collections in the 19th century.

Bellagio occupies the tip of the peninsula that separates the two arms of Lake Como: it's from Bellagio that the Y-shaped view of the lake is most striking. Its stairway alleys (the Salita Serbelloni), terraced gardens, and boutiques make it the most photographed town on the lake. Villa Melzi, whose gardens open directly onto the lake, was built in 1808 for Francesco Melzi d'Eril, first vice-president of the Italian Republic.

activities.text: Walk along the shore of Lake Como westward from the historic center to Villa Olmo: 1.5 km waterfront promenade. The villa's gardens (free entry) open directly onto the lake. Check whether the villa itself is open before you go—restoration work occasionally affects access.

In five minutes by funicular from lower Como, the village of Brunate opens onto a plunging view of the lake at 715 m: different light, mountain air, forest walks. Last departure from Brunate around 10:30 PM in summer.

From the funicular's arrival station in Brunate, a 30 to 40-minute walk on a marked trail leads to the Faro Voltiano, a symbolic 29-meter lighthouse built in 1927 for the centenary of Alessandro Volta's death. From the summit, the panorama over Lake Como, the Prealps, and—on clear days—all the way to Mont Rose is exceptional.

A regular ferry service connects Tremezzo to Bellagio in about twenty minutes. The boat crossing offers the best views of Villa Carlotta's lake-facing façade and allows you to appreciate the Y-shape of the lake from the water. Departures are frequent throughout the day from the dock in front of the villa.

visits.text: Giovanni Battista Cima, called Cima da Conegliano, was born here around 1460 and left his hometown several altarpieces among the most delicate in Venetian painting. His works dot the old town churches. The cathedral houses one of his masterpieces, free visit.

Less known than Venice, yet 60 km away, Conegliano protects a Via XX Settembre lined with Venetian arcades decorated with 15th- and 16th-century frescoes. In September, a grape harvest festival gathers prosecco producers. The rest of the year, tourists are rare here.

The ramparts of the village of Soave, nearly 700 meters long, run up the hill above the vineyards in a state of preservation that would make most French medieval castles blush. The Scaliger castle at the summit dates from the 10th century, expanded in the 13th and 14th centuries. Below, the village is calm, without the mass tourism the appellation's name might suggest. Garganega vines climb right to the feet of the ramparts—the image is beautiful and the volcanic soil visible in cross-section in the embankments explains better than any speech why Soave Classico is different.

Founded in 1876, the Scuola Enologica di Conegliano is Italy's oldest wine school—26 years before Montpellier's. Its graduates have trained several generations of Veneto winemakers, and many estates in Prosecco and Valpolicella are run by alumni. The historic building can be visited, as can the adjacent experimental vineyard. Not the most spectacular site on the route, but a useful stop for understanding why Veneto became Italy's leading wine region by volume.

activities.text: You'll climb to the castello via the path that starts behind the cathedral, about 15 minutes on foot. View over the Prosecco Superiore DOCG hills on clear days. The museo civico is open Tuesday to Sunday.

Pieropan estate in Soave: this is where garganega regained its dignity. In the 1970s, when industrial Soave from the plains had turned the appellation into supermarket plonk, Leonildo Pieropan continued producing terroir-driven Soave on the limestone and volcanic slopes of the Classico zone. His 'La Rocca' bottling, from volcanic tuff, still ages well at ten years. The family continues—the visit is restrained, the tasting direct and precise.

Drive toward Conegliano in late afternoon (about 2 hours from Soave, A4 then A27). Arrival in the Prosecco DOCG capital—Conegliano is the northern gateway to the route and co-capital of the appellation with Valdobbiadene. First glimpse of the terraced hills from the road climbing up: if you're here in October, the grape pickers are in the vineyards. First glass of Prosecco Superiore on a terrace in the town center to calibrate the difference from what you usually drink.

visits.text: Walk the Corso Italia, Cortina's pedestrianised main street - equal parts luxury shopping and people-watching. The bell tower of the Basilica dei Santi Filippo e Giacomo anchors the centre. In summer, the café terraces are the real theatre: Italian glamour meets hiking boots, fur coats next to fleece.

activities.text: Take the Freccia nel Cielo (Arrow in the Sky) cable car up to Tofana di Mezzo (3,244 m) - the highest point you can reach without climbing gear in the Dolomites. Three stages, the last one emerging above the clouds on most mornings. The panoramic terrace at the top offers a 360° view across the Dolomite range. Dress warm - it's often below freezing even in July.

🍽️ LUNCH - SanBrite. Only seven tables in a room of recycled wood with a picture window onto the Ampezzo Dolomites. Chef Riccardo Gaspari grows and farms most of his ingredients at the adjoining El Brite de Larieto farmstead. One Michelin star, zero pretension. The meal starts with mountains of homemade butter and bread with extraordinary texture. Desserts are made without added sugar - and they're the best course.

🍽️ DINNER - Ristorante Tivoli. On the road to the Falzarego Pass, at the base of the Tofane. Chef Graziano Prest has held his Michelin star since 2002 - Cortina's most decorated year-round table. The kitchen bridges Alpine mountain tradition and Venetian seafood (fresh fish arrives daily from Chioggia). The wine cellar leans French and historic Italian. Plan for 2.5 hours.

🏨 NIGHT - Cristallo, a Luxury Collection Hotel. Cortina's original grande dame, opened in 1901. 73 rooms mixing Belle Époque bones with contemporary design. Spa with indoor pool, Turkish bath, and Dolomite-view treatment rooms. Free shuttle to town.

🍽️ DINNER - Il Vizietto di Cortina. Back in town, more casual than the Michelin spots but beloved locally. Wood-fired focaccia, handmade pasta, and a wine list that punches above its weight class. Good for the night when you don't want a 3-hour tasting menu but still want to eat well.
🏨 NIGHT - Cristallo Hotel (second night). The 1224 Terrazza bar on the Grand Hotel Savoia's roof is a short drive for a nightcap with a panoramic view - Cortina's best evening spot.

places.name: Cortina Dampezzo

visits.text: Cortina is fashionable, but not only that: the Ciasa de ra Regoles houses an ethnographic collection of Ampezzo Ladin culture and canvases by Giorgio de Chirico and Filippo de Pisis. The Ampezzans call themselves neither Italians nor Tyroleans—they are Ladins, an alpine people with their own language for centuries. Paid entry, verify hours locally.

Corso Italia at dawn, before the shops open, has something strange and beautiful: the Liberty façades, the white bell tower of Santi Filippo e Giacomo in raking light, and the Tofane in the background beginning to blush pink. The 'Queen of the Dolomites' deserves to be seen before her audience.

Cortina d'Ampezzo hosted the Winter Olympics in 1956—the legendary Tofane downhill—then again in 2026 with Milan. The Olympia delle Tofane course, one of the legendary women's World Cup downhills, is accessible to hikers in summer. The Palazzo del Ghiaccio (Olympic ice rink) remains open off-season.

Bressanone (Brixen in German) is the oldest town in South Tyrol. Its Gothic cathedral dedicated to Mary and Saint Cassian was rebuilt in Baroque style in the 17th and 18th centuries while preserving its 11th-century Romanesque cloister, considered one of the finest in northern Italy: its double columns frame an interior courtyard adorned with medieval frescoes. The neighboring episcopal palace, residence of prince-bishops since the 10th century, houses the Diocesan Museum with a collection of nativity scenes, some dating back to the 17th century.

Lake Braies (Pragser Wildsee in German) sits at 1,496 meters altitude in the Fanes-Sennes-Braies Nature Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009. Its intense emerald-green waters owe their color to the fine suspension of limestone particles. The lake measures 1.2 km long by 300 to 400 meters wide, with a maximum depth of 36 meters. It's framed by the vertical wall of Croda del Becco (Seekofel, 2,810 m). It's the starting point for Alta Via n°1 of the Dolomites, the great traverse from Braies to Belluno. A dock and wooden chalet on the north shore have made it the most photographed lake in the Dolomites.

Cortina d'Ampezzo is nicknamed the "Queen of the Dolomites." Perched at 1,210 meters altitude in the heart of a white-rock mountain cirque, it hosted the 1956 Winter Olympics and will co-host them again in 2026 with Milan. Its Corso Italia, lined with luxury boutiques, runs through a center with a Belle Époque resort atmosphere. From town, the vertical faces of the Tofane (3,244 m) dominate to the northwest, the Cristallo (3,221 m) to the northeast.

Lake Misurina (1,754 m altitude) is the first body of water you encounter while climbing toward the Tre Cime. Stretching 900 meters long, framed by the Sesto Dolomites, it reflects the silhouettes of Sorapiss and Cristallo in calm weather. It's from Misurina that the toll road (about €30) leading to Rifugio Auronzo departs—the base for the hike around the Tre Cime.

The Tre Cime di Lavaredo (Drei Zinnen in German) are the symbol of the Dolomites and one of the most photographed rock formations in the world. They consist of three distinct pillars of dolomitic limestone: Cima Grande (2,999 m, the highest, with a nearly vertical 500-meter north face), Cima Ovest (2,973 m), and Cima Piccola (2,857 m). These rocks formed 200 to 220 million years ago by sedimentation in the tropical waters of the Tethys Ocean. Cima Grande was first climbed on August 21, 1869 by Paul Grohmann. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009. During World War I (1915-1917), the front line ran exactly here: trenches, galleries, and barracks carved into the rock are still visible on the trails.

activities.text: Take the Tofane lifts from lower Cortina to reach around 3,000 m: in clear weather, 360° views over the Dolomites. Check summer schedules in advance—reduced hours off ski season. Windbreaker even in August.

Late afternoon, drive to Passo Falzarego (2,105 m) 10 km from Cortina: the Cinque Torri stand out from the Lagazuoi cable car viewpoint, and the Great War trenches accessible from the upper station restore the scale of the 1915-1918 mountain battles. Return before sunset.

The loop around Lake Braies on foot is 3.9 kilometers and takes 1h15 to 1h30. The west shore, wide and flat, is accessible to all; the east shore is narrower, with steps carved into the rock and ledge passages above the water—more demanding but with the most striking views. In high season (July-September), car access is regulated: shuttles required from valley-bottom parking lots.

The Great Dolomites Road (Strada delle Dolomiti, SS48) links Bolzano to Cortina in 117 kilometers. Construction began in 1901 by decision of the 1897 Austrian provincial law—the primary objective was military, the Austro-Hungarian Empire wanting to control its southern borders. The road was completed in 1909. From Cortina, the loop by car passes through three emblematic passes: Passo Falzarego (2,105 m) with the Lagazuoi cable car (2,835 m, site of World War I battles with tunnels carved into the rock), then Passo Pordoi (2,239 m, highest pass on the route, with a monument to cyclist Fausto Coppi and a cable car to Sass Pordoi at 2,950 m, "terrace of the Dolomites"), and finally Passo Sella (2,244 m) at the foot of the Sella group, with direct views of Sassolungo (3,181 m) and Marmolada (3,343 m, highest peak of the Dolomites).

The classic loop around the Tre Cime starts from Rifugio Auronzo (2,320 m, accessible by car from Misurina via toll road) and covers about 10 kilometers with 500 meters of elevation gain. The trail passes Rifugio Lavaredo, climbs to Forcella Lavaredo (2,454 m) to discover the south face of the peaks, winds around the north to Rifugio Locatelli-Drei Zinnen Hütte (2,405 m) which offers the most famous view: the three towers stand directly ahead, their north walls in full verticality. The descent returns to Rifugio Auronzo via the eastern valley. Allow 3 to 4 hours of walking.

places.name: Erto E Casso

visits.text: The Vajont dam (265 m) is still standing—it was the dam that survived, not the mountain. On the night of October 9, 1963, a landslide of approximately 270 million m³ from Monte Toc created a wave that overtopped the dam and obliterated Longarone below, killing 1,917 people. The dam and the scar in the mountain are now a visitable memorial from Erto e Casso.

From the road through Erto e Casso, the landslide scar—the bare white rock of Monte Toc—remains visible to the naked eye sixty years later. Guided tours of the Vajont site explain the circumstances of the disaster, documented without embellishment. It is established that the catastrophe could have been avoided.

Diga del Vajont - On October 9, 1963, at 10:39 PM, an entire section of Monte Toc (about 260 million cubic meters of rock) slid into the artificial lake behind this 261.6-meter dam (one of the world's tallest at the time). The wave, estimated at 250 meters high, overtopped the dam crest and swept down the valley, obliterating the town of Longarone and several hamlets in four minutes. The death toll reached 1,917. The dam itself, intact, still stands - it was the mountain that failed, not the structure.

Erto e Casso - These two villages perched on heights above the dam were partially spared by the wave but evacuated. Erto has been restored and listed among the 'Borghi più Belli d'Italia' (Italy's most beautiful villages). Its sloping lanes, gray stone houses, and fountains recount mountain life before the catastrophe. An interpretive center traces the drama's chronology.

Monte Toc scar - From the overlook upstream of the dam, you can clearly see the immense gash left by the landslide on the mountainside, and the residual lake reduced to a thin ribbon of water. The contrast between the scar's magnitude and the landscape's current tranquility is striking.

activities.text: Descend to the foot of the Vajont dam to measure the 265 m height from downstream: the perspective is dizzying. Information on the signage documents the disaster and political responsibilities. Free access from Erto e Casso via the canyon road.

Guided tour recommended - Local associations offer guided routes that place the catastrophe in context: ignored geological warnings, industrial and political responsibilities, the subsequent trial. Allow about 2 hours.

visits.text: If you have the energy, continue to Lago di Braies (Pragser Wildsee) - about 1h15 north of Cortina. This turquoise lake surrounded by vertical Dolomite cliffs is arguably the most photographed spot in the Italian Alps. Arrive before 9 AM or after 5 PM to avoid the Instagram crowds. Boat rental (€15/30 min) is the classic shot, but the shoreline walk is free and just as beautiful.

visits.text: Lago di Fedaia deserves the stop beyond a simple stage: at 2,054 m, the reservoir at the foot of the Marmolada's north face presents an intense blue-gray fed by glacial meltwater. From the dam, the gaze rises to Punta Penia (3,343 m), roof of the Dolomites, and the cable car ascends the glacier.

From the Fedaia dam, comparative photographic markers document the retreat of the Marmolada glacier year after year. In July 2022, a serac collapse claimed the lives of several climbers from this face: the site has become a place of climate memory as much as a panorama.

Lago di Fedaia deserves more than a quick stop: at 2,054m, the reservoir at the foot of Marmolada's north face shows an intense blue-gray fed by glacial melt. From the dam, your gaze climbs to Punta Penia (3,343m), roof of the Dolomites, and the cable car rises onto the glacier.

From the Fedaia dam, comparative photo markers document the retreat of the Marmolada glacier year by year. In July 2022, a serac collapse killed several climbers from this side: the site has become a memorial to climate as much as a panorama.

activities.text: Take the cable car from Malga Ciapela (Veneto side) to Punta Rocca (3,265 m) for a 360° view over the Dolomites. The glacier beneath the terrace is visibly shrinking. Check schedules at marmolada.com—access impossible in bad weather.

Take the cable car from Malga Ciapela (Veneto side) to Punta Rocca (3,265m) for a 360° view of the Dolomites. The glacier under the terrace is in visible contraction. Check conditions at marmolada.com—access impossible in bad weather.

visits.text: Lago di Sorapis is a reward, not a stroll: 2 hours hiking from Passo Tre Croci via trail 215, then a final view of a cirque of orange walls and turquoise water colored by suspended glacial particles. Intermediate level, about 4 hours round trip.

Even without doing the Sorapis hike, Passo Tre Croci (about 1,800 m) is worth the stop: view of the Cristallo to the northeast and the first Venetian Dolomites to the south. Starting point for several marked trails. The parking area is free but limited in high season.

activities.text: Leave for Lago di Sorapis before 7:30 AM: ideal conditions and parking still available at Passo Tre Croci. Trail 215 is well marked but has some exposed passages with cables. Hiking boots and water (1.5 L minimum) required.

visits.text: You expect a classic botanical garden—and you find yourself in a natural amphitheater of 12 hectares. The Gardens of Trauttmansdorff Castle, voted 'Most Beautiful Garden in Italy' in 2005, display 80 garden landscapes across 100 m of elevation, from lotus ponds to forest parks to sun gardens. The integrated Touriseum traces 250 years of alpine tourism. Closed in winter.

The scent of cypress and Mediterranean maquis 200 m above Merano: the Tappeiner Promenade winds along the sunny slope with views over the Passirio valley. 3.8 km accessible to all, open year-round. The Powder Tower (14th century) along the route is worth a stop for the panorama.

Merano is the town where Empress Elisabeth of Austria came to recover: the 'Sissi Path' connects the Kurhaus to the Trauttmansdorff gardens via the sites where she resided. This warm, dry microclimate of the Passirio valley was renowned throughout Europe for pulmonary ailments. The town's Belle Époque legacy is still legible in the façades of the Summer Promenade.

Tappeinerweg – a 4-kilometer panoramic promenade built in 1893 at the initiative of Dr. Franz Tappeiner, a Viennese physician and botanist, along the heights of the Passer River's left bank, 100-300 meters above the city. The subtropical vegetation—palms, cacti, agaves, lemon trees—thrives thanks to Merano's exceptional microclimate (270 sunny days per year, 300mm rainfall), created by a mountain corridor sheltered from northern winds by the Ötztal Alps.

Passeggiata Lungo Passirio and historic center – the banks of the Passer River were transformed in the late 19th century into therapeutic promenades for spa visitors, lined with chestnut and willow trees. Merano became the most fashionable spa resort in the Austro-Hungarian Empire after Empress Elisabeth of Austria (Sissi) visited in 1870 and 1871, popularizing the grape cure still practiced every autumn. The historic center preserves the Gothic arcades of Via dei Portici (14th-15th centuries) and the 14th-century Duomo San Nicola.

Giardini di Castel Trauttmansdorff – 12-hectare terraced botanical gardens on the Maia Alta hillside, created in 1906 around the castle where Empress Elisabeth stayed in 1870. The castle was purchased by the Province of Bolzano in 1980 and the gardens opened to the public in 2001. The 80 themed zones showcase 1,000 plant species from five continents, including 20-meter bamboos, giant sequoias, and collections of heritage roses.

Castello Principesco (Landesfürstliche Burg) – residential castle built in 1470 by Sigismund, Archduke of Tyrol, on the foundations of a 13th-century fortified house. One of the rare preserved examples of Tyrolean Gothic residential architecture, featuring carved wooden interior halls, 15th-century ceramic stove tiles, and original furnishings. Property of the Province of Bolzano since 1948.

activities.text: Follow the Passirio in the lower town via the Summer and Winter Promenades, the two opposing riverbank walks that frame the historic center between old cafés and Belle Époque hotels. The Ponte delle Poste leads to the Cathedral of St. Nicholas and Piazza del Duomo for an aperitivo on a terrace.

In 1874, the Kurhaus of Merano opened at the heart of the spa town: this Belle Époque rotunda with high ceilings remains Merano's cultural center, with concerts, exhibitions, and lively terraces on the Passirio all summer. Program at meranofestival.it; free entry to common areas.
Hike the Tappeinerweg from Merano's center to Brunnenburg Castle – a 6-kilometer loop with 200 meters of elevation gain, offering views over the Passer Valley and terraced vineyards.

Wine tasting in the Burggrafenamt – the wine region around Merano has produced Meraner Wein DOC since 1971, featuring rare varietals like Vernatsch (Schiava) cultivated in low Tyrolean pergola style since the Middle Ages.

visits.text: Monte Grappa, at 1,775 meters, was one of the deadliest theaters of the Great War on the northeastern front. The Sacrario Militare at the summit contains the remains of tens of thousands of Italian and Austro-Hungarian soldiers. Access by road from Bassano.

The access road from Bassano climbs in tight hairpins through a beech forest before opening onto the sacrario plateau. The air is several degrees cooler than below. The two ossuaries, one Italian and one Austro-Hungarian, have faced each other since 1935.

activities.text: A military monument yet Monte Grappa is also a popular hiking summit on weekends. The view on clear days embraces the Venetian plain to the Adriatic. The Great War museum at the summit deserves 45 minutes. Open in season, free entry.

visits.text: In Ortisei, the art of wood carving—'intaglio' in Ladin—has been practiced continuously since the 17th century: the School of Wood Carving perpetuates the transmission of a craft born here with the Trebinger and Vinazer families. About 85 to 90% of Ortisei residents speak Ladin as their first language—a Romance alpine language distinct from Italian and German.

The parish church of Sant'Ulrich (15th century) houses some of the finest works of the local carving tradition: crucifixes, statues of saints, and a pulpit in wood worked by valley artisans. Opposite, the Museum of Ortisei traces the history of Val Gardena wood carving since the 17th century.

Lago di Carezza (Karersee) – a 3-hectare glacial lake at 1,519 meters altitude in the Rosengarten Dolomites, whose waters shift from emerald green to deep blue depending on light and season. Local legend tells of a sorcerer who tried to seduce a water nymph by disguising himself as a rainbow—the nymph fled and the furious sorcerer shattered his rainbow into pieces in the lake, explaining the colorful reflections. Protected as a natural monument since 1980, the lake is fed by underground springs with no visible tributaries.

Santa Maddalena in Funes and Chiesa San Giovanni in Ranui – a hamlet of 500 inhabitants at 1,300 meters in Val di Funes, with the San Giovanni in Ranui church (1744) built on a rocky spur before the north face of the Geisler/Odle peaks (3,025m). The baroque church with its onion-domed bell tower is the subject of the world's most reproduced photograph of the Dolomites, with the Odle group as backdrop. The Val di Funes road, built only in 1928, connected hamlets previously accessible only on foot or horseback.

Alpe di Siusi (Seiser Alm) from Compatsch – Europe's largest alpine plateau with 56 square kilometers at 1,680-2,350 meters altitude, closed to motor traffic in season (accessible by shuttle or cable car from Ortisei and Castelrotto). The plateau has been used for grazing since the Neolithic—remains of Bronze Age pastoral huts have been uncovered during excavations. In summer, 1,400 cows and 700 horses graze here between June and September.

activities.text: Stroll through Ortisei's pedestrian center among colorful Tyrolean houses and craft workshops: wood carving galleries display nativity scenes, statues, and furniture made by hand using four-century-old techniques. Stop for Schlutzkrapfen (spinach and ricotta ravioli) at one of the cafés.
Walk around Lago di Carezza – marked 1.2-kilometer trail around the lake with a viewpoint on the north shore offering the classic view of the Latemar reflection.
Easy hike on the Alpe di Siusi from Compatsch – 6-kilometer loop across the plateau with views of Sassolungo (3,181m) and Sciliar (2,563m), with minimal elevation change.

visits.text: At 2,758 m, Passo dello Stelvio is the highest paved pass in the Italian Alps: the air bites even in July, and the 48 hairpins of the Trafoi side stack up below like an engineering lesson. The Ortles massif (3,905 m) dominates the pass from the north and glaciers cover the walls. The pass is closed October through May depending on snow.

Passo dello Stelvio is the second-highest paved pass in the entire Alps, after the Iseran (2,764 m), and it surpasses it in cycling notoriety: regularly the 'Cima Coppi' of the Giro d'Italia. From the pass, you can also descend into Switzerland toward Val Müstair via the Umbrail Pass—the linguistic border between Romansh and German runs through here.

activities.text: From the summit of Passo dello Stelvio, take the trail toward the ridge to the north to escape the bustle of the terraces: 15 minutes on foot is enough to find silence and a view of the Ortles-Cevedale massif. Even in August, bring a windbreaker.

visits.text: The Stelvio Pass (2,757 m) is the second-highest paved road in the Alps and the one every driving enthusiast eventually has to conquer. Approaching from the north (Prato allo Stelvio), 48 numbered hairpins stack up the mountainside like a wall of asphalt - the famous 'North Face.' The Bormio side is arguably the better drive: faster flow, long sightlines, tunnels carved into the rock. Either way, allow 2-3 hours and go early to beat the motorcycle swarms.

activities.text: Stop at the summit for the obligatory photo with the 'Passo dello Stelvio 2757 m' sign. There's a handful of souvenir shops and a couple of cafés - don't expect gourmet, but the hot chocolate is earned. On a clear day you can see deep into the Ortler Alps. The retreating glacier is visible to the south - summer skiing still operates here, usually May to November.

visits.text: Jagged Dolomite towers on both sides, meadows so green they look Photoshopped - the approach to Cortina d'Ampezzo via the Passo di Giau (2,236 m) is one of the most photogenic drives in the Alps. The town itself earned the title 'Queen of the Dolomites' long before the 2026 Winter Olympics put it back on the front page. Allow extra time; you will stop for photos.

days_plan.itin_title: Luxury Alpine Road Trip: Zurich to Salzburg — 14 Days

visits.text: The Dolomites suddenly tip at Passo Falzarego: on one side the Lagazuoi and its vertical walls, on the other the long descent to Cortina. The enrosadira, the limestone's reddening at sunset, is particularly violent here. Arrive 30 minutes before sunset.

Passo Falzarego, at 2,105 meters, isn't the highest of the Dolomite passes but concentrates the best panoramas. The rifugio terrace at the pass offers coffee with a view of the Tofane. Cable car to the Lagazuoi in season.

At Falzarego Pass, 2,105m, the mountain still bears the scars of 1915: underground tunnels, trenches, artillery positions carved into the limestone. The silence here is different from ordinary high-altitude quiet. The Lagazuoi massif, facing the pass, was simultaneously Austrian side and Italian side—the front lines crossed on the same rocks.

From Passo Falzarego, the Lagazuoi cable car climbs in a few minutes to roughly 2,800m: panorama of the Cinque Torri, Marmolada and Antelao massif. The mountain also hides WWI underground tunnels you can explore by headlamp—allow 45 minutes to 1 hour for the full circuit.

activities.text: You'll take the Lagazuoi cable car from the pass to access the Great War trenches carved into the rock at 2,835 meters. The descent on foot through underground galleries takes 1h30. A headlamp is necessary for the tunnels.

Walk to the Cinque Torri, five dolomite towers peaking at 2,361m, roughly 3km from the pass: the marked trail goes via Rifugio Scoiattoli (2,255m) with views over Cortina. One hour each way from Passo Falzarego. Along the way, the 'Sentiero delle Trincee' follows WWI trenches preserved intact.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Traverse, 16 days: Grisons to Trieste
Grand Dolomites Tour: Braies, Cortina and the Mountain Passes

visits.text: Passo Pordoi, at 2,239 meters between the Sella group and the Marmolada, is the highest road pass on the Great Dolomites Route. The vertical walls of the Sella form an amphitheater to the east. Arrive early: in July, cyclists attack it from 7am.

A high-altitude pass yet accessible by car all summer season, Passo Pordoi resembles nothing else in the Alps. The summit restaurants serve strudels at 2,239 meters. The Terrazza delle Dolomiti at the top of Piz Pordoi alone justifies the stop.

It's not mountain beneath your feet, it's the ancient floor of the Tethys Sea: the Sella Group dominating Passo Pordoi (2,239m) was a tropical coral reef hundreds of millions of years ago—the blonde color of the rock, its rectangular blocks, everything explains it. From this legendary Giro d'Italia pass, a monument pays tribute to Fausto Coppi.

Locals call it the 'Terrace of the Dolomites': from the pass, the Sass Pordoi cable car climbs 700m in 5 minutes to 2,950m on the southern spur of the Sella Group. From the Rifugio Maria terrace, you'll see the Marmolada to the southeast, Catinaccio to the west and Piz Boè (3,152m) to the north. In service May to November and winter for skiing.

activities.text: You'll climb to Piz Pordoi by cable car (2,952 meters) for a 360-degree view over all the eastern Dolomites. The climb takes 6 minutes from the pass. Closed in bad weather: check on sas.it.

Hike up to Sass Pordoi from the pass via trail no. 627 if you prefer to earn the view: 700m elevation gain, roughly 2 hours. At the top, the plateau is strangely flat and mineral—true ocean floor at 2,950m. Alternatively, the cable car makes the same trip in 5 minutes and stays open almost year-round.

places.name: San Daniele Del Friuli

visits.text: You'll linger at a San Daniele DOP prosciutto producer in the historic center for a tasting. The difference from Parma prosciutto? San Daniele is recognized by its guitar shape and the paw still attached. A direct tasting at the norcineria is enough to verify.

The aroma of prosciutto aged at least 13 months in Friulian air fills the streets of San Daniele's center. This ham has a sweeter flavor than its Parma competitor, according to locals. The Adriatic wind combined with alpine air creates unique drying conditions.

Centro storico di San Daniele del Friuli - Perched on a hill between the Carnic mountains to the north and the Adriatic to the south, this borough owes its fame to prosciutto DOP but conceals a far richer heritage. The position creates a unique microclimate: warm sea breezes meet cold Alpine currents, generating the gentle ventilation that cures the ham during its 13-month aging.

Biblioteca Guarneriana - Founded October 7, 1466 when humanist Guarnerio d'Artegna bequeathed his 173 manuscript codices to his community, this is Friuli's oldest public library and one of Italy's first. The idea was revolutionary: at that time, libraries were private collections. It now holds about 12,000 antique books, including a 12th-century Byzantine Bible, one of the oldest Florentine copies of the Divine Comedy (late 14th century), illuminated Books of Hours on calfskin vellum, and a wooden room with secret doors sheltering once-forbidden texts.

Chiesa di Sant'Antonio Abate - Nicknamed the "Sistine Chapel of Friuli," this single-nave church was consecrated in 1308 as the hospital chapel, damaged in 1348, then reconsecrated in 1470. Its walls are covered with three fresco cycles: those by Vitale da Bologna (late 14th century) and especially those by Martino da Udine, known as "Pellegrino da San Daniele," painted between 1497 and 1522. The choir vault presents Prophets and Evangelists, and the rear wall a large Crucifixion.

Portonat - Near Piazza Dante, this massive square-based tower (torrione) was erected around 1580, facing toward Gemona. It formed part of the borough's medieval defensive system and today offers an architectural landmark in the network of ancient lanes.

Ponte di Pinzano al Tagliamento - About ten kilometers south, this bridge spans the Tagliamento and offers one of the finest panoramas of the river. Flowing 170 km, the Tagliamento is considered Europe's last major natural braided river: its multiple channels trace gravel meanders bordered by riparian vegetation.

Castello di Villalta - On the heights between Fagagna and San Daniele, this medieval castle dominates the Friulian plain. Its towers and battlements emerge from the vegetation, offering a viewpoint over the surrounding moraine hills.

activities.text: Capital of Friulian dry ham, San Daniele del Friuli also hides an unexpected treasure: the Biblioteca Guarneriana, founded in 1466, preserves medieval illuminated manuscripts among the most precious in northeastern Italy. Visit by reservation. Don't enter with a prosciutto sandwich, even if it's local.

Prosciutto di San Daniele DOP tasting - The borough's salumifici open their doors for tastings. The prosciutto is produced solely with Italian pork leg and sea salt, without preservatives, following centuries-old know-how. In 1563, during the Council of Trent, the Patriarch of Aquileia sent 12 San Daniele prosciutti to the prelates by mule. In 1797, Napoleon's officers plundered a large quantity along with the Guarneriana's treasures.

visits.text: At 2,519 m, the air is crisp and the Odle (Geislerspitzen) cut the sky like a giant saw: the Seceda plateau is one of the most photographed ridges of the Dolomites. Access by cable car from Ortisei. In summer, marked hiking trails from the upper station.

It's from Seceda that the geography of the Dolomites becomes readable at a single glance: the Marmolada, the Sassolungo, and Cortina's Tofane are visible in clear weather. Orientation panels in Ladin, Italian, and German identify each peak from the panoramic terrace.

activities.text: Walk from the Seceda upper station to Col Raiser (2,107 m) along the ridges: 2 km of well-marked panoramic trail, one-hour round trip. From the pass, views over Val Gardena below and the Sella massif to the south. Return by cable car to Ortisei.

places.name: Spilimbergo

visits.text: They're simply called the 'mosaicisti': students at the Scuola Mosaicisti del Friuli have restored mosaics at Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, the Holy Sepulchre dome in Jerusalem, and subway stations in New York. The school accepts weekday visitors by appointment.

The Scuola Mosaicisti del Friuli in Spilimbergo, founded in 1922, is the world's leading mosaic training school. Spilimbergo's duomo itself displays mosaics and bas-reliefs on the Romanesque-Gothic facade. The interior houses remarkable medieval frescoes.

Spilimbergo deserves better than the label 'city of mosaicists': its medieval castello and stone-cut lanes form a harmonious ensemble, rare for a town this size. The view of the Tagliamento from the ramparts alone justifies the stop. Free access.

Duomo di Santa Maria Maggiore - Built in 1284 against the old fortified walls, this Gothic gem incorporated a defensive tower converted into a bell tower. Inside, the three apses preserve 14th-century frescoes: Christ the Judge, the Annunciation to the Shepherds, and scenes from the Old and New Testaments. In the crypt rests the sarcophagus of Walterpertoldo IV, 14th-century lord of Spilimbergo.

Castello di Spilimbergo - Founded in the 11th century by the Spengenberg counts of Carinthia, the castle forms a circular courtyard surrounded by noble palaces. Destroyed and rebuilt multiple times, burned in 1511 during a popular revolt, it preserves two remarkable elements: the Palazzo Dipinto and Palazzo Tadea with its 16th-century stucco salon.

Palazzo Dipinto - The sole building to survive the 1511 fire, this palace is the castle's oldest section, restored between 1390 and 1400 by Count Wanzel. Its façade is entirely covered with frescoes attributed to Andrea Bellunello (15th century) and Pordenone, with Gothic and Renaissance mullioned windows framing two balconies. Emperor Charles V stayed here with his court in 1574.

Corso Roma and historic center - The main street cuts through the medieval borough east to west between two 14th-century towers. Pastel-colored façades line up painted palaces and antique signs. Pause before Palazzo Monaco and its painted façade, then Casa Dipinta (Palazzo Ercole) adorned with 16th-century frescoes depicting scenes from the life of Hercules.

Piazza Duomo and Loggia della Macia - On the square, notice the corner column still bearing the Macia, the ancient length measure used for medieval commercial exchanges. The Palazzo del Daziario, where taxes were paid to the lords, completes the picture of a borough that was an important commercial transit center.

Scuola Mosaicisti del Friuli - Founded in 1922 by mayor Ezio Cantarutti on a suggestion from Milan's Umanitaria, this school trains mosaicists from around the world. Its graduates have created decorations for the Library of Congress in Washington, the dome of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, and the Ground Zero metro station in New York. The visitor route covers techniques from Greco-Roman to Byzantine to contemporary mosaic, with over 800 works on display. You can watch students and masters breaking tesserae with the martellina hammer.

activities.text: You'll visit Spilimbergo's duomo whose Romanesque-Gothic facade is adorned with medieval mosaics and bas-reliefs. The interior houses medieval frescoes often little mentioned in guides. Free, open daily except midday closure hours.

If you pass on a Saturday morning, Spilimbergo's center market gathers Friulian producers: Montasio cheeses, cured meats, wines from neighboring hills. A good opportunity to assemble a picnic before the road to Udine.

Open-air mosaic trail - Spilimbergo is an open-air museum: works created by the Scuola Mosaicisti are scattered throughout town—on façades, at the entrances to the Town Hall and library, in parks, and even on tree trunks. A map available at the tourist office guides visitors from one piece to the next.

visits.text: A red train rolls through the streets of Tirano like a tramway, passing within meters of the Sanctuary of Madonna di Tirano—construction began in 1505 on the site of a 1504 Marian apparition. The carved woodwork of the baroque organ (1608) fills the entire back wall. Free entry; avoid mass times if you're here for the architecture.

Palazzo Salis occupies the historic center of Tirano with its handsome facade and wooded gardens; today it hosts exhibitions and cultural events. Via Bernina and the adjacent lanes reveal an intact Lombard center, walkable in 30 to 40 minutes. Aperitivo in the square afterward—Valtellina wines by the glass at several establishments.

activities.text: Take time for an aperitivo in Tirano before moving on: at 429 meters elevation, you've left the alpine atmosphere for Lombardy. If you're traveling by train, watch the Bernina Express depart from the street: the locomotive rolls on the roadway between cars before climbing toward the pass.

visits.text: Built in the 11th century, Tirol Castle gave its name to the entire Tyrol region: from its ramparts, the view embraces Merano and the Adige valley in a panorama that the Counts of Tyrol dominated in the Middle Ages. The interior houses a museum of South Tyrolean cultural history and a well-preserved Romanesque chapel. Closed Mondays.

View over Merano from the ramparts of Tirol Castle: the spa town spreads across the Passirio valley, framed by the first foothills of the Alps, with vineyards on the south-facing slope in the foreground. The village of Tirolo around the castle is worth a walking tour among cobbled streets and terraced gardens.

activities.text: Walk down from Tirol Castle to Merano via the panoramic trail through terraced vineyards and orchards: 45-minute descent, constant views over the valley. Free trail access; the castle is paid admission.
