visits.text: You'll follow the Adige to reach Trento's Piazza del Duomo from the station, a 10-minute walk past medieval ramparts. The piazza market is lively Saturday mornings. A good introduction before climbing to the castello.

The Castello del Buonconsiglio, residence of the Prince-Bishops of Trento, hosted sessions of the Council of Trent between 1545 and 1563, which reformed Catholicism against the Protestant Reformation. The frescoes of the cycle of Months in the Torre d'Aquila, around 1400, are among the finest in northern Italy. Plan 2h.

Piazza Duomo forms the beating heart of Trento: the Cathedral of San Vigilio, built between the 12th and 16th centuries, faces the baroque Fountain of Neptune (1767). This is where numerous sessions of the Council of Trent (1545-1563) took place—one of the pivotal events of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

Castello del Buonconsiglio, begun in the mid-13th century, served for five centuries as the residence of Trento's prince-bishops. It comprises three distinct architectural cores: the medieval Castelvecchio, the Renaissance Magno Palazzo commissioned by Cardinal Bernardo Clesio (1485-1539), and the Baroque Giunta Albertiana. Don't miss the Torre Aquila and its Cycle of the Months—early 15th-century International Gothic frescoes attributed to a Bohemian artist, depicting peasant and aristocratic activities month by month. Legend has it that an underground passage once connected the castle to the cathedral.

activities.text: You'll continue to the MUSE, Trento's science museum designed by Renzo Piano, at the city's edge. The architecture is worth as much as the exhibitions. Open 10am to 6pm except Monday, rates on muse.it.

Wander through the historic center's narrow lanes, admiring the painted facades characteristic of Trentino. Sample local wines—Trentino produces exceptional Pinot Grigio and Gewürztraminer—at a traditional enoteca in the center.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Traverse, 16 days: Grisons to Trieste
Italy Road Trip: From Trentino to the Amalfi Coast

visits.text: Neither quite Italian, nor anymore Austrian, Trieste has navigated since 1954 between two identities with particular ease. It was the Habsburgs' main port until 1918. Today, it's closer to Ljubljana than Rome in mindset. Arrive by train from Udine to see the sea emerge.

James Joyce settled in Trieste in 1904 to teach English and lived there over a decade. He wrote Dubliners and much of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in his Trieste apartments. Several plaques recall his passage on old center streets.

The saline air of the Adriatic invades Piazza Unità d'Italia, the largest square open to the sea in Italy, in late afternoon. The Bora, the northeast wind that can reach impressive speeds, refreshes the city a few days a year. When it blows, the Triestini go out anyway.

Piazza Unità d'Italia - At 12,280 square meters, this is the largest sea-facing square in Europe. Enclosed on three sides by 19th-century palaces - the Palazzo del Municipio (1875) crowned by its two bronze automatons Micheze and Jacheze that strike the hours, the Palazzo del Lloyd Triestino (1883) by Viennese architect Heinrich von Ferstel, and the Palazzo del Governo (1905) adorned with Murano glass mosaics - it opens dramatically onto the Gulf of Trieste. Its name has evolved with history: Piazza Grande, then Piazza Francesco Giuseppe under the Habsburgs, Piazza Unità in 1918 when annexed to Italy, and finally Piazza Unità d'Italia in 1955 after Trieste's return to Italian sovereignty.

Molo Audace - This 246-meter pier jutting into the gulf takes its name from the destroyer Audace, the first Italian warship to dock in Trieste on November 3, 1918, marking the end of Austro-Hungarian rule. At its tip, a bronze compass rose and a full 360° panorama of the gulf and city rooftops.

Borgo Teresiano and Canal Grande - This neoclassical quarter was built in the 18th century on former salt pans, commissioned by Empress Maria Theresa of Austria. The canal, a former commercial wharf, is lined with palaces whose ground floors served as warehouses while upper floors housed offices and residences. At the canal's head, the chiesa di Sant'Antonio Taumaturgo (1849) closes the vista.

Colle di San Giusto - Crowning the hill that overlooks downtown, the Teatro Romano (1st century AD), partially carved into bedrock and facing the sea, sits beside the Castello di San Giusto, expanded from the 15th to 17th centuries, whose terrace offers a 360° panorama of city and gulf. The Cattedrale di San Giusto, born from the fusion of two churches in the 14th century, preserves Byzantine mosaics in its apses.

Piazza della Borsa - The Stock Exchange (1806), whose Doric-columned facade recalls a Greek temple, symbolizes Trieste's mercantile boom. Next door, the imposing Palazzo del Tergesteo (1842) functioned as a shopping arcade and housed the office of Italo Svevo, one of Trieste's great literary figures. Emperor Charles VI had proclaimed the free port in 1719, launching the city's prosperity.

Castello di Miramare - Built between 1856 and 1860 in white Istrian stone on the Grignano promontory, this castle was designed by engineer Carl Junker for Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg and his wife Charlotte of Belgium. The name 'Miramar' comes from Spanish 'mirar el mar': legend has it that Maximilian chose this site after sheltering here from a storm. The ground floor, in sea-inspired blue tones, houses the private apartments where the bedroom is arranged like a ship's cabin - reflecting the archduke-admiral's passion for the navy. The upper floor, all in red and gold tapestries with imperial symbols, served for receptions.

Parco di Miramare - Maximilian transformed this nearly barren karst promontory into a 22-hectare garden mixing Mediterranean and exotic species brought back from his admiral's voyages around the world. The park combines an English garden, an Italian parterre, and curiosities: the Castelletto (the couple's temporary residence during construction), greenhouses, ruins of the San Canciano chapel with a wooden cross from the frigate Novara, and the 'Swiss House' beside a swan lake. At the harbor entrance, a pink granite sphinx from the 3rd century BC (Ptolemaic era) is the sole survivor of Maximilian's Egyptian collection.

activities.text: You'll head down to the Castello di Miramare following the coast from the center, either 8 km on foot or 15 minutes by bus. The castle was built by Archduke Maximilian of Austria between 1856 and 1860. Enter early: groups arrive around 11am.

Trieste caffè is a science apart: here, a 'caffè' isn't a simple espresso - a 'nero,' a 'capo,' a 'deca' are codes specific to Trieste. Caffè San Marco, open since 1914, remains the best place to learn the vocabulary.

Coffee ritual in the historic cafés - Trieste is Italy's coffee capital (the country's leading import port). The vocabulary here is unique: a 'nero' for an espresso, a 'capo in b' for a macchiato in a glass. The historic establishments downtown, founded in the 19th century, preserve woodwork, mirrors, and the Mitteleuropa literary atmosphere where Svevo, Joyce, and Saba once crossed paths.

Tasting in a Triestine buffet - These typical Trieste counters, an Austro-Hungarian legacy, serve ham in a bread crust baked on-site and carved by hand, accompanied by kren (horseradish) and mustard. Patate in tecia (sautéed potatoes) and gnocchi di pane col gulash complete the meal, washed down with a glass of Terrano from the Carso.

Following Maximilian's tragic destiny - On April 14, 1864, Maximilian and Charlotte embarked here aboard the Novara for Mexico, where he had accepted the imperial crown. Executed at Querétaro on June 19, 1867, his remains returned to Trieste on the same ship. Charlotte lost her sanity and never returned to live at the castle. A persistent 'Miramare curse' holds that anyone spending the night there is doomed to a tragic end far from home.

Walk along the promontory with gulf views - The cliff-side path offers panoramic views across the entire Trieste coastline and, on clear days, to the Slovenian coast and Istria. Park access is free year-round.

places.name: Udine

visits.text: Udine's Piazza della Libertà is often compared to Venice's Piazza San Marco: the Loggia del Lionello (Venetian Gothic, 15th century), the Clock Tower with its two Moors, the column with the Lion of St. Mark (1539)—everything recalls four centuries of Venetian rule. The square was successively called 'piazza del vino' and 'Contarena', before taking its current name in 1945.

For the earliest Tiepolos, you must climb to the castle: the Castle of Udine, perched on the only hill in the Friulian plain, houses the civic museums with Carpaccios and Tiepolos. It was here that Giambattista Tiepolo created his first major works in the 1720s, before becoming the grand master of European Rococo.

After nightfall, Udine comes alive around Piazza Matteotti and its osterie serving Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, and Ramato on wooden counters. Friuli white wine is among Italy's finest—producers from Collio and Colli Orientali frequently exhibit in town. Cena around 8 PM: this is where the alpine rhythm of the journey ends.

Piazza della Libertà - Considered the finest Venetian square outside Venice itself, it gathers the Loggia del Lionello, Loggia di San Giovanni, and the column crowned by the Lion of Saint Mark in one space—a striking summary of four centuries of Venetian rule over Friuli.

Loggia del Lionello - This Venetian Gothic town hall was commissioned in 1441 and built between 1448 and 1456. Its architect, Nicolò Lionello, wasn't a trained architect but a goldsmith, which explains the refinement of every detail. The façade measuring 35.5 meters long and 15.2 meters high alternates bands of white and pink stone, ten pointed arches at ground level, and a central balcony above. Ravaged by fire in 1876, it was reconstructed identically. The Gothic inscription "UTINUM" recalls Udine's Latin name.

Loggia di San Giovanni and Torre dell'Orologio - Facing the Loggia del Lionello, this Renaissance loggia shelters a clock tower inspired by—though squatter than—the one in St. Mark's Square in Venice. It underscores the Serenissima's constant influence on city life.

Arco Bollani and ascent to the Castello - Pass through the arch designed by Andrea Palladio in 1556: it grants access to the ramp climbing toward the castle hill. Along the way, walk beneath the Loggia del Lippomano, an elegant 16th-century portico.

Castello di Udine - Rebuilt in the mid-16th century after the 1511 earthquake, this palace-fortress atop the hill houses the Civic Museums: galleries of Venetian and Friulian paintings from the 14th to 19th centuries, archaeological collections, and prints. From the terrace, views sweep across the city rooftops and, on clear days, the snow-capped Julian and Carnic Alps.

Museo Diocesano e Gallerie del Tiepolo - Set in the Palazzo Patriarcale, residence of the Patriarchs of Aquileia from 1593 to 1751, this museum holds around 700 works. Young Giambattista Tiepolo painted masterful frescoes here between 1726 and 1730: The Fall of the Rebel Angels in the stairwell, Rachel Hiding the Idols in the Gallery of Guests, and The Judgment of Solomon in the Red Room. An entire floor displays polychrome wood sculptures from the 12th to 18th centuries.

Oratorio della Purità - This small chapel shelters a ceiling Assumption painted by Tiepolo: a luminous Madonna surrounded by cascading angels. The intimacy of the space makes the work all the more striking.

Duomo di Santa Maria Annunziata - A Latin cross cathedral rebuilt after the 1348 earthquake, whose entire floor is covered by one of northern Italy's largest Roman mosaic pavements. The side chapels preserve works by Tiepolo and Pordenone.

Piazza Matteotti (Piazza San Giacomo) - A lively square ringed by Renaissance and Neoclassical façades, bordered by café terraces. This is Udine's social heart: locals gather here evenings for a tajut, the glass of Friulian white wine shared at the counter.

Casa Cavazzini - Museo d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea - This restructured 16th-century palace presents a substantial collection of 20th-century Italian artists including De Chirico, Morandi, and Severini, through several donations tracing the evolution of modern art in Italy.

activities.text: Climb to Udine Castle from Piazza della Libertà through the Bollani Gate (1556, designed in collaboration with Palladio): 5-minute walk on cobblestones. From the castle's north terrace, view of the Julian and Carnic Alps—a line of ridges less than 100 km to the north.

Friuli, to close, is the pleasant surprise of the journey: less touristy than Tuscany, more rooted in Central Europe than Lombardy, open to Slovenia beyond the border. Udine is a town of real people, without staging—the best counterpoint to conclude an alpine arc that has crossed nine regions in 14 days.

Wander the Venetian historic center - Meander through lanes between Via Mercatovecchio and its arcades, Via Vittorio Veneto and its colorful palaces. Every Thursday morning, the Mercato del Giovedì sets up stalls of fresh produce, cheeses, and Friulian cured meats on Piazza Matteotti.

Friulian wine tasting - Udine is the gateway to Friuli's great wines: Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso. Wine bars in the historic center offer tastings paired with frico (Montasio cheese fritter) and musetto (local cotechino sausage).

visits.text: Valdobbiadene winemakers claim that the Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG hills, UNESCO-listed in 2019, produce something incomparable to industrial plain prosecco. The Cartizze, 107 hectares of grand cru in a pentagon shape on the hill, is the centerpiece.

The Cartizze bubble holds a flavor of white peach and acacia flower, different from ordinary prosecco. Small family cantinas on the heights open their tasting bars on weekends. Avoid the large cooperatives on the main road: prefer the hills.

San Pietro di Feletto, a 12th-century Romanesque church perched on a hill halfway between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene: the exterior is modest, the interior covered with medieval frescoes that humidity has patiently damaged over eight centuries. It's open, it's free, and it's the kind of place you drive past without stopping and regret. Stop.

The Molinetto della Croda in Refrontolo is Veneto's oldest working water mill—built in 1630, it still turns. Perched above a wooded ravine, surrounded by vineyards, it's also the setting for a local festival in September that brings together several thousand people to drink Colli di Conegliano Refrontolo Passito. Self-guided visit, period wood interior, sound of the wheel.

Cartizze: 107 hectares in the heart of Valdobbiadene, the grand cru of Prosecco. Hectares here trade above one million euros—Veneto's absolute record. The slopes are so steep that all harvesting is done by hand, carrying crates at arm's length on the narrow ciglioni. The wine that emerges is richer, more complex, often slightly off-dry—different from the brut Proseccos drunk at aperitivo. From the road above San Pietro di Barbozza, the view over Cartizze in its amphitheater of hills is worth stopping for even if you're not going anywhere.

activities.text: You'll stop at a family cantina in the hills while driving up the Valmareno road. These small producers sell at the cellar, no appointment needed Saturday mornings. A glass of Superiore with a view of the vines beats the best restaurant in town.

The Strada del Prosecco, founded in 1966, is Italy's first wine route ever created. The 40 kilometers between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene are ideally driven without GPS—just the brown signs and the vineyards on the ciglioni on either side. If you're here in October, harvesting is underway and tractors loaded with glera slow down traffic. That's precisely why you should be here in October.

Tasting at Bisol in Valdobbiadene: the benchmark house for Cartizze, in production since the 16th century in the family. Bisol provides the clearest demonstration of the difference between a basic Prosecco Brut DOCG and their Cartizze—same Charmat method, same Glera grape, but soil, exposure, and yield make a completely different wine. The visit includes the Cartizze vineyard if weather permits.

visits.text: Varenna may be the most beautiful village on Lake Como—and the Passeggiata degli Innamorati proves it: this walkway anchored into the rock, just inches above the water, with its famous red railing, connects the landing pier to the village center. The lake is right beneath you. On weekdays off-season, you'll have it almost to yourself.

Traditionally commissioned by the Lombard Queen Theodelinda, the Castello di Vezio towers over Varenna from 375 m—20-minute walk from the village, 360° lake views. Below, Villa Monastero was founded in the 12th century as a women's monastery: today a house-museum with 14 furnished rooms and botanical gardens on the lake.

Arrive at Varenna by ferry to immediately take the Passeggiata degli Innamorati, a 1.3 km suspended corniche linking the landing stage to the village center by following the lake beneath red iron arches draped with climbing plants. Then climb toward Piazza San Giorgio, the medieval heart of the village, dominated by the 13th-century church of San Giorgio whose austere facade shelters medieval frescoes.

Visit Villa Monastero and its botanical gardens. The villa takes its name from a Cistercian monastery founded in the 12th century and closed by papal decree in 1567 for the nuns' indecorous behavior. Bought by the Mornico family then resold several times, it was enlarged at the end of the 19th century by a Hamburg family and completed in 1904. Now state-owned, its 14 furnished rooms constitute a house-museum. The botanical garden extends nearly 2 kilometers along the shore, in terraces, with some 900 plant species: African palms, Lebanon cedars, cypresses, magnolias, wisteria, citrus trees, and some rarities like Erythea armata.

Climb to Castello di Vezio, a medieval fortress perched on the hill overlooking Varenna for over a thousand years. The tower offers 360° panoramas of the lake and mountains. The castle houses a falconry with regular demonstrations and a permanent exhibition dedicated to the Lariosaurus, a primitive marine reptile whose first fossils were discovered in the province of Lecco and which, according to local legend, was spotted in the lake in 1946.

Stroll through the gardens of Villa Cipressi, dating from the 15th century: terraces descend to the lake, planted with cypresses, exotic flowers, and aromatic plants. Paired with Villa Monastero, it completes Varenna's botanical circuit.

activities.text: Take the ferry from Varenna's pier to Bellagio: 15-minute crossing over the intersection of the lake's three branches, the most beautiful panorama of the Lario. Return possible by the same ferry or via Menaggio on the opposite shore.

Ferry crossing between Varenna and Menaggio or Bellagio: Lake Como's public boat service connects the three points of the 'golden triangle' in 15 to 30 minutes. It's the best way to grasp the lake's inverted-Y geography and appreciate the villas and villages from the water.

visits.text: Venzone was razed by the 1976 earthquake—and rebuilt stone by stone, exactly as before, using the anastylosis technique: each block catalogued, numbered, replaced identically. It's the strangest and most beautiful village in Friuli: both authentically medieval and entirely modern. Elected 'Borgo dei Borghi' in 2017.

The Venzonese discovered in 1647, while moving a sarcophagus, that their dead had become mummies. Forty bodies were naturally preserved thanks to a particular mold in the cemetery soil. The Crypt of San Michele, facing the Cathedral of Sant'Andrea (1308), now houses several of these mummies with paid access. 20-minute visit.

Mura medievali di Venzone - The only 14th-century fortified borough preserved intact in the entire region, Venzone is ringed by a double 13th-century wall pierced by three gates: Porta San Genesio, Porta Italia, and Porta Friuli. In 1258, Patriarch of Aquileia Gregorio da Montelongo granted the borough fortified city status. Declared a National Monument in 1965 and ranked among the "Borghi più Belli d'Italia" (voted Italy's most beautiful borough in 2017), Venzone occupies a strategic position at the confluence of the Tagliamento valley and the Canal di Ferro, on the route of the ancient Amber Road linking the Baltic to Aquileia.

Duomo di Sant'Andrea Apostolo - Consecrated in 1338 by Patriarch Bertrando di San Genesio, this Gothic cathedral was almost entirely destroyed by the May 6, 1976 earthquake (magnitude 6.5), then finished off by September 15 aftershocks. Reconstruction by anastylosis—each hewn stone replaced in its exact original position—mobilized 9,500 blocks inventoried one by one thanks to photographic archives. The work, completed in 1995, is considered one of the world's greatest examples of medieval building reconstruction. The Baroque organ dates from 1792.

Cappella cimiteriale di San Michele - A 13th-century rotunda built on the Duomo's forecourt, this chapel shelters five natural mummies visible to the public in its crypt (out of some forty discovered since the 17th century). The first, nicknamed "il Gobbo" (the Hunchback), was found in 1647 during expansion work. Mummification was caused by a rare fungus, Hypha Bombicina Pers, which dehydrates tissues in about one year. The bodies, dating from the 14th to 19th centuries, weigh between 4 and 8 kg. Napoleon's soldiers in 1797 were so impressed by "il Gobbo" that they removed strips of skin as souvenirs—since then, the mummies wear small protective aprons.

Palazzo Orgnani-Martina - Tiere Motus - This historic center palace houses the permanent museum dedicated to the 1976 earthquake and Friuli's reconstruction. The route traces the stages: the shock of May 6, the summer under tents, the September aftershocks that finished destroying what May had spared, the exodus of 40,000 people to the beach resorts of Grado and Lignano, and complete reconstruction in ten years following the principle "first factories, then houses, finally churches." A multimedia room projects the sequence of tremors on a regional model and displays the names of 989 victims.

activities.text: Walk the circuit of Venzone's ramparts: 1,060 m of wall 8 m high, flanked by 15 towers, encircling the entire medieval village. The exterior walk takes 30 minutes and gives an aerial view of the reconstructed roofs and the Julian Alps to the north. Free access through the main gates.

Walk through the borough rebuilt stone by stone - Stroll lanes where every façade results from meticulous reconstruction work. New stones are still distinguishable from original ones by their slightly different surface: this deliberate choice lets visitors "read" the earthquake's history on the walls. Four 15th-century votive chapels dot a trail on the surrounding heights, following the route of an ancient Celtic path.

visits.text: What a strange town Vittorio Veneto is, born in 1866 from the merger of Ceneda and Serravalle - two distinct towns, two squares, two altitudes, two characters. The Battle of Vittorio Veneto in October 1918 sealed the war's end on the Austro-Hungarian side. A town with a double bottom.

The medieval ruins of Serravalle stand on the hill above the lower town. Saint Mark's lions adorn the Venetian palaces of Piazza Marc'Antonio Flaminio. On summer evenings, residents bring chairs out onto the cobblestones and the piazza stays lively until midnight.

Step into Serravalle (now part of Vittorio Veneto), a medieval fairytale town that ranks among the most picturesque in Italy. Cobbled streets, stone houses with frescoed facades, and an ancient castle create an atmospheric setting that transports visitors centuries back in time.

Visit the Museo del Cenedese for fabulous frescoes, paintings, and works of art, including access to a fully frescoed chapel where babies born in the local hospital were once baptized. The artistic heritage here rivals better-known destinations.

activities.text: You'll visit the Museo della Battaglia at the Castello di San Martino, which traces the 1918 offensive and the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian army. The visit takes 45 minutes. The walk from the lower town offers a fine view over the Venetian plain.
Wander the medieval streets photographing the unique architecture and peaceful squares. Unlike more touristy medieval towns, Serravalle offers authentic atmosphere without crowds.

places.name: Abano Terme

visits.text: Relax in Abano Terme, a town completely dedicated to spa culture where hundreds of hotels and facilities offer thermal treatments. The Romans were the first to bathe in these volcanic waters, and the tradition has continued unbroken for over two millennia.

Experience the therapeutic mud treatments, thermal pools, and steam grottos that have made this region Europe's largest thermal basin. The mineral-rich waters emerge at temperatures up to 87°C from deep underground sources.

activities.text: Explore the elegant spa town's gardens and promenades, where the wellness tradition blends with refined hospitality. The proximity to the Euganean Hills provides beautiful walking opportunities between treatments.

visits.text: Acaya is one of the few surviving Renaissance fortified villages in southern Italy, and you can tell from the Porta Terra, a stone arch dated 1535. Gian Giacomo dell'Acaya, military engineer to Charles V, redrew the entire village on a grid plan. Allow 90 minutes: the whole place fits into four streets.

Built around 1506 and then fortified in 1535-1536, the Castello di Acaya has a trapezoidal plan, a moat and corner bastions. The vaulted halls, the stables and the old prisons are open to visitors. Check the opening days before you come: the castle closes on certain weekdays out of season.

activities.text: Walk the walls from the outside, along the moat, in about twenty minutes. Beyond the walls, the Cappella di San Paolo was one of the pilgrimage sites for victims of tarantula bite, along with Galatina. Park in front of the gate, as the village inside is pedestrian.

visits.text: The Cattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta e San Canio crowns Acerenza at over 800 meters altitude, visible from far away. Consecrated in 1080 by Arnoldo, Abbot of Cluny, it was built atop an early Christian church, itself placed on a temple dedicated to an "Acheruntin" Hercules. The style is Romanesque-Cluniac, rare in the South. The painted crypt is the real prize: ask for it, it's not always open by default.

Set up in the Palazzo Arcivescovile, the Sala degli Stemmi in Acerenza displays dozens of walnut panels painted by a local artist. The Museo Diocesano d'Arte Sacra occupies the same building: sculptures, canvases, manuscripts from diocesan churches. It's small and often deserted. Hours are limited: call the town hall before going up.

Walk to the Torretta in Acerenza, the viewpoint opening onto the entire upper Bradano valley. The borough is girded by high walls and perched on a mount surrounded by the Bradano and Fiumarella torrent: the position explains everything else. Five minutes from the cathedral, uphill. Autumn is the best time, the hills turn orange.

visits.text: Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre - Nicknamed the "Jerusalem of Europe," this 9th-century basilica houses in its Romanesque crypt the world's oldest reproduction of Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre. Legend tells that Matilda of Westphalia, mother of Emperor Otto I, was traveling to Rome with mules laden with gold when the animals refused to advance at Acquapendente. A dream commanded her to build the church here. The 11th-century crypt—24 columns with all-different capitals forming nine naves beneath groin vaults—is a true "stone forest." The current facade is the work of Nicola Salvi, architect of Rome's Trevi Fountain.

Historic center and Torre del Barbarossa - The former double circuit of walls preserves three gates, including the Torre Julia de Jacopo—named after a woman who in 1550 closed the gate under enemy fire to save the town from assault by Orsini troops. On the hill dominating the town, the clock tower is the last vestige of the fortress built by Emperor Henry IV in the 12th century.

Bosco del Sasseto - 12 km from Acquapendente, near the village of Torre Alfina (classified among the Borghi più Belli d'Italia), this monumental forest shelters centuries-old oaks, beeches, and hornbeams whose twisted trunks grow between enormous moss-covered lava boulders. The atmosphere evokes a fairy-tale setting. The neo-Gothic castle of Torre Alfina, restored by Sienese architect Giuseppe Partini, overlooks the wood.

activities.text: Via Francigena stage - Acquapendente is the first Lazio town for pilgrims coming from the north. The Pilgrim House, steps from the cathedral, still welcomes walkers with 25 beds managed by the Confraternity of San Rocco. This is where Saint Roch allegedly performed his first miracle by healing plague victims in the 14th century.

Pugnaloni and traditions - Every third Sunday in May, the Festival of the Madonna del Fiore commemorates the town's liberation from Frederick Barbarossa's yoke in 1166. The "Pugnaloni," giant mosaics composed of flower petals and leaves, are carried in procession through the streets. A tradition unique in all of Italy.

days_plan.itin_title: Tuscia Circuit: Etruscan Sites and Villages of Lazio

places.name: Acquaviva Delle Fonti

visits.text: Four palatine basilicas in Puglia, and one of them is here: the Cattedrale di Sant'Eustachio in Acquaviva delle Fonti, alongside San Nicola in Bari, the cathedral of Altamura, and that of Monte Sant'Angelo. Started in 1529 by the dukes of Atri, finished in 1594, consecrated only in 1823. It takes the Romanesque plan of Bari and Bitonto and pushes it toward the Renaissance: rare in the region.

The historic center of Acquaviva delle Fonti clusters around Piazza Vittorio Emanuele, where the cathedral opens. The town takes its name from the water table running beneath it, and its origins stretch back to the 7th century BC. The painter Carlo Rosa, of the southern Caravaggesque tradition, was born here in 1613. Half an hour's walk is enough.

activities.text: The cipolla rossa of Acquaviva delle Fonti is a Slow Food Presidium, and the municipality hosts a second one, the cece nero della Murgia carsica: two presidia on one territory, which is unusual. At table, ask for the calzone di cipolle, a flatbread stuffed with onions, ricotta forte, and cheese. Eat it warm, never cold.

The WWF Gioacchino Carone oasis, a few kilometers from Acquaviva delle Fonti, is a detour worth taking: two and a half hectares of woodland, dense birdlife including the lesser kestrel. It's small, but it's what remains of the Murge's original forest cover. Access and visits managed by the WWF; check before heading out.

days_plan.itin_title: The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

map_keywords: Cathedral of Sant'Eustachio Acquaviva delle Fonti

visits.text: Pietrabbondante ('abundant stones'), at 966 meters on Monte Saraceno's flank, was the federal sanctuary of the Samnite Pentri tribe. Theater-temple built between 120 and 90 BC, abandoned after the Social War (91-88 BC). The theater, estimated capacity between 1,000 and 2,500 seats according to archaeologists, preserves three rows of stone seats with backrests—rare detail, almost ergonomic. Acoustics still perfect: every summer it hosts the Samnite Theater Festival, unamplified. Sit at the top and look toward the Verrino valley: this is where the Samnite senate deliberated. The panorama is worth as much as the stones.

The Marinelli Foundry of Agnone is probably the world's oldest family business—Nicodemus Marinelli's signature is attested on a 1339 bell, and family activity reportedly dates to the 11th century, around 1040. 27th generation at the helm. They've cast bells for the Vatican, St. Peter's Basilica, Monte Cassino rebuilt after WWII, Buenos Aires cathedral, Pompeii sanctuary, and UN headquarters in New York. In 1924, Pope Pius XI granted them the privilege of displaying papal arms on their bells. The guided tour (€9) shows the clay-and-hemp mold, the casting, and ends with a mini-concert. Photos forbidden. Tours at 11am, 12pm, 4pm, 5pm Monday-Saturday.

Touring Club Orange Flag, fourteen churches in a pocket-sized center: Agnone invites wandering. San Marco with Renaissance portal adorned with a copper lion—vestige of Venetian artists who came in the 11th century to decorate the Borrello family houses. Sant'Emidio (12th century) with wooden statues brought out for Good Friday procession. If you pass December 24, the Ndocciata is a nighttime procession of fir and beech torches descending the corso: pagan-Christian spectacle classified as Italian cultural heritage. Rest of the year, just enjoy the alleys, copper workshops and caciocavallo cheesemakers active for 400 years.

activities.text: Lunch in Agnone at Locanda Mammì (1 Michelin star), one of very few starred tables in Molise. Reinvented peasant cuisine: grilled caciocavallo, lamb, mountain vegetables, handmade pasta. Tasting menu around €70-90, more accessible lunch formula. Essential booking, especially weekends. It's a chance to understand why this overlooked region has a rising gastronomic scene.

Agnone caciocavallo tasting, one of central-southern Italy's finest cheeses. The technique—stretched curd, pear-shaped molding, hanging in pairs—hasn't changed in four centuries. Several caseifici downtown sell and offer tastings of different ages (3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years). Older vintages develop notes close to aged Parmesan.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Molise in 9 Days: Pescara to Naples Through the Samnium

places.name: Agrigento

visits.text: Agrigento's Valley of the Temples, founded in 580 BC as Akragas, contains the largest ensemble of Doric temples outside Greece. Pindar described it as "the most beautiful of mortal cities." The UNESCO site sprawls across 1,300 hectares.

The Temple of Concordia, built around 430 BC, ranks among the world's best-preserved Greek temples. Its survival stems from its conversion into a Christian church in the 6th century. All 34 columns, standing 6.70 meters tall, retain their original golden hue.

The Temple of Hera Lacinia, at the ridge's eastern end, dominates the valley from its 25 partially standing columns. The charring marks on its stones date from the fire set by Carthaginians during the city's sack in 406 BC.

The Temple of Olympian Zeus, erected after the victory over Carthage in 480 BC, was the largest Doric temple ever attempted: 113 by 56 meters, never completed. One of its telamones—7.65-meter atlas figures—lies reconstructed on the ground.

Agrigento's Regional Archaeological Museum houses the reconstructed telamon from the Temple of Zeus (7.65 m tall) and an exceptional collection of Greek vases, coins, and sculptures. Its topographical section illuminates the complete urban layout of ancient Akragas.

Agrigento's Hellenistic-Roman quarter, discovered in 1950, reveals a perfectly gridded street plan with perpendicular roads 6 meters wide, underground drainage systems, and the foundations of atrium houses from the 2nd and 1st centuries BC.

activities.text: Lunch on Via Atenea with macco di fave—dried fava bean soup with olive oil and wild fennel, an Agrigento dish of Greek origin.

Excursion to Caltagirone (40 km): its 142 steps of the Santa Maria del Monte Staircase are covered in ceramic tiles illustrating each century of the town's history. Caltagirone ceramics are classified as UNESCO intangible heritage.
Night visit to the Valley of the Temples on Mondays and Fridays from May to October: the illuminated temples create an extraordinary atmosphere.

visits.text: Agropoli is a real coastal town, not an open-air museum: 21,000 inhabitants, active fishing port, beaches at its feet. The historic center on the promontory (90 m above sea) keeps its medieval layout. You climb the paved ramp to the 16th-century Porta Forte, then wander the alleys to the Castle. Founded by the Byzantines in the 6th century to watch the coast, expanded by the Normans, then by the Aragonese. Spectacular view over the bay and Castellabate to the south.

Agropoli's harbor is one of Cilento's busiest: colorful boats, morning fish auction, ferries to Capri and Salerno in season. The quayside taverns serve catch of the day. Good place to observe local maritime life, far from tourist clichés.

activities.text: Fish lunch at the harbor. Agropoli specialty: alici di menaica, anchovies caught the old way with a net called menaide, hand-salted and marinated. Slow Food Presidium since 1999. Trattoria U' Zifaro for the classic version.

days_plan.itin_title: From Naples to Calabria: The Tyrrhenian Coast
Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: Climb to the acropolis of Alatri, built in the 7th century BC by the Italic Hernici people. The outer wall, stretching over 2 km and nearly intact, is formed of polygonal blocks assembled without mortar, some exceeding three tons. It covers approximately 25 hectares and is considered by archaeologists as the largest pre-Roman acropolis in Italy after Athens. Two monumental gateways survive: the Porta Maggiore, whose lintel is a single monolithic block, and a lower pedestrian gate.

The Church of Santa Maria Maggiore was built in the 5th century on the ruins of a temple of Venus, then reconstructed with a 14th-century facade and bell tower dated 1394. Inside: a 13th-century carved wooden group depicting the "Virgin of Constantinople" and a triptych of the Redeemer attributed to Antonio da Alatri (14th-15th century).

Saint Paul's Cathedral, whose origins date to the 10th century, occupies the very esplanade of the acropolis. Its position is exceptional: it stands on the site of the ancient main temple of the Hernician city, within the cyclopean walls.

The Municipal Archaeological Museum, installed in the Palazzo Gottifredo (a Roman-era building), displays finds from excavations conducted on Alatri's territory since the 19th century: Hernician ceramics, coins, funerary stelae, and architectural fragments from the acropolis.

activities.text: Walk the outer perimeter of the cyclopean walls following the trail that circles the hill: the view over the valley of the Ernici Mountains extends to the ridges of southern Lazio, and you can clearly perceive the defensive logic of the Hernician builders who selected their stones based on natural shape, without any cutting.

days_plan.itin_title: Ciociaria Circuit: Abbeys and Medieval Hilltop Villages

places.name: Alba

visits.text: Asti deserves more than a quick stop: the Gothic cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, built between 1309 and 1354, is one of Piedmont's largest Gothic churches. The Torre Troyana - 40 meters, 12th century - is one of the few medieval towers surviving from the 120 that once marked the city's communal heyday. The historic center is compact, nearly empty of tourists during the week. Allow 45 minutes.

The underground cathedrals of Canelli are the day's main draw. Since the 16th century, Spumante houses have carved galleries into the limestone tuff beneath the town - Contratto, Gancia, Coppo, Bosca - to store their wines at constant temperature. The complex was designated UNESCO World Heritage in 2014 as part of the cultural landscape of Piedmont's vineyards. At Contratto, founded in 1867, the tour descends into cellars that resemble church naves: tuff vaults, rows of riddling racks loaded with bottles in remuage, absolute silence. Reservation required.

Neive is classified among Italy's 'most beautiful villages' - and for once, the label matches reality. Medieval hilltop village in the Langhe, cobbled lanes, 17th-century palazzos, panorama over the Barbaresco vineyards 5 km away. In October, the nebbiolo leaves turn orange and copper red - the village reaches an almost indecent state of beauty. Coffee on the terrace before heading down to Alba.

Barbaresco: 660 inhabitants, a 12th-century medieval tower, and one of Piedmont's two top DOCGs. The tower offers the clearest view over the crus - Rio Sordo, Rabajà, Asili, Martinenga - descending toward the Tanaro below. DOCG since 1980, pure nebbiolo, minimum 26 months aging (50 for Riserva). More floral, more delicate than Barolo, approachable younger - which doesn't mean simpler.

The Enoteca Regionale del Barbaresco occupies the former San Donato church, deconsecrated in the 19th century. Under Romanesque vaults, the entire production of the appellation's estates is available by the glass and bottle - about a hundred references, including the Produttori's single-vineyard cuvées. It's the most honest place for a first comparative tasting: same appellation, same vintage, a dozen producers side by side. Open daily except Tuesday.

The Produttori del Barbaresco was founded in 1958 by 19 winegrowers who refused to sell their grapes to négociants at rock-bottom prices. Today the cooperative includes 56 members across 100 hectares, and its single-vineyard cuvées - Asili, Rabajà, Montestefano - rank among the appellation's absolute references, at prices well below Gaja. The cellar tour is sober and instructive. Reservation recommended.

Alba's medieval center has kept its towers, cobbled lanes and Duomo San Lorenzo - 14th-century Gothic façade, baroque interior remodeled in the 18th century. But what Alba does better than any Piedmontese town is the market: every Saturday morning, Piazza Pertinace, local producers sell their Tonda Gentile hazelnuts, sheep cheeses, tajarin (egg pasta, 40 yolks per kilo of flour - four times the standard proportion). Arrive before 9 AM.

The International White Truffle Fair of Alba runs every Saturday and Sunday from October through early December. Tuber magnatum pico is the world's most expensive truffle - between €3,000 and €5,000 per kg depending on the year, size, and the seller's mood. The covered market is open to all, paid admission (€15), but what you come for is the smell: a 200-gram truffle in a truffle hunter's hand, 10 cm from your nose, is a sensory experience that's hard to describe. Even without buying.

Pio Cesare, founded in 1881 in central Alba, is one of the few major négociant houses still independent and family-owned. The distinctive feature: the cellars are carved beneath the town's 1st-century Roman walls, visible through a glass bay in the tasting room. Five generations of the same family, Barolo and Barbaresco in every style. Walk-in visits during the week.

activities.text: Moscato d'Asti DOCG tasting in Canelli: sweet sparkling wine, only 5.5° alcohol, aromas of white peach and acacia. It's the opposite of Barolo - and that's deliberate. At Contratto or in one of the cellars on Via G.B. Giuliani, ask to compare still Moscato (non-sparkling) and Moscato d'Asti: same grape, same terroir, two radically different vinifications. At €6 per glass, it's one of the most revealing tastings in the region.

Lunch in Canelli or Asti: Monferrato cuisine - Piedmontese fritto misto (offal, vegetables, amaretti fried together in the same oil - sounds odd, tastes delicious), risotto with Barbera, Tonda Gentile hazelnut tart. Osteria dei Binari in Canelli, opposite the train station, offers a lunch menu at €15 that changes according to the morning market.

Tasting at Gaja if you've booked - and if you've booked, it means you planned this 3 months in advance. Angelo Gaja internationalized the Barbaresco appellation in the 1960s-1980s, imposing prestige prices at a time when Piedmontese wine was considered rustic. His Sorì Tildin and Costa Russi cuvées now run €300-500 per bottle. The visit is technical, reserved for serious enthusiasts. Otherwise, drive past the house in the village center - the modesty of the façade is a delicious paradox.

Walk through the vineyards between Barbaresco and Neive: the cru trail runs along the parcels for 4 km on dirt paths, with signs identifying each cru. In autumn, the nebbiolo vines turn orange and copper red - backlit at sunset, it's the Langhe at their most beautiful, and it costs nothing. Walking shoes recommended after rain.

Tajarin with white truffle tasting: tajarin is the local pasta, thin as paper, hand-rolled on wooden boards. With a fried egg and a few shavings of white truffle grated on top - it's the simplest and most expensive dish you'll eat all week. At Osteria dell'Arco, Via Vittorio Emanuele, tajarin with truffle is offered by weight of truffle grated: 5 grams is enough for a complete dish, around €40-50.

Free afternoon in Alba: the town has an abnormal concentration of chocolatiers and pastry shops for 30,000 inhabitants - Ferrero was born here, Nutella was invented here in 1964 (the spread was originally called 'Supercrema'). The factory isn't open to visitors, but artisan hazelnut paste shops are everywhere. At Barbero or Converso, on the main street, buy crema di nocciola in jars: nothing like the industrial version.

White truffle fair Alba Piazza Pertinace

visits.text: Albenga's early Christian baptistery is probably the architectural highlight of this entire itinerary, and almost nobody's heard of it. Built between the 5th and 6th centuries, octagonal plan inside, decagonal outside. The detail that makes it unique: it sits 2.5 meters below current street level—you descend by stairs. The floor you're walking on is the ancient floor of the Roman city. At the back, in a niche, a 6th-century mosaic depicts twelve white doves around the monogram of Christ, on a cobalt blue background. Fifteen hundred years old, intact. Access via the diocesan museum, 9:30am-1pm and 2:30-6:30pm, closed certain holidays.

Albenga's medieval center is recognizable from kilometers away: its red brick towers rising above the rooftops like chimneys. There were about fifty in the Middle Ages, nine still stand, the tallest (Torre Comunale) reaches 32 meters. The street grid still faithfully follows the layout of the Roman castrum—a rare thing in Liguria. Wander without a map, it's small and rectangular, you can't get lost. Obligatory detour through San Michele Cathedral: Byzantine crypt accessible by a discreet staircase behind the main altar—many miss it.

The Museo Navale Romano displays the cargo of a Roman merchant ship that sank off Albenga around 80 BC. Discovered in 1925, scientifically excavated starting in 1950 by Nino Lamboglia—officially the first underwater archaeological dig in history. More than 11,000 wine amphorae were shipping from Campania to Gaul on that vessel, the largest known ancient cargo in the western Mediterranean. Five hundred pieces are on display, plus two 1.5-meter lead anchors. Kids immediately hook in, adults stay longer than planned. Included in the combination ticket.

Alassio, 6 km southwest, deserves the round trip for one thing alone: the Muretto, that little hundred-meter wall in front of Caffè Roma, covered since 1953 with 550 ceramic tiles signed by celebrities who stopped by. Hemingway, Sophia Loren, Dario Fo, Gino Bartali. The idea came from a cafe owner and autograph fan who turned his hobby into a tourist attraction. It's kitschy, it's touristy, but it's a genuine time capsule of 1950s-60s Italy. The seafront promenade behind is worth it too, especially at dusk.

activities.text: Boat or kayak trip around Isola Gallinara, the triangular island facing Albenga. Let's be clear: you do NOT land on it. It's private property and a regional nature reserve since 1989, occupied by a large colony of yellow-legged gulls and inhabited only by the six apartments of the owners. But you circle it at 1.5 km from shore: transparent waters, seagrass beds, and the turtle-shaped silhouette cutting against the open sea. Excursions depart from Alassio, Loano or Albenga, expect €25-35 for 2 hours by boat, a bit more for guided kayak. Sea often choppy in the afternoon with thermal wind—go in the morning.

Wednesday morning market in Albenga, one of the biggest on the entire western coast of Liguria, spread across Piazza del Popolo and surrounding streets. The Albenga plain is famous for its violet asparagus, Cuore di Bue tomatoes, and artichokes; this is where they land straight from the fields. Cheeses, warm focaccia, fresh trofie with pesto to go. Get there before 11am, after that it becomes a contact sport. For focaccia all'olio, trust the queue: the bakers on Vico San Giovanni never empty out—that's a sign.

visits.text: A thousand cones and souvenir shops everywhere: Rione Monti in Alberobello is saturated, and still astonishing. Around 1,030 trulli line its sloping alleyways, their whitewashed rooftops painted with symbols. The quarter is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 1996. Come before 9am or after 6pm; in between, the tour buses unload.

Then cross into Rione Aia Piccola, where no commercial business may operate: that's the rule, and it holds. About 590 trulli, all inhabited, laundry at the windows, no one trying to sell you a fridge magnet. The contrast with Rione Monti, a hundred meters away, is absolute. Keep your voice down; people actually live here.

Trullo Sovrano is the only two-story trullo in town, which is enough to make it a curiosity. Dating from the 18th century, it's set up as a house-museum with original furnishings from the early 20th century: the best place to understand how people lived under a cone. Entry announced at around 2 euros. Fifteen minutes is enough; it's tiny.

A church shaped like a trullo: the idea could have been absurd, and somehow it isn't. The Chiesa di Sant'Antonio, at the top of Rione Monti, uses the same chiancarelle construction and blends into the quarter rather than overpowering it. It's the only church built this way. The climb is steep; save it for the end of the loop, when the light is falling.

Two cones fused at the centre: the Trulli Siamesi owe their name to this shared roofline. Local legend sees two brothers, a story of love and hatred, and a house divided in two. They line Rione Monti, steps from the shops. Five minutes, long enough to study the joint between the two cones.

Find Casa d'Amore at the entrance to the center: this is the first building constructed after Alberobello was freed from the fiscal obligations imposed by the King of Naples, in 1797. It served as the first town hall. Nothing extraordinary to look at, except that it marks the turning point in the town's entire history. Explanatory panel on site, two minutes.

Casa Pezzolla is fifteen cones joined together and converted into the Museo del Territorio. Tools, objects, reconstructions: the place explains how these houses were organized and why they survived. Entry announced as free. Rare for Alberobello, it's quiet inside.

Head up to Belvedere Santa Lucia at the end of the day: this is where you take in the full sea of grey cones in Rione Monti at a single glance. Sunset photos happen here, and everyone knows it. Arrive twenty minutes early; the front row goes fast.

activities.text: If you want to understand rather than just photograph, book a guided tour of Alberobello: the dry-stone construction technique, the symbols painted on the rooftops, the fiscal history of the village, none of it is self-explanatory. The craft shops in Rione Monti also sell local stone and textiles, in between stalls of magnets. Book in advance in summer.

visits.text: Alghero's ramparts were built by the Aragonese starting in 1353 when Peter IV of Aragon settled Majorcan and Catalan colonists here, and they've retained over 70% of their original perimeter with seven 16th-century towers still intact. Catalan remains an officially recognized minority language — street signs bear bilingual names, and the Iberian accent lingers in certain families to this day.

The Bastioni Marco Polo run along the sea for several hundred meters above the limestone rocks. At sunset, golden light spills across the waters of the Gulf of Alghero, drawing locals to the evening promenade as it has for centuries.

Capo Caccia is a limestone promontory rising 170 meters straight out of the sea, 24 km from Alghero. At its base opens the Grotta di Nettuno, a karst cave discovered by a local fisherman in the 18th century, accessible by boat or via the 654 steps of the Escala del Cabirol carved into the cliff face in 1959.

Maria Pia Beach stretches for 2 km north of Alghero, backed by a pine forest of umbrella pines planted in the 1930s to stabilize the dunes. Its fine white sand and shallow waters make it the city's most popular family beach.
Le Bombarde Beach, 8 km north of Alghero in Porto Conte Bay, is framed by rocks and Mediterranean scrubland. The rocky seabed makes it an excellent snorkeling spot.

activities.text: Boat crossing from Alghero port to the Grotta di Nettuno: 3-hour round trip with views of the Capo Caccia cliffs and Porto Conte Bay.
Taste aragosta all'algherese in a harborside trattoria — a Catalan lobster recipe with tomatoes, onion, olive oil, and vinegar that's distinct from the rest of Sardinia.
Swimming and snorkeling in the coves of Porto Conte Bay, a protected marine area with some of the clearest waters in northwest Sardinia.

visits.text: Aliano is the village where Carlo Levi, doctor and anti-fascist writer, was assigned to residence by Mussolini in 1935-1936. He lived there a year and wrote one of 20th-century Italian literature's greatest books: 'Christ Stopped at Eboli.' The house he occupied, on Piazza Garibaldi, is now a modest but moving museum. Letters, drawings, period photos. The village itself has changed little: 853 inhabitants, stone houses, lanes packed on a ridge between two ravines. The Carlo Levi Literary Park scatters plaques with book excerpts through the streets, to read on site.

The Aliano Calanchi are one of southern Italy's most striking landscapes: clay ravines sculpted by erosion, nearly lunar, nearly African scenery. Carlo Levi described them as 'a frozen mineral sea.' Several viewpoints around the village, and several marked hiking trails (Sentiero della Frana, Sentiero dei Calanchi). Golden light at sunrise and sunset.

Aliano's cemetery houses Carlo Levi's tomb (died 1975), according to his wish. He had said: 'I want to be buried in Aliano because that's where I understood who I was.' Simple tomb, among the peasants', but easy to spot: it's the only one covered with small stones that visitors leave in tribute (a Jewish tradition gesture, adopted here despite the writer's professed secularism). Open-air cemetery on the ridge, views over the calanchi.

activities.text: Walk in the calanchi at sunset. The Sentiero dei Calanchi (3 km, 1h30) descends into the ravines and climbs back via the other slope. Good elevation, technical path in places. No shade, bring water.
Dinner at Agriturismo La Riserva in Aliano, serving the dishes Carlo Levi described: pasta con la mollica (fried breadcrumbs), cicoria selvatica, baked lamb, house wine.

visits.text: Alicudi, the most isolated Aeolian island with 100 permanent residents, has no roads, no cars, no motorcycles — only steep trails and donkeys for transport. Electricity arrived only in 1990, telephones in 1991.

Monte Filo dell'Arpa (675 m), accessible via 2,000 steps carved into the rock from the port, is the only way to reach the agricultural terraces. The climb takes 2 hours and offers views of all the Aeolian Islands.

activities.text: Snorkeling and swimming in the port waters, among the clearest in the archipelago thanks to the absence of pollution and maritime traffic.

places.name: Altamura

visits.text: Altamura - Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta: Built by Frederick II between 1232 and 1254 as a palatine chapel — a status that removed it from the Bishop of Bari's authority and placed it directly under imperial authority. In 1248, Pope Innocent IV was forced to accept this fait accompli. The facade features a 14th-century portal carved with 22 Gospel scenes, supported by two stone lions remade in 1533. The upper Gothic section with its two bell towers dates from the 16th century. A 17th-century historian suggested the church occupied the site of a Greek temple dedicated to Castor and Pollux.

Altamura - claustri and historic center: Frederick II founded or refounded Altamura in 1230, bringing in Latin, Greek and Jewish populations. The result was about 80 claustri — small interior courtyards with single entrances, in Greek style (with central well) or Arabic (long and narrow). These micro-community spaces functioned as both social units and defensive structures. In 1993, in the Lamalunga cave on the city's outskirts, the Altamura Man was discovered: a Neanderthal skeleton estimated at 130,000-172,000 years old, one of the oldest and best preserved in Europe.

Gravina in Puglia - canyon and aqueduct bridge: This town is built on the edge of a limestone canyon (the gravina) inhabited since the 8th century BC. The 18th-century aqueduct bridge spanning the ravine is one of the most spectacular structures in inland Puglia — and one of the region's most underrated sites. In 2020, Gravina was chosen as the setting for the James Bond film No Time to Die for a car chase scene on this bridge.

Gravina - San Michele delle Grotte cave church: Carved into the canyon limestone, this church houses human bones stacked on the walls — the presumed victims of a medieval Saracen raid according to local tradition. Partially preserved frescoes testify to a Byzantine monastic presence. The Gravina Sotterranea, a network of caves and tunnels beneath the city, can be explored with a guide.

activities.text: Purchase Altamura DOP bread from an artisanal bakery in the center: This is the only bread in Europe with PDO status. Made from re-milled durum wheat semolina and baked in stone wood-fired ovens, it keeps for an entire week. Horace, traveling on the Via Appia in 37 BC, noted in his Satires that Altamura produced 'the finest bread anywhere' and advised stocking up.

Hiking in the Gravina canyon: A trail descends into the ravine, passes beneath the aqueduct bridge and allows observation of the troglodyte dwellings carved into the canyon walls from below. Allow 1h30 round trip.

places.name: Amalfi

visits.text: The Cathedral of Sant'Andrea in Amalfi, built from 987 onward by Duke Mansone I, is the emblem of the ancient Maritime Republic of Amalfi—first of the four Italian Maritime Republics, which in the 10th-11th centuries controlled part of Mediterranean trade and counted approximately 70,000 inhabitants. It's accessed by a 57-step staircase from Piazza Duomo. The Arab-Norman facade blends golden mosaics, horseshoe arches, bicolor stripes, and ceramics. The bronze doors were cast in Constantinople in 1057—the first of their kind in Italy. The Cloister of Paradise (1266-1268), with its interlaced Moorish-influenced arches on twin columns, served as a cemetery for the Amalfitan nobility.

The Arsenal of the Republic (Arsenale della Repubblica), a 12th-century shipyard preserved in its original state, houses the Museum of the Compass and Maritime Duchy. Amalfi's sailors were among the first in the West to use the compass for navigation. Around 1070, Amalfitan merchants established in Jerusalem founded the Hospital of Jerusalem—origin of the Knights Hospitaller of St. John.

Ravello perches at 365 meters above the Tyrrhenian Sea, on a rocky promontory between Amalfi and Minori. Villa Rufolo, built in the 13th century by the Rufolo family—one of the most powerful in medieval Amalfi's Republic—blends Arab, Norman, and Gothic influences in a unique hybrid architecture. Its belvedere overlooking the Gulf of Salerno impressed Richard Wagner during his 1880 visit: he found here the inspiration for Klingsor's magic garden in Parsifal. In his honor, Ravello hosts an international classical music festival each summer in the villa's gardens.

Villa Cimbrone, whose origins date to the 11th century, was profoundly transformed in the early 20th century by British aristocrat Ernest William Beckett, who created gardens, terraces, and a cloister in mixed styles—neo-Gothic, neo-Moorish, Venetian. Its public gardens extend along the cliff edge. The Terrace of Infinity, a balcony lined with marble busts at 365 meters elevation, offers the Amalfi Coast's most famous panorama: the sea and sky merge on the horizon. Virginia Woolf, Greta Garbo, Winston Churchill, and Gore Vidal stayed here.

Atrani, 700 meters from Amalfi on foot along the coast, is Italy's smallest municipality by area. A former stronghold of the Amalfi Republic, it has preserved its labyrinth of lanes, arches, and stairways without the tourist crowds of its neighbor. Its small pebble beach, sheltered in a cliff hollow, is one of the coast's most tranquil.

Minori, 6 km from Amalfi, houses the remains of a 1st-century Roman maritime villa—proof that the Amalfi Coast was already a resort for Roman nobility. The Basilica of Santa Trofimena (11th-12th century) holds the remains of the village's patron saint. Between Minori and Maiori stretches the Sentiero dei Limoni, a marked 2-km path through lemon terraces overlooking the sea.

activities.text: Boat excursion from Amalfi's port to the Grotta dello Smeraldo (Emerald Grotto), a karst cavity discovered in 1932 whose waters take on an intense emerald color thanks to light filtered through an underwater opening at 4 meters depth. Swimming in a cove from the boat.

After Ravello, descend to Maiori for an afternoon of relaxation on the Amalfi Coast's largest beach. Protected from winds in a natural cove, Maiori's sandy beach contrasts with the pebbles of the rest of the coast. Evening stroll along the waterfront promenade.

Beach day at Maiori or Minori—the coast's only two sandy beaches—to conclude the circuit by the sea. Swimming, seafood lunch at a waterfront trattoria, and leisurely return to Amalfi's port in late afternoon.

visits.text: Amantea—a medieval town of 13,000 on a 177-meter promontory above the Tyrrhenian Sea, 30 km from Lamezia Terme airport. The historic center preserves the 15th-century Torre Aragonese and the 13th-century church of San Francesco d'Assisi with a Gothic portal. The town was an important silk production center until the 19th century, exporting to Naples and Genoa.

activities.text: Final swim on Amantea's fine sand beaches before returning to Lamezia Terme airport (30 km).

visits.text: Anagni Cathedral was built between 1072 and 1104 by Bishop Pietro da Salerno and consecrated in 1105 by Pope Paschal II. This Romanesque-Gothic marvel stretches 80 meters and features a stunning Cosmatesque floor installed in 1231, along with a ciborium sculpted by Vassalletto in 1267. Anagni was the birthplace of four popes, including Boniface VIII (born c. 1235). Within these walls, Alexander III excommunicated Frederick Barbarossa on March 24, 1160, and Clare of Assisi was canonized in 1255.

Descend into the Crypt of San Magno, built simultaneously with the cathedral (1072-1104) and frescoed between 1237 and 1255 across 540 square meters—often called the Sistine Chapel of the Middle Ages. The transition from Byzantine to Romanesque style unfolds panel by panel. Lighting is switched off every half-hour to protect the pigments, with only twenty minutes of illumination per cycle: time your visit accordingly.

The Palace of Boniface VIII, built in the early 13th century by the Conti family in Gothic style, houses a museum with 13th-century frescoes. This palace was the stage for the infamous 1303 "Slap of Anagni," when Sciarra Colonna, acting on behalf of France's King Philip IV, struck Pope Boniface VIII to humiliate papal authority before royal power.

The Palazzo della Ragione, built around 1160 by Jacopo da Iseo, served as the seat of medieval civic assemblies. Its facade overlooking the main square stands as one of the best-preserved examples of Romanesque civil architecture in the region.

activities.text: Wander through Anagni's historic center from the Porta degli Angeli to Piazza Innocenzo III: cobbled lanes reveal 12th and 13th-century cardinal palaces, medieval fountains, and chiseled limestone doorways that remind you at every turn of the era when this town rivaled Rome itself.

days_plan.itin_title: Ciociaria Circuit: Abbeys and Medieval Hilltop Villages

visits.text: Head to Andria, 13 km inland. The town is less pretty than its coastal neighbors, but its Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, founded in the 11th century, holds something unique: the tombs of two of Frederick II's wives, Yolande de Brienne (died in childbirth in 1228 at 16) and Isabella of England (died in 1241 at 27). The crypt, partly carved into an earlier paleo-Christian church, is the most moving part. The cathedral also preserves a thorn from Christ's crown, offered in 1308 by Countess Beatrice, daughter of Charles II of Anjou.

Porta Sant'Andrea, also called Arco di Federico, is the only one of Andria's five medieval gates to survive: the other four were demolished after Italian unification. The inscription carved on the facade, attributed to Frederick II in 1230 on his return from the sixth crusade—"Andria fidelis nostris affixa medullis" (Andria the faithful, engraved in our bowels)—explains why the emperor called the city his "fidelis." Small, sober, restored in the 16th century, but loaded with symbolism.

Palazzo Ducale, on Piazza Catuma, was built by Frederick II on his return from the sixth crusade in 1230, originally as a Franciscan convent. Remodeled in the 16th century as a noble residence for the Carafa dukes, it's now city hall. Visit limited to public spaces, but the courtyard and facade are worth the detour. The square itself, called "Catuma" because of paleo-Christian catacombs underground, is the true heart of Andria.

Andria's historic center explores through its narrow alleys between Porta Sant'Andrea and the cathedral: degraded but inhabited Renaissance palaces, small churches, local product shops. The Torre dell'Orologio, also erected by Frederick II, marks the medieval center. Budget an hour of relaxed wandering, the center is compact.

activities.text: Burrata tasting straight from the source at Caseificio Olanda in Andria. Burrata is mozzarella enveloping a heart of stracciatella and cream: twelve hours freshness maximum after making. Lorenzo Bianchino invented it in Andria in 1956, to avoid losing his milk production during a winter blocked by snow. IGP since 2016. Workshop visit in the morning, tasting in the afternoon with a glass of Castel del Monte DOC.

Dinner in a masseria around Andria. Several addresses between Andria and Castel del Monte offer regional cuisine: Lucanian lamb, fave e cicoria (fava bean puree with wild chicory), homemade pasta. Rustic atmosphere, reasonable prices, essential to book.

visits.text: Stroll through Angera's center and along its quays bordering the southern tip of Lake Maggiore on the Lombard side. The small town is dominated from afar by the crenellated silhouette of the Rocca whose swallowtail merlons can be recognized from the lake.

Visit the Rocca Borromea of Angera, a medieval fortress owned by the Borromeo family since 1449. The earliest traces of the building date back to 1066, when it belonged to the archbishops of Milan. The Visconti took control in 1277 after the Battle of Desio—a victory commemorated in the spectacular frescoes of the Hall of Justice, painted shortly after the event by the 'Master of Angera' and constituting one of the major examples of secular painting from the late Lombard Gothic. Vitaliano I Borromeo bought the complex in 1449 for 12,800 imperial pounds. The Rocca is the harmonious result of five building sections constructed between the 11th and 17th centuries.

Spend an hour at the Doll and Toy Museum, the largest in Europe, founded in 1988 by Princess Bona Borromeo Arese. Its 12 rooms distributed across the Visconti and Borromeo wings display over 1,300 pieces—dolls, French and German automatons from the 19th century, toys from around the world—from the 18th century to contemporary creations. A separate room is dedicated to dolls and toys from non-European cultures.

Explore the Rocca's medieval garden, 2,000 m² enclosed between the vineyards and the crenellated walls overlooking the lake. This garden was reconstructed from historical sources—illuminated codices and period documents—and presents the three types of medieval gardens: the Princes' Garden, the Verzière (vegetable garden), and the Herb Garden.

activities.text: Climb to the Rocca's tower viewpoints to admire the panorama over Lake Maggiore and the Alps. The Torre Castellana offers the highest view of both lake shores—the Lombard side with Angera, and the Piedmont side with Arona, where the Rocca d'Arona once stood before Napoleon ordered its demolition in 1800. Together with Angera, it formed the lake's historic lock.

days_plan.itin_title: Lombardy's Most Beautiful Villages in 5 Days

visits.text: Fortified village of Anghiari: ranked among the most beautiful villages in Italy, Anghiari rises on a hill overlooking the Valtiberina plain, protected by bastions of which a portion survives. The Torre del Campano, dating from the 13th century and rebuilt in the 16th century after its destruction by Vitellozzo Vitelli in 1502, marks the village's silhouette. The Palazzo Pretorio on Piazza del Popolo displays a facade covered in the coats of arms of the Florentine vicars who administered the town after 1440, typical of fortress-towns governed from Florence.

Museum of the Battle of Anghiari — Palazzo del Marzocco: the museum, opened in 2000 and expanded in 2007, traces the history of the battle of June 29, 1440, in which the Florentines led by Micheletto Attendolo defeated the Milanese under Niccolò Piccinino, securing Florence's independence. The battle would have remained a local episode were it not for Leonardo da Vinci, commissioned in 1503 by Gonfalonier Piero Soderini to paint it in the Hall of the Five Hundred of the Palazzo Vecchio. Using experimental encaustic, Leonardo managed only to sketch the "Battle for the Standard" before leaving Florence in 1506; Vasari covered the unfinished work in 1563. The museum holds a 17th-century copy by the Flemish engraver Gérard Edelinck, as well as engravings by Dürer and Chagall inspired by Leonardo's sketches.

Museo Statale di Palazzo Taglieschi: a national museum housed in a Renaissance palace, devoted to the history of Anghiari and the Valtiberina from the Middle Ages to the 18th century. It brings together local sculpture and painting as well as documentation on the tradition of firearm manufacture — Anghiari was in the 18th century a center renowned for the fineness of its arms decorations.

activities.text: Trail of the Battle of Anghiari to the Maestà della Vittoria: a roughly 1-hour hike from the historic center to the exact spot where the Florentines defeated the Milanese in June 1440. The path follows the ancient straight road built in the late 14th century linking Anghiari to Sansepolcro, along which the former Byzantine church of Santo Stefano and traces of Roman centuriation are still visible.

places.name: Anversa Degli Abruzzi

visits.text: Anversa degli Abruzzi - a village of 400 inhabitants on a rocky spur at 660 meters at the entrance to the Gole del Sagittario. Vestiges of an 11th-century Norman castle dominate the village. The Chiesa di Santa Maria delle Grazie preserves a 12th-century Romanesque portal and 15th-century frescoes.

activities.text: View of the Gole del Sagittario entrance from the village belvedere - the 200-meter-high limestone cliffs framing the torrent are visible from the historic center terraces.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo
