visits.text: 110 km route via A5 motorway, 1h45, heading north across the Po plain then climbing Valle d'Aosta beneath the glacial summits of Mont Blanc and Matterhorn. Aosta appears at the confluence of the Buthier and Dora Baltea, at 583 m altitude, boxed into its mineral valley floor. The city was founded in 25 BC by legionaries of Augustus's praetorian cohort on the site of an oppidum of the Celto-Ligurian Salassi tribe, exterminated to open passage of the Alpine passes toward Gaul. Augusta Praetoria—'founded by the praetorians of Augustus'—became Aosta after two thousand years of linguistic wear. Drop bags centro €90-140.

Make the Roman circuit on foot, it's dense and compact. The Arco di Augusto, erected as early as 25 BC at the city's east end to celebrate the foundation, marks the historic entrance: single arch 11.5 m high in travertine, ten engaged Corinthian columns, pediment embedded in the masonry. 200 m away, the Porta Praetoria, eastern gate of the Roman enceinte, double passage boxed between two towers, preserved to 12 m height—one of the very rare complete Roman gates still standing in Italy. The paved threshold bears the ruts of carts worn over two millennia.

Pass through the Porta Praetoria and enter the Teatro Romano, dated to the Claudian period (around 50 AD). The north facade still rises 22 m high, pierced with four rows of arcades, enormous blind facade dominating the excavated gardens. The neighboring amphitheater could receive 20,000 spectators out of a civilian population estimated at 6,000—the disproportion is explained by the military garrison and passing merchants who doubled the numbers during spectacle periods. Combined ticket €10 for theater + Criptoportico Forense (underground gallery of the forum, dated to Augustus, preserved intact over 89 m).

Head southeast via SS26, 40 km, to the Forte di Bard. The fortress bars the glacial lock of lower Valle d'Aosta, where the Dora Baltea narrows between two hard rock walls. A first fortress existed there in the tenth century. In May 1800, the French Reserve Army commanded by Bonaparte found itself blocked for fifteen days by the Austrian garrison of the fort, which controlled the entire valley—Napoleon had to have his 40,000 men detoured by mountain trails and have the cannons passed beneath the walls at night, wrapped in straw to muffle the noise, before racing toward the victory of Marengo on June 14. In reprisal, he ordered complete demolition of the fort in 1800-1801. King of Sardinia Charles Albert had it rebuilt from 1830 to 1838 on three concentric levels, still standing today, and it became in 2006 a modern museum complex (Museum of the Alps, photo exhibitions, glass elevators). Ticket €12.

Drive 25 km climbing back up the valley to the Castello di Fénis, one of the best-preserved in the Western Alps. Built mainly between 1340 and 1392 by the Challant family, vassals of the Counts of Savoy, on a site with no obvious strategic value—no pass to defend, no road to control. It was a showpiece residence intended to impose the social rank of the lineage. Double crenellated enceinte, central pentagonal keep, curtain wall with machicolations, interior courtyard with frescoes (circa 1430, attributed to Giacomo Jaquerio) representing Saint George and the dragon. Guided tour mandatory (€8, departures every 30 minutes, in Italian and French).

If you keep energy in the afternoon, push 15 km further east to the Castello di Verrès, perched on a rocky spur overlooking the town. Built in 1390 by Iblet de Challant, it's a perfect 30 m cube on each side, without corner towers, austere, military—complete opposite of Fénis. The square interior courtyard with superimposed galleries, the monumental honor staircase, the vaulted armory hall make it a perfect example of a late fourteenth-century Savoyard castle. Ticket €6, guided tour 1 hour. If fatigue, skip and stay longer at Fénis—one suffices to grasp the idea.

activities.text: Taste Valle d'Aosta fontina at a caseificio counter downtown. Fontina PDO is produced only between 1,700 and 2,700 m altitude by 200 Valle d'Aosta alpine dairies, raw milk from Valdostana breed cows, minimum 80 days aging in stone cellars. At Caseificio Valdostano, Via Croix de Ville 8, they cut to order, you taste three ages side by side (3 months, 6 months, 12 months), €22-28/kg.

Dinner at Trattoria Praetoria, Via Sant'Anselmo 9, 50 m from Porta Praetoria. Traditional Valle d'Aosta cuisine in vaulted seventeenth-century cellar. Polenta concia (polenta enriched with melted fontina and mountain butter), carbonade valdôtaine (beef in spiced red wine, recipe inherited from Flemish merchants who transited the passes), seuppa vallpellinetze (black bread soup, fontina, cabbage, meat broth, shepherd recipe) served as main course. Count €35-50 per person.

Branch off in late afternoon toward Cogne, 27 km south of Aosta, last village before Gran Paradiso National Park (Italy's first park created in 1922, 70,000 ha, 4,000 ibex, 8,000 chamois). Stroll through the Prato di Sant'Orso, 60-hectare meadow at the foot of glacial summits culminating at 4,061 m, crossed by clear water streams—it's the postcard image of Valle d'Aosta, alpine meadow in a basin ringed by peaks, marmots audible from the trail. One hour of easy walking suffices.

Dinner in Cogne at Lou Ressignon, Rue des Mines 22, mountain institution open since 1966—fifty years of Valle d'Aosta cuisine without concession to fashions. Seuppa à la valpellinentze, aged mocetta (dried ibex and chamois ham, PDO), crunchy tegole butter cookies for dessert. Vaulted cellar, fireplace lit even on some June evenings, tables of skiers in winter, hikers in summer. Book ahead. Return to Aosta 30 minutes after dinner.

days_plan.itin_title: Aosta Valley Circuit: From Roman Gateway to Mont Blanc
Dark Piedmont - 8 days from mystical Turin to Valle d'Aosta
Dark Piedmont - 8 days from mystical Turin to Valle d'Aosta

visits.text: Foro romano e porto fluviale - Founded in 181 BC as a Roman colonia, Aquileia became the Empire's fourth-largest city (after Rome, Milan, and Capua) with a population reaching 100,000. The Forum, the river port with its stone quays, and vestiges of Roman roads testify to this grandeur. The city was the starting point for routes to Noricum and Pannonia.

Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta - UNESCO World Heritage listed, this patriarchal basilica houses one of the world's largest early Christian mosaic floors: over 760 square meters of 4th-century mosaics depicting the cycle of Jonah, pastoral scenes, and geometric motifs. The 12th-century frescoed crypt and the excavation crypt complete the visit. The 73-meter bell tower offers panoramas across the site and lagoon.

Museo Archeologico Nazionale - Reorganized in a modern building, this museum presents exceptional collections: engraved gems, glassware, amber from the Baltic route, funerary portraits, and the richest collection of lapidary inscriptions in northern Italy after Rome's.

activities.text: Climb the basilica's bell tower - 73 meters high for an exclusive view over the archaeological site, the Friulian plain, and the glints of the Grado lagoon on the horizon.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Friuli-Venezia Giulia

visits.text: Piazza Grande: Arezzo's central square since the 13th century, tilted with a 10-meter drop from top to bottom. It is bordered by the apse of Santa Maria della Pieve (12th century), the Palazzo della Fraternità dei Laici (Gothic and Renaissance facade, 14th–15th centuries), the Palazzo Pretorio (14th century) and Vasari's Logge, designed in 1573 and completed in 1595. During its construction in 1553, the Medici fortress unearthed the Chimera of Arezzo — a 78.5-cm-tall Etruscan bronze ex-voto, now in the National Archaeological Museum of Florence. Replicas adorn fountains near the station and at Porta San Lorentino.

Basilica of San Francesco and Piero della Francesca's cycle: a Gothic building erected between the late 13th and late 14th centuries, made famous by the Bacci Chapel, whose decoration was entrusted to Piero della Francesca after the death of Bicci di Lorenzo in 1452. Piero executed the 15 scenes of the Legend of the True Cross between 1452 and 1466, covering the three registers of the side walls. The iconographic program, drawn from the Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine, follows not chronological order but formal and symbolic correspondences between scenes: the meeting of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon mirrors the battle of Heraclius, and the two battle scenes echo each other. A ten-year restoration completed in 2000 returned the frescoes to their original colors.

Cathedral of San Donato: one of the most representative examples of Italian Gothic architecture, its construction spanning from the 13th to the 16th century. It houses the stained-glass windows of Guillaume de Marcillat — including the 1524 rose window depicting Honorius III's approval of the Indulgence of Saint Francis — as well as Piero della Francesca's Mary Magdalene fresco, tucked at the back of the left nave, and a painting by Pietro da Cortona depicting the Nativity.

Church of San Domenico and Cimabue's Crucifix: a medieval church founded in the 13th century with austere Gothic architecture. The Cimabue Crucifix — dated by scholars to the decade 1265–1275 — hangs above the high altar. It's one of the Florentine painter's earliest works, already revealing his break from the Byzantine manner: the body of Christ begins to curve naturally, foreshadowing the humanism of Giotto.

Giorgio Vasari House-Museum: the personal residence that the architect, painter and first art critic of the Renaissance — born in Arezzo in 1511 — decorated himself with frescoes of allegories and portraits of great artists. The building, acquired in 1541 and transformed through 1548, reflects Vasari's taste for Mannerist decoration and his relationship to the history of art that he would codify in his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects (1550).

Santa Maria della Pieve: a 12th-century Romanesque church whose facade of stacked pilasters is adorned with sculptures attributed to Lombard masters. The interior preserves the polyptych by Pietro Lorenzetti (1320–1324), Madonna and Child between Saint John the Baptist, Saint Donatus, Saint John the Evangelist and Saint Matthew, on the high altar. The campanile of the Hundred Holes, pierced by 40 windows across five levels, is one of the most distinctive Romanesque bell towers in Tuscany.

National Archaeological Museum Mecenate: housed in the former convent of San Bernardo, built against the 1st–2nd-century Roman amphitheater. It brings together the Etruscan and Roman collections of the region, including sigillata corallium ceramics — the distinctive production of Arretium whose coral-red color characterized Roman exports — and Etruscan bronzes. The amphitheater exterior, with its surviving arc of seating, can be freely explored.

House of Petrarch and the medieval historic center: Francesco Petrarca, born in Arezzo in 1304, is alongside Dante and Boccaccio one of the three founders of the Italian literary language. His birthplace, at the end of Via dell'Orto, provides access to a biographical museum. The historic center also reveals the medieval Lappoli tower-house on Piazza Grande, and the heritage of a city that was in the Middle Ages a powerful bishopric and a Ghibelline stronghold that resisted the Guelph forces of Florence until the Battle of Campaldino (1289).

activities.text: Giostra del Saracino: a jousting tournament rooted in the Middle Ages, revived in 1931 as a 14th-century reenactment. It takes place twice a year on the Piazza Grande: the penultimate Saturday of June (Joust of San Donato) and the first Sunday of September. The four quarters — Porta Santo Spirito, Porta Sant'Andrea, Porta del Foro and Porta Crucifera — compete in a tournament where mounted knights charge and strike the shield of a pivoting Saracen effigy. The procession mobilizes over 350 costumed participants and 27 horses.

Arezzo Antique Fair: one of the largest antique fairs in Europe, created in 1968 by Ivan Bruschi. On the first Saturday and Sunday of every month, the Piazza Grande and surrounding streets host more than 500 dealers from across Italy, specializing in furniture, paintings, objects and antique jewelry.

Filming locations for Life Is Beautiful: Roberto Benigni's 1997 film, which won three Academy Awards including Best Foreign Language Film, was largely shot in Arezzo. The Piazza Grande serves as the film's central square, and Via Vittorio Veneto was used as the set for the main character's bookshop. Guided film-location tours retrace these sites.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries
Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

visits.text: If the pump hall is open, the Museo della Bonifica in Argenta is a gem of industrial archaeology: six cast-iron pumps in an Art Nouveau setting, canals and expansion basins explained through models. The Saiarino pumping station is still active. Check opening hours before coming (renovation underway).

Designated a Ramsar site since 1972, the Oasi di Campotto spans 1,600 hectares of freshwater wetlands. It's the 6th station of the Parco del Delta del Po. The Museo delle Valli, at Casino di Campotto, serves as a documentation center and starting point for visits.

activities.text: From the Vallesanta observation tower, reed beds and water lilies stretch as far as the eye can see. Access to Vallesanta is free. However, Campotto and the Bosco del Traversante can only be visited with a guide.
Rent a bike at the Ecomuseo to ride along the embankments. The flat landscape, rectilinear canals, and silence of the reclaimed plain create an almost unreal atmosphere. Allow 1 hour for the loop.

days_plan.itin_title: From Ferrara to the Delta in 5 Days: Delizie, Ravenna, and Bertinoro

visits.text: Gesualdo holds Renaissance music's darkest story in a single village. Carlo Gesualdo, Prince of Venosa, born 1566, composer of avant-garde madrigals whose harmonic chromaticism anticipates Wagner and Schoenberg. On the night of October 16-17, 1590, he surprises his wife Maria d'Avalos with her lover the Duke of Andria in his Neapolitan palace: he has them massacred by his men. He takes refuge in this family castle where he lives as a recluse until his death in 1613, at 47, during a penitential flagellation session. The castle is partially open to visitors; the village huddles around it. Guaranteed emotion for music lovers.

Frigento, 10 km from Gesualdo, perched at 911 m on the Ufita valley ridge. Monumental Roman cisterns from the 1st century AD, seven vaulted rooms carved into rock to store water for the entire Hirpinian city, still functional today—visitable by reservation through the town hall. But the real reason to climb is the panorama: on clear days, 360° views over the Ufita valley, Vulture, Matese Apennines, to the Tyrrhenian Sea. Sunset from Piazza Municipio is cinematic.

Ariano Irpino, 'city of art,' was built on the ridge separating Campania from Puglia. Its history pivots in 1140, when Roger II promulgated the Assizes of Ariano here—one of the first written law codes of the Norman Kingdom of Sicily, predating the Napoleonic Code by several centuries. The same year, Roger struck the ducat there. The Norman castle dominates the city, the cathedral (11th-12th centuries, heavily damaged by earthquakes and rebuilt) houses a 12th-century wooden crucifix. The historic center is extensive, allow 2 hours to loop through on foot.

The Museo della Ceramica d'Ariano exhibits 900 years of local production—Ariano is one of three great majolica centers of the South, with Cerreto Sannita and Vietri. Pieces from the 13th to 20th century: souvenir plates of great families, monastic pharmaceutical vases, apothecary jars with orientalizing decorations. One hour suffices, really. Contemporary ceramics shop at the exit, fair prices, a nice set to bring home.

activities.text: On the road between Avellino and Gesualdo, stop at Sant'Angelo dei Lombardi (35 km), epicenter of the 1980 earthquake. The cathedral, whose Romanesque façade was half-destroyed, was rebuilt without hiding the wounds—collapsed section left as is, headless statues, like a memorial. The Castello Imperiale has been restored. The village itself transformed: relocated populations, rethought urbanism. It's the historical counterpart to Apice Vecchia, but here they chose to rebuild and tell the story, not to leave.

Dinner in Ariano: the absolute specialty is cicatielli with caciocavallo podolico, hand-rolled thumb pasta, melted in a podolic cow cheese cream. Also try: salsiccia di Ariano IGP, fennel and red pepper sausage, grilled over wood fire. For wine, you're still in DOCG territory: a Taurasi from the previous dinner completes the logical chain.

days_plan.itin_title: Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia

visits.text: The acropolis of Civitavecchia, at 627 meters altitude above Arpino, is the original core of the Volscian then Samnite city, dating to the 7th-6th centuries BC. Its mortarless polygonal walls extend approximately 3 km. It contains the only known pre-Roman pointed-arch gate in Europe: an ogival arch cut from cyclopean blocks that existed before this type of arch was theorized by medieval Gothic architects. The 1581 land registry still designated it as Civitas Ciceroniana.

Arpino was the birthplace of three great men of Roman antiquity: Cicero (born January 3, 106 BC), Caius Marius (born 156 BC, seven-time consul), and Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa (born 63 BC, architect of the Pantheon of Agrippa in Rome). Plaques and statues recall these illustrious natives throughout the historic center.

Arpino's historic center features cyclopean walls visible even in the lower town, integrated into the foundations of medieval houses. The lanes of the upper section (Civitavecchia) are partially deserted and preserve an atmosphere of partial abandonment since the 18th century.

activities.text: Each year since 1980, the Certamen Ciceronianum Arpinas brings together high school students from around the world for an international Latin translation competition on texts by Cicero. If you're present in late April, the awards ceremony at the teatro comunale is open to the public.

days_plan.itin_title: Ciociaria Circuit: Abbeys and Medieval Hilltop Villages

places.name: Arqua Petrarca

visits.text: Discover Arquà Petrarca, a beautiful stone village built on a hilltop overlooking the majestic Euganean Hills. This atmospheric settlement is famous as the place where the Herald of the Renaissance, Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), spent his final years contemplating nature and composing poetry.

Visit Petrarch's House, preserved much as it was when the poet lived here in the 14th century. His tomb in the village square marks the final resting place of one of the founders of humanism and the Italian literary tradition.

activities.text: Wander the narrow stone lanes, enjoying the views that inspired Petrarch's contemplative verse. The village's unspoiled medieval character and poetic associations make it one of the most atmospheric destinations in the Euganean Hills.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

map_keywords: Oratorio della Santissima Trinità Arquà Petrarca

places.name: Arsoli

visits.text: Castello Massimo di Arsoli — A medieval fortress with origins tracing back to the 11th century, transformed into a noble residence in the 16th-17th centuries by the Massimo family, one of Rome's most ancient patrician houses, who claim descent from Fabius Maximus. The castle retains terraced gardens with centuries-old trees and a Renaissance loggia overlooking the Aniene valley. Arsoli sits at 473 m altitude on the eastern foothills of the Monti Simbruini.

Centro storico di Arsoli — A medieval village with cobbled lanes, the Chiesa di Santa Croce, and vestiges of fortifications. The village occupies a strategic position on the ancient Via Valeria, the Roman road linking Rome to the Adriatic via the Abruzzo.

activities.text: Hiking in the Monti Simbruini — The Parco Naturale Regionale dei Monti Simbruini is Lazio's largest natural park, covering 30,000 hectares of forests, high-altitude pastures, and springs. The Aniene River rises in this massif. Marked trails depart from Arsoli toward the wooded plateaus.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Villages Around Rome and the Castelli Romani

map_keywords: Parco Naturale Regionale dei Monti Simbruini

visits.text: The Villa Medici 'La Ferdinanda,' built in just four years from 1596 to 1600 by Bernardo Buontalenti for Grand Duke Ferdinand I de' Medici, is the last great Medici villa and the masterwork of Buontalenti's old age—too old to travel, he directed the works from his house on Via Maggio in Florence by correspondence. Its nickname, 'Villa of the Hundred Chimneys,' comes from Ferdinand I's desire to equip each room with its own hearth for winter hunting seasons: the chimneys, all different, bristle from the roof like a crown. The interiors are frescoed by Domenico Cresti (Il Passignano) and Bernardino Poccetti. The villa has been a UNESCO site since 2013.

The Archaeological Museum of Artimino 'Francesco Nicosia,' reinstalled since 2011 in the former grand-ducal stables of the village, displays Etruscan finds from the region: tumuli of Montefortini and Boschetti at Comeana (7th century BC, Orientalizing period), necropolis of Prato Rosello in the Artimino hills, and a 4th-century BC Etruscan red-figure krater with its perfectly preserved bronze symposium set. The Pietramarina archaeological area completes the Carmignano Archaeological Park.

The Pieve di San Leonardo ad Artimino, at the village gates, is one of the most significant examples of Romano-Lombard architecture in Tuscany. Its foundation is attributed to Countess Matilda of Canossa. The sober, compact building contrasts with the Medici Villa facing it.

activities.text: Tasting of Carmignano DOCG in a cellar in the Artimino hills. This red wine produced exclusively in the municipality of Carmignano is one of Italy's oldest appellation wines: Cosimo III de' Medici officially delimited its production zone in 1716. The dominant grape is Sangiovese, often blended with Cabernet Franc or Cabernet Sauvignon introduced to the region as early as the 17th century.

days_plan.itin_title: The Finest Stops Around Florence in 7 days

places.name: Asciano

visits.text: Palazzo Corboli Museum: Housed in a 12th-century palace that belonged to the noble Bandinelli family, this museum unfolds over three floors a collection of sacred art and archaeology. The archaeological section gathers Etruscan and Roman remains from the territory, including Ambrogio Lorenzetti's Badia a Rofeno triptych and the remarkable 14th-century Wheel of Barlaam.

Torre della Mencia and Piazza del Grano: Standing 25 meters high, this medieval tower dominates Asciano's oldest square, once Siena's granary. The Fontana della Mengia at the tower's base, with its stone and bronze Gorgon head, is accompanied by a legend: whoever drinks from this fountain always returns to Asciano.

Abbey of Monte Oliveto Maggiore: Founded in 1313 by Bernardo Tolomei, a Sienese nobleman renouncing his fortune for a hermit's life, this red brick Benedictine abbey emerges from the woods of the Crete Senesi. Its Great Cloister is entirely decorated with frescoes by Luca Signorelli (late 15th century) and Il Sodoma (early 16th century) on the life of Saint Benedict—one of the masterpieces of Italian Renaissance painting. The monks still chant Gregorian vespers.

activities.text: Hiking in the Crete Senesi Park: The Crete Senesi Life Park covers the Asciano territory with marked, not-difficult trails through the clay hills. Trail No. 2, starting from Asciano, offers the widest views of the biancane—these characteristic whitish clay formations—and rejoins the historic center to finish at the Corboli Museum.
Palio dei Ciuchi: Every Sunday in September, Asciano's seven districts compete through the village streets—on donkeyback rather than horseback, a popular wink at Siena's Palio.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Siena Province

map_keywords: Abbazia di Monte Oliveto Maggiore Asciano

visits.text: En route, stop at Fermo, an hour from Sarnano. The city dominates a 320-meter hill with views to the Adriatic. On Piazza del Popolo, framed by arcades, the Palazzo dei Priori (13th century) houses the civic picture gallery: Adoration of the Shepherds by Rubens (1608, painted for the Oratorians of Fermo), paintings by Lotto, Vivarini. But Fermo's highlight is beneath the city: Roman cisterns from the 1st century AD, 30 vaulted underground chambers across 2,000 m². Still partly functional, they fed the imperial aqueduct.

Detour via Acquaviva Picena, 25 minutes southeast of Fermo. Probably one of the best-preserved rocche in the Marche—the 15th-century fortress dominating the village was designed by Baccio Pontelli (him again) for the Acquaviva family. Polygonal keep, casemates, rampart walkway. The village is also known for pagliarola, traditional wheat-straw wickerwork braided by local women for centuries.

Full day in Ascoli; best to start with Piazza del Popolo in morning light. The Palazzo dei Capitani del Popolo, begun in the 13th century, was the seat of the captains who governed the free medieval commune. Arcaded interior courtyard. Beside it, the basilica of San Francesco, Gothic begun in 1258 on the saint's orders during his visit to Ascoli, completed in the 15th-16th centuries. Travertine portal sculpted with twisted columns.

Piazza Arringo, the city's oldest square, two steps away. More austere than del Popolo but more monumental: Cathedral of Sant'Emidio (facade designed by Cola dell'Amatrice in the 16th century, crypt with the patron saint's relics), octagonal 12th-century baptistery, Palazzo dell'Arengo (historic town hall, housing the Pinacoteca Civica). The picture gallery displays works by Crivelli, Titian, Van Dyck, plus a 13th-century embroidered cope.

Forte Malatesta, on the banks of the Castellano. Built in the 15th century for Galeotto Malatesta, transformed into a prison from the 16th to 20th centuries. Now a medieval archaeology museum and exhibition venue. Plunging view over the city from the ramparts. Just beside, the Ponte di Cecco, medieval bridge spanning the torrent—legend attributes its construction to the demon, defeated by Cecco d'Ascoli, scholar and heretic burned in Florence in 1327.

The Roman theater at the foot of Colle dell'Annunziata, behind the cathedral: built in the last decades of the 1st century BC, with restorations in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, 95 meters in diameter, partly restored. More modest than those of Fiesole or Verona but well preserved. Beside it, the Annunziata grottoes, possible remains of a 1st-century AD pagan temple.

activities.text: Arrive in Ascoli Piceno mid-afternoon. First visual shock on Piazza del Popolo: paved and bordered by palaces entirely in local travertine, which turns golden in evening light. Aperitivo at Caffè Meletti, opened in 1907 under a neoclassical facade with original Art Nouveau interior restored in 1988. Order the Anisetta Meletti, green anise liqueur invented by Silvio Meletti—created right here.

Evening stroll through the historic center: lighting enhances the travertine, and the local passeggiata animates the square. Ascoli bears the nickname 'city of 100 towers': about fifty remain, some incorporated into houses.

Lunch on olive all'ascolana: large Tenera Ascolana DOP green olives, hand-pitted, stuffed with mixed meats (pork, veal, sometimes chicken) then breaded and fried. Invented in Ascoli in the 19th century. The 180 Gradi shop on Piazza del Popolo serves them in takeaway cones. To sit down: Migliori on Piazza Arringo, or the friggitoria Siamo Fritti near the cathedral.

If you're here the first Sunday in August, don't miss the Quintana: one of Italy's finest historical reenactments, horseback jousts between the city's six sestieri (neighborhoods) in Renaissance costumes. More than 1,500 costumed participants, procession through the streets in the afternoon, ring race in the evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Abruzzo in 8 Days: From Rimini to Pescara, Hills to Wild Nature
Marche & Abruzzo in 8 Days: From Rimini to Pescara, Hills to Wild Nature

places.name: Asiago

visits.text: Sacrario Militare di Asiago - This funerary monument built in 1938 preserves the remains of 54,286 Italian and Austro-Hungarian soldiers who fell on the Asiago Plateau during World War I. The Plateau was one of the war's deadliest theaters: the battles of the Strafexpedition (Austrian offensive of June 1916) and the Italian counter-offensives of 1917-1918 killed tens of thousands for territorial gains of a few hundred meters. The monumental ossuary, with its crypt and galleries, conveys the scale of these battles in what is today a peaceful mountain landscape.

Museo della Grande Guerra di Canove - Inaugurated in 1974, this museum in Canove di Roana presents uniforms, weapons, tactical maps and photographic documents tracing the Plateau's battles from 1915 to 1918. The collections include objects recovered from surrounding battle sites and written testimonies from soldiers on both sides. The museum is one of the most rigorous on the conflict in Veneto.

activities.text: Museo all'Aperto di Monte Zebio - A few kilometers from Asiago, this open-air museum lets you walk through trenches and communication trenches carved into the rock during the Great War. Monte Zebio constituted a strategic Austrian strongpoint between 1916 and 1918. The firing positions, cave shelters and gallery networks are still largely visible. The discovery walk takes about two hours.

Ascent to Forte Verena - This Austro-Hungarian fort, built between 1908 and 1912 at 2,015 meters altitude, was captured by the Italians in 1916 and remained a strategic observation post until the war's end. The climb from Rifugio Verenetta (accessible by car) takes about 1 hour. The summit panorama embraces the entire Plateau, the Venetian plain and, on clear days, the Dolomites. The fort's remains are freely accessible.

Asiago historic center - The town of Asiago was entirely razed during the Great War and rebuilt between 1919 and 1925. Gabriele d'Annunzio called it 'Italy's smallest and brightest city.' Its center, remade in one piece in Liberty and neoclassical style, is exceptional in the mountain landscape. The two main piazzas—Piazza Carli and Piazza Risorgimento—and Corso IV Novembre form a cohesive urban ensemble rare in the alpine zone.

days_plan.itin_title: Vicenza Circuit: Palladian Villas and the Venetian Countryside

map_keywords: Museo Grande Guerra Canove di Roana

visits.text: The Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi is the opposite of the hippie saint you'd imagine: a colossal two-level edifice, begun two years after his death in 1226. But descending into the lower basilica then into the crypt, you rediscover the real Francis—the saint's tomb, miraculously rediscovered in 1818 after 600 years hidden (it had been walled up to prevent pillaging), surrounded by the sepulchers of his four closest companions: Brother Leo, Brother Angelo, Brother Masseo, Brother Rufino. Dark atmosphere, vaulted, silent. Upstairs, Giotto's cycle on Francis's life—foundational frescoes of Western painting. And Death, the Last Judgment, Hell, by the same masters. UNESCO 2000.

Assisi's more troubling side: the Basilica of Santa Chiara preserves beneath the altar the mummified body of Saint Clare, who died in 1253. Visible in a glass reliquary since 1850, skin blackened like parchment, original clothing in tatters. Clare was the first woman to found a Franciscan order (the Poor Clares) and lived 42 years cloistered at San Damiano without ever leaving. The basilica also preserves the painted crucifix before which Francis heard Christ's voice in 1205—starting point of his conversion. All this in a pink-white Subasio limestone church, archetype of Italian Gothic.

The Eremo delle Carceri, 4 km above Assisi in the Monte Subasio forest, is the hermitage where Francis came to pray alone with his companions. Cave where he slept on stone, centuries-old oak under which he preached to the birds according to legend (still alive, 800 years old), small chapel clinging to a rock fissure above a stream. Still a Franciscan site, friars in brown habits, silence imposed. Car access via narrow road or one-hour walk from Assisi. Mystical atmosphere without staging.

San Damiano, 2 km below Assisi, is the other emblematic site of the Francis-Clare pair. This is where Francis heard Christ tell him "Go, repair my house," an order he took literally by rebuilding the abandoned church. This is where Clare lived cloistered for 42 years. This is where she died. This is where a copy of the famous crucifix that spoke to Francis is kept. The convent preserves its 13th-century appearance—Clare's cell, garden, tiny cloister. More moving than the basilica above, because rawer.

activities.text: Dinner at La Fortezza, in upper Assisi near Rocca Maggiore. Traditional Umbrian cuisine: braised wild boar, Castelluccio lentils (which we'll see tomorrow), truffle tagliatelle, lamb. Reasonable prices (30-40 euro menu), terrace with view.

Evening walk through Assisi's deserted alleys after 8 PM, when pilgrims have returned to their hotels. The town regains its medieval atmosphere, pink stone turning orange under streetlights. Perfect route from Piazza del Comune down to the Basilica of Saint Francis.

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Umbria: 8 days Among Mummies, Mystics & Caves

places.name: Asti

visits.text: Admire the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta in Piazza Risorgimento, an imposing 15th-century Gothic building that represents one of Asti's most important monuments. The three-nave interior, decorated in gold and blue colors, contrasts magnificently with the exterior of characteristic Piedmontese red brick.

Explore the medieval towers that dot the historic center, testimony to Asti's glorious past when it was a powerful city-state. Torre Troyana, Torre Comentina, and Torre Rossa are the most famous and offer evocative glimpses among the historic palaces of the center.

Visit the Palazzo Comunale in Piazza Risorgimento, which houses precious ancient frescoes from the Church of San Domenico, including a moving 14th-century Pietà and a panel depicting the Virgin and Child by Macrino d'Alba from 1501.

activities.text: Participate in a tasting of the wines that have made Asti famous worldwide: Asti Spumante DOCG and Barbera d'Asti. The area's wineries offer food and wine experiences that pair great wines with traditional Piedmontese cuisine.

If you're here in September, don't miss the Palio di Asti, one of Italy's oldest horse races held in central Piazza Alfieri. The event is preceded by a magnificent historical parade with over 1,200 participants in medieval costumes.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont Wine & Truffle Road Trip: Turin, Alba & Barolo in 6 Days

map_keywords: Cattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta Asti

visits.text: Atina, holder of the Touring Club's Bandiera Arancione, was founded according to legend by the god Saturn—as were Anagni, Alatri, Arpino, and Ferentino. Cited by Virgil in the Aeneid among the cities allied with Turnus, it was first Volscian then Samnite (Pentri tribe) before being conquered by Rome during the Samnite Wars. Cicero wrote of it: "Atina, mother of many illustrious men, to such an extent that no city of Italy can be said to be richer."

Atina's polygonal walls form a total circuit of over 8,000 meters distributed in two distinct systems: the outer enclosure running along the heights of Monte Morrone, and the inner enclosure defending the hill of Santo Stefano. These works date to the 4th-3rd centuries BC and constitute one of the longest pre-Roman fortification perimeters in southern Lazio.

The Palazzo Cantelmo (ducal palace), built after the 1349 earthquake, features a two-tower facade and Gothic mullioned windows. It illustrates the architectural style of the Angevin lords who governed the region after the destruction caused by the earthquake.

The Giuseppe Visocchi Municipal Archaeological Museum assembles discoveries made on Atina's territory since the 19th century: a Roman funerary lion, elements of a pre-Roman necropolis discovered in 2002, a Roman mosaic uncovered in 1946, and scale models of war machines used by Roman and Samnite armies. Atina has been an episcopal seat since 800, attested by a diploma of Charlemagne.

activities.text: Follow the trail along the best-preserved sections of Atina's polygonal enclosure: blocks of local limestone, some exceeding two cubic meters in volume, interlock without mortar to heights reaching 4 to 5 meters in places. The trail requires no special equipment and offers views over the Comino Valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Ciociaria Circuit: Abbeys and Medieval Hilltop Villages

visits.text: The Parco Archeologico di Aeclanum in Mirabella Eclano comprises 18 hectares of Roman city spread along the Via Appia—the 'Regina Viarum' inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024, passing right through here. Aeclanum was burned by Sulla in 89 BC, then rebuilt as a Roman municipium; the circular macellum (market), baths, domus, and the 5th-century early Christian basilica built atop a domus are accessible on foot along three sections of paved road. In February 2025, ground-penetrating radar located the forum, still buried. Mirabella Eclano is among the ten finalists for the title of Italian Capital of Culture 2028—results announced late March 2026.

In the monumental complex of San Francesco (1222) in the center of Mirabella, two museums are truly worth a stop. The Museo Civico del Carro di Paglia displays the woven straw panels composing the Eclano obelisk—25 meters high, hauled by six pairs of oxen during the Grande Tirata in September. Agricultural tradition turned contemporary performance. Next door, the Museo dei Misteri di Cartapesta: 19th-century papier-mâché sculptures depicting Passion scenes, paraded on Good Friday. An unexpected, kitsch, and fascinating visual universe.

Apice Vecchia, on the road between Benevento and Avellino, is a ghost town—abandoned after the 1962 earthquakes then 1980 (the great Irpinia earthquake, 6.9 on the Richter scale, 2,914 deaths). Residents were rehoused in a 'Apice Nuova' built 2 km away. The old village remained as is: gutted houses, abandoned dishes, collapsed chapel. Entry is free, at your own risk, boots recommended. Consider yourself warned: it's striking, especially at nightfall.

At Atripalda, 3 km east of Avellino, visit Abellinum—ancient Avellino, founded by the Hirpini then became a Roman municipium. The site is small but well maintained: remains of the defensive walls in opus reticulatum, domus, atrium with mosaics. In the 4th century, the city was abandoned due to invasions and the population withdrew to the hill of present-day Avellino—hence the gap. One hour suffices. Next door, San Sabino Church preserves a 4th-century crypt with early Christian sarcophagi, open intermittently.

Avellino's center is quickly toured: Piazza della Libertà with the Bellerophon fountain (17th century, water jet spurting from the winged horse's mouth), Conservatorio Cimarosa, Palazzo Caracciolo. The Museo Irpino deserves a real stop: opened since 1933, it exhibits finds from Aeclanum, Abellinum, and especially Daunian funerary stelae from the north. Pinacotheca section with Baroque and contemporary works. Count 1h. Avellino Castle is in ruins, accessible but unspectacular—skip it if time is tight.

The Sanctuary of Montevergine, 25 minutes northeast of Avellino, perched at 1,270 m on Mount Partenio, is one of the great pilgrimage sites of the South. Founded in 1124 by Saint William of Vercelli, it houses a Byzantine icon of the Madonna di Montevergine considered miraculous. The current basilica is a mix of Romanesque + Gothic + 20th-century reconstruction. Curiosity: the Italian homosexual community makes pilgrimages here on February 2—the Madonna became protector of minorities over the centuries, long story.

Taurasi is the undisputed capital of the South's most prestigious Aglianico DOCG. The Marchionale Ducal Castle (12th-16th centuries) houses the Archaeological Museum, displaying 5th-century BC Attic ceramics found in local tombs—proof that wine trade already existed here in Greek times. The historic center is tiny, walkable in 30 minutes: sloping lanes, stone houses, and everywhere posters announcing tastings. Don't drop into cellars without reservation—it's family-run and personalized.

Tufo, 12 km west, is the origin of Greco di Tufo DOCG. The village was built atop sulfur mines exploited from the 19th century until the 1980s, whose sulfurous soils give the Greco grape its distinctive mineral character. Visits to the old Solfara mines possible by reservation through the Pro Loco—galleries, extraction machinery, period documents. The Castello degli Acciardi dominates the village with broad views over the wine hills. Small town, frozen atmosphere, almost melancholic.

Lapio is the third summit of the DOCG triangle: here they produce Fiano d'Avellino, among Italy's most aristocratic whites. The village overlooks the Calore valley at 600 m altitude. Stroll to the Belvedere del Ponte Principe—abandoned iron railway bridge spanning the valley between Lapio and Taurasi, remnant of a disused line. Today it's a spectacular viewpoint over the vineyards, especially at sunset. Mandatory postcard photo.

Montefusco, 15 km northwest of Avellino, was the capital of the ancient Principato Ultra (province) from the 16th to early 19th century. Its former courthouse became a Bourbon prison where Risorgimento patriots were jailed—Carlo Poerio, Sigismondo Castromediano. The Museo Carcerario exhibits graffiti scratched into walls by inmates, irons, straw mattresses. Not cheerful but interesting for understanding the resistance against the Bourbons. Count 45 minutes.

activities.text: Upon arrival in Avellino, aperitivo must be taken with a glass of Greco di Tufo, one of Irpinia's three DOCGs. White grape with golden-yellow skin, planted on sulfurous soils around the village of Tufo: striking minerality, notes of flint. Bars on Corso Vittorio Emanuele serve it by the glass. Compare with a Sannite Falanghina if you've retained yesterday's memory—they're two different worlds.

Dinner in Avellino at one of the Campetto quarter trattorias. Irpinian cuisine relies on black pork from Caserta, chestnuts (the area produces the Montella IGP chestnut), fusilli al ragù bianco, and fagioli quarantini di Volturara beans. For cheese, ask for caciocavallo podolico—ancient breed cow, cave-aged stretched-curd cheese. Carafe of Aglianico recommended.

The Montevergine cable car departs from Mercogliano at 712 m and climbs to 1,270 m in 8 minutes. It's the fastest and most spectacular access to the sanctuary—on clear days, views reaching Mount Vesuvius and the Gulf of Naples. Built in 1956, modernized in the 2000s. Last departure around 5 PM in winter, 6 PM in summer. If you drive up, winding road but without difficulty, parking at the summit.

Quick stop in Mercogliano on the way back for gelato at Locale tipico or coffee at the local roastery. If you have margin, the Antiquarium di Mercogliano exhibits archaeological finds from the area, but only open weekends and by appointment. For evening, return to Avellino, classic dinner, or switch to an agriturismo in the Taurasi vineyards already—you'll save time tomorrow morning.

For tastings, you're spoiled for choice within a 15 km radius: Mastroberardino in Atripalda (the historic house, founded 1878, which saved Campanian Aglianico after the phylloxera epidemic), Feudi di San Gregorio in Sorbo Serpico (contemporary architecture, very successful modern wines), or Quintodecimo in Mirabella Eclano (boutique winery of the Ercolino couple, rare cuvées). Reservation essential everywhere, even Mastroberardino. Three estates in one day is doable, but alternate with a hearty lunch.

If you prefer sleeping among the vines, several agriturismi offer rooms plus table d'hôte at the heart of the DOCG: Borgo San Gregorio, Tenuta Cavalier Pepe, Antico Borgo. You eat what you see through the window—pasta with Irpinian lamb ragù, podolici cheeses, sheep's ricotta, and all the house wines. Sunrise over the vineyards in the morning—that's the big difference from a downtown Avellino hotel.

places.name: Bagni Di Lucca

visits.text: Historic Thermal Center and Terme Bagni di Lucca: Known since Roman times, Bagni di Lucca's hot springs took off in the 11th century thanks to Countess Matilda of Canossa, before becoming in the 19th century one of Europe's most fashionable spa resorts. Elisa Baciocchi, Napoleon's sister and Princess of Lucca, had the Bernabò establishment built here in 1810, where waters emerge naturally at 39.2°C. The thermal complex has welcomed Byron, Shelley, Montale, Henry James, and Puccini. The English called the place "the Switzerland of Tuscany."

Real Casino of Ponte a Serraglio: Inaugurated in 1839, this casino was one of the very first in Europe—some sources credit Bagni di Lucca with inventing roulette around 1837. The Art Nouveau building, restored and reopened in 2009 after years of closure, overlooks the banks of the Lima and constitutes one of the best-preserved testimonies of 19th-century aristocratic tourism.

Ponte delle Catene (Chain Bridge): This iron suspension bridge designed by Lorenzo Nottolini—the same architect who redesigned Lucca's Piazza dell'Anfiteatro—is one of the oldest metal bridges still standing in Italy. It spans the Lima between the hamlets of Ponte a Serraglio and Villa Fiori.

Italy's first Anglican church and English cemetery: The British community established in Bagni di Lucca from the early 19th century built the country's first Anglican church here. The adjoining cemetery holds the graves of English, American, and other nationalities who chose to end their days in this valley.

activities.text: Hiking in Orrido di Botri: A few kilometers north, this canyon carved by the Pelago torrent through the Apennines offers vertical limestone gorges and waterfalls. The ascent follows the riverbed for several kilometers; a protective helmet is recommended. Access is regulated and best done with a local guide.
Thermal treatments: The Bagni Caldi thermal establishments offer pools, natural steam grottos, and treatments using sulfurous waters whose natural temperature approaches 39°C.

places.name: Bagnoregio

visits.text: Drive 1.5 hours east to Bomarzo, 9 miles southeast of Viterbo. Buy your ticket at the gate (€13, open 8:30 AM-7 PM high season, until 5 PM in winter) and enter the Sacro Bosco. Prince Pier Francesco 'Vicino' Orsini commissioned this garden in 1550, the year his wife Giulia Farnese died. He worked on it for thirty years. The architect Pirro Ligorio (who would finish St. Peter's Basilica after Michelangelo) directed the work: sculpt from the tuff boulders of the forest life-size monsters, with no coherent overall plan, no symmetry, no clear narrative thread. It's deliberate. On the entrance lintel, Orsini had engraved: 'Voi che pel mondo gite errando' - you who wander through the world.

Follow the path in whatever order you like, the park extends over 7 acres with no required circuit. First encounter: the Bocca dell'Orco, gaping ogre mouth 13 feet high that you enter like a salon. Inside, a stone table, and the inscription 'Ogni pensiero vola' - every thought flies away. Further on, Hercules tearing Cacus apart upside down, Hannibal's elephant crushing a Roman legionnaire in its trunk, the giant tortoise carrying Fame on its shell, the dragon attacked by three lions, and the Casa Pendente, a house deliberately built leaning at 8 degrees that gives you seasickness after two minutes inside. Dalí discovered the park in 1948 when it was abandoned to brambles, tried in vain to buy it, made a short film about it in 1949.

Get back on the road heading north, 30 miles, 1 hour. Pass Viterbo without stopping (you'd come back for its own treasures on another trip) and arrive in Bagnoregio in late afternoon. Drop your bags in the upper village center (€60-110), the belvedere over Civita is 500 yards away. Look from up there first: the Etruscan borgo floats on its tuff hill at 1,150 feet, isolated by erosion that has collapsed the entire plateau around it since the 1695 earthquake. It's called la città che muore - the dying city. The edge closes in by 3 feet per decade.

activities.text: Dine in Bagnoregio at Antica Trattoria Da Pippo, Via Garibaldi, twenty covers in a vaulted cellar. Tuscia cuisine: umbrichelli homemade pasta with spicy alla viterbese sauce, pignattaccia (beef stew with wine from Lake Bolsena), agnello scottadito grilled. Try the wine Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, named according to legend in the 12th century by a German servant who marked the best inns on the road to Rome.

Before sleeping, return to the belvedere. At night, Civita lights up alone on its pinnacle, suspended in the darkness above the invisible valley - eleven permanent residents, a few lit windows. The pedestrian bridge a half-mile long that connects it to the world is barely visible, a fragile luminous curve. Free spectacle, never the same depending on the clouds. Allow twenty minutes in peace.

visits.text: This, by tradition, is where the Ottoman fleet landed in 1480 before laying siege to Otranto: the Baia dei Turchi has carried the name ever since. The sand is white and fine, the pine wood dense, and the site belongs to the protected Laghi Alimini oasis. The FAI has listed it among the places it works to safeguard.

Warm resin and needles underfoot: you cross the pine wood that backs the Baia dei Turchi before the sea comes into view, which is exactly what makes the arrival land so well. The dunes carry sea lilies, junipers and broom, on a site of Community importance. Stay on the marked paths.

activities.text: Leave the car before the pine wood and finish on foot along a dirt path, five to ten minutes. No road runs down to the sand. Bring water and something for shade: services are minimal and the bay heats up in the afternoon.

visits.text: The fortress of Bardi sits on a spur of red jasper - a rare metamorphic rock that gives the castle its reddish tint visible from kilometers away. The Landi made it their main residence starting in 1257 and transformed it through four centuries of renovations into a princely residence. In 1551, Emperor Charles V granted them the right to mint coins - a privilege reserved for sovereigns. The archaeological museum inside displays Bronze Age artifacts (1600-1200 BC) discovered in the valley.

The Val Ceno descends from the Apennine ridges to the Po plain in a succession of perched villages, chestnut forests, and torrents. This is Landi and Farnese country, two dynasties that disputed these valleys for three centuries. The road along the Ceno from Bardi to Compiano is among the most beautiful in the Parmesan Apennines.

activities.text: Hike in Val Ceno from Bardi toward the ridge villages - Braia, Metti, Casanova. Marked trails, chestnut trees, views across both Apennine slopes. Allow 3 hours for an accessible round trip.

Visit Bardi's local market if you're there on a Tuesday - valley products: cheeses, cured meats, dried mushrooms, honey. It's the most direct way to understand the mountain economy of the Parmesan Apennines.

visits.text: Duomo di San Cristoforo: Perched at the village's highest point (410 m), this Romanesque cathedral was built in stages from the 11th to 16th centuries in blocks of alberese, a local gray-cream limestone. Its 13th-century marble pulpit, the work of Guido Bigarelli, is supported by four columns, two resting on recumbent lions. Inside: a ciborium of the Holy Oils by Andrea della Robbia, a 14th-century Madonna del Molino, and a medieval polychrome wooden statue of San Cristoforo. From the churchyard, views extend over the entire historic center and, on clear days, to the Apuan Alps.

Palazzo Pretorio and Museo Civico del Territorio: Residence of Florentine commissioners from 1341 to 1859—when Barga chose to submit to Florence rather than Lucca, obtaining exemption from numerous taxes. The palace houses the municipal museum with archaeological collections (prehistory, Ligurians, Romans) and artworks from the Middle Ages and Renaissance. The old medieval prisons are still visitable.

Loggia dei Mercanti and Piazza Salvo Salvi: This loggia with slender columns was built in 1546 on orders from Cosimo I de' Medici to shelter Barga's market, whose main products were silk and salt. The stone lion (Marzocco) on the façade symbolizes Florence's political guardianship. Palazzo Pancrazi, seat of the town hall, displays a diamond-bossed façade characteristic of 16th-century Florentine architecture.

Teatro dei Differenti: Inaugurated in 1689 and rebuilt in 1795, this Italian-style theater is one of the best preserved in Tuscany. It was here that Giovanni Pascoli delivered on November 26, 1911, his famous speech La grande proletaria si è mossa in favor of the Italo-Turkish War in Libya.

Casa Museo Giovanni Pascoli in Castelvecchio (4 km from Barga): Giovanni Pascoli, major poet of Italian Symbolism, purchased this 18th-century country house in 1895 and lived here with his sister Mariù until his death in 1912. He composed here his most celebrated collections, including Myricae and Canti di Castelvecchio, directly inspired by the surrounding landscapes. The museum preserves books, manuscripts, and everyday objects in the state the family left them. Pascoli is buried in the garden chapel, beneath cypresses and wisteria.

Medieval Historic Center of Barga: Classified among "Borghi più belli d'Italia" and labeled Cittaslow (slow cities network for quality of life), Barga has kept its 12th–14th century communal urban fabric almost intact. Enter through Porta Reale—so renamed after Grand Duke Leopold of Lorraine's visit—and climb the cobbled alleys to the Duomo. The presence of a significant Scottish community, heirs of hundreds of Barghigiani who left to settle in Glasgow between the 19th and 20th centuries as ice cream vendors and fish and chips shop managers, has earned Barga the nickname "most Scottish town in Italy."

activities.text: Barga Jazz Festival (August): Since 1986, this internationally renowned jazz festival has animated the squares and alleys of the medieval historic center each summer. Musicians from around the world perform in this medieval setting for a week in August.
Via dei Poeti and Castelvecchio surroundings: Marked trail linking the main sites associated with Pascoli in the countryside around Castelvecchio, with views of the Apuan Alps.

visits.text: Bari Vecchia takes patience: a labyrinth of tight alleys where laundry hangs across balconies and cats follow you to the next piazza. Four kilometers of packed lanes on a spur between two harbors. Look for Via Arco Basso, nicknamed "orecchiette street": the nonnas make the little ear-shaped pasta on trestles outside their doors, and yes, they sell them. Budget two hours to walk through without rushing, more if you get caught by a terrace. Avoid the 1-4pm slot: everything closes and the city naps.

The Basilica of San Nicola doesn't look like much from outside—massive facade, almost austere—and that's for the best: the shock waits inside. Consecrated in 1197 to house the relics of Saint Nicholas, stolen from Myra (present-day Turkey) in 1087 by Barese sailors, it remains a pilgrimage site for Orthodox Christians worldwide. Go down to the crypt: that's where the saint rests, beneath a slab that weeps the "manna," an oily liquid the faithful collect once a year. Free entry, but covered shoulders required.

Shorter lines, fewer crowds, more calm: the Cathedral of San Sabino plays in a different league than its neighbor San Nicola. Rebuilt in the late 12th century in pure Apulian Romanesque style, it houses a Byzantine icon of the Virgin Odigitria that the Barese have venerated since the Middle Ages. Ask to see the Trullo, a small annexed dome too often overlooked. The crypt preserves mosaic fragments from the 6th century. Twenty minutes suffice if you're pressed, a good half hour if you take your time.

Founded by the Normans in 1131, rebuilt by Frederick II in 1233, Bari's Swabian Castle shows what makes Puglia unique: every empire passed through here, and each stacked its layer. Only part is visitable (a good chunk still serves as administrative offices), but the inner courtyard and the gallery of casts—plaster copies of the finest Romanesque portals in Puglia—are worth the 6-euro entry. Nice harbor view from the ramparts. Closed Wednesdays.

Built under Mussolini in the 1920s, long, wide, monumental: the Nazario Sauro promenade borders the sea for nearly five kilometers with Art Deco palazzi on one side and the Adriatic on the other. This is where the Barese come to run, double-park to chat, and watch the sunset. At the Margherita, a former theater built on stilts above the water, grab gelato at Gentile: the specialty is pasta reale, made with almonds.

Return toward Bari to close the loop, about 1 hour by SS170 then SS16. The route crosses the lower Alta Murgia plateau before descending toward the Adriatic coast. If you have time before the flight, a detour through Ruvo di Puglia and its Jatta Archaeological Museum is worth it for the collection of 4th-century BC Apulian ceramics—one of Italy's finest.

Final pass through Bari before the airport, located in Palese, 12 km northwest of downtown. If the flight is late afternoon, save time for a farewell lunch and a last focaccia. The rental agency is on the terminal ground floor: quick return, budget 15 minutes. Allow 2 hours before a Schengen flight, 2.5 hours for the rest.

activities.text: Try focaccia barese at Panificio Fiore in the historic center. Protected recipe: potato-based dough, cherry tomatoes poked into the dough, oregano, olive oil. Sold by weight, to be eaten in the street as tradition demands.

Breakfast Bari-style at Molo San Nicola, in the corner known in dialect as N' dèrr'a la lanze ("at the feet of the boats"). Fishermen have unloaded their red and blue gozzi since dawn and sell the catch raw from trestles: octopus still twisted, sea urchins opened with a knife, mussels, oysters at one euro each on Sundays. Local tradition calls for washing it all down with an ice-cold Peroni at Bar El Chiringuito, open since 1950. Strange breakfast? The Barese have done it for three generations.

Farewell lunch on the return route: Trattoria Antica Bari, in Palombaio (highway exit, 15 km before the airport), serves orecchiette with broccoli rabe and fave e cicoria like they made fifty years ago. Simple cooking, gentle prices, not a word of English. That's the real Puglia cuisine.
If the flight is late, final swim at San Giorgio, public beach between Bari and the airport. Clear water, sand, easy access. Free parking. Showers on site, convenient before returning the car.

visits.text: First morning stop: the Colossus of Barletta, planted in front of the Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre. This 5.11-meter bronze statue represents a late Roman emperor—probably Theodosius II or Valentinian I, the debate has lasted for centuries. Dated to the 5th century, it was probably cast in Constantinople. How did it get to Barletta? Several hypotheses: a Venetian shipwreck in 1204 returning from the sack of Constantinople, or a transfer ordered by Frederick II from Ravenna in 1231. In 1309, the local Dominicans melted down its legs and arms to make bells: what you see today is a restoration from 1491. It's the largest ancient bronze statue to survive intact. Locals call it Eraclio, or Aré in dialect.

500 meters from the Colossus, Barletta's Castello Svevo: the most imposing Norman-Swabian castle on the coast. Founded by the Normans in the 11th century, profoundly remodeled by Frederick II in 1234, then fortified by Charles V in the 16th century with its four massive diamond-pointed bastions. The castle today houses the municipal library and an interesting lapidary museum. Fine harbor views from the ramparts. Budget an hour, more if you love medieval archaeology.

January 15, 1503, during a banquet in this cantina in the historic center: the French knight Charles de la Motte, a prisoner of war, calls the Italians cowards after drinking too much Rosso Barletta. The insult doesn't pass. The Italians issue a challenge: 13 knights against 13 knights. The tournament takes place on February 13, 1503 on the plain between Corato and Andria. The Italians, led by Ettore Fieramosca, win. The cantina is now a small museum with weapons, costumes, and reenactments. Every February 13, Barletta replays the scene in period costume.

Adjacent to the Colossus, the Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre dates from the 12th century. Built by the canons of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem as a stop for departing crusaders, it blends Romanesque, French Gothic, and Oriental influences brought back from the Holy Land. Inside, a 13th-century Byzantine Christ and medieval frescoes being restored.

activities.text: Quick lunch in Barletta: focaccia break at Panificio Cosma on the Corso, or a more substantial pranzo at Antica Cucina 1983, near the castle. The dish to try: cavatelli con cime di rapa, local pasta with wild turnip greens.

visits.text: The castle of Grinzane Cavour has overlooked the vineyards since the 11th century. Camillo Cavour, future first Prime Minister of unified Italy, lived here and conducted viticultural experiments in the 1830s-1840s - he would help spread Barolo style across Europe through his diplomatic connections. Today the Enoteca Regionale holds 500 references of Piedmontese wines, and the Museum of the Langhe traces the region's agricultural history. In October, the world's largest white truffle auction is held here: 500-gram specimens can sell for €100,000.

La Morra is the Côte de Beaune village of the Langhe - its Barolos are the most elegant, most floral, most approachable young. The panorama from the central square covers 180° of vineyards: you can make out Barolo village to the south, Castiglione Falletto to the east, the Alps on clear days to the north. But the real reason for stopping is the Cappella del Barolo, 2 km from the village in the middle of the vines: a 17th-century chapel painted inside and out by Sol LeWitt and David Tremlett in 1999 - abstract geometry, primary colors, surrounded by nebbiolo. It makes no sense and it's perfect.

The WiMu - Wine Museum of Barolo - occupies the village's medieval castle across seven levels. Thematic journey through wine, territory, Piedmontese culture, with contemporary installations designed by François Confino. Less didactic than Beaune's Cité des Climats, more poetic, occasionally bewildering. The castle cellar offers a final tasting at the tour's summit - with views over the vines through arrow slits. Allow 1.5 hours.

The castle of Serralunga d'Alba is one of the Langhe's most photographed silhouettes - 14th-century cylindrical tower, perfect outline against the vines. It's been owned by the same family since around 1340, making it one of Piedmont's best-preserved castelli. Barolos from Serralunga are the appellation's most structured, most tannic - they need 10 to 15 years in the cellar to truly open up. Guided castle tours on weekends, reservation recommended.

Fontanafredda is the opposite end of the spectrum: a vast 100-hectare estate at the foot of Serralunga, founded by King Vittorio Emanuele II in the 19th century as a gift to his mistress, Rosa Vercellana, nicknamed 'la bella Rosin'. The village of workers' houses, red brick cellars, gardens - everything has the scale of a royal estate. Now owned by the Farinetti group (founder of Eataly), it's one of the Langhe's most visitor-friendly cellars: walk-in tours, on-site restaurant.

Monforte d'Alba: hilltop village at 480 meters, stepped lanes, 360° panorama over the Langhe. The Horszowski Theatre is a curiosity - open-air stage carved into the rock, 800 seats, named for pianist Mieczysław Horszowski who performed there at age 99 in 1992. The village is quiet outside festival season, and that's perfectly fine.

activities.text: Tasting at Marchesi di Barolo in Barolo village: this is the house where the appellation took shape. In the 1840s, Marchesa Juliette Colbert Falletti asked French oenologist Louis Oudart to vinify her nebbiolo dry, reducing residual sugar - it was revolutionary for the time. The house, now owned by the Abbona family, remains the appellation's historical reference. Cellar tour and tasting, reservation recommended.

Slow drive through Barolo's 11 communes: La Morra, Barolo, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba, Monforte, Novello, Verduno, Diano d'Alba, Grinzane Cavour, Cherasco, Roddi. Each commune has its own soil, exposure, style: wines from La Morra and Barolo are rounder, those from Serralunga and Monforte more austere and longer-aging. The difference can be read in the geology: Tortonian calcareous marls to the west, more compact Helvetian soils to the east.

Comparative tasting: Barolo La Morra vs Barolo Serralunga, same vintage - it's the most revealing exercise you can do in the Langhe. Same grape, same appellation, same year - and wines that seem to come from different countries. At Enoteca Massimo Camia in La Morra or at the Hotel Barolo bar, request this comparison: most local sommeliers know how to construct it. Expect €20-30 for both glasses.

Lunch at Trattoria della Posta in Monforte d'Alba: historic table, no-frills setting, service by the same family for three generations. Agnolotti del plin mandatory - these tiny hand-pinched ravioli, filled with braised veal and spinach, are eaten here 'al sugo di arrosto' (in roast juices), not with cream. The portion is reasonable, order two. Wine list exclusively local, Barolo by the glass at producer prices.

Piedmont - 3 days in Nebbiolo country, from Torino to Barolo
