visits.text: Su Nuraxi is Sardinia's most complete nuragic complex, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. Built from the 17th century BC using basalt blocks, its central tower originally stood 61 feet high. Archaeologist Giovanni Lilliu excavated it between 1950 and 1957 from beneath an earth mound.

The nuragic village surrounding the tower contains over 50 circular huts inhabited from the 13th to 6th centuries BC. The only entrance still accessible is a doorway about 23 feet high, making the fortress virtually impregnable.
Casa Zapata, a 16th-century Aragonese manor built directly atop a second nuraghe, now houses a museum where the ancient remains are visible through glass floors from the very rooms above.

activities.text: Excursion to the Giara di Gesturi, a basalt plateau at 1,640 feet covered with cork oaks and seasonal ponds—one of the last refuges of Sardinia's wild horse, the cavallino della Giara.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Sardinia Loop: Coastline, Cities & Heartland

visits.text: Su Gorroppu is often called the "Grand Canyon of Europe." The numbers speak: walls up to 400 meters high, width reduced to 4 meters in places, 1.5 km explorable length without technical gear. Carved by the rio Flumineddu through Supramonte limestone. Three difficulty zones: the easy zone (to the first boulders), zone B and zone C requiring harness and rope. The standard hike takes 5 to 6 hours round trip from the S'Abba Arva bridge. Canyon entrance: €5 adult, €3.50 child.

On the road between Dorgali and Baunei, the Genna Silana pass peaks at 1,017 meters and offers one of the island's finest panoramas: Supramonte on one side, Gulf of Orosei on the other. Several picnic areas set up under holm oaks. It's also the alternative starting point for Gorroppu (longer but more panoramic descent). Mandatory photo stop, especially late afternoon when light gilds the limestone.

Baunei, your evening stop, is a large village perched at 480m altitude, in whose municipality starts the legendary Selvaggio Blu trek (5 days on the wild coast), though the official start is at Pedra Longa, near Santa Maria Navarrese. Raw stone architecture, not touristy, pastoral atmosphere. Taste the local porceddu and pane guttiau—pane carasau drizzled with oil and grilled. The center visits in 30 minutes. A few agriturismi welcome in the area, more authentic than seaside hotels.

activities.text: Hike in the Su Gorroppu Gorge: 14 km round trip from the S'Abba Arva bridge, 5 to 6 hours, moderate elevation gain (300m). The trail alternates climbs and descents through maquis, follows the Flumineddu, crosses several cool areas near fountains. At the canyon entrance, walking among blocks polished by water, under vertiginous walls, remains a powerful experience. Good physical preparation necessary. Fresh water at fountains, but count on 2 liters per person anyway. Possibility of 4x4 transfer from Cala Gonone (jeep + guide, €50 per person, saves 1 hour).

For those with dead legs on return, restorative dinner at an agriturismo near Baunei: try Agriturismo Coopgaia or Su Coloru. Fixed menu, €35-45: Sardinian antipasti, homemade pasta primi, grilled meat secondi, traditional dessert. Wine included. Reservation mandatory the day before.

days_plan.itin_title: Sardinia's Wild Interior and Eastern Coast: 6 Days from Olbia to Cagliari

visits.text: Bedonia is an Apennine paradox: a mountain village with a planetarium. The episcopal seminary attached to the Madonna di San Marco sanctuary has housed since the 19th century an ancient library, a natural history museum, a picture gallery, and a planetarium - an improbable cultural ensemble lost in the Val Taro forests. It's also the birthplace of the 'Orsanti,' those itinerant bear trainers who traveled across Europe in the 19th century; the museum dedicated to them in Compiano, 15 km away, pays tribute.

The Madonna di San Marco sanctuary dominates the village from its hilltop. The current building results from four centuries of renovations to a 15th-century oratory. The interior is austere; the interest lies in the seminary's collections - notably the series of woodcuts by artist R. Musa and the local archaeology museum.

The Val Taro from Bedonia is one of the quietest routes in the Parmesan Apennines - beech forests, trout streams, gray stone villages. The Borgotaro IGP Porcino Mushroom Route passes through here: the boletes from this area have obtained protected geographical indication and are harvested from July to November.

activities.text: Evening at Bedonia seminary's planetarium - far from any light pollution, the Apennine sky offers one of Emilia's best starry vaults. Sessions organized according to schedule, best to book ahead.
Trout fishing in Val Taro - rich streams, cold and transparent water. Permits available at Bedonia town hall or certain village shops. Peaceful activity that lets you explore the wooded banks.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand tour of the four provinces in 5 days

visits.text: Explore the steep lanes and cobbled stairways of Bellagio's old town—'Bellus Loci' (beautiful place) to the Romans, and already a summer residence of Pliny the Younger who loved fishing here. The village occupies the tip of the Lariana promontory, at the exact point where the lake's two southern arms meet in an inverted Y. From Piazza della Chiesa, the 12th-century basilica church of San Giacomo, dedicated to Bellagio's patron saint, displays a characteristic bell tower and triumphal arch. From the Punta Spartivento viewpoint, the panorama embraces both lake branches and the Alps simultaneously.

Visit the gardens of Villa Melzi d'Eril, commissioned in 1808 by Francesco Melzi d'Eril, Duke of Lodi and vice-president of the Italian Republic under Napoleon. The neoclassical villa was completed in 1810 in simple, severe lines; the English-style park surrounding it was designed to harmonize with the lakeshore, and a Japanese garden with pond and maples was added in the northern section. Neoclassical, Renaissance, Egyptian, and Etruscan-Roman sculptures are scattered among Lebanon cedars, camellias, azaleas, and centuries-old trees. The orangery now houses works by Appiani and sculptures by Canova.

Book a guided tour of the gardens of Villa Serbelloni, which extend over 18 hectares atop the promontory with panoramic views of both lake arms. Designed in the 18th century, these Italian-style gardens are accessible only by guided tour organized from the village (Tuesday-Sunday). Napoleon, Austrian Emperor Francis I, and Franz Liszt number among their illustrious 19th-century visitors.

Descend to the hamlet of Pescallo east of Bellagio, a former fishing village accessible from the cemetery via via per Pescallo. Its small beach and sailboats anchored in the bay offer an authentic view of Lake Como's eastern branch.

activities.text: Rent a license-free boat from Bellagio's landing stage to explore small coves inaccessible from shore, cruise along historic villas, and reach isolated beaches on the lake's central branch.

days_plan.itin_title: Lombardy's Most Beautiful Villages in 5 Days
Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona
Italian Lakes Road Trip: 8 Days Through Lombardy and Piedmont

visits.text: On the way, detour through Guardia Sanframondi, a medieval village known for two things: its leaning bell tower of San Sebastiano Church (slight tilt due to an 18th-century earthquake) and its Riti Misti—penitential procession held every seven years, where hooded faithful flagellate themselves in the streets. Tough spectacle, pagan and Christian mixed. The next one is in 2031. In normal times, the historic center is still worth the walk: empty lanes, valley views of the Calore, and three or four grocery stores selling locally produced Aglianico del Taburno DOCG.

The Arch of Trajan in Benevento stands 15.60 meters high and was erected in 114 AD by the Roman Senate to celebrate the inauguration of the Via Traiana, a shortcut between Rome and Brindisi. It's one of the best-preserved Roman arches in the world—the Parian marble bas-reliefs are almost intact, while those on the Arch of Constantine in Rome are damaged. Each face tells a chapter of Trajan's reign: Dacian campaigns, alimenta for poor children, founding of colonies. Best visited in the morning, with raking light on the eastern sculptures.

The Cathedral of Santa Maria de Episcopio has a complicated history: 12th-century Lombard façade, interior rebuilt after Allied bombing on September 21, 1943, which destroyed 80% of the building. The famous Janua Major—12th-century bronze door with 72 panels depicting bishops of Benevento—was found fragmented in the rubble and patiently restored. It's now displayed inside, behind glass. Count 20-30 minutes for the cathedral, plus 15 for the crypt with its reused ancient capitals.

Santa Sofia is a church with a six-pointed star plan, built around 760 by Lombard Duke Arechis II—precisely when Charlemagne was about to crush the northern Lombard kingdom. Benevento would become the last Lombard stronghold in Italy, and this church, its national sanctuary. The plan is unique: six reused Roman columns (probably taken from the nearby Temple of Isis) at the center, eight white pillars around them, forming a star. Listed as a UNESCO site in 2011 within the serial site 'Longobards in Italy: Places of Power.' 9th-century frescoes preserved in two of the apses—Annunciation, Visitation. Small but essential.

The 12th-century Romanesque cloister attached to Santa Sofia merits the detour on its own: sculpted capitals depicting hunts, allegories, fantastical animals, in exceptional condition. It provides access to the Museo del Sannio, free with the Santa Sofia ticket. Six sections including Samnite (Aeclanum ceramics, bronzes), Roman, Lombard, and the famous Egyptian section—a 4-meter obelisk from the Temple of Isis built by Domitian in Benevento around 88 AD, plus sphinxes, Apis bulls, and a Horus. Allow 1h30 to properly tour the museum.

The Roman theatre was inaugurated between 125 and 128 AD under Hadrian, expanded under Caracalla, and could accommodate between 10,000 and 15,000 spectators across 90 meters in diameter. During the Lombard period it was buried—medieval houses were built on top, using the arcades as cellars. Excavated between 1890 and 1957, it reopened to the public on June 26, 1957 with Aristophanes' Assemblywomen. Today: 25 arcades on the lower level, sculpted masks in the access corridors, and in summer, opera and ancient theater. The acoustics remained intact—test it by climbing all the way up, a voice from below carries perfectly.

The Hortus Conclusus is Benevento's surprise: in a cloister of the San Domenico convent, Italian artist Domenico Paladino installed a contemporary garden populated with sculptures in 1992—a bronze horse rearing on a wall wearing Agamemnon's golden mask, severed heads, stars. Direct reference to the Trojan horse and to the city's Samnite-Lombard mythology. It's practically free, almost never visited, and it's the best dose of contemporary art in the entire itinerary. Go in late afternoon when light filters through the gallery.

Pietrelcina, 13 km north of Benevento, is the birthplace of Francesco Forgione, alias Padre Pio, born May 25, 1887. Stigmatized in 1918, Capuchin of San Giovanni Rotondo, canonized by John Paul II in 2002—he remains one of Italy's most popular saints. The birth house, the lanes where he grew up, the Madonna degli Angeli church where he was baptized: everything is marked by a pilgrimage route. Even if you're not particularly devoted to the cult, go anyway to observe the fervor—entire busloads of pilgrims, Italians and Poles, candles, ex-votos. It's a slice of Italy you don't see elsewhere.

Montesarchio guards on its hill an Aragonese castle transformed into the Museo Archeologico Nazionale del Sannio Caudino. The centerpiece: the 'Lichas Crater,' a 4th-century BC red-figure vase found in a local necropolis depicting Heracles throwing Lichas into the sea. But it's mainly worth it for the position: the castle overlooks the Furcae Caudinae pass, where in 321 BC the Roman army, trapped by the Samnites, had to pass under the yoke—supreme humiliation engraved in Rome's memory for six centuries.

At Sant'Agata de' Goti (yes, 30 minutes from Montesarchio if you want to loop back), quickly revisit the Annunziata if it was closed on D1—the Last Judgment fresco really deserves the effort. Otherwise, head down to Solopaca to finish the afternoon at a cellar: Fontanavecchia is open on Saturdays without reservation, and their Aglianico del Taburno Vigna Cataratte is probably the best in the DOCG. Compare with the Solopaca rosso, simpler, more immediate.

activities.text: Strega liqueur, electric yellow and highly aromatic, was born in Benevento in 1860 in the Alberti house. Secret recipe with 70 herbs and spices—saffron, mint, fennel, cinnamon, and about sixty others whose complete list only one family member knows. The historic building, facing the station, houses a small museum where you follow production. Tasting at the end (mini-portion, it's potent). The name comes from the Janare, witches supposedly holding their sabbaths under Benevento's enchanted walnut tree.

Castelvenere and Solopaca are Benevento's immediate wine capitals—25 minutes to the west. Castelvenere produces Aglianico del Taburno DOCG, a tannic red for aging that really began to break through in the 2000s against its big brother Taurasi. Solopaca offers Solopaca DOC, more accessible. Local cellars (La Guardiense, Fontanavecchia) welcome aperitivo guests, especially in late afternoon. Reservation required in winter, advised in summer. Plan to dine there or return to Benevento by taxi.

Since Benevento is a nest of witches in local imagination—the Janare gathered under an enchanted walnut tree planted by the Sabato River, according to tradition—the Museo Janua opened in the center to tell this folklore. Small private museum, funny, full of votive objects and amulets against the evil eye, interactive display of the magic formula 'Unguento, unguento, mannaceme allu nuce de Beneviento.' Half an hour suffices. If you have children, they'll love it.

For dinner, head to the Triggio quarter, around the Roman theatre: medieval lanes, no cars, restaurant terraces serving pure and hard cucina sannita. Cécatielli alla beneventana (handmade pasta with lamb ragù and pecorino), Benevento sausage with fennel, panna cotta drizzled with Strega. For wine, stay local: Aglianico del Taburno or Falanghina del Sannio depending on whether you want red or white.

To properly finish the Sannio sequence, return to Benevento in late afternoon for the passeggio on Corso Garibaldi—800 pedestrian meters between Trajan's Arch and the cathedral. It's when the whole city comes out, groups of retirees station in front of shop windows, teens strut their stuff. Aperitivo on Piazza Roma, around 7 PM, with a spritz alla Strega (local variant, very yellow) or an Aglianico before heading to dinner.

If you fancy a nature escape rather than archaeology, the Taburno-Camposauro Massif 30 minutes from Benevento offers marked trails (CAI 916, 917) climbing to the summit of Taburno (1,394 m). Count 4 hours round trip. From the summit, on clear days, views to the Tyrrhenian Sea and Matese peaks. Combine with lunch at a park trattoria, like Cafe' Pizzeria 'A Casalella in Cautano, serving reputed cinghiale al Aglianico.

days_plan.itin_title: Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia
Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia
Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia

visits.text: Area Naturalistica La Bora - a 10-hectare wetland managed by the province of Bologna, featuring breeding ponds for the European pond turtle (Emys orbicularis), a protected species threatened with extinction across northern Italy. The site also hosts a center dedicated to amphibians and aquatic insects.

activities.text: Birdwatching from the purpose-built observation hides: grey herons, kingfishers, and mallards frequent the ponds year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: 10 Natural Wonders Around Bologna

visits.text: Berceto sits at 852 meters, the last stop in Emilia before the Via Francigena crosses the Apennines. In 718, Moderanno - bishop of Rennes en route to Rome - stopped here, hung relics on a tree, and the tree refused to be cut as long as the relics remained. Liutprand, king of the Lombards, took this as a divine sign and founded a monastery. The resulting Romanesque-Lombard duomo blends three centuries of styles; the attached museum preserves a 12th-century Lucchese silk cope attributed to Moderanno himself.

The Passo della Cisa at 1,041 m marks the old border between the Duchy of Parma and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany - wall inscriptions still visible on the old post station. It's the Via Francigena's most difficult passage in northern Italy: thousands of pilgrims have crossed it from Canterbury since the 10th century. The Chapel of Our Lady of the Guard, at the top of a steep stairway, dates from 1921.

Berceto's historic center has preserved its cobbled alleyways, Renaissance portals, and 12th-17th century stone houses virtually intact. Excavations at the foot of the castle ruins (whose stones the inhabitants reused to build their houses after 1805) resumed in 2004 and opened an archaeological park.

activities.text: Walk the Via Francigena between Berceto and Passo della Cisa - 8 km, gradual climb through beech forests and high meadows where herds of horses and cows graze freely. It's one of the most beautiful stages of the entire Italian Francigena. Return by car or shuttle.

Tasting of Berceto Spongata - spiced cake with walnuts, candied fruit and honey, a specialty of the Parmesan mountains for centuries. Also available: Borgotaro IGP porcini mushrooms and mountain Parmigiano Reggiano.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand tour of the four provinces in 5 days

visits.text: Ride the funicular up to Città Alta, one of Italy's best-preserved medieval villages enclosed within the majestic Venetian Walls, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Wandering through the cobbled streets you'll discover centuries of history and Renaissance art in a timeless atmosphere that has captivated travellers of every era.

Admire Piazza Vecchia, the true civic drawing room overlooked by the Palazzo della Ragione, the Civic Tower (Campanone) and the Angelo Mai Library. Every evening the Campanone bell tolls one hundred times, just as in Venetian times when it signalled the closing of the city gates, evoking an atmosphere steeped in historical charm.

Visit the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore with its richly Baroque interiors adorned with tapestries and gilded stuccowork, and the adjacent Cappella Colleoni, a Renaissance masterpiece built as a mausoleum for the condottiere Bartolomeo Colleoni. The chapel's polychrome marble façades rank among the finest in Italy.

Explore the Accademia Carrara, one of Italy's most prestigious art galleries with over 1,800 paintings by artists such as Botticelli, Raphael, Mantegna, Titian and Canaletto. Directly opposite stands the GAMeC, the Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art, creating a unique dialogue between tradition and modernity.

activities.text: Ride even higher on the San Vigilio Funicular to the Castle, crossing breathtaking landscapes with spectacular views of the city rooftops, medieval towers and the Lombard plain. From the castle ramparts you can enjoy one of the most beautiful sunsets in Lombardy.

Lose yourself in the Lorenzo Rota Botanical Garden, a small urban Eden of 2,400 sq m on the panoramic terraces of Città Alta. From here you can admire a spectacular view of the city and surrounding mountains, with the Venetian Walls seeming to merge with the landscape in perfect harmony.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona
Italian Lakes Road Trip: 8 Days Through Lombardy and Piedmont

visits.text: A Romagna village that houses a University of Bologna center in its thousand-year-old rocca: Bertinoro surprises. The fortress, built in the 10th century, hosted Frederick Barbarossa in 1177. Since 2000, it has served as a residential campus. Free exterior visit, interior not open to the public.

Erected in the 13th century on Piazza della Libertà, the Colonna dell'Ospitalità bears 12 rings. Each noble family owned one: the traveler would tie his horse and become the guest of the corresponding family. Dante mentions it in Canto XIV of Purgatorio. The Festa dell'Ospitalità takes place every first week of September.

From the terrace of Piazza della Libertà, the view extends over the Romagna plain to the sea. The nickname 'balcony of Romagna' is well deserved. The neighboring Cathedral, Bramante-inspired, can be visited in 10 minutes.

activities.text: Bertinoro's Albana is drunk chilled, on a terrace, facing the panorama. It was the first Italian white wine to obtain DOCG status. Local producers offer tastings by appointment. The Sangiovese from the surrounding hills also holds its own.

Push on to the Pieve di San Donato in Polenta, 5 km from Bertinoro. This Romanesque basilica predating the 10th century was celebrated by Giosuè Carducci. The place is isolated, quiet, with a sweeping view over the hills. Return by the same route.

days_plan.itin_title: From Ferrara to the Delta in 5 Days: Delizie, Ravenna, and Bertinoro

visits.text: Mura etrusche - Bettona, which was called Vettona in Umbrian-Etruscan times, preserves sections of 4th-century BC Etruscan walls in local sandstone around its perimeter, covered in the 13th-14th centuries by medieval ramparts that used them as foundations. From Porta Romana, several sections of this irregular polygonal apparatus characteristic of Etruscan construction are still visible. On the outskirts, on the Perugia road at the locality called Colle, an Etruscan tomb entirely built in local sandstone is accessible. In 1352, Perugia almost completely destroyed the town during a siege, leaving only the churches intact.

Belvedere and panorama - From the highest point of the village perched at 353 meters, the view embraces the Umbrian plateau across its full width: Assisi with the Basilica of Saint Francis recognizable in the distance, Foligno, Spello and the foothills of Monte Subasio to the east, the Tiber valley to the northwest and the hills toward Perugia. Bettona was the outpost that controlled, beyond the Tiber, the border between Umbrian territory and Etruscan lands.

Pinacoteca comunale - The 14th-century Palazzo dei Priori houses an art gallery assembling works from the Umbrian and Tuscan schools. Notable pieces include paintings from Giotto's school from the 14th century, a collection of 15th-16th century altarpieces, and detached frescoes from local religious buildings. The Oratory of Saint Andrew preserves a 13th-century carved wooden coffered ceiling with a cycle on the Passion of Christ attributed to Giotto's school (1394).

Centro storico - Via di Mezzo, the former axis of the Roman town, crosses Bettona from Porta Vittorio Emanuele to Porta Romana. The perpendicular alleyways, accessible only on foot, are lined with stone houses and hanging gardens. Piazza Cavour brings together the main civic and religious monuments in a very compact space.

activities.text: Walk along the outer ramparts - The outer rampart path allows you to walk along the medieval fortifications over a large part of the perimeter. In autumn, the vines and olive trees on the slopes color the landscape rust and gold.

days_plan.itin_title: Umbria Itinerary: Medieval Villages & Rolling Hills

places.name: Bevagna

visits.text: Piazza Silvestri - This asymmetrical square is one of Umbria's most architecturally coherent. It brings together face to face two 12th-century Romanesque churches built by masters Binello and Rodolfo: San Silvestro (1195, sober façade with elegant portal and three-nave interior with medieval crypt) and San Michele Arcangelo (flat façade with rose window, sculpted portal depicting Saint Michael slaying the dragon, three-nave interior). Between them stands the Palazzo dei Consoli (1270), former Gothic town hall with external staircase and mullioned windows, now home to Teatro Francesco Torti since 1886. A Roman column with Corinthian capital completes the ensemble. Bevagna occupied ancient Mevania, a Roman city on the Via Flaminia, founded at least since the Iron Age.

2nd-century Roman baths - On Via di Porta Guelfa, these public baths rediscovered in 1891 preserve a remarkable black and white mosaic floor depicting fantastic sea creatures: tritons, seahorses, lobsters, squid. They testify to Mevania's prosperity in the 2nd-3rd centuries, when the city drew its wealth from the waterway and commerce.

Medieval craft workshops - The Mercato delle Gaite cultural association has reconstructed medieval craft workshops in the hamlet accessible for visits year-round by reservation: coin-minting workshop, silk-weaving loom (with a wheel of complexity close to an industrial machine), parchment-making, and apothecary's workshop.

Cinta muraria - Bevagna's medieval ramparts, erected on foundations of earlier Roman walls, are almost entirely preserved. Their circumference is punctuated by square, round, and polygonal towers and four Gaite (access gates). It's possible to walk along part of the outer ramparts.

activities.text: Mercato delle Gaite (June) - For ten days in June, Bevagna's four historic quarters recreate medieval life in competition: crafts, cuisine, banners, and games. Residents wear period costumes and workshops operate in public. It's one of Umbria's most authentic medieval recreations.

days_plan.itin_title: Umbria Itinerary: Medieval Villages & Rolling Hills

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Michele Arcangelo Bevagna

places.name: Bibbiena

visits.text: Historic center of Bibbiena: the administrative capital of the Casentino, Bibbiena is documented since 979 and developed as a medieval fortress of the bishops of Arezzo atop a hill overlooking the Archiano river. After the Battle of Campaldino (1289), the Florentine Guelphs sacked it for eight days. Rebuilt, it became one of the strategic castles of the Tarlati da Pietramala in the 14th century before passing to Florence in 1384. Of the original walls, the Tarlati Tower on Piazza Tarlati survives as the sole remnant of the medieval castle. The square offers a view over the entire Casentino valley.

Church of San Lorenzo: erected in the 15th century, it preserves two remarkable glazed terracottas by Andrea della Robbia — a Deposition and an Adoration. These late 15th-century works rank among the finest examples of Della Robbia art in the Casentino.

Church of Saints Ippolito and Donato (Propositura): the main religious building in the historic center, built in the early 12th century on the site of the Tarlati castle chapel, consecrated in 1314. The interior houses a 13th-century wooden sculpture of the Madonna and Child, a triptych by Bicci di Lorenzo and an Annunciation by Balducci.

Casentino Archaeological Museum Piero Albertoni — Palazzo Niccolini: the museum traces the valley's history from prehistory to the Middle Ages through local discoveries. The highlight is the collection of Etruscan bronzes from the Lago degli Idoli (Lake of the Idols), an artificial lake on the flank of Monte Falterona where over 14,000 Etruscan ex-votos were excavated, some of which are now in the British Museum and the Louvre.

activities.text: Sanctuary of Santa Maria del Sasso: a Renaissance complex 1 km from the historic center, built to the design of Giuliano da Maiano in Renaissance style on the site of a Marian apparition in 1347. The sanctuary contains a Madonna and Child by Bicci di Lorenzo, a Nativity of the Virgin by Ligozzi, an Assumption by Fra' Bartolomeo and Fra' Paolino, and a remarkable Renaissance cloister.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

map_keywords: Propositura dei Santi Ippolito e Donato Bibbiena
Santuario di Santa Maria del Sasso Bibbiena

visits.text: The Sanctuary of Oropa, at 1,200 meters altitude in the Biella Prealps, is the largest Marian sanctuary in the Alps and has been part of UNESCO World Heritage since 2003 (Sacri Monti). Its origins reportedly date to the 4th century, when Bishop Eusebius of Vercelli placed a statue of the Virgin there according to tradition. In 1620, during the first coronation of the Black Virgin statue, baroque works accelerated. Filippo Juvarra designed the Porta Regia in the 18th century, Guarino Guarini participated in the overall design. The twelve chapels of the Sacro Monte (built from 1620) recount the life of Mary in polychrome statues and frescoes by Giovanni d'Enrico. The new basilica, consecrated in 1960, rises over 80 meters to its dome.

The medieval quarter of Piazzo, the upper part of Biella accessible by funicular from the lower town, preserves a Piazza Cisterna surrounded by 15th-century arcades, the Romanesque church of San Giacomo, and Palazzo Gromo Ternengo (16th century). The cathedral baptistery, built between the 7th and 11th centuries with a central plan and four apses, is one of the most significant examples of Piedmontese Romanesque art. Above the door, a Roman bas-relief depicting Hercules in reuse testifies to continuity of occupation since antiquity.

Biella is first mentioned in 826 as Bugella, in a donation act by Louis the Pious to a Count Busone. From 1245, city statutes reference weaver and wool worker guilds. In 1695, a silk manufactory was built there; in 1835, the same building was converted to a mechanical wool mill, placing Biella at the forefront of European textile industry. Cittadellarte - Fondazione Pistoletto, installed in a former mill on the Cervo river, is a contemporary art center founded in 1996 by artist Michelangelo Pistoletto.

activities.text: Cable car from Oropa to Rifugio Savoia (1,900 m), then 15-minute hike to Lake Mucrone: panorama over the plain to Turin and Milan on clear days. Return via old shepherd trails.
Forest hike in Burcina-Felice Piacenza Natural Park, south of Biella: reserve known for its spectacular rhododendron collection (blooming May-June). Bronze Age tools have been found in this massif.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Valleys of Piedmont: Occitan Alps, Lakes & Baroque Savoy

places.name: Bienno

visits.text: Enter Bienno's historic center, built on the geometric grid of a 1st-century BC Roman foundation. The name comes from the Latin 'biennium,' a term designating the canals that channeled waters from the Grigna torrent to the workshops. The defensive Avanzini tower (dating from 1075) and Morandini tower flank the oldest nucleus. Renaissance palace facades preserve exterior frescoes; Palazzo Francesconi Rabajoli, two 16th-century noble houses united, shelters frescoes attributed to Fiamminghino.

Follow Via Artigiani along the Vaso Re, an artificial canal built around the year 1000 to channel water from the Grigna to the forges. In the 17th century, fifteen forges operated in the village. Visit the Fucina Museo, a forge-museum acquired by the municipality in 1985: the enormous hydraulic hammers, driven by the waterwheel according to Archimedes' principle, still function and are demonstrated. This is the heart of the Ethnographic Museum of Iron, Arts, and Popular Traditions of Bienno, founded in 1988.

Visit Bienno's Mill-Museum, the other pillar of the village's industrial heritage, adjacent to the Fucina. Together, these two buildings form the museum's founding nucleus and illustrate the complete chain of metal transformation from ore in the prehistoric Camunian mines to the finished tool.

Climb to the Colle di Cristo Re to see the golden statue of Christ the Redeemer, a 1929 work by Timo Bortolotti. Nearby, the church of the Maddalena is adorned with frescoes. The Gothic church of Santa Maria Annunciata, built in the 15th century with its exposed-stone rose window, preserves frescoes by Romanino and Pietro da Cemmo, two great Lombard painters.

activities.text: Thematic walk along the Vaso Re canal titled 'Discovering Vaso Re, along the story told by water': this marked trail crosses the village's old forges converted into a Forge School and Iron Playroom, allowing you to follow Bienno's industrial history from the Middle Ages to the 1980s, when the last active forges closed.

visits.text: A Bronze Age megalithic tomb dating from 2300 to 1750 BC, the Chianca dolmen, 5 km inland from Bisceglie, is the stop you don't expect to make in Puglia. Discovered by chance in 1909 by two archaeologists, Samarelli and Mosso. Corridor of 7.6 m, burial chamber covered by a slab weighing more than 10 tons, oriented due east toward the rising sun. Inside, six adult and child skeletons, stone knives, a bronze pendant. UNESCO recognized it in 2011 as "heritage testifying to a culture of peace." Free access, follow SP 138 from Bisceglie, last kilometer on dirt road.

Return toward the coast through the historic center. The medieval town centers on the Cathedral of San Pietro (begun in 1073, facade redone in the 18th century) and the Castello Svevo, another fortress of Frederick II. Small streets descending toward a still-active fishing harbor. Budget an hour for the tour, more if you grab an aperitivo at Piazza Vittorio Emanuele. Bisceglie stays authentic: few souvenir shops, plenty of old men playing cards.
Cala San Giacomo, a small cove 3 km south of downtown, offers a seaside break mid-day. Rocky bottom, transparent water, few people on weekdays. No beach bar, bring your towels and picnic.

activities.text: Quick swim at Cala San Giacomo. Water shoes recommended, the pebbles are sharp. Good compromise to break the rhythm before tackling Trani.

visits.text: A griffin in mosaic beneath a cathedral: the Concattedrale of Bitonto was built over an Early Christian church, whose crypt preserves an 11th-century opus sectile pavement, remarkably intact. Lion's body, eagle's head, symbolizing the dual nature of Christ. The building, inspired by San Nicola in Bari, is regarded as the finest example of Apulian Romanesque.

Look at the central doorway of the Cattedrale di Bitonto before entering: its narrative sculpture has no equivalent in Apulian Romanesque. Above it, a sixteen-petalled rose window, topped by a relieving arch with a sphinx, flanked by two lions on suspended columnettes. The portico planned in front was never built. Piazza Cattedrale.

The Torrione Angioino guards the entrance to Bitonto's medieval quarter, near Porta Baresana: this is where all guided visits begin, and it's the right way to read the city. Bitonto was a Roman municipium, then Lombard, Byzantine, Norman, and Swabian: no period of rule missed the appointment here. Walking loop from the gate.

Palazzo Sylos Calò is the civic showpiece of Bitonto: a 15th-century triple portico and a 16th-century loggia, around Piazza del Sedile, where churches, museums, and noble palaces line up. This is the square the town gathered in, literally. Twenty minutes, looking up.

The Lama Balice rings Bitonto: it's the bed of the former Tiflis torrent, now a nature park, and the reason the town was defensible. Trails, vegetation, and the contrast with the olive groves covering the surrounding territory. Bring water; there are no facilities on the route.

activities.text: Bitonto's olive oil comes from the local Ogliarola di Bitonto variety, on groves that cover the territory to the horizon: the mills welcome tastings and explain production. The town also has its frantoi ipogei, underground olive mills carved beneath the historic center. The Galà dell'Olio marks the local calendar.

visits.text: The Ponte Gobbo is hunchbacked, twisted, irregular - eleven arches of different heights spanning 273 meters. Legend says the Devil built it in one night in exchange for the first soul to cross it: San Colombano sent his dog across, and the Devil stormed off, kicking the structure as he went. The reality is even older: Roman construction, remodeled over the centuries. Hemingway saw it from the banks of the Trebbia and described it as 'the most beautiful valley in the world.'

San Colombano Abbey is the reason Bobbio exists. An Irish monk named Columbanus founded it in 614 after crossing all of Europe from Ireland to evangelize the Lombards. The abbey became one of Europe's most important cultural centers: its library held 700 manuscripts in 982. Gerbert d'Aurillac - future Pope Sylvester II - received the abbey in commendam from Otto II that same year, but the monks quickly expelled him. The scriptorium, cloister, and crypt with Columbanus's sarcophagus can still be visited.

Bobbio's historic center has preserved its medieval layout intact. The 11th-century Santa Maria Assunta cathedral, Piazza San Fara with its arcades, aristocratic palaces with carved portals - an hour's walk covers everything. Look for the house where filmmaker Marco Bellocchio (born in Bobbio) grew up: the address circulates around the village.

activities.text: Swimming in the Trebbia. Hemingway wasn't wrong: the water is remarkably transparent, the white pebble banks are natural beaches frequented by Italians from the plains in summer. The Rio Foino thermal baths, free-access sulfur springs just outside the center, are 5 minutes on foot from Ponte Gobbo.
Dinner of maccheroni alla Bobbiese - wide homemade pasta typical of Bobbio, served with meat or mushroom ragù depending on the season. The trattorias on Piazza San Fara are the village's best tables.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand tour of the four provinces in 5 days

visits.text: Saepinum is as fascinating as Pompeii with zero crowds. The Romans took the Samnite city Saipins, perched on the mountain above, around 290 BC at the end of the third Samnite War; inhabitants descended to the plain and founded the new Roman city, Saepinum, shortly after. Walls, gates and towers were financed in the 1st century AD by Tiberius and Drusus—the monumental inscription on Porta Boiano mentions both names. Forum, basilica with varied capitals, semi-circular theater 61.5 meters in diameter, baths, Porta Boiano, cattle market: it's all here. Peculiarity: in the 18th century, peasants built their houses atop the theater tiers, which follow the curve. Stunning effect. The site, long open access, is now managed by the ministry since 2024 (€10, two museums included). Allow 2.5 hours.

Three kilometers above the Roman site, the medieval village of Sepino also merits a stop. Saepinum's inhabitants took refuge here in the 9th century after Saracen raids. Santa Cristina church (14th century), remains of old walls, winding streets following Matese relief. The castle was destroyed by the 1805 earthquake, but the panoramic position remains striking. 45 minutes, it's small.

Down in the plain, Bojano doesn't look like much: 8,000 inhabitants, modern town without great charm. But it's ancient Bovianum, Samnite capital of the Pentri taken by Rome in 311 BC. Civita Superiore, the fortified borgo above, preserves ruins of Frederick II's imperial castle—you must climb to understand. The Biferno springs gush here, crystalline water feeding central Molise—they've made the area's pastoral wealth since antiquity. 1 hour for Civita Superiore and the springs.

Nicknamed the 'village of brigands,' Roccamandolfi clings to Matese slopes beneath ruins of Maginulfo Castle—destroyed by Frederick II's troops in the 13th century because Roger and Thomas of Molise had taken refuge there. Today the borgo of 800 inhabitants revolves around San Giacomo Maggiore church (18th century, altar and wooden statue by Molise sculptor Di Zinno). The Documentation Center on Brigandage recounts a little-known episode: after Italian Unification in 1861, brigand bands of the South resisted the nascent state for years—and Roccamandolfi was a hotbed.

Roccamandolfi's Tibetan bridge is the day's sensation. Metal structure 234 meters long suspended 140 meters above the canyon carved by the Callora torrent. Access via a marked trail from the castle ruins, 20-minute walk. The walkway is made of metal slats with handrails: secure, but you feel the void. Round trip about 1 hour. Free, open access. Don't attempt in high wind.

Small reward after the Tibetan bridge: the Rio waterfall, in Roccamandolfi territory. Short trail from the borgo, 30 minutes one way. Water cascades down a succession of small drops in a wooded canyon. In spring, powerful flow; in summer, you can dip your feet in pools. Little frequented, you'll mostly encounter locals.

Largest WWF oasis in continental Italy (3,137 hectares): the Guardiaregia-Campochiaro oasis protects a remarkable portion of the Matese. Deep Quirino gorge, waterfalls, karst caves, emblematic fauna: Apennine wolf, wildcat, golden eagle in passage. Visitor center at Guardiaregia, marked trails of varying difficulty. If you have good shoes, the Quirino Waterfall trail is worth an extra hour.

activities.text: Caciocavallo tasting at a Matese farm, near Sepino or Bojano. This pear-shaped cheese, tied in pairs to a rope, is made from raw Podolica cow milk. Aged from a few months to several years, it develops hazelnut and hay notes. Many fattorie offer visits with tasting, some open by reservation only. Allow 1 hour—brief but memorable.

Walk on a tratturo, those grassy transhumance paths that have structured Molise for 2,000 years. The Pescasseroli-Candela tratturo passes by Saepinum and totals 211 km. A well-marked section starts right beside the archaeological site. One hour suffices to understand how, for centuries, hundreds of thousands of sheep shaped these landscapes.

Winter season: Campitello Matese, ski resort at 1,400 meters on the slopes of Monte Miletto (2,050 meters, highest peak in the massif). 40 km of slopes, perfect for relaxed skiing—not Alpine scale, but family atmosphere and gentle prices. In summer, hikes to the Miletto summit: on clear days, views of both Adriatic and Tyrrhenian seas. It's unique in Italy.

Dinner in Bojano at a family trattoria. Ask for cavatelli with lamb ragù, typically Molise pasta shaped like small shells, handmade with semolina and water. Traditional Sunday dish. With Tintilia or neighboring Aglianico, it's hefty and filling—exactly what's needed after a day of Matese hiking.

visits.text: Before leaving Modena province, devote the morning to the Ferrari Museum in Maranello, located 20 km south of Modena. Opened in 1990, this museum traces the history of the Scuderia and the Prancing Horse through legendary Formula 1 cars, prototypes, and GTs. You can also try a driving simulator. If you're a true enthusiast, combine it with the Enzo Ferrari Museum in central Modena, housed in the founder's birthplace—a combined ticket lets you visit both within 48 hours.

Arriving in Bologna by early afternoon, head to Piazza Maggiore, the city's heart. The Basilica of San Petronio dominates the square with its deliberately unfinished facade—construction began in 1390 and it remains the world's fifth-largest church. Inside, you'll find a meridian line traced on the floor in 1655 by astronomer Cassini, stretching 66 meters long. Entry is free.

The Two Towers are Bologna's symbol. The Torre degli Asinelli, rising 97 meters, is Italy's tallest leaning medieval tower still standing. Climb its 498 steps: the panorama over Bologna's red rooftops, the hills, and on clear days the Alps is exceptional. Beside it, the Torre Garisenda, smaller at 48 meters, leans even more than the Tower of Pisa—it's not accessible for safety reasons. In the 12th century, Bologna had over a hundred such towers; about twenty remain.

Bologna deserves a second day. Start at Palazzo dell'Archiginnasio, the former seat of the University of Bologna—founded in 1088, it's the oldest university in the Western world. Dante, Petrarch, and Copernicus studied here. Inside, don't miss the Teatro Anatomico, a room entirely clad in fir wood adorned with sculptures, where medical professors gave anatomy lectures before tiers of students. The atmosphere is both scholarly and slightly macabre.

Continue to Piazza Santo Stefano, one of Bologna's most beautiful squares. The Basilica of Santo Stefano is actually a complex of several interlocking churches and cloisters, built between the 5th and 13th centuries—sometimes called "the seven churches." The medieval cloister, with its Romanesque columns and central basin, radiates absolute serenity. Take time to sit for a moment.

Pass through Piazza Nettuno to admire the Neptune Fountain, sculpted in bronze by Giambologna between 1563 and 1567. The sea god, trident in hand, dominates a basin adorned with mermaids and dolphins. Just behind stands Palazzo Re Enzo, where Emperor Frederick II's son was imprisoned for 23 years after being captured by the Bolognese in 1249.

Wander through the university quarter around Via Zamboni. With 100,000 students—a quarter of the population—Bologna pulses with distinctive energy. Independent bookshops, lively cafes, walls covered in posters: this is where you'll feel why Bologna also bears the nickname "la Dotta" (the learned one). Continue to Palazzo Poggi, the university's current seat, which houses fascinating scientific collections.

If you're seeking a quiet moment, the Baroque church of San Domenico is worth the detour. It houses the Arca di San Domenico, the monumental tomb of Saint Dominic, worked on by renowned sculptors including the young Michelangelo—three statuettes on the tomb are attributed to him. The wooden choir is also remarkable.

activities.text: Bologna is the only city in the world where you can walk for kilometers without ever being exposed to rain or sun. Its porticoes, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021, extend over 40 km in the historic center. Let yourself wander beneath these arcades, from Via dell'Indipendenza to Strada Maggiore. For the more athletic, the San Luca portico climbs 3.8 km and 666 arches up to the sanctuary perched on the hill—allow 1h30 round trip.

Bologna earned the nickname "la Grassa" (the fat one) for good reason. Lose yourself in the Quadrilatero, the old medieval guild quarter, now a permanent market where the aromas of cheeses, cured meats, and fresh fish mingle. Taste tortellini in brodo—tiny pasta parcels served in capon broth—and mortadella Bologna IGP, far more refined than the deli meat you might know as "bologna." Pair it all with a glass of Pignoletto, the local sparkling white wine.

Bologna is a city best discovered by bike. The historic center is largely flat and pedestrianized, and operators offer rentals by the hour or day. It's the best way to cover the 40 km of porticoes without exhausting yourself, and to easily reach outlying neighborhoods like the Giardini Margherita, the large public park south of the center.

For complete immersion in Bolognese gastronomy, join a cooking class to learn how to make tagliatelle al ragù—the real ragù Bolognese, a thick and savory sauce served with egg pasta, which bears no resemblance to the "spaghetti Bolognese" found abroad. Operators offer 2- to 3-hour workshops, often in welcoming settings in the historic center.

visits.text: Lago di Bolsena - Europe's largest volcanic lake (114 km², maximum depth 151 m), formed in a caldera of the Volsini mountains approximately 300,000 years ago. Its clear, fish-rich waters contain two islands: Bisentina (former Farnese property, with Renaissance chapels) and Martana (where, according to tradition, Amalasuntha, Queen of the Ostrogoths, was strangled in 535). Swimming is permitted on several black volcanic sand beaches.

Basilica di Santa Cristina in Bolsena - This 11th-century basilica is linked to the Eucharistic Miracle of Bolsena (1263): a Bohemian priest on pilgrimage, doubting transubstantiation, saw the host bleed onto the corporal during Mass. Pope Urban IV, then in Orvieto, instituted the feast of Corpus Christi in response. The Cappella del Miracolo, in the catacombs beneath the church, preserves the altar of the episode. The 4th-century Christian catacombs, carved into tufa, are accessible by guided tour.

Castello Monaldeschi in Bolsena - 13th-century fortress dominating the lake from the medieval town. It houses the Museo Territoriale del Lago di Bolsena, devoted to the geological, archaeological (Etruscan and Roman remains from ancient Volsinii), and natural history of the lake.

Montefiascone - Perched on the crater's southern rim, this town offers circular panoramas over the lake and countryside. The Duomo di Santa Margherita has one of Italy's largest domes after St. Peter's in Rome, visible from afar. It's also the birthplace of Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone DOC wine, whose name comes from a medieval anecdote: a German bishop en route to Rome sent his cupbearer ahead to mark "Est" (there is some) on taverns with good wine; arriving at Montefiascone, the cupbearer inscribed the word three times, so pleased was he with the wine.

activities.text: Tasting Est! Est!! Est!!! wine - Montefiascone's cellars offer tastings of this DOC dry white, accompanied by local products: acquacotta (Tuscia peasant soup), sbroscia (lake fish soup), and grilled eels.

Boat excursion to Isola Bisentina - Boats depart from the ports of Bolsena and Capodimonte to reach this wooded island housing seven Renaissance chapels, including one attributed to Vignola, and Italian gardens. Booking recommended.

places.name: Bomarzo

visits.text: Sacro Bosco (Park of the Monsters) of Bomarzo - Created from 1552 onward by Prince Vicino Orsini, this 3-hectare park is the world's oldest modern sculpture garden. After his wife Giulia Farnese's death, Orsini commissioned architect Pirro Ligorio (who completed St. Peter's Basilica after Michelangelo) to create dozens of colossal creatures carved from peperino: an ogre with gaping mouth, an elephant bearing a combat tower, two wrestling giants, a dragon, sphinxes. The leaning house, built on a tilted block, disorients visitors. Abandoned for 400 years, the park was rediscovered by Salvador Dalí in 1938.

Tempietto of the Sacro Bosco - Atop the hill, this small temple attributed to Vignola crowns the route. Its dome echoes in miniature that of Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence. Vicino Orsini dedicated it to his wife's memory.

Etruscan Pyramid of Bomarzo - In the sacred wood, a peperino monolith carved into a stepped pyramid puzzles archaeologists. Likely a sacrificial altar or rock sanctuary, it remains shrouded in mystery. Access via a forest trail.

Vitorchiano, the "suspended village" - 15 minutes from Bomarzo, this grey peperino village seems to merge with the volcanic cliff. Classified among the Borghi più Belli d'Italia and awarded the Touring Club's Bandiera Arancione. The profferli (external staircases), the 13th-century fountain on Piazza Roma, and the Capitoline Wolf engraved on facades recall the unique status of "land faithful to Rome" granted in 1265. Director Mario Monicelli filmed "L'armata Brancaleone" here with Vittorio Gassman in 1966.

Moai of Vitorchiano - In 1990, eleven craftsmen from Easter Island (Rapa Nui) sculpted this 6-meter, 3-ton statue from a local peperino block—the only Moai in the world made outside Easter Island using ancestral techniques. Tuscia's volcanic peperino resembles Rapa Nui stone. The statue stands watch over the belvedere overlooking the Vezza valley.

activities.text: Vitorchiano belvedere - From Largo Padre Ettore Salimbeni (where the Moai stands), the view plunges over the borgo clinging to its cliff, the Vezza valley, and the oak forests of the Cimini Mountains. Tuscia's best photo spot, especially in late afternoon light.

visits.text: Ponte della Maddalena (Devil's Bridge): This humpback bridge spans the Serchio with a main arch rising 18.50 meters flanked by four smaller asymmetric arches—a silhouette that has intrigued travelers since the 16th century, notably Michel de Montaigne who described it in his 1581 Travel Journal. The structure probably dates to the 11th century, but its current appearance is due to Castruccio Castracani, lord of Lucca, who had it rebuilt between 1324 and 1327. On the Via Francigena pilgrimage route from Canterbury to Rome, the bridge held during World War II: retreating German troops had mined it but it was never destroyed, which proved crucial for the Allies. Legend tells that the mason, despairing of floods from the Serchio, made a pact with the devil to finish the work in one night—in exchange for the first soul to cross the bridge. The village priest sent a dog across, outwitting the devil. They say this white dog still walks the bridge on October evenings.

places.name: Borgo San Lorenzo

visits.text: The Pieve di San Lorenzo, founded in 941, is the largest rural Romanesque building in the Florentine countryside. Its hexagonal bell tower with a semi-dodecagonal brick base, placed directly on the apse, is unique in Tuscany. The interior preserves a Madonna attributed to Giotto, a Crucifix from Giotto's school, a Virgin Enthroned attributed to Agnolo Gaddi, and a Virgin with Saints by Matteo Rosselli. The apse is entirely frescoed by Galileo Chini. On the right side facade, a polychrome terracotta tabernacle by Fornaci Chini (1926), created for the centenary of Saint Francis's death, is one of the finest street pieces of the Art Nouveau movement in Tuscany.

The Chini Museum in Villa Pecori Giraldi traces the history of the Fornaci San Lorenzo manufactory, founded in 1906 by Galileo and Chino Chini, two cousins born in Borgo San Lorenzo. Galileo Chini was one of the leading representatives of Italian Art Nouveau: his ceramics—first with floral motifs inspired by Botticelli, then with metallic-luster Deco designs—adorn the Salsomaggiore thermal baths, several Florentine palaces, and Borgo San Lorenzo's town hall. In 1911-1913, the King of Thailand invited him to Bangkok to decorate the Sathon Throne. The villa's rooms are frescoed by the Chini family: a high-quality Saint George cycle, medieval geometric motifs, and coats of arms of Florentine nobility.

activities.text: Art Nouveau Trail of Mugello: a walking or driving route among Chini works scattered throughout the town—Misericordia facade, mayor's office decorated on floors and windows, Santissimo Crocifisso oratory. Borgo San Lorenzo was named 'Città della Ceramica' (City of Ceramics) by the Italian Ministry of Economic Development in 2017.

visits.text: Castello Malaspina has stood since the late 13th century on Serravalle hill, 260 feet above the Temo River. It contains the chapel of Nostra Signora de Sos Regnos Altos, whose 14th-century frescoes illustrate the rare scene of "The Meeting of the Three Living and the Three Dead," the only known example of this Franciscan theme in Sardinia.

The Sa Costa quarter is Bosa's medieval heart, with ochre, yellow, and rose-colored houses pressed together on the slopes above the Temo. The Ponte Vecchio, built from red trachyte, links this quarter to the quays.

The church of San Pietro extra muros, a 12th-century Romanesque structure, stands apart from the center on the far bank of the Temo, where ancient Roman Bosa once stood. It's one of Sardinia's oldest Christian churches.

activities.text: Boat ride on the Temo, Sardinia's only navigable river, between the city quays and the river mouth at Bosa Marina. Every first Sunday in August, a procession of decorated boats carries the Virgin's statue upriver.

Taste Malvasia di Bosa DOC in one of the wine cellars in the nearby villages of Magomadas or Modolo. This sweet, amber white wine, produced from a grape variety of Greek origin, is one of Italy's rarest wine productions.
Swim at Cala Managu or Bosa Marina beach, about a mile from the center, on a coastline still uncrowded and bordered by basalt cliffs.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Sardinia Loop: Coastline, Cities & Heartland

visits.text: A crown of branches as wide as a village square: the Quercia Vallonea, known as the oak of the Hundred Horsemen, stands around 25 metres tall with a trunk more than 5 metres round, and is reckoned to be over seven centuries old. It rises in the Bosco di Tricase, with free access.

The Bosco di Tricase forms part of the Costa Otranto-Santa Maria di Leuca regional nature park and mixes oaks, maquis and old drystone walls. The paths are flat and short. Carry water, as there is nowhere to stock up on site.

activities.text: The Quercia fair is traditionally held at the foot of the tree, a farmers' market inherited from far back. Allow an hour walking under the oaks. Check the dates with the town council in Tricase, as they shift from year to year.

places.name: Botromagno

visits.text: The Botromagno archaeological zone and the cave crypt of the Padre Eterno are on the outskirts of Gravina in Puglia, and together they hold the oldest layers of the city. The Sette Camere hypogeal complex completes the series, with the pre-Christian temple turned into the Madonna della Stella. This is a territory, not a checklist: allow half a day.

visits.text: Sant'Agata di Puglia overlooks the border between Daunia and Irpinia at 800 m altitude—on clear days, you can see five regions from the castle belvedere. The imperial fortress, built by the Lombards then remodeled by Frederick II in the 13th century, watched over the road from Benevento to Brindisi. The village kept its medieval layout intact: stone lanes, stairs, arches passing overhead. Awarded the Orange Flag. If you explore the surroundings, Neolithic statue-menhirs from the late 3rd millennium BC were found at Serbaroli locality, among the oldest human statues in Puglia.

Deliceto, 20 km northeast, features an imposing castle clinging to a spur (12th century, reworked under the Swabians), a Baroque chiesa madre built on Lombard foundations, and—above all—the abbey of the Consolazione, founded in the 16th century, where Saint Alphonsus Liguori spent several summers. The Centro del Gusto in the center offers tastings of local products: Daunia DOP olive oil, Tavoliere cherry tomatoes, caciocavallo. It's a short stop, 45 minutes suffices, unless you eat on-site.

Bovino, 'the balcony of Puglia,' is one of Italy's Most Beautiful Villages. The Castello Ducale (10th century, extended by the Guevara) dominates the main square. The cathedral, a minor basilica, rests on the remains of ancient Vibinum's forum—a Roman town where an honorary base dedicated to Emperor Caracalla was found, displayed at the Museo Civico Carlo Gaetano Nicastro. The museum, open since 1925, also preserves 7th-6th century BC Daunian anthropomorphic stelae—proto-human statues resembling stone sentinels.

Three km from Bovino, at Casalene locality, ruins of a large Augustan-era Roman villa (1st century BC). Inhabited until the 6th century, it yielded black-and-white mosaics, private baths, and an oil press. Site less spectacular than Aeclanum but free access, never crowded. For the picturesque, it's the perfect stop with a thermos of coffee.

activities.text: Bovino has a brigand reputation. In the 19th century, after Italian unification (1861), armed bands held the surrounding mountain area and ransomed travelers on the route from Foggia to Naples. Brigand Carmine Crocco, the 'general' of Vulture, operated in the sector. The Pro Loco organizes thematic walks 'Sulle orme dei briganti' combining hiking and history—19th-century trails, hideout caves, local anecdotes. By reservation, essentially in Italian.

Dinner in Bovino: try the ragù di brigante, slow-cooked mixed meats (pork, rabbit, beef) in red wine—rustic preparation linked to bandits who ate what they stole. Pasta with orecchiette or Puglian cavatelli. Local wine: Cacc'e Mmitte di Lucera DOC, light red very much Daunian-style, or an Aglianico from the neighboring zone. Hotels and B&Bs in town, several restored in noble palaces.

days_plan.itin_title: Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia

visits.text: Castello Orsini-Odescalchi — A Renaissance fortress begun in 1470 under Napoleone Orsini's commission, likely built by the very masons working simultaneously on the Sistine Chapel. Napoleone's brother, Cardinal Latino Orsini, served as chamberlain to Pope Sixtus IV. Construction was completed in 1495 under his son Gentil Virginio's supervision. The complex incorporates five towers on five corners and three concentric defensive walls. In 1558, Duke Paolo Giordano Orsini married Isabella de' Medici and converted the fortress into a ducal palace, bringing in the Zuccari brothers to fresco several rooms. When the Orsini line died out in 1696, the castle passed to the Odescalchi family, nephews of Pope Innocent XI, who remain the owners today. The museum route covers twenty rooms displaying weapons collections, period furniture, and paintings spanning the 15th to 19th centuries.

Anguillara Sabazia — A lakeside village perched on a promontory of the Sabatini Mountains overlooking Lake Bracciano, with the 16th-century Collegiata dell'Assunzione and medieval lanes clinging to the hillside. From the belvedere in the central piazza, you look straight across the lake to the wooded shores of Parco Regionale di Bracciano-Martignano, designated a protected natural area in 1999.

Trevignano Romano — A small fishing village on the lake's northern shore, with a parish church built on the ruins of a medieval castrum. The main piazza, perched above the water, offers one of the most sweeping panoramas of Lake Bracciano's 56.5 km² expanse. These waters have supplied Rome since the 17th century via the Acquedotto Paolo.

activities.text: Swimming on the shores of Lake Bracciano — A volcanic crater lake 160 meters deep, ranked among the cleanest lakes in central Italy. The best access points are at Trevignano and Anguillara, where you'll find pebble beaches and picnic areas within the natural park.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Villages Around Rome and the Castelli Romani
Grand Tour of Lazio: Etruscan Sites and Volcanic Lakes

visits.text: Kitsch, yes, but Brescello plays the game with sincerity. The village was the backdrop for the five Don Camillo and Peppone films shot between 1951 and 1965 with Fernandel and Gino Cervi. The crucifix that spoke to Don Camillo is still in the parish church. Combined ticket at 6 euros for all three museums.

On Piazza Matteotti, the tank from the film stands in front of the Museo Peppone e Don Camillo. Inside: Peppone's motorcycle, Don Camillo's bicycle, shooting photos and the reconstruction of Peppone's kitchen. Small but touching.

The Museo Archeologico Romano Albino Umiltà surprises in this context: Roman remains attest that Brixellum was an important center in the 2nd century. The combined ticket also includes the Guareschi museum, more recent and better curated.

activities.text: Climb up to the argine of the Po for a walk or bike ride. The crucifix that conversed with Don Camillo comes out once a year for the solemn blessing of the river. The rest of the time, it waits in the church.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

visits.text: Explore the Museo di Santa Giulia, an extraordinary monastic complex and the city's main museum housing treasures of exceptional historical and artistic importance. From the ninth-century Cross of Desiderius to the incredible frescoes of the Nuns' Choir, from the remains of ancient Roman Domus houses to the marvellous interiors of the Basilica of San Salvatore, it is part of the UNESCO site in the heart of Brescia.

Admire the Roman Archaeological Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site comprising Piazza del Foro, the Capitolium with the hall dedicated to the Winged Victory, the Republican Sanctuary, the ancient theatre and the Roman Basilica. This extraordinary complex bears witness to the greatness of Brixia, one of northern Italy's most important cities in the Roman era.

Visit Piazza Loggia, the beating heart of Brescia characterised by a splendid blend of styles with a clear Venetian imprint. The Palazzo della Loggia, built between 1492 and 1570 with contributions from Palladio and Sansovino, dominates the square alongside the Clock Tower with its ancient astronomical clock.

Discover the Pinacoteca Tosio Martinengo, one of northern Italy's most important galleries with works by Raphael, Foppa, Moretto, Romanino, Lotto, Ceruti and Hayez. The route through 21 exhibition halls offers an intense journey from late Gothic to the early nineteenth century through the great Brescian Renaissance painting.

activities.text: Climb to Brescia Castle on the Colle Cidneo, a great fortress built between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries in a commanding position over the city. A favourite destination for relaxing walks in the greenery, it houses the Luigi Marzoli Arms Museum and offers breathtaking views of the city and the Bergamo valleys.

Stroll through Piazza Paolo VI admiring the Duomo Vecchio, a rare example of Romanesque architecture with a circular plan, and the Duomo Nuovo completed in 1825. Then lose yourself in the ancient Carmine quarter with its evocative lanes, traditional taverns and bohemian atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona
Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: The Matterhorn (14,692 feet), the Alps' fifth-highest summit, is the world's most recognizable mountain for its nearly perfect pyramidal shape—the result of four intersecting glacial cirques. From Breuil—renamed Cervinia in 1936-37 at the urging of Senator Dino Lora Totino to assert the resort's Italian identity—the Lion Ridge rises toward the summit. On July 17, 1865, Valtournenche guide Jean-Antoine Carrel opened the first Italian route up the Matterhorn via this ridge, three days after Englishman Edward Whymper's triumph from Zermatt. Whymper's descent cost four companions their lives. In 1890, Carrel perished on the mountain he had conquered, caught in a storm while descending after bringing his clients to safety.

Cervinia's Blue Lake, a 45-minute walk from the village, offers the Matterhorn's reflection in turquoise waters. This glacial cirque lake at 7,064 feet is surrounded by a mineral amphitheater whose hues shift from turquoise to cobalt depending on the hour. It's the starting point for trails to the Oriondé (Duca degli Abruzzi, 9,193 feet) and Carrel (12,566 feet) refuges—the two stages of the Matterhorn ascent by the Italian route.

The Matterhorn Alpine Crossing, inaugurated July 1, 2023, links Breuil-Cervinia to Zermatt by cable car for the first time without skis, crossing the Alps' highest border crossing. The Plateau Rosa (11,417 feet) to Klein Matterhorn (12,739 feet) section crosses the Italian-Swiss frontier above the glaciers, with direct views of the Matterhorn from both flanks.

activities.text: Hike to Oriondé Refuge (Duca degli Abruzzi, 9,193 feet) from Breuil: ascend the route of the first alpinists, pass the Carrel cross, view the Matterhorn's south face. Round trip approximately 5-6 hours.

In summer, ride the cable car to Plateau Rosa (11,417 feet): panoramas of Matterhorn and Monte Rosa glaciers, summer ski slope, walking access to the seracs. In winter, international ski domain linked to Zermatt.

days_plan.itin_title: Aosta Valley Circuit: From Roman Gateway to Mont Blanc

places.name: Brindisi

visits.text: Warm marble under your palm, the sea below: the Roman Column of Brindisi marks the very end of the Via Appia. It stands 18.74 m tall, its twin collapsed in 1528, and its capital is kept at Palazzo Granafei-Nervegna. Climb the steps late in the day and the low light does all the work.

Consecrated in 1089 by Pope Urban II, Brindisi Cathedral was largely rebuilt after the 1743 earthquake. The result is a plainer interior than you might expect, with fragments of medieval floor mosaic still in place. Come in the morning: by afternoon the nave fills with cruise-ship groups.

The Tempio di San Giovanni al Sepolcro is a squat, almost windowless Templar rotunda from the 12th century. Inside, worn frescoes and a carved doorway flanked by lions are worth the ten minutes. Opening hours are unpredictable, so ask at the tourist office on Piazza Duomo before crossing the old town.

The Castello Svevo is mostly one for the outside view: the Navy still occupies it and visits are rare and strictly supervised. Frederick II began building it in 1227 to keep watch over the harbour. Walk the quayside circuit, then head for the inner port.

Pale stone, a painted ceiling and silence a few minutes from the airport: Santa Maria del Casale is the ideal last stop. Built around 1300 by Philip of Anjou, it combines two-tone banded stonework on the facade with frescoes attributed to the circle of Rinaldo da Taranto; the Last Judgement covers the entrance wall. The trial of the Templars was held here in 1310. It mainly opens in the morning, so call ahead.

The capital of the column that collapsed in 1528 is kept at Palazzo Granafei-Nervegna, in the centre of Brindisi. The building now serves as a cultural and exhibition space. It is the logical companion to the Roman Column seen on day one, and takes half an hour to walk through.

activities.text: Head down to the Lungomare Regina Margherita in the late afternoon, when the boats come in and the cafes bring out their tables. The promenade runs along the inner harbour, the one the Romans called the gateway to the East. The water-facing terraces fill up at sunset, so get there before.

If your flight leaves late in the day, the local ferry between central Brindisi and the Casale shore takes a few minutes and costs a few euros. It gives the best view of the inner harbour. The AP bus route then links Piazza Crispi, the station and the airport.

Brindisi in 2 Days: Byzantine Crypts and Torre Guaceto
Brindisi in 2 Days: Byzantine Crypts and Torre Guaceto

map_keywords: Santa Maria del Casale Church Brindisi

visits.text: Brisighella greets you with an unforgettable silhouette: three rocky pinnacles of selenite dominate the village, each crowned by a monument—the Rocca Manfrediana fortress, the Clock Tower, and the Sanctuary of Monticino. Ranked among Italy's most beautiful villages, this medieval hamlet in Ravenna province has remained remarkably intact. Start with the Via degli Asini, the village's most famous attraction. This covered, elevated street, built in the 12th century, originally served as a defensive rampart before housing the stables of carters who transported gypsum from nearby quarries with their donkeys. Its arched windows, wooden beams, and irregular paving make it unique in Italy.

Climb up to the Rocca Manfrediana, the 14th-century fortress that dominates the village. From up here, the view over the Lamone valley and hills covered with olive groves and vineyards is superb. The fortress houses the Museum of Man and Gypsum, which traces the thousand-year history of mining this mineral that shaped the village and its landscape. Allow 45 minutes for the climb, visit, and panorama.

Descend and take the path leading to the Torre dell'Orologio, perched on the second rocky pinnacle opposite the fortress. This 13th-century tower has a peculiarity: its clock shows only six hours, a historical detail that intrigues every visitor. The view from its summit complements that from the Rocca.

If you have time, make a detour to the Pieve del Tho (Pieve di San Giovanni in Ottavo), a Romanesque church located a few minutes from the center. Erected between the 8th and 10th centuries, it contains reused Roman fragments and ancient frescoes. It can be visited freely on Sunday afternoons; other days require booking.

activities.text: Brisighella sits within the Regional Park of the Vena del Gesso Romagnola, a striking landscape of white gypsum ridges, caves, and forests. Several hiking trails start directly from the village—the most accessible connects the three hills in a loop of about 1h30. For the more motivated, longer paths wind through the gypsum formations with spectacular views over the Romagna hinterland.

Brisighella is also a village of flavors. Its extra virgin olive oil PDO "Brisighello," obtained from the Nostrana variety cultivated only on these hills, was the first in Italy to obtain PDO certification in 1996. Local producers offer mill visits with tastings. Pair the oil with cured meats from Mora Romagnola, a local pig breed, and a glass of Sangiovese DOC.

Milan to Chianti Circuit: Design, Art, and Wine

places.name: Buggiano Castello

visits.text: The Palazzo Pretorio of Buggiano Castello, a building from the first half of the 14th century, displays on its restored facade 57 coats of arms of the podestàs who governed the commune from the 14th to 17th centuries. It houses the municipal historical archive and 15th-century frescoes in its halls. It's one of the most complete examples of medieval civic architecture in the Valdinievole.

The church of Madonna della Salute e San Nicolao, founded as a Benedictine monastery in the 11th century, features an austere 12th-century Romanesque campanile. The three-nave interior preserves a 13th-century baptismal font, 16th-century paintings by G. Brina, and the remains of an adjoining cloister. The castle is documented from 1038 when the "da Buggiano" family founded the abbey there.

The Rocca and its clock tower, at the village's highest point, are the remnants of the defensive structure erected by the "da Buggiano" family who, in 1167, obtained from the Emperor a diploma confirming their possessions. The clock tower was completed with its mechanism in 1510.

Uzzano Castello, 3km from Buggiano, is a hilltop village perched on the hill dominating the Pescia valley. It's renowned for producing Bianco della Valdinievole, a DOC white wine from Trebbiano Toscano grapes. The medieval castle and its white limestone lanes can be visited in an hour.

activities.text: Walk through the citrus gardens of Buggiano Castello: the exceptionally mild microclimate of the village—sheltered from the north and open to the south—has favored since the Middle Ages the cultivation of orange, lemon and citron trees in private gardens, hence the nickname "Village of Citrus." Every two years, the village cultural association organizes "La campagna dentro le mura" (The countryside within the walls), opening these secret gardens to the public.
Olive oil and wine tasting from the Buggiano hills: the terraced olive groves surrounding the village produce a recognized IGP olive oil. Several estates offer cellar visits and farm tastings.

days_plan.itin_title: Pistoia Province Circuit: Hill Towns & Thermal Spas

map_keywords: Chiesa della Madonna della Salute Buggiano

places.name: Buonconvento

visits.text: Porta Senese and ramparts: Buonconvento is one of the Italian villages that best preserves its medieval ramparts. Built from the late 13th century by Siena to protect this strategic node of Val d'Arbia on the Via Cassia, the walls still completely encircle the center. The Porta Senese, to the north, preserves its massive original wooden doors—the Porta Romana on the south side was destroyed in 1944 during the German retreat to delay the Allied advance.

Museum of Sacred Art of Val d'Arbia: Housed in the Palazzo Ricci Socini, a 19th-century building restored in Art Nouveau style in 1907 by architect Gino Chierici, this museum is a double curiosity—Sienese paintings from the 13th to 19th centuries displayed in a still-intact Liberty interior. The collection founded in 1926 by Father Don Crescenzio Massari includes the Madonna of Buonconvento by Duccio di Buoninsegna (1290-1295), Pietro Lorenzetti, Luca di Tommé, and canvases from the 17th-century Sienese school.

Church of Saints Peter and Paul and Palazzo Podestarile: The 14th-century church, rebuilt in the 18th century, was according to tradition the death place of Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg in 1313—an engraved marble stone on its left façade bears the date 1103, possibly that of its foundation. The neighboring Palazzo Podestarile, with its Clock Tower and 25 podestà coats of arms, recalls that Buonconvento was Val d'Arbia's most important administrative center.

activities.text: Nova Eroica: Every spring, Buonconvento hosts this amateur cycling ride on dirt roads (strade bianche) with routes for all levels, including families and children—an accessible version of Gaiole's Eroica.
