Chiesa dei Santi Pietro e Paolo Buonconvento

visits.text: Touristy, yes, but Verdi's birthplace in Le Roncole is worth every minute. Born here on October 10, 1813 in this countryside tavern, the composer lived here for ten years. Eight tablets with audio guides walk you through the rooms one by one. Combined ticket available with the Teatro Verdi in town.

Push open the door of the Teatro Verdi in the center of Busseto: the restored Italian-style theater still hosts concerts. The small adjoining museum displays sheet music and stage costumes. Closed Mondays.

The organ in the Church of San Michele Arcangelo in Le Roncole is the one young Verdi learned to play. The instrument dates from 1797, since restored. The church opens on request to the custodian, free entry.

activities.text: Take the Strada del Culatello south toward Polesine: the road runs along low farmhouses between poplars and cornfields, a landscape typical of the Bassa Parmense. Stop at a caseificio to watch Parmigiano-making in the morning before 10 a.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

visits.text: Nora earns your effort and rewards it: founded by Phoenicians between the 9th and 8th centuries BC, probably around 700 BC, conquered by Carthage, then by Rome in 238 BC, abandoned in the 8th century AD after Vandal and Arab raids. This is where the Nora Stele was found (late 9th-early 8th century BC), considered the oldest written document in the West—it bears the word "Shrdn," first written mention of the name Sardinia. On the site itself: Roman theater from the 1st century AD (still used for summer shows), baths with well-preserved mosaics, temple of Aesculapius, forum, Punic tophet. Rare advantage: part of the ruins is underwater, visible while snorkeling. €8.50 entry, guided tour included. Allow 1h30.

Sant'Efisio in Nora, right next to the archaeological site, is an 11th-century Romanesque church by the sea, with three naves. Major pilgrimage site for over 350 years: each May 1st, the saint leaves Cagliari in procession on an ox cart and arrives here the next day—it's the island's largest festival, with traditional costumes from all villages. Sparse interior, almost austere, but the seaside location is striking.

Cagliari, your arrival point, deserves at least half a day. The city sits on seven hills like Rome, dominated by the Castello quarter, fortified by Pisans in the 13th century. From the Bastion of Saint Remy, 360° view over the Gulf of Angels and salt marshes where flamingos live. The Santa Maria cathedral has a baffling Baroque interior. The National Archaeological Museum on Piazza Arsenale keeps the Nora Stele and nuragic bronzetti—unique pieces in the world. €7 entry. Allow 1h30.

activities.text: Lunch in Cagliari's Marina quarter, the city's colorful working-class heart. Several good addresses: Antica Cagliari for spaghetti alla bottarga (dried mullet roe), Lillicu for fregola con arselle, Crackers for meat lovers. Count on €25-35 per person with wine. Relaxed atmosphere, miles away from haute Costa Smeralda.

If you have time before the flight, Poetto beach 10 minutes from center—8 km of white sand, shallow water, summer vibe. Or San Benedetto historic market, one of Italy's largest covered markets: impressive fish market on ground floor, fruits-vegetables-cheese-charcuterie upstairs. Open mornings, closed Sunday. Good opportunity to buy pecorino sardo, bottarga, mirto to bring home.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Sardinia Loop: Coastline, Cities & Heartland
Complete Sardinia Loop: Coastline, Cities & Heartland
Sardinia's Wild Interior and Eastern Coast: 6 Days from Olbia to Cagliari

visits.text: Cala Gonone is the Gulf of Orosei's most authentic seaside resort. Built in the 1950s by families of fishermen and reconverted miners, it remains human-scale: no large hotels, just guesthouses and a lively port from which all excursions depart toward coves inaccessible by road. Facing due east: the sun disappears behind Supramonte by 3pm, so plan beach in the morning, shade in the afternoon. The Lungomare is pleasant at sunset.

The Grotte del Bue Marino, 3 km south of Cala Gonone by sea, owe their name to the Mediterranean monk seal that lived there until the 1980s ("bue marino" = sea ox). A vast karst cave up to 70m high in places, with underground lake and stalactites. Guided visit by boat only, 1h30, around €17 with round-trip shuttle. Light show through natural openings quite impressive. Book the day before in high season at calagononecrociere.it.

activities.text: Cala Luna by boat from Cala Gonone: it's the signature beach of the Gulf of Orosei, 800m of sand bordered by white cliffs, five large natural caves serving as sun shelters. The crossing takes 30 minutes, around €18 round trip with flexible return times (first departure 9am, last return 6pm). Bring picnic and water, the on-site snack bar is expensive and limited. If you're fit, walk back via the coastal trail (2h to Cala Fuili, then taxi or walk).

If you prefer autonomy, rent a no-license boat at Cala Gonone port: €120/day + fuel for a 40hp Zodiac (maximum power without license). You head south in the gulf, Cala Mariolu, Cala Biriola, Cala Sisine—all inaccessible by road. Quick briefing at departure. With skipper, €190/day, more relaxed. Book the day before via Prima Sardegna or directly at the port.

days_plan.itin_title: Sardinia's Wild Interior and Eastern Coast: 6 Days from Olbia to Cagliari

activities.text: If Lama Monachile is packed, fall back on Cala Paura, a bit north of Polignano a Mare: pebbles and rock, fewer people, same water. Parking remains the weak point. Come early or late afternoon, and don't expect natural shade.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia

places.name: Cala San Vito

visits.text: Cala San Vito, fishing hamlet nestled around a natural harbor 3 km from Polignano, is dominated by the Abbazia di San Vito Martire, 10th-century Benedictine foundation. The abbey is private, but the church opens for Sunday mass around 9 am, and exteriors, port and beach are freely visited. Beside it, a 17th-century watchtower. Mid-June, the saint departs in procession on the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

places.name: Calcata

visits.text: Monterano Antica — A ghost town abandoned after a malaria epidemic in the late 18th century. The ruins include a partially standing baroque church and an ornate fountain featuring a lion, attributed to Bernini's circle. The site sits within the Riserva Naturale Monterano, where collapsed houses disappear beneath advancing vegetation. The gradual abandonment accelerated after 1799 when French troops ravaged the area.

Calcata Vecchia — A medieval village perched on a red tuff spur in the Treja valley, declared uninhabitable by fascist decree in 1935 due to the risk of the cliff collapsing. Its residents were relocated to Calcata Nuova, built 2 km away. In the 1960s-70s, artists, intellectuals, and hippies from across Europe and America recolonized the abandoned houses, transforming the village into a creative community that thrives to this day. The 15th-century Palazzo Baronale degli Anguillara now houses the visitor center for Parco Valle del Treja. The small Chiesa del Santissimo Nome di Gesù, built in the 14th century and restored in 1793, preserves a reliquary in a 15th-century tabernacle. Local legend claims that the Holy Prepuce, stolen during the 1527 Sack of Rome, was kept here until the 1980s.

activities.text: Hiking in the Parco Regionale Valle del Treja — The Treja River, a tributary of the Tiber, has carved gorges through volcanic tuff for several kilometers. Trail 015 leads to the ruins of the ancient Faliscan city of Narce on the rocky spur opposite Calcata, with a necropolis dating to the 8th century BC. The Cascate di Monte Gelato, a series of small waterfalls and pools formed by the river, lie 5 km away.

Visiting artists' workshops in Calcata — The caves and cellars carved into the tuff house workshops for ceramics, sculpture, jewelry-making, and furniture restoration. Several artists welcome visitors into their working spaces, continuing the tradition that repopulated the village since the 1960s.

places.name: Calci

visits.text: The Certosa Monumentale di Calci, founded in 1366 by Pisan noble families, stands as one of Italy's best-preserved Carthusian monastic complexes. Transformed into a sumptuous Baroque residence during the 17th century—complete with frescoes, Carrara marble, and elaborate woodwork—it houses 15 monk cells arranged around a grand cloister, a refectory adorned with Bernardino Poccetti's Last Supper (1597), and the sacristy where the Calci Bible is displayed: an illuminated four-volume codex from 1168 that returned here in 2015 after a decade at Pisa's San Matteo Museum. Visits are guided only, by reservation.

The Natural History Museum of the University of Pisa occupies the certosa's former service quarters—granaries, cellars, wine press, stables—converted since 1979. Founded in 1591 by Grand Duke Ferdinand I de' Medici, it preserves four centuries of scientific collections: zoology, paleontology, minerals, and one of Europe's most important cetacean skeleton galleries. The granary, nearly 100 meters long, houses the collection's largest specimens.

The Pieve dei Santi Giovanni ed Ermolao, in the hamlet of La Pieve, is a late 11th-century Romanesque-Pisan building surrounded by terraced olive groves. First documented in 934, the church faces not the canonical west but toward the gate of the old castle—a detail suggesting it predated the fortified village itself.

activities.text: Hike to the Rocca della Verruca, a 13th-century Pisan Republic fortress perched at 537 meters on a rocky spur. Leonardo da Vinci surveyed the site in 1503 for the Florentine army, which made it their final stronghold during Pisa's siege—the fortress capitulated on June 18, 1503, sealing Pisan independence. Two trails connect the site from Calci or Vicopisano; ascent takes about an hour one-way. Views sweep across the Pisan plain, the Arno, and on clear days, the sea.

Stroll through the Valle Graziosa around the charterhouse. Along the stream crossing Calci, more than a hundred mills still operated a century ago. Ancient olive trees on the slopes create one of the most peaceful landscapes in the Pisan Mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

map_keywords: Pieve dei Santi Giovanni ed Ermolao Calci

places.name: Calimera

visits.text: Kalimera means good morning in Greek, and the village of Calimera carries the name without a trace of irony: Griko was still spoken fluently here in the early 20th century. Athens gave the town a marble stele in 1960 as a token of shared identity. It can be seen freely, at any hour.

The Casa-Museo della Civilta Contadina e della Cultura Grika gathers photographs, tools and documents on peasant life and on the Griko language. It is small, thoroughly local, and says far more than any information board. Opening hours depend on the volunteers, so call before making the detour.

activities.text: If the Casa-Museo is shut, fall back on the Chiesa Matrice of San Brizio, on Piazza del Sole, built in 1689 on the remains of a church of the Greek rite. The square holds most of what passes for local life. Half an hour is enough for a loop of the centre.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

map_keywords: Museum of Peasant Life and Griko Culture Calimera

visits.text: Leave Caserta heading east and plunge into the countryside hinterland. After 2 hours driving through the mountains of Irpinia, you reach Calitri—nicknamed the "Positano of Irpinia" by the Italian Touring Club. The village is perched at 530 meters altitude on a tuff ridge, at the border of three regions: Campania, Basilicata, and Puglia. Its triangular silhouette of colorful houses, stacked in parallel tiers, is visible from afar in the landscape.

Climb to Borgo Castello, the upper part of the historic center built around the ruins of the 13th-century medieval castle, erected under Frederick II. The 1980 earthquake devastated this area—then inhabited—and froze it in time. Today, the ruins have been partially restored and the Ceramics Museum is installed there. Calitri is a member of the Italian Ceramic Towns: the pottery tradition dates back to Antiquity, with kilns and workshops documented since the 17th century.

Descend into the labyrinthine centro storico of narrow lanes. You'll encounter portals in carved local stone, noble palaces that survived the earthquakes, and the famous "cupe"—underground passages carved into the rock that once served as cellars. Step through the door of the church of San Canio, the village's patron saint celebrated on May 25, whose Baroque interior contrasts with the exterior sobriety.

Walking the streets, you'll notice caves carved into the tuff beneath the houses. Some still serve to age Caciocavallo di Grotta, a stretched-curd cheese hung in these natural cellars where humidity and constant temperature ensure slow aging. It's a typical product of eastern Irpinia, and local artisans will gladly let you taste it.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a wine tasting from Irpinia at one of the surrounding estates. The region produces three great vintages: Taurasi DOCG (Aglianico, often compared to Barolo), Fiano di Avellino DOCG (mineral and elegant white), and Greco di Tufo DOCG (white with almond notes). Irpinia is one of Italian wine's best-kept secrets—the vineyards grow between 400 and 700 meters altitude, yielding wines of remarkable freshness.

Late in the day, taste local specialties: acqua sala (slices of bread soaked in salted boiling water with hard-boiled eggs and spicy oil), cavatelli with beans, and Calitri's bread, baked in a wood oven according to ancestral tradition, whose aroma fills the lanes on baking days. It's peasant cooking, no frills, that warms the heart.

days_plan.itin_title: From Naples to the Lucanian Dolomites: Secret Campania and the Amalfi Coast
Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

places.name: Camaiore

visits.text: Collegiata Santa Maria Assunta: Founded in the 13th century and profoundly remodeled in the Baroque era, this collegiate church is Camaiore's central monument. Its Romanesque façade contrasts with the decorative richness of the Baroque interior. The adjoining sacred art museum collections preserve furnishings, objects, and paintings from the 14th–16th centuries, including several noteworthy works of local provenance.

San Pietro Abbey: Founded by Benedictine monks between the 8th and 13th centuries, this three-nave Romanesque abbey with bell tower constitutes one of the oldest testimonies of Christianity in Versilia. Accessible on foot from the center via an olive-lined path, it's approached through a 14th-century gate preserving part of the original convent walls. The sober architecture in local limestone reflects Benedictine austerity.

Pieve dei Santi Giovanni e Stefano: Erected in the 12th century at the junction of the Via Francigena (of which Camaiore is the 26th stage), this Romanesque parish church has a bell tower with twin windows on three levels. Inside, the baptismal font was carved from a 3rd-century BC Roman sarcophagus—a characteristic reuse of medieval religious architecture.

Archaeological Museum of Palazzo Tori Massoni: Installed in a Renaissance palace, this museum preserves discoveries covering prehistoric, Ligurian, Etruscan, Roman, and medieval periods. The Camaiore region (from the Roman Campus Major, the great plain) was inhabited since the Neolithic, as attested by finds from the woods of Lucese.

activities.text: Hiking in the hills of Versilia around Camaiore: The hills rising toward the Apuan Alps offer routes through vineyards, olive groves, and perched villages like Monteggiori, Casoli, or Gombitelli, with views of the sea and countryside. Camaiore is an ideal starting point for hikes toward Monte Prana.

days_plan.itin_title: Lucca Province Circuit: Hill Towns and Coast

map_keywords: Pieve dei Santi Giovanni e Stefano Camaiore

visits.text: Monastery of Camaldoli: founded in 1046, roughly twenty years after the hermitage, on a former pilgrim hostel called Fontebuona for the quality of its water. The current monastic building was rebuilt from the 16th century and completed in 1611. The church contains seven panels by Giorgio Vasari, including a main altarpiece depicting the Deposition from the Cross. The library, founded in 1622 with a coffered ceiling painted with the Evangelists, held hundreds of codices and incunabula before the Napoleonic suppression of 1810. The monastery's historic pharmacy, heir to a tradition dating back to the Camaldolese origins, produces and sells natural remedies, liqueurs and body-care products according to recipes handed down for centuries.

Eremo di San Romualdo: hermitage founded around 1023 by Saint Romuald of Ravenna at 1,100 meters, 3 km from the communal monastery — the very distance representing the intended separation between eremitic and cenobitic life. Romuald installed the first five hermit cells and the oratory dedicated to the Holy Savior Transfigured, consecrated in 1027 by the Bishop of Arezzo. The current enclosure contains twenty cells. Among the spaces open to visitors: Saint Romuald's former cell, the 16th-century chapter house, and the church whose baroque facade with two towers dates from 1713–1714. The Camaldolese order, a Benedictine branch combining eremitism and cenobitism, is distinguished from other Benedictines by its white habit and full beard.

activities.text: Hike through the Camaldoli forest: the monumental forest surrounding the hermitage is composed mainly of centuries-old white firs planted by the monks for their commercial value — their timber was used notably for the construction of the dome of Florence's Duomo and the fleet of Pisa and Livorno. Marked trails lead to the Laghetto Traversari, an artificial pond dug in the early 15th century by the monks to raise fish, now naturalized and incorporated into the Camaldoli biogenetic reserve.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

visits.text: Head to the Sila plateau, Calabria's "green lung." At 73,695 hectares, this national park extends between 1,000 and 1,928 meters altitude (Monte Botte Donato). Begin with the Giants of Sila Nature Reserve, at Fallistro, between Camigliatello Silano and Silvana Mansio. You'll find 58 Corsican black pines - an endemic variety of the plateau - nearly 400 years old, reaching 45 meters high with trunks 2 meters in diameter. This forest was planted in the 17th century by the Mollo barons. In the 1980s, Baroness Paola Manes-Mollo chained herself to a tree to prevent logging planned by a farmer who wanted to plant potatoes. Allow 45 minutes for the marked trail among these plant cathedrals.

Continue to Lake Cecita, the largest of the Sila's artificial lakes, at 1,130 meters altitude. By the lake, the Cupone Visitor Center offers a botanical garden, a wolf museum, and a wildlife observatory. The Fossiata and Gallopane forests surrounding the lake are among the park's most beautiful. If you're lucky, you'll spot reintroduced deer, roe deer, or black squirrels - an endemic subspecies of southern Italy.

activities.text: Take the road to Lake Arvo (1,278 m altitude), where the village of Lorica offers electric boat rides with spectacular views of the surrounding mountains. The trail around the lake is family-friendly - allow about 2 hours for the complete loop. In summer, operators also offer kayaking and canoeing.

If you pass through San Giovanni in Fiore, step inside the Florense Abbey, founded by Joachim of Fiore around 1189 - this visionary Cistercian monk is one of the most fascinating figures of the Calabrian Middle Ages. The abbey preserves Romanesque and Gothic elements. Also enjoy mountain specialties: mpanata (soup with ricotta and stale bread) and Sila porcini mushrooms.

days_plan.itin_title: Calabria: From Cosenza to Reggio, Between Mountains and Ionian Sea

places.name: Camogli

visits.text: First glimpse of Camogli from the sea or the corniche: a wall of seven- or eight-story houses painted in Naples yellow, ochre, and terracotta pink, with their feet in the water. Trompe-l'oeil everywhere on the façades—pediments, pilasters, false windows, false balconies—painted to imitate the architectural ornaments of palaces at lower cost (the façades are plaster and brick, not carved stone), and to signal the house to sailors returning from offshore: each family had its palette. The village name supposedly comes from casa moglie, the house of wives: while the men sailed for months, the women ran the village. Park up top at piazza Matteotti, descend on foot to the port in 10 minutes.

The Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta has dominated the little port since the 12th century, remodeled several times, current façade from the 19th. Late Baroque interior, polychrome marbles, a silver Saint Fortunato (town patron) carried in procession on the second Sunday of May. The evening before, the village lights traditional fires on the beach representing the old Porto and Pineto quarters. And on Sunday, it's the Sagra del Pesce: three tons of fish fried in a 6-meter diameter pan, entered in the Guinness Book of Records.

The Abbey of San Fruttuoso is the day's highlight. Wedged at the back of a cove between Camogli and Portofino, it's accessible only on foot (2 hours' walk from Camogli via San Rocco) or by boat (30 minutes, €15 round-trip). Legend: in the 8th century, Greek monks supposedly brought the relics of Saint Fructuosus of Tarragona, a Catalan bishop burned alive under Valerian in 259, while fleeing the Arab conquest of Spain. Rebuilt around the year 1000 by Adelaide, widow of Emperor Otto I. In the 13th century, the Dorias added their family tomb—the famous tombs in black and white marble bands you see on the ground floor. Medio-Byzantine dome adorned with 17 arcades.

At 17 meters depth in the bay of San Fruttuoso rests the Christ of the Abyss. A 2.5-meter bronze statue, arms raised in blessing, submerged on August 22, 1954 at the initiative of diver Duilio Marcante in memory of his friend Dario Gonzatti, the first Italian to use autonomous diving equipment, who died there four years earlier. Sculpted by Guido Galletti, cast from donated bells and naval elements. Restored in 2003-2004 after corrosion tore off a hand. Dive requires Level 1 minimum. Non-divers can see a replica in the church.

activities.text: Hike from Camogli to San Rocco to Punta Chiappa. 1.5 hours one way, moderate elevation gain, through Portofino Regional Park: pine forests, olive groves, old churches like San Nicolò di Capodimonte. Punta Chiappa is a flat tongue of rock jutting into the sea—you swim there, you picnic. A small ferry goes back up to Camogli for those who don't want to walk back. Good shoes, water, early departure in summer.

Taste the focaccia di Recco, just 4 kilometers away. Not the usual Ligurian focaccia—this one's unleavened, two very thin sheets of dough filled with fresh stracchino, baked at 320°C, crispy outside, molten inside. IGP certified since 2015. Manuelina in Recco is the historic institution (since 1885). Expect €12-15 per portion. Better to get there by train from Camogli (5 minutes).

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Beaches in Italy: Secluded Coves and Turquoise Waters
Genoa to Sestri Levante via the Tigullio: 2 Days on the Riviera di Levante
Deep Dive into Tigullio & Golfo Paradiso: 3 Days on the Eastern Riviera
Riviera di Levante in 1 Days - Tigullio Essentials
6-Day Grand Tour of the Riviera di Levante

map_keywords: Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta Camogli

visits.text: Campli - a medieval town of 7,000 inhabitants at the foot of the Monti Gemelli, between the Siccagno and Fiumicino valleys. The Scala Santa is a replica of Pontius Pilate's staircase in Jerusalem, brought to Rome by Saint Helena in the 4th century. Campli's version, built in 1480 on commission from the Farnese family, has 28 steps that pilgrims climb on their knees.

activities.text: Quick stop at the Palazzo Farnese, a 15th-century Renaissance building testifying to the powerful Roman family's patronage in the region.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

visits.text: 300 inhabitants clinging to a sandstone spur at 500 meters altitude—Civitacampomarano is the village where street art held abandonment at bay. Since 2016, the CVTà Street Fest invites international artists annually to paint the walls: 50+ murals today, signed by Alice Pasquini, Francisco Bosoletti, Add Fuel, Jaune, Cinta Vidal, Icy & Sot. Above the main gate, the word RESISTE painted in red on cracked background, responding to the national joke 'Il Molise non esiste' (Molise doesn't exist). The festival runs late May-early June, but the works remain visible year-round. Interactive map available at Casa Cuoco.

The Castello Angioino dominates Civitacampomarano. Built in the 14th century under Charles of Anjou, Di Sangro coat of arms above the main portal—the family obtained the fief from Alfonso I of Aragon in the 15th as reward for betraying the Angevins. Inside, courtyard with a Samnite fountain adorned with four zoomorphic faces—reused vestige. Casa Cuoco, steps away, is the birthplace of Vincenzo Cuoco, Enlightenment philosopher and historian (1770-1823) who wrote the Historical Essay on the Neapolitan Revolution.

Molise hydraulic anomaly: Lake Guardialfiera, 20 minutes south, is an artificial reservoir created in 1976 on the Biferno. Peculiarity: during very low water (dry summer), an ancient Roman bridge reemerges from the waters—the ponte romanico, vestige of the road linking Larino to Bovianum. Fishermen in boats report you can still make out the submerged pillars even when water is high. Picnic area provided, rich birdlife (grey heron, kingfisher).

Arrive in Campobasso late afternoon via the winding roads of central Molise. Regional capital at 700 meters altitude, the city stretches its alleyways along a hillside dominated by Castello Monforte. We'll save the detailed visit for tomorrow. Tonight, just a first reconnaissance of the medieval centro storico (upper) and Murattian centro (lower, 19th century, orthogonal plan). Hotel in the modern city, more practical for parking.

Castello Monforte dominates Campobasso from 800 meters altitude. Quadrangular, stocky, the bulk dates to the 15th and 16th centuries, after the 1456 earthquake collapsed the original. From the terrace, panorama over the Matese and, on clear days, all the way to the Adriatic. Next door stands the small church of Santa Maria del Monte. The ascent can be made via a tree-lined avenue, or by car if the slope discourages you. Ideal at sunset, when the city lights up below.

To understand who these warrior-shepherds were who held Rome at bay during three Samnite Wars (343-290 BC), stop by the Museo Sannitico in Palazzo Mazzarotta down in the city. Samnite weapons, armor and sculptures found at regional sites—Pietrabbondante, Saepinum, Bovianum. Small but well done. Crested helmets, bronze belts, votive statuettes. Budget-friendly admission. Allow 1 hour, and leave with mental keys for Pietrabbondante tomorrow.

Bring good shoes: Campobasso's historic center stretches on steep slopes along the castle hill, climbing and descending relentlessly. San Giorgio church (12th century, Romanesque, probably the city's oldest), built atop a pagan temple. San Bartolomeo church (13th century). San Leonardo (13th century). To try en route: Campobasso confetti, artisan sugared almonds made here since the 14th century. Several confectioneries on Corso Vittorio Emanuele.

Green breath at the heart of the Murattian city: Villa De Capoa, 18th-century Italian-style garden. Statues, geometric pathways, castle views. Campobasso's lung, frequented by locals on weekends. Next door, the Museo dei Misteri recounts the Corpus Domini procession unique to Campobasso: processional machines invented in the 18th century by Paolo Saverio Di Zinno, where children and adults in costumes float in the air on camouflaged metal structures. Spectacular—at least see it on video if you miss the procession (60 days after Easter).

activities.text: Casacalenda, 25 minutes from Civitacampomarano, hosts Molise Cinema Festival every early August, created in 2003 to bring independent cinema to isolated areas. Open-air screenings in palace courtyards, meetings with Italian actors and directors. If passing early August, the detour is worth it. The village itself, perched at 600 meters, is pleasant—Riserva Bosco Casale, WWF oasis, nice hikes in beech forest.

Dinner in Campobasso featuring aged cheeses and Molise charcuterie. To order: pezzata, mutton boiled long with garlic, parsley and tomato—true transhumant shepherd cuisine, festive dish. Or sagne e fagioli, homemade lasagnettes with cannellini beans. Red Tintilia to accompany.

Lamb lunch with cacio e ova, Molise peasant dish: lamb stewed with beaten eggs, pecorino and parsley, sauce coating the meat. A few downtown trattorias still serve it. Pair with Tintilia, an endemic red grape of Molise, little known outside the region—good chance to taste before it becomes fashionable.

Visit a Tintilia winery around Campobasso (Sepino, Frosolone, Macchiagodena). The grape, nearly extinct in the 1970s, was saved by a few stubborn producers. PDO since 2011. Dense, spicy red wine, ideal with Molise red meats. Several cellars welcome for tastings by reservation. Allow 1.5 hours, tasting plus vineyard tour.

Grand Tour of Molise in 9 Days: Pescara to Naples Through the Samnium
Grand Tour of Molise in 9 Days: Pescara to Naples Through the Samnium

places.name: Campodimele

visits.text: Campodimele, perched at 647 meters between the Ausoni and Aurunci Mountains, holds the European title of "Village of Eternal Youth." In 2000, it counted 14 centenarians among 660 inhabitants. In 1985, the World Health Organization sent researchers on site: they discovered a cholesterol rate half the Italian average and very low blood pressure. A 2012 study by La Sapienza University in Rome identified a mutation of the ANGPTL3 gene that protects against cholesterol and diabetes. The village is accessible only on foot via its cobblestone lanes that wind between stone houses, covered passages, and small gardens.

The Church of San Michele Arcangelo, at the village's highest point, dates from the 11th century and was built on a former pagan worship site. Damaged by an earthquake, it was faithfully rebuilt. Inside, a tabernacle, ancient paintings, and wooden statues merit attention.

The Monastery of Sant'Onofrio, founded in the 11th century, suffered several destructions over the centuries before being restored in the 1980s. Its position below the fortified enclosure offers a viewpoint over the fertile valley below.

activities.text: Walk the medieval ramparts: the fortified enclosure, erected to protect inhabitants from Saracen raids, comprises twelve recently restored cylindrical towers. A path known to locals as the "Lovers' Walk" (Passeggiata dell'Amore) circles around it, offering panoramic views of the green valleys and Aurunci Mountains. On the Municipio square, an elm planted in 1789 allegedly commemorates the French Revolution.

Tasting of local products: the secret of longevity also lies in diet—little red meat, plenty of fruits, vegetables, and legumes from the garden, olive oil from the surrounding terraces. The village is part of "The Most Beautiful Villages in Italy" and has received the orange flag from the Italian Touring Club.

days_plan.itin_title: Latina Province Circuit: Lepini Mountains and Coast

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Michele Arcangelo Campodimele

visits.text: You descend a ramp, the temperature drops ten degrees: the Ipogei Lagrasta in Canosa di Puglia are carved into calcarenite, via Generale Cadorna. Three Daunian tombs from the 4th century BC; Lagrasta I has nine rooms arranged in a cruciform plan. Objects found are in Bari's archaeological museum. The visit is by reservation: call the day before.

The Basilica di San Sabino in Canosa dates from 1080 and preserves two rarities: the episcopal chair signed by Romualdo and the tomb of Bohemond of Taranto, son of Robert Guiscard, in a separate chapel. The mausoleum is open-air, against the church's flank. Twenty minutes is enough, but avoid siesta hour: everything closes between 1 PM and 3 PM.

Dating from the 6th century, the Battistero di San Giovanni dominates the Parco Archeologico di San Giovanni in Canosa. The plan and mosaics recall that the city was a major episcopal seat before disappearing from maps. The site is open-air, no shade. Come in the morning or late afternoon, and bring water.

Continue to the Parco Archeologico di San Leucio, on a hill planted with olive trees outside Canosa: it preserves the remains of an ancient temple reused as an early Christian basilica. The panorama over the Ofanto valley is the real bonus. Opening varies, often morning only: check before going up.

activities.text: Locals call their town "little Rome," for its seven hills. The wink is also drinkable: Rosso Canosa earned its DOC in 1979, from vines in the Ofanto valley. A few wineries receive by appointment. Call the day before, you don't just show up here.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia
Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

visits.text: The white sandstone cliff surges from the hills like a raised fist. Little remains of the Castello di Canossa, gnawed by landslides, but the position is striking. This is where the phrase 'andare a Canossa' was born, known in every European language. Closed Mondays.

Almost nothing survives of the triple ring of walls that protected the fortress, and that's precisely what makes the place poignant. The cliff is roughly 80 m long by 30 wide. Foundations show through; archaeologists unearthed them in 1877 and 1893. National monument since 1878.

Visit the Museo Naborre Campanini, housed in a building set against the old castle walls. Model of the reconstructed castello, twelfth-century baptismal fonts, manuscript by Donizone of Canossa. The ticket includes the guided tour. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10 a.m.–5 p.m. weekdays, 10 a.m.–6 p.m. weekends.

activities.text: On 27 January 1077, Emperor Henry IV waited three days barefoot in the snow outside Canossa to obtain Pope Gregory VII's forgiveness. Matilda arbitrated. Panels on site tell the episode in detail. Bring good shoes for the climb to the cliff.

days_plan.itin_title: Matilda's Lands: The Countess's Castles in 5 Days

visits.text: Capalbio is a medieval village whose urban layout has remained virtually intact since the 15th century. Its double-walled ramparts with walkway, built between the 11th and 15th centuries, can be walked entirely. The Porta Senese preserves its original massive wooden doors from the 15th century. Inside, the Rocca Aldobrandesca adjoins the Palazzo Collacchioni, a richly frescoed Renaissance noble residence. The village was given in 805 by Charlemagne to the abbey of Saints Anastasius and Vincent alle Tre Fontane in Rome—one of the oldest donation acts in the Tuscan territory.

The church of San Nicola, built in the Middle Ages atop the hill around which the village wraps, is an architectural palimpsest: Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance are layered one upon another. It preserves a fresco cycle from the Umbrian-Sienese school, and the Oratory of Providence outside the walls contains 18th-century frescoes attributed to Pinturicchio's workshop.

Talamone, 25 km north on the coastal road, is a tiny port dominated by the Rocca degli Aldobrandeschi, a medieval fortress in excellent condition perched on a rocky promontory plunging into the sea. In 1860, Garibaldi stopped here with his Thousand to resupply arms before sailing to Sicily—a plaque commemorates the event. The village retains the atmosphere of an authentic fishing port, with a few hundred permanent residents.

activities.text: The Tarot Garden (Giardino dei Tarocchi), 2 km from Capalbio at the foot of the hamlet of Capalbiole, is a sculpture park created by Franco-American artist Niki de Saint Phalle starting in 1979, inspired by Gaudí's Park Güell in Barcelona. The 22 major arcana of the tarot are represented by monumental sculptures covered in ceramic mosaics, mirrors, and colored glass. Saint Phalle lived for several years inside the Judgement sculpture, transformed into an apartment. The garden opened to the public in 1998.

Walk along Capalbio's rampart walkway with panoramas over the Maremman countryside, the Tyrrhenian Sea, and on clear days Giglio Island and Monte Argentario. Local legend reports that Tiburzi, the Maremma's most famous brigand, spent much of his 19th-century flight here.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Grosseto Province

visits.text: Villa Baciocchi occupies the site of the former castle of the Della Gherardesca counts, who founded Capannoli in the Middle Ages. The current building, in late Baroque and Neoclassical style, was restructured in the mid-18th century, then acquired in 1833 by Count Felice Baciocchi, husband of Elisa Bonaparte, Napoleon's sister. The villa now houses a Zoological Museum (taxidermied animals and dioramas) and an Archaeological Museum of the Valdera. The botanical park contains 160 plant species and 12 monumental trees.

The hamlet of Santo Pietro Belvedere preserves the urban structure of a medieval castle-borgo mentioned as early as 1175 in a treaty between Pisa and Lucca. The bell tower of San Pietro church, built by Luigi Bellincioni between 1881 and 1883, is founded on the remains of the old castle tower—whose Ghibelline battlements were still visible in 1789. The Oratorio di San Rocco contains a painted panel of the Virgin and Child attributed to the school of Benozzo Gozzoli.

activities.text: The municipality of Capannoli is part of the Pisan Hills Wine Route. Valdera wine estates offer tastings of local wines (Sangiovese, Vermentino, Trebbiano) paired with typical products: olive oil, truffles, pecorino.

Hiking or cycling on marked CAI trails crossing the hills between Capannoli, Peccioli, and Terricciola. The landscape of vineyards, olive groves, and isolated farms corresponds to the classic model of 16th-century Tuscan rural settlement.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

activities.text: Head down to Capitolo, Monopoli's beach frazione: long strip of equipped lidos, beach clubs, and free sections, with ample parking. It's the services option, not the nature option. A few minutes' drive from the center. In July-August, reserve a sunbed in the morning or arrive before 10 AM.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia

visits.text: Palazzo Farnese - An absolute masterpiece by Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola, this palace built between 1559 and 1575 for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese the Younger rests on the foundations of a pentagonal fortress begun in 1530 by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger. Vignola kept the five-sided shape but hollowed out the center to create an extraordinary circular courtyard with double superimposed porticoes. The Scala Regia, a helical staircase supported by 30 Doric columns, is so wide that - according to legend - the cardinal rode up it on horseback to the piano nobile. The halls are covered with 6,000 m² of Mannerist frescoes by brothers Taddeo and Federico Zuccari. The Sala del Mappamondo presents a map of the known world in 1574 painted by Giovanni Antonio Vanosino, surmounted on the ceiling by a representation of the zodiac. The Sala degli Angeli (or degli Echi) conceals an acoustic effect: two people whispering at opposite corners can hear each other as if standing side by side - a cardinal's stratagem for monitoring conversations.

Giardini Farnesiani - Behind the palace, two secret gardens (one summer, one winter) extend the architecture into the open air, with fountains, boxwood parterres, artificial grottos (Grotto of the Satyrs, Grotto of the Tartars), and statues. Higher up the hillside, the monumental park extends through woods to the Casina del Piacere, an isolated hunting lodge that served as summer residence for President Luigi Einaudi (1948-1955). The gardens are closed on Sundays and holidays.

Via Dritta and the town of Caprarola - Vignola wasn't content with just the palace: he had part of the medieval town razed to trace the Via Dritta, a 500-meter straight artery rising from the lower square to the palace piazzale, creating a theatrical perspective. The tufa and peperino houses of the side alleys preserve the atmosphere of a Tuscia Viterbese village.

activities.text: Tasting of Cimini Mountain hazelnuts - Caprarola lies at the heart of the nocciola dei Cimini production zone, a round, fragrant hazelnut used in creams, cakes, and torroni. The town's bakeries offer them in every form.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Lazio: Etruscan Sites and Volcanic Lakes

visits.text: Caraglio, at the entrance to Valle Grana, houses the Filatoio Rosso, one of Europe's oldest silk mills, built in 1678. The red brick building now hosts the Piedmont Silk Museum. Valle Grana stretches twenty kilometers between the Cottian and Maritime Alps, climbing to Punta Tempesta (2,679 m).

Climb to the Sanctuary of San Magno at 1,761 meters altitude, at the head of Valle Grana. In 1475, Enrico Allemandi built the first Gothic chapel. Growing devotion required expansion in 1514—the decorations by Giovanni Botoneri, still visible, retain their original colors. The current sanctuary was completed in 1716 with the high altar added in 1775 and side porticos between 1861 and 1868. Excavations in 1894 unearthed a Roman altar dedicated to Mars and coins dating to around 250 AD, proof of occupation since imperial Roman times. Among the ex-votos hung inside, numerous portraits of cattle: the saint is considered protector of livestock.

The alpine pastures surrounding Castelmagno are the birthplace of Castelmagno DOP, a whole cow's milk cheese considered one of Italy's oldest. Produced only in the communes of Castelmagno, Pradleves, and Monterosso Grana according to aging techniques passed down through generations, it obtained protected designation of origin status. The village of San Pietro Monterosso preserves a settlement of dozens of Babaciu, life-size wooden figures inhabiting the alleyways.

activities.text: Ascent to Colle Fauniera (2,481 m) from the Sanctuary of San Magno, a pass famous for Giro d'Italia stages. A monument honors Marco Pantani. 360° views over the plain and border ridges.
Castelmagno DOP tasting with alpine producers in Castelmagno or Pradleves, with visit to an artisanal cheese dairy (aging in natural caves).

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Valleys of Piedmont: Occitan Alps, Lakes & Baroque Savoy

places.name: Caramanico Terme

visits.text: Caramanico Terme - a thermal village of 1,900 inhabitants on a spur at 650 meters, at the confluence of the Orfento and Orta rivers in the heart of Parco Nazionale della Majella. The sulfurous springs have been exploited since Roman times; modern thermal baths use the waters for respiratory and rheumatological treatments.

Chiesa di Santa Maria Maggiore - a 1476 Gothic building with a façade carved with plant and animal motifs. The interior preserves 15th-century frescoes, a 14th-century wooden crucifix, and a 16th-century Flemish tapestry depicting the Virgin and Child.

activities.text: Hike through the Gola dell'Orfento - a 6-kilometer gorge carved by the Orfento torrent into the Majella limestone, accessible from Caramanico. Habitat of peregrine falcon and otter.
Thermal cure at Caramanico's establishments - sulfurous water treatments recommended for respiratory conditions, open from May to November.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

map_keywords: Chiesa di Santa Maria Maggiore Caramanico

places.name: Carmignano

visits.text: Pontormo's Visitation (1528-1530) is preserved in the Church of Saints Michael and Francis in Carmignano—currently undergoing restoration for water infiltration. During the works, the painting is temporarily displayed at the Villa Medici of Poggio a Caiano. The painting (202 × 156 cm, oil on wood panel) depicts the meeting of Mary and Elizabeth in a city street, surrounded by two witnesses with fixed, vacant gazes. Acid colors—reds, greens, and iridescent grays—elongated bodies apparently lifted on tiptoe, monumental drapery: Florentine Mannerism at its most accomplished. American artist Bill Viola drew inspiration from it for his video The Greeting (1995).

The Tumuli of Montefortini and Boschetti at Comeana, in the hills below the village of Artimino, are monumental tombs from the Orientalizing period (7th century BC) among the best preserved in central Tuscany. The Montefortini tumulus, about 60 meters in diameter, houses two burial chambers accessible for visits.

activities.text: Hiking or cycling through the vineyards of the Carmignano DOCG route, between the medieval village of Artimino and the wine estates of the Montalbano hills. In October the Palio dei Ciuchi takes place, a traditional race of the town's four neighborhoods on donkeys in medieval costumes.

days_plan.itin_title: The Finest Stops Around Florence in 7 days

map_keywords: Chiesa dei Santi Michele e Francesco Carmignano

visits.text: Quick morning detour via Selva di Fasano, a hamlet perched at 400 metres amid an oak forest—fresh air, panoramas over the coast and the Valle d'Itria. It's been the hill station for Apulians since the early 20th century. A few Liberty villas, game restaurants, and the belvedere sweeping from Ostuni to the Adriatic. Brief halt but refreshing after yesterday's underground galleries.

Ceglie Messapica, one of the most authentic towns of the Valle d'Itria—less touristy than Ostuni, which lies right next door. Self-proclaimed and recognised gastronomic capital of Puglia: one of its restaurants won the region's first Michelin star in 1996. In the centre, the Castello Ducale (14th century, on Norman foundations) flanks Piazza Plebiscito, with its clock tower. Four Messapian megalithic circuits from the 8th century BC still encircle the old town.

Carovigno, final stop: whitewashed historic centre à la Ostuni but quieter, dominated by the Castello Dentice di Frasso (15th-17th century), recognisable by its spur tower. The town is small, you can walk round it in an hour, but it mainly serves as a base for the nature reserve.

activities.text: Torre Guaceto Nature Reserve: 3,300 hectares, 8 km of Adriatic coastline preserved between Brindisi and Carovigno, jointly managed by WWF Italia and the state. Sandy beaches framed by dunes up to 10 metres high, marshes where herons and bitterns nest, and nesting zone for the Caretta caretta turtle. The 16th-century Aragonese tower that gave the site its name (from the Arabic Al Gawsit, the place of fresh water) guards the entrance. Options for walking, cycling (dedicated trail from Serranova), diving and snorkelling.

Aperitif in Ceglie Messapica on Piazza Plebiscito, when the square transforms into an open-air stage (mid-July to August, almost every evening: jazz, classical, folk). The Antico Caffè, founded in 1861 on Corso Garibaldi, still serves espresso just as it did on opening day—this is where the village elders gather for their daily ritual.

days_plan.itin_title: Puglia: 3 days through the Murgia Barese, from Polignano's cliffs to the Tarantine ravines
The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

visits.text: Alberto III Pio transformed the medieval fortress of the Pio into a Renaissance residence in the 16th century, with a Bramantesque-style courtyard of honor. The Palazzo dei Pio houses three museums, the library and the archives. The Torre Passerino from 1320 and the Uccelliera from 1480 frame the castle's silhouette.

The Piazza dei Martiri stretches over about 17,000 square meters: it's one of the largest in Italy. The name recalls the sixteen civilians and partisans shot here by the fascists on August 16, 1944. The porticoes that surround it give the whole a theatrical solemnity.

The Museo Monumento al Deportato shakes you: designed in 1973, it evokes deportation through contemporary artworks and testimonies. Free the first Sunday of the month. Not an easy museum, but a necessary one.

activities.text: Stroll under the porticoes of Piazza dei Martiri and spot the Duomo, facing the Palazzo. The Museo della Xilografia, dedicated to Ugo da Carpi, inventor of chiaroscuro woodcut around 1516, is integrated into the Palazzo tour. Single ticket.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

visits.text: Climb the 90 steps of the Castello di Carpineti mastio: the 360° view takes in the Apennines, the Secchia valley and, on clear days, the Alps. A panoramic binocolo is installed at the top. The small museum in the tower traces Matilda's life panel by panel. Weekends only, 10 a.m.–12.30 p.m. and 3–7 p.m.

After the Canossa meeting in 1077, Matilda chose Carpineti to host Pope Gregory VII. The castle was then nicknamed 'la nuova Roma'. It also received Popes Urban II and Paschal II, and in 1092 the assembly that decided to continue the war against Henry IV.

The centro storico of Carpineti, huddled around the Palazzo degli Amorotti, merits a ten-minute stop. Amorotto, a sixteenth-century bandit-lord, ruled these mountains after Matilda's death. The borgo is quiet, a few bars and an open view over the valley.

activities.text: If the day is limpid from the summit of Monte Antoniano (over 900 m), search out the Alps on the northern horizon. The castle itself sits on a rocky spur accessible only by a steep provincial road. Fill up with petrol before climbing.

The small Romanesque church of Sant'Andrea, built by Matilda inside the fortified complex, preserves elements of proto-Romanesque architecture. No fixed hours: it's generally open during the castle's visiting slots.

days_plan.itin_title: Matilda's Lands: The Countess's Castles in 5 Days

places.name: Carpineto Romano

visits.text: Norma and Parco Archeologico di Norba — Norma sits on the 'Rave,' a limestone spur at 433 m plunging over 400 m sheer above the Pontine Plain. One kilometer from the modern village lie the ruins of ancient Norba, founded in the 5th century BC by the Volsci as a fortress controlling the plain. The 2.5 km circuit of opus polygonale walls—massive limestone blocks dry-fitted without mortar—culminates in two acropolises. Norba sided with Marius against Sulla and was destroyed in reprisal around 82 BC; abandoned, it was never rebuilt. From the site, on clear days the panorama stretches to Nettuno, Terracina, and the Pontine Islands.

Segni — A village at 668 m in the Monti Lepini with Cyclopean walls from the Republican Roman era among the best preserved in Lazio. The Porta Saracena, a monumental arch in 3-meter-high polygonal blocks dating to the 4th-3rd century BC, was frequently reproduced by Grand Tour artists. The Cattedrale di San Pietro e Paolo preserves a 12th-century Romanesque apse.

Carpineto Romano — A village at 745 m in the heart of the Monti Lepini, a feudal holding of the Colonna from the 14th to 17th centuries, with a preserved medieval historic center of sloping lanes and several noble palaces. The 16th-century Collegiata di Santa Maria Assunta preserves an altarpiece from the Roman school.

activities.text: Hiking the trails of the Monti Lepini around Carpineto — The limestone massif offers routes between 700 and 1,500 m altitude through beech and oak forests. The villages of Segni, Norma, Bassiano, and Sermoneta are all accessible via marked trails of the Comunità Montana dei Monti Lepini.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Villages Around Rome and the Castelli Romani

map_keywords: Cattedrale di San Pietro e Paolo Segni
Collegiata di Santa Maria Assunta Carpineto Romano

visits.text: Before leaving Lunigiana, stop at Bagnone, on the route to Carrara (15 minutes' detour from Pontremoli). This small medieval village clings to a hillside above the torrent of the same name, which rushes down from the Apennines forming natural waterfalls. The castle, dominated by an imposing cylindrical keep, was built in the 14th century by the Malaspina - the powerful feudal family who controlled all of Lunigiana for centuries and sheltered Dante during his exile. The village divides into two parts: the upper section around the castle, and the lower, the old merchant quarter called 'Gutula', with its arcades and artisan workshops. Half an hour suffices to wander the alleys and admire the 14th-century medieval bridge over the torrent.

Arriving in Carrara, head up to the quarries of the Fantiscritti basin. Since Roman times (the port of Luna already exported marmor Lunensis under Julius Caesar), the Apuan Alps have been carved by quarries that supplied the raw material for some of the greatest works of Western sculpture. Michelangelo came personally to choose his blocks - it was Carrara marble that gave birth to the David (now in Florence) and the Pietà (St Peter's Basilica, Rome). Donatello, Bernini and Canova used it after him. The open-air museum at Fantiscritti, free of charge, traces the evolution of extraction techniques. The spectacle of white walls cut into giant tiers, like an amphitheatre carved into the mountain, is breathtaking.

Continue to the village of Colonnata, 8 km from Carrara, perched on the mountainside amid the quarries. This hamlet of 300 inhabitants is famous throughout Italy for its lardo - not simple lard, but an exceptional cured meat prepared since around the year 1000. The fat layer from the pig's back is seasoned with aromatic herbs and sea salt, then matured for 6 to 10 months in basins carved from marble, the 'conche'. In the past, this was the quarrymen's meal, which they slipped into their bread loaves with tomatoes to face the steep climbs and exhausting extraction work. Taste it sliced paper-thin on lightly warmed bread.

Descend into Carrara's historic centre to Piazza Alberica, lined with noble palaces with marble facades, then the Duomo (Cathedral of Sant'Andrea), built between the 11th and 14th centuries in local white marble, with its Gothic rose window. The town also preserves the Malaspina-Cybo Castle, transformed into a princely residence during the Renaissance.

activities.text: Tour operators offer guided 4x4 visits into the active quarries, including underground quarries - veritable cathedrals carved into the mountain. The Ravaccione gallery, accessible through the old marble railway tunnels (the 'Marmifera'), is where Michelangelo allegedly spent three years searching for the perfect block for the Pietà. Allow 2 to 3 hours for a complete visit with lardo tasting in Colonnata.

days_plan.itin_title: From Lunigiana to Cinque Terre: Between Tuscany and Liguria

places.name: Casale Monferrato

visits.text: Admire the Cathedral of Sant'Evasio, consecrated in 1107, with its grand and rare Narthex that represents a masterpiece of architectural engineering. Inside you can admire a precious 13th-century wooden Crucifix and visit the Cathedral Treasure Museum in the Open Sacristy.

Visit the Jewish Complex, one of the most important in Italy, with the extraordinary Baroque Synagogue built in 1595. The interior decorations of surprising richness testify to the prosperity of the Jewish community of Casale. The complex also includes the Silver Museum and the Museum of Lights.

Explore the Civic Museum and Bistolfi Plaster Cast Gallery, which in addition to the Picture Gallery houses works by Symbolist sculptor Leonardo Bistolfi and an exhibition dedicated to Carlo Vidua, the traveling count who explored the Far East from the 19th century.

Discover the Castle of Monferrato in central Piazza Castello, today home to the Tourist Office, the Regional Enoteca of Monferrato, and cultural events. An unmissable visit to discover the wines and typical products of the territory.

activities.text: Taste the Krumiri Rossi, the symbolic biscuits of Casale Monferrato whose recipe dates back to 1878 by pastry chef Domenico Rossi. This tradition has been carried on since 1953 by the Portinaro Family, guardians of the secret of these unique sweets.

Reach the Sacro Monte di Crea, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in a splendid panoramic position. This devotional complex includes the Sanctuary, 23 chapels, and 5 hermitages built between 1589 and 1612 in a place of ancient Marian worship.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont Wine & Truffle Road Trip: Turin, Alba & Barolo in 6 Days

map_keywords: Sinagoga di Casale Monferrato Casale Monferrato
Sacro Monte di Crea Serralunga di Crea

places.name: Casalmaggiore

visits.text: From the argine maestro, the bend of the Po reveals the entire town of Casalmaggiore at once. This strategic position made it the object of covetousness between Milan, Mantua and Venice for centuries. The neoclassical Duomo at the end of via Favagrossa is worth a look.

The Santuario della Madonna della Fontana was built in 1463 on the site of a spring reputed to be miraculous. In the crypt, water still flows into a 17th-century basin. The 15th-16th century frescoes are worth the trip, and tradition has it that Parmigianino is buried here.

The Casalaschi have venerated their Santuario since the great plague of 1497. Pilgrims still come to drink the fountain water in the crypt. The Gothic layout and Renaissance cotto portal form a surprising mix. Free access.

activities.text: Visit the small Museo del Bijou, dedicated to the costume jewelry that made Casalmaggiore prosperous in the 20th century. A rare curiosity. Open weekends, modest entry fee.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

map_keywords: Sanctuary of the Madonna della Fontana Casalmaggiore

places.name: Casalrotto

visits.text: It's nicknamed the Sistine Chapel of cave art, and the comparison holds up: the chiesa rupestre di San Nicola at Casalrotto, near Mottola, is carved into tufa, three naves, an iconostasis in the Byzantine style, a cycle of frescoes restored in 1972. On one arch, two superimposed images of the saint: one from the 11th century, one from the 13th.

A cave church arranged on two levels of circulation: the chiesa di Sant'Angelo is embedded in the cave village of Casalrotto, on the territory of Mottola. It hides in a valley that lacks the scale of the great ravines, which is exactly why people walk past it without seeing it. A guide is essential to find it.

Around a hundred caves carved on both sides of the ravine: the villaggio rupestre di Casalrotto, below Mottola, is reached by an old tratturo, a transhumance track. You descend to the floor through a stepped cut in the rock. The whole site lies within the Parco Naturale Regionale Terra delle Gravine, among Aleppo pines, ancient olive trees, and rosemary.

days_plan.itin_title: The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

map_keywords: Cave Church of San Nicola Mottola

visits.text: A blue village in a region that paints everything white: the historic center of Casamassima is a maze of alleyways, arches, and chiassi, those dead-end passages, where the lime has been tinted azure. The tradition attributes this to a vow to the Madonna against the plague, in the mid-17th century. The color has faded, but the effect remains. Come in late afternoon, when the light catches it.

The Porta dell'Orologio is the scenic entrance to the Casamassima village, built in the 19th century to replace the medieval gate. It opens from Piazza Aldo Moro, where the chiesa del Purgatorio, built around 1700, also stands. It's the starting point on foot and the town's symbol. Park on the square.

Under the arch of Via Santa Chiara in Casamassima, a 17th-century fresco depicts the Madonna di Costantinopoli: it's from the colour of her mantle that Duke Vaaz is said to have drawn the village's blue, in gratitude for the end of the epidemic. A less romantic version holds that housewives reused blue-tinted washing water to whitewash the walls. Choose your story.

Founded in 1573 by Antonio Acquaviva d'Aragona with his sister Dorotea's money, the Monastero di Santa Chiara is the most imposing building in Casamassima's historic center. Built as an orphanage, it became a Clarisses monastery a century later, then after Italian unification, a prison, school, cinema-theatre, and housing. Few buildings have accumulated this many lives.

The Chiesa Matrice di Santa Croce in Casamassima was built over a 12th-13th-century church, and its courses of polished, regular blocks speak to the care of the original construction. It's in the old town, with the Palazzo Ducale a few steps away. Hours follow the services.

The Polish Military Cemetery in Casamassima has nothing to do with the rest of the visit, and that's exactly why you should stop: it holds the Polish soldiers who fell during the Second World War. Silence, rows of graves, dates. A reminder that these hills witnessed more than harvests.

activities.text: Schedule your stop in Casamassima for the end of the day: the blue walls only work in raking light; at noon they disappear. The Balcone Fiorito festival animates the village with exhibitions, concerts, and markets, and includes a cena azzurra, a picnic that's entirely blue, tablecloths included. Dates published by the municipality.

days_plan.itin_title: The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

places.name: Casarano

visits.text: One of the oldest early Christian churches in southern Italy looks like nothing much from the street: Santa Maria della Croce, in Casaranello, keeps 5th-century mosaics on the dome and the vault of the presbytery. Byzantine and Gothic frescoes carry on from there. Opening hours are very tight, often weekends in the late afternoon.

Midnight blue ground, a gold cross, a starry sky: the dome of Santa Maria della Croce holds the heart of the mosaic decoration, while the nave carries 13th-century frescoes, among them a Kiss of Judas and a Last Supper. The lighting is dim, so bring a torch.

activities.text: Push on into the Casaranello district, the original core of Casarano, to understand why the church stands here and nowhere else. The rest of the town has lived off shoemaking for decades. Phone the parish before you come: with nothing open, the stop loses all its point.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

map_keywords: Santa Maria della Croce Church Casarano

visits.text: Take the morning ferry back to Naples, then drive 30 km north to Caserta. The Reggia di Caserta awaits: with its 1,200 rooms spread over 5 floors, 245-meter facade, and more than 2 million cubic meters of volume, it's the world's largest royal residence. Charles of Bourbon had it built from 1752 by architect Luigi Vanvitelli to rival Versailles. The king never slept there—called to the Spanish throne in 1759, he left Naples before construction was completed.

Inside, don't miss the Grand Staircase of Honor, which inspired the one in Saint Petersburg's Alexander Palace. The Palatine Chapel, inspired by Versailles' chapel, features a polychrome marble floor beneath majestic colonnades. The Royal Apartments alternate between 18th-century Baroque decor and Empire style—Joachim Murat, King of Naples from 1808 to 1815, remodeled several rooms. The Royal Theatre, inaugurated in 1769, has a unique feature: its backstage could open onto the park, creating a natural backdrop.

The Royal Park extends 120 hectares behind the palace. A 3-km axis aligns fountains, basins, and monumental cascades in perspective. The Grande Cascade, 78 meters high, is fed by the 38-km-long Carolino Aqueduct. At the foot of the cascade, the Fountain of Diana and Actaeon stages the goddess and her nymphs in a spectacular sculptural group. You can traverse the park on foot, by bicycle, or by carriage. Allow at least 1.5 hours to reach the cascade and return.

Before leaving the park, explore the English Garden, laid out in the late 18th century by botanist John Andrew Graefer on orders from Queen Maria Carolina of Austria. The atmosphere radically differs from the French garden: bodies of water hidden in vegetation, fake ruins, a cryptoporticus imitating a Roman temple, and the Bath of Venus with its statue of the goddess emerging from a basin. More than 200 botanical species coexist here.

activities.text: Late afternoon, drive up to Casertavecchia, the medieval village perched on the hill overlooking the modern town. At 400 meters altitude, this town founded by the Lombards in the 8th century has preserved its medieval charm intact: cobbled lanes, Norman tower, and the splendid 12th-century Romanesque cathedral with its tuff dome and Arab-Norman-inspired interlace. The panorama over the plain of Caserta and distant Vesuvius is worth the climb.

If you still have time, detour to the Belvedere di San Leucio, 3 km north of Caserta. This hamlet was transformed in the late 18th century by Ferdinand IV into a model silk manufactory, with a socially avant-garde set of rules: compulsory education, equal pay for men and women, ban on dowries. The palace and workshops are UNESCO-listed along with the Reggia.

days_plan.itin_title: From Naples to the Lucanian Dolomites: Secret Campania and the Amalfi Coast

places.name: Casole D Elsa

visits.text: Medieval walls and circular towers: The ramparts of Casole d'Elsa have a characteristic elliptical shape, about 420 meters long on the main axis and 130 meters wide. Two circular towers built in 1481 on the eastern perimeter are the work of Francesco di Giorgio Martini, the greatest military architect of the Renaissance. Contested between Volterra, Siena, and Florence throughout the 13th century, the town definitively passed under Sienese rule in 1260.

Rocca Senese and Arte Viva Art Gallery: A 14th-century fortress now housing the town hall, the Rocca hosts a collection of drawings and paintings created by children from across the province, gathered by artist Giuseppe Ciani. The façade shows traces of defensive apparatus on corbels shaped like inverted pyramids.

Collegiate Church of Santa Maria Assunta: Consecrated in 1161, the Romanesque-Gothic church houses the cenotaph of Beltramo Aringhieri, a remarkable 14th-century funerary sculpture. In the adjacent presbytery, the Archaeological Museum of the Collegiate displays Etruscan pieces, paintings, and goldwork.

activities.text: Hiking in Selva di Sogno Park: Between Casole and Chiusdino, this forest park features sculptures and murals integrated into an oak wood. Marked trails, free access.

places.name: Cassino

visits.text: Isola del Liri — A unique phenomenon in Italy: an 89-foot waterfall in the town center. The Liri river, at the height of the Castello Boncompagni-Viscogliosi (built around 1000 AD, residence of the Dukes of Sora from 1579), splits into two arms around a travertine outcrop, creating a natural island and two waterfalls: the Cascata Grande (89 feet, vertical drop) and the Cascata del Valcatoio. In the 19th century, hydraulic power attracted French industrialists: Charles Lefebvre of Pontarlier founded a modern paper mill in 1812 whose 'endless' paper was exported to London to print the Times. The town was nicknamed 'Little Paris' or 'Manchester of Italy.' The former Cartiera Lefebvre, swallowed by vegetation, was rediscovered in 1995. The former Cartiera Boimond still preserves its continuous machine. The Liri Blues Festival (since 1988, sister-city partnership with New Orleans) animates the square in July. In May 1799, during the triennio giacobino, over 500 people were massacred in the church.

Abbazia di Montecassino — Italy's oldest monastery, founded in 529 by Saint Benedict of Nursia at 1,692 feet elevation, on the ruins of a Roman temple to Apollo and Jupiter from ancient Casinum. Here Benedict wrote his Rule ('Ora et labora') that structured European monastic life. Benedict and his sister Scholastica are buried beneath the high altar. The monastery was destroyed four times: Lombards (577), Saracens (883), earthquake (1349), Allied bombing on February 15, 1944. That day, 142 heavy and 114 medium bombers dropped 353 tons of bombs believing (wrongly) that Germans occupied the abbey. About 400 civilian refugees perished. The octogenarian abbot Gregorio Diamare survived and refused to sign a Nazi propaganda memorandum. The Battle of Cassino lasted 128 days (Jan-May 1944): over 55,000 Allied dead, 30,000 German. Polish soldiers took the ruins on May 18. Rebuilt identically (plans by Cosimo Fanzago, 17th-18th centuries), consecrated by Paul VI on October 24, 1964. Free entry. The 11th-century bronze door (survivor), the tabernacle by Nicola Salvi, the tomb of Pietro de' Medici, and the Codice Cassinese 512 of the Divine Comedy are among the treasures preserved. The Polish military cemetery (1,072 graves) bears the inscription: 'For our freedom and yours, we Polish soldiers gave our souls to God, our bodies to Italian soil, our hearts to Poland.'

activities.text: Admire the Cascata Grande from Piazza Boncompagni. Cross the Parco Fluviale along the Liri to see the Cascata del Valcatoio. Taste finifini (ultra-thin fettuccine with ragù), a local specialty.

Drive up to Montecassino via the scenic road. Cross successive cloisters: entrance cloister (former Apollo temple), Cistern cloister, Loggia del Paradiso, Benefactors' cloister. Basilica rebuilt with polychrome marbles. Crypt with bronze reliquary urn. Polish military cemetery.

places.name: Castagnole Delle Lanze

visits.text: Castagnole delle Lanze takes its name from the Lancia family - from the nickname Lancifero (lance-bearer) awarded to Lord Manfredo at Frederick Barbarossa's court in the twelfth century. Its history then follows that of the commune of Asti from the thirteenth century, then the Visconti in the fourteenth, finally Emanuele Filiberto of Savoy from 1573. The village sits in the UNESCO buffer zone of the Vineyard Landscapes of Langhe-Roero and Monferrato. Its vineyards primarily produce Moscato d'Asti, Barbera d'Asti, and Ruchè - a rare aromatic red wine from a grape variety typical of this zone.

Climb to the historic borgo of San Pietro, perched on the hill at 298 meters. The parish church of San Pietro in Vincoli, built in 1681 in Ligurian-Piedmontese baroque style, houses 230 carved cherubs, gilded stuccoes, and wooden altars inside - unexpectedly rich decor for a village of this size. The nineteenth-century panoramic tower, commissioned by Count Paolo Ballada di Saint Robert for his astronomical observations, dominates the Rimembranza park and offers a 360° view over the UNESCO buffer zone.

Along Via Ener Bettica, the arcades of the historic center are adorned with murals by local artist Vincenzo Piccato - thirteen arches in the colors of the seasons and wine constitute an open-air gallery on the nature of the Langhe and Monferrato. The church of the Confraternity of the Battuti Bianchi (1668), now deconsecrated, hosts exhibitions and concerts; it houses the Museum of Peasant Civilization of the Alto Monferrato.

activities.text: Tasting of Moscato d'Asti DOCG (sweet sparkling wine) and Barbera d'Asti in local cellars. The Adopt a Row of Vines initiative, launched in 2010 by the town hall, allows visitors to adopt ten meters of Barbera and receive ten bottles of wine - unique in Italy.

visits.text: First true inland detour at Atri, an hour south of the trabocchi coast. The cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta from the 13th century houses one of Abruzzo's finest quattrocento fresco cycles, signed Andrea De Litio between 1481 and 1497: on the choir walls, the life of the Virgin in 22 panels, earning the artist the nickname 'Piero della Francesca of Abruzzo.' The crypt sits atop remains of a Roman cistern. 10 minutes from the center, the Riserva dei Calanchi: clay terrain eroded into sharp ridges and white ravines, lunar appearance, one of central Italy's most singular landscapes.

Climb toward Campo Imperatore via Castel del Monte. The high plain stretches 20 km long and 7 km wide, between 1,600 and 1,800 m elevation, completely flat, treeless, enclosed on all four sides by peaks exceeding 2,500 m. Its winds and appearance earned it the nickname 'little Tibet.' Here Mussolini was detained at Hotel Campo Imperatore (2,130 m altitude) from August 28, 1943, after his deposition by the Fascist Grand Council. On September 12, 1943, ten German DFS 230 gliders landed on the plateau—Operation Eiche, under Luftwaffe General Kurt Student's overall command. Major Harald Mors directed the ground detachment from Assergi; SS-Hauptsturmführer Otto Skorzeny commanded the glider-borne commando. Mussolini was extracted without a shot fired. Nazi propaganda credited everything to Skorzeny, but recent research largely re-credits Mors. The hotel still stands, transformed into a museum and seasonal lodging.

activities.text: Arrive late afternoon in Castel del Monte, the village, not to be confused with Frederick II's castle in Apulia. Stone village at 1,346 m altitude, former capital of the Carapelle barony. Slow walk through the alleys before dinner. The local specialty, lamb arrosticini, are grilled on iron fornacelle, by the dozen skewers.
