visits.text: Craco, perched on a clay pinnacle at 391 meters, is one of Italy's most photogenic ghost towns: gutted houses, solitary bell tower, collapsed noble palaces, alleys overgrown with vegetation. Final evacuation in 1963 after a major landslide, followed by the 1972 flood then the 1980 Irpinia earthquake that finished everything. The 1,800 inhabitants were rehoused in Craco Peschiera in the valley, 3 km away, and the old town was never touched again. Visit by guided tour only with mandatory helmet, 11 euros, 1.5 hours, departures from Craco Peschiera.

Film set. Mel Gibson shot part of "The Passion of the Christ" (2004) here, Marc Forster "Quantum of Solace" (James Bond 2008), and Francesco Rosi "Christ Stopped at Eboli" (1979)—perfect loop with Aliano and Matera. More recently, the producers of Patty Jenkins's "Wonder Woman" also set up cameras here. The guide points out filming locations: it's touristy, but well done.

The Craco badlands, surrounding the village, are even more impressive than those of Aliano 30 km away: wider, whiter, more arid. The contrast between the pale clay and the dark stones of the village gives the place a post-apocalyptic hue. Panoramic viewpoint on the approach road, free, ideal in late afternoon when golden light blankets the gullies.

activities.text: Dinner in a Basilicata masseria, several nearby (Masseria Lo Prino, Masseria Santo Stefano). Lucanian peasant cuisine: oven-roasted lamb, pasta con la mollica (fried breadcrumbs), peperoni cruschi, Aglianico wine. Overnight stay possible on-site in rural boutique guesthouse.

days_plan.itin_title: Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy
Dark Apulia: 8 Days from Bari to Esoteric Naples

visits.text: Castello Ducale di Crecchio - a 14th-century fortress with four corner towers, dominating the village from a 265-meter hill. The castle houses the Museo dell'Abruzzo Bizantino ed Altomedievale, whose centerpiece is the Reggio treasure, a collection of 7th-century gold jewelry discovered in 1955. The last king of the Two Sicilies, Francesco II, took refuge here in 1861 after the fall of Gaeta.

activities.text: Quick stop in the medieval center's narrow streets before continuing to Penne.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

visits.text: Cattedrale di Cremona and Torrazzo - Romanesque-Gothic cathedral built between 1107 and the 14th century, with the Torrazzo rising 112.7 meters - the world's tallest brick bell tower and Italy's third-tallest campanile. The Torrazzo was constructed between 1250 and 1309 and connected to the cathedral in 1490 by a soaring Gothic tribune. The cathedral façade integrates 12th-century Romanesque elements with 13th-14th century Gothic additions.

Piazza del Comune di Cremona - medieval square surrounded by the Palazzo del Comune (1206), Palazzo dei Giureconsulti (13th century), Romanesque Battistero (1167), and Loggia dei Militi (1292). The ensemble forms one of the best-preserved examples of Lombard medieval civic architecture, with five distinct monuments comprising a single integrated complex.

Museo del Violino - museum housed in the Palazzo dell'Arte dedicated to Cremonese violin-making, whose history traces back to Andrea Amati (circa 1505-1577), the first documented violin maker. Antonio Stradivari (1644-1737) crafted over 1,100 instruments in Cremona, of which approximately 650 are still accounted for worldwide. The museum preserves eleven Stradivari violins, including the Cremonese from 1715, which are regularly played during concerts in the museum's integrated performance hall.

activities.text: Visit to a violin-making workshop in the luthiers' quarter around Piazza del Comune - Cremona still counts about one hundred active luthiers, concentrated in the alleys surrounding the cathedral. Several workshops accept visitors by appointment.

Tasting of Cremona's torrone - nougat made from honey, egg whites, and almonds or hazelnuts, crafted in Cremona since the 15th century according to archival documents dating to 1441, during the wedding banquet of Francesco Sforza and Bianca Maria Visconti.

days_plan.itin_title: Milan to Chianti Circuit: Design, Art, and Wine

places.name: Crespi D Adda

visits.text: Walk down Crespi d'Adda's main avenue to grasp the master plan of this workers' village founded in 1877 by Cristoforo Benigno Crespi, one of Italy's greatest textile industrialists. His son Silvio, trained in England and Germany, designed its final layout: identical workers' houses arranged in a perpendicular grid, each with a garden and vegetable plot, following a paternalistic model inspired by British company towns.

Step inside the textile factory and its grounds: inaugurated in 1878, it sprawled across nearly two square kilometers and counted 120 mechanical looms, 4,000 workers, and a daily output of 50,000 meters of fabric at its peak. Its monumental entrance features a red wrought-iron gate with floral decorations crafted by Milanese artist Alessandro Mazzucotelli. Power came from a hydroelectric plant Crespi himself built on the Adda River.

Explore the village's communal buildings: the school (where books, meals, and teachers' lodging were covered by the company), the Renaissance-style church faithfully copied from the church in Busto Arsizio, the Crespi family's birthplace, the theater, the food cooperative, the hospital, and the public baths with a covered pool and hot water—all financed entirely by the family. The village was also the first in Italy equipped with Edison-system electric street lighting.

Climb the cypress-lined path to the workers' cemetery, where the community's social hierarchy still reads in stone. The simplest workers' graves stand in rows like a military cemetery, while foremen's and managers' tombs occupy the sides. At the far end, dominating the ensemble, rises the Crespi family's pyramid-shaped mausoleum, encircled by walls that seem to embrace 'their' workers protectively. The entire complex was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.

activities.text: Bike ride or walk along the Adda riverbanks around the village, following the industrial canal Crespi dug to power his hydroelectric plant. The landscape blends Lombard meadows, poplars, and industrial ruins—a setting that illuminates why UNESCO called Crespi 'the most complete and best-preserved example of a company town in southern Europe.'

days_plan.itin_title: Lombardy's Most Beautiful Villages in 5 Days

map_keywords: Villaggio Crespi d'Adda Capriate San Gervasio
Chiesa di Santa Maria Nascente Crespi d'Adda
Fabbrica Tessile Crespi Capriate San Gervasio

activities.text: If you only book one thing in Matera, book the Cripta del Peccato Originale, about fifteen kilometers away, above the Gravina di Picciano. Its 8th-9th century frescoes earn it the nickname "Sistine Chapel of rupestrian art"; the anonymous painter is called the Pittore dei Fiori. Delicious detail: the forbidden fruit depicted is a fig, not an apple. Guided tour only, limited capacity, reservation required.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia
The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

places.name: Cripta Di San Biagio

visits.text: The Cripta di San Biagio is the real reason for the detour near San Vito dei Normanni: a Byzantine sanctuary carved into the rock in contrada Jannuzzo, covered with frescoes from the late 13th century that draw partly on the apocryphal gospels. Two side caves served as refectory and dormitory. The visit must be booked in advance.

activities.text: Turn up without a booking and you will stay outside: the guided visit has to be requested from the town council of San Vito dei Normanni. The site sits at the centre of a rock-cut settlement strung along the Canale Reale. Wear closed shoes, as the floor is uneven and damp.

days_plan.itin_title: Brindisi in 2 Days: Byzantine Crypts and Torre Guaceto

map_keywords: Crypt of San Biagio San Vito dei Normanni

places.name: Cripta Di San Giovanni

visits.text: Dated to the 13th century, the Cripta di San Giovanni opens in contrada Cafaro, two kilometres from the previous one, along the Canale Reale. Its walls carry a Déesis, a series of saints and, among the Latin inscriptions, one in Arabic. Two neighbouring caves have collapsed.

activities.text: You reach the crypt on the path that follows the Canale Reale, flat and shaded in places. Allow an hour there and back from San Biagio. Access is not free: ask for the guided visit at the same time as the one for San Biagio, since both can be arranged as a single outing.

days_plan.itin_title: Brindisi in 2 Days: Byzantine Crypts and Torre Guaceto

places.name: Cuneo

visits.text: Begin at Piazza Galimberti, whose neoclassical design by Benedetto Brunati was approved in 1832 and implemented over fifty years. The square measures over 23,000 m² and is framed by ten identical arcaded palaces with round-arched vaults—a symmetrical arrangement inherited from the Napoleonic alignment plans of 1801, when the demolition of the ramparts finally permitted the city's southward expansion. Originally named Piazza Nizza, then Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II, it has borne since May 21, 1945 the name of Duccio Galimberti, a Cuneo lawyer and Resistance hero killed in 1944, who lived in Palazzo Osasco facing the square.

Walk the entire length of Via Roma: this medieval artery stretching over 800 meters, now pedestrianized, has always been Cuneo's commercial center. The porticos were gradually added to medieval facades to shelter activities under cover—in some buildings, you can still see the joint between the original masonry and the added arches. The 52-meter-high Civic Tower, built in 1317, and the Cathedral of Santa Maria del Bosco, whose dome and interior frescoes date from the 19th century, punctuate the route. From the tower's summit, accessible by elevator, guards would spot enemies and sound the alarm.

Explore Contrada Mondovì, Cuneo's former Jewish quarter: one of Piedmont's oldest ghettos since the 15th century, it now forms a picturesque pedestrian zone with several historic shops. Continue to the Church of San Francesco, built between the 13th and 15th centuries in Gothic style: its marble portal from 1418, crowned by a rosette pediment, is the city's most important medieval testimony. Its cloister houses the Civic Museum.

Visit the Museo Casa Galimberti, housed in the palace where Duccio Galimberti was born, an anti-fascist resistance fighter shot on December 3, 1944 at age 35. The museum includes a gallery of paintings by Piedmontese artists, the family library, and the hero's mementos. The building stands on Piazza Galimberti, at the very spot where the first call to armed resistance in Italy was pronounced on July 26, 1943.

activities.text: Walk through the Parco Fluviale Gesso e Stura, along the banks of the two torrents that define the plateau on which Cuneo was founded in 1198. Cuneo—whose name comes from the Piedmontese 'cùneo,' meaning wedge or point—occupies precisely the point of this natural triangle formed by the confluence of the Gesso and Stura di Demonte, at 534 meters altitude at the foot of the Maritime Alps.

Aperitivo beneath the porticos of Piazza Galimberti: the arcades allow you to travel from end to end of the square and Via Roma without ever being exposed to the weather—making Cuneo one of the European cities with the longest continuous covered gallery route. Taste the Cuneesi al rhum, small chocolates filled with meringue and rum, a local pastry specialty present in every shop window.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy Road Trip from Nice: Riviera & Alps in 2 Days

map_keywords: Parco Fluviale Gesso e Stura Cuneo

places.name: Cutigliano

visits.text: The Palazzo dei Capitani della Montagna, built in 1377 to house the Florentine governor charged with administering the Pistoiese mountains, displays 95 stone and polychrome terracotta coats of arms on its facade—the heraldic shields of each successive Captain, dated from 1444 to 1742. The first to reside here was Baldo Altoviti, a Florentine nobleman. The Captains' Loggia opposite was where justice was dispensed and notarial acts signed. The Marzocco column, bearing Florence's lion with the Republic's lily, recalls that Cutigliano was an outpost of Florentine power in the mountains.

The Chiesa della Madonna di Piazza (15th century), steps from the Palazzo, preserves a terracotta by Benedetto Buglioni representing the Virgin and Child with Saint Anthony Abbot and Saint Bernardino of Siena. San Bartolomeo church, whose campanile rises from an ancient Lombard watchtower, houses 14th-century works.

activities.text: Stroll through the stone lanes of Cutigliano (678m altitude), certified among Italy's most beautiful villages (Bandiera Arancione). The village preserves its intact medieval layout: green sandstone fountains, vaults, covered passages and hand-cut stone facades.

days_plan.itin_title: Pistoia Province Circuit: Hill Towns & Thermal Spas

map_keywords: Palazzo dei Capitani della Montagna Cutigliano
Chiesa della Madonna di Piazza Cutigliano

places.name: Delta Del Po

visits.text: Explore the Delta del Po Regional Park, where Italy's longest river meets the Adriatic Sea in a landscape of extraordinary natural beauty. This vast wetland ecosystem is home to over 400 bird species including flocks of wild pink flamingoes that create spectacular displays against the marshy backdrop.

Visit the Giardino Botanico Litoraneo di Porto Caleri, a coastal botanical garden offering walks through lush vegetation at the edge of the sea. The diverse habitats - from dunes to pine forests to marshlands - support unique plant and animal communities.

activities.text: Discover wild beaches, island resorts, and the unique landscape where freshwater and saltwater ecosystems merge. The area offers exceptional opportunities for cycling, birdwatching, and boat excursions through the labyrinthine waterways.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

map_keywords: Parco Delta del Po Porto Tolle

places.name: Demonte

visits.text: The Forte Albertino di Vinadio, built between 1834 and 1859 by the Kingdom of Sardinia under King Charles Albert, stands as one of Europe's last great star fortifications. Its pink granite bastions, pierced by 8 km of galleries, could house up to 4,000 soldiers and withstand a six-month siege. The fort was designed to guard the Maddalena Pass (1,996 m) against any French incursion from Dauphiné. It was abandoned at the end of the 19th century without ever facing assault.

The Sanctuary of Sant'Anna di Vinadio (2,035 m altitude) is Europe's highest car-accessible Marian sanctuary. Construction dates to the 15th century at the initiative of the upper valley communes. On the night of July 25-26, the annual Saint Anne gathering draws thousands of pilgrims—a torchlit procession descends toward the plain through darkness. The site sits surrounded by alpine meadows with direct views onto the Franco-Italian border ridges.

The Casa del Contrabbandiere in Argentera is a museum-ecomuseum dedicated to the smugglers of the upper Stura: salt, tobacco, alcohol, and textiles crossed the Maddalena Pass by human or mule back, by night, throughout the 18th and 19th centuries. Exhibits include period equipment, oral testimonies, and maps of clandestine routes. In Aisone, caves carved into molasse have yielded traces of human occupation dating back 9,000 years.

The Terme di Vinadio thermal baths capture sulfurous water at 31°C flowing at 620 liters per minute from a geological fault at 900 meters altitude. The current facility, rebuilt in the 20th century, builds on a spa tradition dating to the 16th century, documented in the House of Savoy archives.

activities.text: Hike to Rifugio Migliorero from Vinadio (Valle Stura): ascent through alpine pastures between 1,400 and 2,100 meters, spotting chamois and marmots. Return via abandoned shepherd huts of the valley.
Session at the Terme di Vinadio after the hike: outdoor and indoor sulfurous water pools, thermal treatments. Reservation recommended in high season.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Valleys of Piedmont: Occitan Alps, Lakes & Baroque Savoy

map_keywords: Santuario di Sant'Anna di Vinadio Vinadio

places.name: Desenzano Del Garda

visits.text: Explore the Castle of Desenzano del Garda, an imposing fortress erected in the early Middle Ages probably on the remains of an ancient Roman castrum. Of the original construction, portions of walls and truncated corner towers survive; from the panoramic observatory at the top you can enjoy a spectacular view of Lake Garda that amply rewards the climb.

Visit the Cathedral of Santa Maria Maddalena, a splendid example of late Brescian Renaissance built between the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Inside it houses important works by Andrea Celesti, and in the Chapel of the Blessed Sacrament you can admire G.B. Tiepolo's celebrated Last Supper from 1738, a masterpiece of eighteenth-century Venetian painting.

Discover the Roman Villa, the most important testimony to the great late-antique villas of northern Italy. Built between the first and fourth centuries AD and accidentally discovered in 1921, it preserves over 240 sq m of extraordinary polychrome mosaics featuring cupids, maenads, satyrs and wild animals, bearing witness to the refinement of Roman life on the lake.

Admire the Giovanni Rambotti Archaeological Museum, rich in prehistoric finds from the Lake Garda area dating mainly from the Bronze Age. Among the treasures it houses is what is considered the oldest wooden plough in the world, a precious testimony to the first farming communities that inhabited these shores.

activities.text: Stroll through the picturesque Porto Vecchio, one of Desenzano's most evocative corners overlooked by the broad arcades of Palazzo Todeschini. The dock took shape in the days of the Venetian Republic; don't miss the curious Stone of the Unemployed from 1555, where town criers and those condemned for bankruptcy would stand.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona

Duomo Santa Maria Maddalena Desenzano del Garda
Museo Archeologico Rambotti Desenzano del Garda

visits.text: Diamante - a coastal town of 5,000 inhabitants whose historic center boasts over 150 wall murals created since 1981 by Italian and international artists as part of the Museo all'Aperto (Open-Air Museum) project. The themes explore local life, mythology, and politics, transforming the narrow lanes into an outdoor art gallery. Diamante is also the world capital of Calabrian peperoncino (chili pepper), celebrated at an annual September festival.

activities.text: Stroll through the historic center's lanes to discover the wall murals - a route map is available from the local tourist office.
Sample Calabrian peperoncino in all its forms: dried, powdered, preserved in oil, and especially as 'nduja, the spicy spreadable sausage typical of the Tyrrhenian coast.

days_plan.itin_title: From Naples to Calabria: The Tyrrhenian Coast

visits.text: Tre Cime di Lavaredo – the three most famous dolomite towers in the Alps: Cima Grande (2,999m), Cima Ovest (2,973m), and Cima Piccola (2,857m), formed by differential erosion of an Upper Triassic limestone plateau. The north face of Cima Grande (500 meters of vertical wall) is one of the six great north faces of the Alps, first climbed in 1933 by Comici and the Dimai brothers. The toll road from Rifugio Auronzo (2,333m) allows you to reach the trailhead by car.

Lago di Landro (Dürrensee) – 15-hectare glacial lake at 1,408 meters on the road between Dobbiaco and Cortina, with reflections of Tre Cime in calm weather from the north shore. The German name Dürrensee (dry lake) recalls that the lake level drops considerably in summer through evaporation and that the lake was nearly dry before construction of a regulatory dam in the 19th century.

Lago di Braies (Pragser Wildsee) – 32-hectare glacial lake at 1,496 meters in the Foresta di Braies, framed by Sasso del Signore (2,448m) and Swiss stone pine forests. The waters reach emerald green to turquoise depending on light conditions, resulting from dissolved carbonates in glacial meltwater. In May 1945, 139 prisoners of war and important hostages (including members of the Italian government) were liberated here by American troops after being transferred from concentration camps.

activities.text: Hike around Tre Cime from Rifugio Auronzo – 9.5-kilometer loop with 350 meters of elevation gain, passing Rifugio Locatelli (2,405m) with views of the north faces of the three towers.
Walk around Lago di Braies – marked 3.5-kilometer trail around the lake with wooden rowboat rentals from the hotel on the south shore.

days_plan.itin_title: Dolomites Loop: Alpine Lakes, Mountain Pastures & Limestone Peaks

visits.text: Dolceacqua's medieval bridge is the postcard image of the Nervia Valley. A single humpback arch, 33 meters span, built in the 15th century to link the Terra (old quarter) to the Borgo (the new one, on the opposite bank). Claude Monet painted it in 1884 and called it, in a letter, a jewel of lightness. The phrase stuck. Best viewpoint: from the Borgo bank, late afternoon, when the light turns the stones crimson and the castle looms above.

Look up from the bridge: those two square towers dominating everything, that's the Doria Castle. And the entire history of the valley lives in that building. Built in 1151 by the Counts of Ventimiglia, purchased in 1270 by Oberto Doria—the Genoese captain who had just crushed the Pisans at the Battle of Meloria. Franco-Spanish armies bombarded it in 1746 during the War of Austrian Succession, the 1887 earthquake finished the job. The 6€ entrance fee seems steep for a partly ruined castle, but the panorama from the keep silences all complaints.

Apricale, 5 kilometers from Dolceacqua, ranks among Italy's most beautiful villages. Founded by the Counts of Ventimiglia in the 10th century, sold in 1276 to the Doria family, briefly French under Napoleon. The village is a vertical labyrinth of caruggi, staircases and vaulted passages, perched on a spur. On the main square: two churches, the town hall and the ruins of Castello della Lucertola, from the 10th century, now a museum. Park below, walk up. And look up: contemporary frescoes cover several facades.

Odd surprise when you reach Pigna: its houses spiral in concentric circles around the baroque church of San Michele, like scales. Hence the name (pigna = pinecone). Thermal waters known since Roman times—a modern hammam has set up shop for those the alleys tire out. The medieval center, fortified in the 13th century, is a maze of stairs and covered passages. Surprising detail: Pigna became part of the Terres Neuves of Provence in 1388 and shared three centuries of history with the County of Nice. That's why you still find French signs and surnames here.

activities.text: Wine tasting of Rossese di Dolceacqua in a village cellar. It's the first Ligurian wine to receive DOC status, in 1972. Light ruby color, notes of strawberry and pepper, produced in only fourteen communes. Napoleon drank it, so did Pope Paul III Farnese. Several family cellars in the Borgo offer tastings at 10-15€. Ask for the cru bottling—some winemakers bottle vineyard by vineyard.

Try the michetta, Dolceacqua's signature brioche, perfumed with anise and fennel, traditionally prepared for Saint Michael's Day on August 16th. Local legend: it commemorates a popular revolt against Lord Doria in the 15th century. Borgo bakeries make it year-round. One for an afternoon snack with a strong espresso is plenty—it's dense.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy Road Trip from Nice: Riviera & Alps in 2 Days
Riviera di Ponente and Ligurian Hinterland in 3 Days
Grand Tour of the Riviera di Ponente in 4 Days

visits.text: The Dolmen della Chianca aligns its slabs in the olive-grove countryside since the 3rd millennium BC. Discovered in 1909 by archaeologists Samarelli and Mosso, this Bronze Age tomb shows a chamber and a 7.5 m corridor. Free visit without reservation: ideal early morning.

days_plan.itin_title: Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

visits.text: Set in the middle of an olive grove 3 km from Calimera, the Dolmen Placa is a megalithic tomb with a single chamber, a broad horizontal slab on short supports. Access is free and the site is unguarded. The dirt track carries no sign at all: save the GPS point before you set off.

The Dolmen Gurgulante lies a few hundred metres from the first, in the same chequerboard of olive trees. Lower and stockier, it completes Calimera's small megalithic group. Both can be seen in half an hour, with closed shoes advisable because of the brambles.

activities.text: In summer, come early: there is no shade on site and the dirt track heats up fast. Leave the car on the verge without blocking the tractors, as the land is still farmed. Mobile coverage is weak, so download the map beforehand.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: The Su Gologone spring has been a natural monument since 1998. Water gushes from a limestone fault at over 300 liters per second, sometimes 4,000 in heavy rains. Explored depth: more than 135 meters, making it one of Italy's deepest karst springs. The icy blue-green water is striking. Small picnic area under cork oaks, free access, free parking. Avoid weekends in July-August, it's packed. 20 minutes by car from Oliena.

Tiscali is the day's adventure. A nuragic village dated between the 15th and 8th centuries BC, built inside a giant collapsed doline on Mount Tiscali (515m). Unique case in Sardinia: the circular stone huts are lodged in the open-air cave, invisible from outside. The trail starts from the Lanaittu valley, climbs via an old charcoal burner's path, passes through a narrow fissure before opening onto the doline. Excavations date from 1999; some artifacts suggest repopulation in the 2nd-1st centuries BC, likely a refuge against the Romans. The silence up there is striking. €5 site entry.

Dorgali, your evening stop, is a large town of 8,500 inhabitants at 400m altitude, halfway between Supramonte and the Gulf of Orosei. Historic center in light stone, living traditions: carpets, ceramics, leather. Several workshops open to visit on Via Lamarmora. The archaeological museum presents objects found at Tiscali, Serra Orrios and other local sites—useful for contextualizing what you saw during the day. €3 entry. In the evening, terrace on the main square, the sunset over Supramonte is worth it.

activities.text: Hike to Tiscali: 3h round trip from Sa Barva parking (Lanaittu valley), 7 km, 350m elevation gain. Medium difficulty, rocky terrain, a few easy scrambling sections. Good shoes essential, 1.5L water minimum per person, cap. No shade in the doline. Guide recommended for first-timers (€40 per person, several cooperatives in Oliena or Dorgali). Departure before 9am in summer to avoid the heat.

If you still have energy late afternoon, the Sa Oche cave (10 minutes from Su Gologone) shelters an underground river that literally roars after heavy rains—its name means "the voice" in Sardinian. Guided tour of 1 hour, €12, regular departures April to October. Helmet provided.

days_plan.itin_title: Sardinia's Wild Interior and Eastern Coast: 6 Days from Olbia to Cagliari

visits.text: Dozza is a museum-village in the literal sense. Ranked among Italy's most beautiful villages, this small medieval hamlet perched on a hill between Bologna and Imola has become an open-air art gallery thanks to the Painted Wall Biennial, launched in 1960. Over 200 Italian and international artists have painted house facades, arches, and walls over the decades. The works are everywhere: look up, peer into corners, venture down alleys. Among the best-known are "The Angel of Dozza" by Giuliana Bonazza (1993) and "The Rainbow" by Alfonso Frasnedi (2000). The village consists of two parallel streets, Via XX Settembre and Via De Amicis—you can't get lost.

At the top of the village rises the Rocca Sforzesca, a fortress built in 1245 whose current appearance dates from work by Caterina Sforza starting in 1480. She added the two large round corner towers with machicolations. Inside, you'll discover rooms furnished with furniture from the Campeggi and Malvezzi families who inhabited the fortress until 1960, dungeons and oubliettes, and a picture gallery preserving sketches of the wall frescoes. From the rampart walk, the view over the valley vineyards and hills is remarkable.

In the Rocca's cellars, don't miss the Enoteca Regionale dell'Emilia-Romagna, installed here since 1970. It's the showcase for wines from across the region—over 1,000 labels from 200 producers. You can taste on-site using a self-service system, or simply buy a bottle to take home. The setting of vaulted cellars adds to the pleasure. Try the Sangiovese di Romagna, Albana DOCG (the first Italian white to obtain DOCG status), and Pignoletto.

activities.text: If you visit Dozza in September of an even year, you'll catch the Painted Wall Biennial in full swing: over a weekend, artists paint live on the village facades, before the public's eyes. It's a unique moment when you can watch a work being born and chat with its creator. Even in odd years, the village hosts cultural events and wine tastings.

To close this itinerary in style, treat yourself to lunch at one of the village's restaurants. Romagna cuisine takes center stage: fresh pasta, grilled meats, piadina (Romagna flatbread), and local cheeses. Tables are set on terraces as soon as good weather arrives, with views over the hills. Pair the meal with a glass of regional wine—you're in the heart of the Strada dei Vini e Sapori of the Colli d'Imola.

days_plan.itin_title: 10 Natural Wonders Around Bologna
Gourmet Emilia: From Parma to Bologna Through the Hills

visits.text: The Ponte del Diavolo of Dronero, built in 1428 over the Maira torrent, is the village's centerpiece. Three unequal arches, crenellated in swallowtail style (Ghibelline pattern), rise 18 meters above two irrigation canals. The main arch measures 27 meters in diameter and 6 meters wide. A drawbridge existed on the village side until 1810, its iron hinge discovered beneath the paving. Legend tells that the mayor, desperate as floods swept away every bridge, struck a pact with the devil for the soul of the first being to cross. He threw a bread crust—a stray dog bolted across and fled. The devil, cheated, abandoned the bridge. The original construction receipt is preserved in the municipal archives: 700 florins paid to one magister Antonius.

Espaci Occitan, headquarters of the Piedmont Occitan cultural association, houses the Museo Sòn de Lenga devoted to Occitan history and culture in the region. Dronero appears as Dragonerium from the 12th century, its coat of arms displaying a rampant dragon. The historic center preserves medieval arcades, Gothic capitals, and 15th-century noble palaces.

Climb the Valle Maira toward Chialvetta and Viviere on the old paved mule trail. Along 177 km of marked paths, the Occitan Routes traverse hamlets, votive chapels, and sites linked to the former Marquisate of Saluzzo. The San Salvatore chapel in Macra preserves 14th-15th century frescoes depicting the Dance of Salome and Genesis.

Viewpoint above Acceglio facing the Monviso massif (3,841 m), highest peak of the Cottian Alps. The Maira rises in a glacial basin nearby, its waters flowing between pine forests before carving caves in travertine. The village of Acceglio is one of the valley's most isolated, at 1,220 meters altitude.

activities.text: Hike the Cyclamen Trail starting from Bedale (hamlet of Macra): between July and September, meadows of orchids and cyclamens beneath ash and wild cherry trees. Duration about 3h, moderate elevation gain.
Introduction to rock climbing on the valley's equipped cliffs (beginner to intermediate routes, top-ropes installed). Local providers offer half-day guided sessions.

In June, don't miss the Fiera degli Acciugai (Anchovy Fair) in Dronero, recalling the valley inhabitants' old trade: in winter, they descended to Liguria to buy salt-preserved anchovies, which they resold throughout the region. It's believed the anchovies originally served to conceal smuggled salt.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Valleys of Piedmont: Occitan Alps, Lakes & Baroque Savoy

visits.text: Erected in the 4th century BC, the Messapian walls of Egnazia enclose an entire city left open to the sky, on the coast near Fasano. The first settlement dates to the 16th century BC and life continued here until the 13th century AD. Fifteen hectares of archaeological park, with not a tree in sight. Hat and water are non-negotiable; there is no shade anywhere.

Walk the Via Traiana, the road Emperor Trajan had built between 108 and 110 AD to link Benevento to Brindisi, as an alternative to the Appian Way. At Egnazia, it separates the public buildings from the residential and craft quarters. The ruts worn by cart wheels are still visible in the stone. It's the best thread to follow through the site.

The cryptoporticus is the best-preserved section of the Egnazia park, and you can walk through it entirely: a covered underground passage, cool and intact. Next to it, the Basilica Civile with its aula delle Tre Grazie, the shrine to eastern deities, the colonnaded square, and the baths. Allow two hours for the park alone.

Pomegranates painted on the walls of a tomb: the Tomba delle Melagrane at Egnazia is a Messapian funerary chamber from the 4th century BC. The necropolis, outside the walls, lines up pit graves, semi-chamber tombs, and full rock-cut chambers, some decorated with frescoes. An aristocracy wealthy enough to commission underground rooms for its dead.

The Museo Nazionale Giuseppe Andreassi completes the park across seven sections, from the 16th century BC to the 13th century AD when the site was abandoned. Eleven bright pavilions arranged around two courtyards. In the 19th century, the tombs were looted first by foreign officers and then by agricultural workers: much of the funerary furnishings is now scattered. Multilingual audio guides available.

activities.text: Take a guided tour of the excavations and museum at Egnazia: without commentary, the site looks like a field of stones; with it, a city comes back to life. Systematic excavation campaigns started in 1912 and continue today. Extended hours from April to September, until 7:15pm. Book morning slots in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

visits.text: Pieve di Santa Anatolia — the oldest building in the village, Romanesque in origin and documented as early as 1180. Its 13th-century stone portal is one of the most complete Romanesque examples in the province of Macerata. Embedded in the base of the bell tower is a 1st-century Roman inscription, proof of Augustan-era occupation. The interior, entirely rebuilt in the 18th century, retains the baptismal font and the altar of the patron saint.

Palazzo Varano (Town Hall) — a 14th-century fortified residence of the Da Varano lords of Camerino. During restoration after the 1997 earthquake, medieval frescoes were uncovered depicting a cavalry parade with Giulio Cesare da Varano in old age and his son Giovanni Maria — the only chivalric fresco cycle of its kind in Le Marche. The entire municipal council chamber is decorated with this 15th-century sequence.

Casa delle Tre Porte and the Fonte del Borgo — a medieval house still inhabited today on Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, with three arches serving three distinct purposes: the everyday door, the bridal door, and the 'porta del morto' (walled up and reopened only for the passage of a coffin). The 13th-century village fountain in river stone has two separate basins — one for people, one for animals.

Il Roccone and Eremo di San Cataldo — the Roccone is a 13th-century polygonal watchtower with angular spurs on the slopes of Monte Corsegno, reachable on foot from the centre. The Eremo di San Cataldo, at 766 metres, built over a medieval defensive tower, is dedicated to the Irish saint the community proclaimed as patron in the 17th century. Legend holds he stopped a boulder threatening the village — a large rock bearing the 'imprints of the saint' is visible along the path.

activities.text: Stroll through the 'filetta' — Esanatoglia's nickname for its spindle-shaped elongated form. Corso Vittorio Emanuele II runs from Porta Sant'Andrea at the top to Porta Panicale at the bottom, with side streets branching off perpendicularly toward the seven bell towers that punctuate the village skyline.

Try the Frostingo — an ancient sweet made with nuts, dried fruits and spices — along with local specialities: cotiche with beans, tagliatelline al tartufo nero and artisan honey (Esanatoglia is known as the 'City of Honey').

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

visits.text: Explore Este, a 3,000-year-old walled town that gave its name to the powerful Este dynasty who later ruled Ferrara. The Archaeological Museum houses remarkable pre-Roman artifacts from the ancient Venetic civilization, including the famous Situla Benvenuti bronze bucket with detailed figural scenes.

Walk through the walled park where Este's medieval castle once stood, now a peaceful garden enclosed by battlemented walls and towers. The romantic ruins and ancient trees create an atmospheric setting for exploration.
Discover the town's thriving ceramics industry, a tradition dating back centuries, with artisan workshops producing distinctive hand-painted majolica in the local style.

activities.text: Combine your visit with the nearby Arquà Petrarca (18 minutes by bus) or Monselice (8 minutes by train) to explore multiple Euganean Hills gems in a single day.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: Orange Flag holder from the Touring Club, Fanano surprises with its density of heritage for a mountain village. The 8th-century core preserves a radial medieval layout. In 749, the Lombard nobleman Anselmo founded a Benedictine monastery here that became a religious center for the entire Apennines.

Stop in Piazza Corsini in front of the Palazzo Lardi from 1340 and the Torre dell'Orologio from 1609. The oratorio di San Rocco, housed at the tower's base, preserves 15th-century frescoes. A giant thermometer hanging on the tower wall doesn't go unnoticed.

The Pieve di San Silvestro, founded in 749, is considered one of the oldest in the Modena Apennines. The interior has undergone transformations over the centuries, but the building remains endearing. The 17th-century church of San Giuseppe next door is one of the most beautiful in the area.

activities.text: If the sky is clear at Passo della Croce Arcana, the view reaches far across the Tuscan and Emilian ridges. The pass marks the border between Emilia-Romagna and Tuscany. Accessible by car.

The Simposio Internazionale di Scultura has produced more than 250 stone works scattered throughout the village and surroundings. Fanano has been a stone carver's village for generations. The sculptures line the hiking trails.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Apennines: From Montefiorino to Rocchetta Mattei

visits.text: The shade under the arches hits you all at once: the Portici delle Teresiane in Fasano are what remains of a Carmelite convent built in 1628, now a covered shopping arcade. The nuns built these arcades to link several streets of the center under cover, sheltered from rain and heat. Today they're where the Fasanesi meet. Reliably cool at 3pm.

Piazza Ignazio Ciaia is Fasano's vital center: quadrangular, surfaced in white limestone, dedicated to a local poet and patriot. The cafés open early. It's the logical starting point before heading up toward the Selva or down to Savelletri and the sea.

Step into the Chiesa Maria Santissima del Rosario, adjoining the Portici: a single nave, and above all the remains of the enclosure, the grilles, and the opening cut into the wall through which communion was given to the nuns attending Mass from their choir loft. A rare and slightly unsettling detail. Five minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

visits.text: Favignana, the main Aegadian island, witnessed the Battle of the Aegates in 241 BC — antiquity's first decisive naval battle, where Rome defeated Carthage at sea for the first time. Since 2005, 200 bronze rams from sunken warships have been recovered from the seabed.

The yellow tuff quarries, excavated since the 16th century, have created a unique landscape of canyons and vertical terraces. Some have been transformed into hanging gardens; others, now flooded, form natural swimming pools.
Cala Rossa, a cove with red-orange waters caused by iron oxides in the submerged tuff rocks, is Favignana's most spectacular swimming spot. Accessible by bike from the port (4 km).

The Ex-Stabilimento Florio, a 19th-century industrial tuna processing plant converted into a museum, documents the mattanza — the ritual bluefin tuna fishing practiced since Arab times. The labyrinth of nets, the rais (fishing chief) ritual, and period tools are preserved through archival audiovisual materials.

activities.text: Bike rental for the island circuit (27 km): flat, well-marked route connecting Cala Azzurra, Cala Rossa, and Cala Rotonda. Favignana is flat and bans motorcycles in high season.

Ferry excursion to Levanzo (20 min, Liberty Lines) for the morning: visit the Grotta del Genovese with its 10,000 BC prehistoric frescoes — the Mediterranean's most important cave paintings. Afternoon return.
Snorkeling at Cala Rotonda, east of Favignana, with seagrass meadows and visibility up to 25 meters.

places.name: Feltre

visits.text: Discover Feltre, a charming town huddled on a small hill and picturesquely surrounded by the powerful peaks of the Dolomites. Tall stone houses with frescoed façades and whimsical chimneys capture the imagination, while the stunning main square - Piazza Maggiore - anchors the historic center.
Explore the museums, churches, lovely theatre, and medieval streets that give Feltre its distinctive character. The blend of Venetian elegance and Alpine setting creates a unique atmosphere.

activities.text: If you have a car, venture to the nearby 11th-century Sanctuary of St. St. Vittore and Corona, a remarkable Romanesque church in a peaceful rural setting with important early frescoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

map_keywords: Santuario dei Santi Vittore e Corona Feltre

visits.text: Ferrara is one of the great cities of the Italian Renaissance, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995. Start with the Castello Estense, the imposing red-brick castle that dominates the city centre. Built in 1385 by the Marquis Niccolò II d'Este following a violent popular uprising, it's the only castle in Italy still surrounded by water-filled moats. Inside, you'll discover the sumptuous ducal apartments with painted ceilings, the kitchens and—in a darker vein—the underground dungeons where the Este family imprisoned their enemies. Climb to the top of the Torre dei Leoni for exceptional panoramic views across the entire city.

A stone's throw from the castle, the cathedral of San Giorgio blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its marble façade, begun in the 12th century, is adorned with elaborate sculptures depicting biblical scenes, including a striking Last Judgement. Notice that the lower section is Romanesque, with rounded arches, while the upper levels are Gothic, with pointed arches. The stone lions guarding the main entrance are copies—the originals are preserved inside.

Don't miss the Palazzo Schifanoia, whose name literally means 'escape boredom'—this was the residence where the Este came to be entertained. Built in 1385 by Alberto V d'Este and then enlarged by Borso d'Este in the 1470s, it houses the Hall of the Months, a fresco cycle painted by the finest artists of the Ferrara school, including Francesco del Cossa. Each panel represents a month of the year with its zodiac sign, fieldwork and court entertainments. It's one of the most beautiful ensembles of secular painting from the Italian Renaissance.

Lose yourself in the Via delle Volte, one of the most atmospheric medieval streets in Italy. About 2 km long, it's punctuated by brick arches that connect buildings above your head—these passages once linked merchants' warehouses to their homes on the other side of the street. The atmosphere is unique, especially late in the day. If you have time, push on to the Palazzo dei Diamanti (8,500 stone points on the façade, designed by Biagio Rossetti in 1493)—it mainly hosts temporary exhibitions, so check the programme before going.

activities.text: Ferrara is the cycling city par excellence—they say every resident owns three bikes. Rent a bicycle to ride the 9 km of Renaissance ramparts that encircle the old town. This green circuit, almost entirely intact, offers changing views of interior gardens, tiled roofs and the surrounding countryside. It's the best way to understand why UNESCO described Ferrara as 'an outstanding example of a planned Renaissance city'.

Ferrara's cuisine has its own specialities, distinct from the rest of Emilia-Romagna. Try cappellacci di zucca—ravioli stuffed with pumpkin, a local classic—and salama da sugo, a long-simmered sausage served with mashed potato. Wash it down with a glass of Fortana, the local red wine from the delta. The trattorias in the medieval centre, around Via delle Volte, are your best bet.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Po Delta to the Romagna Riviera: Ferrara, Ravenna and Rimini

visits.text: The Duomo di Fidenza is worth the detour for its Romanesque façade sculpted by Benedetto Antelami at the end of the 12th century. The bas-reliefs tell the life of San Donnino, beheaded on Emperor Maximian's orders, and guide pilgrims on the Via Francigena. The crypt preserves a 2nd-3rd century Roman sarcophagus.

Climb to the matroneo to discover the Museo del Duomo: medieval goldwork, a chalice of San Donnino and a dove-shaped acquamanile that historian Jacques Le Goff was fond of. Inaugurated in 1999, the museum occupies the adjoining Palazzo Vescovile.

If you're following the Via Francigena, the crenellated tower at the end of the bridge marked the northern entrance to the city in 1364, under the Visconti. Fidenza was called Borgo San Donnino until 1927, when the Roman name Fidentia was restored.

activities.text: Allow yourself a shopping break at Fidenza Village, an open-air outlet on the edge of town. Prices are good on Italian brands. Open every day, free parking.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

visits.text: The archaeological area of Fiesole—Roman theater, thermal baths, Etruscan-Roman temple, and museum—spreads across three hectares in the heart of the hillside. Fiesole (ancient Faesulae) was founded by the Etruscans between the 9th and 8th centuries BC and only became a Roman colony in the 1st century BC, after the Romans had already settled in the valley below to establish Florence. The theater, carved into the hillside in the 1st century BC, still hosts performances each summer during the Estate Fiesolana festival. The layered Etruscan-Roman temple—first dedicated to Minerva (a bronze owl attests to this), then converted to a Roman temple in the 1st century BC—was destroyed by fire following the Roman conquest. Cyclopean Etruscan walls remain visible on the site's northern edge. The museum, built in 1914 as an Ionic temple, preserves a fragment of a bronze Capitoline wolf and the Costantini collection of Greek and Etruscan ceramics.

The Villa Medici in Fiesole, built between 1451 and 1457 by Michelozzo for Giovanni di Cosimo de' Medici—son of Cosimo the Elder—is the first pleasure villa of the Renaissance: it broke definitively with the medieval fortress model by making the loggia and panorama the pivots of its architecture. Lorenzo the Magnificent inherited it in 1469 and turned it into a meeting place for the Platonic Academy: Marsilio Ficino, Pico della Mirandola, and Poliziano philosophized here. The villa has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2013. A singular detail: this is where the Medici first introduced citrus cultivation to Tuscany, imported from southern Italy. An assassination attempt on Lorenzo the Magnificent by the Pazzi family took place during a gathering within these walls.

Villa Peyron al Bosco di Fontelucente, 2 km from central Fiesole, is a 20th-century Italian garden designed between 1934 and 1960 by Paolo Peyron—without an architect, following only his own instinct—across 40 hectares of wooded estate. Thirty terraced levels descend toward Florence, linked by double-hedged boxwood parterres, 29 fountains fed by a 16th-century spring, statues in Vicenza stone (replacing originals destroyed during the war), and an artificial lake. Bequeathed to the Bardini-Peyron Foundation in 1998, the complex is classified as an exemplary 20th-century garden by Florence's Monuments Authority.

activities.text: Panoramic views of Florence from Piazza Mino da Fiesole or from the Villa Medici gardens, with vistas over Brunelleschi's dome, the bell towers of Santa Croce, and the Arno Valley extending to the Apennines. Evening light is particularly striking.
Hike the Sentiero dei Borghi trail between Fiesole and Settignano, through olive groves and historic villa gardens. The path follows the Etruscan walls for part of the route.

days_plan.itin_title: The Finest Stops Around Florence in 7 days

places.name: Figline Valdarno

visits.text: Figline Valdarno is the birthplace of Marsilio Ficino (1433-1499), the Neoplatonist philosopher who, under the patronage of Cosimo de' Medici then Lorenzo the Magnificent, translated into Latin the entire works of Plato (1482 edition), Plotinus's Enneads, and the Corpus Hermeticum—thus restoring to the West texts lost since Antiquity. He directed the Platonic Academy of Florence, founded by Cosimo de' Medici in 1459. The main square bears his name. The Collegiate Church of Santa Maria (founded 1257) houses the Madonna Enthroned by the Master of Figline (1317) and a terracotta Saint Joseph attributed to Andrea della Robbia.

The Castello di Sammezzano, 8 km north in Leccio (municipality of Reggello), is a Moorish castle transformed between 1853 and 1889 by Marquis Ferdinando Panciatichi Ximenes d'Aragona—a Florentine noble of Spanish origin. Inspired by the Alhambra in Granada, he had 365 rooms built decorated with arabesque ceilings, stalactite vaults, polychrome mosaics, and horseshoe arches, employing only local artisans. In 1878, King Umberto I was received here. The castle is currently closed to the public for restoration work (new ownership since April 2025, reopening envisioned at the earliest in 2028). The 65-hectare park—one of Tuscany's largest, with Italy's largest group of giant sequoias—remains accessible.

activities.text: Hiking in Castello di Sammezzano park among giant sequoias, romantic alleys, and Moorish architectural elements of the garden (bridge, artificial grotto with statue of Venus, pools). Ideal in spring and autumn.

visits.text: Filicudi, a 9.5 km² island with 200 permanent residents, remains one of the least touristy Aeolian islands. Its agricultural terraces, abandoned in the 1950s, now bloom with wild capers and fig trees. A single road connects the port to Valdichiesa at 390 meters elevation.

The Grotta del Bue Marino (Sea Ox Cave, named for the now-extinct Mediterranean monk seal), accessible only by sea, is a 35-meter-deep marine cavern whose walls reflect turquoise water in shimmering patterns.

activities.text: Hike to Monte Fossa Felci di Filicudi (773 m) from the port: 2h30 round-trip on a trail through terraced vineyards and caper plants, with views of Alicudi and Salina.

days_plan.itin_title: Sicily's Island Circuit: Aeolian, Aegadian & Pantelleria

visits.text: Two kilometers from the sea, behind a 13th-century wall, you stumble upon Finalborgo. And there, it's a bit like opening a chest: the village has barely budged since the Renaissance. Perfect quadrangular plan, four monumental gates, paved alleys, Del Carretto palaces recalling it was the capital of a marquisate—and quite a one. The Basilica of San Biagio (17th century) hides, in the Santa Maria degli Oliveri chapel, one of the finest cycles of medieval frescoes in all of Liguria. And the octagonal Gothic bell tower, right next door, dates from the 14th. Park outside the walls, the center is pedestrian—and good thing too.

Castel Gavone, on the hill above Finalborgo, was the palace of the Del Carretto marquises from the 12th century. Now in ruins, it preserves the Torre dei Diamanti, a cylindrical tower adorned with diamond-point rustication—marble cut into pyramids—that made the facade shimmer in the sun. Very few equivalents in Italy. Hike on foot from Finalborgo in 30 minutes, stony but easy path, good shoes.

Varigotti, 6 km east, is the other postcard image of Finale. Houses in ochre, red, Naples yellow, set with their feet in the sand, nestled against a big rock. Nicknamed the Saracen village for its Moorish influences, but it's actually a former Byzantine port. The Baia dei Saraceni, at the foot of Cape Noli, is one of Liguria's finest beaches: fine sand, translucent water, white cliff. 30 km from Finale by trails (Sentiero del Pellegrino) or 10 minutes by train from Finalmarina.

The Archaeological Museum del Finale, in the Santa Caterina convent in Finalborgo, displays finds from the caves of the Manie plateau: Arene Candide, Caprazoppa, Pollera. Centerpiece: the burial of the Young Prince, a young man about 12,000 years old buried with a staff made of deer bone and shells, one of the most important Upper Paleolithic discoveries in Italy. Also: a skull of Ursus spelaeus, the cave bear that disappeared 24,000 years ago. Count an hour.

activities.text: The Sentiero del Pellegrino, one of the Riviera's finest trails. From Finalmarina to Varigotti via Cape Noli, 2-3 hours of walking, aerial sea views, white limestone cliffs, Captain Albertis' hermitage perched at the summit. Halfway: the Grotta dei Briganti and Punta Crena. Start early in summer, little shade, and finish with a swim at Baia dei Saraceni. Return train from Varigotti to Finale in 5 minutes.

Finale is Italy's mountain biking capital. The Manie plateau offers over 200 km of single-tracks, limestone cliffs, karst rockscapes, and over 4,000 equipped climbing routes. Several rental shops (50-80€/day) offer electric mountain bikes with shuttle to climb to the plateau. If you don't climb, walk: the trails are also very good on foot.

places.name: Fiorenzuola Di Focara

visits.text: Village gateway and the Dante plaque — the only true promontory on the northern Adriatic between Trieste and Ancona's Monte Conero, 177 metres above the cliff. The village appeared between the 10th and 13th centuries as part of a defensive system alongside Casteldimezzo, Gradara and Granarola, at the crossroads between the jurisdictions of Ravenna and Pesaro, later between the Malatesta of Rimini and those of Pesaro. At the village entrance, a stone plaque engraves the lines from Canto XXVIII of Dante's Inferno (vv. 88–89): Guido da Montefeltro foretells that the winds of Focara would be so deadly that no prayer or vow would suffice. 'Focara' derives either from the fuochi — fires lit at the summit to guide sailors by night — or from the fornacelle where bricks were fired (from the Romagnol fuchèr).

Pentagonal wall circuit and Sant'Andrea campanile — of the original five bastions, three survive. The walls along the cliff edge are being gradually eroded by the sea below. 17th-century doorways with inscriptions decorate the lanes. The church of Sant'Andrea dates to the 12th century — demolished by the 1916 earthquake, only its bell tower remains standing, its clock still working, striking the hour in this near-silent village.

Belvedere on the cliff — Sentiero dell'Amore — The village lanes describe concentric semicircles converging toward the cliff's edge, then rising back toward the old bell tower. From the belvedere at the wall's edge, the drop to the sea is sheer and vertiginous. The Sentiero dell'Amore is a path laid along the old rampart walkway, running along the cliff face.

activities.text: Descent to the beach at Fiorenzuola — the wild beach of Fiorenzuola di Focara is accessible on foot from the village via the Strada della Marina. A must on any day spent at Focara. Turquoise water, shallow seabed, within the Parco Naturale del Monte San Bartolo: ranked among the 40 most beautiful beaches in Europe by The Guardian in 2019. In summer, a shuttle connects the village to the beach.

Hiking in the Parco del Monte San Bartolo — from Fiorenzuola, several trails in the Parco Naturale Regionale del Monte San Bartolo head north toward Casteldimezzo or south toward Pesaro. Trail 151 runs along the coast, alternating between Mediterranean scrubland and open views over the Adriatic.

visits.text: Lucca - morning stop en route to Florence (Lucca sits on the A11 highway, halfway between Pisa and Florence). City Walls - Passeggiata sulle Mura: Lucca's ramparts form a 4.2-kilometer Renaissance enclosure built between 1504 and 1645. Unlike most Italian fortifications, they were never breached and remain virtually intact. Their flat crown, 30 meters wide and shaded by centuries-old plane trees, was converted into a public promenade in the 19th century. Eleven star-shaped bastions punctuate the circuit, designed to withstand artillery using the military engineering techniques of the era.

Torre Guinigi - Built in the second half of the 14th century by Paolo Guinigi, Lord of Lucca from 1400 to 1430, the Guinigi Tower rises 45 meters in red Romano-Gothic brick. Its absolute singularity is the hanging garden at its summit: seven holm oaks (Quercus ilex), symbols of rebirth in the Guinigi family tradition, grow in a soil-filled chamber 45 meters above ground. In the early 15th century, Lucca counted nearly 250 towers; the Guinigi is one of the few still standing. Local legend claims that the tallest tree was planted by Paolo Guinigi himself, and that it lost all its leaves when the lord was imprisoned by Francesco Sforza. The 230 steps lead to a panorama over the entire medieval center.

Torre delle Ore - Lucca's medieval public clock tower dates from the 14th century and was one of Tuscany's first mechanical public clocks. The climb is optional but offers a different view over the rooftops and the nearby Torre Guinigi.

San Michele in Foro - Built on the site of the Roman forum, the church of San Michele in Foro is one of the finest achievements of Pisan Romanesque architecture in Lucca. Its four-tiered facade, adorned with twisted columns, marble lozenges, and polychrome inlays, was erected between the 11th and 14th centuries. The facade is deliberately higher than the nave to impress merchants in the square.

Piazza dell'Anfiteatro - This elliptical square, unique in the world, is built on the foundations of a 1st-century AD Roman amphitheater that could hold up to 10,000 spectators. The tiers were gradually integrated into medieval houses, whose facades still follow the exact curve of the ancient arena. Four vaulted passages, heirs to the Roman entrances, are the only access points to the enclosed square.

Cathedral of San Martino - The Cathedral of Lucca preserves one of the most venerated relics of the Middle Ages: the Volto Santo, a cedar wood crucifix representing the face of Christ, which tradition attributes to Nicodemus, a disciple of Jesus. The tomb of Ilaria del Carretto (1406), a masterpiece by Jacopo della Quercia, is one of the most moving examples of Italian Gothic sculpture.

Ponte Vecchio and Lungarno - The Ponte Vecchio owes its existence to an earlier Roman bridge built around 120 AD on the Via Cassia. Destroyed by a flood in 1333, it was rebuilt in stone in 1345 by Taddeo Gaddi and Neri di Fioravante with three arches, the largest measuring 30 meters. In 1593, Ferdinand I de' Medici, bothered by the smells of butchers and fishmongers when crossing the Vasari Corridor above, ordered that only jewelers and goldsmiths could keep shops there—a regulation still in effect today. The Vasari Corridor, built in 1565, runs above the bridge for nearly a kilometer.

Piazza del Duomo - Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore, Brunelleschi's Dome, Giotto's Campanile - The Cathedral of Florence, whose construction began in 1296 under Arnolfo di Cambio, is crowned by Brunelleschi's dome completed in 1436: with its 45-meter diameter and 91-meter height, it remains the world's largest brick dome. Brunelleschi had to invent new construction techniques because no contemporary knew how to close such a cupola. Giotto's Campanile, begun in 1334, reaches 84 meters and offers from its 414 steps a direct view of the dome. The Baptistery of San Giovanni, whose 'Gates of Paradise' were sculpted by Ghiberti between 1425 and 1452, is one of the city's oldest buildings.

Mercato Centrale (San Lorenzo) - The halls of the Mercato Centrale, built in iron and glass between 1870 and 1874 by architect Giuseppe Mengoni (also architect of Milan's Galleria Vittorio Emanuele), constitute one of Tuscany's liveliest covered food markets.

Piazza della Signoria - Loggia dei Lanzi - The Palazzo Vecchio, whose construction began in 1299 under Arnolfo di Cambio, was the seat of the Florentine Republic and later of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Its 94-meter tower is offset from the facade because it incorporates a pre-existing medieval tower. In the square, a circular plaque marks the spot where Savonarola was hanged and burned in 1498. The Loggia dei Lanzi houses Benvenuto Cellini's Perseus (1554) and Giambologna's Rape of the Sabine Women (1583).

Palazzo Pitti and Boboli Gardens - The Palazzo Pitti, whose construction began in 1458 for banker Luca Pitti on a design attributed to Brunelleschi, was acquired by the Medici in 1560. It's the largest palace in Florence with a 205-meter facade. The Boboli Gardens, laid out from 1549, constitute one of the first examples of Italian-style gardens with their geometric paths, fountains, and statues.

Oltrarno Quarter - The neighborhood situated beyond the Arno retains a more authentic atmosphere. The Basilica of Santo Spirito, designed by Brunelleschi in 1436, and the alleys around Piazza Santo Spirito concentrate artisan workshops, antique dealers, and trattorias frequented by Florentines.

activities.text: Bike ride on Lucca's ramparts - The complete circuit of the ramparts is 4.2 km and takes 30 to 45 minutes by bike. Rental shops are located at the main city gates.

Walking loop through Florence's historic center (Duomo → Signoria → Ponte Vecchio → Oltrarno) - The entire historic center of Florence has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982. The loop covers approximately 3 km.
