Riserva Naturale Valli del Mincio Mantova

places.name: Grazzano Visconti

visits.text: Explore the Castle and Historic Park of Grazzano Visconti, the most precious part of this unique village. The 14th-century castle, completely restored by Giuseppe Visconti di Modrone in eclectic style, offers guided tours through the courtyard, the richly furnished reception rooms, and the bedrooms on the first floor.

Wander through the Castle Park, 15 hectares of English and Italian gardens designed by Giuseppe Visconti. Statues, vases, columns, fountains, and an extraordinary variety of trees and shrubs create a fairytale atmosphere, completed by the delightful little girls' cottage that seems straight out of a storybook.

Visit the Wax Museum with statues of figures connected to Piacenza's history, and the Torture Museum in the Palazzetto dell'Istituzione, small but complete, with torture instruments accompanied by explanatory panels. Adjacent is an Escape Room themed around the Inquisition.

Admire the Parish Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, the oldest building in the village with 17th-century renovations. Inside, the Chapel of Our Lady of Lourdes houses numerous ex-votos, testimony to popular devotion through the centuries.

activities.text: Lose yourself in the white lanes of the village, admiring the cottages with frescoed façades, the arcades, and the statues. In the Cortevecchia you'll find the statue of Aloisa, the famous ghost of Grazzano Visconti, and a small museum of agricultural tools under the long portico.

Explore the numerous craft shops and souvenir stores, open in every season on weekends. This rare example of revivalist architecture, recognized as a City of Art by the Emilia Romagna Region in 1986, will make you feel catapulted back in time 700 years.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles of the Piacenza Hills: A 2-Day Medieval Road Trip Through Northern Italy

map_keywords: Castello di Grazzano Visconti Grazzano Visconti
Chiesa dei Santi Cosma e Damiano Grazzano Visconti

visits.text: Valle del Lys (Gressoney Valley) was colonized in the 13th century by the Walser, a Germanic population originating from the Valais canton in Switzerland. Departing from Zermatt via the Theodul Pass (3,317 m) to the west and Monte Moro (2,984 m) to the east, they settled in a then-inhospitable region in exchange for rights and freedoms granted by local feudal lords. They still speak titsch (in Gressoney) and töitschu (in Issime) today, Alemannic dialects close to German—in Issime, titsch is still taught in primary school.

Castel Savoia in Gressoney-Saint-Jean was built between 1899 and 1904 by Queen Margherita of Savoy, wife of King Umberto I, who particularly appreciated this valley for her summer stays. Its neo-Gothic towers and English gardens contrast with the alpine landscape. The queen received botanists and alpinists here. Period furniture is largely preserved.

The hamlet of Alpenzu (1,776 m), above Gressoney-La-Trinité, is one of the best-preserved Walser villages in the Alps. Its stadel—larch granaries on stilts—date from the 16th-17th centuries. The Walzer Weg (Walser Path) links Gressoney-Saint-Jean to Alpenzu crossing alpine pastures and larch forests. The Walser Kulturzentrum in Gressoney-Saint-Jean documents the architecture, traditional costume, and language of this community.

activities.text: Hike the Walzer Weg from Gressoney-Saint-Jean to Alpenzu: ascent through alpine pastures, view of the Monte Rosa glacier. Duration about 3h round trip.
In summer, the cable car from Gressoney-La-Trinité climbs to 3,200 meters on the Monte Rosa massif, offering direct access to glaciers and high-mountain routes.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Valleys of Piedmont: Occitan Alps, Lakes & Baroque Savoy

places.name: Greve In Chianti

visits.text: Piazza Matteotti in Greve in Chianti has been the commercial center of the vineyard for five centuries. Its atypical triangular shape—surrounded by arcades under which merchants displayed wines and oils—is crossed by the Via Chiantigiana, the only road between Florence and Siena until the 18th century. At the center stands a statue of Giovanni da Verrazzano, born in 1485 at the nearby Castello di Verrazzano, who discovered New York Bay in 1524—his name is preserved in the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge between Brooklyn and Staten Island. In 1716, Cosimo III de' Medici officially delimited the Chianti production zone here, in the first European legal act delimiting a wine appellation.

The medieval village of Montefioralle, 2 km from Greve, is classified among Italy's Most Beautiful Villages. Still enclosed by its medieval walls, it preserves a compact plan of stone houses and streets virtually unchanged since the 13th century. The family of Amerigo Vespucci, the Florentine navigator who gave his name to America, originated from this village.

activities.text: Tasting of Chianti Classico DOCG in cellars of hillside estates. In 1906, major landowners founded the Chianti Wine Union here, precursor to today's Consorzio. The Gallo Nero (Black Rooster) label, emblem of the town, certifies the strictly local origin of the wines. The Chianti Classico Expo, every second weekend of September, brings together about sixty producers in the main square.

The Abbey of Badia a Passignano, 8 km northwest of Greve, is a Vallombrosian abbey founded in the 11th century. The Antinori group vinifies Chianti Classico Riserva Badia a Passignano in its medieval cellars, and produces its Tignanello nearby—one of the first Super Tuscans. Estate visits and tastings can be reserved.

days_plan.itin_title: The Finest Stops Around Florence in 7 days

map_keywords: Borgo di Montefioralle Greve in Chianti
Museo del Vino Greve in Chianti

visits.text: Rocchetta Mattei - an eclectic castle built from 1850 onward by Count Cesare Mattei (1809-1896) atop the ruins of a medieval fortress at 370 m elevation. Mattei, inventor of electrohomeopathy (an alternative medicine he marketed worldwide), financed the construction of this residence-laboratory for 46 years. The architecture blends medieval Gothic, Moorish style (domes, horseshoe arches, Hispano-Moorish ceramics), and Renaissance elements in a labyrinth of 60 rooms.

Museo Giorgio Morandi a Grizzana - the Bolognese painter Giorgio Morandi (1890-1964), famous for his still lifes of bottles and carafes, spent every summer in Grizzana from 1913 to 1964. The municipal museum presents reproductions of his works and documents his relationship with the Bolognese Apennine landscape that influenced his earthy color palette.

activities.text: Take a guided tour of Rocchetta Mattei—the route winds through decorated halls, the Moorish room with Spanish ceramics, the neo-Gothic chapel, and terraces with views over the Reno valley.
Hike the ridge trails around Grizzana with views across the Reno and Setta valleys—the wooded hillscape that inspired Morandi for half a century.

days_plan.itin_title: 10 Natural Wonders Around Bologna
Modena Apennines: From Montefiorino to Rocchetta Mattei

visits.text: Perched on an ophiolitic rock spur above a rushing stream, the Castello di Gropparello looks more like a fairytale set than a fortress. Built around 789, granted by Charlemagne to the Bishop of Piacenza in 808, it weathered centuries of feuds between Guelphs and Ghibellines. Open Sundays and holidays from March to November; free parking at the entrance.

Built around 789 on a Roman castrum, the site preserves what may be a Celtic sacrificial altar carved into the bedrock. The inner courtyard, unreachable from below, explains why no attacker ever took the fortress. The medieval tavern in the park serves local dishes with DOC wines from the Piacenza hills.

activities.text: If you're traveling with children, the Parco delle Fiabe at the castle's foot offers a forest adventure trail with medieval characters. Adults can join without embarrassment. Open during castle hours, combined ticket available.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

visits.text: The water shifts from turquoise to emerald in this pool carved into white rock: the Grotta della Poesia, at Roca Vecchia, was a Messapian sanctuary dedicated to the healing god Thaotor Andirahas. Its walls bear millennial carvings. Come early in the morning in summer to avoid the crowds.

activities.text: If you can swim, slip into the basin from the rock ledges: bathing in the Grotta della Poesia is the experience that made Roca Vecchia famous. Access is on foot from the nearby paid parking lots. Bring water shoes—the stone is sharp.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce

visits.text: A site cited worldwide, and almost invisible on the ground: the Grotta delle Veneri at Parabita yielded two female figurines carved in bone in the mid-1960s. They are kept at the archaeological museum in Taranto, not here. The cave is looked at from outside, so do not count on going in.

activities.text: If the subject really grabs you, pair the stop with a trip to the Taranto museum, or ask at the Parabita town hall about occasional openings. On site there is neither a sign nor a made-up path. Wear closed shoes, as the ground is scrubby.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: Fishermen named it after the zinzuli, the rags: the stalactites of the Grotta Zinzulusa hang from the vault like washing put out to dry. The cave runs about 160 metres, of which 150 are open to the public. The guided visit takes around thirty minutes.

Open to the public, yet mostly closed off: beyond the first 150 metres, the Zinzulusa shelters a pool known as il Cocito and partly flooded galleries, sealed because of the importance of their biodiversity. Access is granted only for research. The visitable stretch is enough to show why the site is watched so closely.

activities.text: When the sea is rough, the Zinzulusa closes: the entrance sits right at water level, about 2 km north of Castro Marina. An underground crustacean, Spelaeomysis bottazzii, was described here in the early 20th century and carries the name of the physiologist Filippo Bottazzi. Come first thing, as the queue builds quickly.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce
Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: The smell of wet clay hits you before the alleyways do: the Quartiere delle Ceramiche in Grottaglie clings to the gravina di San Giorgio, with workshops and kilns carved directly into the rock. In dialect they're called li Camenn're, the chimneys. You reach them by steps, along the walls of the Castello Episcopio. Come in the morning, when the ceramicists are at the wheel.

A symbol of the feudal power of the bishops of Taranto, the Castello Episcopio raises its 14th-century square tower over the historic center. It houses the Museo della Ceramica, which traces the evolution of local production century by century. Courtyard, halls, panoramic terrace. In the evening, lit up from the ceramics quarter, it's worth looking at from below too.

The Collegiata Maria Santissima Annunziata is Grottaglie's chiesa madre, at the top of the historic center, steps from the castle. It's the classic starting point for guided tours of the town, before heading down to the workshops. Quick, but it puts everything else in context. Fifteen minutes.

The Chiesa del Carmine in Grottaglie houses a cave crypt dedicated to the Madonna della Grotta, with an adjoining convent. On the way, spot the ceramic pumi placed on balconies, those stylized buds said to bring good luck, and the Cappella dei Santi Pietro e Paolo. Palazzo Pignatelli is visible from the street.

The Gravina di Riggio is the most impressive of the ravines encircling Grottaglie, and a waterfall runs at its floor. The other ravines, Fullonese, Fantiano, San Biagio, complete the picture; the last one houses a chapel with frescoes and Greek inscriptions. Allow half a day if you're descending into Riggio, and wear shoes that grip.

Street art murals in the middle of a ceramics town: Grottaglie opened its walls to street artists, often in the most unexpected corners of the historic center. They coexist with ancient palaces and medieval kilns without anyone finding this strange. Look for them between Via Crispi and the terraces overlooking the Ionian countryside.

activities.text: Walk into a bottega in Grottaglie's ceramics quarter and ask: most craftspeople are happy to explain the stages, from the wheel to the firing. You can buy pumi, tableware, one-of-a-kind pieces. The contemporary ceramics competition Mediterraneo is held in the rooms of the Castello Episcopio, running without interruption since 2004.

If you're there in late July, Vino e Musica fills the Quartiere delle Ceramiche: tasting route, street performers, music in the lit alleyways. The Festa dell'Uva, dedicated to the local Noscia grape variety, rounds out the calendar. Two occasions to see the quarter as more than a shop window.

days_plan.itin_title: Puglia: 3 days through the Murgia Barese, from Polignano's cliffs to the Tarantine ravines
The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

places.name: Grottammare

visits.text: Piazza Peretti — the beating heart of the borgo antico, framed by the town hall, the Chiesa di San Giovanni Battista and the Teatro dell'Arancio. From the theatre's loggia, the view sweeps all the way down to the Riviera delle Palme.

Teatro dell'Arancio — built in the final decade of the 18th century by Ticinese architect Pietro Maggi, this intimate theatre takes its name from an orange tree that once stood in the square, whose care was entrusted each year to a local family in exchange for a tax exemption. During the Spanish flu epidemic (1918–1920), with no wood available for coffins, the interior woodwork was stripped out entirely. Restored in 2003, it now houses the Gianni Ottaviani museum space.

Torrione della Battaglia — a 16th-century fortification tower commanding sweeping views of the coastline. Its rooms hold 250 works by local sculptor Pericle Fazzini (1913–1987), the man behind the monumental silver Resurrection in the Vatican's Nervi Hall.

Museo Sistino — housed inside the Chiesa di San Giovanni Battista on Piazza Peretti, it brings together sacred objects from the village's churches, including a chalice donated by Pope Sixtus V, who was born in Grottammare in 1521.

Resti del Castello — at the hilltop, the ruins of a fortress built between the 8th and 9th centuries by the monks of Farfa as a defence against Saracen raids. The surrounding park offers the highest viewpoint over the sea.

activities.text: Wander the alleyways of the borgo antico between brick houses and orange trees, following two marked trails: one tracing the footsteps of Pope Sixtus V, the other leading to Fazzini's sculptures scattered throughout the village.
Taste the brodetto alla sambenedettese — the iconic fish soup of the Picene coast — and the frustingo, a Christmas cake made with dried figs, walnuts, raisins and cooked wine.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Giovanni Battista Grottammare

visits.text: Discover the Grotte di Caglieron, where wooden walkways lead through a series of caves with countless waterfalls streaming down rocky gorge sides. This area of extraordinary natural beauty combines geological wonders with human history stretching back centuries.

Explore the unique cheese caves where a local dairy company matures cheese in the natural cool humidity. You can purchase slabs of this cave-aged cheese, adding a delicious souvenir to your nature adventure.

activities.text: Hike the trails through this remarkable gorge where water, rock, and time have created a magical landscape. The combination of natural caves and quarried grottos offers insights into both geological and human history.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

places.name: Grotte Di Castellana

visits.text: The air drops to 16-18°C in an instant, seventy meters below the Murge plateau: the Grotte di Castellana open through the Grave, the only cavern connected naturally to the surface, 100 meters long, 50 wide, 60 deep. The opening of sky above you lingers for a moment, then disappears. Bring a light layer and flat-soled shoes, even in August.

Pay for the full route, not the short one: the Grotta Bianca is only accessible on the 3km tour, roughly 100 minutes of walking. Near-translucent alabaster, walls that reflect the spotlights back at you. The partial route covers 1km in 50 minutes and stops before reaching it. Tickets sell out fast in summer; book online.

The Museo Speleologico Franco Anelli, at the cave exit, is named after their discoverer. Scale models, exploration equipment, workshops for children: it's brief but puts the visit in perspective. The underground network extends far beyond the section open to the public. Ask at the ticket desk what's included in your ticket.

activities.text: If you're there on a summer evening, look out for the Speleonight: the tour runs in darkness, which changes everything, including the acoustics. Dates are limited and so are spots. Failing that, aim for the first slot of the morning, fewer crowds and a less rushed guide.

days_plan.itin_title: The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days
Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

map_keywords: Franco Anelli Speleological Museum Castellana Grotte

visits.text: Gualtieri, listed among the Borghi più belli d'Italia, hides behind its porticoed piazza a palace disproportionate for a village of this size. The Palazzo Bentivoglio, erected from 1594 by Ippolito Bentivoglio, was meant to rival the great courts of the Po. In 1751, half of it was demolished to contain the river's floods.

In the Salone dei Giganti, frescoes inspired by Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered cover 17-meter-high walls. Restored and reopened in 2025, the space also serves as a performance hall. The effect is striking.

The Museo Antonio Ligabue exhibits works by the painter born in Zurich in 1899, who died in Gualtieri in 1965. Self-taught and tormented, he painted wild beasts and self-portraits of rare intensity. Next door, the Donazione Tirelli shows film costumes by Visconti and Zeffirelli. Entry 3 euros.

activities.text: Take the free audioguide for the Palazzo Bentivoglio visit: available in Italian and English. On weekends, free guided tours are offered. The 44-meter civic tower dominates the piazza.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

places.name: Guardiagrele

visits.text: Guardiagrele - a town of 9,000 inhabitants at 576 meters, at the eastern foot of Majella, renowned since the Middle Ages for its goldsmiths and ironworkers. Nicola da Guardiagrele (c. 1385-1462), a goldsmith considered one of the greatest 15th-century Italian artists, was born here. His repoussé silver works are preserved in museums in Chieti, L'Aquila, and the Vatican.

Collegiata di Santa Maria Maggiore - a 12th-century Romanesque cathedral with a 14th-century Gothic portal attributed to the school of Nicola da Guardiagrele. The 42-meter octagonal bell tower dominates the historic center. Preserves a silver polyptych by Nicola da Guardiagrele (1434).

activities.text: Discover the Presentosa in goldsmith workshops - this traditional gold or silver filigree jewel, circular and adorned with geometric motifs, is Abruzzo's emblematic jewelry piece, offered to women to ward off the evil eye.
Tasting of Sise delle Monache - a three-humped pastry filled with ricotta cream and chocolate, a specialty invented by Clarissan nuns from the local convent in the 18th century.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

map_keywords: Collegiata di Santa Maria Maggiore Guardiagrele

visits.text: Guarene dominates the right bank of the Tanaro from a strategic position that allowed the Radicati to establish a fortress here in the Middle Ages. In the eighteenth century, Count Carlo Giacinto Roero di Guarene - friend and student of court architect Filippo Juvarra - decided to transform the fortress into a prestige residence. Work began on September 13, 1726, the date and hour recorded in the archives. The building, 25 meters high over three levels and surrounded by Italian gardens begun in 1740, is a rare example of Piedmontese baroque commissioned by an aristocrat who was himself an amateur architect.

In 1773, King Victor Amadeus III of Sardinia and the Queen visited the castle, leaving traces in the furnishings of several rooms. From the terraces, the view embraces 60 kilometers of UNESCO-classified territory - from the Langhe of Barolo to Barbaresco, the Monferrato, and the Alpine chain from the plain of Alba and beyond. Today converted into a luxury hotel and listed as a historic monument since 2011, the castle preserves all its period furniture, tapestries, and family portraits of the Roero.

On the hill of San Licerio, the Parco d'Arte presents works by Italian and international artists installed among Nebbiolo vines and woods. Born in 1975 from a local painting competition, the collection has grown to constitute a unique free open-air museum in the Roero.

activities.text: Tasting of Roero Arneis - Piedmont's great dry white - and Roero Rosso made from Nebbiolo in local cellars. Walk through the Roero vineyards along the "Rocche," spectacular sandy cliffs carved by erosion that characterize this north side of the Tanaro.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont's Most Beautiful Villages in 2 Weeks

visits.text: Cesare I Gonzaga had the Palazzo Ducale of Guastalla rebuilt in the 16th century by Francesco da Volterra. Tasso and Guercino were received here. Now a city museum with the Quadreria Maldotti, the palace reopened after a long post-earthquake restoration. The ducal apartment has been accessible since 2025.

Piazza Mazzini opens with the statue of Ferrante I Gonzaga at its center. Under the porticoes, the Biblioteca Maldotti houses rare volumes. The piazza is more intimate than Carpi's, but the Renaissance setting is intact.

The Concattedrale dei Santi Pietro e Paolo, facing the Palazzo, preserves a spacious Baroque nave. The Santuario della Beata Vergine della Porta, at the town entrance, merits a detour for its ex-votos and popular atmosphere.

activities.text: Head down to the Po for a stroll on the argine: the view embraces the plain and the river. Guastalla is well connected by bus from Reggio Emilia (line 87). On Saturday and Sunday, the UIT on the ground floor of the Palazzo provides maps and information.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

places.name: Gubbio

visits.text: Gubbio is arguably the most austere of Umbria's medieval towns: grey stone from Monte Ingino, dark roofs, tight alleys climbing steeply. No Florentine softness here. The town preserves its intact medieval layout, 13th-century stone palaces aligned on four terraced levels clinging to the mountainside. The Palazzo dei Consoli, perched above Piazza Grande, is the archetype of the Italian medieval commune: 60 meters tall, massive blind facade, crenellations. It houses the Tabulae Iguvinae, seven bronze tablets inscribed in Umbrian alphabet from the 2nd century BC—one of the oldest preserved pre-Roman religious texts.

The Church of San Francesco in Gubbio carries the memory of one of the loveliest Franciscan legends: this is where the man-eating wolf that terrorized the town in the early 13th century supposedly lived. Francis, visiting, reportedly tamed it before the townsfolk—he extended his hand, the wolf placed its paw, and both sealed a pact: the wolf would kill no more if the town fed him. The wolf's tombstone, found in 1873 beneath the threshold of the neighboring Chiesa di San Francesco della Pace, is displayed inside—the bones themselves have vanished. Medieval frescoes from the 13th and 14th centuries inside.

To climb to the Basilica di Sant'Ubaldo (827 meters altitude, town patron), take the funivia (cable car in open two-person cages) departing from Colle Eletto. Six minutes ascending standing in a metal cage, feet dangling—not for the vertigo-prone or claustrophobic. The basilica houses the incorrupt body of Ubaldo, who died in 1160, displayed in a glass reliquary above the altar. As well as the three Ceri, enormous 4-meter wooden candles carried in a frantic race through town every May 15—Corsa dei Ceri festival, listed as UNESCO intangible heritage in 2013.

Piazza Grande, a panoramic terrace suspended above the town, is one of Italy's most spectacular squares. Four enormous stone vaults support it above the void since the 14th century—medieval engineering trick to create a flat square on steep terrain. Views across the Umbrian plain to the Apennines. Also the starting point for the annual Ceri race on May 15.

activities.text: Dinner at Taverna del Lupo, the name says it all. Classic Umbrian cuisine in a vaulted medieval cellar: braised wild boar, Apennine black truffle, porcini gnocchi, spit-roasted lamb. Moderate prices (40-50 euro full menu). Reserve, especially weekends.

Evening drink at Tana del Coniglio, centro wine bar—selection of Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG and Rosso di Montefalco, powerful Umbrian reds built for Apennine charcuterie. Budget 6-10 euros per glass, cheese board included.

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Umbria: 8 days Among Mummies, Mystics & Caves

map_keywords: Funivia Colle Eletto cable car Gubbio

visits.text: Nuraghe Genna Maria, 1 km from Villanovaforru, deserves the stop before Iglesias. Perched at 408m altitude, it offers a panorama of 53 Sardinian villages on clear days, from the Gulf of Oristano to the Gulf of Cagliari. It's a complex nuraghe erected in the 15th century BC: 10m central keep surrounded by three towers and a bastion added a century later. In the Punic-Roman era, it becomes a sanctuary dedicated to Demeter and Kore—over 600 votive oil lamps, coins and offerings were found. €4 guided tour, €7 with archaeological museum in the village.

Iglesias is the former center of Sardinia's mining epic. 27,000 inhabitants, founded by Pisans in the 13th century who already exploited the silver and lead from neighboring mountains. Its name means "churches" in Spanish—the Aragonese renamed it in the 14th century. Compact historic center, dominated by the Santa Chiara cathedral (13th-14th centuries) and the San Francesco church, one of the finest intact Catalan Gothic architectures in Sardinia. Holy Week here has Seville airs: Mysteries processions on Holy Tuesday and Friday, obvious Spanish heritage.

The Mining Art Museum in Iglesias, in the early 20th-century Liberty-style Asproni institute, traces the zone's industrial history. Reconstructions of galleries, mineral collection, original extraction machines. The Sardinian Geo-mining Park has been recognized by UNESCO since 1997 as the first geo-mining park on the world list. Allow 1 hour. Good preamble to tomorrow's Porto Flavia visit.

activities.text: Aperitivo and dinner on Piazza Sella in Iglesias, the city's heart. Several tapas bars and trattorias serve local specialties: malloreddus alla campidanese (Sardinian gnocchi with sausage-tomato-saffron sauce), fregola con arselle (pearl couscous with clams), Sardinian porceddu. The city comes alive at nightfall, relaxed atmosphere, lots of students.

Quick detour to Villamassargia (15 km south of Iglesias) for the S'Ortu Mannu park: historic olive grove with about 700 monumental olive trees. The most imposing, nicknamed Sa Reina ("the Queen"), displays a trunk over 16 meters in circumference and estimated age around 900 years—possibly the largest olive tree in the Mediterranean basin. For Sardinia's absolute elder, you need to see S'Ozzastru in Luras, a wild olive estimated at 4,000 years. Free access to S'Ortu Mannu, simple signage. Allow 45 minutes on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Sardinia's Wild Interior and Eastern Coast: 6 Days from Olbia to Cagliari

places.name: Imperia

visits.text: Climb to the Parasio, the medieval promontory of Porto Maurizio, via the spiral road or the elevator from sea level. This quarter constitutes the original nucleus of Imperia: for centuries Porto Maurizio was an autonomous port and the Mediterranean's leading center for olive oil production and trade, under the protection of the Republic of Genoa. Only in 1923 did a government decree merge it with Oneglia—its Piedmontese rival separated by 3 kilometers—to form the municipality of Imperia. Inhabitants of the two towns still call each other 'ciantafourche' and 'cacelotti,' nicknames inherited from centuries of rivalry.

Enter the Basilica of San Maurizio, the largest church in Liguria, built between 1781 and 1838 on the site of an earlier chapel. Its neoclassical facade dominates the square at the Parasio's exit. Inside: frescoes, paintings, and 19th-century sculptures. On the adjacent Via Santa Caterina, visit the birthplace of San Leonardo da Porto Maurizio, born in 1676 in the Parasio and canonized in the 19th century: the house converted into a museum preserves his habit, his hair shirt, and the funeral cast of his face.

From the Logge di Santa Chiara, the panoramic loggias of the Convent of the Sisters of Santa Chiara atop the Parasio, the view embraces the Ligurian coast on both sides. Nearby, the Tower of Prarola rises directly from the sea west of the historic center: this cylindrical watchtower was built to monitor Saracen pirate raids, a constant threat on this coast until the 17th century.

Visit the Museo dell'Olivo Carlo Carli in Oneglia, housed in a Liberty-style palazzo and spread across eighteen rooms. The Carli brothers, olive oil industrialists, assembled a collection tracing olive cultivation techniques from Ancient Greece to the 20th century: Roman amphorae, parts of animal-drawn or hydraulic mills, documents on cosmetic and medicinal uses of oil. A reconstruction of a Roman ship's hold and a 17th-century press stand in the courtyard. The Taggiasca olive, cultivated in these hills since its Benedictine introduction in the 7th century, was the source of the entire region's historic wealth.

Visit the Basilica of San Giovanni Battista in Oneglia, consecrated in 1762 by architect Gaetano Amoretti and elevated to basilica status in 2017. This late Genoese Baroque building houses polychrome marbles, frescoes, and an 1874 three-keyboard organ. For centuries Oneglia was the main port of Piedmont under the Savoys, rival to Porto Maurizio which answered to Genoa—a rivalry so intense that in 1792, a French fleet bombarded Oneglia without touching neutral Porto Maurizio.

Stroll through Villa Grock, commissioned in the 1920s by Adrien Wettach—known as Grock—one of Europe's most famous clowns, born in Switzerland in 1880. The villa mixes Art Nouveau, references to the circus world, and elements recalling Dalí, Picasso, and Gaudí. It now serves as a museum of clowning and an architectural monument.

activities.text: Walk the Passeggiata degli Innamorati, the path that follows the cliffs at the base of the Parasio and connects Porto Maurizio to Borgo Marina. This promenade suspended between the medieval quarter and the sea offers the best views of the coast, particularly at sunset.

Sketching or photography session by Porto Maurizio's harbor, equipped with a long protective pier whose lighthouse provides the best viewpoint over the entire coast. Since 1986, Imperia has periodically hosted the Vele d'Epoca, a gathering of historic sailboats over 20 meters arriving from around the world.

Wander beneath the arcades of Piazza Dante in Oneglia: this lively square is Oneglia's commercial and social heart, surrounded by cafes and boutiques. Wednesday mornings host the local producers' market—Taggiasca olives, olive oil, vegetables, and cured meats from the hinterland.

Bike or walk a section of the Riviera dei Fiori cycle path between Imperia and San Lorenzo al Mare: the Imperia section, inaugurated in 2025, connects the two parts of the city and links to the existing route toward Sanremo. This stretch passes converted former stations and follows the sea for nearly the entire route.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy Road Trip from Nice: Riviera & Alps in 2 Days
Italy Road Trip from Nice: Riviera & Alps in 2 Days
Riviera di Ponente and Ligurian Hinterland in 3 Days
Grand Tour of the Riviera di Ponente in 4 Days

map_keywords: Basilica di San Giovanni Battista Oneglia

visits.text: The Basilica-Sanctuary of Santa Maria all'Impruneta was consecrated on January 3, 1060, on the site of an Etruscan place of worship. Its foundation rests on the legend of the discovery of an icon of the Virgin during construction: the oxen carrying the materials knelt at a precise point, indicating the site of the sanctuary. This Madonna—a 12th-century painted panel—has since been the principal Marian devotion of Tuscany. In 1711, she was proclaimed co-patron of Florence. The left chapel preserves a Madonna and Child by Giovanni Pisano (1317); the Treasury Museum houses a cross attributed to Ghiberti and illuminated choir books from the 14th-16th centuries.

Impruneta has been the world's principal center of terracotta production since at least 1098 (first documented mention). The local clay, refractory and extremely durable, was used by Brunelleschi for the tiles of the dome of Santa Maria del Fiore, and by the Della Robbia workshops for their glazed ceramics. The oil jars and garden vases of Impruneta adorn the gardens of Tuscany's greatest villas.

activities.text: Visit an active terracotta workshop in Impruneta: throwing, drying, firing, and glazing according to traditional techniques. Production covers jars, tiles, sculptures, and garden pots—the same ones that adorned the Uffizi and Medici palaces.

The Fair of Saint Luke, October 18 in Impruneta, is one of Tuscany's oldest fairs, attested since the Middle Ages: originally a cattle fair linked to the Madonna procession, it now brings together markets, banquets, and horse races on Piazza Buondelmonti.

days_plan.itin_title: The Finest Stops Around Florence in 7 days

visits.text: Ingria, at 827 meters elevation in Val Soana, counts 46 permanent residents - but groups together some thirty hamlets scattered across the slopes, linked by ancient trails. This commune in Gran Paradiso National Park is one of Canavese's most isolated and best-preserved villages. The uncertain etymology suggests either the Lombard Ingrich, or the Latin ingredire, linked to the Roman bridge spanning the Soana torrent - true gateway to the valley. The local language, Valsoanin, is a variant of Arpitan (Franco-Provençal), still spoken in the hamlets.

The 1719 bell tower, standing opposite the parish church of San Giacomo, is the village symbol. The permanent outdoor exhibition Le case raccontano presents panels with old black-and-white photographs captioned in Arpitan and Italian, along the alleys. The most typical hamlets like Camprovardo (three- to four-story houses connected by exterior wooden staircases) and Pasturera (sixteenth-seventeenth century round-arch stone arcades) are discovered on foot.

activities.text: Hike to Punta Arbella or Monte Betassa from Ingria, in Gran Paradiso National Park - one of Italy's oldest parks (1922), created to protect the ibex after Carlo Felice's 1821 hunting ban. The Soana torrent is suitable for canoeing depending on water levels. In August, Cose d'altri tempi (Tchouse d'auti ten) is a Franco-Provençal festival with music, dance, and ancient crafts.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont's Most Beautiful Villages in 2 Weeks

places.name: Iseo

visits.text: Monte Isola is the largest inhabited island in European lakes: 5 km², 600 meters at its highest point, about 1,800 inhabitants spread across 11 hamlets. No cars circulate here. The first document mentioning the island dates from 905, when it was property of the monastery of San Salvatore in Brescia. The tradition of fishing net manufacturing has been documented here for over 600 years; the local company La Rete, which revived the activity in the 1970s, has become Europe's leading manufacturer of sports nets. In 2016, artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude installed "The Floating Piers" here, yellow floating walkways connecting the island to the mainland.

The Sanctuary of Madonna della Ceriola stands at the island's highest point, at 600 meters altitude. It's Monte Isola's oldest church, founded in the 13th century. It preserves a 12th-century wood sculpture. The ascent from Peschiera Maraglio by trail requires about 400 meters of elevation gain and offers views over both shores of Lake Iseo.

In Pisogne, at the northern end of Lake Iseo, the church of Santa Maria della Neve houses a fresco cycle painted by Girolamo Romanino between 1532 and 1534: the entirety of the walls and vaults is covered with scenes of Christ's Passion, with sibyls and prophets in imposing poses on the Gothic vaults. Critic Giovanni Testori nicknamed the ensemble the "Sistine Chapel of the poor." The church, built in the late 15th century at the request of Pisogne's inhabitants, is free to enter.

activities.text: The ferry to Monte Isola departs from Sulzano, a few kilometers from Iseo. The crossing takes less than 10 minutes. On the island, the coastal perimeter loop on foot or by bike is about 9 kilometers and takes 2h30 to 3h: you pass through the fishing villages of Sensole, Carzano (where shipyards still build mahogany wooden boats according to a 350-year tradition) and Siviano.

days_plan.itin_title: Italian Lakes & Dolomites Road Trip: Piedmont to Venice

map_keywords: Santuario Madonna della Ceriola Monte Isola
Chiesa Santa Maria della Neve Pisogne

visits.text: Saepinum is as fascinating as Pompeii with zero crowds. The Romans took the Samnite city of Saipins, perched on the mountain above, in 293 BC; the inhabitants descended to the plain and founded the new Roman city, Saepinum, around 290 BC. The ramparts date from Tiberius's reign (between 2 BC and 4 AD)—inscriptions to prove it. Forum, basilica with varied capitals, semicircular theater 61.5 m in diameter, baths, Porta Boiano, cattle market: it's all there. Peculiarity: in the 18th century, peasants built their houses right on top of the theater's tiers, which follow its curve. Stunning effect. The site, long freely accessible, has been managed by the ministry since 2024 (€10, two museums included). Allow 2h30. Arrive at opening; in the morning the light on the limestone is magnificent.

Pietracupa, halfway between Saepinum and Isernia, is the village that grew into the rock. Houses carved into a limestone tuff spur, rupestrian church of Madonna delle Grazie, lanes cut into the stone. 200 inhabitants off-season. It's small, you can visit in 45 minutes, but the site is striking—especially seen from below, from the winding road. Park at the village entrance; the center is pedestrian.

Before reaching Isernia, the Museo Paleolitico della Pineta is worth the detour: it houses one of Europe's oldest human occupation sites, dated to 730,000 years ago. Stone tools, faunal remains, hearth vestiges. The pavilion covers the excavations; you see the original ground. Small, didactic, perfect after a day of Roman and Samnite archaeology.

The Marinelli Foundry in Agnone is probably the world's oldest family business—Nicodemus Marinelli's signature is attested on a bell from 1339, and family activity dates back to the 11th century, around 1040. The 27th generation is now in charge. They've cast bells for the Vatican, St. Peter's Basilica, Monte Cassino rebuilt after World War II, Buenos Aires Cathedral, the Sanctuary of Pompeii, and the UN headquarters in New York. In 1924, Pope Pius XI granted them the privilege of affixing the papal coat of arms to their bells. The guided tour (€9) shows the clay and hemp mold, the casting, and ends with a mini-concert where the master rings several bells. Photos prohibited. Tours at 11am, noon, 4pm, 5pm Monday to Saturday.

Pietrabbondante ('stones in abundance'), at 966 m on the flank of Monte Saraceno, was the federal sanctuary of the Samnite Pentri tribe. Theater-temple built between 120 and 90 BC, abandoned after the Social War (91-88 BC). The theater, estimated capacity between 1,000 and 2,500 seats depending on archaeologists, preserves three rows of stone seats with backrests—a rare detail, almost ergonomic. Acoustics still perfect: every summer the Samnite theater festival is held here, without amplification. Sit at the top and look at the Verrino valley: this is where the Samnite senate debated. The panorama is worth as much as the stones.

On the return road to Isernia, stop at the Sanctuary of Castelpetroso. Picture this: a hundred years of construction, 1890-1975, three generations of Molisan stone carvers, and a floor plan shaped like a heart pierced by seven swords symbolizing Mary's seven sorrows. Full neo-Gothic, 52 m dome, facade entirely hand-carved. Originally, two shepherdesses reportedly saw the Virgin in March 1888; the sanctuary was built downstream to make the pilgrimage accessible. Nicknamed 'Italy's little Lourdes.' John Paul II visited in 1995. Free entry, open daily 9am-6pm.

activities.text: Caciocavallo tasting at a Matese farm, near Sepino or Bojano. This pear-shaped cheese, attached in pairs to a rope, is made from raw milk of Podolica cows. Aged from a few months to several years, it develops notes of hazelnut and hay. Many fattorie offer visits with tasting, some open only by reservation. Allow 1 hour—brief but memorable.

Walk along a tratturo, those grassy transhumance paths that have structured Molise for 2,000 years. The Pescasseroli-Candela tratturo passes through Saepinum and totals 211 km. A well-marked portion starts right next to the archaeological site. An hour is enough to understand how, for centuries, hundreds of thousands of sheep shaped these landscapes.

Lunch in Agnone at Locanda Mammì (1 Michelin star), one of Molise's very rare starred tables. Reinvented peasant cuisine: grilled caciocavallo, lamb, mountain vegetables, handmade pasta. Tasting menu around €70-90, more accessible midday formula. Essential reservation, especially weekends. It's the chance to understand why this little-known region has a rising gastronomic scene.

Stroll through Agnone's center, classified Bandiera Arancione. Fourteen churches, including San Marco with its Renaissance portal adorned with a copper lion—remnant of Venetian artists who came in the 11th century to decorate the Borrello family's houses. If you pass in late December, the Ndocciata is a nocturnal torchlight procession of fir and beech torches descending the corso: a pagan-Christian spectacle classified as Italian cultural heritage. The rest of the year, content yourself with the alleys, copper workshops, and caciocavallo cheesemakers in business for 400 years.

places.name: Isola Del Liri

visits.text: The Cascata Grande of Isola del Liri plunges 27 meters right in the town's historic center—a phenomenon unique in Italy. The waterfall is produced by the bifurcation of the Liri River, which splits into two arms around a natural island: the left arm forms the Cascata Grande, while the right feeds the Cascata del Valcatoio (or Gualcatojo), converted in the 19th century into hydroelectric power. A painting of the waterfall by Isabelle Bidault is now preserved in the Louvre; Philipp Hackert also depicted it.

The Boncompagni-Viscogliosi Castle is documented from the 12th century and has served as a noble residence since the year 1000. It sits precisely at the bifurcation of the Liri, atop both waterfalls. Its medieval tower and Renaissance halls are visible from the riverbanks.

The Museum of Paper and Telecommunications Civilization, housed in the former Béranger-Coste paper mill, traces the industrial history of Isola del Liri: in the 19th century, the town was one of Europe's largest paper manufacturing centers. In the early 20th century, it became the first city in the world to produce and distribute hydroelectric power for both public and private use.

activities.text: Walk down the banks of the Liri on both sides of the island to see both waterfalls from water level: the Cascata Grande from the bridge on Via Argine, and the Cascata del Valcatoio from the trail on the right bank. Morning light on the main falls is particularly photogenic between 9 and 11 a.m.

visits.text: Riserva Naturale Foce dell'Isonzo - At the mouth of the Isonzo River where it flows into the Adriatic, this wetland covering over 2,300 hectares ranks among Europe's most important for migratory birds. Marshes, reed beds, flooded meadows, and oxbow lakes create a habitat mosaic where more than 300 bird species have been recorded.

Isola della Cona - The heart of the reserve, this 'island' accessible via a boardwalk trail hosts a herd of white Camargue horses living semi-wild, introduced to manage vegetation through natural grazing. Wooden observation hides punctuate the paths.

activities.text: Bird watching - Migration months (March-May and August-October) offer the richest sightings. Herons, egrets, flamingos, snipes, buzzards, and hawks follow in succession. Binoculars are essential; the visitor center sometimes lends them.
Cycling along Valle Cavanata - The flat cycle path follows the salt marshes and joins the Grado lagoon, through an amphibious landscape balanced between land and water.

places.name: Itri

visits.text: Monte San Biagio, a small village with labyrinthine alleyways climbing a hill between the Ausoni Mountains. The Church of San Giovanni Battista dominates the village. From Viale Littoria below, the panorama embraces the plain of Fondi, the three lakes, and the coast stretching to the Pontine Islands on clear days.

Castello di Itri, perched on Colle Sant'Angelo, has controlled the Via Appia since the 9th century. The first nucleus—a pentagonal tower—was erected in 882 by Duke Docibilis I of Gaeta. His grandson Marino I added around 950 a second tower, taller and wider. In the 13th century, the Caetani built the residential section and the cylindrical tower called the "Tower of the Crocodile": according to legend, prisoners condemned to death were thrown in as prey to a reptile kept in its waters. The walkway connects the towers and offers views to the coast.

The Church of San Michele Arcangelo, in Itri's upper section, is the village's oldest sacred building, dating back to the 11th century. In Arab-Norman style with three naves, it preserves 14th-century frescoes attributed to the Neapolitan Roberto Oderisio. Its square bell tower, decorated with colored majolica plates, is positioned centrally against the façade.

The Museum of Brigandage recounts the life of Michele Pezza, known as Fra' Diavolo, born in Itri on April 7, 1771. Initially wanted for murder, he became a colonel in the Neapolitan army against Napoleon's troops, using the castle's underground passages to ambush enemies on the Via Appia. Captured in 1806, he was hanged in Naples' Piazza del Mercato at age 35. Auber's opera "Fra Diavolo" (1830) and the Laurel and Hardy film (1933) made his name famous worldwide.

activities.text: Climb to the Sanctuary of Madonna della Civita, at 673 meters altitude on Monte Fusco, 13 km from the village in the Aurunci Mountains Park. According to tradition, two Basilian monks fleeing iconoclasm hid an icon of the Virgin and Child from Constantinople; a deaf-mute shepherd found it on the mountain and recovered his hearing and speech. The first historical document of the sanctuary dates from 1174. The icon, called Madonna Nera, was crowned in 1777 and 1877. From the forecourt, spectacular views of the mountains and the Gulf of Gaeta.

Hike along the Via Appia Antica: in the Gola di Sant'Andrea, between Itri and Fondi, a 2-km section of the ancient route has been excavated and enhanced. The Roman basalt paving winds between opus quadratum constructions and polygonal walls. On the ruins of a 1st-century BC Roman villa stands a fortino used by Fra' Diavolo as a rear base against the French in 1798.

days_plan.itin_title: Latina Province Circuit: Lepini Mountains and Coast

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Michele Arcangelo Itri

visits.text: Rocca Calascio first thing morning, 30 minutes from Castel del Monte. The fortress at 1,460 m altitude is the highest in the Apennines, built in white limestone around a central mastio dating to the year 1000. The four cylindrical corner towers were added around 1480 by Antonio Piccolomini, after the devastating 1461 earthquake. Historical curiosity: the castle never endured battle; it was earthquakes—the 1461 and 18th-century ones—that ruined it. The setting seduced Hollywood—Ladyhawke (1985) with Michelle Pfeiffer was filmed here, as were sequences from The Name of the Rose and The American (George Clooney, 2010). Park at the village base and climb 30 minutes on foot. The octagonal church of Santa Maria della Pietà, on the path, is one of Abruzzo's most recognizable images.

Santo Stefano di Sessanio 10 minutes from Calascio, on the route. Medieval village at 1,250 m, orange Touring Club medal. Stone houses huddled against rock, former Medici properties (the Florentine lily coat of arms still appears on some doors). The village has been partly restored as an albergo diffuso—a hotel dispersed through old houses, whose initiator Daniele Kihlgren revived local tourism. The 14th-century Medicean tower collapsed in the 2009 earthquake; its identical reconstruction was completed in 2021.

Descent to L'Aquila in the afternoon. The Abruzzo capital, founded in 1254 on Frederick II's order, was struck by a magnitude 6.3 earthquake on April 6, 2009 at 3:32 AM: 309 dead, 1,600 injured, more than 65,000 homeless. Reconstruction is still ongoing, which makes the visit singular—shored-up palaces, scaffolding, and completed buildings in total restoration coexist. The basilica of San Bernardino (15th century, Renaissance facade signed Cola dell'Amatrice) reopened in 2015. The Fontana delle 99 Cannelle, a medieval fountain with 99 faces spouting water, symbolizes the 99 castelli that supposedly founded the city according to legend. Compact historic center, to cover on foot.

activities.text: L'Aquila dinner: maccheroni alla chitarra (pasta cut on a stringed frame), lamb cacio e ovo (beaten egg and cheese), zafferano dell'Aquila DOP—Abruzzo saffron, among the world's most expensive, 1 kg = 200,000 hand-harvested stigmas. Several trattorias in the center.

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Abruzzo in 8 Days: From Rimini to Pescara, Hills to Wild Nature

places.name: La Maddalena

visits.text: The town of La Maddalena, the archipelago's only settlement, preserves in the Church of Santa Maria Maddalena a crucifix and two candlesticks offered by Admiral Nelson in 1804, who called this harbor "the most beautiful in the world" and used it as a fleet base while pursuing the French.

On Caprera Island, the Compendio Garibaldino is the house where Giuseppe Garibaldi spent the last 26 years of his life, from 1856 until his death on June 2, 1882 at 6:21 PM. The bedroom clock remains stopped at that hour. His red shirt, bed, wheelchair, and the rough granite tomb where he's buried are on display.

La Maddalena Archipelago National Park, created in 1994, groups 62 islands and islets along 112 miles of granite coastline. Spiaggia Rosa on Budelli Island, famous for its pink sand made from coral and shell fragments, is now protected and accessible only by sea.

activities.text: Ferry crossing from Palau (15 minutes) to the main island of La Maddalena.

Boat excursion around Spargi, Budelli, and Santa Maria islands, accessible only by sea. Spargi Island preserves the wreck of a 2nd-century BC Roman ship whose cargo of amphorae has been partially recovered.
Swim at Cala Coticcio on Caprera Island, nicknamed "Sardinian Tahiti" for its transparent waters in shades of turquoise and deep green. Access is on foot via a trail or by sea.

places.name: La Morra

visits.text: Admire the viewpoint at Piazza Castello, the most famous panoramic terrace in the Langhe offering a 360-degree view over vineyards dotted with villages and castles. On clear days, the gaze extends to the Alps, offering one of Piedmont's most breathtaking natural spectacles.

Climb the 31-meter-high Bell Tower, built in 1710, to enjoy an even wider view of the surrounding hills. Near the viewpoint stands the monument to the winegrower, a bronze statue paying tribute to those who work the vines and produce Barolo.

Visit the Church of San Martino, an elegant Baroque building with a brick façade and interiors decorated with precious frescoes. It's one of the most representative churches in the area and houses artworks of great value.

activities.text: Seek out the giant benches of the Big Bench Community Project scattered around La Morra. These colorful installations, created to enhance the landscape of the Langhe, allow you to enjoy spectacular views of the vineyard-covered hills from an unusual and fun perspective.

Join a tasting at the historic cellars of La Morra, one of the most important areas for Barolo DOCG production. Cantina Mascarello, Cantina Marcarini, and Cantina Oddero offer guided tours with tastings and vineyard walks.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont Wine & Truffle Road Trip: Turin, Alba & Barolo in 6 Days

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Martino La Morra

visits.text: Technical Naval Museum of the Italian Navy - Considered one of the world's oldest naval museums, the Museo Tecnico Navale is housed in the military naval arsenal built in 1869. Across more than 3,000 square meters, it preserves ship models, navigation instruments, 28 figureheads (the oldest dating to 1738), and a section dedicated to Guglielmo Marconi, who conducted his first long-distance wireless communication experiments in the Gulf of La Spezia in 1897.

Castello San Giorgio and Archaeological Museum - Documented from the second half of the 14th century, the Castello San Giorgio houses the Civic Archaeological Museum with collections from Lunigiana from Prehistory to the Middle Ages, notably the famous anthropomorphic statue-menhirs from the Copper and Bronze Ages. The ramparts offer a panorama over the Gulf of La Spezia.

Via del Prione and historic center - The main pedestrian artery of La Spezia's historic center is lined with arcades and 19th-century palaces. The Museo Civico Amedeo Lia, installed in a 17th-century Franciscan convent, preserves a collection spanning the 13th to 18th centuries including works by Tintoretto and Titian.

Harbor promenade and Passeggiata Morin - From the Molo Italia, a panorama extends over the Cinque Terre. The Gulf of La Spezia, nicknamed the 'Gulf of Poets' since Dante, Shelley, and Byron stayed here, is one of the largest protected natural gulfs on the Ligurian coast.

Riomaggiore - Marina and stairway alleys - The southernmost village of the Cinque Terre was reportedly founded in the 8th century by Greek refugees. Its five- to six-story houses, painted in ochre, yellow, and terracotta, are built directly on rock—an ancient technique that allowed sailors to recognize their home from the sea. The Via dell'Amore, a ledge carved into the cliff during the construction of railway tunnels in the 1920s, is partially reopened.

Manarola - Belvedere and postcard view - Manarola is renowned for its production of Sciacchetrà, a sweet, amber-colored white wine obtained by drying the grapes. Its belvedere on the rocky promontory is the most famous photographic viewpoint of the Cinque Terre. The church of San Lorenzo, built in 1338, preserves a medieval rose window and bell. The giant Christmas nativity scene installed on the cliffs every year since 1961 is visible from several kilometers at sea.

Corniglia - Village perched 100 meters above the sea - Corniglia is the only one of the five villages without direct access to the sea. Perched at 100 meters altitude, it is preceded by the Lardarina, a staircase of 382 steps from the station. The 14th-century church of San Pietro is adorned with a rose window in white Carrara marble. Less crowded than its neighbors, Corniglia offers the calmest atmosphere of the Cinque Terre.

Vernazza - Port, Piazza Marconi, and Castello Doria - Vernazza is regularly cited among Italy's most beautiful villages. Its natural port, protected by a medieval breakwater, is the only true mooring harbor of the Cinque Terre. The Castello Doria, built in the 11th century on the rocky ledge, is one of the oldest fortifications of the Cinque Terre and offers the most iconic view of the village and harbor.

Monterosso al Mare - Medieval borgo and Fegina beach - Monterosso is the largest of the five villages, divided into two parts: the medieval borgo (Colle di San Cristoforo) and the beach resort of Fegina, which has the only true sandy beach of the Cinque Terre. The statue called Il Gigante, a 14-meter reinforced concrete sculpture representing Neptune, was erected in 1910. The 14th-century church of San Giovanni Battista in Ligurian Gothic style striped with white and green marble is the largest in the Cinque Terre. The hinterland of Monterosso produces the Monterosso lemon, a local variety used for limoncino.

activities.text: Logistics reconnaissance for the Cinque Terre - La Spezia Centrale station is the main departure point for the Cinque Terre. The regional train serves all five villages in a maximum of 20 minutes. The Cinque Terre Card (train + trail access) is available at the station.

Cinque Terre Card train between villages (south) - The regional train connects La Spezia to Riomaggiore, Manarola, and Corniglia in less than 15 minutes. The Cinque Terre Card allows unlimited boarding.

Hike Manarola → Corniglia (trail 586/506) - The route takes the heights from Manarola, crossing terraced vineyards, holm oak forest, and a pass at 360 meters before descending to Corniglia. Allow 2h30-3h.

Hike Sentiero Azzurro Monterosso → Vernazza - This 3.6 km section is one of the most spectacular and demanding of the Sentiero Azzurro. The trail climbs through terraces of lemon and olive trees, skirts cliffs above the drop, crosses the hamlet of Prevo, then descends toward Vernazza by a steep staircase. Total elevation gain of about 400 meters. Allow 1h30-2h.
Cinque Terre Card train between villages (north) - The train connects Vernazza and Monterosso to La Spezia in 20 minutes.

places.name: La Verna

visits.text: Sanctuary of La Verna — Basilica and Chapel of the Stigmata: Mount Alverne was given to Saint Francis in 1213 by Count Orlando Cattani di Chiusi, who described it as "a solitary and wild place suited to those who wish to do penance." It was here, on September 17, 1224 — two years before his death — that Francis received the stigmata of the Passion, becoming the first stigmatist officially recognized by the Catholic Church. The Chapel of the Stigmata marks the exact spot of the miracle, indicated by a tablet in the floor. The great Basilica dedicated to Santa Maria Assunta was built from 1348 and completed in 1509 thanks to donations from the Senate of Florence. It was raised to the rank of minor basilica by Pope Benedict XV in 1921. Inside, 15th-century glazed terracottas by Andrea della Robbia decorate the chapel and the basilica — including the large Crucifixion altarpiece, one of the master's last works.

Small church of Santa Maria degli Angeli: the original nucleus of the complex, commissioned by Francis himself in 1216. This is the chapel where the eremitic life on the mount began. It is the starting point of the daily 3 PM procession to the Chapel of the Stigmata.

activities.text: Monumental forest of La Verna: protected by the Franciscan brothers for centuries, this forest of ancient beeches and firs includes trees reaching 50 meters in height. Marked trails cross the forest and lead to the summit of Monte Penna (1,283 m), from which the view extends over the entire Casentino and Valtiberina. Deer, wild boar, wolves and numerous bird species inhabit these woods.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

map_keywords: Chiesa di Santa Maria degli Angeli La Verna

places.name: Labro

visits.text: The village of Labro, a "stone borgo," rises at 2,060 feet between Monte Terminillo and Lago di Piediluco. First mentioned in 956 when Emperor Otto I enfeoffed the site to Aldobrandino de' Nobili, it preserves its intact medieval terraced plan: castle and tower at the top, noble palaces in the middle, common houses below. Nearly abandoned in the 1960s, it was the first village in Lazio to be entirely restored, thanks to the initiative of a Belgian architect who used materials and forms faithful to the original. A Bandiera Arancione from the Touring Club Italiano, Labro is also certified among Italy's "most beautiful skies" for stargazing.

Push open the door of Palazzo Nobili Vitelleschi, a manor house founded between the 10th and 11th centuries, still inhabited by descendants of the family. The rooms preserve the complete family archive and refined furnishings. The Chiesa di Santa Maria Maggiore (1508), whose portal was the old castle entrance, crowns the village's highest point with a panorama from Terminillo to Lake Piediluco.

Lago di Piediluco, at 1,230 feet elevation, is considered the most beautiful natural lake in central Italy. Its calm waters, nestled among wooded hills, serve as a basin for national rowing competitions. The small village of Piediluco, with its colorful houses at the water's edge and the ruined medieval Rocca at the summit, is accessible in 5 miles from Labro.

The Cascata delle Marmore, 4 miles from Terni and about 30 minutes from Labro, is Europe's highest man-made waterfall at 541 feet, divided into three cascades. It was created in 271 BC by Roman consul Manius Curius Dentatus, who dug a canal to drain the stagnant waters of Lacus Velinus—the ancient marshy lake of the Rieti plain—into the Nera river below. The water is now regulated by a hydroelectric plant and the falls operate on a precise schedule. Two viewpoints allow observation: the Belvedere Superiore (at the top, level with the falls) and the Belvedere Inferiore (at the bottom, facing the wall of water). A network of trails connects the two viewpoints.

activities.text: Walk along Labro's parapet path, locally called the "Passeggiata dell'Amore" (Lovers' Walk), which follows the medieval walls with plunging views over the Fuscello valley and Lake Piediluco. The Torrione watchtower, at the highest point, offers a 360° panorama.

Hike between the two viewpoints of the Cascata delle Marmore on the park trails. The main route (Sentiero 1) climbs in switchbacks through the humid vegetation to the Balcone degli Innamorati (Lovers' Balcony), a rocky terrace behind the curtain of water.
Boat or kayak tour on Lago di Piediluco, a natural lake fed by the same Velino waters. The wooded shores and the medieval Rocca overlooking the village offer a peaceful setting, far from crowds.
