visits.text: Conza della Campania is one of the 1980 earthquake's most powerful images. The Hirpinian then Roman city of Compsa rose on the hill; in November 1980, it collapsed. Political decision: don't rebuild, relocate the village 4 km lower. Old Conza remains as is, and thanks to this catastrophe, archaeologists could excavate freely—unearthing a Roman forum, baths, ramparts. Today it's both an archaeological park and a ghost town. Three hours minimum visit if you want to see everything.

Bisaccia rises at 860 m, dominated by its Castello Ducale (11th century, expanded in the 15th by the Pignatelli). The castle houses the Archaeological Museum, rich in Daunian ceramics and Oriental bronzes found in the nearby Hirpinian necropolis—the area traded with Phoenicia in the 8th century BC. The town is a maze of sloping lanes, punctuated with small Baroque churches. Bisaccia is also famous for its tartufo nero pregiato, which can be tasted in season (November-February) at the three or four trattorias in the center.

Calitri catches your eye from afar: a cone of stone houses packed on their hill, whose façades were decorated in the 2010s by contemporary artists with ceramic murals. Unexpected urban mosaic, artist Beatrice Borrelli's 'Borgo Mosaicato' project. Count 1 hour to walk through the center, looking up at every street corner. Calitri also hosts the Sponz Fest in late August, folk music festival directed by Vinicio Capossela, a local native—if you happen upon it, go for it.

Trevico, 30 km south of Lacedonia, is the 'roof of Irpinia': at 1,094 m, it's Campania's highest municipal seat. Only 956 inhabitants. The village froze around its cathedral and former episcopal castle, and the view from the Belvedere carries on clear days to Basilicata and Puglia. Trevico is also the birthplace of Ettore Scola, director of A Special Day, who made it the setting for Trevico-Turin (1973). Twenty minutes walking through the center, dinner on the square, then quiet night.

activities.text: Cairano, 450 inhabitants, at 600 m altitude, is the most experimental art project on the circuit. The village has been emptying for forty years (earthquake, emigration), and since 2009 it hosts the 'Cairano 7x' festival planting contemporary art installations in deserted lanes. Large-format photographs pasted on gable walls, sculptures in courtyards, videos projected in former stables. Outside the festival, many works remain in place. Brief but unexpected visit, one hour suffices.

To end the day, dinner in Lacedonia or at a nearby agriturismo with cucina povera irpina menu: pancotto (stale bread cooked in wild chicory broth), roast lamb, local tome. Wines start veering more toward Basilicata here—Aglianico del Vulture, more austere than Taurasi. Good transition before switching toward Puglia tomorrow.

days_plan.itin_title: Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia

visits.text: Most people come here for the beach, which is a pity: the Laghi Alimini form two basins joined by a channel called Lu Strittu, the brackish Alimini Grande and the Alimini Piccolo, fed by freshwater springs. Dunes, pine wood and maquis separate them from the sea. The site is classified as of Community importance.

The spiaggia degli Alimini stretches north of Otranto, pale sand with a seabed that shelves very gently, alternating free stretches with lidos. It is the easiest beach in the area with children. The lidos turn into bars in the evening, and August nights here are loud.

activities.text: With a bike, the path around the lakes makes an easy loop before you head for the beach. In a sirocco or a tramontana the sea gets up and the surfers arrive. Parking along the litoranea is paid in season.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: Explore the Park of the Hundred Lakes (Parco dei Cento Laghi), a stunning natural area in the Parma Apennines featuring dozens of glacial lakes scattered across the mountain landscape. Lago Santo Parmense, the largest and most accessible, sits at over 1,500 meters altitude surrounded by forests and peaks, offering a refreshing mountain escape especially welcome on hot summer days.

Hike through the alpine-like scenery where crystal-clear lakes mirror the surrounding peaks and forests. The park encompasses some of the highest terrain in the Parma province, with trails leading to panoramic viewpoints on Mount Aquilotto and other summits offering sweeping vistas over the lake-dotted landscape.

activities.text: Discover the diverse mountain flora and fauna protected within the park boundaries. The area offers exceptional hiking opportunities ranging from gentle lakeside walks to challenging peak ascents, all set within landscapes that feel far removed from the plains of Emilia-Romagna below.

days_plan.itin_title: Emilia-Romagna's Hidden Treasures: Castles, Apennines & the Great Labyrinth

visits.text: Lago di Suviana and Lago del Brasimone - two artificial lakes created in the 1920s-1930s for hydroelectric power in the Bolognese Apennine valleys. Lake Suviana (capacity 32 million m³) is ringed by beech and conifer forests between 500 and 900 m altitude. Lake Brasimone, smaller, is managed as a nature reserve with restricted access to protect aquatic wildlife.

activities.text: Swimming and boating on Lake Suviana from the Bargi beaches—canoes and pedalos in summer, forest trail hiking in any season.

days_plan.itin_title: 10 Natural Wonders Around Bologna

activities.text: If you have binoculars, descend to Lago di Acerenza, an artificial basin created in 1984 at the base of the borough. From the bird blind installed on the east bank, you can observe kites, sparrowhawks, and falcons; walking and cycling trails circle it. Sport fishing is permitted. Count ten minutes' drive from the cathedral.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia

visits.text: Every photo is true—and that's a kind of miracle. Lago di Braies at 1,496m, in the Fanes-Sennes-Braies nature park, truly delivers on its promise of turquoise water with red boats moored at the dock. Lake loop: 4km, roughly 1.5 hours. Arrive before 9 a.m. to avoid crowds and access restrictions (road closed to cars 9:30 a.m.–4 p.m. from early July to early September).

Listed as part of the Dolomites UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009, this lake draws summer crowds—yet keeps something unreal about it in the evening when the last visitors leave. Local legend says Braies is a gateway to the underground kingdom of Fanes. True or not, the emerald water in November, with no one around, will make you believe it. Off-season: free access and parking.

activities.text: Rent a red rowboat at the Lago di Braies dock: 15 to 20 minutes of rowing takes you to the end of the lake, facing the vertical Dolomite walls dropping into the water. Check prices on-site. Private watercraft (kayaks, paddleboards) are banned throughout the nature park.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Dolomites Tour: Braies, Cortina and the Mountain Passes

places.name: Lago Di Cornino

visits.text: Lago di Cornino - Born about 10,000 years ago as glaciers retreated, this small lake shimmers in intense turquoise year-round. Fed by underground aquifers, it maintains a constant temperature of 8-9°C and crystalline clarity due to its calcium sulfate content. The lake is oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) but still shelters white-clawed crayfish. At Christmas, divers install a presepe subacqueo (underwater nativity scene) on the bottom.

Riserva Naturale Regionale del Lago di Cornino - This 487-hectare reserve, on the southeastern edge of the Carnic Prealps, houses the free visitor center of the Progetto Grifone with aviaries for convalescing raptors, a museum dedicated to vultures, and an ornithological observation hide.

activities.text: Trail around the lake - Easy 2.5 km loop (about 50 minutes) circling the lake, with panoramic platform and stretch along the Tagliamento River. Swimming prohibited.

Griffon vulture observation - The Progetto Grifone, launched in the late 1980s, is Italy's first reintroduction program for these birds. The colony numbers about 150 individuals in winter and over 200 in spring-summer, with thirty nesting pairs. Wingspan nearly 3 meters, weight 7 to 12 kg. Morning observation recommended.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Friuli-Venezia Giulia

map_keywords: Lago di Cornino Forgaria nel Friuli

visits.text: Conclude your grand tour at Lake Fimon, the oldest lake in Northern Italy at 35,000 years of age - predating even Lake Garda. This tranquil natural setting offers a peaceful escape for walking, picnicking, or simply contemplating the landscape.

Explore the shores and surrounding Berici Hills, where nature and agriculture create a pastoral landscape within easy reach of Vicenza. The lake's ancient origins add geological interest to its natural beauty.

activities.text: Enjoy a leisurely walk around the lake, perhaps with a picnic. The peaceful atmosphere provides a perfect finale to your exploration of the Veneto's extraordinary diversity of cultural and natural treasures.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: At Lago di Misurina, 1,754m, the Tre Cime di Lavaredo and Sorapiss massif reflect in the still morning water—three rock fingers pointed at the sky. Lake loop on foot: 2.6km, flat, accessible to all, 45 leisurely minutes. Former center for childhood asthma treatment thanks to the exceptionally pure air at this altitude.

From the shore of Lago di Misurina, the toll road to the Tre Cime di Lavaredo begins: 7km of hairpins to Rifugio Auronzo at 2,333m, starting point of the classic loop (roughly 9.5km, 3 to 4 hours). Toll roughly €30 per car in 2024-2025, parking included. In case of crowds, shuttle from Misurina. Avoid July-August midday.

activities.text: Do the Lago di Misurina loop in late afternoon when the Tre Cime hikers have left: the low light gilds the Cadini di Misurina and the Cristallo turns pink. A quiet hour on flat trail, with the full Dolomite panorama to yourself.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Dolomites Tour: Braies, Cortina and the Mountain Passes

visits.text: The Teatro del Silenzio is a natural amphitheater created in 2006 at the initiative of Alberto Bartalini and tenor Andrea Bocelli, born in Lajatico on September 22, 1958. The concept: a theater that remains silent 364 days a year and comes alive once each summer for a single concert. Tuscan travertine block terraces surround an artificial basin at whose center a different contemporary artist's sculpture is installed each year. The first edition, July 27, 2006, was dedicated to Bocelli's father. Since then, Placido Domingo, José Carreras, Dua Lipa, and Zubin Mehta have performed here.

The borgo of Lajatico, perched on a spur overlooking the Valdera, was first a castle of the Bishop of Volterra before being conquered by Pisa then Florence. The civic tower, Palazzo Pretorio, and cobbled alleyways form the heart of a village of about 1,000 inhabitants that claims, statistics in hand, to be Italy's municipality with the highest average per-capita income.

activities.text: Hike to the Rocca di Pietracassia, a ruined medieval fortress at 550 meters altitude in the Valdera woods, about 40 minutes' walk from Lajatico. Built in the Lombard era to control the route to Montecatini's copper mines, it was disputed and sold several times before passing definitively to the Pisans in 1434. Its name comes from a fissure (cassia) in a limestone spur.

The mofeta di Borboi, between Lajatico and Orciatico: a geothermal carbon dioxide emission typical of ancient volcanic zones. The stream water appears to boil from gas rising from underground. Best seen between October and May, when the watercourse is fuller.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

visits.text: Nicastro—the historic heart of Lamezia Terme and former capital of the Norman County of Calabria in the 11th century. The Castello Normanno-Svevo, built by Roger I around 1060 on a 320-meter spur, served as Frederick II of Hohenstaufen's residence during his Calabrian visits in the 13th century. The devastating 1638 earthquake—one of Italy's deadliest with 10,000 deaths in the Savuto Valley alone—reduced the castle to ruins that still brood over the valley today.

activities.text: Swimming at Gizzeria Lido beach, 10 km from the airport—a sweep of fine sand along the Tyrrhenian coast, perfect for unwinding after arrival before heading south to Pizzo the next day.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Calabria Loop: Tyrrhenian and Ionian Coasts

places.name: Lanciano

visits.text: Lanciano - a town of 35,000 inhabitants whose medieval center is divided into four historic quarters: Civitanova, Lancianovecchia, Sacca, and Borgo. In the Middle Ages, the town was an important commercial crossroads hosting international fairs that attracted Venetian and Oriental merchants.

Santuario del Miracolo Eucaristico - an 8th-century building housing what is considered the first documented Eucharistic miracle in Catholic history, dated 750 AD. A Basilian monk reportedly witnessed the host transform into flesh and wine into blood. The relics are preserved in gilded urns, scientifically examined in 1971: analyses identified human cardiac tissue of blood type AB.
Torri Montanare - two 14th-century medieval towers connected by an arch, remnants of the town's ancient Angevin fortifications. They constitute Lanciano's visual emblem.

Cattedrale della Madonna del Ponte - a baroque cathedral built between 1687 and 1791 on a 1st-century AD Roman bridge with five arches, still visible below. This juxtaposition of two eras is unique in the region.

activities.text: Walk through the Lancianovecchia quarter, the oldest district, with its medieval alleyways, carved portals, and 15th-century palaces.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

map_keywords: Cattedrale della Madonna del Ponte Lanciano

places.name: Lanzo Torinese

visits.text: The Ponte del Diavolo of Lanzo Torinese, built from 1378 to 1380 over the Stura di Lanzo, rises 16 meters above the river. Its construction cost 1,400 florins, financed by a wine tax for ten years. It allowed travelers to avoid the hostile territories of the princes of Acaja and Montferrat when reaching Turin. In 1564, a gate was installed on the bridge to block travelers during plague epidemics. Its name comes from a natural cavity 7 meters high and 6 meters at the base carved by waters in the left wall—the Giant's Cauldron—which locals attributed to the devil.

The Civic Tower of Aymon de Challant (1329-1357), 20.50 meters tall, was the gateway to the medieval borough. It bears the name of its builder, castellan of Lanzo from 1332 to 1357 in service to Margaret of Savoy. The church of Loreto was built in 1618 in just three months by the inhabitants, modeled on the Santa Casa of Loreto, at the initiative of Margaret of Savoy. Via San Giovanni Bosco is the old heart of town with its terracotta porticos, ogival windows, and medieval decorations.

The Ecomuseum of the History of Alpinism of the Valli di Lanzo, installed at the headquarters of the Italian Alpine Club of Lanzo, traces the history of these valleys considered the cradle of Piedmontese alpinism. Over 360 marked trails covering 1,000 km constitute the hiking network. The ethnographic museum of textile art is housed in the 17th-century Palazzo degli Estensi.

The Casa del Grissino in Lanzo recalls the invention of the Turin breadstick: physician Pecchio reportedly developed this thin, crispy bread to treat young Vittorio Amedeo II, unable to digest ordinary bread. The Lanzo grissino is distinct from the rubatà grissino of Chieri.

activities.text: Hike to Lago Monastero from Ala di Stura (Val Grande di Lanzo): alpine lake surrounded by rhododendrons, panorama over high-altitude pastures. Ala di Stura preserves medieval buildings and was connected to Turin by the Turin-Ceres railway in 1916.
Via ferrata or mountain safety workshop in the Valli di Lanzo (several equipped sectors available depending on season, inquire with local providers).

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Valleys of Piedmont: Occitan Alps, Lakes & Baroque Savoy

map_keywords: Torre di Aymone di Challant Lanzo Torinese
Ala di Stura Ala di Stura

places.name: Lari

visits.text: The Castello dei Vicari has dominated Lari since the year 1000—the first documented mention dates to 1043, when land was sold for a sword. After Florence took Lari in 1406, it became the seat of a Florentine vicariate administering almost the entire Tuscan coast from Livorno to Pontedera. The inner courtyard bears 92 ceramic coats of arms of the vicars who governed here for over four centuries. The cistern built in 1448, topped with the Pitti and Scali family arms, sits halfway up the 95 access steps. The complex served as a prison until World War II, damaged by bombing. Open to visitors since 1991.

Grand Duke Leopold II, during his visit, wrote: "I arrived at Lari and from its fortress was shown a vast country, the most beautiful part of Tuscany." The terrace indeed offers a 360° panorama: from the Pisan Mountains to the Balze of Volterra, from the Livorno coast to Peccioli.

The Porta Pisana, also called Maremmana, is the only one of the three original gates still equipped with a counter-gate. The tight space between the two openings created a trap for attackers who had breached the first defense. The Porta Volterrana, demolished in 1798, still had a drawbridge at that date.

The 15th-century parish church of San Leonardo and Santa Maria Assunta preserves paintings by Melani and two marble statues attributed to Andrea Pisano. It was severely damaged by the 19th-century earthquake that also remodeled the neighboring market loggia.

activities.text: Tasting of Lari cherries: 19 local varieties, some found only in this area of the Pisan hills. Local producers sell baskets, jams, and liqueurs in the village square. The cherry festival is one of Tuscany's oldest.
Stroll through the borgo's medieval alleyways, whose original stone structure and Renaissance-Gothic dwellings have remained intact—the world wars never touched the village.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

map_keywords: Chiesa di Santa Maria Assunta Lari

visits.text: Larino remains a gap in the guidebooks—take advantage: there's almost nobody. Ancient Larinum, Samnite then Roman, preserves a 1st-century elliptical amphitheater that could seat around 11,000 spectators—respectable size for a provincial city. Free access, you can wander as if in a field, no ticket booth or fence. Spot the still-legible cavea and vestiges of the entrances. Next door, the Roman quarter has yielded 2nd-century mosaics (Leopard, Lion) currently under restoration. Allow 1.5 hours at the site.

San Pardo Cathedral, Romanesque with Gothic influences, dates to the 12th century. Consecrated in 1319, it preserves a highly expressive Romanesque portal and remarkable rose window above. Inside, partially preserved medieval frescoes and the patron saint's reliquary. The historic center around Piazza Duomo can be covered in 30 minutes: Renaissance palaces, winding alleys, shaded terraces. Late February-early March, the San Pardo festival parades with 100+ flower-covered carts pulled by oxen—a spectacle unique in Molise.

Fifteen minutes from Larino, you enter one of the three Arbëreshë villages of lower Molise: Ururi, colonized by Albanians fleeing Ottoman invasion after 1456. The Arbëresh language (old Albanian) is still spoken orally, especially by elders—odd effect hearing Albanian words behind a Molise door. Santa Maria delle Grazie church, baroque facade consecrated in 1730 atop ruins of a 1026 church destroyed by the 1456 earthquake. On May 3, Ururi lives for the Carrese: cart race with ox-drawn chariots galloping 4 km, three teams competing (Giovani, Giovanotti, Fedayn). Off-season, just the village and its history—already beautiful.

Portocannone, 10 km away, completes the Arbëreshë triangle with San Martino in Pensilis. Its own Carrese takes place on Pentecost Monday. Santa Maria di Costantinopoli church, Byzantine icon venerated since the 16th century—said to have been brought by Albanian refugees. The village is tiny but cultural identity remains vibrant: bilingual signage, traditional dishes (kanazet, beurr e zi). Quick visit, 30 minutes.

activities.text: Olive oil tasting in Larino, capital of the olive in lower Molise. The Gentile di Larino cultivar is endemic—medium fruity, notes of green almond and cut grass. Several frantoi (mills) open their doors in autumn to witness trituration. Off-season, tasting possible directly at producers. Festa dell'Olio in November.

Dinner in Larino at a downtown trattoria. Must-try: pampanella, signature dish of lower Molise—pork marinated in sweet pepper and wild fennel, slow-cooked in wood oven. Originating from San Martino in Pensilis, it's eaten cold or warm, accompanied by country bread. With a red Tintilia, it's one of Molise cuisine's most convincing pairings.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Molise in 9 Days: Pescara to Naples Through the Samnium

visits.text: Massafra, nicknamed the Thebaid of Italy for the concentration of rock-cut churches in its 11 ravines. Descend the 125 steps of the Baroque staircase leading to the bottom of the Gravina della Madonna della Scala (4 km long, 40 metres deep, once the Valley of Roses). At the bottom, the Baroque sanctuary of Madonna della Scala, construction of which began in 1729 on the site of the miracle of the hinds: according to legend, two deer hunted by hunters knelt around 1300 before the Byzantine fresco of the Virgin hidden in the rock. 200 metres on, the Farmacia del Mago Greguro, a complex of 12 interconnected monastic cells carved into the tuff, where Basilian monks stored their medicinal herbs.

Castellaneta, birthplace of Rudolph Valentino, the great seducer of silent cinema born here in 1895. The Museo Valentino, housed in the former convent of Santa Chiara, holds thousands of posters, films, stage costumes and personal items—€3.50, guided tour and video included. The Gravina di Castellaneta, known as Gravina Grande, carves 10 km long and over 100 metres deep just behind the historic centre. Several rock-cut churches—Padre Eterno, Santa Maria del Pesco—remain virtually inaccessible there, but the borgo's viewpoints offer vertiginous vistas.

Laterza, highlight of the day. Laterza PDO bread, baked in traditional wood-fired ovens, scents the streets morning and afternoon: dark crust, soft crumb, round format, you find it nowadays as far as Milan. The MuMa, Museo della Maiolica, tells the story of 17th-18th century Laterza majolica with a well-designed multimedia tour. And the Fontana dei Mascheroni, right in the centre, its bronze mascarons spouting water, long served as trough and washhouse for the locals.

activities.text: Hike along trail no. 3 of the LIPU oasis above the Gravina di Laterza: 11 km return, considered the Grand Canyon of Puglia. 12 km long, up to 400 metres wide, vertical walls over 200 metres high. It's one of the deepest gorges in Europe, protected by the Terra delle Gravine Regional Nature Park since 2005. You can spot the lesser kestrel, the eagle owl, and with a bit of luck the Egyptian vulture.

Gourmet stop in Laterza: the focaccia laertina, usually topped with olive oil, oregano and tomato, comes out of the ovens mid-day. In the evening, the rosticcerie line up their charcoal grills—local meats, bombette (meat rolls stuffed with cheese), everything goes on the fire. It's what Apulians call cucina dei fornelli, a social ritual as much as a meal.

days_plan.itin_title: Puglia: 3 days through the Murgia Barese, from Polignano's cliffs to the Tarantine ravines
The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

places.name: Laveno Mombello

visits.text: Visit the prepositural Church of Saints Philip and James, known as the old church, a religious building dating from 1315 that is the historic spiritual heart of Laveno. Beside it stands the Church of Sant'Ambrogio, built in 1940 by architect Paolo Mezzanotte in a modern style, together forming the sacred heritage of this charming lakeside town.

Discover Villa De Angeli Frua, an elegant eighteenth-century residence donated to the municipality and now home to the public library. The magnificent Parco delle Terrazze surrounding it offers breathtaking views of Lake Maggiore, with an evocative entrance tunnel that in spring is draped in blooming wisteria, creating a fairy-tale setting.

Ride the cable car up to Poggio Sant'Elsa for a privileged perspective of Lake Maggiore. This panoramic excursion offers spectacular views of the blue lake waters, the Borromean Islands in the distance and the Alpine skyline, delivering an unforgettable experience for nature and photography lovers.

activities.text: Stroll along the Laveno lakefront, one of Lake Maggiore's most evocative promenades offering views of the town, Stresa on the opposite shore and the famous Borromean Islands. From here ferries depart for Verbania, giving you the chance to explore both sides of the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona

map_keywords: Chiesa Santi Filippo e Giacomo Laveno-Mombello

visits.text: Stroll through Lazise, whose Scaliger Castle (not open for visits) and defensive walls create a picturesque medieval ensemble on Lake Garda's shores. The atmospheric lakefront promenade offers views across the water to the distant mountains, perfect for a relaxing evening passeggiata.

Visit the Church of San Nicolò, an ancient Romanesque church within the castle walls featuring medieval frescoes. The intimate scale and historic atmosphere capture the authentic character of a traditional lakeside community.

activities.text: Enjoy the beautiful lakeside setting, perhaps with a gelato from one of the local shops. The colorful boats bobbing in the harbor and the castle silhouette create postcard-perfect views at every turn.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

places.name: Le Castella

visits.text: First head to Capo Colonna, 10 km south of Crotone, on the promontory that once closed the Gulf of Taranto. Here stood one of the most important sanctuaries of Magna Graecia: the temple of Hera Lacinia, built around 470-460 BC. Of this Doric temple that counted 6 columns by 14, only a single 8-meter-high column remains today, standing before the Ionian Sea for 25 centuries. It was from here that Hannibal embarked for Carthage after his Italian campaign, engraving his exploits on a bronze column. The site's Archaeological Museum displays finds from the excavations, including a gold diadem and bronze votive objects.

In town, the National Archaeological Museum of Crotone traces the history of Kroton, a city founded around 710 BC by Achaean colonists from the Peloponnese. The city was famous in antiquity for its athletes - Milo of Croton won the Olympic wrestling games six times - and for Pythagoras, who founded his school there. On the second floor, the rooms dedicated to the sanctuary of Hera Lacinia present the gold diadem and a mysterious Nuragic bronze ship, testimonies of Mediterranean exchanges.

End the day at Le Castella, 35 km south of Crotone. The Castello Aragonese stands on an islet connected to land by a thin sandy isthmus - the image is spectacular. The foundations date back to the Magna Graecia era (5th century BC), and Hannibal himself allegedly took refuge here. The current core dates from the Angevin period (13th century), reinforced by the Aragonese in the 15th century with spurred bastions. Climb to the top of the tower for a circular view over the Capo Rizzuto marine protected area - Italy's largest - and its turquoise waters.

activities.text: Enjoy the Le Castella beach for a swim in the crystal-clear waters of the marine reserve. Operators offer boat trips around the castle and protected seabeds. If you're a diver, the Capo Rizzuto marine area offers snorkeling spots accessible directly from the beach.

days_plan.itin_title: Calabria: From Cosenza to Reggio, Between Mountains and Ionian Sea

map_keywords: Capo Colonna tempio Hera Lacinia Crotone

visits.text: The Riserva Naturale Le Cesine covers 348 hectares of coastal marsh, the last remnant of the wetland that once ran from Brindisi to Otranto. Two ponds, the Salapi and the Pantano Grande, are cut off from the sea by a belt of dunes. More than 150 bird species have been recorded here.

Brine and Aleppo pine in the air, bird calls across the water: the trails through the oasis alternate pine woods, holm oak stands and garrigue. Observation towers and hides punctuate the route, one of them accessible to visitors with reduced mobility. The visitor centre is at the Masseria Cesine.

activities.text: Between October and May the guided walk leaves at 10.30am; in summer, at 4.30pm. The rest of the time only the main track and the via del Pesce stay freely open. Booking with the WWF is compulsory, and outings are dropped in the rain.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: Santa Croce's facade took 150 years to build (1549-1695) and it shows: every square centimeter is carved - atlantes, grape clusters, rosettes, chimeras. Pietra leccese, local soft golden limestone, cuts like fresh butter and hardens with age. Result: baroque of almost obsessive precision, barely darkening over centuries unlike marble. The interior is austere - all the energy is outside.

Piazza del Duomo is closed on three sides - cathedral, 70-meter bell tower, episcopal palace, seminary - giving it rare acoustics and intimacy for a city this size. The cathedral has two facades: a monumental lateral one on the piazza, a main one facing a secondary alley. The opposite of what you'd expect. The bell tower, built in 1682, illuminates in the evening in a way worth the detour.

Lecce's Roman amphitheater dates from the 2nd century AD and was discovered by accident in 1901, during bank construction on piazza Sant'Oronzo. It remained buried beneath the city for 1,700 years. Original estimated capacity of 25,000 spectators - more than Lecce's population today. Half remains under adjacent buildings, unexcavated.

Otranto Cathedral's floor (1163-1165) is a world apart: 800 m² of medieval mosaic representing the Tree of Life, with Alexander the Great ascending to heaven on an eagle, sirens, centaurs, King Arthur - the entire 12th-century bestiary in a single image. The priest Pantaleone conceived and executed it in three years. Look for the intentional errors: in the Middle Ages, only God could create something perfect.

Santa Maria di Leuca: the extreme point of the boot's heel, where the Adriatic and Ionian meet. Theoretically. In practice, the boundary between the two seas is invisible to the naked eye - local sailors say you see it in different colors during mistral winds. The Virgin's sanctuary atop the cape rests on the foundations of a Temple of Minerva. The monumental 236-step staircase descends to the basilica.

Gallipoli - not the Turkish one, the Salento one - is an entire old town on an islet connected to the mainland by a 17th-century baroque bridge. 14th-century Angevin castle facing the sea, baroque cathedral, alleyways where fishing nets still dry between houses. In the 18th century, Gallipoli was one of the Mediterranean's largest lamp oil export ports - the city's palaces still testify to this wealth.

activities.text: Breakfast leccese before anything else: pasticciotto (shortcrust pastry filled with pastry cream) and caffè in ghiaccio con latte di mandorla - espresso over crushed ice with almond milk. Not optional, mandatory. Caffè in ghiaccio is a Salento specialty, unknown in Naples, and one of the best arguments for traveling south. Bar Alvino or Caffè Alvino, Piazza Sant'Oronzo.

Tasting at Cosimo Taurino in Guagnano (30 km from Lecce): the Patriglione cuvée, 100% negroamaro, has been an absolute Salento classic since the 1980s. Firm tannins, black cherry, tobacco - a wine that convinced the world negroamaro wasn't just for cutting northern wines. The house also makes a reference Scaloti rosé.

Salento rosé deserves particular attention: tradition dating back to the 1940s, dark salmon to 'partridge eye' color, negroamaro-based - nothing like pale Provençal rosé. Fuller-bodied, more structured, more apt to stand up to spicy cuisine. Castello Monaci in Salice Salentino offers a reference version with cellar and vineyard tours.

Frittura di paranza in Gallipoli: small fish from the day's catch - goby, red mullet, squid - fried in olive oil and served in newspaper. The technique has been the same for centuries, the oil changes everything: no greasy frying, no burnt smell. With a well-chilled Alezio DOC rosé, it's the circuit's best lunch.

Final tasting at sunset over the Ionian Sea: a negroamaro-based rosato del Salento, served cold (10-12°C), facing the sea. Salento's light at day's end turns golden orange - the same orange as in the pietra leccese. It's the right moment to finish the circuit.

places.name: Levanto

visits.text: Levanto, the northern gateway to the Cinque Terre, but without the crowds. The central beach stretches nearly a kilometer, sand mixed with gravel, and it's one of the very rare surf spots in all of Liguria—the bay is open and receives western swells. Several schools rent boards (€35-50 per day with wetsuit). No monumental big waves, but a relaxed surf vibe that stands out on the coast. Free beach accessible, paid bagni in the center.

Levanto's medieval center remains largely pedestrian. 13th-century Loggia Comunale, perfectly preserved—its stone arches still support the old town hall. All around, arcaded alleys recalling those of Chiavari but on a smaller scale. The Church of Sant'Andrea, façade in black and white marble bands from the 13th century, remarkable Gothic rose window, sober interior. The medieval town was fortified—remnants of walls visible in several places.

Levanto's castle, at the top of the town, dates from the 16th century. Built to defend the town from Barbary incursions, transformed into a private residence in the 19th century. Not open to visits (private), but the climb through the alleys and the view from the adjacent belvedere are worth it. Five minutes on foot from the center.

Punta Mesco marks the cape separating Levanto from Monterosso, first of the Cinque Terre. The trail climbing it (3 hours round-trip, 400 m elevation gain) crosses pine forests and old terraced vineyards. At the summit: ruins of the Church of Sant'Antonio (13th century), lighthouse, and one of the most beautiful views over the Cinque Terre from offshore. Marine protected area below. Doable in half a day if you start early.

activities.text: The day's highlight—and one of the most singular things on the Ligurian coast: the Maremonti cycle path Levanto-Bonassola-Framura. 5.5 km flat on the old Genoa-Pisa railway line, opened in 1874, abandoned in 1970 when a new double-track route was built further inland. Lit tunnels (cool in midsummer—18°C inside, 35°C outside), coves accessible by stairs between tunnels, permanent sea views at the openings. Converted to a trail 2010-2011. Bike rental in Levanto (€10-15 per day at Cicli Raso or Onda Sport). Allow 1h round-trip by bike, 2h on foot.

Tasting of Cinque Terre DOC in a Levanto cellar. Vermentino and Bosco, dry white with notes of almond blossom and yellow fruit, aged on terraced vineyards plunging toward the sea. Several local producers open their cellars (around €15-20 for tasting with four wines and focaccia). Also possible to taste Sciacchetrà, very rare straw wine, sometimes up to €80 per half-bottle.

days_plan.itin_title: From Lunigiana to Cinque Terre: Between Tuscany and Liguria
6-Day Grand Tour of the Riviera di Levante

map_keywords: Maremonti Cycle Path Levanto Bonassola Framura

visits.text: The Torre Federiciana dominates the center of Leverano with its tall medieval silhouette, commissioned by Frederick II around 1220 to watch the nearby coast. It's among the oldest monuments in Salento. Climb if access is open: the view extends over the surrounding vineyards.

activities.text: Leverano gives its name to a DOC wine available in red, rosé and white, made mainly from Negroamaro and Malvasia. Surrounding wineries open their doors for tastings. Head to one late in the day, when light gilds the vine rows.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce

visits.text: If you arrive on an open day, the Castello di Levizzano Rangone can be visited in 75 minutes with a mandatory guide. The Torre Matildica is linked to the feudal palace by an underground gallery you walk through with a flashlight. €5 per person, free under 12. Reservations at experiencemore.it.

Local winemakers nickname Levizzano the jewel of Grasparossa. The Museo Rosso Graspa, within the castle walls, tells the story of local viticulture through antique tools and period photos. Included in the guided castle tour.

activities.text: From the castle loggia, vine-planted hills roll down to the plain. Best moment: late afternoon, when the light gilds the rows. Small Napoleonic cemetery Campo San Rocco below; quick 5-minute detour.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Hills: Balsamic, Ferrari, and Mud Volcanoes

visits.text: Pontile di Lido di Camaiore: The wooden pier of Lido di Camaiore, symbol of the seaside resort, extends into the Tyrrhenian Sea facing the Apuan Alps. Less frequented than those of Forte dei Marmi or Viareggio, this promenade on stilts offers a peaceful panorama over the Versilia coastline.

activities.text: Beach and waterfront: Lido di Camaiore stretches for several kilometers of fine sand between the Tyrrhenian Sea and the pine forest. Less fashionable than Forte dei Marmi, the resort offers family beach establishments with all the infrastructure of traditional Italian beach culture. The coastal bike path links Lido di Camaiore to Forte dei Marmi in the north and Viareggio in the south.

Versilia bike path: The path runs along the waterfront for over 20 km, from Viareggio to Marina di Pietrasanta, allowing you to connect the main seaside resorts of Versilia by bike while riding directly along the sea.

days_plan.itin_title: Lucca Province Circuit: Hill Towns and Coast

visits.text: Stroll through the historic center of Limone Piemonte, a village in the Vermenagna Valley at 1,000 meters altitude on one of the historic routes linking France, Piedmont, and the Ligurian coast—once traveled by convoys transporting salt from the Mediterranean inland. Inhabited since Roman times, Limone was one of the first villages in the Southern Alps to develop mountain tourism. Restaurants, shops, and refuges form a compact village center reachable from the train station within minutes on foot.

Visit the Museo dello Sci Agostino Bottero, opened in 2012, which traces the history of skiing in the Riserva Bianca from the first Alpine troops' training sessions in 1907 on the slopes of Monte Vecchio, to the 2006 Winter Olympics that modernized the resort. In 1937, 'lo slittone'—a large motorized sled—was the first mechanical lift installed in southern Piedmont, allowing riders to climb 700 meters of elevation.

activities.text: Skiing or snowboarding session on the Riserva Bianca slopes (season December to early April): the ski area extends from 1,050 to 2,085 meters altitude over 80 kilometers of slopes divided into 41 runs served by 16 lifts. The difficulty distribution is 25% beginner, 55% intermediate, and 20% red and black runs. From the summits—notably Mont Alpetta at 2,070 meters—on clear days, the Mediterranean and Corsica are visible to the south, the Matterhorn and Monte Rosa to the north. Italian and French national teams have conducted training camps here.

Outside ski season, snowshoe or hiking trek on one of the 12 marked trails around Limone and Limonetto, some leading to 19th-century military forts built around the Colle di Tenda—Fort Alto, Fort Pernante, Fort Giaura, and Fort Margherita to the west, Fort Taburda and Fort Pepino to the east. These defensive works of the Kingdom of Sardinia then the Kingdom of Italy controlled the historic pass between Italy and France.
Excursion to the Cascate del Saut, waterfalls located in the valley near Limone Piemonte, particularly impressive in winter under snow and in early spring during the melt.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy Road Trip from Nice: Riviera & Alps in 2 Days

places.name: Limone Sul Garda

visits.text: Explore the historic center of Limone sul Garda, nestled between limestone cliffs and the lake. The village name doesn't derive from lemons but probably from the Latin 'limes' (border) or the Celtic 'lemos' (elm). Until 1932, the village was road-inaccessible and could only be reached by boat or mountain paths—a fact that contributed to an exceptional genetic peculiarity: in 1974, researchers from the University of Milan discovered ApoA-1 Milano in local residents, a mutation of the apolipoprotein A-I protein inherited from a common ancestor born around 1780. This protein eliminates arterial fats at high speed, conferring on its carriers natural resistance to cardiovascular disease despite very low HDL cholesterol. About 60 out of 1,100 residents still carry it today.

Climb to the Limonaia del Castèl, an 18th-century lemon greenhouse bought and restored by the municipality in 1995. Limonaie are open-air structures facing due south, with thick walls, tall white stone columns, and wooden planks placed in winter to protect the trees from cold. Franciscan monks introduced lemon cultivation on these shores as early as the 13th century, making Limone one of the northernmost points in the world for commercial citrus growing. Goethe described these terraced gardens in September 1786 during his Italian Journey. The limonaia now houses an educational pathway and more than a hundred producing lemon trees.

Descend to Limone's small historic harbor, the village's original heart. The San Rocco church, on its terrace by the water, offers a vantage point on Monte Baldo across the lake. At the northern edge of the village, a museum recounts the history of fishing and PDO olive oil production, another local specialty.

activities.text: Walk the Busatte-Tempesta panoramic walkway, inaugurated July 14, 2018, after two years of construction costing 7 million euros. Suspended from the cliff face about 50 meters above the lake on a 2-kilometer route, it follows the municipality to the Trentino border. The round-trip from the village center is entirely on foot.

visits.text: Early morning, embark at Milazzo for Lipari (1 hour by hydrofoil, around €22). The Greeks placed here the home of Aeolus, god of winds, and Vulcan's forge. The Aeolian archipelago has been UNESCO since 2000 for its seven active volcanoes. Lipari is the largest island - 37 km² - and its center is organized around the Castello, a citadel perched on a basalt outcrop inhabited since the Neolithic. Excavations have uncovered 2,500 tombs superimposed over six millennia: it became the Museo Archeologico Eoliano, one of the richest in southern Italy for Mediterranean prehistory. €6 entry.

In the afternoon, a 10-minute crossing to Vulcano, the island that gave its name to all volcanoes in the world. According to the Odyssey, this is where Vulcan forged the gods' weapons with the help of the Cyclopes - Homer placed the cosmic anvil here. The last major eruption dates from 1888-1890 and inspired the term 'Vulcanian eruption' in modern volcanology. Today, the crater is at rest but fumaroles persist. Basic but well-placed, the arrival port opens directly onto the black beach and the crater trail.

activities.text: Climb to the Gran Cratere della Fossa, 391 m, easy ascent in 1 hour on an ash trail. The sulfur fumaroles catch in your throat - powerful rotten egg smell - and the ground is burning hot under your soles, sometimes 80°C at the surface. The bright yellow mineral flowers on the crater's edges are sulfur crystals pushed out by the exhalations. From the summit, complete panorama of Lipari, Salina in the distance, and on clear days Stromboli smoking on the northern horizon. Avoid on windy days, the vapors become suffocating.

Bath in the fanghi, sulfurous mud pools at 30°C supposedly good for rheumatism (€3-5 entry). It stinks for kilometers, sticks to your skin for three days, permanently stains swimsuits, and that's perfect: it's the quintessential local experience. Mandatory rinse in the sea right next door, warm water even in May. Don't wear silver jewelry, the sulfur blackens it permanently.

Return to Lipari for the night. Dinner at E Pulera, Via Diana, garden under bougainvillea, raw gambero rosso from Mazara, sheep's ricotta ravioli and seared tuna with Salina capers. Reservations essential, 30-40 covers.

days_plan.itin_title: Sicily's Island Circuit: Aeolian, Aegadian & Pantelleria

Haunted Sicily - 8 Days from the Capuchin Crypts to Stromboli

places.name: Lizzano In Belvedere

visits.text: Santuario della Madonna del Faggio - a hermitage built in the 17th century in the Bolognese Apennine beech forests at 1,150 m elevation, according to legend at the spot where woodcutters discovered a terracotta image of the Virgin beneath a great beech tree. The 4 km access path from Lizzano passes through dense beech forest.

Castello Manservisi - a 19th-century neo-Gothic castle overlooking the village of Lizzano, restored and open for visits. It preserves works by the local painter Giacomo Lolli (1859-1940), including landscapes of the Bolognese Apennines.

activities.text: Hike to the Santuario della Madonna del Faggio from Lizzano—4 km through beech forest with 300 m elevation gain.

days_plan.itin_title: 10 Natural Wonders Around Bologna

places.name: Locorotondo

visits.text: The pointed rooftops catch the light differently here than in Alberobello: in Locorotondo, they belong to the cummerse, white houses with pitched roofs covered in chiancarelle limestone slabs. The historic center is laid out in concentric rings, hence the name, locus rotundus. A one-hour walk covers it. Look for the Latin inscriptions carved into the lintels.

A 16th-century facade and a 35-meter dome: the Chiesa Madre di San Giorgio dominates the central square, wildly out of proportion with the village. It's the landmark that brings you back to the center when you get turned around in the alleyways. Open mornings and late afternoons, closed at siesta.

Locorotondo's lungomare has no sea: it's a panoramic road suspended above the Valle d'Itria, with views all the way to Martina Franca. Trulli, vineyards, and dry-stone walls as far as the eye goes. The name is a local joke, fully intended. Come in late afternoon when the valley turns golden.

Make a point of walking past Palazzo Morelli at Via Morelli 30, dated 1819: carved doorway, family coat of arms, one of the finest examples of civil architecture in the village. It's a private residence, not a museum; you admire it from the street. Two minutes, then back into the alleyways.

Porta Napoli marks the entrance to Locorotondo's historic center, with the town's coat of arms engraved in the ground. It opens onto Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II, the village's living room, formerly Piazza Castello. The Torre dell'Orologio rises above it, now housing the municipal historical archives. The best starting point for the walking loop.

Find the Chiesetta di San Nicola di Myra, tucked into the white facades: from the outside, nothing sets it apart from the houses on either side. Built in 1660, it conceals a vault painted in its entirety, devoted to the life and miracles of the saint. It doesn't open every day; try in the morning, it's free and worth the detour.

activities.text: The best moment of the day in Locorotondo is aperitivo on the lungomare: vineyards surround the village and the bars in the center pour the local white by the glass for a few euros. Dry, light, drink it young, not a wine for aging. The Valle d'Itria is right in front of you, the light is falling, and you won't want to move.

If you enjoy details, hunt for the Latin inscriptions carved into the lintels of houses in Locorotondo. Parva sed apta mihi, small but right for me. Invidia invidenti nocet, envy harms the envious. There are dozens, each one chosen by a homeowner. Look at door-height as you walk.

days_plan.itin_title: The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

map_keywords: Chiesa Madre di San Giorgio Locorotondo

visits.text: Loreto conceals history's most well-traveled house: according to Catholic tradition, the Holy House of the Virgin—the one from Nazareth where Mary received the Annunciation—was transported here in 1294 from Palestine by angels, to protect it from Muslim invasions. Official Church version until the 20th century, more prosaic modern version: the Angeli family ("angels" in Italian) orchestrated the transfer by ship, and chroniclers embroidered the miracle. The sanctuary, erected in 1469, houses the small stone house blackened by centuries, encased in a Renaissance marble shell.

Inside the Holy House, the Black Madonna of Loreto: cedar of Lebanon statue (the original burned in 1921, the current one is a 1922 copy) above the altar, blackened over centuries by candle smoke and oil lamps. Patron saint of aviators since 1920—obvious symbolism with her aerial journey. The house itself is made of stones actually compatible with Nazareth geology, which has revived hypotheses: ship transfer during the Crusades, organized by a family called Angeli. Curious.

The sanctuary square, designed by Bramante in the 16th century, is one of the Marche's most harmonious. The Gothic-Renaissance basilica, the apostolic palace on the side, and the Baroque fountain at center form a cohesive ensemble. In the evening, especially off-season, silence is total—Loreto remains a pilgrim town, empty after 6 PM.

activities.text: Dinner at Andreina, just outside Loreto. Wood-fired oven, Conero regional cuisine: roast pigeon, lamb, Apennine charcuterie. Michelin-starred address, elevated prices (60-80 euro tasting menu) but an experience that justifies the splurge.

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Umbria: 8 days Among Mummies, Mystics & Caves

places.name: Lucca

visits.text: Piazza dell'Anfiteatro: Lucca's oval plaza is no reconstructed set piece—it traces the exact perimeter of a 2nd-century AD Roman amphitheatre that once held 10,000 spectators. Medieval residents built their houses directly against the ancient stone tiers, erasing the arena but preserving its elliptical form. The 19th-century restoration by architect Lorenzo Nottolini cleared the square and opened the four arched passages that still produce the element of surprise described by Grand Tour travelers. Enter through one of the vaulted passages to understand how an entire city grew from the bones of a Roman monument.

San Martino Cathedral: Founded in the 6th century by Bishop Fridian, rebuilt from the 11th century onward, and completed in the 16th–17th centuries, the cathedral displays a distinctive asymmetrical façade—the architect had to narrow the final arcade to fit the pre-existing bell tower, creating an elegant dissonance. Inside, the main treasure is the Volto Santo, a 13th-century wooden crucifix traditionally attributed to Nicodemus and carried in a candlelit procession every September 13th since the Middle Ages. In the sacristy, the tomb of Ilaria del Carretto (1406) sculpted by Jacopo della Quercia shows the young wife of Paolo Guinigi lying with a dog at her feet—a symbol of marital fidelity—in a style that would influence Donatello.

Torre Guinigi: The Guinigi family's red brick tower, erected in the late 14th century, reaches 44.25 meters. Its unique feature is a garden of holm oaks planted at the summit—a symbol of rebirth chosen by the Guinigi, then lords of Lucca. Paolo Guinigi, who ruled the city from 1400 to 1430, made this tower the emblem of his mercantile and banking power. Climb the 230 steps for sweeping views of tiled rooftops, ramparts, and, on clear days, the Apuan Alps.

San Michele in Foro Church: Built on the site of the ancient Roman forum, San Michele displays a 12th-century Pisan-Lucchese façade with four tiers of sculpted columns, each different from the next. Throughout the Middle Ages, the building also served as the courthouse for the Republic of Lucca. Inside: a 14th-century frescoed Virgin and Child and a glazed ceramic Madonna by Luca della Robbia.

Puccini's Birthplace (Museo Puccini): Giacomo Puccini was born on December 22, 1858, in this apartment on Corte San Lorenzo, where the Puccini family had served for five generations as organists and chapel masters at the cathedral. The museum preserves the Steinway & Sons piano purchased in 1901 on which he composed Turandot, opera manuscripts, costumes, and stage photographs. Puccini bought back the family apartment after his sister sold it—proof of the composer's attachment to his native city.

Palazzo Mansi - National Museum: Built in the 17th century for a wealthy family of Lucchese merchants, this palace preserves its state apartments almost intact—music room with allegorical frescoes, hall of mirrors, painting collections from the Medici and Grand Duchy holdings. Lucca built its fortune between the 13th and 15th centuries on silk trade, exporting fabrics as far as England and Flanders. This palace is the direct architectural expression of that wealth.

Palazzo Pfanner and Gardens: Built in 1660 for the Moricani family, then purchased in the mid-19th century by the Austrian-origin Pfanner family—who still own it. It opens onto one of the rare Italian-style gardens still preserved within the walls, with a central fountain surrounded by statues of deities and seasons. Jane Campion's film Portrait of a Lady was partly shot here.

Via Fillungo and Historic Center: The main artery of the pedestrian center concentrates historic cafés, artisan shops, and fragments of medieval architecture. The Torre delle Ore, whose first clock dates to 1390, marks its northern end. Puccini frequented Caffè Di Simo, an establishment opened in 1875 whose Art Nouveau storefront is still visible.

Villa Guinigi - National Museum: Former country residence of Paolo Guinigi, lord of Lucca from 1400 to 1430, built outside the medieval walls in the style of Venetian Palladian villas with an arcaded loggia. The museum houses collections ranging from 8th-century BC Etruscan discoveries to medieval sculptures from churches suppressed during the Napoleonic era.

activities.text: Bike ride on the ramparts: Built between 1513 and 1650 along a 4.2 km circuit, Lucca's Renaissance walls constitute one of the best-preserved examples of modern fortifications in Europe. Thirty meters wide at the base and 12 meters high, they never saw combat—Lucca maintained its independence through diplomacy until 1799. Today they're transformed into a tree-lined promenade bordered by plane trees and oaks, accessible on foot or by bike. Rentals are available at the main gates.

Colline Lucchesi DOC wine tasting: The Colline Lucchesi appellation covers the hills immediately north and east of Lucca. It produces Trebbiano-based whites and Sangiovese-based reds cultivated on these slopes since Roman times. Several estates in the province offer tastings.

Antiques market: Every third Sunday of the month, the antiques market spreads across the main squares of the historic center—Piazza San Martino, Piazza San Giovanni, Piazza Bernardini—with several hundred vendors. It's one of the most frequented antiques markets in Tuscany.

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Michele in Foro Lucca

visits.text: The Cathedral of Troia is probably the most singular building of the entire itinerary. Built between 1093 and 1125, it synthesizes Pisan, Byzantine, and Arab-Norman styles into a unique façade. But it's the rose window that mesmerizes: eleven rays in openwork columnettes, unmatched stone lacework technique. Added in the 13th century under the Angevins, it postdates the Romanesque nave by an entire century—hence the clash of styles on the same façade. Why eleven rays? The symbolism remains debated: some see the eleven faithful apostles without Judas, others a numerological reference to macrocosm (6) plus microcosm (5). No other rose window in the world has this number. The main bronze door, cast by Oderisio da Benevento in 1119, shows portraits of previous bishops, panel by panel. Inside, thirteen marble columns.

On the road between Troia and Lucera, Troia's historic center deserves the walk. Via Regina Margherita lines up 17th-18th century noble palaces. Pasticceria La Passionata on the square serves the dolce of the same name—historic almond, ricotta, and cinnamon cake, 18th-century recipe. One bite and you understand why Troia proclaims itself 'capital of the sacred': they even take pastry seriously. Troia is also on the Via Francigena del Sud, explaining the wealth of its churches for such a small town.

Lucera, 2025 Italian Capital of Culture, keeps a history told nowhere else. Between 1223 and 1225, Emperor Frederick II deported 16,000 to 20,000 rebellious Muslims from Sicily here—this is 'Lucera Saracenorum.' For 75 years the city became a unique Muslim enclave in Christian Europe, with mosques, hammams, and the emperor's Muslim personal guard. Between August 15-24, 1300, Charles II of Anjou razed it: massacre, deportation, slavery. It was rebaptized Civitas Sanctae Mariae. Today almost nothing remains of this history—only names and the Angevin Gothic cathedral replacing the central mosque.

The Swabian-Angevin Fortress on Colle Albano is immense: 900 m of ramparts, twenty-four towers still standing. The inner palatium is what remains of Frederick II's palace built around 1233—32 rooms on two floors, with Arab-Norman decorations (lost). Charles of Anjou added the great outer fortress between 1269 and 1283. Unbeatable panoramic view over the Tavoliere delle Puglie, the great grain plain. Count 1h30 to walk around. And right next door, the Augustan Roman Amphitheater—one of Puglia's largest.

activities.text: Lucera's cathedral, Angevin Gothic, is exactly the counterpoint to Troia: sober, austere, monumental. Built between 1300 and 1317 by Charles II on the site of the destroyed central mosque—political symbol above all. Inside, polychrome wooden statue of the Brown Virgin offered by Charles of Anjou, considered miraculous, still paraded on August 15. The MAU Museum next to the cathedral exhibits archaeological fragments from Roman, Saracen, and Angevin periods, plus a section on medieval urbanism. One hour.

For dinner, Lucera offers cuisine between Daunia and flat Puglia: orecchiette with cime di rapa, troccoli (long pasta with traditional machine), grilled cardoncelli mushrooms (Puglian porcini). Local wine: Cacc'e Mmitte di Lucera DOC, made from a very typical Uva di Troia (Nero di Troia) grape blend. Three or four historic trattorias around Piazza del Carmine, including Osteria Catervino which has been making the same legume soup with stale bread for thirty years.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Puglia: Frederick II's Castles, Hidden Hinterland & Forgotten Villages
Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia

places.name: Lucignano

visits.text: Elliptical layout of Lucignano: the village, Etruscan in origin and developed between the 13th and 16th centuries, is one of the best-preserved examples of medieval town planning in Tuscany. Its streets coil in four concentric elliptical rings around the hilltop, like a snail shell. This singular layout earned it the Bandiera Arancione label from the Italian Touring Club. Its position on the boundary of the former territories of Florence, Arezzo, Siena and Perugia gave it a strategic importance still visible in the thickness of its ramparts.

Municipal Museum — the Albero d'Oro: on the ground floor of the former Palazzo Pretorio, this 2.70-meter gilded copper reliquary is one of the masterworks of Italian goldsmithing. Created between 1350 and 1471 — a 120-year project — thanks to a bequest from one Madonna Giacoma, it was intended for the church of San Francesco and held Franciscan relics and splinters of the Cross of Christ. Its tree form draws on the Lignum Vitae (1259–1260) by Saint Bonaventure. The tree is displayed in the Sala delle Udienze, the former tribunal hall decorated with a fresco cycle (1410–1479) depicting illustrious figures from Antiquity, from Solomon to Aristotle. The museum, founded in 1924, also holds two panels by Luca Signorelli and works from the 14th-century Sienese school.

Church of San Francesco: built in the 12th century, recognizable by its travertine and local sandstone facade. Inside, a polyptych attributed to Luca di Tommè depicting a Madonna holding the castle of Lucignano recalls the town's role as a marquisate contested between Siena and Florence until the Battle of Scannagallo in the 16th century.

activities.text: Walk through the concentric rings: following the four elliptical streets that encircle the village from the outside is the only way to perceive the exceptional urban layout. The Medici Fortress, built in the 16th century on orders from Cosimo I de' Medici, offers a panorama over the Valdichiana and Lake Trasimeno.

Palio delle Contrade of Lucignano: a medieval historical reenactment in costume held every year in May. In September, the Festa degli Sposi commemorates the symbolic link between the Albero d'Oro and love, celebrated since the Japanese designer Yumi Katsura chose Lucignano for a bridal gown presentation.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

places.name: Lugo Di Vicenza

visits.text: Villa Godi Malinverni - This villa built between 1537 and 1542 in Lonedo, a hamlet of Lugo di Vicenza, is the first villa designed by Andrea Palladio—he wasn't yet thirty. The commission came from brothers Girolamo, Pietro and Marcantello Godi, from a powerful noble family specializing in silk trade across Europe. The facade is sober, almost austere, with two massive projecting blocks framing a central loggia with three arches, without the classical ornaments that would characterize his mature works. Palladio himself notes in the Four Books of Architecture that it 'stands on a hill with an admirable view, beside a river that serves for fishing.' The interior is decorated with frescoes by Gualtiero Padovano, Giovanni Battista Zelotti and Battista del Moro. A park pavilion houses the Pierluigi Malinverni paleontological museum, which preserves notably the world's longest fossil palm, and a second museum is dedicated to the British presence in this territory during the Great War, with documents on the Prince of Wales (future Edward VIII) and pacifist writer Vera Brittain.

Buso della Rana - In Monte di Malo, about twenty kilometers from Lugo, opens the entrance to Veneto's longest cave. The speleological network extends over more than 10 kilometers of galleries. The portion accessible to the public, about 500 meters of equipped galleries, crosses rooms of limestone concretions—stalactites, stalagmites, columns—formed over millions of years. The constant temperature of 9°C makes it an appreciated excursion in summer. The guided visit lasts about an hour.

activities.text: Visit to Villa Godi's historic gardens - The villa's centuries-old park, recently restored thanks to PNRR funds as part of the 'Gardens of Palladio' project, alternates Italian gardens with regular embroidery, alleys of century-old boxwood and an English wooded park with trees planted in the 19th century. A fountain, a network of paths and a view over the Astico valley and Vicentine Prealps complete the walk.

Exploring the Buso della Rana galleries - Guided cave tours depart every hour from the prepared entrance. The route crosses several remarkable rooms including the 'Sala del Bivio' and 'Sala delle Cascate,' with explanations of the karst geology of the Asiago Plateau, of which the Buso is one of the natural drains.
