visits.text: Twenty meters of stairs into darkness, the air suddenly cools: the Grotta di San Michele in Minervino Murge burrows beneath the village at the end of a karst ridge. The oldest written mention appears on a parchment from the year 1000 preserved at Monte Cassino abbey. The neoclassical entrance contrasts with the raw cavity. Guided tours, often dramatized, require booking.

Minervino Murge bears the nickname "Balcone delle Puglie": perched above 400 meters on the last limestone step, the terrace opens from the Ofanto basin to the Lucanian Apennine mountains, with Vulture in the distance and Gargano on clear days. A lighthouse built under fascism, then dedicated to all war dead, completes the scene. Come with a north wind: that's when the view extends.

Climb into the borgo antico Scesciola, the oldest part of Minervino Murge: narrow lanes, stairs, small balconies, arches connecting facades. Everything is on foot and it climbs steeply. It's short—twenty minutes—but forget strollers and smooth soles.

activities.text: Locals make the trip for this: the Grottino in Minervino Murge, a friggitoria serving giant panzerotti in three versions—mushroom, mozzarella-tomato, salami. Paper tablecloths, plastic utensils, pushed-together tables: the decor isn't the point. The wait can be long. Arrive before 1 PM or after 2 PM.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia
Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

visits.text: Villa Romana di Minori - a 1st-century AD Roman seaside villa, the only archaeological site on the Amalfi Coast open to the public. This 21,500-square-foot complex includes baths with hypocaust underfloor heating, reception halls decorated with frescoes and opus sectile floors, and a terraced garden overlooking the sea. Unearthed in 1932 during construction work, the villa likely belonged to a wealthy Roman merchant engaged in maritime trade across the Tyrrhenian Sea.

Basilica di Santa Trofimena - a basilica built in the 9th century to house the relics of Saint Trophimena, a 3rd-century Sicilian martyr whose body, according to legend, drifted to Minori in an unmanned boat. The 9th-century crypt preserves the original white marble sarcophagus. The current building, reconstructed after the 1954 earthquake, faithfully reproduces the proportions of the early Christian basilica.

activities.text: Tasting ndunderi di Minori - ricotta-filled pasta documented since the Middle Ages, considered one of Italy's oldest stuffed pasta shapes, served with tomato-basil sauce or ragù. The recipe is registered in Italy's traditional agri-food products (PAT) registry.
Strolling Minori's lungomare among fishing boats and potted lemon trees in front of the houses - this 1,300-foot waterfront is one of the few on the coast accessible on foot without stairs.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Villages of the Amalfi Coast: From Praiano to Salerno

places.name: Minturno

visits.text: The Archaeological Complex of Minturnae, on the Via Appia at km 156, preserves the vestiges of the Roman port-city founded in 295 BC on the ruins of an Auruncian town. The 1st-century AD Roman theater, built in opus reticulatum, accommodated more than 4,000 spectators; its restored cavea still serves as a setting for summer performances since 1960. Beneath the tiers, the Antiquarium displays statues, ex-votos, epigraphs, and coins recovered from the Garigliano River. An original section of the Via Appia, paved with basalt blocks, crosses the site. It was at Minturnae that General Gaius Marius, fleeing Sulla's assassins, hid in the marshes before being discovered—an episode recounted by Plutarch.

The Church of San Pietro Apostolo, the main church of Minturno's hilltop village, stands at the heart of the medieval historic center. Some of its marbles come directly from the ancient site of Minturnae, reused over the centuries in local constructions.

The Castello Baronale dominates the historic center from an elevated position. The village of Minturno was called Traetto until 1879, a name inherited from the Middle Ages when inhabitants of the ancient city, driven to the heights by the Lombards around 580 and by the swamping of the plain, rebuilt their village on the hill.

activities.text: Walk through Minturno's historic center (formerly Traetto), a hilltop village with picturesque alleyways and views over the Garigliano valley. The Memory Trail passes commemorative plaques recalling World War II events; near the archaeological site stands the British Commonwealth War Cemetery, where 2,049 soldiers who fell in 1943-1944 rest.

Pass by the Ponte Real Ferdinando over the Garigliano, Italy's first iron suspension bridge, designed by engineer Luigi Giura and inaugurated in 1832 by King Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies. The bridge connected the Papal States to the Kingdom of Naples. Destroyed during World War II, it was restored in 1998 and can be visited.

days_plan.itin_title: Latina Province Circuit: Lepini Mountains and Coast

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Pietro Apostolo Minturno

visits.text: Discover Villa Foscari La Malcontenta, another stunning Palladian masterpiece rising elegantly from the banks of the Brenta Canal. This 16th-century villa showcases Andrea Palladio's genius for proportion and harmony, with breathtaking interior frescoes that rank among the finest examples of Venetian villa decoration.

Explore the Brenta Riviera, the historic waterway connecting Padua to Venice that was once lined with over 70 noble villas. The canal served as the summer escape route for Venetian aristocracy, who would travel by burchiello (traditional boat) to their countryside retreats.

activities.text: Consider a scenic boat cruise along the Brenta Canal, following the historic route that Venetian nobles traveled for centuries. The journey passes multiple villas and offers a unique perspective on this remarkable concentration of architectural heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: Leaving Parma, stop in Reggio Emilia, the city that gave birth to the Italian flag. Head straight to Piazza Prampolini, the city's heart, where the cathedral and town hall stand. Inside this communal palace is the Sala del Tricolore, where on January 7, 1797, representatives from Reggio, Modena, Bologna, and Ferrara adopted the green-white-red flag as the emblem of the Cispadane Republic—forerunner of unified Italy. The room, designed by architect Lodovico Bolognini in 1774, is free to visit. The small adjacent Tricolore Museum traces the flag's history with period documents.

A few steps from Piazza Prampolini, step into the Basilica della Ghiara, one of the region's finest Baroque buildings. Built between 1597 and 1619, it preserves remarkable frescoes and a miraculous image of the Virgin. The contrast with the Romanesque austerity of the neighboring cathedral is striking. Allow 20 minutes.

Arriving in Modena by midday, make your way to Piazza Grande. Modena's cathedral, begun in 1099, is a masterpiece of Lombard Romanesque art, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1997 along with its bell tower, the Ghirlandina, and the square itself. Inside, don't miss the richly sculpted 13th-century rood screen that separates the nave from the elevated choir above the crypt—quite rare in Italian churches. Cathedral entry is free.

The Torre Ghirlandina, the cathedral's bell tower, rises 86 meters and dominates all of Modena. If you have the energy to climb, the view over the city's terracotta rooftops and surrounding hills is worth the effort. Allow 30 minutes for the ascent and descent.

The Palazzo Ducale, imposing residence of the Este dukes who ruled Modena from 1598 to 1859, sits just a few minutes' walk away. The palace now houses the Military Academy—you can't visit inside, but the facade and courtyard merit a detour. The Este family had made Modena a refined little capital after being forced to leave Ferrara.

activities.text: Modena is the capital of traditional balsamic vinegar PDO, a product that bears no resemblance to the industrial balsamic vinegar sold in supermarkets. Here, grape must (from Trebbiano and Lambrusco) is slowly cooked then aged for 12 to 25 years in batteries of small barrels made from oak, cherry, juniper, and mulberry, stored in house attics. Local producers open their doors to reveal this fascinating process. Book ahead—it's an experience you won't forget.

For lunch or late afternoon, visit the Mercato Albinelli, Modena's historic covered market open since 1931. Under its beautiful halls, you'll find stalls selling cured meats, cheeses, fresh pasta, and of course balsamic vinegar. You can buy on the spot and sit down to eat—a very local way to discover Modenese gastronomy. Try the tortellini, the region's specialty.

days_plan.itin_title: Gourmet Emilia: From Parma to Bologna Through the Hills
Modena Hills: Balsamic, Ferrari, and Mud Volcanoes

visits.text: Charles I of Anjou commissioned it in 1277 and had it designed two years later by Pierre d'Agincourt: the Castello Angioino of Mola di Bari, star-polygon fortress set at the edge of the Adriatic to guard the coast from pirates. In one cell, strange graffiti of oared ships have been recorded. Open intermittently: check, otherwise the exterior view suffices.

activities.text: Sit down at the port of Mola, one of Puglia's busiest, for fish of the day and the local Cima di Mola oil. In August, the Sagra del Polpo celebrates octopus with concerts and tastings. The last stop before the return to Bari, 20 km away.

days_plan.itin_title: Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

visits.text: Not the postcard charm of Giovinazzo, but something rarer: an Old Cathedral of San Corrado planted directly on the harbor, with its three aligned domes and two twin bell towers. Started around 1150, completed in the 13th century, the church is the purest example of Apulian Romanesque with domes: you can detect Byzantine, Romanesque, and Arab-Sicilian influences blended without forcing. No Baroque retouches, because in the 18th century it lost its cathedral title and was forgotten. Free entry, closed Sundays.

Molfetta's harbor remains one of the busiest fishing ports in the lower Adriatic: fleet of trawlers, morning fish auction, shipyards still working. Walk to Banchina Seminario to see the Old Cathedral from the sea, as its builders intended. Coffee on the terrace at Piazza Municipio on the way back.

A discreet but very real trace of the Templars, the Sala dei Templari occupies the former church of San Nicola, attested in Molfetta since 1148. The knights maintained an embarkation point here for the Holy Land, until the order's dissolution in 1312. Today the building serves as an exhibition and congress hall. Open only during events, check on site.

activities.text: Fish lunch at the harbor. Molfetta specialty: the local fish soup called "ciambotto," a mix of small fish cooked in spicy tomato sauce. Simple, reliable address: Osteria del Porto.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari Loop: 7 days Along Puglia's Northern Coast
Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia
Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

visits.text: Mombaldone is the only village in the Langa Astigiana still encircled by its intact original walls, with its urban plan unchanged since foundation. The first written mention dates to 991, in the foundation act of the abbey of San Quintino in Spigno Monferrato. In 1208, the fief passed to the Del Carretto family, Marquises of Finale Ligure. In the seventeenth century, the village alone resisted Napoleonic troops - armor and muskets from French soldiers are still found in the Bormida plain - while the rest of Piedmont opened its doors to the victorious army. A once-imposing square tower, now partially ruined, still dominates the village summit.

Walk through the single main street from which branch alleys and vaulted passages, interior courtyards and portals carved from centuries-old wood. Notice the engraved lintels and stone arches testifying to unchanged medieval craftsmanship. The Palazzo Fortezza, partially inhabited by descendants of the Del Carretto family - whose name spans more than eight centuries of continuous presence - faces the main street.

Leaving the village, climb a few hundred meters toward the surrounding countryside. The calanchi are deep ravines carved by erosion in the gray sandstone of the Langa Astigiana hills - a lunar and overwhelming landscape, unique in this wine region. Herds of goats whose milk produces Robiola di Roccaverano DOP graze these slopes.

activities.text: Hiking or cycling in the Bormida di Spigno valley, on trails crossing fields and vineyards. Canoeing on the Bormida for the more athletic, possible depending on water levels. In August, the Historia Montis Baudonis historical reenactment and classical music festival animate the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont's Most Beautiful Villages in 2 Weeks

visits.text: Rocca Roveresca — masterpiece of Renaissance military architecture — Built between 1482 and 1492 on the orders of Giovanni Della Rovere — nephew of Pope Sixtus IV and son-in-law of Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino — by Sienese architect Francesco di Giorgio Martini. The mastio is octagonal with a broad base, its ten irregular trapezoidal faces tapering upward in a helical spiral: a geometry designed to deflect cannonballs by presenting oblique angles rather than flat walls. Martini himself wrote in his treatise of 'geometrie che disegno mostrar non può' — forms that drawing alone cannot convey. A torricino di rinfianco protects the walkway leading to a semi-circular torrione, connected by an entrance ravelin. Seen from above, the ensemble traces a crossbow — Martini's habitual signature. The rocca was never struck by a single cannonball. Converted into a prison from 1631 until the 19th century after the Della Rovere line died out. Left unfinished following the simultaneous deaths of both Martini and Giovanni Della Rovere in 1501. In the moat, since 2000, reconstructed war machines built after Martini's original drawings.

Museum of historical re-enactment — 5 levels — From the basement to the top floor of the mastio: an armoury in the ravelin (a mascolo — the terminal section of a bombard weighing more than six quintals — along with moschettoni, falconetti, spingarde, halberds and ornately decorated bladed weapons), then four floors of reconstructed Renaissance scenes: a wedding banquet, a prison and torture chamber, an oven, a munitions store. Period-costumed mannequins inhabit every room. Single ticket including the Museo Civico and the village theatre.

Piazza Della Rovere and Porta Cavour — the main square was created in the 17th century by vaulting over the rocca's northern moat. It still bears the name of the commissioning family. Porta Cavour, the village gateway, is a well-preserved circular cassero.

activities.text: Full visit of the Rocca Roveresca — walk all five levels of the mastio, through the narrow passages and spiral staircases that give a concrete sense of life in a 15th-century military castle. End on the camminamenti di ronda to observe from outside the mastio's ten irregular faces and the war machines in the moat.

Caccia al Cinghiale — historical re-enactment (13–15 August) — Three days of Renaissance living history: Mondavio's historical archers in period costume, tournaments, crossbow competitions, banquets with local products in a village transformed into a 15th-century settlement.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

places.name: Mondolfo

visits.text: Double ring of walls — Mondolfo is one of the few villages in Le Marche with two concentric circuits of walls. The inner ring dates in part to the 6th century (partially visible from the Byzantine period), the outer to the 15th-century medieval construction. The 19th-century Porta Fanestre and Porta Santa Maria give access to the outer enclosure. The walkways along the walls lead to a belvedere from which, on a clear day, the Croatian coast is visible.

Palazzo Comunale and Torre Civica — a neo-Gothic building from 1931, rebuilt with bricks salvaged from the original structure destroyed by an earthquake the same year. Three symbols decorate the façade: the municipal coat of arms in gold and azure (the colours of fields and sea), the campanone San Gervaso, and a stone escutcheon held in a lion's mouth — the city's heraldic device. The central square bears the name of Piazza Mario del Monaco.

Bastione di Sant'Anna and Belvedere — a former military bastion converted into an Italian-style garden with a limonaia (orangery). The belvedere at the top offers a panorama over the valley, the coast at Marotta and Monte Conero to the south. On clear days the Croatian coastline is visible on the horizon.

Galleria senza soffitto — an open-air museum spread throughout the village. Murals, black-and-white photographs by Mario Giacomelli — a photographer from nearby Senigallia, one of the major figures in 20th-century Italian photography, whose series Io non ho mani che mi accarezzano il volto was inspired by a poem by David Maria Turoldo. The Scalinata del Pianoforte is one of the village's most photographed landmarks.

Chiesa di Sant'Agostino — a large single-nave church with barrel vault and twelve gilded carved wooden altars. Two 17th-century paintings stand out: Madonna del Rosario and Madonna col Bambino. Above the entrance, a 1776 organ by Gaetano Callido, one of the greatest Venetian organ builders of the 18th century. The campanone known as 'Cristo Re' is the one that rings on Sundays in a concert of bells.

Abbazia di San Gervasio di Bulgaria — a 5th–6th-century abbey a few hundred metres from the centre, founded on the Via Flaminia. Its basilica plan is directly inspired by the great basilicas of Ravenna. In the crypt, the largest Ravenna-style sarcophagus in Le Marche, dating to the 6th century, decorated with Christian symbols, crosses, laurel wreaths and two peacocks symbolising immortality. One of the oldest archaeological sites in the province.

activities.text: Walk the camminamenti di ronda to the belvedere — follow the walls from inside the village along the old walkways to the highest panoramic point. Along the way, an old cannon recalls the bastion's defensive past.

Museo Civico — the 1858 clock mechanism — installed in the cloister adjoining the Chiesa di Sant'Agostino. The centrepiece: an 1858 clock movement, still working, wound by hand, chiming every 15 minutes. Exhibition on accordion makers — a craft tradition of the region.

La Cacciata — historical re-enactment (summer) — a Renaissance living history event featuring the pallone col bracciale (a ball game played with a leather brace, once as popular in 16th-century Italy as football is today), sword tournaments, archery and flag-throwing. Banquets with local products.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

map_keywords: Abbazia di San Gervasio di Bulgaria Mondolfo

visits.text: Unique feature in Italy: to enter Moneglia from Riva Trigoso, you pass through five alternating one-way road tunnels, controlled by traffic lights that open three times per hour in each direction. Former railway tunnels from the Genoa-Pisa line, dating from 1874, decommissioned in 1970, recycled into a single-lane automobile road. It's narrow, it's lit, it's very Ligurian. Riva Trigoso side, departures from Moneglia at :05, :25, :45 of each hour; Deiva side, every 10 minutes. Check beforehand, otherwise you wait 20 minutes at a red light in the sun. And between tunnels, rocky coves for diving.

The Castello di Monleone dates from 1173: it's one of two fortresses built by the Republic of Genoa to defend Moneglia (the other, Villafranca, is in ruins). In the 19th century, transformed into a neo-Gothic private castle. Today a luxury hotel. The climb to reach it (5 minutes on foot from the center) remains public and worthwhile for the panorama: Moneglia, its bay, and the coast stretching toward the Cinque Terre. The castle even appears on the municipal coat of arms.

The Castello di Villafranca is the other fortress, opposite the village, on the east side. Reduced to ruins by Allied bombing during World War II, partially restored. What you visit today is mainly its park and botanical garden. Strategic position: it watched for Barbary pirate arrivals from offshore. The tower gives its silhouette to the entire bay.

The Church of Santa Croce, former 12th-century parish church, rebuilt in 1726. Inside, two major works: an altarpiece by Luca Cambiaso (Genoese Mannerist painter born in Moneglia in 1527, one of the greats of the Genoese school) and a statue by Anton Maria Maragliano, the Baroque sculptor who dressed almost all Ligurian processions in the 18th century. Next door, the Baroque oratorio dei Disciplinanti preserves a cycle of ancient frescoes. The Church of San Giorgio, higher up, dates from 1396 and keeps a beautiful Franciscan cloister.

activities.text: Moneglia beach. One kilometer of granular sand, shallow sea for the first meters—one of the rare family beaches truly usable with small children on the Riviera di Levante. Blue flag every year since 1990. Free beach widely accessible from both sides, paid bagni in the middle (€15-25 per lounger). The further east you go (toward the tunnels), the more the coast closes into small coves of pebbles and rocks, perfect for snorkeling.

Hike the Sentiero Verde Azzurro between Moneglia and Deiva Marina, about 6 km, 2 hours. The trail climbs toward Lemeglio then San Pantaleo (high point 325 m), pine forests, olive groves, vertiginous views over the coast. Level reserved for experienced hikers (EE in Italian classification)—some passages are steep. Return train from Deiva to rejoin Moneglia (3 minutes, €1.80).

days_plan.itin_title: 6-Day Grand Tour of the Riviera di Levante

visits.text: Monforte d'Alba - the Mons Fortis - takes its name from the ramparts that once crowned the hill at 480 meters. In 1028, Milan's Archbishop Aribert d'Intimiano besieged the village to eradicate a Cathar community. The deported population, condemned to the stake in Milan after refusing to recant, suffered an episode that preceded the Béziers massacres by two centuries. The medieval center has preserved its fan-shaped plan following the contour lines, with tortuous alleys bordered by carefully restored stone buildings.

The Auditorium Horszowski is an open-air venue carved into the hill's natural morphology - a 800-seat cavea whose exceptional acoustics are produced by the terrain configuration between the Romanesque bell tower (sole remnant of the old church demolished in the early twentieth century), the baroque oratory of Santa Elisabetta, and the walls of Palazzo Scarampi. Pianist Mieczysław Horszowski, then 91 years old, inaugurated it in 1986. Since then, the Monfortinjazz festival has welcomed internationally renowned artists every summer, from Paolo Conte to Caetano Veloso.

Palazzo Scarampi, built in the eighteenth century on the ruins of the medieval castle (itself rebuilt after 1706 by the Del Carretto family then restored in 1833), now houses the town hall. Its facade opens directly onto the auditorium and serves as a backdrop for concerts. Right beside it, the oratory of Saint Augustine and Saint Boniface presents a brick facade and a bronze portal with medieval symbols.

activities.text: Wine walk through the UNESCO-classified Langhe vineyards (2014) - Monforte is one of the 11 Barolo DOCG production communes. Local estates offer cellar visits with tastings of Barolo, Nebbiolo, and Dolcetto d'Alba.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont's Most Beautiful Villages in 2 Weeks

places.name: Monopoli

visits.text: Built in the 16th century to ward off Turkish raids, the Castello di Carlo V did its job: the town was never taken. Its irregular pentagonal layout even encompasses an ancient Basilian church, San Nicola della Pinna. It served as a prison until the 1950s. Not everything is accessible, as part of it houses municipal offices, but the view from the bastions over the Porto Vecchio is more than worth it.

The Cattedrale Maria Santissima della Madia tells the story of a raft. In 1117, tradition holds, a boat loaded with timber arrived in the harbor, carrying an icon of the Madonna, and the wood was used to finish the church roof. Some of the beams are preserved as relics. The present building is an 18th-century Baroque reworking with polychrome marble and gilding. Every December 16, the scene is reenacted in a procession on the sea.

Blue on white: the fishing boats of Monopoli's Porto Vecchio stand out against the ramparts. This isn't a set piece; the fishermen still go out, mostly for octopus. The best vantage point for photos is from the jetty facing the castle, boats in the foreground. Just after sunset, the lights reflect on the water and the basin changes completely.

Get lost between Piazza Garibaldi, Piazza Palmieri, and Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II: Monopoli's historic center threads through narrow alleys that suddenly open onto these broad squares. The contrast is the whole point. Notice the white loggia of Palazzo Martinelli along the way, 18th century, almost Venetian in feel. Put the map away; the old town is too small to get truly lost.

If Baroque churches interest you, Monopoli's Museo Diocesano completes the cathedral, just a few steps from Largo Cattedrale. The territory also has cliff-face cave churches carved into the coastal cliffs, far less visited than the center. Museum hours are reduced off-season; call ahead before making the trip.

activities.text: The best swimming in town isn't at Capitolo but at Cala Porta Vecchia, right at the foot of the ramparts: you jump in the water from the historic center itself. It's small and fills fast. The Capitolo beaches further south are wider but cost money and are packed in August. Arrive before 10am for Cala Porta Vecchia.

The locals call it a sporcamuss, literally dirty-mouth: a puff pastry soaked in custard and dusted with icing sugar, physically impossible to eat neatly. The name is a warning, not a metaphor. You'll find it in pastry shops throughout the center, best eaten warm. Bring a napkin, seriously.

The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days
Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

map_keywords: Cathedral Maria Santissima della Madia Monopoli

visits.text: Monreale Cathedral, built by William II between 1172 and 1189, shelters 6,340 square meters of Byzantine mosaics—the largest mosaic surface in the world after Istanbul's Hagia Sophia. The 130 scenes from the Old and New Testaments were created by Constantinople craftsmen under the direction of Benedictine monks.

Monreale's cloister, formed by 228 twin columns—no two identical—blends mosaics, Arab interlacing, lion heads, and Apocalypse scenes. The southwest corner houses an Arab fountain with a twisted column, the sole remnant of the original Norman royal palace's Islamic architecture.

activities.text: Lunch at the trattorias surrounding the cathedral with views over the Conca d'Oro—the golden basin of orange and lemon groves encircling Palermo—before driving to Trapani (100 km, ~1h40).

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Sicily

visits.text: Visit Monselice Castle, housing one of the finest collections of medieval arms and armor in the Veneto, second only to the Doge's Palace in Venice. The castle's remarkable fireplaces are themselves works of art, showcasing the refined craftsmanship of medieval artisans.

Climb the Seven Churches Sanctuary (Santuario delle Sette Chiese), a pilgrimage route of seven chapels ascending the hillside that once granted the same indulgences as visiting Rome's seven pilgrimage churches. The Via Sacra offers beautiful views of the surrounding hills.
Explore the Old Cathedral and the elegant Villa Duodo, designed by Vincenzo Scamozzi, surrounded by gardens and offering panoramic views from its hillside position.

activities.text: Walk the fortified historic center, where medieval walls, towers, and gates create an authentic atmosphere. The town's strategic hilltop position made it an important defensive stronghold for centuries.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

places.name: Montagnana

visits.text: Discover Montagnana, renowned for producing some of Italy's finest prosciutto and encircled by one of Europe's best-preserved medieval defensive walls. The nearly complete circuit of walls, punctuated by 24 towers, creates a dramatic silhouette visible for miles across the Veneto plain.

Explore the castle, the elegant main square, and the stunning Cathedral with its notable works of art. The town center retains its medieval character within the protective embrace of the mighty fortifications.

activities.text: Experience the annual Prosciutto Festival celebrating the local cured ham tradition. The town's Prosciutto Veneto Berico-Euganeo DOP is produced following centuries-old methods in the unique microclimate of the Euganean Hills.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

map_keywords: Duomo di Santa Maria Assunta Montagnana

places.name: Montalcino

visits.text: Fortress of Montalcino: Built in 1361 by reusing earlier 13th-century structures, this pentagonal fortress was the last bastion to resist during the fall of the Republic of Siena to the Medici in 1555—Sienese refugees held out here until 1559. Its interior enoteca allows you to taste Brunello in the very symbol of republican resistance. From the ramparts, the view stretches across Val d'Orcia, Monte Amiata, and the Maremma.

Piazza del Popolo and Palazzo dei Priori: The 13th-century communal palace, adorned with heraldic coats of arms from Montalcino's history, has a slender bell tower whose carillons still punctuate the life of the town. It's the central square of a network of narrow, steep lanes typical of Sienese medieval urbanism.

Civic and Diocesan Museum of Sacred Art: Housed in the former 14th-century convent of Sant'Agostino (with its two 16th-century cloisters), this museum preserves over 200 works on three floors, including the 12th-century Crucifix of Sant'Antimo, a Madonna by Simone Martini, and the Coronation of the Virgin by Bartolo di Fredi.

Abbey of Sant'Antimo: Ten kilometers south via the SP55, in a valley hollow planted with cypresses and olive trees, this Benedictine Romanesque abbey is mentioned as early as 813 in an act of Louis the Pious. The main church, built in the 12th century in the Cistercian Burgundian style, is one of the finest examples of French Romanesque architecture in Italy. Since 1992, a community of Premonstratensian canons has sung the Gregorian offices—vespers at 6:30 PM can be heard from afar.

activities.text: Brunello di Montalcino tasting: Brunello is produced exclusively from Sangiovese Grosso on the commune's territory. Clemente Santi was the first to get it recognized in 1869. The fortress cellars or surrounding estates (Poggio di Sotto, Ciacci Piccolomini) offer tastings of the current vintage and riserva.
Sagra del Tordo: Every last Sunday in October, Montalcino's four districts compete in archery in this medieval festival commemorating the region's hunting traditions.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Siena Province

map_keywords: Museo Civico e Diocesano d'Arte Sacra Montalcino

places.name: Monte Sant Angelo

visits.text: First stop in Lucera, an ancient Roman colony that became, under Frederick II, a Muslim enclave populated with Saracens deported from Sicily—a unique political experiment in medieval Italy. Visit the Roman amphitheater (circa 16-10 BC, one of southern Italy's largest) then climb up to the Angevin fortress. The 900-meter ramparts dominate the Tavoliere, Puglia's vast grain-growing plain.

Lucera's cathedral, raised between 1300 and 1317 on the ruins of the mosque destroyed by Charles II of Anjou when he expelled the Saracens in 1300, offers a rare synthesis of Angevin Gothic in southern Italy. Pause before the lateral portal and its tympanum depicting the Virgin.

Arrive in Monte Sant'Angelo by late afternoon, a village perched at 843 meters altitude on the southern slopes of the Gargano. Sweeping views over the Gulf of Manfredonia. The air turns noticeably cooler: bring a layer.

Don't miss the Sanctuary of Saint Michael the Archangel. You descend 86 steps carved into the rock to reach the sacred grotto. The archangel appeared to the Bishop of Siponto in 490 AD. A continuous pilgrimage site for fifteen centuries. UNESCO-listed since 2011 (Lombards in Italy).

Inside the cave, the marble statue of Saint Michael attributed to Andrea Sansovino (early 16th century) occupies the main altar. Around it, frescoes and ex-voto offerings from pilgrims. Climb back up via Frederick II's octagonal bell tower, erected in 1273 as both watchtower and campanile.

activities.text: Wander through the Rione Junno, a historic quarter dating to the 6th century. Tightly packed white houses, staircases, laundry hanging overhead. While you're there, look for the pagghiaraziz, dry-stone shepherds' huts used by local herders.

Dine on paposcia (local stuffed bread) with melted caciocavallo podolico cheese and 'nduja. In local trattorias, you'll also find orecchiette all'erbe del Gargano: pasta with wild herbs from the promontory (wild mint, oregano, nepitella).

days_plan.itin_title: Gargano & Northern Puglia - The Spur of the Italian Boot

map_keywords: Sanctuary San Michele Arcangelo Monte Sant'Angelo

places.name: Monte Sole

visits.text: Parco Storico di Monte Sole - a 6,300-hectare park between the Reno and Setta valleys, established in 1989 as a memorial to the Marzabotto massacre. Between September 29 and October 5, 1944, SS troops from the 16th Panzergrenadier Division murdered 770 civilians (women, children, elderly) in the Monte Sole villages—the largest massacre of civilians in Western Europe during World War II. The devastated villages of Marzabotto, Caprara, and Casaglia are preserved as ruins.

activities.text: Walk the 8 km waymarked memorial trail linking the park's ruined villages, with interpretive panels at massacre sites. The silence of the oak and chestnut forest that has reclaimed the ruins makes the visit particularly haunting.

days_plan.itin_title: 10 Natural Wonders Around Bologna

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Martino Monte Sole

places.name: Monte Terminillo

visits.text: Cittaducale, founded in 1309 by King Charles II of Anjou (hence its name meaning "ducal city"), preserves a typical medieval bastide orthogonal plan with rectilinear streets converging on the central square. The Chiesa di Santa Maria del Popolo (14th century) and the Chiesa di San Francesco with its Gothic portal merit a stop. From the ramparts, view the Velino valley and Terminillo.

The Terme di Cotilia, a few miles from Cittaducale, were known to the Romans as Aquae Cutiliae. Emperor Vespasian, born in nearby Sabina (at Vicus Phalacrinae, today's Cittareale), stayed here regularly and died here in 79 AD. Titus also died here in 81 AD. The sulfurous springs still gush into a small lake.

The Tempio di San Francesco al Terminillo, a contemporary church built at 5,322 feet at Pian de' Valli, stands out with its 171-foot bell tower and its 3,767-square-foot apse mosaic, one of the world's largest modern mosaics, depicting the Creation. Engraved on the main bell is a prayer for peace meant to resonate across the mountains.

activities.text: Climb toward Terminillo on the scenic road from Cittaducale via Rieti. The road winds through beech forests, gaining 3,300 feet over 12 miles, with viewpoints over the Rieti plain opening at each hairpin turn.

Panorama from Pian de' Valli (5,315 feet) over the Valle Santa: on clear days, you can distinguish the four Franciscan sanctuaries arranged in a cross around the Rieti plain—Fonte Colombo, Greccio, La Foresta and Poggio Bustone.

Hike to the summit of Monte Terminillo (7,274 feet), nicknamed "Rome's Mountain." The massif, whose meltwater feeds the lakes of the nature reserve below, offers trails through beech forests and alpine meadows with views of the Abruzzo, Sibillini Mountains and, on exceptional days, the Tyrrhenian coast.

days_plan.itin_title: Rieti, Holy Valley & Sabine Lakes Circuit
Rieti, Holy Valley & Sabine Lakes Circuit

map_keywords: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Popolo Cittaducale

activities.text: The Parco del Vulture spreads across the slopes of an extinct volcano, just above Melfi: protected area, forests, marked trails. It's the green counterpoint to a day spent in stone. An hour's walk is enough to completely change landscapes. In summer, leave before 10 AM: there's no shade on the ridges.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia

places.name: Montecarlo

visits.text: Rocca di Cerruglio: The village of Montecarlo owes its name to Charles IV of Luxembourg—Mons Charoli in Latin—who contributed in 1333 to liberating Lucca from Pisan occupation. The Republic of Lucca then had the destroyed village rebuilt on Cerruglio hill and erected this three-tower fortress: the semi-circular keep, the Tower of the Apparition, and the Tower of Saint Barbara, the latter named for a legend that the Virgin appeared to defend the village during a 15th-century Pisan siege. The fortress is open to visitors with views over the plain of Lucca and the Valdinievole.

Collegiata di Sant'Andrea: In the heart of the village, this collegiate church founded in the 14th century preserves its original Gothic façade and portal, remodeled in Baroque style in the 18th century. Inside, a fresco of the 15th-century Florentine school depicts the Madonna del Soccorso snatching a child from the devil's claws. Two plaques commemorate visits by poet Giuseppe Ungaretti in the 1960s and composer Giacomo Puccini.

Teatro dei Rassicurati: Built in the early 18th century, this tiny Italian-style theater ranks among the five smallest in Italy. It takes its name from the Academy of the Rassicurati, a local learned society founded in 1690. Puccini visited several times. The auditorium, with its lacquered wooden boxes and ceiling frescoes, has remained almost unchanged since construction.

Pieve di San Piero in Campo: At the foot of the hill, this 12th-century Romanesque parish church with three naves is one of the oldest Christian buildings in Lucca province. Its sober limestone façade and austere interior contrast with the Baroque exuberance of the collegiate church perched atop the village.

activities.text: Montecarlo DOC tasting at family estates: Montecarlo's winemaking tradition dates to Roman times, but it was in 1870 that a local landowner imported French grape varieties from Bordeaux (Sauvignon, Sémillon, Cabernet, Merlot) and Burgundy (Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris) to blend with Tuscan Trebbiano. Montecarlo Bianco DOC—recognized in 1969—has been celebrated since the 15th century: Pope Gregory XII praised it in the early 1400s. Village estates welcome visitors year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Lucca Province Circuit: Hill Towns and Coast

map_keywords: Pieve di San Piero in Campo Montecarlo

places.name: Montecassiano

visits.text: Palazzo dei Priori — a Gothic 14th-century building dominating the Piazza Unità d'Italia, with crenellated crown, a banditore balcony and a grand connecting arch to the Palazzo Compagnucci. A Roman funerary stele of Cassia Orestina, preserved inside the palazzo, testifies to the village's post-Roman origins — traditionally said to have been founded by nobles fleeing the destruction of Helvia Ricina in 408. The Pinacoteca Civica Girolamo Buratto, in the Pompeian-decorated rooms of Palazzo Compagnucci, holds a rare work by Ioannes Hispanus (a 16th-century Iberian painter, Madonna in Trono con Santi) and paintings by Girolamo Buratto, a pupil of the Pomarancio.

Collegiata di Santa Maria Assunta — founded by the monks of Fiastra Abbey. It holds the village's masterpiece: an enamelled and painted terracotta altarpiece by Fra' Mattia della Robbia (1527–1532), the only authenticated work by one of the last members of Florence's famous della Robbia dynasty.

Museo di Arte Sacra 'Giovanni da San Guglielmo' — installed in the 16th-century Chiesa di San Giovanni Battista. It holds the oldest bell in Le Marche, cast in 1358, along with reliquaries, chalices and liturgical goldsmithery by master silversmith Domenico Piani.

Mura e Parco del Cerreto — 15th-century walls with three crenellated gate towers (Porta San Giovanni, Porta Diaz, Porta Battisti). From the terrace of the Parco del Cerreto (1.2 hectares), panoramic views west to the Sibillini and east to the Adriatic.

activities.text: Walk the concentric lanes of the village — Montecassiano is shaped like an onion, with alleyways spiralling toward the central piazza. Via Catena, Vicolo Santa Chiara, Vicolo San Francesco: look for the inner courtyards visible through half-open doorways.

Try the sughitti — sweet polenta made with grape must, cornmeal and walnuts, prepared after the grape harvest since at least the 15th century. Once a peasant dish offered to local dignitaries as a mark of esteem.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

map_keywords: Collegiata di Santa Maria Assunta Montecassiano

visits.text: The Terme Tettuccio constitutes the most representative building of European Belle Époque thermalism: rebuilt in the 1920s by architect Ugo Giovannozzi, it combines a circular colonnade, an English-style garden with fountains, and four drinking galleries where the waters of the Tettuccio, Rinfresco, Regina and Leopoldina springs flow. The interior frescoes and mosaics are the work of Galileo Chini, Italy's leading Art Nouveau artist. Montecatini has been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2021 in the "Great Spas of Europe" category.

Montecatini Alto, accessible via the funicular inaugurated in 1898—the oldest still in service according to Wikipedia—is the ancient medieval village perched at 300 meters altitude above the spa town. The town walls were razed in 1554 by Cosimo I's Florentines during their conquest of the territory. The village preserves some cobbled lanes, the Rocca, and panoramic views across the entire Valdinievole. The 8-minute journey aboard the historic red carriages "Gigio" and "Gigia" is an experience in itself.

The Viale Verdi and its "Passi di Gloria": since 2011, over 200 bronze plaques embedded in the sidewalks between Piazza del Popolo and the Terme Tettuccio trace the visits of the most notable personalities—from Giuseppe Verdi to Puccini, from Ruggero Leoncavallo to Marie Curie, from Gary Cooper to Audrey Hepburn, all who came to take the waters. The early 20th-century Palazzo Municipale, designed by Raffaello Brizzi, borders this promenade.

activities.text: Thermal cure or wellness session at Terme Tettuccio or Terme Excelsior: Montecatini's four springs, which rise from depths of over 60 meters, produce sulfate-saline bicarbonate-sodium waters, traditionally used for digestive, hepatic and metabolic conditions. The thermal season runs from May to October.
The Teatro Verdi, built in 1950 in the thermal park, hosts the summer music season. Puccini, who stayed regularly in Montecatini, reportedly said it was one of his favorite places to compose.

days_plan.itin_title: Pistoia Province Circuit: Hill Towns & Thermal Spas

visits.text: From the outside it's an austere fortress with a deep moat and thick walls. Inside, the Castello di Montechiarugolo reveals Renaissance halls with delicate frescoes and a luminous Salone delle Feste. Legend has it that the ghost of Fata Bema, mistress of Count Pio Torelli (beheaded in 1612), still haunts the corridors. Guided tour compulsory, €6.

The inner garden of the Castello di Montechiarugolo, tidy and flower-filled, contrasts sharply with the raw mass of the ramparts. You access it during the tour. Also spot the prigioni in the tower and the walkway for views over the torrente Enza.

activities.text: Request the weekend guided tour of the Castello di Montechiarugolo: the guides know every nook and tell the story of the Torelli with storytelling flair. Bring flat shoes for the narrow walkway. The castle is 16 km from Parma, 19 minutes from Reggio Emilia.

days_plan.itin_title: Matilda's Lands: The Countess's Castles in 5 Days

places.name: Montecosaro

visits.text: Chiesa di San Rocco — built in 1447 on an octagonal plan, on the path leading up to the historic centre. It holds magnificent frescoes attributed to Simone de Magistris (1576), a Marchigian painter trained under Lorenzo Lotto. In the apse, the village of Montecosaro itself appears as a backdrop in a religious scene — a rare 16th-century visual document of how the village once looked.

Complesso Agostiniano (Palazzo Comunale) — a medieval complex comprising the Chiesa di Sant'Agostino and a former convent now serving as the town hall. The church, though restructured in 1773, retains a gilded Byzantine-style reliquary and a Gaetano Callido organ (1792). Inside the palazzo, a 2nd-century white marble Roman sarcophagus was recovered from the Chienti valley.

Collegiata di San Lorenzo and Teatro delle Logge — the collegiata was built in 1723 over the ruins of the old pieve, of which the 10th-century Romanesque campanile survives. It holds a pre-Giotto crucifix (12th–13th century) with Byzantine influences. The adjoining Teatro delle Logge, inaugurated in 1809 (stalls and three horseshoe tiers of iron boxes), was the site in 1568 of the execution of Enea Galizia and twelve conspirators, hanged from the railings after their failed uprising against the Cesarini family.

Abbazia di Santa Maria a Piè di Chienti (Montecosaro Scalo) — 4 km below the village, one of the finest Cluniac architectural achievements in Le Marche, consecrated in 1125. First documented in 936. Its two-storey interior (women's galleries, timber roofs, alabaster windows) blends Lombard and Burgundian influences. The bell tower's campana carries the date 1425 and the oldest known municipal coat of arms.

activities.text: Stroll through the lanes between the 13th-century Porta San Lorenzo (the last surviving gate, now embedded in the Marinozzi palazzo) and the Parco del Cassero at the highest point, with panoramic views over the Sibillini and the Adriatic.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

map_keywords: Abbazia di Santa Maria a Piè di Chienti Montecosaro Scalo

visits.text: Perched on a rocky spur between the Scoltenna and Leo valleys, the Castello di Montecuccolo dominates the Frignano forests. The feudal structure, towers and Guelph merlons, recalls the Matildic castles of the Reggio area. Restored since the 1970s by the municipality of Pavullo, it's open to the public.

A medieval castle housing Italy's highest balsamic vinegar cellar, at 873 m altitude. The Torre del Trebbo holds this small room where balsamic vinegar ages beneath the roof tiles. On the piano nobile, the collections of Gino Covili and Raffaele Biolchini, two Pavullo artists with opposing styles.

Raimondo Montecuccoli, born here in 1609, was one of the greatest military strategists of his century. The museum dedicated to him, inaugurated in 2021, occupies the first floor. The Museo Naturalistico del Frignano, on the upper floors, presents rocks, fossils, and local fauna.

activities.text: Finish with a meal in the castle's former guesthouse, transformed into a mountain osteria. Frignano cuisine with local products. Reservations recommended.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Apennines: From Montefiorino to Rocchetta Mattei

visits.text: The gateway — the only entrance to the castello — Montefabbri first appears in documents in 1216, having developed from the 9th–10th century around the pieve of San Gaudenzio. The name comes from Monte Fabrorum — the mountain of the Fabbri family, the earliest feudal lords. In 1578, the Duke of Urbino granted the village as a fief to Francesco Paciotti, a civil and military architect who brought a long period of prosperity and ceramic craftsmanship. The gateway is the only opening in the enclosure wall. The medieval arch once supported a drawbridge — the niches where the bridge arms rested are still visible in the vestibule. On the valley-facing façade above the arch, a small 15th-century sandstone carving depicts a Madonna lattante. On the inner façade, the white marble arms of Count Francesco Paciotti preside over the entrance. In 1799, insurgents from the surrounding countryside captured Napoleonic soldiers here who had sought refuge on the walls after the sack of Urbino.

Pieve di San Gaudenzio — the original nucleus of the village — one of the four oldest pievi in the Archdiocese of Urbino, founded between the 7th and 8th centuries and dedicated to the first bishop of Rimini, martyred in 360. Rebuilt and extended in 1570, as recorded by a tablet at the back of the church. The interior preserves 16th–17th-century works and a collection of scagliole — stucco decorations considered the oldest in Le Marche. The Gothic chapel of Santa Marcellina (12th century) has held the saint's remains since 2 November 1666. The baptismal font is carved from an ancient Roman marble cippus. The 15th-century bell tower (25 m) dominates the village.

Belvedere over the Foglia and Apsa valleys — at 319 metres on the ridge separating the two valleys, Montefabbri has remained virtually unchanged since the 15th century — 70 inhabitants, no new construction for decades, only careful restorations. The lanes radiate from the pieve like spokes, with tightly packed fired-brick houses pressing against the walls. From the village's high points, the view spans one side across the Foglia valley toward Pesaro, and the other across the Apsa valley toward Urbino.

activities.text: Full walk through the village — Montefabbri can be explored in 30 to 45 minutes. Enter through the single gateway, walk the inner walls, visit the pieve and its scagliole, then step outside along the outer enclosure to see the Madonna lattante. The village, with its 70 residents, flowering balconies and deep quiet, is one of the most intimate stops along the entire itinerary.

A cena in famiglia — storytelling dinner (seasonal event) — the association 'Un paese cento storie' opens the homes of Montefabbri residents to strangers for a shared dinner: the grandparents tell the history of the village over a meal. Seasonal initiative — contact the Comune di Vallefoglia for details.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

places.name: Montefalco

visits.text: Complesso Museale di San Francesco - This Gothic church built between 1335 and 1338 by the Friars Minor was converted into a municipal museum in 1990. Its apse preserves Benozzo Gozzoli's most important fresco cycle in Umbria: in 1450-1452, this Florentine painter (student of Fra Angelico in Florence) covered the five sections of the apse with twenty episodes from the Life of Saint Francis in three ascending registers, symbolically rising from Birth to celestial glory. In the scene of the meal at the knight Celano's (episode 12), a carafe of red wine is visible on the table—likely an allusion to local Sagrantino. On the counter-façade, a 1503 Nativity by Perugino (Pietro Vannucci) completes the pictorial ensemble. The Franciscan cellars discovered during 2006 restoration yielded a pressing vat and period tools.

Piazza del Comune - This semicircular square, also called Piazza del Certame, is the hamlet's heart. It's surrounded by the Palazzo del Comune with its bell tower, the Municipal Theater, and Palazzo Bernardino de Cuppis. All of Montefalco's streets converge here from the ramparts. A covered passage connects the palace to the vineyard sector below.

Santuario di Santa Chiara della Croce - This sanctuary houses the chapel decorated with 14th-century frescoes of the Franciscan order, attributed to a student of Giotto. Adjacent, a cloistered Poor Clares monastery preserves a vegetable garden and a stone cloister. It's one of the most silent spiritual places in central Umbria.

Ramparts and panorama over the "Ringhiera dell'Umbria" - Montefalco's nickname comes from the expression Ringhiera dell'Umbria (Umbria's balcony): from its medieval ramparts at 473 meters altitude, the 360° view covers Assisi, Spoleto, Foligno, the Sibillini Mountains and, on clear days, Perugia. The town itself owes its name to Frederick II of Swabia who, visiting in the 13th century, noted the abundance of falcons in the region and baptized the hamlet Montefalco in their honor.

activities.text: Tasting of Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG - Sagrantino is a black-berry grape variety native to this single micro-region of Umbria, one of the most tannic of all Italian grapes. Its red DOCG wine (Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita) comes from long vinification and barrel aging. Wine estates surrounding the hamlet offer guided tastings with vineyard and cellar visits.

days_plan.itin_title: Umbria Itinerary: Medieval Villages & Rolling Hills

map_keywords: Santuario di Santa Chiara della Croce Montefalco

visits.text: Rocca dei Papi - Fortress built in the 13th century by Pope Innocent III at Montefiascone's highest point. A favored summer residence for several popes thanks to fresh breezes and an impregnable position. Archaeological excavations are uncovering vestiges of Etruscan occupation. Climb to the tower's summit: the panorama embraces all of Lake Bolsena, the volcanic domes, and Orvieto in the distance.

Cathedral of Santa Margherita - Its 17th-century dome, visible throughout the region, dominates Montefiascone's profile. Architect Michele Sanmicheli designed the general structure in the early 16th century. A fire ravaged it in 1670; it was restored and reopened in its current form in 1893. The neoclassical portal dates from the mid-19th century.

Church of San Flaviano - An original construction on two superimposed levels: Romanesque-Gothic arcades below, 16th-century loggia above—and the two churches face opposite directions. The walls preserve medieval frescoes. Near the entrance, look for the tombstone of German bishop Johannes Defuk (died 1113), origin of the Est! Est!! Est!!! wine legend.

activities.text: Panorama over Lake Bolsena - Europe's largest volcanic lake (114 km², 151 meters deep) spreads at Montefiascone's feet. Two small islands, Martana and Bisentina, emerge from the waters. From the Rocca dei Papi terrace, you can take in the entire caldera.

Est! Est!! Est!!! wine tasting - The DOC appellation (since 1966) takes its name from a 12th-century legend: Bishop Johannes Defuk sent a scout ahead to mark good wine inns with "Est!" (there is!) on the door. At Montefiascone, the scout wrote "Est!" three times, so pleased was he with the wine. The bishop settled there... and never left. The white wine, based on Trebbiano and Malvasia, is produced on volcanic soils around the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Tuscia Circuit: Etruscan Sites and Villages of Lazio

places.name: Montefiore Dell Aso

visits.text: Polo Museale di San Francesco — housed in a 14th–16th-century former convent, this museum holds Carlo Crivelli's triptych, painted around 1471–1475 for the Chiesa di San Francesco. Originally a five-panel polyptych, it was sold off piece by piece in the mid-19th century — the Franciscan fathers accepted over a thousand scudi, ostensibly to fund convent repairs. The central Pietà now hangs in the National Gallery in London. The six remaining panels include a figure of the Maddalena widely regarded as one of the most beautiful Crivelli ever painted.

Chiesa di San Francesco — built between 1247 and 1303 through alms collected by the friars. It was for this church's altar that Crivelli created his polyptych. Adjacent to the museum, the church retains several 16th-century chapel works.

Collegiata di Santa Lucia — the main church of the village, dominating the historic centre. Its interior decoration was enriched during the 1900 Holy Year by artists of the Fermana school: a coffered stucco ceiling, frescoes by Luigi Fontana depicting the life of Saint Lucy, and a 17th-century walnut choir.

Belvedere De Carolis — a panoramic viewpoint over the Valdaso valley, named in honour of Adolfo De Carolis (1874–1928), the Symbolist painter born in Montefiore and D'Annunzio's celebrated illustrator. The Valdaso still holds the intact hillside and farmhouse landscapes that Renaissance painters once used as backdrops in their works.

activities.text: Wine tasting from the Valdaso: Falerio DOC and Rosso Piceno, in a territory where vineyards descend in terraces to the valley floor.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

map_keywords: Polo Museale di San Francesco Montefiore dell'Aso
Chiesa di San Francesco Montefiore dell'Aso
Collegiata di Santa Lucia Montefiore dell'Aso

places.name: Montefiorino

visits.text: From atop the Rocca di Montefiorino, the view sweeps across the Dolo and Dragone valleys, once Montecuccoli territory. The museum inside chronicles the first partisan Republic in Italy, born on June 18, 1944, when partisans seized this fortress from the Republican National Guard. The exhibition, renovated in 2015, is modern and accessible.

On June 18, 1944, partisans from the Brigata Modena entered the Rocca. For forty days, a free zone spanning several municipalities governed itself with an elected mayor. On August 1, the Germans razed Montefiorino. A howitzer used by the partisans is displayed in the central hall. Free admission.

activities.text: Take time to read the names on the plaque at the Rocca entrance. Montefiorino was awarded the Gold Medal of the Resistance. The surrounding trails are part of the Gothic Line route. Easy hike from the Rocca toward the ridges.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Apennines: From Montefiorino to Rocchetta Mattei

map_keywords: Rocca di Montefiorino Resistance museum Modena

visits.text: Continue your wellness journey in Montegrotto Terme, another thermal town offering modern spa facilities rooted in ancient curative traditions. The therapeutic properties of the local thermal springs have attracted visitors seeking health and relaxation for millennia.

Visit the Butterfly House and Fairy Forest, a delightful attraction combining a large butterfly conservatory with a whimsical forest inhabited by fantastical creatures. Hundreds of colorful tropical butterflies flutter freely around visitors in the warm, humid environment.

activities.text: Explore the archaeological remains of Roman thermal baths discovered in the area, testament to the ancient appreciation of these healing waters. The surrounding Euganean Hills provide a scenic backdrop for spa relaxation.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: Piazza del Comune — Palazzetto del Podestà and Torre Civica — the 14th-century Palazzetto with its five-arch loggia and pointed Gothic windows houses the Pinacoteca Civica 'Corrado Pellini' on the upper floor. Its centrepiece is the Madonna Immacolata by Flemish painter Ernest Van Schaych (1631). The Torre Civica bears the oldest coat of arms in the village and a clock, crowned with swallowtail Ghibelline battlements.

Teatro Storico Nicola Degli Angeli — inside the Palazzo Comunale, rebuilt during the Napoleonic period (1807–1814) by architect Ireneo Aleandri. Two tiers of boxes, ceiling frescoes by Domenico Ferri (1887). Aleandri also designed the theatre in Senigallia and the Fontana del Pasquino in Rome.

Chiesa di San Francesco (13th century) — founded in 1251 and later remodelled in the baroque style. The 18th-century wooden choir, four statues of the Theological Virtues (1752) and the 1753 organ form a harmonious ensemble. Above the high altar, a Madonna del Latte whose attribution remains debated among local scholars.

Abbazia di San Firmano — 3 km away, founded around 980 by the Grimaldi family and rebuilt in the 13th century in Romanesque style. The crypt holds the relics of San Firmano, the village's patron saint. On the apse vault, a fresco by Giacomo di Nicola da Recanati (1456) depicts the Madonna in Trono tra San Firmano e San Sebastiano. The abbey overlooks an agricultural landscape that has remained almost entirely unchanged.

activities.text: Urban trekking along the 15th-century town walls (roughly 1 km), with towers of rectangular and pentagonal base — the pentagonal ones marking the period of Malatesta rule. Near Porta del Trebbio, the visible join between two sections of wall built at different periods.
Taste the carciofo di Montelupone — the local artichoke celebrated each spring — and the vincisgrassi, layered pasta with mixed meat ragù and offal, the defining dish of the Macerata tradition.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

places.name: Monteprandone

visits.text: Piazza dell'Aquila — the village's main square, dominated by the Palazzo Comunale and the 16th-century Palazzo Campanelli, recognisable by the sundial painted on its façade.

Santuario di San Giacomo della Marca — a Franciscan convent founded in 1449 by San Giacomo himself, following special authorisation from Pope Nicholas V. Below the chapel altar rests the saint's body, repatriated from Naples in 2001. The 19th-century cloister is decorated with a tempera fresco cycle by Emidio Tegli (1848) depicting key moments of his life in vivid popular scenes.

Museo Civico dei Codici di San Giacomo — preserves 61 manuscripts from the saint's personal library, a collection that once held over 180 codices in this small convent, including Latin and Greek classics and an excerpt from the Qur'an. A remarkable library for a 15th-century Franciscan friar.

Collegiata di San Niccolò — the village's main church, rebuilt in the 19th century on a foundation dating to the year 1000. The neoclassical interior is the work of Pietro Maggi — the same architect behind Grottammare's Teatro dell'Arancio.

activities.text: Walk along the 15th-century town walls with a triple panorama stretching across the Adriatic, the Sibillini Mountains and the Gran Sasso.
Sample the olives all'ascolana — the Piceno region's signature dish: large olives stuffed with meat, breaded and fried. Monteprandone is one of their historic heartlands.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

map_keywords: Santuario di San Giacomo della Marca Monteprandone

visits.text: Piazza Grande: At the hilltop (605 m), this Renaissance square is surrounded by the 15th-century Palazzo Comunale (a miniature Sienese version of Florence's Palazzo Vecchio, with panoramic tower), the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta begun in 1592 by Ippolito Scalza, Palazzo Contucci by Antonio da Sangallo, and Palazzo Tarugi. At the center, the Pozzo dei Grifi e dei Leoni, a Renaissance well designed by Sangallo.

Historic cellars of Vino Nobile: Beneath the Renaissance palaces of the center, a network of tunnels carved into tuff and brick vaults houses the oak barrels in which Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG rests. The Contucci family has produced wine here since the 11th century; the Cantina De' Ricci extends over several medieval levels. Vino Nobile, based on Prugnolo (local Sangiovese), was already being exported to the Medici court in the 15th century.

Tempio di San Biagio: Five hundred meters below the ramparts, this Renaissance church begun in 1518 by Antonio da Sangallo the Elder is one of the finest examples of central-plan Renaissance architecture in Italy—inspired by Bramante's Tempietto. The travertine façade dominates the Valdichiana vineyards.

Strade bianche and Val d'Orcia: Montepulciano is the natural starting point for exploring the white roads from Val di Chiana to Val d'Orcia. The road toward Monticchiello (4 km) runs along vineyards and cypresses with views of classic Tuscan panoramas.

activities.text: Vino Nobile DOCG tasting: The cellars in the center offer guided tours of the tunnels carved into tuff with comparative tastings of Rosso di Montepulciano DOC, Vino Nobile DOCG, and Vino Nobile Riserva.

Bravio delle Botti: Every last Sunday in August, Montepulciano's eight districts compete by pushing 80 kg barrels along Via Gracciano nel Corso to Piazza Grande—a tradition documented since the 14th century.

places.name: Monterchi

visits.text: Museum of the Madonna del Parto: a 260 × 203 cm fresco painted around 1460 by Piero della Francesca for the church of Santa Maria di Momentana, located away from the village — a site linked to traditions of Marian devotion and fertility rites. It was painted for the hometown of the painter's mother, according to Vasari during a return to Sansepolcro upon her death. Analysis of the fresco suggests it was executed in roughly seven days. It depicts the pregnant Virgin standing, opening her mantle with one hand, flanked by two symmetrical angels produced from the same cartoon reversed. The church was demolished in 1785 to make way for a cemetery; the fresco, forgotten in the masonry of a funerary chapel, was only rediscovered in 1889. After restoration, it was transferred in 1993 to the former village primary school, now converted into a museum. A legal dispute between the municipality of Monterchi, the Catholic Church and the Ministry of Culture over its ownership remains unresolved.

Historic center of Monterchi: perched on an isolated hill on the border with Umbria, the village retains a typically medieval character despite several earthquakes in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its name derives from Mons Herculis — Hill of Hercules — recalling presumed ancient cults on this promontory. The Museum of the Balance, housed in the center, holds one of Europe's most important collections of antique scales and weights, with an interactive educational trail.

activities.text: Exploring the Valtiberina countryside: the surroundings of Monterchi are dotted with Romanesque parish churches, castles and rural hamlets typical of the upper Tiber valley landscape. The road between Arezzo and Monterchi passes through several well-preserved farming villages, with panoramas over the wooded hills that herald the Tuscan Valtiberina.

places.name: Monteriggioni

visits.text: Medieval walls of Monteriggioni: Built between 1214 and 1219 by the Republic of Siena to defend against Florence, the circular wall measures 570 meters in perimeter and rises 2 meters thick. Its 14 square towers, regularly spaced, have remained almost intact since the 13th century. Dante Alighieri immortalized them in the Inferno of the Divine Comedy, comparing these giant towers to the guardians of the abyss—'Monteriggioni di torri si corona.' From the ramparts open to the public, the view sweeps across Chianti and Val d'Elsa.

Monteriggioni in Arme Museum: Housed in the village's former buildings, this museum presents life-size reproductions of medieval and Renaissance armor and weaponry, siege machines, and knight's equipment. According to local legend, a Ubisoft developer stayed here and drew inspiration from the place to make it Ezio Auditore's birthplace in Assassin's Creed II—a story not officially confirmed by Ubisoft, but one that has introduced Monteriggioni to new generations.

Church of Santa Maria Assunta and Piazza Roma: At the heart of the walls, the 13th-century church blends Romanesque and Gothic on a simple stone façade. Piazza Roma, with its central well and a handful of palaces, sums up the scale of the village—three parallel streets connect the two gates, Porta Franca on the Siena side and Porta di Ponente on the Florence side.

activities.text: Walk on the ramparts: The accessible section runs along the north, east, and west faces for a partial loop of about 500 meters with views of Chianti Colli Senesi vineyards. In July, the medieval festival Monteriggioni di Torri si Corona transforms the village into a life-size recreation of 13th-century crafts.

Local products tasting: The village produces Chianti Colli Senesi Monteriggioni DOC and extra virgin olive oil from the olive trees surrounding the ramparts—shops on Via Matteotti offer these specialties.

places.name: Montopoli In Val D Arno

visits.text: Montopoli was nicknamed the "castello insigne" by Boccaccio, impressed by its powerful fortifications. Disputed between Pisa, Florence, and Lucca since the 11th century—the Arno once flowed beneath its eastern walls—the town resisted numerous sieges. The Torre di San Matteo (15th century), built by the Florentine Republic, is today the best viewpoint over the Pisan Valdarno, reaching the Apuan Alps on clear days. The Arco di Castruccio Castracani marks the spot where the famous condottiere was wounded during the 1328 siege.

The Battle of San Romano (1432), fought near Montopoli between Florence and the Milanese troops of Niccolò Piccinino, was immortalized by Paolo Uccello in three paintings now preserved at the Uffizi in Florence, the Louvre, and London's National Gallery. The town voluntarily submitted to Florence in 1349, after the decisive battle. In 1412, podestà Jacopo degli Albizzi divided Montopoli into two peoples—Santo Stefano and San Giovanni—whose rivalry is reenacted every September during the Disfida con l'Arco.

The Museo Civico in Palazzo Guicciardini displays archaeological finds dating back to the 3rd century BC (Etruscan period, Volterran style), medieval collections, and a section devoted to local ceramics—Montopoli had a tradition of kilns and potters from the 16th century, perpetuated in the 19th century by Dante Milani.

activities.text: Disfida con l'Arco: every second Sunday in September, Montopoli's two historic quarters (Santo Stefano and San Giovanni) compete in an archery tournament in medieval costume, preceded by a parade. The event commemorates the 1412 decision that divided the town.

Stroll through the centro storico: 17th-century noble palaces, Villa Capponi Piaggio (16th century, acquired in 1953 by Enrico Piaggio), and the Tenuta di Verramista with its oaks, chestnuts, and white firs exceedingly rare in the Pisan plain.

places.name: Morano Calabro

visits.text: Begin your Calabrian journey at Morano Calabro, perched at 694 meters altitude in the heart of Pollino National Park. Nicknamed the "Presepe del Pollino" (the Nativity scene of Pollino), the village forms a maze of red-roofed houses clinging to a conical hill. Climb up to the ruins of the Norman-Swabian castle (12th-13th century), expanded in the 16th century by the Sanseverino princes: the view from the summit encompasses the entire Coscile valley and the peaks of Pollino. Then descend toward the church of San Bernardino da Siena, founded in 1452, whose golden stone ogival portal and ship's hull ceiling - unique in Calabria - are worth the visit alone. Don't miss the Polyptych by Bartolomeo Vivarini (1477), painted in Murano, which gleams with gold on the altar. Allow about 2 hours to explore the historic center at a leisurely pace.

Continue to the collegiate church of Santa Maria Maddalena, recognizable from afar by its dome covered with green and ochre majolica tiles. Inside, you'll find a Madonna degli Angeli by Antonello Gagini dated 1505 and, in the San Silvestro chapel, the Sanseverino Polyptych. On your way down, pass by the church of Saints Peter and Paul, the village's oldest, founded around the year 1000 - it preserves four marble statues by Pietro Bernini, father of the famous Gian Lorenzo.

A 20-minute drive away, the village of Civita transports you to another world. Founded in the late 15th century by Albanian refugees fleeing the Ottoman occupation, it's one of the oldest Arbëreshë communities in Italy. Wander through the lanes organized in gjitonia - these semicircular neighborhoods around a mother house and a small square. Look closely at the façades: the "Case Kodra" (named after artist Ibrahim Kodra) have human faces formed by windows and chimneys. These sculpted comignoli are genuine works of art, with each family decorating them according to their social status.

From Civita's center, descend to the Ponte del Diavolo spanning the Raganello gorges. According to legend, the devil built this bridge in one night in exchange for the soul of the first person to cross - but the clever owner sent a sheep across instead, and the furious devil tried to destroy his own work without succeeding. Beyond the legend, the panorama from the bridge over the vertiginous canyon walls is breathtaking. Arrive early morning or late afternoon to avoid summer crowds.

activities.text: If you enjoy thrills, operators offer canyoning excursions in the Raganello gorges - expect 3 to 4 hours of walking in water between the canyon walls. Check weather conditions before committing: after heavy rains, the gorges may be closed. Alternatively, a hiking trail accessible from Civita follows the Raganello ridge with plunging views over the canyon.

End the day in Civita by visiting the Arbëreshë Ethnic Museum, which displays traditional embroidered costumes, gold jewelry of oriental craftsmanship, and everyday objects. Don't leave the village without tasting local specialties: handmade pasta and soppressata accompanied by Pollino rosé wine.

days_plan.itin_title: Calabria: From Cosenza to Reggio, Between Mountains and Ionian Sea

map_keywords: Collegiata Santa Maria Maddalena Morano Calabro

visits.text: Torre Eptagonale — a 25-metre 12th-century tower with seven sides, unique in Europe. Today it houses the TOMAV (Torre Moresco Arti Visive), a contemporary art centre. From the top, on a clear day, the eye travels from Monte Conero to the Gran Sasso — and all the way to the Croatian coast. The Ghibelline battlements visible today were rebuilt in the early 20th century after the original arabesque spire collapsed.

Piazza Castello — the village's only square, triangular in shape, with a 16th-century portico that is all that remains of the left nave of the demolished Chiesa di Santa Maria in Castro. Under the groin vaults, a fresco by Vincenzo Pagani depicts the Madonna con Bambino.

Torre dell'Orologio and ex-Chiesa di Santa Sofia — a 14th-century tower marking the original village gateway, flanked by a 16th-century portico. Passing under the tower leads to the former Chiesa Santa Sofia, now a performance space nicknamed 'lu teatrì'. The church retains a fresco from the school of Carlo Crivelli (15th century).

Sala Consiliare of the Palazzo Comunale — preserves an altarpiece by Vincenzo Pagani (1540) depicting the Madonna in Gloria con i Santi Lucia, Lorenzo, Rocco e Nicolò. Pagani, born in Monterubbiano around 1490, is the author of both frescoes visible in the village.

activities.text: Taste the ciauscolo — a soft pork salami you spread like pâté, seasoned with pepper and garlic — a signature product of the Valdaso, along with the organic peaches from the Val d'Aso cultivated at the foot of the village.
Walk the rampart path around the village (elliptical in shape, roughly 600 inhabitants) with views down over the Valdaso, its orchards and olive groves.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

places.name: Morro D Alba

visits.text: Camminamento di Ronda 'La Scarpa' — Morro d'Alba claims a record unique in Italy: the only fortified village whose entire inner walkway is covered and lined with arcades along its full length. The irregular pentagonal wall circuit with six bastions dates to the 13th–15th centuries. The covered inner walkway, known as 'La Scarpa' (from the scarped inclination of the walls), runs 300 metres, punctuated by six watchtowers and a long row of windows opening onto the countryside — the Sibillini on one side, the Conero and the sea on the other. Two panoramic towers bear the names Torre Teodorico (east, hillside views, now a cultural venue) and Torre Federico I (west, sunset views).

Sotterranei di Morro d'Alba — beneath the village houses, inhabitants carved out from the 14th to 15th centuries a labyrinth of caves and galleries on multiple levels — an entire underground city. These spaces served to preserve food, shelter livestock in winter and take refuge during attacks. In the galleries, the oldest known bombarda (primitive firearm) in Italy was discovered — the original is now at the Museo Storico Nazionale di Artiglieria in Turin. Part of the galleries houses the Museo Utensilia, which documents the life of Marchigian sharecroppers (mezzadri) through seven reconstructed environments: a press, weaving workshop, cellar, barn and farmyard, with scythes, baskets, barrels, ploughs and agricultural tools.

Piazza Tarsetti and Torre Civica — the village's main square. The fountain bears a graffito by Maestro Enzo Cucchi, born in Morro d'Alba in 1949, one of the leading figures of Italian Transavanguardia. The clock tower preserves a 1504 bas-relief of a rampant lion — the symbol of Jesi, to which Morro d'Alba still belonged at that time. Opposite, the Chiesa di San Gaudenzio (1763), recently restored, holds several paintings including Claudio Ridolfi's altarpiece (1630) Incoronazione della Vergine e Santi, and a 17th-century canvas depicting San Michele Arcangelo, the village's patron saint.

activities.text: Lacrima di Morro d'Alba DOC tasting — Lacrima is a red wine with violet hues, fruity and lightly tannic, from an ancient grape variety whose skin is so fragile it tears at full ripeness, allowing the juice to seep out — hence the name. More than ten wineries offer visits and tastings: the Antica Cantina Sant'Amico (founded 1850, one of the oldest in Le Marche) is an ideal starting point. Morro d'Alba also falls within the production zone of Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC.

places.name: Mottola

visits.text: At the entrance to Mottola, roadside, the church of San Gregorio descends into a large cave complex: a Greek-cross plan, three naves, three semicircular apses, four large pillars on circular bases with square capitals. In the apse calotte, a half-length blessing Pantocrator, solemn face, forked beard, compared to the one at Monreale.

activities.text: Book a guide before coming to Mottola: the three cave churches, Sant'Angelo, San Nicola, and San Gregorio, are locked and impossible to find without accompaniment, hidden in the valleys. Local cooperatives and the town's visitor information office organize the visits. The historical file on Casalrotto is available on the municipal website, worth reading beforehand.

activities.text: Cross the ravine and climb to the Murgia Timone belvedere: it's from the opposite bank, in the Parco della Murgia Materana, that Matera is properly seen, the whole city in one frame. The park covers about 8,000 hectares, UNESCO-listed, with its prehistoric caves and cave churches. Sunset is non-negotiable. Plan for a car or a shuttle; it's not walkable.
