map_keywords: Necropoli del Crocifisso del Tufo Orvieto

visits.text: Ostana counts barely fifty permanent residents today - down from 1,200 in 1921 - yet this Occitan village perched at 1,250 meters beneath Monviso has become an international model of alpine renaissance. In 1985, mayor Giacomo Lombardo and architect Renato Maurino launched a restoration project following strict rules respecting original materials and volumes. This continuous effort transformed Ostana into an "open-air alpine architecture laboratory" in Legambiente's words, which awarded it the Bandiera Verde in 2005. In 2008, Ostana joined the Borghi più belli d'Italia network.

Wander through the hamlets scattered across the slope: La Villo (the administrative center with the town hall flying the Occitan flag), Champanho surrounded by maples and ash trees, Miribrart completely restored with European funds and home to a film school founded in 2012. In the small chapel of San Bernardo, a recently uncovered medieval fresco represents a rare testament to high-mountain sacred art. The ethnographic museum I Rënèis, housed in the town hall, presents traditional ways of life in the Po valley.

activities.text: Hike the Monviso Horizon route, a 50-kilometer loop connecting all the upper Po valley villages, also suitable for mountain biking. In winter, ski touring and snowshoeing at the foot of Monviso. Ostana is also a recognized climbing destination with summer routes and winter ice cascades.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont's Most Beautiful Villages in 2 Weeks

places.name: Ostuni

visits.text: A Gothic cathedral in Puglia is almost an anomaly: the Cattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta in Ostuni was built between 1435 and 1495, when the region was building Romanesque or Baroque. Its central rose window has 24 petals. National monument since 1902. It occupies the highest point of the old town: the climb earns it, so go early.

The Arco Scoppa spans the alleyway in front of Ostuni's cathedral, connecting the Palazzo Vescovile to the old seminary. Originally built in wood, it was reconstructed in stone in 1750 on the orders of Cardinal Scoppa. Locals simply call it la Loggia. It's the town's mandatory photograph: come before 9am if you want it without a crowd underneath.

The locals call it la Terra: Ostuni's historic center was once whitewashed throughout, which is where the white city nickname comes from. Alleyways, hidden courtyards, medieval arches, staircases, all climbing the highest of three hills. Nothing to check off, everything to wander through. Flat shoes essential; the slopes are serious.

A pregnant woman who died more than 25,000 years ago: Delia is preserved at the Museo di Civiltà Preclassiche della Murgia Meridionale, housed in Ostuni's former Carmelite monastery. She was found in a local cave, crouching, her foetus still in position. She's the single exhibit that justifies the ticket on its own. The museum is small; allow an hour.

Opened in 2017, the Museo Diocesano di Ostuni occupies the Palazzo dell'Episcopio, right next to the cathedral: the Collezione Archeologica Capitolare alongside works from surrounding churches and monasteries. It also serves as a temporary exhibition space. Useful when the midday heat drives you off the alleyways at 2pm.

Piazza della Libertà is Ostuni's main square at the foot of the old town: the Chiesa di San Francesco, the former Franciscan convent converted into the Palazzo di Città, and the guglia di Sant'Oronzo, the column dedicated to the town's patron. Everyone ends up here in the evening. Terraces fill from 7pm in summer.

Walk the Aragonese walls of Ostuni for the view: the plain of olive trees runs all the way to the sea, eight kilometers away. Two ancient gates still stand, Porta Nova and Porta San Demetrio. This is the best place to understand why the town was built here and nowhere else. Late afternoon, when the light rakes across the olive groves.

activities.text: Stop before entering Ostuni: it's from the outside, from the surrounding countryside, that the white city works best, perched on its three hills among the olive trees. The viewpoints just outside the historic center give the same effect. Late afternoon photo, when the white turns golden. In the morning, the contre-jour kills the shot.

Taste Ostuni's olive oil where it's made: ancient olive trees cover the plain between the town and the coast, and local mills welcome visitors for tastings. Some trees have trunks that look like sculpture. The harvest runs in autumn: that's the best time to visit a working frantoio.

days_plan.itin_title: Puglia Wine Route - 7 Days
The Bari Loop: trulli, ravines and Matera in 13 days

map_keywords: Museum of Pre-Classical Civilisations of the Southern Murge Ostuni

visits.text: You walk on it, literally: the entire floor of Otranto cathedral is covered by a mosaic made between 1163 and 1165 by the monk Pantaleone, running from the entrance to the apse. The Tree of Life, carried by two elephants, shares the ground with King Arthur and Alexander the Great. Come at opening time, before the groups.

The Chapel of the Martyrs, at the end of the right-hand nave, was enlarged in 1482 to hold the remains of the townspeople killed after the Ottomans took Otranto in 1480. The bones are visible behind glass, alongside the stone said to have been used for the executions. Pope Francis canonised them in 2013.

A real fortress, not just a backdrop for fiction: the Castello Aragonese closes off the old town of Otranto on the harbour side, with its bastions and moat, rebuilt at the end of the 15th century after the siege. It now hosts temporary exhibitions. Horace Walpole took loose inspiration from it for The Castle of Otranto, published in 1764.

The cathedral crypt gets rushed through, which is a shame: dozens of salvaged marble columns, often mismatched, hold up a forest of small vaults. It is the coolest place in town at midday. Go down after the mosaic; the way in is from the nave.

activities.text: People here call Otranto the city of the Martyrs: walk the walls at sunset, then drop back towards the harbour through the white lanes. The historic centre takes twenty minutes to cross. Around 14 August the feast of the Holy Martyrs takes over the town, and you can expect to give up on parking.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce
Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: Pacentro - a village of 1,200 inhabitants built entirely from white Majella stone at 720 meters altitude. The Castello Caldoresco, with its three 14th-century cylindrical towers, dominates the village. Madonna Ciccone, whose ancestors are from Pacentro, visited the village in 1995 to trace her roots.

activities.text: Climb to the castle towers for panoramic views of Valle Peligna and the Majella foothills.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

visits.text: Discover Padova, one of Italy's oldest cities with legendary origins traced to the Trojan warrior Antenor. The UNESCO-listed Scrovegni Chapel houses Giotto's revolutionary 14th-century frescoes that changed Western art forever with their emotional realism and innovative use of color. Book your timed entry in advance for this artistic treasure.

Explore the Palazzo della Ragione, a vast medieval law court featuring one of the largest unsupported roofed halls in Europe, its walls covered with allegorical frescoes and celestial symbols. Below the arcades, discover Sotto il Salone - said to be Europe's oldest indoor food market where artisan shops have operated for generations.

Visit the Basilica of Saint Anthony (Il Santo), a major pilgrimage destination housing the saint's marble tomb and chapels frescoed by Giotto and other masters. The basilica combines Romanesque, Gothic, and Byzantine architectural elements into a unique synthesis of styles.

Stroll through Prato della Valle, one of Europe's largest squares, featuring the central Isola Memmia ringed by a canal and 78 statues of Padova's most illustrious figures. This grand public space transforms from market venue to evening promenade as locals gather.

activities.text: Experience the Padova Urbs Picta UNESCO trail connecting eight sites of 14th-century frescoes, including the glowing dome of paradise by Giusto de' Menabuoi in the Baptistery. The 48 or 72-hour card provides access to all sites.

Visit Palazzo del Bo, seat of the University of Padua founded in 1222, to see the Teatro Anatomico - the world's first permanent anatomy theatre - and Galileo's actual lecturing podium in guided tours of this historic academic institution.

Explore the Orto Botanico, the world's oldest university botanical garden still in its original location, a UNESCO World Heritage Site founded in 1545 with over 6,000 species including a palm tree planted in 1585 that inspired Goethe.

Stop at Caffè Pedrocchi, the legendary café open continuously from 1831 to 1916, where poets, professors, and revolutionaries gathered. The Sala Verde famously welcomed even those who couldn't afford coffee - giving rise to the Italian expression 'essere al verde' (to be broke).

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: The Certosa di San Lorenzo in Padula is one of Europe's largest monasteries: 51,500 m², 320 rooms, and a monumental cloister of 12,000 m² considered the world's largest. Founded in 1306 by Tommaso Sanseverino, transformed into a baroque masterpiece in the 17th-18th centuries. Beyond the numbers, the experience is unique: the walk through vaulted corridors stretching 200 m, the library with majolica-tiled floors, the legendary kitchen (thousand-egg omelet for Charles V), and the final helical staircase, a baroque feat. UNESCO since 1998. Plan 2.5 hours minimum.

The town of Padula, on the hill facing the charterhouse, deserves an hour's stroll. Medieval historic center, 17th-18th century noble palaces, and the Joe Petrosino Museum: museum dedicated to the Italian-American policeman born here in 1860, first cop in the anti-Mafia fight, assassinated in Palermo in 1909. Small, but distinctive.

activities.text: Lunch in Padula at Hosteria del Borgo. Vallo di Diano cuisine: handmade cavatelli, wood-grilled meat, mountain cheeses. Fair prices, family welcome.

days_plan.itin_title: Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: Three Doric temples in the open plain, standing for twenty-five centuries: Paestum is one of Europe's most striking archaeological sites. Founded around 600 BCE by Greek colonists from Sybaris, the city was then called Poseidonia. Abandoned in the Middle Ages due to malaria, it was forgotten for a thousand years and rediscovered in 1750 by builders of the royal road, who literally crossed through the forum. The Temple of Neptune (450 BCE) is the best preserved of the three and the most monumental—six columns on the façade, fourteen on the sides. Plan a full day for the temples, museum, and necropolis with its painted tombs.

The archaeological museum of Paestum, opposite the site, houses the famous Tomb of the Diver (480 BCE): five painted slabs depicting a funeral banquet, and on the lid, a young man diving into water. It's the only figurative Greek wall painting from the archaic-classical period preserved in its entirety—all other known examples on perishable supports (wood, stucco) have vanished. Endless interpretations have been offered: passage to the afterlife, philosophical metaphor, simple decoration. Priceless treasure, yet the room is rarely crowded.

The Temple of Hera (550 BCE), the oldest of the three, was long mistaken for a Roman basilica—hence its nickname in old guidebooks. Nine columns on the façade, eighteen on the sides. More archaic, stockier than Neptune's. Next door, the smaller Temple of Ceres (500 BCE) actually served Athena: an identification mix-up by early excavators.

activities.text: Visit a buffalo farm. Cilento is home to authentic mozzarella di bufala campana DOP. Several dairies offer tours: Tenuta Vannulo (1 km from the archaeological site) is the most famous, but reservations required three weeks ahead. Otherwise, Caseificio Barlotti, more accessible. Tour of the buffalo, production, tasting. An hour and a half.
Sunset over the temples. The site is open until 7:30 PM in summer (last entry 6:45 PM). Golden light on the columns, without the daytime crowds. Classic photo of the Temple of Neptune facing west.

days_plan.itin_title: From Naples to Calabria: The Tyrrhenian Coast
Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: Toiano is a ghost village perched among the Pisan hills and tuff calanchi reminiscent of Volterra's Balze. Tuff spurs up to 40-50 meters high line the access track, 3 meters wide. The village, inhabited until the 1960s (521 souls in the 19th century), was gradually abandoned when Valdera factories—including Piaggio—drew labor to the plain. Its history was marked by the unsolved 1947 murder of "beautiful Elvira" (Elvira Orlandini, 22), a case that mobilized all of postwar Italy and remains a cold case. The borgo is listed by FAI (Fondo per l'Ambiente Italiano) among the "places of the heart" to be preserved.

The Pieve di San Martino of Palaia, outside the walls, was built between 1270 and 1300 to Andrea Pisano's designs—it is listed in the catalog of Italian national monuments. A Romanesque building with three naves of five bays, ending in a raised presbyterium with three chapels. On the floor, funerary slabs of the village's illustrious figures; on the walls, those of Palaia's parish priests.

Villa Saletta, another ghost village near Palaia, is an example of a completely self-sufficient 16th-17th century villa-fattoria belonging to the Florentine Ricciardi family. The main square, manor villa, and clock tower have remained virtually intact. Films have been shot here, including the Taviani brothers' La Notte di San Lorenzo and Virzì's Me and Napoleon. In summer, a popular theater festival brings it to life.

activities.text: Visit the Museum of Rural Civilization in Montefoscoli, installed in a house dating from the year 1000: cellars, oil mill, agricultural tools, reconstruction of the Valdera peasant world. Next door, the "Casa Museo Vaccà Berlinghieri" celebrates Andrea Vaccà, famous surgeon at the University of Pisa and personal physician to Paolina Bonaparte. Best visited early morning before heading to Toiano and Villa Saletta.

Hike on wooded trails between Palaia and its hamlets—Alica, San Gervasio, Colleoli. The Tuscan expression "Peggio Palaia" (worse than Palaia) dates, according to tradition, from the 1435 siege by Niccolò Piccinino, who took the castle by starvation after failing to force it.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

visits.text: Palena - a village of 1,500 inhabitants at 875 meters in the heart of Parco Nazionale della Majella, entirely rebuilt after its near-total destruction by German troops in 1943. The Castello Ducale, the only surviving medieval building, houses the Museo Geopaleontologico with Majella fossils.

Area Faunistica dell'Orso Marsicano - a natural enclosure of several hectares where Marsican bears unfit for wild life are housed, visible from a marked discovery trail. The Marsican bear (Ursus arctos marsicanus) is an endemic subspecies of Abruzzo, with a total population estimated at 50-60 individuals.

activities.text: Hike to the Eremo della Madonna dell'Altare - a 16th-century hermitage perched on a rocky spur at 1,100 meters, accessible by a marked 2-kilometer trail from the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

visits.text: The name of Palermo's airport - Falcone-Borsellino - sets the tone for this journey. The two judges who brought down the Mafia were blown to pieces 23 km from here in 1992; we'll come back to that tomorrow. First, drop your bags in the Vucciria or Kalsa neighborhoods, where crumbling baroque palaces still have laundry hanging from the windows and street vendors start shouting at 7 AM. Practical tip: book accommodation with courtyard views - the alleyways stay loud until 2 AM.

First shock of the trip: descend into the Capuchin Catacombs, Piazza Cappuccini 1, open 9 AM-12:30 PM and 3-5:30 PM, €5 entry. You're standing above 8,000 mummified bodies, of which 1,252 are displayed upright in the corridors, organized by sex and profession - men, women, priests, doctors, lawyers, military officers. The monk Silvestro da Gubbio inaugurated the collection in 1599 when the Capuchins noticed the dry air naturally mummified their brothers. By the 17th century, it had become the ultimate status symbol: families paid to have their dead preserved in formal dress, and returned regularly to change the outfits. Allow an hour, longer if you read the plaques.

At the far right of the catacombs, the children's chapel. This is where Rosalia Lombardo rests, two years old, dead of pneumonia on December 6, 1920. The chemist Alfredo Salafia embalmed her with a formula whose recipe was found in his notes in 2009: formalin, zinc salts, glycerin, salicylic acid, alcohol. The body is intact, eyelashes in place, blonde curls still there. They call her 'the world's most beautiful mummy'. The illusion that she opens her eyes was debunked in 2009 - an optical effect on eyelids that were never completely closed. You won't walk out the same person.

The Palazzo Steri, Piazza Marina 61, housed the Spanish Inquisition Tribunal in Sicily from 1601 to 1782. Go down to the basement prisons: the walls are covered with graffiti, prayers, drawings, blasphemies carved by the condemned in every language that circulated through Palermo - Italian, Latin, Sicilian, Arabic, Hebrew. Leonardo Sciascia wrote that it was one of the most moving places in Italy. He was right. €8 entry, allow 90 minutes. Avoid Tuesday, it's closed.

The Falcone Tree, Via Notarbartolo 23, isn't an official monument. It's a century-old ficus in front of the building where the judge lived, which spontaneously became a civic altar after the Capaci bombing on May 23, 1992 - 600 kg of TNT under the highway, five dead. Photos, letters, children's drawings permanently hang from the branches. A 15-minute walk away, Via D'Amelio, where Paolo Borsellino was blown up 57 days later, July 19 at 4:58 PM, in front of his mother's house. Toto Riina, who ordered both assassinations, celebrated with champagne. Died in prison in 2017.

Palermo Cathedral mixes everything: Norman, Arab, Gothic, Baroque, Neoclassical. Climb to the rooftops - brilliant view over the red domes - then descend to the royal tombs to see the sarcophagus of Frederick II of Hohenstaufen, in red porphyry. He was called stupor mundi, 'wonder of the world', an emperor excommunicated twice and suspected of every heresy, speaking six languages including Arabic, surrounded by Muslim astrologers. His Palermo court in the 13th century was the freest in Europe. Rooftops €7, tombs €3.

activities.text: Dinner at Trattoria Ai Cascinari, Via D'Ossuna 43-45, real working-class Palermitan cooking: pasta con le sarde and caponata. No reservations possible before 8 PM, it's been that way for forty years, nobody minds. The dining room is small, the kitchen is open, diners talk to each other across tables.

Evening walk through the Vucciria, a medieval market turned nightlife district. Arancini are sold at all hours from the friggitorie around Piazza Garraffello. Worth seeing: the Palazzo Mirto and the ruins bombed in 1943 and never rebuilt - Renato Guttuso painted his famous market scene here in 1974.

Street food lunch at Mercato di Ballarò, the oldest of Palermo's three historic markets. Try the pani ca' meusa: boiled veal spleen sandwich. Yes, really. It's delicious, very rich, and eaten at the counter with half a lemon and a glass of beer. Otherwise: panelle (chickpea fritters), sfincione (thick focaccia with anchovies), arancini. Budget €8-12 to fill up.

Evening, dinner at Trattoria del Massimo Plaja near Teatro Massimo. Classic Sicilian cuisine well executed, family atmosphere, reasonable prices. The neighboring Teatro Massimo is the third-largest opera house in Europe by size - its steps are where the final scene of The Godfather Part III was filmed in 1990.

Complete Tour of Sicily
Haunted Sicily - 8 Days from the Capuchin Crypts to Stromboli
Haunted Sicily - 8 Days from the Capuchin Crypts to Stromboli

visits.text: Guadagnolo — Lazio's highest village at 1,218 m altitude in the Monti Prenestini, reached via a winding road from Capranica Prenestina. On clear days, the panoramic belvedere sweeps across a 180° arc covering Rome, the Tyrrhenian Sea, and the Apennines. The village's permanent population barely exceeds twenty residents.

Castel San Pietro Romano — A tiny village at 763 m overlooking Palestrina from the summit of Monte Ginestro, listed among the Borghi più Belli d'Italia. Medieval houses step along the rocky ridge, incorporating vestiges of ancient Praeneste's acropolis, with polygonal walls in opus cyclopeum identical to those of the sanctuary below.

Santuario della Fortuna Primigenia — The largest religious complex in Republican Roman Italy, built in the late 2nd century BC across seven cascading terraces on Monte Ginestro's flank. The sanctuary dedicated to Fortuna Primigenia—'Jupiter's firstborn' and oracular goddess—was consulted throughout the Empire. The oracle functioned through the drawing of wooden lots (sortes), and Cicero reported that Romans considered no site more suited to divination. The structure employed Roman concrete made with pozzolana on a grand scale for the first time, its durability proven by its preservation two millennia later. In 1944, Mussolini demolished several hundred medieval houses obstructing the complex, revealing the terraces in their current state.

Museo Archeologico Nazionale Prenestino and the Nile Mosaic — The museum, installed in Palazzo Barberini built directly atop the ancient structures, preserves on its third floor the Nile Mosaic, a Hellenistic masterpiece measuring 5.85 m × 4.31 m. Created in the 1st century BC by Alexandrian craftsmen, the mosaic depicts the Nile's course from the Ethiopian sources to the delta, populated with hippos, crocodiles, pygmy hunters, and a walled city flanked by four colossal statues. Discovered in 1507 still in place within the sanctuary, it was cut into 27 pieces in 1625 by Palestrina's bishop, transported to Rome, then returned to Palestrina by Cardinal Francesco Barberini in 1640 after several restorations. It has been displayed here since 1956.

activities.text: Walking through Palestrina's historic center — The medieval town developed directly atop the sanctuary's ramps and terraces, such that some cellars and basements of houses still reveal Roman masonry in opus incertum. The Cattedrale di Sant'Agapito, dedicated to the 2nd-century local martyr, preserves a paleo-Christian crypt.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Villages Around Rome and the Castelli Romani

visits.text: Capo Palinuro, a limestone promontory jutting into the Tyrrhenian Sea, takes its name from Palinurus, Aeneas's pilot in Virgil's Aeneid: he supposedly drowned here, thrown into the sea by the god Sleep. Legend aside, the cape is a geological marvel: sea caves, turquoise waters, 180 m cliffs. The boat tour from the port is the signature activity—Blue Grotto (lesser-known equivalent to Capri's), Blood Grotto (reddened by oxides), Bones Grotto (prehistoric remains). Two-hour trips in traditional boats.

Buon Dormire beach ('good sleep'), at the foot of the Natural Arch, is emblematic of the cape. White sand, limestone arch sculpted by the sea, water of saturated turquoise. Accessible only by boat or on foot from Marinella beach via a one-hour trail. No beach bar, no drinks stand, just the beach. That's its charm.

Palinuro center itself is modest—a few streets, the harbor, some hotels—but it's the ideal base for exploring the cape. The departure harbor for boat tours, several kayak rentals, and decent restaurants along the beach.

Baia degli Infreschi, 15 km south of Palinuro toward Marina di Camerota, regularly ranks among Italy's most beautiful beaches. Semicircular cove, emerald water, wooded cliffs, accessible only by boat or a 2-hour trail. No buildings, no roads. Cold water springs gushing directly into the sea (hence the name Infreschi, 'the fresh ones'). Marine protected area.

Cala Bianca, right next to Infreschi, is southern Cilento's second iconic beach: white pebbles, transparent sea, same postcard scenery. Accessible by boat, or on foot from Lentiscelle via the Infreschi trail (1h30 one way, moderate elevation). No services on site, bring everything.

Marina di Camerota, heading back north, is the ideal anchorage for trips to Infreschi. Quieter than Palinuro crowd-wise, with more authentic local life. The center retains several 16th-century palaces and a Castello Marchesale under restoration.

activities.text: Boat tour of Capo Palinuro with swimming stop in the Blue Grotto. Several operators leave from the port, duration 2-3 hours, price €20-30. Small groups, local captain, commentary in Italian and English.
Sunset aperitif on the terrace of Lido Ficocella, 2 km north of the center. Private beach with bar, cape views, relaxed atmosphere. Spritz and tagliere of local products.
Boat excursion Infreschi + Cala Bianca + Marina di Camerota. Several options, half-day or full day with lunch on board (fish grilled on deck). Excellent time-to-views ratio.

days_plan.itin_title: From Naples to Calabria: The Tyrrhenian Coast
Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy
Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: Piazza Grande di Palmanova - At the precise geometric center of this star-shaped fortress city founded on October 7, 1593 by the Venetian Republic, the hexagonal plaza forms the heart of an architectural masterpiece. The foundation date commemorates the 1571 Battle of Lepanto victory over the Ottomans. The original name "Palma" symbolized that triumph; Napoleon later added "nova" two centuries on. Stand on the central platform to grasp the perfect symmetry of six radiating streets leading toward nine defensive bastions.

Duomo del Santissimo Redentore - Dominating Piazza Grande, this church traditionally attributed to Vincenzo Scamozzi, Palladio's pupil, features a deliberately squat bell tower: it couldn't be visible from outside the ramparts, denying potential attackers a targeting reference point. This single detail encapsulates Palmanova's dual nature as both Renaissance utopian city and military machine.

Fortezza di Palmanova - Three concentric rings form three nested nine-pointed stars. The first two were built by Venice between 1593 and 1690, the third added by Napoleon between 1806 and 1813 under General Chasseloup's direction. Each curtain wall measured roughly 400 meters—exactly matching the cannon range of the era, so a single bastion could defend the entire adjacent front. UNESCO-listed since 2017, Palmanova remains the only perfectly preserved star-shaped Renaissance fortress city in existence.

Museo della Grande Guerra e della Fortezza - Housed in the dungeons of Porta Cividale, this museum chronicles the fortress's military history from its 1593 founding through the 20th century. Weapons, uniforms, and documents illustrate the Venetian, Napoleonic, and Austro-Hungarian periods.

Bastioni e Gallerie di Contromina - Descend into the underground galleries of Baluardo Donato: these secret tunnels connected the bastions to the 4-kilometer outer moat, allowing soldiers to move under cover. The pointed bastion design deflected cannonballs, reducing impact force. Above, the rampart walkway offers a 4.3-kilometer circuit on foot or by bike around the entire fortress.

Porta Aquileia, Porta Udine, and Porta Cividale - The three monumental gates facing Aquileia, Udine, and Cividale were the fortress's only entry points. Each was protected by counter-gates and drawbridges. Push through to appreciate the wall thickness and the perspectives opening toward Piazza Grande.

activities.text: Complete rampart circuit on foot or by bike - The Anello delle Fortificazioni (4.3 km) traces all three Venetian and Napoleonic defensive rings, past bastions, ravelins, and lunettes. Interpretive panels line the route. Each September, the "Palma alle Armi" historical reenactment draws over a thousand costumed participants in 16th-century dress.

days_plan.itin_title: Udine & Friuli Circuit: Hidden Treasures

places.name: Palmi

visits.text: Palmi—a town of 19,000 perched on a 240-meter promontory above the Tyrrhenian Sea, with sweeping views of the Aeolian Islands and the Strait of Messina. The Museo Calabrese di Etnografia e Folklore, founded in 1965 in the Casa della Cultura Leonida Repaci, houses one of Calabria's most important ethnographic collections: traditional costumes, musical instruments, rural life objects, and a section dedicated to the Varia di Palmi—an 18-meter processional machine inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Heritage list in 2013.

activities.text: Stop at Palmi's belvedere for the view across the Strait of Messina to Mount Etna before descending toward Scilla.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Calabria Loop: Tyrrhenian and Ionian Coasts

map_keywords: Casa della Cultura Leonida Repaci Palmi

visits.text: The prehistoric village at Capo Milazzese, perched on an eastern promontory, dates to the Bronze Age (15th-13th century BC). Its 23 elliptical dry-stone huts rank among the Mediterranean's best-preserved prehistoric settlements.

Cala Junco, a cove accessible on foot (20 minutes from the port), forms a natural pool enclosed by granite and obsidian cliffs. Its intense blue-green water makes it Panarea's most photographed beach.

activities.text: Boat excursion around the satellite islets — Basiluzzo, Lisca Bianca, Dattilo, and Bottaro. The islets harbor underwater thermal springs where the sea bubbles between the rocks.

days_plan.itin_title: Sicily's Island Circuit: Aeolian, Aegadian & Pantelleria

visits.text: Pantelleria, a volcanic island 70 km from Tunisia, is nicknamed "the Black Pearl of the Mediterranean" for its basalt rock. Its Dammusi — domed stone dwellings inherited from 9th-century Arab architecture — collect rainwater and maintain coolness through 90 cm-thick walls.

Specchio di Venere (Venus's Mirror), a crater lake at 836 meters elevation, reaches 40°C in geothermal zones. Its gray-green silt, used as a body mask since antiquity, is harvested directly by bathers.

The Mursia prehistoric site includes a Bronze Age village (2000-1000 BC) and a sesi — a funerary monument unique to Pantelleria, built of dry-stacked volcanic stone, whose function remains debated by archaeologists.
Cala Gadir on the northeast coast is a small black rock cove where underwater geothermal springs heat the sea to 30-35°C. Accessible on foot from Gadir village in 10 minutes.

Montagna Grande, the island's highest point at 836 meters, offers views of the Tunisian coast on clear days from its hiking trail. The Mediterranean forest of kermes oak and mastic that covers it is among the most intact in the central Mediterranean.

activities.text: Bathing at the Thermae San Calogero, natural 60°C geothermal springs in a black stone cave on the north coast, used since the Bronze Age.
Tasting Passito di Pantelleria DOC, a sweet white wine produced from Zibibbo grapes sun-dried in July — the only Sicilian wine awarded the grand prize by the International Union of Oenologists.
Island circuit by scooter (50 km, circular coastal road) to reach Cala dei Cinque Denti — a cove with five finger-like lava rocks emerging from the sea, accessible on foot via a 20-minute trail.

days_plan.itin_title: Sicily's Island Circuit: Aeolian, Aegadian & Pantelleria
Sicily's Island Circuit: Aeolian, Aegadian & Pantelleria

places.name: Pantheon

visits.text: The Pantheon is the best-preserved building from ancient Rome. The first temple was erected by Agrippa in 27 BC and burned in 80 AD. The current structure is the one Hadrian rebuilt between 118 and 125 AD—yet he kept Agrippa's inscription on the pediment, erasing his own name. Its hemispherical unreinforced concrete dome (43.30 m in diameter) remains the world's largest in this category. The interior height exactly equals the diameter, inscribing a perfect sphere within the rotunda. The central oculus (8.92 m diameter) is the only source of light: rain enters directly and drains through 22 nearly invisible outlets in the original marble floor. Each year at Pentecost, a shower of rose petals descends through the oculus. Raphael is buried here, along with Italian kings Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I. Michelangelo called this building an 'angelic and not human design.'

Santa Maria sopra Minerva, steps from the Pantheon, is Rome's only Gothic church. Built in the 13th century atop the ruins of a temple to Minerva, it contains Michelangelo's Christ Bearing the Cross (1521), the Caraffa Chapel decorated by Filippino Lippi, and Fra Angelico's tomb. In front of the façade, Bernini's marble elephant bearing the obelisk (1667) is one of Rome's most whimsical monuments.

activities.text: Watch the Pantheon's oculus in the rain: water falls directly onto the ancient marble floor and vanishes into Roman drains that still function perfectly. The effect is mesmerizing.

days_plan.itin_title: Rome: Historic Center, Ancient Ruins & Vatican Treasures

map_keywords: Basilica di Santa Maria sopra Minerva Roma
Chiesa di Sant'Ignazio di Loyola Roma

visits.text: Incense and white light: the Basilica Santuario della Madonna della Coltura, built from 1913 to designs by Napoleone Pagliarulo, houses a painted monolith that resurfaced when the old chapel was demolished in 1912. It carries Greek inscriptions. Free entry, and the evening mass draws a crowd.

The Byzantine crypts of Santa Marina and the Cirlici complete the picture in Parabita: the second is a natural cavity turned into a place of worship in the 12th century. They only open on request. Call at the parish or the town hall in the morning to try your luck.

activities.text: Walk past the 14th-century Angevin castle, then the palaces of the centre: Palazzo d'Alfonso, Palazzo dei Veneziani, Palazzo Ferrari. Parabita takes an hour to cross on foot. The monumental cemetery, a work of contemporary architecture, can also be visited and catches most visitors off guard.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

places.name: Parco Della Maremma

visits.text: Exploration of Parco Naturale della Maremma and hike to the wild beach of Marina di Alberese.
Observation of local wildlife and landscapes between sea and forest.

activities.text: Moment of relaxation on the beach bordered by driftwood and natural dunes.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Beaches in Italy: Secluded Coves and Turquoise Waters

map_keywords: Spiaggia di Marina di Alberese Alberese

places.name: Parma

visits.text: Begin your discovery of Parma at Piazza del Duomo, one of Italy's most beautiful squares. The cathedral, built between 1060 and 1073 in pure Romanesque style, welcomes you with its simple facade in pale stone. Look up inside to discover the dome painted by Correggio in the early 16th century—an Assumption of the Virgin so breathtaking it seems to open onto the heavens themselves. Entry is free, so take your time soaking it all in.

Right beside the cathedral stands the octagonal baptistery in pink Verona marble, the work of Benedetto Antelami, begun in 1196. This monument bridges Romanesque and Gothic styles and ranks among Italy's finest baptisteries. Step inside: the frescoes covering the walls and dome are remarkable, and the light filtering through the windows creates an extraordinary atmosphere. Allow about 30 minutes; a combined ticket includes the adjacent diocesan museum.

Head next to Palazzo della Pilotta, just a hundred meters from the main square. This vast 16th-century complex, built by the Farnese family, houses the National Gallery, the archaeological museum, and above all the Teatro Farnese. Built in 1618 by Giovan Battista Aleotti on orders from Duke Ranuccio I, this entirely wooden theater could seat 4,000 spectators—in a city that had only 20,000 residents. It was used just nine times over a century. Almost completely destroyed by bombing on May 13, 1944, it was reconstructed identically in the 1950s. It's the world's first theater with a permanent proscenium arch. They even staged mock naval battles here thanks to a system that could flood the pit.

Don't miss the Basilica of Santa Maria della Steccata, erected in 1521. This Renaissance church shelters an image of the Virgin venerated for centuries in Parma. You'll also see frescoes by Parmigianino in the apse. Entry is free and the visit is quick—allow 20 minutes.

Finish with a stroll through Piazza Garibaldi, the lively heart of the historic center. Entirely paved, it's bordered by the Palazzo del Comune and the Governor's Palace with its clock tower. This is where locals gather for aperitivo. From here, Via Farini—a pedestrian shopping street—leads you to the Teatro Regio, built in 1829 on the initiative of Marie Louise of Austria, Napoleon's wife and Duchess of Parma.

activities.text: Parma is the capital of Italy's Food Valley, and you can't leave town without tasting its two treasures: Parmigiano Reggiano and Prosciutto di Parma. Tour operators offer combined visits to the city outskirts to discover a cheese dairy and a ham curing facility—allow half a day. Alternatively, head to the covered market or gourmet food shops in the center for a more flexible tasting. Pair everything with a glass of local Lambrusco.

Treat yourself to a walk in the Ducal Park, Parma's grand Italian-style garden located just across the Torrente Parma. Its tree-lined paths, fountains, and small lake make it the perfect spot to digest after all those tastings. The Ducal Palace, once Marie Louise's residence, can be viewed from outside—it now houses the Carabinieri headquarters.

days_plan.itin_title: Gourmet Emilia: From Parma to Bologna Through the Hills
Milan to Chianti Circuit: Design, Art, and Wine
Emilia-Romagna's Hidden Treasures: Castles, Apennines & the Great Labyrinth

map_keywords: Basilica Santa Maria della Steccata Parma

visits.text: Villa Manin - This monumental complex of 8,500 square meters and 18 hectares was built in the 17th century by Friulian nobleman Antonio Manin. The forecourt, inspired by St. Peter's Square in Rome, opens onto a semicircular colonnade. The central building was redesigned in the 18th century by Giorgio Massari, one of Venice's great Settecento architects. Napoleon Bonaparte lodged here for two months in 1797 with Joséphine de Beauharnais, conducting negotiations that led to the Treaty of Campoformio signed October 17, 1797—ending a thousand years of Venetian Republic. Napoleon's bedroom and period bed remain on display.

Cappella Sant'Andrea - Built in 1708 by Domenico Rossi outside the square courtyard, this octagonal chapel adorned with marble statues by sculptor Pietro Baratta was connected by corridors to the villa's upper floors, allowing the Manin family to attend services without mingling with Passariano villagers.

Permanent collections - The former stables house a collection of antique carriages and a 350-piece armory from Udine's Casa della Contadinanza. Since 2004, the villa has also served as a Contemporary Art Center with rotating exhibitions featuring international artists and park installations.

activities.text: Stroll through the French-style gardens - Designed in 1714 by a French architect modeled on Versailles, the park blends centuries-old trees, small lakes, hillocks crowned with mythological statuary, and vast lawns. In spring, the central meadow carpets itself with yellow daffodils. Even Carlo Goldoni was dazzled by the site's magnificence during a visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Udine & Friuli Circuit: Hidden Treasures

visits.text: Duke Francesco IV had the Palazzo Ducale of Pavullo built between 1830 and 1844 as a summer residence, at the end of the Via Giardini connecting Modena to the mountains. Austere neoclassical style, rigorous symmetry. Today, the building houses the Gallerie d'Arte Contemporanea and the library. Free admission.

Stroll through the Parco Ducale beneath the Lebanon cedar that locals call the Pinone. The gardener Karl Huller designed this park in the 19th century on uneven terrain behind the palace. Free access year-round, even when the palace is closed.

If you love gliding, Pavullo's Aeroporto Paolucci hosts Italy's only winch-launch gliding school. Even without flying, watching the gliders take off from the green bowl of the Piani di Pavullo is a spectacle in itself.

activities.text: Pavullo's crescentine and borlenghi are the local specialty: thin flatbreads cooked on stone griddles, filled with lard or pesto modenese. Look for them at summer sagre or in the town center's trattorie.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Apennines: From Montefiorino to Rocchetta Mattei

visits.text: The MACCA (Museo d'Arte Contemporanea a Cielo Aperto) of Peccioli brings together over 70 permanent installations scattered throughout the municipal territory. The Anfiteatro Fonte Mazzola, built in 2007 in tuff slabs without concrete using bio-construction techniques, can accommodate 2,000 spectators with the hills as backdrop. In July it hosts the 11 Lune festival. In 2024, Peccioli won RAI's national "Il Borgo dei Borghi" competition.

The medieval borgo of Peccioli has been inhabited since the Neolithic, with attested Etruscan and Roman occupations. Its Piazza del Popolo brings together the Palazzo Pretorio, the Pieve di San Verano, and the Archaeological Museum—excavations have yielded Greek and Etruscan ceramics. Walking Patrick Tuttofuoco's Endless Sunset footbridge, which connects the centro storico to the modern part in a ribbon of colors, is one of the most surprising strolls in the Pisan hills.

The hamlet of Ghizzano houses permanent works by Alicja Kwade and Patrick Tuttofuoco, and house façades bear the signature of British artist David Tremlett. The entire territory of Peccioli functions as a museum without walls—the "Sistema Peccioli": revenues from the waste treatment and recovery plant (biogas, recycling) have financed culture, art, and public facilities since the 1990s, a model cited as a reference at the European level.

activities.text: 11 Lune Festival at the Anfiteatro Fonte Mazzola, every July: theater, music, and dance by national and international artists, with the Valdera hills as natural backdrop. The festival attracts about 15,000 spectators per edition.
Wine and local product tasting in the cellars of the Pisan Hills Wine Route. In October, the Sagra del Tartufo brings Peccioli alive with markets, tastings, and performances.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

visits.text: Penne - the city of red brick, built across four hills (Sacro, Romano, Castello, and Cappuccio) at 438 meters altitude. The entire historic center, ranked among Italy's most beautiful, is constructed from locally fired bricks that give the streets a characteristic orange hue, unique in Abruzzo.

Cattedrale di San Massimo - a Romanesque cathedral rebuilt in the 12th-13th centuries on the foundations of a Roman temple. The red brick façade and 14th-century octagonal bell tower make it the most representative building of Penne's architecture.

Chiesa dell'Annunziata - a 15th-century church with a late Gothic carved portal, central to Holy Week ceremonies with the Good Friday procession that has united the entire town since the 16th century.

activities.text: Visit the Riserva Naturale Lago di Penne - a 146-hectare WWF reserve around an artificial lake created in 1959. Home to grey herons, redshanks, and otters. Visitor center with exhibitions on local fauna.

places.name: Pergola

visits.text: Museo dei Bronzi Dorati della Città di Pergola — the major archaeological treasure of Le Marche. In 1946, farmers near Cartoceto di Pergola unearthed while ploughing four gilded bronze statues from the 1st century BC: an equestrian warrior, a noblewoman and two divine or priestly figures, in exceptional condition. Their origin is still debated: some historians identify the equestrian group as depicting Publius Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria. They are the only gilded equestrian bronzes from Roman antiquity preserved anywhere in the world. Displayed since 1999 in a museum purpose-built for them.

Duomo di Santa Maria Assunta and historic centre — the cathedral was rebuilt in the 19th century on a medieval foundation, with a freestanding 12th-century campanile. The interior holds a Crucifixion attributed to Raffaellino del Colle, a pupil of Raphael. The Piazza Municipale is lined with Renaissance palaces, including the Palazzo dei Priori with its loggia.

Convento di San Francesco — founded in the 13th century, the church preserves 15th-century frescoes and works recovered from rural churches across the Pergola area. The cloister is one of the few intact Franciscan ensembles surviving in the province of Pesaro-Urbino.

activities.text: Walk through the historic centre to admire the arcaded houses typical of the Pergola area, and look for Roman milestones repurposed as door lintels in several façades — traces of the Via Flaminia that once ran nearby.

Taste the formaggio di fossa from Pergola — cheese aged in tufa pits — and the crescia al formaggio, a wood-fired leavened bread with pecorino and eggs, an Easter speciality throughout the Pesaro area.

visits.text: The Pertosa-Auletta Caves, on the route between Roscigno and the climb northward, have a unique feature in Europe: you enter by boat, on an underground watercourse—the Negro River, which runs about 3 km of galleries before emerging into open air. Occupied by humans since the Neolithic about 8,000 years ago, occupied in the Bronze Age, then abandoned. Stalactites, cathedral halls, gour formations. Three possible routes, from 1 hour to 2.5 hours. Constant temperature 16°C, sweater recommended even in high summer.

The Museo Integrato dell'Ambiente (MIdA), at the cave entrance, recounts local geology and prehistoric occupation of the site. Small archaeological section with Bronze Age objects found in the caves. Thirty minutes suffice.

activities.text: Lunch in Auletta, small medieval town near the caves. Simple address: Antica Trattoria della Posta. Specialty: cicoria selvatica con fagioli (wild chicory with beans).

days_plan.itin_title: Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: Perugia hides a ghost city beneath its feet: the Rocca Paolina, massive papal fortress built in 1540 by Pope Paul III to crush the Perugian revolt against the salt tax. To build it, they razed an entire quarter of Baglioni family medieval palaces—without destroying the ground floors. Today you traverse these ghost streets via a series of public escalators, descending level by level into the city's belly. Houses, vaults, alleys, fountains, preserved intact beneath the fortress. Dismantled by the Perugian mob in 1860 upon Italian unification—symbol of papal oppression, only the underground was kept. Free entry, access from Piazza Italia.

The Pozzo Etrusco (Etruscan Well), Piazza Danti, descends 37 meters into bedrock since the 3rd century BC—one of the largest known Etruscan wells. Built in travertine blocks without mortar, with a stone vault that defies the laws of statics. It supplied the Etruscan city of Perusia with filtered rainwater. Walkway above the water, descent possible to the lower level. Three euros, claustrophobes beware.

The Fontana Maggiore at the center of Piazza IV Novembre, sculpted in 1278 by Nicola and Giovanni Pisano, is one of Italy's most beautiful medieval fountains: two superimposed pink marble basins, carved with 50 bas-reliefs depicting the months of the year, the zodiac, Aesop's fables, the founding of Rome, and even the liberal arts. A little lesson in medieval civilization in stone. Topped by three bronze nymphs who poured the water (now copies, originals in the Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria next door).

Seven kilometers east of Perugia, the Ipogeo dei Volumni—one of Italy's finest Etruscan tombs. Discovered in 1840, dating from the 2nd century BC, it houses the sarcophagi of a noble Perugian family, the Volumni. Central burial chamber with a statue of the deceased reclining on the urn lid, fixed gaze, eternal banquet. Seven other rooms around, totally intact, as if abandoned yesterday. Timeless atmosphere, few visitors. Possible combination with the Etruscan Well.

The Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria, in Palazzo dei Priori on Corso Vannucci, is one of central Italy's greatest picture galleries. Perugino (Raphael's master, born in nearby Città della Pieve), Pinturicchio, Piero della Francesca, Beato Angelico. And the entire Umbrian School that preceded then influenced the Florentine Renaissance. If time is short, target at least the Perugino rooms.

activities.text: Final lunch at Osteria a Priori, in a vaulted cellar in the center. Authentic Umbrian cuisine with local products only: strangozzi with black truffle, herbed lamb, Pienza cheeses. Budget 35-50 euros. Good pre-departure point near the station.
Return to Bologna by train from Perugia Fontivegge station—Trenitalia Frecciargento direct, 2h-2h30, around 35-45 euros. Return rental car in Perugia beforehand. Much faster than driving (3h30).

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Umbria: 8 days Among Mummies, Mystics & Caves

visits.text: Centro storico di Pesariis - This hamlet of Prato Carnico, at 750 m elevation in Val Pesarina (the 'Valley of Time'), lines up stone houses with scandole roofs (wooden shingles) carefully rebuilt after the 1976 earthquake. Here, from the late 17th century, families of skilled blacksmiths began making weight-driven iron clocks. The border position between the Venetian Republic and the Habsburg Empire, with its customs house and pesa pubblica (public scale), favored the exchange of ideas and know-how.

Museo dell'Orologeria Pesarina - Over a hundred clocks trace nearly 300 years of production: from 17th-century domestic pendulum clocks to monumental tower clocks, including the revolutionary 'palette' clock (mechanical digital display) invented in 1948 by the Solari company. These flip-panel displays, where numbers turn like book pages, equipped airports and train stations worldwide, up to a reconstructed example for the TWA Hotel at JFK Airport in New York.

Percorso dell'Orologeria Monumentale - 15 giant and entirely different clocks line the village lanes: water turbine clock, planetary clock (solar system), giant perpetual calendar (showing day, month, zodiac, day and night length), mariners' nocturnal planisphere. On the piazzetta before the Church of Saints Philip and Jerome (1861), the carillon clock rings the ancient Marian chant 'Us saludi, o Marie' on eleven bells at set hours.

Casa Bruseschi - This 17th-century Carnian bourgeois house, owned by the parish, hosts a small ethnographic museum: the fogolâr (traditional Friulian hearth), period furniture, manuscripts, and utensils recounting daily life in Carnia.

activities.text: Clock treasure hunt through the village - A map available at the museum guides visitors from one orologio to the next through the viottoli (narrow lanes). The mechanisms are visible and operating: you can study the gears up close. Allow about 1h30 for the museum and complete route.
Cascata di Fuas - 20 minutes on foot from the Solari factory, following 'Fuas' signs, a woodland path leads to this discreet waterfall in a green setting.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Friuli-Venezia Giulia

places.name: Pescara

visits.text: Start with Pescara Vecchia, the neighborhood that survived the demolition of the military fortress during D'Annunzio's childhood. Corso Manthonè, the main street, preserves its layout as a small Adriatic port. Low-slung houses, pastel facades, restaurants and bars that come alive in the evening—this is where Pescara's movida concentrates. The modern city, west of the Pescara River, holds little interest: stick to the borgo side. Two hours is enough to get your bearings, but this is by far the most charming part of town.

Gabriele D'Annunzio's birthplace stands at 116 Corso Manthonè. The poet was born here on March 12, 1863, spending his first eleven years before leaving to study in Prato. Mussolini declared the house a National Monument in 1927—at the poet's own request. Nine rooms on the first floor, period furnishings, clothing (the red hunting coat, golden summer sandals), first editions of his books, and the death mask cast over his body on the night of March 1, 1938. Full admission around €5. Allow 1 hour. Controversial figure—proto-fascist, who left Ronchi in September 1919 with about 200-300 Sardinian grenadiers, his column swelling en route to 2,000-2,600 men upon arrival in Fiume—but the writer remains central to twentieth-century Italian literature.

San Cetteo Cathedral, steps from the D'Annunzio house, was partially financed by the poet himself—his mother is buried here. Austere white stone facade, Fascist-era exterior styling, three-nave interior with a Guercino Ecstasy of Saint Francis. It's quick (20 minutes), but an aging D'Annunzio's devotion to his hometown reads clearly here. Construction was completed in 1938, the year of his death.

Late afternoon, walk the Lungomare and cross the Ponte del Mare, a pedestrian-cycling bridge inaugurated in 2009—one of Italy's most beautiful modern bridges, an elegant white curve spanning the river mouth. Cross it at sunset, golden light washing the Adriatic, fishermen returning to port in view. It's become Pescara's modern symbol, as much as the D'Annunzio house is its historical one.

The Aurum occupies a former Fascist-era bathing establishment, now a cultural center. Amusing anecdote: the building, designed in the 1930s, once housed production of Aurum liqueur—orange and brandy—created for D'Annunzio himself, who invented the name (Latin for 'gold'). Today: temporary exhibitions, concerts, outdoor cinema in summer. Sober rationalist architecture, views over the d'Avalos pine forest. If the current exhibition speaks to you, take an hour. Otherwise, the building can be seen from outside in 15 minutes.

Next door, Pescara's green lung: 53 hectares of pine forest including 35 hectares of preserved ancient woodland. Aleppo pines, umbrella pines, a small lake, an open-air theater dedicated to D'Annunzio (summer concerts). The official name—Pineta d'Avalos—comes from the noble family that ruled the marquisate during the Bourbon era, but everyone calls it Pineta Dannunziana. Perfect for catching your breath after a morning in town. 1 hour of easy walking suffices, trails well-marked.

If you have 1-1.5 hours and regional culture interests you, the Museo delle Genti d'Abruzzo is worth the stop: 13 interconnected rooms covering Bronze Age, pastoral civilization, transhumance, brigandage, traditional crafts. Dense, sometimes dated in its museography, but it's the most complete introduction to Abruzzo you'll find. Useful before tackling neighboring Molise, which shares much of this pastoral tradition.

Piazza Salotto, nicknamed so because locals settle into its terraces as if in their living room. Nerve center of modern Pescara, lined with cafés, lively from morning to evening. Next door, the Fontana Nave di Cascella, Pietro Cascella's travertine marble sculpture evoking a sailboat putting out to sea—one of the city's emblems. 30-minute coffee break, then back toward the borgo.

activities.text: Evening at the fish market and dinner at a trattoria on Corso Manthonè. Pescara remains above all a fishing port: Adriatic-style raw fish, brodetto pescarese (different from Termoli's version, more tomatoey), fritto misto. Ask for arrosticini, Abruzzo's signature lamb skewers—5-6 cm bites ordered by the dozen, grilled on long narrow braziers. It's the region's flagship dish, simple but unbeatable with a glass of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.

Evening stroll on Pescara beach. Fine sand stretching for kilometers, shallow waters, very family-friendly. Outside summer season, you'll have the beach to yourself in late afternoon. It's also an ideal launching point for water sports in July-August: sailing, kitesurfing, windsurfing.

Cycling along the Bici-Litorale, a bike path following the Adriatic coast for 17 km south from Pescara (Francavilla, Ortona). Flat, partially shaded, it runs alongside beaches and bathing establishments. Several rental shops in town. It's the best way to understand Abruzzo beach culture—the stabilimenti, paid establishments with parasols aligned in military rows, organize the entire summer life along the coast. Ideal half-day.

Last evening in Pescara: back to Corso Manthonè, dinner at a borgo enoteca, tasting of white Trebbiano d'Abruzzo and red Montepulciano. Abruzzo vineyards have been moving upmarket for twenty years, particularly the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG. Ask to taste—several wine merchants in the neighborhood are passionate and open for tastings until late.

visits.text: The Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise National Park is Italy's oldest in continuous operation, created in 1922 on 12,000 hectares—today extended to 50,000 hectares. It saved the Marsican brown bear (Ursus arctos marsicanus), an endemic sub-species of the central Apennines scientifically described in 1921 by naturalist Giuseppe Altobello. The first reliable censuses of the 1950s estimated the population at around thirty individuals; today, we count 50 to 60. It's one of western Europe's last great bears. And 40 to 50 Apennine wolves distributed across 8-10 packs. The Pescasseroli visitor center, the park's capital, provides context before hikes.

Civitella Alfedena, medieval village at 1,100 m, houses the Museo del Lupo (Wolf Museum). Beside it, the wildlife area presents some wolves and a lynx in semi-freedom—injured animals, rescued and impossible to release. Pedagogically useful, especially with children. The village itself spans five parallel lanes, tight stone houses, end-of-the-world atmosphere.

Lake Barrea, the park's largest body of water, formed by a dam on the Sangro. Emerald waters bordered by beech forests. Lake tour by car in 30 minutes (15 km), with stops at Barrea (village perched at 1,066 m on a spur, ruined Aragonese castle), Villetta Barrea (deer cross the streets in the evening, verified fact), and Opi (perched on its ridge at 1,250 m, plunging view over Val Fondillo).

activities.text: Val di Rose hike from Civitella Alfedena, 6 km, 700 m elevation gain. The trail climbs through an ancient beech forest (among Europe's oldest, beeches over 500 years old, UNESCO-listed since 2017) to alpine pastures above 1,800 m. From there, near-guaranteed observation of the Apennine chamois (Rupicapra ornata)—endemic subspecies also saved from extinction by the park. In June-July, regulated access: guide mandatory above a certain altitude to avoid disturbing bears.

At sunset, return to Villetta Barrea to hear the deer rut in September, or simply observe herds in the village gardens. Deer come to graze in the streets, unafraid of humans—a phenomenon that's become emblematic of the park.

places.name: Peschici

visits.text: Peschici's historic center, founded in 970 AD by Croatian colonists (Ragusan Slavs) fleeing Byzantine invasion, displays the characteristic urban plan of early medieval Adriatic defensive towns: cubic whitewashed houses, flat rooftops, narrow alleyways, and stone staircases. The village perches on an 80-meter limestone cliff overlooking a horseshoe-shaped bay.

The Norman-Swabian castle, built in the 10th century on a rocky promontory, underwent defensive reinforcement under the Angevins in the 13th century, then transformation into a military fortress under Charles V. Since 2013, it has housed a permanent exhibition on medieval torture instruments, relocated from Certaldo.

Drive next toward the Foresta Umbra, heart of Gargano National Park (established 1991, 118,144 hectares). The primary beech forest—a remnant of the vast "Nemus Garganicum" that once blanketed the entire promontory—was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2017 as part of Europe's Ancient Beech Forests. Protected area: 10,000 hectares, elevations between 300 and 800 meters.

The Casa Umbra visitor center provides maps, audio guides, and access to marked trail #1 (3.5 km, 1h30, moderate elevation change). Several remarkable tree species: beech trees over 500 years old, European yew, Italian maple, endemic orchids (spring). Documented presence of the Italian red deer, reintroduced in 1953.
Board early at Peschici harbor for the Tremiti Islands. One hour crossing, €35 round-trip by hydrofoil. The archipelago: five islands 22 km offshore, a marine protected reserve since 1989.

Disembark at San Nicola, the most historic island. Climb the medieval ramp to the Abbey of Santa Maria a Mare, founded in 1045 by Benedictine monks. Both fortress and place of worship, it served as a papal prison then political jail until 1943.

Inside, you'll see a 15th-century Venetian wooden polyptych on the main altar, a 12th-century Byzantine crucifix, and 10th-century mosaic flooring. The abbey retained its defensive character: arrow slits, an Angevin tower, ramparts that plunge straight into the sea.
Transfer to San Domino by shuttle boat (5 min). The 2 km² island is covered with Aleppo pines. No cars. Small electric buses circle the island.

activities.text: Zaiana Bay, accessible via a steep road from Peschici, features pale sand and shallow water suitable for families. Paid parking in summer (€8), limited seasonal facilities.

Dinner in Peschici. Local gastronomy combines seafood (swordfish, anchovies, squid) with promontory products (caciocavallo podolico cheese, extra-virgin DOP olive oil, Gargano lamb). Signature dish: troccoli pasta with octopus ragù.

Two-hour boat tour around the archipelago. You'll skirt San Domino's cliffs and its evocatively named caves: Grotta del Bue Marino (former habitat of the monk seal), Grotta delle Viole (wild violets in spring), Grotta delle Rondinelle. Swimming stop at the underwater statue of Padre Pio (14 meters deep).

Lunch at Cala delle Arene, the archipelago's only sandy beach. Beach restaurant, spaghetti alle vongole, water at 24°C in summer. Mask and snorkel essential: the seabed is remarkably rich in fish life.
Return to Peschici late afternoon (departure 5-6 pm depending on season). Sunset over the sea behind the cliffs. Light seafood dinner at the harbor.

places.name: Peschiera Del Garda

visits.text: Explore the Fortress of Peschiera del Garda, an extraordinary example of military architecture enclosing the entire old town. Its walls, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017, bear witness to centuries of history: from Roman fort to Scaliger stronghold, from sixteenth-century Venetian fortress to Habsburg citadel. Enter through the monumental Porta Verona or Porta Brescia to discover this defensive gem.

Visit the Sanctuary of the Madonna del Frassino, a splendid monumental church nestled in nature at the foot of the Lake Garda hills. Built between 1511 and 1514 on the spot where the Madonna appeared to the farmer Bartolomeo Broglia, the sanctuary kept by the Franciscan Friars Minor features a single nave and two marvellous frescoed chapels.

activities.text: Stroll along the Lungolago Mazzini, a wonderful lakeside promenade stretching about 700 metres from the old town to the Lido dei Cappuccini. This panoramic route, perfect at sunset, is lined with elegant establishments and offers spectacular views of the crystal-clear waters of Lake Garda.

Relax at the Lido Cappuccini, one of the lake's most popular bathing establishments where you can hire sun loungers and pedalos, swim in the clear waters and enjoy a refreshing break on the pebble beach, with lifeguard service and a restaurant right on the waterfront.

visits.text: Pescia Cathedral is mentioned as early as 951 in the form "Sita loco Piscia." Elevated to episcopal status by Pope Benedict XIII in 1726, it preserves its sober baroque architecture. Pescia was declared a noble city by Cosimo III de' Medici in 1699 and received on that occasion the Porta Fiorentina, a commemorative triumphal arch with the peculiarity of not being connected to any walls—built solely to celebrate the elevation in status.

The Palazzo del Vicario and Piazza Grande form the heart of Pescia's civic center, structured in the 13th century in "fifths"—four quarters on the right bank of the Pescia river and one on the left bank—with a fortified bridge ensuring the connection. This double town center (religious cathedral pole / civic palazzo pole) is an urban organization preserved intact since the Middle Ages.

San Francesco church preserves a collection of 14th-15th century paintings including the Triptych by Bonaventura Berlinghieri (1235), one of the earliest representations of Saint Francis of Assisi painted during his lifetime or shortly after his death, commissioned by the Franciscans of Pescia.

activities.text: Pescia's flower market: the city is Italy's capital of cut flowers, primarily carnations. The tradition dates back to the 1920s-1930s when, after the decline of silk manufactures and paper mills, farmers converted their land to horticulture. The first covered reinforced concrete market, built in 1950-1951 on plans that won awards in Brazil in 1953, is now reopened as a multipurpose cultural space. The region exports millions of flowers and indoor plants throughout Europe.

Stroll along the lungofiume of the Pescia: the river flows through the city between the two medieval poles, beneath ancient bridges. The landscaped banks offer a pleasant walk between gardens and palace facades.

days_plan.itin_title: Pistoia Province Circuit: Hill Towns & Thermal Spas

places.name: Pescocostanzo

visits.text: Pescocostanzo - a village of 1,000 inhabitants at 1,400 meters in the Altipiani Maggiori d'Abruzzo, considered one of Abruzzo's best-preserved towns. The historic center dates mainly from the 17th century, rebuilt after the 1706 earthquake in a sober baroque style with local stone houses and wrought-iron balconies.

Collegiata di Santa Maria del Colle (La Collegiata) - an 11th-century basilica rebuilt between the 14th and 17th centuries. The interior features a 17th-century gilded coffered ceiling, carved wooden choir stalls, and wrought-iron grilles from local workshops considered masterpieces of Abruzzese ironwork.

Museo del Tombolo - the bobbin lace museum, an art practiced in Pescocostanzo since the 17th century. The village's lacemakers produced commissions for the royal courts of Naples and Madrid. A few artisans still perpetuate the tradition.

activities.text: Walk through the Bosco di Sant'Antonio - a monumental 1,200-hectare forest of black pines, beeches, and maples 6 km from the village, one of Italy's oldest managed forests, with some trees exceeding 500 years.

visits.text: The nickname is well-earned: Pescoluse, called the 'Maldives of Salento,' stretches nearly 4 kilometers of white sand and shallow, transparent water, in the municipality of Salve. Blue Flag since 2009. Vegetated dunes border the beach. Arrive early—parking fills up fast in summer.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a half-day with your feet in the water at Pescoluse: the seabed slopes gently for dozens of meters, perfect for families. Rent a beach chair at a beach club or lay your towel on the free section. Bring a picnic and parasol—natural shade is scarce.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce

places.name: Petritoli

visits.text: Tre Archi — the village gateway: three neo-Gothic arches built in 1874, flanked by two 15th-century cylindrical towers. Local tradition holds that the name Petritoli comes from the merging of three ancient castles — Petrosa, Petrania and Petrollavia — represented by the three blue lozenges on its coat of arms.

Torre Civica and Piazza della Rocca — a tower with a square base, hexagonal body and cylindrical top, at the village's highest point. From here the view stretches from the Sibillini to the Adriatic. At the tower's foot, look for the porta del morto: a small opening in the wall reserved exclusively for the passage of the deceased, so their spirit would not linger in the house.
Convento delle Clarisse — built between the 16th and 17th centuries, now the town hall. The building retains several rooms with artworks and a council chamber of elegant, restrained beauty.

Chiesa di Santa Maria dei Martiri — built at the end of the 16th century with an adjoining Franciscan convent. Inside: a 17th-century wooden octagonal coffered ceiling painted in tempera on Franciscan themes, and a Callido organ from the 18th century — one of the finest instruments in the province.

Teatro dell'Iride — a small 19th-century Italian-style theatre with gilded wooden boxes and balconies, still in use today. Across the street, notice the Palazzo Vitali Rosati with its Venetian-inspired façade decoration, built in the late 19th century by the Vitali family.

activities.text: Excursion to the Santuario della Madonna della Liberata, a few kilometres from the village on a wooded hillside. Inside, a votive painting from 1529 by Giovanni Battista Morale gives thanks to the Virgin for protecting the inhabitants from French troops and plague. The holy water stoup is carved from a Roman funerary cippus.
Taste the olive oil of the Valdaso: Petritoli is surrounded by olive groves and mulberry trees, at the heart of a little-industrialised farming landscape.

places.name: Pettorano Sul Gizio

visits.text: Pettorano sul Gizio - a medieval village of 900 inhabitants at 720 meters overlooking the confluence of the Gizio and Sagittario rivers. The 13th-century castle, successively owned by the Cantelmo and Caracciolo families, preserves its square keep and curtain walls. At its foot, the Riserva Naturale Monte Genzana Alto Gizio protects ancient beech forests.

activities.text: Stop at Piazza del Municipio to view the castle-village ensemble from the central fountain before continuing on.

places.name: Piacenza

visits.text: Admire Piazza Cavalli, the beating heart of Piacenza dominated by two majestic Baroque equestrian statues of Alessandro and Ranuccio Farnese. Commissioned in 1600 and crafted by Mochi da Montevarchi over 13 years of work, they represent the third and fourth Duke of Parma and Piacenza in a breathtaking masterpiece of bronze casting.

Visit the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta and Santa Giustina, one of the best-preserved examples of Romanesque architecture in Italy. Built between the 11th and 12th centuries, it conceals behind its sober façade a richly frescoed interior, crowned by the extraordinary dome painted by Guercino in the 17th century. Climb the 136 steps to reach the 27-meter-high dome.

Explore the Museums of Palazzo Farnese, a sumptuous period building housing seven different exhibition areas: the Picture Gallery, the Carriage Museum, the Civic Museum, the Rizzi Vaccari Collection, the Ceramics Museum, the Risorgimento Museum, and the Archaeological Museum. A journey through centuries of Piacenza's history and art.

Discover the Ricci Oddi Modern Art Gallery, a museum established in 1931 that houses the famous Portrait of a Lady by Gustav Klimt. The painting, stolen in 1997 and found over twenty years later in a hidden trapdoor within the museum itself, has been visible again since 2020 and is one of the most mysterious masterpieces in art history.

activities.text: Stroll beneath the arcades of the historic center to the Basilica of Santa Maria di Campagna, a jewel of Renaissance art with its frescoed chapel blending religious and pagan figures. Since 2024, visitors can climb to the dome to admire the details of the masterpieces from a unique perspective.

Visit the Municipal Theater, inaugurated in the early 19th century and considered among the most beautiful in Italy, as Stendhal himself proclaimed. The three-quarter ellipse auditorium, revolutionary for its time, offers extraordinary acoustics and interior decorations of meticulous elegance.
