map_keywords: Basilica di Santa Maria di Campagna Piacenza

visits.text: Rocca Aldobrandesca: A quadrilateral fortress in lava stone first mentioned in 1194 in a diploma of Emperor Henry VI, it successively belonged to the Abbey of San Salvatore, the Aldobrandeschi family, the Orsini of Pitigliano, then the Republic of Siena which seized it between 1415 and 1430. Its two towers—the large one serving as keep, and the small one defending the gate—are characteristic of Aldobrandeschi fortresses on Amiata. Now a museum, it offers panoramic views of the Paglia valley.

Church of San Francesco and Palazzo Bourbon del Monte: The church, from a 15th-century convent, has a façade preceded by a simple loggia and preserves fragments of frescoes from the 14th-century Sienese school. The Palazzo Bourbon del Monte, at the village's edge, was the residence of feudal lords from 1601 to the late 18th century, when Grand Duke Leopold I made Piancastagnaio the capital of an autonomous community.

activities.text: Hiking in the chestnut woods of Monte Amiata: The forests surrounding Piancastagnaio are dominated by the Amiata chestnut, a protected species. Trails depart from the village for loops of 5 to 10 km up to the first slopes of the extinct volcano (1,738 m).

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Siena Province

places.name: Piazza Armerina

visits.text: The Villa Romana del Casale, 5 km south of Piazza Armerina, shelters 3,500 square meters of in-situ 4th-century Roman mosaics—the world's largest surface. Its hunting scenes, athletes, and the famous "bikini girls"—ten women exercising—represent a unique depiction in ancient art. UNESCO-listed since 1997.

Piazza Armerina, founded by Normans in the 11th century, preserves a Baroque center with its blue-domed cathedral dominating the hill. The town counted 40 noble families in the 17th century for just 5,000 inhabitants—hence its nickname "city of one hundred thousand."

activities.text: Lunch in the upper town with pasta al ragù di maiale nero dei Nebrodi—black pig from the Nebrodi mountains, an Iberian breed raised semi-wild in Sicily's interior forests.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Sicily

map_keywords: Villa Romana del Casale Piazza Armerina
Mosaico delle Ragazze in Bikini Piazza Armerina
Duomo di Piazza Armerina Piazza Armerina

places.name: Piazza Di Spagna

visits.text: The Scalinata di Trinità dei Monti (1723-1726) ranks among Europe's grandest monumental staircases: 135 travertine steps divided into 11 ramps that serpentine and converge, designed by Francesco De Sanctis with funds bequeathed by French diplomat Étienne Gueffier. The original plan called for a statue of Louis XIV at the summit; Pope Innocent XIII refused, and a garden was planted instead. At the base, the Barcaccia fountain (1629) by Pietro Bernini—father of the more famous Gian Lorenzo—depicts a half-submerged boat commemorating the 1598 Tiber flood that allegedly beached a vessel at this very spot. Each April, the entire staircase vanishes beneath azaleas during the annual exhibition celebrating Rome's birthday.

The church of Trinità dei Monti, built between 1502 and 1585 at the request of Charles VIII of France, stands as one of the rare examples of late French Gothic style visible in Rome. Its Renaissance façade with twin bell towers—the work of Giacomo della Porta and Carlo Maderno—remains under French state care to this day. Inside, six chapels house remarkable artworks. In front of the entrance, the Sallustiano obelisk (13.91 m) is a Roman creation imitating Egyptian hieroglyphs, gifted to Pope Clement XII by the Ludovisi family in 1783.

activities.text: Climb the scalinata early in the morning, before the tourist rush, to watch Rome stretch out beneath Via dei Condotti: the street's vanishing perspective at dawn is one of the city's most photographed vistas.

Coffee at Caffè Greco (Via dei Condotti 86), open since 1760—Rome's oldest café and Italy's second oldest. Stendhal, Goethe, Byron, Liszt, and Keats all took their coffee here. The walls are covered with portraits and dedications from artists who frequented the place.

days_plan.itin_title: Rome: Historic Center, Ancient Ruins & Vatican Treasures

map_keywords: Scalinata di Trinità dei Monti Roma
Chiesa della Trinità dei Monti Roma

places.name: Piazza Navona

visits.text: Piazza Navona occupies the exact footprint of the Stadium of Domitian, built in 86 AD for Greek-style games that could accommodate 30,000 spectators. Its elongated shape (roughly 275 m by 55 m) is the direct imprint of that structure. At the center, the Fountain of the Four Rivers (1648-1651) is Gian Lorenzo Bernini's masterwork, commissioned by Pope Innocent X Pamphilj: four white marble giants represent the Nile (Africa, veiled because its source was unknown), the Ganges (Asia, holding an oar), the Danube (Europe, touching the pope's coat of arms), and the Rio de la Plata (Americas, holding a bag of gold). A 16-meter obelisk from the Circus of Maxentius crowns them. The legend of the Bernini-Borromini rivalry is apocryphal: the fountain was completed before Borromini began the façade of neighboring Sant'Agnese. The heavy statues rest on a hollow travertine base—visually impossible, a deliberate demonstration of Bernini's genius.

The church of Sant'Agnese in Agone (begun 1652, Borromini's façade) marks the spot where, according to tradition, the young Agnes was exposed naked before her martyrdom under Diocletian, miraculously protected by her hair which grew to cover her.

activities.text: Eat or drink in the alleys behind the square (Via del Governo Vecchio) rather than on the piazza's terraces: authentic Roman atmosphere, prices cut in half.

days_plan.itin_title: Rome: Historic Center, Ancient Ruins & Vatican Treasures

map_keywords: Chiesa di Sant'Agnese in Agone Roma

visits.text: The Vittoriano—or Altare della Patria—is the neoclassical monument erected between 1885 and 1935 in homage to Victor Emmanuel II, first king of unified Italy. Designed by Giuseppe Sacconi after his victory in the 1882 competition, it's built from white Botticino marble (Brescia)—a choice that outraged Romans accustomed to local travertine. The structure measures 135 m wide and 70 m high. Romans nicknamed it the 'typewriter' or 'wedding cake.' Its construction required demolishing a medieval quarter and revealed, during excavations, a section of the Servian Wall (6th century BC)—both walls are still visible in the foundations. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, installed in 1921, is permanently guarded. At the inauguration, a banquet was held inside the bronze equestrian statue of Victor Emmanuel—guests entered through the horse's mouth.

activities.text: Ascend to the panoramic terrace (paid elevator access or free stairs to the intermediate level): stunning views of the Imperial Forums, the Colosseum, and Rome's hills.

days_plan.itin_title: Rome: Historic Center, Ancient Ruins & Vatican Treasures

places.name: Piazzola Sul Brenta

visits.text: Marvel at Villa Contarini, a palace so vast it resembles a royal residence of a small country. This monumental Baroque villa features stunning architecture, extensive grounds, and regularly hosts one of Italy's largest antique and vintage markets.
Explore the villa's grand facades, ornate interiors, and the surrounding park. The scale and ambition of this aristocratic estate rivals any palace in Europe.

activities.text: Time your visit for one of the monthly antique markets held in front of the villa, combining architectural appreciation with treasure hunting among vintage and antique wares.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

map_keywords: Parco Villa Contarini Piazzola sul Brenta

visits.text: Picinisco, certified as one of I Borghi più Belli d'Italia, occupies a ridge at 850 meters altitude in the Comino Valley, at the heart of the Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise National Park. Its name first appears in 1017 in a donation to the Abbot of Montecassino. The castle has four towers, the oldest—la Torretta—dating to the 11th century; a larger tower was built in the 15th century, incorporating it. The village is crossed by five historic gates: Porta Saracina, Porta Codarda, Porta Rione, Porta della Prece, and Porta della Piazza.

The Church of San Lorenzo was built in 1305 and expanded several times. Its bell tower, dated to the 11th century, originally served as a military watchtower before being integrated into the religious building.

The writer D.H. Lawrence stayed in Picinisco in 1919 and completed his novel The Lost Girl there. The house where he lodged is now an agriturismo. Additionally, some 60% of Italians in Scotland originate from Picinisco: a massive exodus at the end of the 19th century and after World War II populated Scottish cities with families from this single village.

activities.text: Hike in the Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise National Park starting from Picinisco: marked trails climb toward the high-altitude pastures of Monte Meta (2241 m), where wolves and Apennine chamois are regularly observed. The park is one of Italy's oldest (founded in 1923) and one of the last refuges of the Apennine brown bear.

Taste Pecorino di Picinisco, a sheep's milk cheese recognized by local producers as a high-altitude specialty: the sheep graze on aromatic Apennine herbs between May and October, giving the cheese a slightly herbaceous flavor and a natural ocher-colored rind.

days_plan.itin_title: Ciociaria Circuit: Abbeys and Medieval Hilltop Villages

visits.text: Piazza Pio II and Renaissance ensemble: In 1459, Pope Pius II—born Enea Silvio Piccolomini in the village of Corsignano—commissioned Bernardo Rossellino, a student of Leon Battista Alberti, to transform his birthplace into a model city. In just three years (1459-1462), Rossellino erected the cathedral, Palazzo Piccolomini, Palazzo Borgia, and the trapezoidal Piazza—the first concrete realization of Renaissance humanist urban ideals. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

Cathedral of the Assumption: Built between 1459 and 1462 by Rossellino, its exterior façade is purely Renaissance in travertine, while the three-nave interior draws on the late Gothic of South German churches—a compromise wanted by Pius II, influenced by German cardinal-philosopher Nicholas of Cusa. It houses the Assumption by Il Vecchietta, the Madonna in Majesty by Matteo di Giovanni, and Flemish tapestries in the basement.

Palazzo Piccolomini: Pope Pius II's summer residence built in 1459 by Rossellino on the model of Florence's Palazzo Rucellai. The triple-level loggia on the south side opens onto a hanging garden with panoramic views of Val d'Orcia, Monte Amiata, and Enea Silvio's birthplace, Corsignano. The interior preserves period furniture, a library, and a weapons collection.

activities.text: Fiera del Cacio: On the first Sunday in September, Pienza's six districts compete in the game of cacio al fuso—rolling a wheel of Pecorino di Pienza as far as possible—along with tastings and markets.
Pecorino di Pienza tasting: Pienza's sheep cheese comes in fresh, semi-stagionato, and stagionato varieties. The shops on Corso Rossellino offer tastings with Val d'Orcia DOC wines.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy Road Trip: From Trentino to the Amalfi Coast
The Most Beautiful Villages of Siena Province

places.name: Pietra Di Bismantova

visits.text: Experience the Pietra di Bismantova, a dramatic isolated rock formation rising from the Apennine foothills that inspired Dante's description of Purgatory in the Divine Comedy. This massive sandstone plateau, reaching 1,047 meters in altitude with sheer cliffs on all sides, creates one of the most distinctive natural landmarks in the entire region.

Explore the trails leading around and atop this remarkable geological formation, where centuries of erosion have sculpted the distinctive flat-topped profile. The hermitage of Santa Maria carved into the rock face adds spiritual significance to this already awe-inspiring natural monument.

activities.text: Hike to the summit plateau for panoramic views extending across the Apennines and toward the distant Po Valley. The Pietra di Bismantova offers climbing routes on its impressive cliff faces and easier walking paths that circle the base, making it accessible to visitors of all abilities.

days_plan.itin_title: Emilia-Romagna's Hidden Treasures: Castles, Apennines & the Great Labyrinth

Eremo di Bismantova Castelnovo ne' Monti
Santuario della Beata Vergine Castelnovo ne' Monti
Sentiero della Pietra Castelnovo ne' Monti

visits.text: Pietracamela - a village of 300 inhabitants at 1,005 meters altitude, perched on a rocky spur at the foot of Corno Piccolo (2,655 m) in the Gran Sasso. The medieval center preserves characteristic dry-stone houses built side by side and vaulted alleyways. Starting point for climbers ascending Corno Grande (2,912 m), the roof of the Apennines.

activities.text: Stop at Prati di Tivo (1,450 m), a ski station and alpine meadow 4 km from the village, with sweeping views of the Gran Sasso walls.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

visits.text: Pietrapertosa is Castelmezzano's mirror on the other side of the Volo dell'Angelo: even higher perched (1,088 m, Basilicata's highest municipality), even more gripped by rock. The lanes of the Arabata quarter, the oldest, date from the Arab-Norman occupation of the 10th-11th centuries—hence the name. Houses carved into the stone, some with entire rooms in the rock. The Saracen Castle at the summit, ruined, keeps its prow silhouette against the sky. Climb by stairs, sustained elevation.

The Castle belvedere offers the reverse view of Castelmezzano's: you see Castelmezzano head-on, 1.5 km as the crow flies, and the entire Dolomiti chain. If you did the Volo dell'Angelo the day before, this vantage point best visualizes the route.

activities.text: Via Ferrata Marcirosa, for enthusiasts: 2.5-hour equipped sports route on the walls around Pietrapertosa, 350 m elevation, Nepalese bridge included. Intermediate level. Equipment rental and mandatory guide on site.

Lunch at Osteria al Becco della Civetta, the village's gastronomic restaurant. Revisited Lucanian cuisine, reasonable prices for the quality. Specialty: Lucanian lamb with peperoni cruschi (fried, dry, crispy peppers).

days_plan.itin_title: Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: Piazza del Duomo and Duomo San Martino: Pietrasanta's rectangular square is the artistic heart of the town. San Martino Cathedral, whose construction dates to the 14th century, presents a façade clad in local marble and an interior enriched with 19th-century frescoes and artworks from preceding centuries. The brick bell tower, commissioned around 1520 from Donato Benti—a collaborator of Michelangelo—conceals an extraordinary self-supporting helical staircase in brick, long overlooked. It was during the period when Michelangelo stayed in Pietrasanta to extract marble destined for the façade of San Lorenzo in Florence that this staircase was designed, according to most historians.

Museo dei Bozzetti (Museum of Sketches) - Chiostro di Sant'Agostino: Created in 1984 in the former convent of Sant'Agostino (14th century), this museum unique in the world documents the creative process of more than 350 Italian and international sculptors who have worked in Pietrasanta. It preserves over 700 maquettes and plaster models that preceded marble or bronze works now dispersed in museums and public spaces worldwide. Botero, Mitoraj, Folon, Cascella, Pomodoro, Miró, and Henry Moore are represented.

Marble and bronze workshops - Parco Internazionale della Scultura Contemporanea: Pietrasanta houses some fifty marble sculpture workshops and artistic bronze foundries. The town, nicknamed "Little Athens," has welcomed since the 15th century—when Michelangelo stayed here to work marble from nearby quarries—sculptors from around the world. Henry Moore was among the first modern foreigners to discover Pietrasanta in the 1950s; he was followed by Noguchi, Miró, Mitoraj, and Botero. The International Park of Contemporary Sculpture presents over 70 monumental works donated to the town, visible in the streets and squares.

Museo Archeologico Bruno Antonucci (Palazzo Moroni, 16th century): Located on Piazza del Duomo, this museum presents collections ranging from prehistory to the medieval era, with Etruscan and Roman pieces discovered in the Versilia territory.

activities.text: Stroll among art galleries and sculptors' workshops: Pietrasanta counts more than one gallery per 1,200 inhabitants—a record density even in Tuscany. Several workshops open their doors to the public, allowing observation of artisans working marble or bronze.

Thursday weekly market and antiques market (1st Sunday of month): The Thursday market covers Piazza del Duomo and adjacent streets with food, crafts, and local products. The first Sunday of the month, antique dealers set up in the same squares.

days_plan.itin_title: Lucca Province Circuit: Hill Towns and Coast

visits.text: Lago Santo Modenese, at 1,501 m, is the largest lake in the Modena Apennines. Glacial in origin, ringed by beeches and scree, it's reached in ten minutes on foot from the parking area. In winter, the surface freezes entirely. A local legend tells of two shepherd lovers who drowned crossing the ice in spring.

The torrent beneath the Ponte della Fola, a medieval bridge in Pievepelago's center, rushes toward the Scoltenna. It's the starting point for a hiking trail to Roccapelago, about 1h30 on foot. The bridge is the village symbol, often photographed.

In Roccapelago, a tiny hilltop village near Pievepelago, the church preserves a collection of mummies discovered in the crypt during construction work. The Museo delle Mummie displays these naturally mummified bodies and the textiles that accompanied them. Small admission fee, limited hours.

activities.text: Head up to Rifugio Vittoria for polenta ai funghi or wild boar ragù overlooking the lake. Tex, the rifugio keeper, sometimes offers vin brûlé at the end of the meal. Paid parking (€4 per day) at the trailhead.

If you've still got legs left, Lago Baccio is thirty minutes' walk from Lago Santo, doable even with children. Its oval shape is unique in the entire northern Apennines. The smaller Lago Turchino is forty-five minutes away.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Apennines: From Montefiorino to Rocchetta Mattei

visits.text: Piglio is the heartland of Cesanese del Piglio, Lazio's first and only red wine DOCG (awarded in 2008, after DOC status dating to 1973). The indigenous Cesanese d'Affile grape has been cultivated on the slopes of the Ernici Mountains since antiquity: Emperor Nerva built a palace at Piglio to secure his wine supply, and Popes Innocent III and Boniface VIII were documented enthusiasts. The vineyards cover approximately 15,300 hectares across Piglio, Serrone, Acuto, Anagni, and Paliano.

Serrone, perched on the slopes of Monte Scalambra just a few kilometers from Piglio, offers a sweeping panorama from its belvedere over the Sacco Valley and the ridges of the Ernici. The village preserves its tight medieval layout with lanes of local limestone and several 17th-century palaces.

activities.text: Visit a DOCG-zone winery to discover the three expressions of Cesanese del Piglio: the base version (minimum 12°, red and black fruit aromas, silky tannins), the Superiore (minimum 13°), and the Riserva (minimum 14°, aged at least 20 months). This ruby-hued grape with violet reflections carries a slightly bitter finish—a distinctive character that local winemakers proudly claim as their signature.

Hike through the vineyards of the Ernici Mountains on marked trails connecting Piglio to Serrone via terraced vineyards: in autumn, harvest activity is still visible in some parcels, and cellars welcome drop-in visitors without appointments.

days_plan.itin_title: Ciociaria Circuit: Abbeys and Medieval Hilltop Villages

visits.text: Piazza del Duomo—nicknamed Piazza dei Miracoli, a name invented by writer Gabriele D'Annunzio in his 1910 novel—gathers four Romanesque buildings constructed between the 11th and 14th centuries on a single lawn carpet, inscribed together on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1987. The cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, begun in 1064 by architect Buscheto after the Pisan fleet's victory over the Saracens in Sicily, is the founding monument of the Pisan Romanesque style characterized by blind arcades and pale marble bands.

The Baptistery, begun in 1153 by architect Diotisalvi, is Italy's largest: 54.86 meters in diameter and 55 meters high. Its exceptional acoustics—a guide can produce a three-note chord simultaneously by singing in echo—has attracted visitors since the Middle Ages. Inside, the pulpit sculpted by Nicola Pisano in 1260 marks a decisive break with Byzantine art by returning to direct study of ancient Roman sarcophagi, opening the path to Renaissance sculpture.

The Leaning Tower, begun in 1173 and completed in 1372 after two long interruptions due to unstable alluvial terrain, measures 55.86 meters on the south side and 58.36 meters on the north—the visible asymmetry reflects successive corrections attempted during construction to compensate for subsidence. It weighs approximately 14,500 tons and had 294 steps until its closure in 1990. Consolidation work conducted through 2001, consisting of removing earth from beneath the higher side, reduced the tilt from 5.5° to 3.97°, stabilizing it for at least two hundred years. Galileo supposedly conducted his falling-bodies experiments from the summit, according to unverified tradition.

The Camposanto—literally 'holy cemetery'—is a monumental rectangular cloister begun in 1278. According to legend, its soil was brought back from the Holy Land by Archbishop Ubaldo Lanfranchi at the end of the Crusades so the dead could rest in sacred earth. Its galleries sheltered 14th-century frescoes including the famous Triumph of Death attributed to Buonamico Buffalmacco, severely damaged by fire during a 1944 bombing—the explosion melted the roof lead onto the paintings—then partially restored.

activities.text: Pisa retains a little-visited historic center beyond the Piazza dei Miracoli: the Arno embankments, the lanes of the Borgo Stretto quarter, and the markets around Piazza delle Vettovaglie offer a glimpse of daily life in a Tuscan university town.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern to Central Italy Circuit: Milan to Rome

places.name: Pistoia

visits.text: Piazza del Duomo brings together the four pillars of medieval power in a single theatrical space: San Zeno Cathedral, the Baptistery, Palazzo del Podestà, and Palazzo dei Vescovi. The campanile tells the city's history in stone—originally a Lombard defensive tower, then heightened in the 12th and 13th centuries in Pisan Romanesque style. Each floor marks a different era, from the austere lower masonry to the elegant Pisan arcading at the summit.

San Zeno Cathedral shelters one of medieval Europe's most extraordinary goldsmithing treasures: the Silver Altar of Saint James, begun in 1287 and enriched over two centuries by Tuscany's finest goldsmiths, including a young Filippo Brunelleschi who worked on it around 1399-1400. The crypt holds the relics of Saint Zeno, while Coppo di Marcovaldo's monumental Crucifix from the 1270s dominates the central nave with its hieratic figures against a shimmering gold background.

The Ospedale del Ceppo, founded according to tradition in 1277—its name comes from a dry tree stump that miraculously flowered to mark the site—operated as a hospital for over seven centuries until 2013. Its early 16th-century loggia bears one of the Renaissance's finest glazed terracotta friezes: commissioned from 1511 by the monk Leonardo Buonafede, it united the rival workshops of the Della Robbia and Buglioni families. Giovanni della Robbia created the 1525 roundels depicting scenes from Mary's life; the narrative frieze illustrates the Seven Works of Mercy in 16th-century settings and costumes, a vivid documentary of daily life in Renaissance Pistoia.

The Hospital Museum del Ceppo, installed in the former wards since 2017, displays several hundred surgical instruments from the 17th to early 20th centuries, exhibited in bed-shaped vitrines along the old men's ward. The visit culminates in the neoclassical oval Anatomical Theater, built 1785-1787, where medical students learned anatomy. A wooden and leather birthing machine, loaned to London's Science Museum in 1913 and returned to Pistoia a century later, is now on display.

San Giovanni Fuorcivitas—"outside the walls," as it was originally built beyond the first Lombard ramparts—presents one of the most spectacular side facades in Pisan Romanesque architecture: a densely packed alternation of white marble and green Prato serpentine bands, constructed from the 12th to 14th centuries. The north portal's architrave, carved in 1166 by Gruamonte with the Last Supper, is one of the earliest examples of Pistoiese Romanesque sculpture. Inside, three masterpieces await: Fra Guglielmo da Pisa's pulpit (1270), disciple of Nicola Pisano; the central holy water font attributed to Nicola Pisano and his workshop; and Luca della Robbia's Visitation in glazed terracotta (1445), the first surviving freestanding sculpture created by the Della Robbia workshop using the invetriatura technique.

The Basilica della Madonna dell'Umiltà traces its origin to a miraculous image of the Virgin dated 1490. The foundation stone was laid in 1495 following plans by Giuliano da Sangallo. Cosimo I later commissioned Giorgio Vasari to roof the building: the dome he constructed from 1561, visible across the entire city, deliberately references Brunelleschi's in Florence and ranks among Tuscany's largest domes.

The Antico Palazzo dei Vescovi, facing the cathedral across Piazza del Duomo, houses the Cathedral Museum with its collections of sacred goldwork and medieval art. Excavations in the basements have uncovered superimposed Roman and Lombard remains, visible in the underground archaeological route.

San Bartolomeo in Pantano—"in the swamp," as it was built on marshy ground outside the first ramparts in the 8th century—preserves the third great Pistoiese pulpit: created in 1250 by Guido da Como, it's the oldest of the three major medieval pulpits surviving in the city, with reliefs of the Annunciation, Nativity and Adoration of the Magi set against polychrome marble panels.

Marliana, a farming village at 500 meters altitude on the north slope of Montalbano, is surrounded by olive groves and vineyards producing the oils and wines of the Pistoiese hills. Its medieval Rocca commands views across the Pistoia plain to the Apennines. The village long served as one of the wine-producing outposts supplying Pistoia's merchants.

activities.text: Pistoia Sotterranea: beneath the Ospedale del Ceppo's forecourt runs a network of brick-vaulted tunnels following the ancient course of the Brana torrent, channeled and covered as the city expanded. The public route covers about 650 meters of the total 1,200-meter network, with panels showing the successive phases of urban expansion and the remnants of walls, towers and bridges integrated into the underground.

The Pieve di Sant'Andrea houses the absolute masterpiece of Pistoiese pulpits: Giovanni Pisano's pulpit, completed in 1301. Its reliefs of shattering expressiveness—the Massacre of the Innocents, the Nativity, the Crucifixion—achieve a sculptural depth and dramatic tension unmatched in early 14th-century Tuscany. Pistoia is the only city in the world to possess so many major medieval pulpits within such a compact area.

The Civic Museum of Ancient Art (Palazzo del Podestà) preserves works from the 13th to 16th centuries, including the famous altarpiece by Giuliano da Rimini and panels by Pistoiese masters. The 13th-century palace facade, with its rounded arches and massive tower, stands as one of Tuscany's best-preserved examples of communal palace architecture.

Wander through the daily market in Piazza della Sala, where stalls cluster around a medieval well surrounded by arcades. Here Pistoia shows its living face, amid displays of citrus fruits, cheeses and cured meats from the Pistoiese Apennines.

Pistoia Zoo, founded in 1970, occupies 7 hectares in the northern part of the city and is home to over 500 animals of 100 species. It's known for its endangered species conservation programs and naturalistic habitats, ranking among central Italy's most active zoological institutions.

Walk through the nursery district around Pistoia: the plain between Pistoia and Pescia forms Italy's main ornamental plant nursery zone, exporting millions of plants annually throughout Europe. Marked paths wind through greenhouses and ornamental plant fields from October to April.

The Embroidery Museum (Palazzo Rospigliosi) traces the history of Pistoiese embroidery, a craft of excellence that dressed European courts from the 17th century. The Rospigliosi family, one of whose members became Pope Clement IX in 1667, were among the great patrons of this art.

places.name: Pitigliano

visits.text: Leave Volterra early and cross the Maremma via the SS73, a long 3.5-hour descent south. The road winds between bare hills and holm oak woods, passes through Massa Marittima where you can stop for an hour at the Cathedral of San Cerbone (Pisan-Romanesque facade, scandalous fresco of the Albero della Fecondità painted in 1265 - a tree whose fruits are phalluses, rediscovered under whitewash in 1999). Get back on the road. Pitigliano appears around a bend, 3 miles away: a village carved into a golden yellow tuff cliff, suspended at 1,027 feet above the gorges of the Lente. Visual gut punch.

Pitigliano has been called 'little Jerusalem' since the 19th century. A Jewish community settled here in 1555 after Pope Pius V expelled Jews from the Papal States: the Orsini, local counts, welcomed them and granted them rights. In the 19th century, they represented a fifth of the population. Today only a few families remain, but the ghetto is intact. Descend Via Zuccarelli then Vicolo Manin: the synagogue, founded in 1598 and restored in 1996 after the 1960 collapse, retains its gilded wooden ark and bronze bimah. Combined ticket €5.

Below the synagogue, descend by steep stairs into the underground rooms carved directly from the tuff: unleavened bread oven with its stone still blackened with flour, mikveh (ritual immersion bath) dug in 1598 and fed by rainwater filtered through the rock, kosher wine cellar, and tanning workshop. The Jews of Pitigliano produced a kosher white wine famous throughout central Italy, Bianco di Pitigliano, still vinified today by the Cantina Cooperativa according to rules of ritual purity. Available by the glass in any enoteca in the village.

If you're here between April and October, descend early in the morning to the Via Cava di San Giuseppe, access from the Sovana road, free parking half a mile from the village. Slip into the defile: for half a mile, the vertical tuff walls rise 65 feet high, leaving only a 5-foot-wide corridor in some places. The Etruscans carved these roads between the 7th and 3rd centuries BC with pickaxes, in rock that's soft when wet, hard when dry. No one has pierced their function: funerary routes linking necropolises and villages? Hydraulic drainage? Trade routes? Chthonic rituals to the world of the dead? Hypotheses have accumulated for 150 years. The walls are marked with medieval crosses meant to exorcise a place deemed demonic.

Drive in the afternoon to Sovana, 5.5 miles northwest. The village is just one street, 90 inhabitants. Its Cathedral of San Pietro, built at the end of the 11th century on an Etruscan temple, preserves a Romanesque crypt with columns recycled from Etruscan tombs - capitals carved from inverted cinerary urns. A detail unique in Italy. Sovana is also the birthplace of Hildebrand, who became Pope Gregory VII in 1073, the man who forced Emperor Henry IV to wait three days kneeling in the snow at Canossa in 1077.

Walk a half-mile at the western exit of the village to the Necropoli Etrusca di Sovana, accessible by marked trail. The crown jewel of the site is the Tomba Ildebranda, carved in the 3rd century BC directly into the tuff cliff like a six-columned temple: the rock preserves the capitals, friezes, fragments of stucco painted red and blue. No other Etruscan rock-cut tomb in Italy imitates Greek temple architecture to this extent. Further on, the Tomba della Sirena (winged siren sculpted above the entrance) and the Tomba dei Demoni Alati. Ticket €5, allow 1.5 hours for the complete trail.

activities.text: Try the cucina giudeo-pitiglianese, a unique blend of Jewish tradition and Maremma products. At Hostaria del Ceccottino, Piazza San Gregorio VII, order the sfratti, stick-shaped biscuits invented in the 17th century to recall the bailiff's staff used to evict Jews before they were welcomed - filled with honey, walnuts, orange and nutmeg. They're sold year-round, you bite them like a cultural wafer. The vaulted dining room is carved directly into the tuff, cool in summer at a constant 64°F.

At dusk, exit the village through Porta della Cittadella and walk 200 yards on the panoramic road to Manciano. Turn around, and see Pitigliano all at once, head-on, the cliff lit like a stage set. It's probably the most beautiful sunset over tuff in all of central Italy. Photographers: short lens, golden light, twenty minutes max before everything turns gray.

Tasting at Caseificio Sociale Manciano, on the return road to Pitigliano, open until 6 PM. The pecorino toscano of the Maremma, PDO, is aged in tuff caves: three months for fresh, nine months for aged, eighteen for riserva. Taste all three side by side, it's striking. The cheesemaker cuts with a machete, has you smell, explains. Buy vacuum-sealed to take home, expect €18-25/kg.

Evening in Pitigliano, dinner at La Magica Torre, Via Cavour, panoramic terrace over the Lente valley. Try the buglione di agnello, Maremma lamb stew with white wine and tomato, a centuries-old shepherd recipe. The interior dining room is carved into the tuff, low-vaulted, underground atmosphere.

Dark Tuscany - 7 Days from the Etruscans of Volterra to Occult Rome

map_keywords: Via Cava di San Giuseppe Pitigliano

visits.text: Castello Aragonese di Pizzo—an Aragonese fortress built in 1486 by Ferdinand I on a rocky promontory commanding the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia. In this castle's courtyard, Joachim Murat, King of Naples and Napoleon's brother-in-law, was arrested on October 8, 1815, after attempting to reclaim his throne with 250 men landed from Corsica. Five days later, on October 13, he faced a firing squad at age 48. His detention cell remains preserved with personal artifacts.

Chiesa di Piedigrotta—a cave church carved into the volcanic tuff cliffs at sea level, founded in the 17th century according to legend by Neapolitan sailors shipwrecked here, who sculpted a Virgin into the rock in gratitude. Inside, dozens of tuff sculptures depict religious scenes and contemporary figures, including a 17th-century Pietà and 20th-century additions that blur sacred and secular.

Centro storico di Pizzo—a medieval town perched on 35-meter cliffs, with Piazza della Repubblica surrounded by 18th-century palazzi. The town's fame rests on centuries of bluefin tuna fishing in the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia, with traditional mattanze (collective tuna hunts) documented since the 16th century.

activities.text: Tasting the tartufo di Pizzo—an ice cream creation born in Pizzo in the 1950s: a chocolate-hazelnut gelato sphere with a molten chocolate core, dusted in bitter cocoa. The gelaterias around Piazza della Repubblica still guard the original recipe.
Sunset walk along Pizzo's lungomare with views across the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia to the Aeolian Islands hovering on the horizon.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Calabria Loop: Tyrrhenian and Ionian Coasts

visits.text: Pizzo Calabro is perched on a promontory above the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia, on the Tyrrhenian Sea. Begin with the Castello Murat, an Aragonese fortress built in 1492 by Ferdinand I of Aragon. It was here that Joachim Murat - Napoleon's brother-in-law and King of Naples - met a dramatic end. Landing at Pizzo on October 8, 1815 with 250 men to attempt to reconquer his throne, he was arrested, tried by a military commission, and shot on October 13 in the castle courtyard, just five days after his arrival. The interior museum reconstructs his final moments - he asked to write a last letter to his wife in Trieste, with locks of hair in the envelope.

One kilometer from the center, descend to the Chiesa di Piedigrotta, carved into the tufa just meters from the sea. According to tradition, 17th-century shipwrecked sailors sculpted this chapel to thank the Virgin for their rescue. The interior is populated with statues and bas-reliefs carved directly into the rock - a place between folk art, faith, and geology that resembles nothing else in Italy.
Climb back to the Duomo di San Giorgio Martire, which houses Joachim Murat's tomb, then stroll through the colorful lanes of the historic center, among arches, flowered balconies, and sea views.

activities.text: Settle on Piazza della Repubblica, Pizzo's beating heart, to taste the famous tartufo di Pizzo. This frozen dessert, born in the 1950s from an improvisation by pastry chef Giuseppe De Maria called "Don Pippo" (he had run out of molds and shaped the ice cream by hand), became the first ice cream in Europe to obtain IGP certification. It's a hazelnut and chocolate ice cream hemisphere with a molten chocolate heart, rolled in bitter cocoa. Each artisanal gelateria has its recipe - locals don't agree on the best, but the debate is part of the charm.

End the day at Pizzo beach or the Passerella, a pier offering superb views of the cliffs and castle at sunset. Pizzo is also a tuna fishing port - in the evening, trattorias serve pesce spada (swordfish) and alici (anchovies) freshly caught.

days_plan.itin_title: Calabria: From Cosenza to Reggio, Between Mountains and Ionian Sea

places.name: Poggio A Caiano

visits.text: The Villa Medici at Poggio a Caiano, designed by Giuliano da Sangallo for Lorenzo the Magnificent beginning in 1485 and completed under Pope Leo X in 1519, is the prototype of the Renaissance villa: raised on an arcaded podium with an Ionic loggia on the facade, it established the relationship between building and landscape that would influence all European villas for two centuries, including Palladio's. A UNESCO site since 2013, it was the scene of three historic Medici marriages: Alessandro de' Medici and Margaret of Austria (1536), Cosimo I and Eleanor of Toledo (1539), Francesco I and Bianca Cappello (1579).

The Salone di Leone X, on the first floor, houses one of the most important fresco cycles of Florentine Mannerism. The painters were summoned under Leo X (son of Lorenzo the Magnificent) around 1520 according to a program by Paolo Giovio: Pontormo painted Vertumnus and Pomona (an allegory of the seasons and agriculture), Franciabigio the Triumph of Cicero, Andrea del Sarto the Tribute to Caesar (alluding to gifts received by Lorenzo from the Sultan of Egypt in 1487). Leo X died in 1521, the works stopped. They were only completed in 1578-1582 by Alessandro Allori under Francesco I. Since 2007, the second floor houses the Museum of Still Lifes: 200 paintings from the late 16th to mid-18th century from the Medici collections.

activities.text: Walk in the villa park and visit the former stables renovated in 2000. The garden preserves rare plant species and terracotta statues. The complex includes the Cascine di Tavola—Medici agricultural estate—which defined the model of the 'villa-azienda' combining prestigious residence with productive rural exploitation.

places.name: Polenta

visits.text: Perched on a hill 5 km from Bertinoro, the Pieve di San Donato in Polenta is a Romanesque basilica predating the 10th century. Giosuè Carducci dedicated a famous poem to it. The building is austere, in stone, with a small squat bell tower. The view over the Romagna hills from the churchyard is magnificent. Free access.

activities.text: Spot the cipresso della Francesca, a centuries-old tree linked to the legend of Francesca da Rimini mentioned by Dante. The road from Bertinoro crosses vineyards of Sangiovese and Albana. Return by the same route in 10 minutes.

visits.text: A 13th-century castle transformed into a temple of culatello: the Antica Corte Pallavicina in Polesine houses the Museo del Culatello e del Masalén. The Spigaroli family, former tenant farmers of Verdi, restored the place over twenty years. In the great underground hall, hundreds of culatelli hang from the vaulted ceiling.

The Spigaroli family, former tenant farmers of Verdi turned restaurateurs, raise the maiale nero di Parma on site. The museum tells the complete cycle: territory, fog, salt from Salsomaggiore, the art of the norcin. The Card of the Musei del Cibo grants access to seven food museums across the province.

activities.text: Book a culatello tasting at the Antica Corte Pallavicina: you'll taste the difference between maiale rosa and nero. The DOP culatello can only be produced in eight communes of the Bassa. Expect about 15-20 euros per person for a full platter.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

places.name: Polignano A Mare

visits.text: Lama Monachile lives up to its reputation: a pebble cove wedged between two cliffs at the mouth of an ancient stream bed carved through limestone. The name is said to derive from the monk seals that once frequented these caves. The Bourbon bridge arching above it, some fifteen meters high, dates from the early 19th century. In August the beach is packed by 9am: come at sunrise or resign yourself to standing.

Built in the 13th century and consecrated around 1500, the Chiesa Matrice Santa Maria Assunta faces Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II, known locally as the Clock Square because of the neighboring Casa dell'Orologio, which once housed the university. Apulian Romanesque on the outside, reworked within. Polignano's historic center has no great monument to tick off: it's a backdrop, not a museum. Step in, then step back out and wander.

The locals simply call them the poems: the verses painted on steps, doors, and walls throughout the historic center are the work of Guido Lupori, known as Guido il Flâneur, who started in 1984. Even the Mark Twain quote on one wall is his, and Twain never set foot here. Look for them by lifting your eyes; most visitors walk right past.

A three-meter bronze figure with arms flung wide, which sounds excessive, and yet the statue of Domenico Modugno works. The singer of Nel blu dipinto di blu, better known as Volare, was born here in 1928; Hermann Mejer's sculpture shows him facing the Adriatic, jacket catching the wind. It stands on the seafront promenade that bears his name, two minutes from Lama Monachile. Queues for photos form in the late afternoon.

The Museo Pino Pascali on Lungomare Cristoforo Colombo is the contemporary art stop nobody expects to find in Polignano. The museum is named after an Apulian artist and also hosts temporary exhibitions. It's small, air-conditioned, and quiet when the town is heaving: the right move during the hot hours, between 2pm and 5pm.

activities.text: Touristy, but the only real way to see Polignano: a boat trip along the sea caves that pierce the cliff face, including the famous Grotta Palazzese, home to the cliff-side restaurant. From the water, you understand why the white houses seem to float in midair. Departures from the harbor in late afternoon for the best light. Rough seas mean cancellation, so build in a backup plan.

The caffè speciale smells of almond and cream before it even reaches you: it's Polignano's specialty, served at the counter in bars throughout the center. Another local curiosity is the carota di Polignano, a Slow Food Presidium since 2013, worth tasting raw from market stalls. And yes, the octopus sandwich at Pescaria is worth the queue, just not at 1pm.

visits.text: The Istituto Lama Tzong Khapa, founded in 1977 by Lamas Thubten Yeshe and Thubten Zopa Rinpoche, is Europe's largest center for Tibetan Buddhist studies. It bears the name of Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelugpa monastic order. The Dalai Lama has taught here on several occasions. The library, meditation halls, gompa (prayer room), and retreat cottages spread across the Pisan hills 40 km south of Pisa. Courses in Buddhist philosophy, psychology, and meditation are offered year-round.

The statue of Cenresig (Avalokiteshvara, the Buddha of Compassion), inaugurated by the Dalai Lama in June 2014, is the tallest in Europe. Its story is singular: created by film set designer Dante Ferretti for Martin Scorsese's Kundun (1997), it risked destruction after filming in Morocco. Saved and transported to Italy, it was restored by sculptor Alessio Pazzini according to strict Buddhist iconographic canons.

activities.text: Participate in a guided meditation session in the institute's gompa, open to visitors on certain days according to the Tibetan calendar. Prayer flags, white stupas, and prayer wheels surrounding the main building create an unexpected atmosphere in the heart of Tuscany.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

visits.text: Locals call it the little Sabbioneta: in 1579, Giulio Cesare Gonzaga redesigned Pomponesco as his 'ideal city,' with a hexagonal castle and a grid of symmetrical streets. The castle was razed by the French, but Piazza XXIII Aprile remains intact, lined with porticoes and colorful houses.

If Bertolucci chose it as the backdrop for 'Novecento,' it's no accident. Pomponesco is among the Borghi più belli d'Italia. The 14th-century church of Santa Felicita and the Gonzaga stables frame the square. Few tourists, plenty of charm.

activities.text: Climb the argine to photograph the colorful houses from above. The Riserva naturale della Garzaia, 96 hectares of golenale zone, shelters herons and black-winged stilts. Marked trails along the Po.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

visits.text: The bell tower of Pomposa Abbey rises from the green plain like a brick lighthouse. Founded in the 6th-7th centuries on the Insula Pomposia, a wooded island between two branches of the Po, the abbey reached its zenith under Abbot San Guido after the year 1000. The mosaic pavement of the basilica blends geometric patterns with fantastic animals. Ticket €3.

It was here that the monk Guido of Arezzo invented the musical notation based on seven notes. The Sala Capitolare preserves frescoes by a direct pupil of Giotto, featuring a Crucifixion and figures of apostles. The refectory displays a cycle attributed to a master close to the Rimini school.

Opposite the basilica, the Palazzo della Ragione was used to administer justice in the 11th century. Today it houses the museo pomposiano: capitals, bas-reliefs, sacred objects. Small but dense. Included in the entrance ticket.

activities.text: Reach Pomposa by bike from Codigoro via the dedicated cycle path (5 km). Along the route, murals from Giorgio Bassani's literary itinerary adorn the town walls. Return the same way or by taxibus 638.

days_plan.itin_title: From Ferrara to the Delta in 5 Days: Delizie, Ravenna, and Bertinoro

visits.text: The Roman bridge at Pont-Saint-Martin, built around the 1st century BC under Augustus to span the Lys torrent, stands as one of Italy's best-preserved Roman arches. Anchored directly into bedrock on both banks, it soars 82 feet above the water with a single span stretching 115 feet. At its base, you can still see slots carved into the rock where wooden support beams were fitted during construction. The bridge formed part of the Route des Gaules linking Eporedia (Ivrea) to Augusta Praetoria (Aosta), then onward to the Great and Little Saint Bernard passes. Though replaced for traffic in 1836, it survived even the Allied bombing of May 25, 1944, which devastated much of the village. Legend, celebrated annually during the historic carnival, tells how Saint Martin negotiated the bridge's construction with the devil: he threw bread across the gorge, and a starving dog raced over first, claiming the promised soul. Outwitted, the devil vanished into the Lys waters.

Fort Bard rises from a rock outcrop commanding the valley's narrowest point. The first defensive works date to the 10th century (first documented in 1034, belonging to Viscount Boso of Aosta). In May 1800, the fort—defended by just 400 soldiers under Captain Stockard von Bernkopf—held up Napoleon's reserve army for two weeks, forcing 40,000 men and 50 cannons to bypass the fortress under cover of night, their cannon wheels wrapped in hay to muffle the sound. Napoleon ordered the fort razed after his victory. King Charles Albert of Sardinia had it rebuilt between 1830 and 1838, designed by engineer Francesco Antonio Olivero. Decommissioned in 1975, purchased by the Region in 1990, and renovated over 10 years at a cost of 45 million euros, it reopened in 2006 as a cultural hub. The Museum of the Alps (in the Carlo Alberto building) offers an interactive journey through Alpine geography, cultures, and glaciers from Slovenia to France. The medieval village of Bard at its foot is accessible by panoramic elevator.

Two miles from the fort at Donnas, the Route des Gaules is carved directly through living rock for 725 feet, topped by an arched passage 13 feet thick, 13 feet high, and nearly 10 feet wide. It's one of the most spectacular testimonies to Roman road engineering in the Alps, still visible in its original state.

activities.text: Hike in Mont Avic Natural Park, established in 1989 and accessible from Pont-Saint-Martin: over 30 lakes and peat bogs, vast Swiss pine forests, wild landscapes untouched by tourist infrastructure. One of the Aosta Valley's most pristine natural spaces.

Historic Carnival of Pont-Saint-Martin (February/March): over 1,000 costumed performers recreate the town's Roman history. On Shrove Tuesday night, an effigy of the devil is burned beneath the Roman bridge arch in a spectacular pyrotechnic display.

days_plan.itin_title: Aosta Valley Circuit: From Roman Gateway to Mont Blanc

places.name: Ponte Ciolo

visits.text: Suspended about thirty meters above a steep-sided fjord, the Ponte del Ciolo, in Gagliano del Capo, offers one of the most striking panoramas on the coast. A long flight of steps descends to a small pebble cove. The name comes from the magpies that nested in the crevices.

activities.text: Spectacular but dangerous: dives from the Ponte del Ciolo regularly cause serious injuries, including a serious accident in July 2026. Stick to swimming from the cove and the hiking trail along the gorge. Don't jump, despite the temptation.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce

map_keywords: Ponte del Ciolo Gagliano del Capo

visits.text: Pontremoli is Tuscany's northernmost town, nestled at the foot of the Apennines on the border with Liguria and Emilia-Romagna. This ancient stop on the Via Francigena - the medieval pilgrimage route between Canterbury and Rome - retains its historic centre crossed by the Magra river and its tributaries, spanned by medieval stone bridges. Start by climbing to the Castello del Piagnaro, whose name comes from the 'piagne', sandstone slabs used for roofing in Lunigiana. Built around the year 1000 to control the mountain passes, this castle dominates the village and houses the Museum of Lunigiana Statue-Menhirs, founded in 1975 by Professor Augusto Cesare Ambrosi.

The museum displays over 80 statue-menhirs, human figures carved from sandstone between the 4th and 1st millennium BC - one of Europe's most important collections of megalithic art. These abstract silhouettes, with their 'carabiniere hat' shaped heads and U-shaped faces, represent men armed with daggers and women adorned with jewellery. Their exact meaning remains partly enigmatic: protective deities? Ancestors? Territorial markers? The museum staging, renovated in 2015, plunges the statues into semi-darkness with lighting that reveals every detail - allow a good hour to explore thoroughly.

Descend into Pontremoli's centre to visit the Duomo, designed in the 17th century by Alessandro Capra from Cremona, with its broad dome and Latin cross plan. On the edge of town, stop at the church of the Santissima Annunziata, which preserves a small polychrome marble temple attributed to Jacopo Sansovino. Then wander through the medieval alleys, beneath the arcades, among the stone bridges and towers - Pontremoli has retained its authentic atmosphere as a pilgrims' staging post on the road to Rome.

activities.text: Spend your evening in Pontremoli savouring testaroli, Lunigiana's absolute speciality. These are thick pancakes made from flour and water, cooked between two scorching cast-iron plates (the 'testi'), then cut and reheated in boiling water like pasta, served with pesto, olive oil or pecorino cheese. It's one of Italy's most ancient dishes - some consider it the ancestor of all pasta.

If you arrive early in the day and weather permits, push on to the Giaredo gorges just outside Pontremoli - a succession of canyons where the Gordana torrent has carved the rock for dozens of metres. The path follows the cliff walls and offers total escapism. Allow 1.5 hours return for the section accessible without equipment.

days_plan.itin_title: From Lunigiana to Cinque Terre: Between Tuscany and Liguria

visits.text: Crossing and Porto di Ponza — Ferry from Formia (2h30 on traghetto, 1h15 on aliscafo) to the largest of the Pontine Islands (2.9 sq mi, 928 feet at Monte La Guardia). The porto borbonico (1772-1793), built on a Roman port by Ferdinand IV's engineers (Antonio Winspeare and Francesco Carpi), is an amphitheater of colorful houses—one of the Mediterranean's most beautiful boat arrivals. The island, inhabited since the Neolithic, was colonized by the Phoenicians, then the Greeks (8th century BC), then the Romans (312 BC) who made it a resort and exile destination. Benedictine monks founded the abbey of Santa Maria, destroyed by Saracens. After centuries of pirate raids (the Turks blew up the port tower in 1655), the Bourbons repopulated the island in 1771 with settlers from Ischia (20 boats) and Torre del Greco (50 boats for coral fishing). Ischian surnames (Scotto, Migliaccio, Mazzella) and the Neapolitan dialect survive.

Grotte di Pilato and island tour — Hypogean and underwater archaeological complex from the 1st century AD: 5 caves carved into the tuff, connected by underwater tunnels and an external basin. Called 'Antico Murenaio Romano': the Romans bred moray eels here, a sacred fish. The main basin had 5 openings closed by sluice gates (saracinesche) to control water and transfer fish. In 1997, at the bottom of the main cave, a white marble statue (Apollo or Dionysus), a tuff altar and oil lamps were discovered—suggesting cultic use. The caves were connected by a stairway to Emperor Augustus's villa on the Collina della Madonna. The name 'Pilato' comes from a legend: young Pontius Pilate, a Roman noble, was sent to Ponza to quell a revolt and gained his surname before being sent to Palestine. The Cisterna della Dragonara (town center) is one of three large Roman cisterns. Continuing the tour by gozzo: Chiaia di Luna (white tuff cliff in a half-moon, 330 feet high), Piscine Naturali (volcanic rock pools), Cala Feola (only sandy beach), Faraglioni della Madonna.

activities.text: Climb the colorful lanes of the centro: church of SS. Silverio e Domitilla, Giardino Botanico. Rent a gozzo (~€80-150/day) or take an organized excursion for the island tour.

Gozzo tour with swimming stop at Grotte di Pilato (mask and snorkel to explore underwater tunnels). Chiaia di Luna for the monumental cliff. Swimming at Piscine Naturali. Fish dinner at sunset on the port.

days_plan.itin_title: Ulysses Riviera: Secret Gardens, Ancient Caves & Southern Lazio Islands
Hidden Beaches in Italy: Secluded Coves and Turquoise Waters

visits.text: Castle of the Conti Guidi of Poppi: first mentioned in writing in 1169, when it belonged to the abbey of San Fidele di Strumi. By the late 12th century, it had passed to the Conti Guidi, a feudal family whose territories stretched from the banks of the Po to the Apennines. The tower and keep were erected in the second half of the 13th century — the architect Arnolfo di Cambio is said to have used it as a prototype for the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence, which he designed shortly after. The Guidi Chapel is covered in frescoes by Taddeo Gaddi, a pupil of Giotto. Dante took refuge in the castle of Poppi during his exile, in 1307 and again in 1311; tradition holds that he composed Canto XXXIII of the Inferno here, dedicated to Count Ugolino della Gherardesca. A bust of the poet on the square before the castle recalls this connection. In 1440, the Guidi sided with the Milanese at Anghiari and were exiled, ending 350 years of dominion over the Casentino.

Pieve di San Pietro a Romena: one of the finest Romanesque parish churches in the Casentino, 5 km from Poppi in the commune of Pratovecchio. Tradition holds it was built at the request of Countess Matilda of Canossa. Dante mentions it in the Divine Comedy (Canto XXX of the Inferno), in connection with the counterfeiting of gold florins carried out at the nearby castle of Romena by Master Adam of Brescia on behalf of the Guidi di Romena — around 1280 at least. The sandstone building, with its three apses and plain facade, is a representative example of Tuscan Romanesque architecture.

Castello di Romena: a Conti Guidi di Romena fortress founded by the Marquises of Spoleto probably in the 11th century, atop a 626-meter hill. The castle reached its peak in the 13th century, in Dante's time. It retains three large fortified towers and the remains of three concentric walls. In 1902, the poet Gabriele d'Annunzio stayed there as a guest of the Goretti counts and wrote part of Alcyone.

Pratovecchio: birthplace of Paolo di Dono, known as Paolo Uccello (c. 1397), master of Renaissance perspective. The medieval village houses two convents of Camaldolese and Dominican nuns, and several remarkable artworks in its churches. The castle of Porciano, a 13th-century Guidi fortress, commands the valley from a neighboring hill.

activities.text: Hike in the Casentino Forests National Park from Poppi: the park, covering the forested massifs between Tuscany and Romagna, is one of the best-preserved forests in central Italy. Deer, wild boar, wolves and golden eagles inhabit these beech and fir woods. The Sasso Fratino Integral Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is off-limits to the public, but peripheral trails cross ancient-growth forests.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

places.name: Porlezza

visits.text: Explore the Grotte di Rescia, a fascinating system of natural cavities rich in stalactites and stalagmites bearing witness to millennia of geological activity. This underground spectacle offers a unique experience among limestone formations of bizarre and evocative shapes, wrapped in an atmosphere of mystery and natural wonder.

Visit the Church of San Vittore il Moro, the religious heart of the Porlezza community built in the seventeenth century over a pre-existing fifth-century structure. Inside you can admire the frescoes by Giulio Quaglio di Laino depicting episodes from the saint's life, a precious Baroque altar, eighteenth-century stuccowork and fine wooden sculptures.

Discover the Oratory of San Maurizio Martire, a small church set just outside the centre that still preserves its original layout. This gem of religious architecture is a precious testimony to local devotion through the centuries.

activities.text: Enjoy the Lombard shore of Lake Lugano, a body of water shared between Italy and Switzerland offering views of rare beauty. Porlezza is a renowned holiday resort prized for its crystal-clear waters, equipped beaches and relaxed atmosphere that draws visitors from all over Europe.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona

map_keywords: Chiesa San Vittore il Moro Porlezza

visits.text: Terme di Porretta - a spa town in the upper Reno valley, whose sulfurous waters have been known since antiquity and exploited in organized fashion since the 14th century. The current spa buildings, built in late-19th and early-20th-century liberty style, offer treatments for respiratory and digestive ailments. The town developed as a resort for the Bolognese bourgeoisie from 1864 onward with the opening of the Porrettana railway line.

activities.text: Take the waters at the Porretta spa—treatments using sulfurous-saline-bromine-iodine waters recommended for respiratory conditions, open March to November.

Discover the Porretta Soul Festival—since 1959, every July Porretta Terme has hosted a soul, rhythm and blues, and gospel festival that drew artists including James Brown, Otis Redding, and Wilson Pickett. The festival, born from a local spa doctor's passion for African-American music, is now one of Europe's oldest soul festivals.
Hike the waymarked trails through the Reno valley from Porretta—chestnut and oak forests, perched villages, and views to the Apennine ridge.

days_plan.itin_title: 10 Natural Wonders Around Bologna

places.name: Porto Cervo

visits.text: Porto Cervo was designed by architect Luigi Vietti and inaugurated in 1964, two years after the creation of the Consorzio Costa Smeralda on March 14, 1962, by Prince Karim Aga Khan IV. The Aga Khan had discovered these deserted shores in the late 1950s aboard a 12-meter sailboat and decided to create an anti-Côte d'Azur. The Consorzio still manages 3,114 hectares today, of which 96% remain undeveloped.

The Stella Maris church, designed by architect Michele Busiri Vici and inaugurated in 1968, overlooks Porto Cervo's old harbor from its hilltop. Its clean white facade and square bell tower exemplify the pan-Mediterranean style the Aga Khan wanted so that each building would integrate with the granite landscape.

Spiaggia del Principe (Prince's Beach) is said to have been the Aga Khan's favorite beach, where he regularly went with his architects during the site's early explorations. Accessible via a 10-minute walk from the road, its intense blue-green waters are framed by pink granite rocks.
Capriccioli Beach, at the back of a sheltered bay, is a succession of small coves separated by rocks you walk along. Its shallow, clear waters make it an excellent snorkeling spot.
Liscia Ruja is the longest beach on the Costa Smeralda at about 800 meters of golden sand. Bordered by juniper and mastic trees, it faces the Mortorio and Soffi islets in the open sea.

activities.text: Stroll through Porto Cervo's piazzetta, the heart of the village designed by Vietti in 1964, whose arcades and white-plastered facades reproduce the vernacular architecture of Gallura.
Swimming and snorkeling in the Costa Smeralda's coves — Capriccioli and Spiaggia del Principe count among the clearest seabeds in the Mediterranean.
Visit the village of San Pantaleo, 10 km inland, a pink granite village with narrow alleys known for its craft market and local artists' galleries.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Sardinia Coast: Beaches & Hidden Coves

map_keywords: Piazzetta di Porto Cervo Porto Cervo

visits.text: Shallow and transparent water for kilometers: Porto Cesareo stretches along a marine protected area created in 1997, one of the richest in Salento. A marine biology museum completes the visit. The village lives around its fishermen and fishmongers. Ideal for a fresh fish lunch.

activities.text: Walk across to the Isola dei Conigli: the depth barely exceeds a meter between the coast and this white sand island, also reachable by pedal boat or canoe. No shops on site—the island is protected. Bring water and parasol, and leave no trash.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce

visits.text: Porto Ercole is guarded by three Spanish fortresses built in the 16th century during the Hispanic domination of the State of Presidi. Forte Stella—whose six-pointed star shape allowed enemy targeting from each point—was begun in 1548 by Giovan Battista Belluzzi and completed by Giovanni Camerini under Cosimo I de' Medici; it's the most accessible and most photographed. The Rocca Spagnola, an irregular four-bastion star form, dominates the borgo antico. Forte Filippo, on the northern promontory, was built for Philip II of Spain according to a design by Giovanni Camerini.

The borgo antico of Porto Ercole, accessible only on foot from the Porta Pisana topped by a clock tower, is a labyrinth of alleys and staircases clinging to the hillside. Piazza Santa Barbara, above the bastion of the same name, offers the village's most iconic panorama over the bay and fortresses. The Palazzo dei Governatori, built in the early 16th century under Siena, served as residence of the Spanish commander and then the summer governor of the State of Presidi. The church of Sant'Erasmo (17th century), at the village's highest point, is the tallest building.

Caravaggio died in Porto Ercole on July 18, 1610, at age 39, in circumstances still debated. Fleeing a death sentence for murder, he had left Naples with three paintings intended for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, the price of an expected papal pardon. His death certificate, found in 2001 in the Sant'Erasmo parish register, indicates he died at the Hospital of Santa Maria Ausiliatrice, probably from malaria. A monument honors him in the historic center.

activities.text: The Duna Feniglia Nature Reserve is a wooded dune 6 km long separating the open sea from the Orbetello lagoon. A dirt path traverses it under pines, inhabited by semi-wild fallow deer. According to local tradition, it was on this beach that Caravaggio was found dying in 1610—though his death certificate found in 2001 indicates he died in hospital, the exact circumstances remaining debated. Car access is prohibited: the dune is explored on foot or by bicycle.

Orbetello, a town perched on the narrow sand strip between the two tomboli of Argentario, is a discovery in its own right: 16th-century Spanish walls, compact old town, lagoon classified as a nature reserve (flamingos, herons, egrets). From the lagoon's edge, the view of Monte Argentario's green promontory rising from the sea is one of the most beautiful on the Tuscan coast.

Spiaggia Lunga beach, accessible from Porto Ercole by a steep path descending behind Forte Stella. Sand and pebble beach below the fortress, surrounded by Mediterranean scrub. Further along the same trail, the Acqua Dolce beach, accessible behind the Hotel Pellicano, is one of Argentario's most preserved coves.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Grosseto Province

visits.text: A stone bouncer has guarded this cove for almost a thousand years: the Abbazia di Santo Stefano, founded in 1086 by Goffredo, count of Conversano, planted on a peninsula above the sand. Below, Porto Ghiacciolo, whose name (ice cube) is no joke: cold springs rise here, and the contrast wakes you upon entering the water. Small sheltered beach, sandy bottom, good spot for snorkeling. Arrive early in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Bari, Castel del Monte, Matera: 14 Days Through the Murgia
Puglia: Terra di Bari in 9 Days, Castel del Monte

places.name: Porto Miggiano

visits.text: The Cala di Porto Miggiano is the most sheltered swim on this stretch of coast, and the only true cove between the cliffs of Santa Cesarea Terme and Castro. You go down by a staircase cut into the rock. Sand is scarce and rock dominates.

activities.text: In August, get there before 9am: the cove is small and fills up fast. Rock shoes are useful, as you enter the water from the platforms. The car park above charges in season and sits a few hundred metres away.

Walk through Mediterranean scrubland and pine forests.

activities.text: Discovery of sea caves and swimming in the clear waters of Salento.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Beaches in Italy: Secluded Coves and Turquoise Waters

visits.text: Portofino, let's be clear: it's touristy, it's expensive, and it's still absolutely beautiful. One hundred eighty year-round residents, multiplied by fifty in summer, horseshoe harbor lined with tall ochre and pink houses that have served as backdrop for at least thirty films since the 1950s. The harbor Piazzetta is the village's only real square, twelve cafés lined up where a Negroni costs €22 - fair warning. Park obligatorily in the upper lot (€5/hour!), or come by boat from Santa Margherita (10 min, €5). Coming by car would be masochistic.

Castello Brown dominates the harbor at 70m elevation, a former 16th-century Genoese fort purchased in 1867 by British consul Montagu Yeats Brown - who transformed it into a private residence. Sold to the municipality in 1949, opened to the public since 1961. Two floors of rooms with period furniture, changing temporary exhibitions, and above all a high terrace with plunging views over the bay. Rate €5, closed certain Mondays off-season. Allow 30 minutes for the visit, 15 minutes more to catch your breath on the terrace.

The path to Portofino Lighthouse starts from Castello Brown and continues south for 800m, carved into the cliff above the sea. Allow 20 minutes of easy walking, open views over the Gulf of Tigullio all the way to La Spezia in clear weather. The lighthouse itself isn't visitable - it's an automated building in service since 1917. But the bar-viewpoint just before serves an Aperol spritz for €12 with probably the best view in Liguria. Shameless and deserved. Avoid midday, the path is exposed full south.

San Giorgio church, above the harbor, is so discreet you easily miss it. First building from the 12th century, rebuilt after 1944 bombing. Inside are preserved relics attributed to Saint George, brought back from the Holy Land by Genoese crusaders in 1098 - hence the name. Small, unadorned, absolute calm after the Piazzetta chaos below. Festa di San Giorgio on April 23, procession, fireworks, probably the only day the village is still Italian and not international.

activities.text: The Portofino Regional Park comprises 1,200 hectares of wooded promontory created in 1935 - one of Italy's oldest protected areas. Over 80 km of marked trails. The classic hike: Portofino - Pietre Strette - San Fruttuoso (2.5 hours one way, 350m elevation gain, red-white trail), return by boat or same path. Forests of holm oak and maritime pine, clear views over both sides of the promontory. Water and serious hiking shoes required, the terrain becomes rocky in places. Free maps at Portofino tourist office.

If Portofino has wrung out your wallet, Santa Margherita Ligure 5 km to the north is the perfect antidote: elegant seaside resort but 30% cheaper, real neighborhood life behind the palm trees, covered food market every morning (except Sunday). Vittorio Veneto seafront promenade, gelato at Centrale (since 1964), aperitivo on Piazza Caprera. Direct train from Genova-Brignole in 35 minutes - ideal alternative base for those who don't want to sleep in Portofino itself.

days_plan.itin_title: Genoa to Sestri Levante via the Tigullio: 2 Days on the Riviera di Levante
Deep Dive into Tigullio & Golfo Paradiso: 3 Days on the Eastern Riviera
Riviera di Levante in 1 Days - Tigullio Essentials

visits.text: Today, dedicate the entire day to Portovenere and Palmaria island - take your time. Portovenere is UNESCO-listed alongside Cinque Terre. A practical tip: the access road is a dead-end often jammed in summer. Arrive early morning, or better still, take the boat from La Spezia (regular shuttles, 30 minutes). The village stretches along a row of medieval tower-houses with colourful facades, squeezed together facing the harbour. This 'palazzata' - continuous facade of fortified houses - served as a defensive wall on the sea side.

Climb to the church of San Pietro, perched on a rocky spur at the tip of the promontory - built in the 13th century in black and white marble in the Ligurian Gothic style, it overlooks the sea with Palmaria island as backdrop. The spot is extraordinary at sunset, but even in daylight the light on the rocks and sea is striking. Below, the Grotta Arpaia (known as 'Byron's Cave') is a natural cavity where the English poet Lord Byron came to meditate and swim - he swam across the gulf to Lerici, according to legend.

Climb up to the Castello Doria, a 12th-century Genoese fortress dominating the village from the hilltop. The view from the ramparts embraces the entire Gulf of Poets, Palmaria island and, on clear days, the Cinque Terre coast to the north. Descending, stroll along Via Capellini, the village's main street, lined with shops and trattorias.

activities.text: In the afternoon, take the boat from Portovenere harbour to Palmaria island (5-minute crossing). It's the largest of the Ligurian islands, UNESCO-listed. The island offers hiking trails through Mediterranean maquis, swimming coves accessible on foot, and the Grotta Azzurra (Blue Grotto), visitable by boat. The path circling the island takes about 2 hours - otherwise, just enjoy the cove on the Portovenere side for a swim. Last boat back around 6pm in summer.

Dine in Portovenere as evening falls, facing the harbour. Ligurian specialities are essential: focaccia, trofie with pesto, fritto misto of gulf fish, Monterosso anchovies. The waterfront terraces are magical when the lights from the tower-houses reflect in the harbour.

days_plan.itin_title: From Lunigiana to Cinque Terre: Between Tuscany and Liguria

places.name: Positano

visits.text: Drive up to Ravello first thing in the morning, perched 350 meters above the sea, 7 km from Amalfi. Villa Rufolo, built in the 13th century, inspired Richard Wagner for Klingsor's garden in Parsifal—he stayed there in 1880. Every summer, a classical music festival is held there on a terrace suspended above the sea. The gardens, with their medieval towers and palm trees, offer a vertiginous panorama over the Gulf of Salerno.

A few minutes' walk away, Villa Cimbrone boasts the famous Terrazza dell'Infinito—the Terrace of Infinity. Bordered by 18th-century marble busts, it overlooks the sea from 350 meters high. Gore Vidal, who stayed there regularly, described it as the most beautiful view in the world. The gardens mix statues, neoclassical temples, and grottoes in a romantic setting. Arrive early—the terrace fills up quickly.

Head back down toward the coast and stop at the Grotta dello Smeraldo (Emerald Grotto) at Conca dei Marini, 4 km from Amalfi. This sea cave, discovered in 1932, owes its name to the emerald color the water takes under the effect of light filtering through an underwater opening. You reach it by elevator carved into the cliff or by boat from the sea. Inside, stalactites and stalagmites frame a turquoise pool.

Continue west on the SS163. Stop at Praiano, between Amalfi and Positano. This village clinging to the mountain is far less touristy than its neighbors. The church of San Gennaro, with its colorful majolica dome, dominates a small square from which the view over the coast is superb. Below, the cove of Marina di Praia—a tiny beach squeezed between two cliffs—is one of the coast's most photogenic spots.

Devote the morning to Positano itself. The former fishing village became a chic resort in the 1950s when writer John Steinbeck introduced it to the world in an article for Harper's Bazaar. Stroll the stepped lanes among artisan shops, art galleries, and bougainvillea. For more tranquility, follow the cliff west to Fornillo beach, smaller and less crowded than Spiaggia Grande.

activities.text: Arrive in Positano late afternoon. Descend the stairs to the Chiesa di Santa Maria Assunta, recognizable by its yellow, green, and blue majolica dome gleaming in the sun. Inside, a 13th-century Byzantine icon of the Black Madonna. Continue to Spiaggia Grande to enjoy the golden evening light on the village—this is when the colors are most beautiful and the crowds begin to disperse.

Set out on the Sentiero degli Dei (Path of the Gods), one of Italy's most beautiful hikes. The 7-km trail links Bomerano (hamlet of Agerola) to Nocelle (above Positano), at 630 meters altitude. Allow 2 to 3 hours walking on a moderate-difficulty path, among rosemary bushes, olive trees, and vertiginous coastal panoramas. Legend has it that this path was traced by gods descending from heaven to save Ulysses from the sirens' song. From Nocelle, 1,700 steps descend to Positano.

Late in the day, treat yourself to a tasting of artisanal limoncello. The Amalfi Coast produces sfusato amalfitano lemons, larger and more fragrant than ordinary lemons. Limoncello is prepared by macerating the zest in pure alcohol for at least a month. Several local producers offer tastings accompanied by lemon cakes—a gentle end to the day after the morning's exertion.

visits.text: Isola di Dino - a 50-hectare limestone island 400 meters offshore from Praia a Mare, accessible only by boat. The system of sea caves perforating the island includes the Grotta Azzurra, whose waters glow electric blue through light refraction on the white seabed - a phenomenon comparable to Capri's famous Blue Grotto.

activities.text: Boat excursion around Isola di Dino with swimming stops in hidden coves and a visit to the Grotta Azzurra - departures from Praia a Mare beach.
