visits.text: Rosazza is a village of about a hundred inhabitants in the upper Cervo valley (province of Biella), carved from local syenite. It owes its fame to Federico Rosazza Pistolet (1813-1899), Kingdom senator, Mazzinian philanthropist, and Grand Master of Biellese freemasonry. After the deaths of his wife and daughter, he devoted the last thirty years of his life to architecturally refounding his native village, in collaboration with painter-architect Giuseppe Maffei, according to an aesthetic blending Masonic symbolism and romantic neo-Gothic style. Today Rosazza is twinned with Rennes-le-Château in France.

Decipher the symbols carved into every building: compasses and squares, five-petaled roses (lodge emblem), hourglasses, five-pointed stars, and a swastika - a Neolithic cosmic symbol used by freemasons - adorn the facade of the parish church of Saints Peter and George, built between 1876 and 1880 on a former cemetery. Its interior ceiling is painted midnight blue and scattered with thousands of stars, like an invitation to spiritual elevation. The church connects to the village by a bridge decorated with crosses and five-pointed stars.

Federico Rosazza's neo-Gothic castle, completed in 1899 the year of his death, is a labyrinth of esoteric references with its false romantic ruins, high tower, and moss-covered walls - a composition seemingly extracted from a fantasized medieval tale. The monumental cemetery, accessible via a three-arch stone bridge adorned with hourglasses, houses the Rosazza family tombs in a setting of crypts and Masonic funerary symbolism. The Palazzo Comunale, where Rosazza held his lodge meetings, still houses period decor.

activities.text: From Rosazza, panoramic road to the Sanctuary of Oropa (one of Italy's most important Marian sanctuaries, at 891 meters) via a road built between 1889 and 1898 by Federico Rosazza himself, passing through a 367-meter gallery dug by hand. Hike to the alpine pastures and Alpe Desate.

days_plan.itin_title: Piedmont's Most Beautiful Villages in 2 Weeks

visits.text: Roscigno Vecchia is a ghost village in Cilento, abandoned since 1902 by civil engineering order: the hill was sliding inexorably, threatening the houses. Residents were relocated 2 km uphill to Roscigno Nuova. The old village remained frozen in its early-20th-century state: central square with centuries-old plane trees, San Nicola church, fountain and public washhouse, stone houses with sealed doors. Nicknamed 'Pompeii of the 20th century.' For decades, a single resident—Giuseppe Spagnuolo, who died in 2024 at 87—refused to leave, gave tours to tourists, fed the cats. Since his death, the village is totally empty permanently, tended by volunteers who open a few house-museums during the day. Atmosphere unique in Italy, UNESCO-listed.

The Museum of Peasant Culture, in one of the village's restored houses, displays the tools, clothing, and furniture of Cilento peasant life before rural exodus. Modest but touching. Run by volunteers, variable hours.

activities.text: Silent stroll through the empty lanes. A few houses under restoration now host artist residencies. If you meet one at work, ask for a visit—they're usually delighted to talk.

days_plan.itin_title: Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: This is the best-preserved Matildic castle in the entire network. The Castello di Rossena, built around 960 by Adalberto Atto (Matilda's great-great-grandfather), raises its 21 rooms on an ophiolitic cliff 2 km from Canossa. Restored in 1999 for over €2 million, it also houses a 54-bed ostello. Guided tour by reservation.

If you've got the lungs, climb up to the Torre di Rossenella, a lookout tower isolated on a pinnacle facing Rossena. The trail takes ten minutes on foot. From up there the view embraces the cliff of Canossa, the hills and, below, the little medieval borgo of Rossena with the church of San Matteo.

activities.text: The trail between Rossena and the Riserva Naturale della Rupe di Campotrera crosses volcanic outcrops rare in Emilia. The dark rocks (ofioliti) contrast with the green of the meadows. Allow 45 minutes return. Accessible year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Matilda's Lands: The Countess's Castles in 5 Days

visits.text: From Maratea, reach the western slope of Pollino National Park (about 1 hour 15 minutes of mountain driving). With its 192,000 hectares spread between Basilicata and Calabria, it's Italy's largest national park. The massif culminates at Serra Dolcedorme at 2,267 meters. Base yourself in Rotonda, a small gateway town to the park—it has nothing touristy in itself, but it's the best base camp for exploring Pollino, with accommodations, restaurants, and the visitor center.

Drive to San Costantino Albanese (30 minutes from Rotonda), one of the last Arbëreshë (Albanian) villages in Basilicata. Founded in the 15th century by Albanian refugees fleeing the Ottoman invasion, it still preserves the language, traditional costumes, and Byzantine rite. The church of the Madonna della Stella celebrates its services in Old Albanian. During certain festivals, inhabitants wear gold-embroidered costumes centuries old.

Explore Pollino's eastern slope. Drive to Terranova di Pollino (30 minutes from Rotonda), a lost village at 926 meters altitude, departure point for trails to the summits. The medieval village, clinging to the rock, has preserved its stone alleyways and mountain water fountains. It's one of Basilicata's least populated municipalities—you'll encounter practically no one.

Descend to Viggianello, one of Pollino's "Most Beautiful Villages of Italy." The ancient Castrum Byanelli, mentioned in 1079, preserves a Sanseverino castle transformed into a noble residence in the 16th century. The centro storico's alleyways, lined with Byzantine churches (including San Sebastiano, remodeled in the 15th century) and noble palaces, offer a concentrate of Lucanian medieval architecture. The surrounding beech and fir forests are among the densest in southern Italy.

activities.text: In the afternoon, hike toward the loricato pines (Pinus heldreichii), Europe's oldest trees. Some Pollino specimens are over 900 years old—twisted trunks, bleached by sun and wind, growing on ridges between 1,800 and 2,200 meters altitude. The trail from Piano Ruggio (1,550 m) is the most accessible: allow 2 to 3 hours round trip to reach Serra di Crispo, nicknamed the "Garden of the Gods." From the summit, the view simultaneously embraces the Tyrrhenian coast to the west and the Ionian coast to the east.

If you're athletic, descend the Raganello Gorges, on Pollino's Calabrian side (1 hour drive from Rotonda, via Civita). This 17 km canyon, up to 700 meters deep in places, is traversed by canyoning with a licensed guide. The lower route (3 hours, accessible to beginners) crosses passages of crystal-clear water between vertiginous limestone walls. Civita, the Albanian village above the gorges, is worth a stop for its architecture and panoramic bridge suspended over the void.

For a more contemplative end to your trip, opt for a walk in the beech forests of Pollinello or a horseback ride in the high-altitude meadows. Several agriturismi around Rotonda and Viggianello offer equestrian outings. In the evening, taste the peperone di Senise IGP (dried pepper, base of Lucanian cuisine) and Pane di Matera IGP.

visits.text: Discover Rovigo, a provincial capital often overlooked in favor of Venice and Verona but rich with unexpected treasures. Torre Donà, at 66 meters, remains one of Italy's tallest medieval brick towers - a remnant of the city's 10th-century castle that once dominated the landscape.

Visit La Rotonda (Church of Madonna del Soccorso), designed by a pupil of Palladio to house a miraculous image of the Madonna. The church's entire interior is covered with remarkable 17th-century frescoes creating an immersive artistic experience.

Explore the Pinacoteca dei Concordi in the Renaissance Palazzo Roverella, housing originals by Tiepolo, Giovanni Bellini, and Palma the Elder. The archaeological collection and temporary exhibitions add depth to this cultural visit.

activities.text: Wander the historic center admiring remnants of medieval fortifications including Porta San Bortolo, Torre Grimani, and Torre Pighin. The main Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II offers beautiful buildings for photography, especially during the peaceful afternoon riposo hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

places.name: Ruvo Di Puglia

visits.text: A 19th-century private collection preserved as its owners intended: the Museo Nazionale Jatta in Ruvo di Puglia occupies four rooms of Palazzo Jatta, arranged in enfilade. Local ceramics from the 6th to 3rd centuries BC, Greek vases from Corinth and Attica, classified "by degrees of beauty" according to period taste. The family founded it in the early 19th century, the state purchased it in 1991. Rare, and rarely crowded.

The Concattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta in Ruvo, 12th-13th century, is one of the pinnacles of Puglian Romanesque: stone facade, central rose window, detached bell tower at the rear. Entry is free. The ipogeo beneath the building costs €2 and reveals Peucetian traces, Roman domus mosaics, and a small necropolis: that's where the real visit happens, not in the nave.

Portal adorned with skulls, stairs descending into darkness: the Chiesa del Purgatorio in Ruvo di Puglia, second half of the 17th century, conceals the Grotta di San Cleto, fitted into a former Roman cistern. Cletus is considered the third pope. The two-nave interior also houses a 16th-century polyptych. Opening erratic outside Mass times.

activities.text: Climb to the top of the Torre dell'Orologio in Ruvo di Puglia: the town is set on a hill, on the edge of the Alta Murgia National Park, and the view extends over vines and olive groves to the woods. The staircase is narrow. Check opening with the info point, it's not daily.

visits.text: Sabbioneta - Renaissance ideal city built from nothing between 1554 and 1591 by Vespasiano Gonzaga (1531-1591), inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 alongside Mantua. Vespasiano, a prince and condottiere in the service of Philip II of Spain, conceived his city according to the humanist theories of Alberti and Vitruvius - orthogonal plan, hexagonal fortifications spanning 2.5 kilometers, monumental public buildings designed for a city of 10,000 inhabitants that today numbers only 4,000.

Palazzo Ducale - palace of Vespasiano Gonzaga built between 1568 and 1578, featuring the Hall of Rivers decorated with allegorical frescoes and a cycle of full-length portraits of the Gonzaga sovereigns. The gilded hall, with its golden coffered ceiling, served as the throne room.

Teatro Olimpico di Sabbioneta - one of Europe's first permanent covered theaters, built by Vincenzo Scamozzi in 1590 on commission from Vespasiano, with a capacity of 250 spectators. The antique-style interior decoration - colonnaded loggias, painted friezes - ranks among the best-preserved from the late Renaissance. Not to be confused with Palladio's Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza (1580).

Galleria degli Antichi - 97-meter-long gallery built in 1584 by Vespasiano to house his collection of antiquities and sculptures, one of the first museum galleries in European history. The 97-meter length was calculated to allow cavalry exercises indoors during inclement weather.

Chiesa dell'Incoronata - octagonal church built between 1586 and 1588 to house the mausoleum of Vespasiano Gonzaga, with a bronze equestrian statue of the founder (1588) and frescoes by Bernardino Campi. The octagonal form, symbolizing resurrection, draws direct inspiration from Florence's baptistery.

activities.text: Walk along Sabbioneta's ramparts - the 2.5-kilometer hexagonal fortifications with five bastions and two gates (Porta Vittoria and Porta Imperiale) feature an accessible walkway offering views across the Po plain.

days_plan.itin_title: Milan to Chianti Circuit: Design, Art, and Wine

visits.text: Centro storico di Sacile - Nicknamed the 'Garden of the Serenissima' for its close ties to Venice, this small town developed on two islets formed by branches of the Livenza River. Sixteen bridges span the canals and offer picturesque views of Renaissance facades and their reflections in the water. The compact, pedestrian urban fabric recalls a miniature Venice transplanted into the Marca Trevigiana countryside.

Piazza del Popolo - The main square, lined with Venetian arcades and painted-facade palaces, opens onto the Livenza. The Duomo di San Nicolò, rebuilt in the 15th century, houses an altarpiece from the Venetian school. The Palazzo Ragazzoni (16th century), with its facade frescoes, testifies to the prosperity of local merchants under the Venetian Republic.

activities.text: Walk along the Livenza - The river banks, lined with willows and old mills, offer a tranquil route between ponticelli (little bridges). In August, the Sagra dei Osei (bird fair, one of Italy's oldest, documented since 1274) brings the town to life.
Strolling under the arcades - The piazza's porticos and adjacent streets shelter shops, cafés, and bacari (wine counters) in the purest Venetian tradition.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Friuli-Venezia Giulia

places.name: Salerno

visits.text: Vietri sul Mare - a town of 8,000 at the eastern gateway to the Amalfi Coast, the historic center of majolica ceramic production since the 16th century. Potter workshops produce tiles, tableware, and decorative objects in glazed terracotta featuring fish, lemons, and maritime scenes. The Museo della Ceramica, housed in Villa Guariglia in Raito, displays pieces from the 16th to 20th centuries including a collection of ceramics made by German artists who took refuge in Vietri in the 1930s.

Cattedrale di San Matteo in Salerno - a cathedral built between 1076 and 1085 by Robert Guiscard, the Norman warlord who made Salerno his capital. The crypt houses the relics of Saint Matthew the Evangelist, brought from the East in 954. An atrium lined with 28 ancient columns salvaged from Paestum precedes the facade. The cathedral witnessed the coronation of numerous Norman princes and sheltered Pope Gregory VII in exile in 1084.

Scuola Medica Salernitana - Western Europe's first secular medical school, active from the 9th to 13th centuries. Legend attributes its founding to four masters from different traditions: Greek, Latin, Arab, and Hebrew. The Regimen Sanitatis Salernitanum, a preventive medicine treatise written between the 10th and 12th centuries, was translated into 16 languages and remained Europe's standard medical manual until the 1600s. The Museo Virtuale della Scuola Medica Salernitana traces the institution's history.

Castello di Arechi - a 6th-century Byzantine fortress perched at 860 feet overlooking the Gulf of Salerno, expanded by the Lombard prince Arechi II in the 8th century who made it the residence of the Principality of Benevento. The square towers and ramparts, preserved along 2,600 feet, offer 180-degree views over the Gulf of Salerno and the Picentini Mountains.

activities.text: Strolling Salerno's Lungomare Trieste - a palm-lined 2-mile waterfront promenade, redesigned in 2008 and regularly cited among southern Italy's most beautiful.
Visiting Salerno's covered market in the centro storico - a 19th-century food hall with local producers selling mozzarella, Cetara anchovies, citron, and limoncello from the Amalfi Coast.

places.name: Salina

visits.text: Salina, the greenest Aeolian island with its twin extinct volcanic cones — Monte Fossa delle Felci (962 m) and Monte dei Porri (860 m) — takes its name from ancient salt pans. Its dense vegetation of capers, vines, and fig trees contrasts sharply with neighboring islands' arid landscapes.

The Pollara cove on the northwest coast served as the natural set for Michael Radford's film Il Postino (The Postman, 1994). Its volcanic tuff cliffs plunge into emerald waters, creating one of the Mediterranean's most stunning natural amphitheaters.
Lingua village in the south is the production center for Salina IGP capers — considered Italy's finest by top chefs — cultivated on volcanic terraces since antiquity.

Monte Fossa delle Felci (962 m) is the Aeolian Islands' highest peak. The ascent from Santa Marina through vineyards and giant ferns (felci) takes 2 hours to reach a 360° panorama of all seven islands. On clear days, the Calabrian coast appears on the horizon.

activities.text: Tasting granita alle more di gelso (mulberry sorbet) and Malvasia delle Lipari DOC at Santa Marina's cafés — specialties exclusive to Salina.
Swimming at Rinella, the black sand beach in the village of the same name on Salina's south coast, accessible by local bus from Santa Marina.

places.name: Salse Di Nirano

visits.text: You could swear you're in Iceland, but you're 15 minutes from Maranello. The Salse di Nirano are cold mud volcanoes: methane rises from the depths, pierces through clay, and forms little gray cones that gurgle in silence. Emilia-Romagna's first nature reserve, created in 1982, covers 200 hectares. Free access year-round.

Stop by the Cà Tassi visitor center to grasp the geology behind the phenomenon. Panels explain how an ancient seabed trapped beneath clay produces these cold eruptions. Small free museum; useful before your walk.

activities.text: The gurgle of methane breaking through clay is audible from six feet away. Trail No. 1, on wooden boardwalks, loops around the active cones in 45 minutes. Flat terrain, accessible to all. In summer, avoid the hottest hours: the central zone has no shade.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Hills: Balsamic, Ferrari, and Mud Volcanoes

map_keywords: Salse di Nirano Nature Reserve Fiorano

visits.text: Mondaino - This fortified village conceals a rare architectural curiosity: a semicircular arcaded square (Piazza Maggiore), shaped like a half-moon, designed in the 18th century. Surrounded by brick porticoes, it served as a covered market and gathering place. The Rocca Malatestiana, at the summit, offers a viewpoint over the wooded hills of the Valconca. The small Paleontological Museum displays marine fossils from the Miocene and Pliocene found in the surrounding hills.

Montegridolfo - This tiny fortified village, enclosed by almost intact walls, can be visited in a few minutes but concentrates a dense charm: flowered lanes, clock tower, ochre stone walls, and open views over the hills. The Museum of the Gothic Line, installed in a former church, traces the passage of the German defensive line Gothic Line in 1944 through objects, photographs, and World War II testimonies.

Saludecio - Perched at 343 meters altitude, this walled medieval village has become an open-air museum: colorful murals painted on façades represent the great inventions of the 19th century (the telephone, the vaccine, cinema, the automobile). The Chiesa di San Biagio, the parish church, preserves sacred art works. The Torre dell'Orologio marks the entrance to the historic center.

activities.text: Circuit among the three villages - The rolling road linking Mondaino, Montegridolfo, and Saludecio crosses landscapes of hills cultivated with olive groves and vineyards, with panoramas over the Romagna coast on one side and the ridges of the Montefeltro on the other. Total distance of about 25 km.

Tasting olive oil and Sangiovese - The hills between Saludecio and Mondaino produce a full-bodied, fruity Sangiovese di Romagna DOC. Farms offer tastings combining local extra virgin olive oil, formaggio di fossa (cheese aged in pits since the Middle Ages), and red wine.

days_plan.itin_title: Romagna Circuit: Medieval Fortresses and Hilltop Villages

visits.text: Saluzzo served as capital of an independent marquisate for over three centuries (founded by Manfred I around 1125, annexed to France in 1548, then to Savoy in 1601 by the Treaty of Lyon). Its medieval historic center climbs cobbled lanes toward the Castiglia, the marquises' fortress built in 1270 and radically remodeled in 1492 by Ludovico II for the arrival of his bride Marguerite de Foix. The 55-meter circular tower dominates the entire plain to Monviso. The castle houses two museums unique in Italy: the Museum of Chivalric Civilization and the Prison Memory Museum. The civic tower of 1462 and its 14th-century ramparts are remarkably preserved.

Casa Cavassa is a 15th-century Renaissance palace, residence of the Cavassa family in service to the marquises. Its interior courtyard features wall frescoes, wooden balconies running the full width of facades, and coffered ceilings. It houses the Civic Museum with the Labors of Hercules in grisaille by Flemish painter Hans Clemer and the Madonna della Misericordia. The pediment bears the French motto 'droit quoi qu'il soit,' trace of the period of French rule.

The Abbey of Staffarda, 9 km from Saluzzo in the commune of Revello, is one of Italy's most complete medieval monastic complexes. Founded in 1135 by Manfred I on marshland given to the Cistercians, it was for three centuries a major agricultural and commercial center—the monks drained 1,300 hectares and created a covered market whose Gothic arcades survive. The Romano-Gothic church with three naves alternates gray stone and red brick; each pillar differs from the others. The high altar preserves the Polyptych of Pascale Oddone (1531), eight ovals of gilded and polychrome carved wooden statues. In 1690, French General Catinat took the abbey during the Battle of Staffarda, burning the archives and refectory.

Castello della Manta, 5 km south of Saluzzo, is a 13th-century fortified house transformed into a lordly residence around 1420 by Valerano di Saluzzo, son of Marquis Thomas III. Its baronial hall is covered with a late Gothic fresco cycle depicting the nine Heroes and nine Heroines in near life-size, with the Fountain of Youth—a rare example of early 15th-century secular painting. Belongs to FAI (Italian Environment Fund).

activities.text: Stroll through Saluzzo's medieval center: from Piazza Castello, climb to the castello via cobbled lanes with views of Monviso. Pass through Piazzetta dei Mondagli and the birthplace of Silvio Pellico, poet and patriot whose My Prisons inspired Risorgimento revolutionaries.

Wine tasting from the Marquisate: Pelaverga, Quagliano, and Chatus, native grape varieties from the Saluzzo hills in DOC Colline Saluzzesi. Accompany with tomini (small valley cheeses) and local hazelnut gianduja.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alpine Valleys of Piedmont: Occitan Alps, Lakes & Baroque Savoy
Piedmont Wine & Truffle Road Trip: Turin, Alba & Barolo in 6 Days

visits.text: Nicknamed the Lombard Cluny, the Abbazia di Polirone was founded in 1007 by Tedaldo di Canossa, grandfather of Matilda. Giulio Romano restructured the interior in 1540 with a sense of decor that recalls a palace more than a church. The complex includes three cloisters, a refectory and a museum.

In the refectory, an early Correggio covers the back wall. It's one of the few works by the painter visible outside Parma. The late-Gothic chiostro di San Simeone, with its slender columns, is the most beautiful of the three.

Cross the three cloisters to reach the Museo Civico Polironiano: a collection of farm tools and period marionettes occupies the former dormitories. The 17th-century Scalone Barberiano leading there is spectacular.

activities.text: Matilda di Canossa was buried here in 1115. Her body was transferred to St. Peter's in Rome in the 17th century, but the sarcophagus remains in the basilica. The complete guided tour of the complex lasts about 1.5 hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

places.name: San Casciano Dei Bagni

visits.text: Etruscan-Roman Sanctuary of Bagno Grande: Excavations conducted from 2019 uncovered in November 2022 more than twenty-four bronze statues dated from 200 BC to 100 AD, perfectly preserved in the mud of thermal springs—including five nearly a meter tall representing Apollo, Hygieia, and matrons. With over 5,000 pieces in gold, silver, and bronze, Jacopo Tabolli's team (University for Foreigners of Siena) called this discovery 'the most important since the Riace bronzes in 1972.' The sanctuary, founded in the 3rd century BC by the Etruscans, was developed by the Romans under the name Balnea Clusinae. The thermal water (42°C) preserved the Etruscan and Latin inscriptions of donor families.

Archaeological site of Bagno Grande: The bronzes from the 2022-2024 excavations are circulating in a traveling exhibition (Quirinale, Naples, Reggio Calabria, Berlin in 2025) while the permanent museum—planned in a 16th-century palace in the historic center—is under construction, with a first inauguration expected in late 2026. Meanwhile, the site itself is visitable via guided tours organized every Saturday in summer by the municipal archaeological group, departing from the Stanze Cassianensi at the Palazzo Comunale.

activities.text: Thermal baths: The springs of San Casciano dei Bagni have been known since the 9th century BC and are still used today for their therapeutic properties. Modern thermal establishments welcome visitors year-round.

places.name: San Felice Circeo

visits.text: Antica Norba — Archaeological site on a plateau in the Lepini Mountains, towering 1,640 feet above the Pontine plain with sheer cliffs. Roman colony founded in the 5th century BC, nicknamed 'the Republican Pompeii of Lazio.' Its cyclopean walls in opus polygonal (massive limestone blocks fitted without mortar) extend 1.5 miles and enclose 94 acres—among the best-preserved in ancient Italy. Four monumental gates: the Porta Maggiore (26-foot jambs, semicircular bastion) is the most spectacular, with walls standing up to 33-40 feet tall. Two acropolises (major and minor) housed temples to Diana and Juno Lucina (goddess of childbirth, bronze inscriptions found). In 81 BC, during the civil war between Marius and Sulla, the inhabitants sided with Marius. Besieged by Sulla's troops, they chose to burn their homes and kill each other rather than surrender—the 'House of Burnt Seeds' still bears traces of this conflagration. The city was never rebuilt. Free access.

San Felice Circeo — Village perched on the Circeo promontory (1,775 feet), which Greek mythology identifies as the island of the sorceress Circe (Odyssey, Book X). Homer describes Ulysses climbing to a 'lookout rock' to see the island surrounded by sea—the profile of Monte Circeo indeed resembles an island when viewed from the south. The acropolis of ancient Circeii preserves megalithic walls in opus polygonal at 985 feet elevation. The medieval borgo centers on the Torre dei Templari (13th century) in the main square. Parco Nazionale del Circeo (founded 1934, one of Italy's oldest) protects the lowland forest (one of Italy's last), coastal lakes (Paola, Caprolace, Monaci, Fogliano), dunes and the island of Zannone. Grotta Guattari, on the promontory's eastern flank, was sealed by a rockfall 53,000 years ago and rediscovered in 1939: a Neanderthal skull at the center of a stone circle, first interpreted as ritual cannibalism, later explained by hyena activity. In 2021, remains of 9 more Neanderthals were unearthed—one of Europe's most important sites for studying this species. Cave visitable a few times yearly by reservation (Soprintendenza/Pro Loco).

activities.text: Walk the paved streets of Norba between the two acropolises, explore the baths, cisterns and underground passages. Extraordinary view over the Ninfa oasis below and across the Pontine plain to the sea.

Climb to the Circeii acropolis for the megalithic walls and panorama. Possible excursion in the National Park: trail to Picco di Circe (summit 1,775 feet, 360° view) or walk in the mesophilic forest. Swimming at Cala dei Pescatori, the bay where legend says Ulysses landed.

days_plan.itin_title: Ulysses Riviera: Secret Gardens, Ancient Caves & Southern Lazio Islands

map_keywords: Torre dei Templari San Felice Circeo

visits.text: Built in 1568 as a watchtower, the Torre di San Foca scanned the horizon for Turkish raids. Restored, it now houses the harbour master's office. A small 18th-century chapel stands beside it. The best view is from the wooden jetties in the port.

Diesel, wet nets and coffee: the porticciolo at San Foca is still a fishing harbour before it is a marina. The two beaches flanking it are called dei Brigantini and degli Aranci. On a clear day with a northerly, the mountains of Albania show on the horizon.

activities.text: If the sea is flat in the morning, take a boat from San Foca out to the sea caves along this coast, which cannot be reached from land. Departures cluster before midday. Check the forecast the day before: at the first hint of sirocco, trips are cancelled without warning.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

Visit to the medieval abbey of San Fruttuoso, nestled by the water's edge.

activities.text: Swimming in the turquoise waters of the cove and relaxing on the beach.

places.name: San Ginesio

visits.text: Collegiata di Santa Maria Assunta — founded in 1090 on an early Christian place of worship, considered the only true masterpiece of ornate Romanesque-Gothic architecture in Le Marche. The façade is divided in two registers: the lower in travertine with a richly carved portal, the upper in modelled fired brick (cotto) across five compartments, completed in the 15th century by master builder Enrico l'Alemano. The civic tower flanks the façade — note that this is not the campanile, which stands on the transept flank. Damaged in the 2016 earthquake and undergoing priority restoration. The square bears the name of Alberico Gentili (1552–1608), a jurist from San Ginesio at the court of Elizabeth I of England, considered one of the founding fathers of international law and author of the treatise De Jure Belli.

Porta Picena and Ospedale dei Pellegrini — the 14th-century Porta Picena is the main gateway, with a wide esplanade in front. The Ospedale dei Pellegrini (1295), built beside it in Romanesque style with a characteristic portico, once served as a staging post on the Rome–Loreto pilgrimage route. Its architecture remains clearly legible today.

Chiesa di San Francesco and Museo-Pinacoteca Gentili — the church (11th century) preserves a Giottesque fresco cycle in the Gothic apse, untouched by the earthquake. The Museo Gentili, in the adjacent former convent (now the town hall), brings together works from the 15th to 17th centuries: a canvas attributed to Ghirlandaio's workshop, Simone de Magistris' Pietà, the Pala della Battaglia tra i Ginesini e i Fermani by Nicola d'Ulisse (15th century), and communal parchments and manuscripts going back to 1199 — one of the best-preserved medieval archives in Le Marche. Partial closure post-earthquake: check access before visiting.

Colle Ascarano — the 'balcony of the Sibillini'. Via Capocastello leads to this viewpoint beyond the walls, where the eye sweeps from the Gran Sasso to Monte Conero, from the Sibillini to the Majella — and on clear days, all the way to the Adriatic. The hill's name recalls the betrayal of the 'Ascari' during a medieval siege, explained by a plaque at Porta Ascarana.

activities.text: Walk the mura di San Nicola — walls built in sandstone from 1308, completed 150 years later, with battlements and a walkway. Local tradition holds that Saint Nicholas braced his knee against the masonry to prevent it from falling during a siege.

Taste the Polentone di San Ginesio — oven-baked polenta served with meat ragù or sausage and pecorino cheese — and the award-winning Ciauscolo 'Il Campagnolo' from San Ginesio, which has claimed first prize at the national competition four years running.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

Chiesa di San Francesco San Ginesio

places.name: San Giovanni In Fiore

visits.text: Head to the Giganti della Sila reserve at Fallistro (near Camigliatello Silano). Marked 700-meter trail among centuries-old laricio pines: 60 trees recorded, some 350 years old, over 45 m tall, trunks 6 m in circumference. Managed by FAI since 1987.

Drive to Lake Arvo at Lorica (1,314 m altitude). Reservoir 8.7 km long, 70 million m³ of water. Pine forests descending to the water—Scandinavian atmosphere in the deep south. Multiple viewpoints from the road.

Ascend to the summit of Monte Botte Donato by road or cable car from Lorica. 1,928 m, highest point of the plateau. On clear days, 360° view of the park, both seas, and Pollino to the north. Ski station in winter with four runs.

Descend to San Giovanni in Fiore to visit the Florense Abbey. Founded around 1189 by monk Joachim of Fiore (1135-1202), visionary theologian who fascinated even Dante. Single nave, Romanesque crypt, mosaics. The village has 15,000 inhabitants, largest settlement in the park.

activities.text: Sample local cured meats in a village salumeria: soppressata, capicollo, salsiccia piccante. Everything is pepper, black pork and ancestral curing technique. Around €30 per kilo on average.

For active types, easy 4-km trail around Lake Ampollino (flat, ideal for families). Mountain biking, horseback riding and pedal boats available at Lorica. Sila air is ranked among the purest in Europe by the Italian INRA.
Dine on Sila porcini mushroom soup and lamb with aromatic herbs. Caciocavallo Silano PDO cheese to finish. Wine: red Magliocco, typical Calabrian varietal.

days_plan.itin_title: Calabria - From Tropea to the Giants of Sila

places.name: San Leo

visits.text: Fortress of San Leo - Rising atop a limestone spur with vertical walls, this citadel has dominated the Valmarecchia from a position renowned as impregnable. A first Roman fortification already occupied the site. Between 961 and 963, King Berengar II of Italy withstood a siege here against Otto I of Saxony. The Malatesta and Montefeltro fought over the stronghold for two centuries; in 1441, the young Federico da Montefeltro retook it by a daring climb up the sheer walls. He entrusted its reconstruction to Sienese architect Francesco di Giorgio Martini, who designed circular bastions and crossfire adapted to firearms—a masterpiece of Renaissance military engineering.

Cagliostro's Cell - From 1631 onward, the fortress became a papal prison. Its most famous prisoner, Count Cagliostro (Giuseppe Balsamo, born in Palermo in 1743), alchemist, Freemason, and adventurer, was imprisoned here in 1791 after his condemnation by the Roman Inquisition. Initially held in a standard cell, he was transferred after an escape attempt to the 'cella del pozzetto': a dungeon of about 3 by 3 meters, accessible only through a trapdoor in the ceiling, with a single opening to the outside. He died there in 1795 of apoplexy.

Parish Church of Santa Maria Assunta - Considered the oldest place of worship in the Montefeltro, this small pre-Romanesque sanctuary reuses columns and capitals from Roman times. Its single, low, austere nave exudes an archaic atmosphere of contemplation.

Cathedral of San Leone - Built of cut stone in Lombard Romanesque style, this cathedral was consecrated to the patron saint Leone, who came from Dalmatia in the 3rd century to evangelize the region. The austere façade and cul-de-four apse dominate the main piazza. Dante Alighieri, struck by the vertiginous aspect of the place, cites San Leo in Canto IV of Purgatory: 'Vassi in Sanleo e discendesi in Noli...'

Piazza Dante and Historic Center - The small square is surrounded by the Palazzo Mediceo (1517–1523), the residence of the Severini-Nardini counts (13th–16th century), and the Palazzo Della Rovere. Together they form a condensed showcase of Montefeltro civic architecture. The sole access road to the village is carved into the rock—a feature that reinforced its impregnable character.

activities.text: Climb on foot to the fortress - From the piazza, a paved path of a few hundred meters climbs to the fort's entrance. The view from the ramparts embraces the Marecchia valley, wooded hills, and, on clear days, the Adriatic coast. Wear comfortable shoes.

Alchimia Alchimie Festival - Every late August, San Leo celebrates the memory of Cagliostro with a festival dedicated to mystery and the occult sciences: markets, street performances, lectures, and fireworks animate the village for three days.

places.name: San Luigi Dei Francesi

visits.text: The church of Saint Louis of the French (built 1518-1589), constructed by Domenico Fontana following plans by Giacomo della Porta, has served as France's national church in Rome since its consecration in 1589. Its Renaissance travertine façade bears the coat of arms of France and statues of Francis I (with the royal salamander) and Charlemagne. Inside, the fifth chapel on the left—the Contarelli Chapel—houses Caravaggio's three canvases painted between 1599 and 1602: the Calling of Saint Matthew, the Martyrdom of Saint Matthew, and Saint Matthew and the Angel. This was the painter's first major public commission in Rome and the official starting point of the Baroque. The initial version of Saint Matthew and the Angel was rejected by the patrons: the saint was depicted as an old peasant with dirty feet, deemed unworthy of an evangelist. The bearded figure at the back of the Martyrdom is likely a self-portrait of Caravaggio.

activities.text: Spot the French royal symbols on the façade: fleur-de-lis from the coat of arms, Francis I's salamander. The church also holds the tomb of Frédéric Ozanam, founder of the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, and that of Blessed Pauline de Beaumont, erected by her lover Chateaubriand.

days_plan.itin_title: Rome: Historic Center, Ancient Ruins & Vatican Treasures

map_keywords: Chiesa di San Luigi dei Francesi Roma

visits.text: In Gavinana, the Museo Ferrucciano honors Francesco Ferrucci, condottiere of the Florentine Republic killed here on August 3, 1530, in the final battle of the Florentine republican resistance against Charles V and the Medici. The house on the square—according to tradition, the very threshold where Ferrucci was finished off with dagger blows by Fabrizio Maramaldo as he lay mortally wounded and told him: "You kill a dead man"—was transformed into a museum in 1931. The enemy commander Filiberto di Chalon, Prince of Orange, also died that day beneath Gavinana's walls, struck by two arquebuses.

activities.text: The Ponte Sospeso delle Ferriere connects Mammiano Basso to Popiglio via a steel-cable footbridge inaugurated in June 1923: 227 meters long, 36 meters above the Lima torrent, only 80 centimeters wide. It was built on the idea of Vincenzo Douglas Scotti, director of the Mammiano Basso rolling mill, to allow workers from Popiglio to reach the factories in 3 minutes instead of a 6-kilometer detour. In 1990, the Guinness Book of Records certified it as the world's longest pedestrian suspension bridge—a title it held until 2006, when it was surpassed by Japan's Kokonoe Yume bridge.

days_plan.itin_title: Pistoia Province Circuit: Hill Towns & Thermal Spas

visits.text: Rocca Guaita (First Tower) - The oldest and largest of San Marino's three towers, built directly on the rock of Monte Titano in the 11th century, without foundations. Encircled by the first of the city's three fortified walls, it houses an interior courtyard, the chapel of Santa Barbara, and former prisons. The view from the battlements sweeps across the Adriatic coast, the Romagna plain, and the Apennines.

Torre Cesta (Second Tower) - Erected in the 13th century at the highest point of Monte Titano (755 m), this pentagonal tower houses the Museum of Ancient Weapons: over 700 pieces (crossbows, swords, armor, firearms) from the Middle Ages to the 19th century. The path linking Guaita to Cesta, carved along the rocky ridge, offers vertiginous panoramas on both sides of the mountain.

Torre del Montale (Third Tower) - The smallest of the three, connected to Cesta by a woodland path. Not accessible inside, it contains a prison 8 meters deep called the 'fondo della torre' (tower pit). Its strategic role was crucial during wars against the Malatesta of Rimini. Large stones primitively stacked around its base testify to very ancient construction.

Piazza della Libertà and Palazzo Pubblico - The political heart of the Republic, this compact square overlooks the valley. The Palazzo Pubblico (1894), designed by Roman architect Francesco Azzurri and inaugurated with a speech by Giosuè Carducci on 'perpetual liberty,' is the seat of government and the Consiglio Grande e Generale. At the center of the square, the statue of Liberty in Carrara marble brandishes a lance shaped like a halberd (symbol of San Marino) and a crown adorned with the three towers. The square rests on ancient cisterns that once supplied the city with water.

Basilica of San Marino - Neoclassical church housing beneath the main altar the relics of the founding saint, rediscovered on March 3, 1586. The small adjacent Chiesetta di San Pietro preserves, according to tradition, the niches carved in the rock where Saint Marinus and his companion Saint Leo slept.

State Museum - On Piazza Titano, this museum gathers about 5,000 pieces: archaeology (including fine ancient Greek vases), paintings (Guercino, Pompeo Batoni, Elisabetta Sirani), and the Gothic goldwork jewel of the Domagnano Treasure, the only piece of this ensemble still preserved in the Republic (the others are scattered in the world's great museums).

activities.text: Path of the Three Towers (Passo delle Streghe) - The ridge path linking the three towers of Monte Titano (about 2 km) winds between cliffs, oak woods, and viewpoints. The 'Witches' Passage,' between Cesta and Montale, crosses steep rocky terrain. On clear days, the view extends to the Croatian coast.

La Cava dei Balestrieri - This pit carved in the rock at the foot of the ramparts still serves as a competition ground for San Marino's crossbowmen. Every year on September 3 (national holiday, anniversary of the Republic's foundation in 301 AD), a crossbow tournament in medieval costume takes place here.

visits.text: Parco di Villa Smeraldi - an 18th-century estate with an English-style landscape park and centuries-old trees. Home to the Museo della Civiltà Contadina, one of Emilia-Romagna's most important museums of rural life, with over 50,000 objects documenting agricultural work and artisan crafts across the Po plain from the 19th to the 20th century.

activities.text: Stroll the villa's landscape park among the centuries-old trees before continuing onward to Bentivoglio.

places.name: San Miniato

visits.text: The Rocca di Federico II of San Miniato, whose tower was erected between 1217 and 1221 (reconstructed in 1958 after bombing), is the borgo's emblem. From the summit, views carry across the Valdarno, the Volterra hills, the Apennines, and the sea. In the Middle Ages, the borgo was called San Miniato al Tedesco: Otto I of Saxony made it a center of imperial administration in 962, and Frederick II of Swabia in 1218 a tax collection point for all central Italy. Bishop Sigeric of Canterbury stopped here on the Via Francigena around 990, confirming its place among the route's historic stations.

The cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta and San Genesio, begun in the 12th century and elevated to cathedral status in 1622, presents a sober façade adorned with 26 ceramic bowls mainly of Tunisian origin (the originals are preserved in the Diocesan Museum). The Baroque interior houses several large altarpieces, including works by Francesco d'Agnolo known as Lo Spillo, Aurelio Lomi, and Cosimo Gamberucci. A tragic episode: on July 22, 1944, an American artillery shell killed 55 people gathered in the cathedral cemetery by German soldiers.

The Palazzo Comunale houses on the first floor the Sala delle Sette Virtù, the building's oldest room, decorated with frescoes by Cenni di Francesco di Ser Cenni: the Virgin nursing the Child surrounded by the four cardinal virtues and three theological virtues. The Palazzo del Seminario, on Piazza della Repubblica, is recognizable by its length and façade entirely painted with repetitive motif frescoes and Latin maxims.

The archaeological area of San Genesio, a few kilometers from the historic center, is one of the historic stages of the Via Francigena mentioned by Sigeric. Recent excavations have uncovered the foundations of an important medieval city, now an archaeological site open to visitors.

activities.text: White truffle hunting in the forests of San Miniato, with a guide and his dogs. The white truffle of San Miniato (Tuber Magnatum Pico) is one of Italy's most renowned. Local production represents about one-fifth of national production. The National White Truffle Fair has taken place the last three weekends of November since 1969; in 1954, a truffle weighing over 2 kg was offered to President Eisenhower.

Tasting of local products in the historic center: white truffle tagliatelle, mallegato (medieval charcuterie still produced by peasant families), spuma di gota di maiale (pink pork pâté). San Miniato is a Slow Food member.

visits.text: A Valpolicella fruttaio looks like a large, well-ventilated barn—that's exactly what it is. Between September and January, thousands of bunches of corvina, corvinone, and rondinella dry on wooden racks for 100 to 120 days. The water in the grapes evaporates, the sugars concentrate, and what remains produces a must that ferments bone-dry to create a wine at 16-17% alcohol: Amarone. Legend has it that a winemaker forgot a sweet Recioto in his cellar, found it fermented dry and furious—and called it 'amaro' (bitter). The failed Recioto became the region's great wine.

The Valpolicella Classico zone—Negrar, Fumane, Marano, Sant'Ambrogio, San Pietro in Cariano—is the historic heart of the appellation, the steepest, the most complex. Vines trained in pergola veronese (traditional horizontal trellis) cover the hills almost continuously. Look up while driving the small road climbing toward Fumane: it's dense, compact, green everywhere—the image of Italian vineyard in its most literal sense.

activities.text: Allegrini in Fumane is the modern benchmark for Valpolicella—the estate that showed in the 1980s you could make structured Amarone without waiting twenty years. The tour of the cellars and fruttaio is educational, the tasting covers the appellation's four wines: Valpolicella DOC, Ripasso, Amarone, Recioto. The Ripasso—Valpolicella re-fermented on still-warm Amarone pomace—is often the best introduction to the house style.

Masi in Gargagnago revived Amarone commercially in the 1950s—before them, the wine existed but didn't sell outside the region. Their Costasera remains one of the most reliable entry-level bottlings in the appellation. Tour of cellars carved into tuff, explanation of the double appassimento method used for certain cuvées. More touristic than Allegrini, but instructive.

Lunch at Trattoria Caprini in Torbe—a family table in the vineyards, Verona market cooking, pasta al ragù d'Amarone (the wine in the sauce, not just on the table), local cheeses. The address that winemakers in the zone recommend to their visitors—which is the best possible recommendation.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto in 8 days: Verona, Valpolicella, Soave, Prosecco, and Venice

places.name: San Polo D Enza

visits.text: Before the Canossa, the Etruscans already occupied this site at the confluence of the Enza and the plain. The insediamento at Servirola, a kilometre to the north, has yielded remains exhibited at the Musei Civici in Reggio. San Polo d'Enza is the gateway to the Matildic lands.

Pass beneath the medieval Torre dell'Orologio to enter the fortified borgo of San Polo d'Enza. A handful of porticoed houses surround the Rocca, the former Gherardini castle turned town hall. The fifteenth-century torrione remains intact. A quick glance; ten minutes will do.

A kilometre north, the Pieve dei Santi Pietro e Paolo stands beside the old road along the Val d'Enza. A basilica plan from its origins, reworked over the centuries, it's one of the many Matildic pievi in the area. Free, often open in the morning.

activities.text: The Thursday market in San Polo d'Enza is a chance to taste local parmigiano reggiano and salame felino straight from the producers. If you pass another day, the botteghe in the centre sell the same products.

days_plan.itin_title: Matilda's Lands: The Countess's Castles in 5 Days

map_keywords: Pieve dei Santi Pietro e Paolo San Polo d'Enza

places.name: San Quirico D Orcia

visits.text: Collegiate Church of Saints Quirico and Giulitta: One of the masterpieces of Romanesque architecture in Val d'Orcia, first mentioned in 712 during a dispute between the bishoprics of Siena and Arezzo. Its three portals are of different styles and periods: the main 12th-century Romanesque portal, supported by two columns on two lions with crocodiles in the architrave; the 13th-century Lombard portal attributed to Giovanni Pisano (Gothic inscription 'Iohes' in the spire); and a third Baroque one. Inside, a polyptych by Lucas Cranach the Elder offered by Frederick III of Germany in 1504.

Horti Leonini: An Italian garden created around 1581 by Diomede Leoni on land offered by Francesco I de' Medici. The diamond-shaped plan of the lower part, with its boxwood hedges and triangular parterres, is one of the rare Renaissance public garden achievements open to travelers—Leoni had wanted it accessible to Via Francigena pilgrims. At the center, a statue of Cosimo III de' Medici by Giuseppe Mazzuoli (1688). Above, a Roman-era double-headed Janus marks the boundary between the geometric garden and the wild ragnaia.

Palazzo Chigi Zondadari: Built in the second half of the 17th century by Cardinal Flavio Chigi, nephew of Pope Alexander VII, this palazzo faces the Collegiate Church and dominates Via Dante Alighieri. Seriously damaged during World War II, it now belongs to the commune.

Chapel of the Madonna di Vitaleta: Three kilometers southeast of San Quirico, at the end of a marked 800-meter dirt path, this small 16th-century chapel surrounded by cypresses is one of the most photographed images of Val d'Orcia. The cypress avenue is most evocative at sunrise.

activities.text: Festa del Barbarossa: Every last weekend in June, San Quirico commemorates the 1155 meeting between Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and Pope Adrian IV's emissaries. Medieval costume parades, flag throwing, and archery competitions.

Val d'Orcia hiking trails: San Quirico lies at the intersection of stage 35 and stage 36 of the Tuscan Via Francigena. The section toward Bagno Vignoni (4 km) runs along cypress fields and vineyards of the Orcia DOC appellation.

places.name: San Secondo Parmense

visits.text: The battered exterior of the Rocca dei Rossi doesn't prepare you for the shock inside. Built in 1413 by Pier Maria I, transformed into a Renaissance residence, it preserves thirteen rooms on the piano nobile with frescoes by pupils of Giulio Romano. The Sala delle Gesta Rossiane recounts the clan's history in seventeen panels.

The Sala delle Gesta Rossiane alone is worth the trip: seventeen scenes of the family painted in the 16th century, in a rare state of preservation. Two portraits attributed to Parmigianino ended up at the Museo del Prado in Madrid. Guided tour on weekends, no reservation needed.

days_plan.itin_title: Bassa Padana: Verdi, Guareschi and the Gonzaga in 8 Days

places.name: San Vito Dei Normanni

visits.text: In 1943, King Victor Emmanuel III took refuge in Brindisi with Badoglio and set up here: the Castello Dentice di Frasso in San Vito dei Normanni housed the Italian head of state during the collapse. Its Norman tower from the 11th-12th centuries stacks three rooms; the rest was added from the 15th century onward. Decorated halls, paintings, hunting trophies, restored archives.

The frescoes of the Cripta di San Biagio are captioned in Greek, save one: that of Saint Nicholas, which carries a Latin inscription. This Byzantine sanctuary is carved into the rock near the masseria Jannuzzo, with the monks' cells still visible, mixing Orthodox and Latin saints on the same walls. Access by reservation only; don't turn up unannounced.

Built in 1571, the Basilica di Santa Maria della Vittoria is what the people of San Vito simply call the chiesa madre. It faces the center of town. Nothing spectacular, but it's the landmark that anchors everything else. Five minutes in passing.

The Museo della Civiltà Rurale in the Chiostro dei Domenicani in San Vito dei Normanni is worth a visit: opened in 2001, it gathers the objects of an agriculture that disappeared within a generation. Tools, utensils, reconstructions. The cloister alone is worth the visit. Reduced hours; call ahead.

Only discovered in 1985, the Castello di Alceste occupies the highest point in the San Vito dei Normanni territory, on a rise in the middle of open countryside. The name misleads: it's an archaeological site, not a castle. Nothing is set up for mass tourism, which is exactly the point. Ask in town about access before heading out there.

activities.text: Take a break at the Villa Comunale in San Vito dei Normanni, which the locals call la Pineta because of its maritime pines: it's the town's green lung, with species that have been there for generations and the obligatory palm trees. A shaded bench at 2pm is worth more than a closed church.

places.name: Sanremo

visits.text: Enter La Pigna through the Porta di Santo Stefano, a Gothic stone arch from the 14th century marking the boundary between the medieval town and the modern city. The quarter takes its name from its spiral form wrapping around the hillside, recalling the scales of a pine cone—a deliberately defensive design conceived after the 9th-century Saracen raids, ensuring that any invader entering the alleys would become lost without being able to advance. The Piazza della Cisterna, with its large underground medieval reservoir, shows how the quarter compensated for the absence of springs by collecting rainwater in a network of cisterns.

Climb to the Sanctuary of the Madonna della Costa, built in 1630 on the site of an earlier chapel, at the summit of the Pigna hill. The church was erected to celebrate Sanremo's liberation from the tutelage of Genoa's Doria family in 1361—an event the city still celebrates today. The Baroque interior houses wooden statues by Maragliano, paintings by Domenico Fiasella, and a 14th-century Madonna and Child. The facade is visible from the sea and has long served as a landmark for navigators.

Visit the Cathedral of San Siro, one of Sanremo's oldest churches, built in the 12th century in Romanesque style with round arches and an ashlar stone nave. It occupies the western edge of La Pigna, steps from the medieval quarter. In 1538, the Manara house at number 21 Via Palma hosted Pope Paul III, en route to Nice where he would sign a ten-year truce between Charles V and Francis I.

Spot the Saracen Tower, built between August and October 1550 in response to repeated attacks by Barbary corsairs. Cylindrical and slender in form, it was connected to the Pigna ramparts and its single vaulted interior room was occupied by guards during alerts. It now stands isolated from the rest of the quarter but remains visible from the base of the hill.

Admire the exterior of the Casino di Sanremo, designed by French architect Eugène Ferret and inaugurated on January 12, 1905 under the name Kursaal. Mussolini's 1927 decree officially made it a casino. Sanremo is one of only four Italian cities authorized to have one, alongside Venice, Campione d'Italia, and Saint-Vincent. Its Art Nouveau halls have welcomed figures like King Farouk of Egypt (a regular in the 1950s after his exile), King Gustav of Sweden, and Princess Grace of Monaco. Poet Francesco Pastonchi created the tradition of Literary Mondays there.

Visit the park of Villa Ormond, on Corso Felice Cavallotti. The villa was built in 1889 by Swiss architect Émile Réverdin for Michel Louis Ormond, a wealthy Swiss entrepreneur, after the 1887 earthquake damaged the foundations of the original villa purchased in 1875. The municipality bought the villa and park in 1928. The garden is organized into themed zones: the palm grove, the orangery, the ficus area, and a Japanese garden in homage to Atami, Sanremo's sister city. Empress Elisabeth of Austria and the Princes of Prussia were among the Villa's guests.

Visit Villa Nobel, on the same Corso Felice Cavallotti, 200 meters from Villa Ormond. Alfred Nobel chose Sanremo in the late 19th century for health reasons and to set up a laboratory. The Moorish-style villa dates from 1870. It was here that he drafted the 1895 will in which he bequeathed his entire fortune to the foundation that would create the prize bearing his name. The salons, study, and bedroom are preserved with original furnishings; the exhibition traces the technological evolution of the 19th century and the role of his inventions.

Walk to the Fort of Santa Tecla, near the old port. Built by the Genoese in just eleven months and inaugurated on March 12, 1756, this star-shaped fort was erected to suppress Sanremo's independence aspirations vis-à-vis the Republic of Genoa. It now hosts cultural exhibitions and events.

activities.text: Stroll through the lanes of La Pigna from Piazza Santo Stefano to the summit: take the Rivolte San Sebastiano, a covered alley with high, uneven steps, then Via Palma—the former main street of La Pigna where the most illustrious families lived. Push open the door of the Oratory of San Sebastiano, built after the 1502 plague and restored: the 1642 inscription on the entrance colonnade and the 18th-century interior frescoes are well preserved.

Evening walk along the Corso Imperatrice, named in honor of Tsarina Maria Alexandrovna who gifted the city with palm trees during a stay on the Riviera. These palms, some of which are the Tsarina's originals, still line this marble promenade adorned with a Spring statue by sculptor Vincenzo Pasquali. Steps away, the Russian Orthodox Church of Saint Basil, inaugurated on December 23, 1913 in the presence of the Tsar's ambassador, served Sanremo's Russian community, which then numbered a thousand people.

Bike rental and ride on the Pista Ciclabile Riviera dei Fiori, built on the former Genoa-Ventimiglia railway line relocated inland from the coast starting in 1998. The path follows the sea for 32 kilometers between Ospedaletti and San Lorenzo al Mare, passing through converted former stations and coastal tunnels. The first Sanremo-San Lorenzo al Mare section was inaugurated in 2009; the extension to Imperia was completed in 2025. Bike rental points available at Sanremo's former station.

Stroll along Corso Matteotti, Sanremo's main shopping street: on the sidewalk slabs, brass plaques engraved with the name of each Italian Song Festival winner since its creation. The Teatro Ariston, which has hosted the festival every year since the 1970s, faces this same street.

visits.text: Civic Museum of Sansepolcro — The Resurrection: Piero della Francesca was born in Sansepolcro around 1412 and died there on October 12, 1492. The Museo Civico, housed in the Palazzo della Residenza whose current structure dates from 1456, is the only museum in the world to hold more than three works by the master. The Resurrection — a 225 × 200 cm fresco from the 1460s — was painted directly on the wall of the audience hall where the town council sat. Aldous Huxley called it in 1925 "the greatest painting in the world." In 1944, a British officer, Anthony Clarke, remembering that essay, halted the order to bomb Sansepolcro, then believed occupied by German soldiers — saving the fresco. The Polyptych of the Misericordia (commissioned in 1445) is Piero's first documented work.

Historic center and cathedral of Sansepolcro: the town, founded according to tradition by two pilgrims returning from the Holy Land in the 9th century with relics of the Holy Sepulchre, retains the character of a Renaissance art city with its stone palaces and 14th–16th-century buildings. The cathedral, rebuilt between the 14th and 16th centuries, houses a 12th-century wooden crucifix and frescoes. The birthplace of Piero della Francesca, in present-day Via Aggiunti, can be glimpsed from outside.

activities.text: Palio della Balestra: a crossbow competition pitting Sansepolcro against Gubbio, held every second Sunday of September on Piazza Torre di Berta since 1594. In medieval dress, the balestrieri of the two rival towns compete at shooting a wooden target — one of the oldest crossbow tournaments in Italy.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

places.name: Sant Agata De Goti

visits.text: Perched on its tufa terrace between the Martorano and Riello torrents, Sant'Agata de' Goti is a peculiar suspended village: you see its houses bursting from the cliff face like a single piece of rock. Today's center developed atop ancient Saticula, a Samnite settlement first mentioned in 343 BC during the battle of the same name, then taken by consul Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus in 315 BC after a two-year siege. In the 6th century AD, Goths converted to Nicene Christianity settled here and left the town their name. Awarded the Touring Club's Orange Flag and listed among Italy's most beautiful villages. The best way to grasp the topography: walk down to the bridge spanning the Martorano and look up. The village reveals itself like an inhabited geological cross-section.

The Cathedral of the Assumption was remodeled in Baroque style in 1728 but preserves a Romanesque crypt with ancient reused columns—fourteen different columns salvaged from local Roman buildings. Just steps away, the Church of San Menna, founded by the Normans in the 11th century, displays rare Cosmatesque flooring in Campania: polychrome marble in geometric patterns laid directly on the nave. Don't miss the Church of the Annunziata on Via Roma, whose vault shelters a 15th-century fresco of the Last Judgment, dark and poorly lit—bring a phone flashlight.

The Ducal Castle dominates the village to the east. Built during the Lombard period then remodeled under the Normans, Swabians, and finally the Acquaviva family during the Renaissance, it lost its military function to become a noble residence. Rooms with 16th-century frescoes are open to visitors only when not rented out for weddings. Clear views over the Isclero valley. Count on 30 minutes if you manage to get inside; otherwise, the exterior belvedere alone is already superb.

activities.text: Cantine Mustilli is the stop that transforms your day. The Mustilli family carved their cellars into the tufa in the 12th century, 16 meters beneath the historic center: you descend into a labyrinth of cool galleries where the Falanghina del Sannio ages—a grape variety they revived in the 1970s. They're the ones who rescued this cultivar from oblivion. Tours plus tastings available by reservation, in Italian or English. Midday Falanghina, a bit of bread, a bit of pecorino bagnolese: you'll stay longer than planned.

If you happen upon the Corpus Domini feast (60 days after Easter, so late May or early June depending on the year), you'll witness the Infiorata taking over the street: 700 meters of Via Roma carpeted with flower tapestries laid on the ground, depicting religious or mythological scenes composed overnight. At 10 AM, the procession passes and everything is trampled—that's the ritual. Outside the festival season, stroll in late afternoon when the golden stone catches the low sun. Dinner at one of the two or three family-run restaurants in the center: Locanda da Domenico serves excellent paccheri al ragù di castrato.

places.name: Santa Cecilia In Trastevere

visits.text: The basilica of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere is built on the house where, according to tradition, Cecilia—a 3rd-century Christian Roman noblewoman—suffered her martyrdom: she was locked for three days in the calidarium (steam bath) without perishing, then beheaded. In 1599, during the church's renovation, Cardinal Sfondrati had the saint's sarcophagus opened: the body was found intact, dressed in white, wounds to the neck visible. Stefano Maderno sculpted from Carrara marble an effigy reproducing the exact position of the body lying on its side—it's one of the most moving sculptures of the early Baroque. Pietro Cavallini's fresco of the Last Judgment (1293), hidden in the choir, was covered during a 1725 restoration and rediscovered only in 1900. Cavallini introduced a new realism in the faces and drapery that prefigured Giotto. In the crypt, excavations uncovered a 2nd-century domus and remnants of the baths of the ancient house.

activities.text: Access Cavallini's frescoes in the nuns' choir (paid entry, restricted morning hours): one of Rome's least known and most powerful medieval works.

visits.text: A dome and Moorish arches set above the drop: the Villa Sticchi is the building that appears in every photo of Santa Cesarea Terme, built at the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries. It is mainly seen from the outside, from the seafront. The neighbouring Villa Raffaella completes the set.

The sulphurous waters of Santa Cesarea surface at around 30C in four sea caves: Gattulla, Fetida, Sulfurea and Solfatara. The smell of sulphur reaches the promenade, and that is no exaggeration. The treatment season broadly runs from May to December, while the sulphur pool follows a summer calendar.

activities.text: Take the steps cut into the tufa down to the bathing platforms below the village. The coast is rocky, with no sand beach. The platforms fill from mid-morning onwards in summer.

places.name: Santa Fiora

visits.text: The Pieve delle Sante Flora e Lucilla, a parish church built before the year 1000 and reconstructed in the 13th century, preserves one of the world's most important collections of glazed terracotta from Andrea della Robbia's workshop. The pieces, created between 1464 and 1490, include a Coronation of the Virgin, a Saint Francis Receiving the Stigmata, a Madonna della Cintola, and several polychrome altarpieces with the characteristic blue background. The reliquary of Saints Flora and Lucilla, jointly offered by the Sforza and Aldobrandeschi families, bears the arms of both houses and materializes the county's passage from one dynasty to the other in 1439.

The Palazzo Sforza Cesarini, erected in 1575 on the foundations of the Aldobrandeschi fortress whose two medieval towers still survive on Piazza Garibaldi, now serves as the town hall. Dante mentioned Santa Fiora in Purgatorio (VI, 111) when the Ghibelline county of the Aldobrandeschi was prey to pillaging—the plaque affixed to the square reproduces this verse. Since 2002, the palace has housed the Museum of Mercury Mines of Monte Amiata, with 22 panels documenting the technical and social history of mercury extraction, the dominant activity on the massif between the 19th and mid-20th centuries.

The church of Madonna della Neve, a small Renaissance building from the 15th century adjoining the Peschiera, contains a unique feature: its floor is a transparent glass slab beneath which flows the official source of the Fiora River. The river literally springs to life beneath visitors' feet. The interior frescoes, attributed to Francesco Nasini, and a glazed terracotta bas-relief by Della Robbia complete the ensemble.

activities.text: La Peschiera, a medieval basin redesigned in the 16th century by the Sforza for trout farming in the Fiora's waters, was transformed into an English garden in the 19th century. Art critic Cesare Brandi wrote that it alone justified the journey. From its shaded banks, the village walls reflect in the water. It's one of the most photographed sites in Grosseto province, virtually unknown outside Italy.

Hiking in the beech forests of Monte Amiata, an extinct volcano reaching 1,733 meters, the highest mountain in southern Tuscany. The massif is geothermally active—steam columns from geothermal plants (including Bagnore 3 and 4) punctuate the landscape. Marked trails depart from Santa Fiora toward the state forest of Selva.

places.name: Santa Margherita Ligure

visits.text: Santa Margherita Ligure - Port and waterfront - Santa Margherita Ligure developed its tourist vocation from the 19th century when aristocrats from across Europe discovered its Gulf of Tigullio. The town was long known as Pescino before being renamed in 1863. Its marina, Belle Époque villas, and tree-lined promenade form the backdrop of a resort that maintains its elegance without Portofino's ostentation. The town is included in the Portofino Regional Natural Park, created in 1935.

Portofino - Piazzetta and harbor - Portofino, founded in the 10th century as a simple fishing port, became in the 19th century one of the most sought-after destinations on the Italian Riviera. Its Piazzetta, surrounded by pastel houses overlooking the horseshoe-shaped harbor, concentrates cafés, boutiques, and prestige yachts. Lord Byron swam in the bay. The Castello Brown, a medieval fortress renovated in the 16th century and purchased by British consul Montague Yeats Brown in the 19th century, offers the most complete panorama over the village.

Paraggi - Protected bay and beach - Nestled between Santa Margherita and Portofino, the bay of Paraggi is one of the rare sandy beaches on this Ligurian coast. Its clear, shallow waters, protected by the Portofino promontory, make it one of the most frequented swimming spots on the Riviera.

Camogli - Port and waterfront - Camogli is one of the most preserved fishing villages on the Ligurian Riviera. Its name reportedly comes from 'Casa dei Mogli' (house of wives). Its five- to six-story houses, painted in bright colors to be visible to sailors, overlook a lively harbor. The Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta, built directly at the water's edge on rocks, was rebuilt several times after storms. Camogli is known for the Sagra del Pesce, fish festival celebrated on the second Sunday of May since 1952, when thousands of sardines are fried in a giant 4-meter diameter pan.

Abbey of San Fruttuoso - Accessible only by boat or on foot, the abbey occupies a secret cove between Camogli and Portofino. Its foundation dates to the 7th century, when Greek monks fleeing the Muslim conquest of Hispania brought the relics of Saint Fructuosus of Tarragona. The current structure dates largely from the 11th century, built at the request of Adelaide of Burgundy, widow of Emperor Otto I. In the 13th century, the Doria family added the Gothic cloister and family tombs in black and white marble. A defensive tower was erected in 1562 to repel pirates. In 1954, the Christ of the Abyss statue was submerged at 17 meters depth—a 2.5-meter bronze created by Guido Galletti in memory of diver Dario Gonzatti who died here in 1947. The FAI has managed the site since 1983.

activities.text: Coastal trail Santa Margherita → Portofino via Paraggi - This 5.3 km trail follows the coast overlooking the sea, passing through the bay of Paraggi before descending to Portofino. Elevation gain of only 47 meters: one of the most accessible coastal routes on the Riviera. Local boats provide the return service.
Boat crossing Camogli → San Fruttuoso - Golfo Paradiso company boats connect Camogli to San Fruttuoso in about 30 minutes. The crossing follows the Portofino promontory.

Hike San Rocco di Camogli → San Fruttuoso - The trail descends through the holm oak forest of Portofino Natural Park to the bay of San Fruttuoso. The descent takes about 1h30 but the climb back is demanding—prefer the boat for the return.

places.name: Santa Maria Di Barsento

visits.text: The Chiesa di Santa Maria di Barsento stands alone in open countryside, a few kilometers from the town center. Built according to tradition in 591 at the request of Pope Gregory the Great, it has a basilical plan with a chiancarelle roof: the same technique used for trulli, roughly a thousand years before trulli. Checco Zalone filmed a baptism scene here. Dirt track at the end; wear proper shoes.

visits.text: Built on an ancient temple of Minerva, the Sanctuary of Santa Maria de Finibus Terrae marks, at Santa Maria di Leuca, the extreme point of the Italian heel. A place of pilgrimage for centuries, it overlooks the sea at nearly 50 meters. Entry is free year-round.

254 steps, but the view is worth it: the lighthouse of Santa Maria di Leuca, standing about 47 meters high, is among Italy's tallest. On clear days you can make out the Albanian coast. They say the two seas meet here, but it's mostly tradition: the Ionian begins further north. Check if the terrace is open.

activities.text: Embark on a boat excursion from the port of Leuca: the surrounding coast conceals dozens of marine caves accessible only by sea. Count on a morning. Book the day before in summer and bring sun protection—shade is scarce on board.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce

visits.text: Santa Severina appears from afar like a stone ship perched on a tufa cliff, overlooking the Neto valley. This village of 2,000 inhabitants, classified among the "Borghi più Belli d'Italia," bears the traces of more than a thousand years of history. Begin with the Castello, one of the best-preserved medieval fortresses in Calabria. Built in the 11th century by Robert Guiscard on an earlier Byzantine fortification, it features a square keep flanked by four cylindrical towers. The archaeological museum it houses displays artifacts ranging from the 3rd century BC to the Norman era - don't miss the skeleton with an ancient coin placed on the jaw, testimony to ancient funerary rites.

Right next to the castle, on Piazza Campo, the cathedral of Santa Anastasia (13th century) preserves its original portal despite numerous renovations. But the real treasure hides alongside: the Byzantine Baptistery, the only one still intact in Calabria. With a circular plan and four arms in a Greek cross, it preserves frescoes dating from the 10th to 12th centuries. This small edifice - discovered and studied by archaeologist Paolo Orsi in 1911 - takes you directly back to the era when Santa Severina was the Byzantine metropolitan seat in Calabria.

Wander through the lanes of the historic Grecìa and Iudìa quarters. The former, of Byzantine origin, clings to the panoramic spur with houses pressed against each other. The latter, the old Jewish ghetto, testifies to the coexistence of different cultures over the centuries. Push on to the church of Pozzoleo, in the Grecìa quarter - considered the last spark of Byzantine civilization in 12th-century Calabria.

activities.text: Enjoy the panoramic view from the castle ramparts at sunset - the Neto valley turns golden and you can glimpse the Ionian Sea in the distance. If you visit between May and June, you might attend the Medieval Festival, with extras in Norman costumes, jugglers, flag throwers, and tastings.

Taste sàuza, a spring fava bean soup with mint flavored with a drizzle of vinegar and served warm with pancetta. The aranciàru, a local orange variety with particular taste properties, is another emblematic village product.

days_plan.itin_title: Calabria: From Cosenza to Reggio, Between Mountains and Ionian Sea

places.name: Santa Teresa Gallura

visits.text: The Longosardo Tower, built under Philip II of Spain in the 16th century, is the largest Spanish tower in Sardinia. From its summit, the view extends to the white cliffs of Bonifacio 12 km away, the La Maddalena archipelago, and on clear days, all of Corsica. The town was founded in 1808 by Victor Emmanuel I of Savoy, who named it after his wife Maria Teresa.

The Capo Testa promontory, connected to the mainland by a narrow isthmus, is the ancient granite quarry from which the Romans extracted stone for their columns. Unfinished column shafts abandoned in the rock are still visible on site. The Valley of the Moon on the isthmus is a chaos of white granite blocks sculpted by wind into rounded, labyrinthine forms.
Rena Bianca Beach, right in the town center, is a 700-meter cove framed by granite rocks. A Blue Flag beach since 1987, its shallow waters allow direct views of the Corsican cliffs on the horizon.

activities.text: Ferry crossing to Bonifacio in Corsica (50 minutes), a town perched on white limestone cliffs directly across the strait. A day trip is possible from the port of Santa Teresa.
Hike the trails of Capo Testa among the granite blocks and maquis, with access to Rena di Ponente and Rena di Levante beaches, sheltered from winds depending on their orientation.
Sample Vermentino di Gallura DOCG, a dry white wine produced on the Gallura granites, at the waterfront restaurants.

places.name: Santarcangelo Di Romagna

visits.text: Rocca Malatestiana - Towering over the village from the summit of Colle Giove, this fortress was built in the 14th century by the Malatesta family and remodeled in the 15th century by Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta. The crenellated walls and square tower offer sweeping views across the Romagna plain to the Adriatic Sea. The rocca is now privately owned but open for guided tours.

Tufa Caves - Beneath the historic center lies a network of underground galleries carved into the calcareous tufa, whose origin remains debated: some archaeologists date them to Roman times (cisterns or silos), others to the Middle Ages (storage cellars). Part of the network is accessible by guided tour; the cool, constant temperature and rounded vaults create a unique atmosphere.

Parish Church of San Michele Arcangelo - One of the oldest Romanesque churches in Romagna, dating back to the 6th–7th century. It reuses ancient Roman columns and capitals. The simplicity of the single nave and semicircular apse contrasts with the medieval additions.

Historic Center - Sloping lanes climb from Piazza Ganganelli (with its neoclassical triumphal arch dedicated to Pope Clement XIV, a native son) toward the rocca. Ochre and brick-faced palaces, artisan workshops practicing mangano (printing on fabric with carved wooden blocks, a centuries-old technique still alive here), and shaded piazzas compose a village of real character.

activities.text: Wandering among palaces and artisan workshops - Santarcangelo's mangano is one of the last workshops in Italy still printing fabrics using rust-based dyes and hand-carved pear-wood blocks, a technique inherited from the 17th century. The production of fabrics with motifs of roosters, grape clusters, and foliage is a living craft tradition.
