Ulysses Riviera: Secret Gardens, Ancient Caves & Southern Lazio Islands

visits.text: Crossing to the island of Elba and discovery of Sansone beach, famous for its white pebbles and translucent water.
Exploration of marine caves and observation of colorful fish while snorkeling.

activities.text: Coastal navigation around Portoferraio and swimming in neighboring coves.

days_plan.itin_title: Hidden Beaches in Italy: Secluded Coves and Turquoise Waters

visits.text: The Modenese call it black gold—not oil, but traditional balsamic vinegar. The Museo dell'Aceto Balsamico in Spilamberto, opened in 2002, is housed in Villa Fabriani. The first room is shaped like a giant barrel. You follow the mosto cotto from vine to cask, then through 25 years of waiting. Open Saturday and Sunday, 9 a.m.–1 p.m. / 3–6 p.m.

Villa Fabriani is worth the visit for its social acetaia in the attic alone: the Consorteria's battery of casks has been aging there since 1967. Created by Rolando Simonini, the Consorteria also organizes the Palio di San Giovanni, an annual competition for tasters.

activities.text: If you come on the second Saturday of October, witness the cottura dei mosti in the open air: 16 to 17 copper cauldrons over wood fires, from morning till evening, right in the piazza. The smell of caramelized must fills the village. Outside this date, tastings are possible by reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Modena Hills: Balsamic, Ferrari, and Mud Volcanoes

places.name: Sternatia

visits.text: Here the street signs are bilingual, Italian and Griko: Sternatia is the village where the language has held on best. The Byzantine rite was celebrated here until 1661. Wander without a map, as the historic centre fits into a few hundred metres.

The Cripta di San Sebastiano was cut into a block of rock between the 9th and 11th centuries. Its wall decorations carry Greek inscriptions dated to 1114-1115 and to 1509-1510. Access is from the west side, and generally on request at the town hall.

Eight metres below the street, the air smells of damp stone and rancid oil: the frantoio ipogeo at Porta Filia is an underground press carved out of the tufa. Men worked and slept down here for months at a stretch. The visit lasts about twenty minutes, with a local guide.

activities.text: Locals call the grain silos cut into the rock fossiata, on the esplanade of the Palazzo Granafei, a fortified residence reworked in the 19th century, one wing of which served as a tobacco factory. The best move is to call at the town hall: it coordinates the openings.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

places.name: Stia

visits.text: Piazza Tanucci and Pieve di Santa Maria Assunta: the heart of Stia is an irregular, gently sloping square lined with porticoes and decorated balconies — one of the most charming in the entire Casentino. It is named after Bernardo Tanucci, born in Stia in 1698, a jurist and royal adviser to the Kingdom of Naples. The Pieve di Santa Maria Assunta, erected in Romanesque style in the 12th century with a later-modified facade, preserves a glazed-terracotta Madonna and Child from the Della Robbia workshop.

Museum of the Art of Wool — Lanificio di Stia: housed in the former Stia wool mill — one of the most important in Italy in the first half of the 20th century, employing over 500 people — the museum traces the history of the Panno Casentino, a woolen cloth with its famous looped texture produced in the valley since the 14th century. The mill bell set the rhythm of village life for decades. The factory ceased production in 2000 before being converted into a museum. Samples, period photographs and pre-mechanization machines illustrate the evolution of this fabric, which became an internationally recognized fashion article in the 20th century.

activities.text: Hike to the source of the Arno from Passo della Calla: drive or cycle to the pass on the Romagna border, then about 2 hours' walk round trip to reach the source of the Arno on the slopes of Monte Falterona, at around 1,350 meters. The river, which will go on to flow through Florence before reaching the sea at Pisa after 241 km, begins here as a thin stream among the beeches.

Castle of Porciano: an 11th-century Conti Guidi di Romena fortress commanding the upper Casentino valley from a hill near Stia. The 13th-century crenellated tower and keep are accessible. Local legend says Dante Alighieri found refuge here during his exile from Florence. The castle was abandoned, then restored from the 1960s onward.

days_plan.itin_title: Casentino Circuit: Art, Villages and Sanctuaries

map_keywords: Pieve di Santa Maria Assunta Stia

visits.text: Climb to the Cattolica di Stilo on the slopes of Mount Consolino. Small Byzantine church 7.5 m on a side, five domes on drums, built in brick in the 10th century. It appears on page 9 of the Italian passport and has been on the UNESCO tentative list since 2006.

Inside, examine the four columns: each comes from a different ancient temple. On one, a cross engraved in Greek; on another, an Arabic inscription (Muslim shahada) from the 11th century—trace of a Saracen occupation. Fragmentary Byzantine frescoes: Christ Pantocrator, Dormition of the Virgin (1552).

Descend to the town of Stilo. The Duomo (12th century) blends Norman, Arab and Byzantine styles—Gothic portal with pointed arch, Arab rose window. Facade redone after earthquakes, baroque interior. Tommaso Campanella, author of The City of the Sun (1602), was born here in 1568.

Wander the main lane. San Francesco church (13th century) preserves a beautiful coffered ceiling and 16th-century frescoes. The houses are tightly packed, many with carved stone portals. Two hours suffice for the center.

activities.text: Lunch on the terrace of an agriturismo in the valley. Ask for maccheroni al ferretto (pasta rolled on a knitting needle) with goat ragù. Around €25 for a full menu with house wine. Pizzata di fichi for dessert: fig and honey tart.

For hikers, take the Monte Consolino trail (2 hours round-trip, 400 m elevation gain). At the summit, ruins of the Norman castle and panoramic view of the Ionian Sea 10 km to the east. Closed shoes required.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Calabria Loop: Tyrrhenian and Ionian Coasts
Calabria - From Tropea to the Giants of Sila

visits.text: La Pelosa Beach, 2.5 km north of the village, takes its name from the posidonia seagrass that carpets its seabed — 'sa pelosa' in Sardinian. Its 10-meter Aragonese tower, built in 1578 on a small island accessible on foot through the shallow waters, has become the beach's iconic symbol. Access is now limited to 1,500 people per day to protect the fragile ecosystem.

Stintino was founded in 1885 by 45 fishing families expelled from Asinara Island when the Italian state established a penal colony there. The 'Communion of the 45' — the cooperative that gave birth to the village — is commemorated by the Piazza dei 45 in the town center. The old tonnara (tuna fishery), active until the 1970s, is now a museum of tuna fishing.

The Torre del Falcone, perched atop Capo Falcone promontory at 200 meters elevation, offers a 360° panorama over the Stintino peninsula, Asinara National Park, and Sardinia's west coast. The name comes from the peregrine falcons that nest in the rocky crevices.

activities.text: Boat excursion to Asinara National Park, an island closed to the public for 115 years due to the presence of a maximum-security penal colony. Now a nature reserve, it's home to albino donkeys, dolphins, and pristine vegetation.
Swimming at La Pelosetta, the neighboring beach to La Pelosa, less crowded, with the same Aragonese tower in the background and shallow waters perfect for children.
Sample bottarga di tonno and lobster soup at the harbor trattorias — specialties drawn directly from the village's tuna-fishing heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Sardinia Coast: Beaches & Hidden Coves

visits.text: Marvel at Villa Pisani, lauded as the Queen of the Venetian Villas, a palatial estate as grand as a royal residence. This magnificent 18th-century villa features fully frescoed rooms including Tiepolo's stunning ceiling masterpiece, a lush garden with an intricate hedge maze, and fascinating historical connections to Napoleon.

Visit the adjacent Villa Foscarini Rossi, home to a unique Shoe Museum displaying hundreds of examples of Italian footwear craftsmanship. The elegant villa provides insight into the refined lifestyle of Venetian nobility along the Brenta Riviera.

activities.text: Explore the extensive gardens of Villa Pisani, featuring formal parterres, ornamental ponds, and the famous labyrinth. The grounds offer a perfect setting for a leisurely stroll through centuries of landscape design.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: Explore Isola Bella, the jewel of the Borromean Islands housing the splendid Palazzo Borromeo, a perfectly preserved noble residence with precious paintings, tapestries and antique furnishings. The magnificent Borromean Gardens, created in the seventeenth century in pure Italian Baroque style, cascade over ten terraces towards the lake with an extraordinary variety of floral species and monumental statues.

Visit Isola Madre, the largest and most evocative of the Borromean Islands, wrapped in a quiet, suspended atmosphere. The sixteenth-century palace houses vast collections of period objects and a curious display of historic puppets, while the lush botanical garden is celebrated for its magnificent camellias, azaleas and exotic plants.

Admire Villa Pallavicino, an elegant nineteenth-century residence surrounded by a vast English-style garden hosting a fascinating zoological park. Among magnificent avenues lined with ancient trees and a wonderful botanical garden, you can encounter kangaroos, fallow deer, zebras and llamas in a beautifully kept natural setting, ideal for families with children.

Discover the Church of Sant'Ambrogio in the heart of Stresa, an elegant example of Neoclassical architecture with a Greek-cross plan completed in 1790. Inside lie the relics of San Vitaliano, a young Christian martyr venerated as protector of children, whose cult was introduced in 1835 following the transfer of his remains from the Roman catacombs.

activities.text: Ride the cable car to the summit of the Mottarone at 1,491 metres, from where you can admire one of the most spectacular panoramas in the Alps. The view stretches from Lake Maggiore to the Po Plain, from the peaks of Monte Rosa to the charming Giardino Botanico Alpinia, creating an unforgettable experience in every season.

Stroll along the romantic Stresa lakefront, lined with magnificent noble villas, exclusive historic hotels and manicured gardens lapped by the waters of Lake Maggiore. From here boats depart for the enchanting Borromean Islands and the extraordinary panorama of the Alps reflected in the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona
Italian Lakes & Dolomites Road Trip: Piedmont to Venice
Italian Lakes Road Trip: 8 Days Through Lombardy and Piedmont
Italian Lakes Road Trip: 8 Days Through Lombardy and Piedmont

visits.text: Stromboli is tiny - 12 km² - and the village of the same name stretches along the northeast coast in single-story white houses, no cars, just paved paths where electric Apes circulate. The philosopher Nietzsche came here in 1882. Several specialists think this volcano inspired his famous phrase from Zarathustra about the 'gate of hell'. The Strombolian eruption - geological term coined here in the 19th century - became the worldwide archetype of a volcano in regular activity. Sailors in Antiquity already called it 'the lighthouse of the Mediterranean' because it glows at night and has for at least 2,500 years.

The church of San Vincenzo, on the village square, offers a perfect view of the smoking cone. Next door, the house where Roberto Rossellini lodged Ingrid Bergman during the filming of Stromboli in 1949 - their affair, the beginning of an international scandal, produced Roberto Rossellini Jr nine months later and cost Bergman seven years of Hollywood exile. A discreet plaque commemorates it. In the morning and early afternoon, rest: the evening ascent will demand all your energy.

activities.text: Around 4-5 PM depending on season, departure for the guided sunset ascent. Local guides are mandatory above 290 m since the major 2019 eruption, which killed a hiker. Budget €30-35 per person, agencies Magmatrek or Stromboli Adventures on site. Ascent 2.5 hours in black ash, you arrive at 290 m just before nightfall, facing the Sciara del Fuoco - that steep black slope where lava tumbles down to the sea. Explosions every 15-25 minutes: showers of incandescent lava thrown 100-200 m, rumbles you feel in your chest. Descent by headlamp through 600 m of black ash.

Not hiking? Plan B is very beautiful: boat excursion at sunset off the Sciara del Fuoco (€40-50, 2 hours, departure around 6 PM). You see the explosions from the sea, at a safe distance, sometimes with flows plunging into the water in a cloud of steam. Touristy, but well done.

Late dinner on the terrace at L'Osservatorio, positioned precisely facing the Sciara, open late. Decent pizza, local wine, and breathtaking views of the volcano's explosions while you eat. It's kitschy, it's touristy, and it's one of the most memorable dinners you can have in the Mediterranean.

days_plan.itin_title: Sicily's Island Circuit: Aeolian, Aegadian & Pantelleria
Haunted Sicily - 8 Days from the Capuchin Crypts to Stromboli

places.name: Subiaco

visits.text: Monastero di Santa Scolastica - The oldest Benedictine monastery in the world (founded by Saint Benedict in the 6th century, sole survivor of the twelve monasteries he established in the Aniene valley before departing for Monte Cassino). Its Romanesque cloister and Cosmatesque cloister frame a still-active community. The Biblioteca Statale holds approximately 150,000 volumes, 440 manuscript codices, and 213 incunabula. In 1465, two disciples of Gutenberg from Mainz, Konrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz, installed Italy's first printing press here and produced the peninsula's first printed book: Cicero's De Oratore, followed by Saint Augustine's De Civitate Dei, each in 275 copies. The typographical style created here is called "stile Subiaco."

Monastero di San Benedetto (Sacro Speco) - Clinging to the cliff like an eagle's nest, this sanctuary is built around the cave where Saint Benedict lived as a hermit for three years (around 500 AD) before writing his Rule, foundation of Western monasticism. The walls of the cave and the superimposed chapels (upper church and lower church) are entirely covered with frescoes from the 11th to 14th centuries. Among them, the oldest known portrait of Saint Francis of Assisi - painted during his visit in 1223 - shows him without a halo and without stigmata, evidence it was made during his lifetime. The stairway carved into the rock leading to different levels offers vertiginous views over the valley.

Rocca Abbaziale - This fortress has dominated the town of Subiaco since the 11th century. Built for the abbots who controlled the valley, it was remodeled in the 16th century and now hosts temporary exhibitions. From its terraces, plunging views over the tufa rooftops, the medieval bridge of San Francesco, and the Aniene valley.

activities.text: Stroll through the medieval town of Subiaco - The sloping alleys of this town, listed among Italy's most beautiful, descend from the Rocca toward the bridge of San Francesco, a Gothic arch spanning the Aniene. The path between the two monasteries (about 2 km) traverses a holm oak forest in the Regional Park of the Simbruini Mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Lazio: Etruscan Sites and Volcanic Lakes

map_keywords: Monastero di San Benedetto Sacro Speco Subiaco

places.name: Sulmona

visits.text: The basilica of Santa Maria di Collemaggio early morning, just outside L'Aquila's walls. Gothic-Romanesque edifice founded between 1287 and 1288 by Pietro da Morrone, a Benedictine hermit of the Maiella. Rectangular facade in white and pink stone, adorned with polychrome geometric motifs and three rose windows—a design unique in Italian architecture. Here in August 1294, before 200,000 faithful, the hermit was crowned pope as Celestine V. A month later, he instituted the Perdonanza, annual plenary indulgence celebrated August 28-29—the world's first jubilee, classified UNESCO intangible heritage in 2019. The basilica thus houses the world's first Holy Door, predating Saint Peter's. The 2009 earthquake collapsed the transept and dome. Restoration, financed by Eni, completed in 2017, won the 2020 Europa Nostra European Heritage Award.

Descent to Sulmona, an hour south of L'Aquila. The birthplace of the poet Ovid (43 BC), enclosed in the Peligna Valley between the Morrone and Maiella massifs. On Piazza Garibaldi, the 13th-century medieval aqueduct deploys its 21 arches over 100 meters—built under the reign of Manfred, son of Frederick II of Swabia. Corso Ovidio lines up palaces and Gothic churches: Annunziata complex (1320 palace), San Francesco della Scarpa, San Panfilo cathedral (Baroque interior on 11th-century edifice).

Visit to the Pelino confetti museum and factory, 10 minutes from the center. Founded in 1783, it's Sulmona's oldest confectionery still operating—the city disputes the title of world capital of the confetto, sugar-coated almond. Recognized as a national monument in 1992, the museum presents a reconstituted 18th-century workshop, machines, antique gift boxes. Sulmona confetti reached British royal weddings. Two-ingredient recipe only: Sicilian almond (Mandorla di Avola or Pizzuta) and refined white sugar, lengthily coated.

If energy follows, climb to the Hermitage of Sant'Onofrio al Morrone, 15 minutes by car then 20 minutes on foot via a steep path. Clinging at 620 m beneath a Morrone cliff, this is where Pietro da Morrone lived as a hermit when the cardinals' delegation came to announce his election to the papal throne in 1294. The grotto beneath the chapel preserves a dripping effect—pilgrims still come to wet themselves with the drops for healing. Plunging view over the Peligna Valley and Sulmona below.

activities.text: Dinner on Piazza Garibaldi beneath the aqueduct's arches, watching the Morrone tint in the setting sun. Specialties: pizza fritta sulmonese, lamb with Maiella black truffles, panzerotti with local ricotta.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo
Marche & Abruzzo in 8 Days: From Rimini to Pescara, Hills to Wild Nature

map_keywords: Santa Maria di Collemaggio Basilica L'Aquila

visits.text: Leave Turin early via SS25, 35 km west to Sant'Ambrogio di Torino. The Sacra di San Michele appears as you climb, clinging to the summit of Monte Pirchiriano at 962 m, grey stone mass inseparable from the rock it extends. Park at the lower lot (€5/day), climb on foot via the sentiero dei pellegrini in 1 hour for the sporty (350 m elevation gain), or drive to the upper parking 700 m from the portal. Founded between 983 and 987 by Hugues de Montboissier called 'the Ripped', Auvergnat noble to whom Pope John XV supposedly imposed penance for his sins by building a sanctuary to Saint Michael—Sylvester II would confirm the foundation by bull after the fact. It became in two centuries one of Europe's greatest Benedictine centers.

Attack the entrance portal. You first climb the Scalone dei Morti—the staircase of the dead—carved directly into the rock in the twelfth century, 243 steps boxed between oozing walls. The lateral niches contained until 1936 the mummified skeletons of Benedictine monks, preserved upright and visible to pilgrims as reminder of human finitude. Health authorities had the remains buried in 1936, but the empty niches still gape like black mouths on the sides. At the top, the Portale dello Zodiaco carved by Maestro Niccolò in 1128-1130: twelve zodiac signs on the right, twelve constellations on the left, interlace framing—one of Europe's finest Romanesque portals.

The upper church, consecrated in 1148, is embedded right at the rocky summit of Pirchiriano. A fragment of raw rock pierces the floor at the center of the choir, left apparent. Then exit toward the Torre della Bell'Alda, set apart on a vertiginous promontory facing the Susa valley. Legend places here a young girl from Sant'Ambrogio who threw herself into the void to escape soldiers in the fifteenth century—saved by Archangel Michael who set her down intact at the foot of the cliff. Overcome by pride, she tried to repeat the leap the next day before mocking witnesses, and killed herself. Umberto Eco supposedly took the Sacra as model for the abbey in his Name of the Rose in 1980—the attribution is traditionally repeated by local guides, but Eco never clearly confirmed it and the fictional abbey of the novel, apart from its perched position, resembles the actual Sacra rather little. Ticket €8.

activities.text: Take the road back due west toward Susa, 25 km, 30 minutes, alpine valley climbing toward Col du Mont-Cenis. Drop bags in town center (€60-110), old centro around the Duomo. On foot, spot the Arco di Augusto erected in 9-8 BC in pink travertine, 13.3 m high monument raised to celebrate the alliance pact between Celto-Ligurian king Cottius and Emperor Augustus. It's one of Italy's best-preserved Roman arches, still legible on all four faces with sculpted frieze of the founding sacrifice. Just beside, ruins of the third-century amphitheater that could accommodate 5,000 spectators.

Dinner in Susa at Ristorante della Torre, Via San Francesco 1, mountain cuisine in an old house with low vaults. Taste the agnolotti del plin (hand-pinched ravioli, filled with three braised meats, melted butter and fresh sage)—classic Piedmontese recipe prepared by pinching each raviolo with thumb and forefinger, hence the name 'plin' (pinch). Polenta concia with Bra and Toma as accompaniment, house génépi as digestif.

days_plan.itin_title: Dark Piedmont - 8 days from mystical Turin to Valle d'Aosta

places.name: Sutri

visits.text: Roman Amphitheatre of Sutri - Carved between the 2nd and 1st centuries BC directly into the tufa hillside, this elliptical amphitheatre measuring 49 by 40 meters could hold between 5,000 and 9,000 spectators across three tiers. Not a single masonry stone was used—everything was sculpted from volcanic rock. Buried under vegetation for centuries, locals rediscovered and excavated it between 1835 and 1838.

Etruscan Necropolis - Along the cliff below the town, 64 tombs carved into tufa date from the 6th to 4th centuries BC. You'll find niches for cinerary urns, chamber tombs with dromos entrances, and columbaria. A paved path winds between the sculpted rock faces. Sutri bore the title "Gateway to Etruria"—this monumental cemetery proves it.

Mithraeum and Church of Santa Maria del Parto - Three adjoining Etruscan tombs were transformed into a sanctuary dedicated to the god Mithras under the Roman Empire, then converted into a Christian church. Step inside to discover 14th-century frescoes depicting the Virgin and sacred scenes, painted directly onto the tufa walls. Local legend claims this cave was where Bertha, Charlemagne's sister, gave birth to Roland, the legendary paladin.

Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta - Built in the 12th century in Romanesque style, remodeled in the 17th century as Baroque. The original Romanesque bell tower and medieval crypt survive. In 1046, Emperor Henry III convened a council here to resolve the crisis of three rival popes.

Palazzo Doebbing - Former episcopal palace until 1986, restored between 2010 and 2018. The museum occupies five levels and blends ancient and contemporary art: sculptures, architectural fragments, and frescoes from surrounding churches.

activities.text: Walk through the Archaeological Park - Lazio's smallest regional nature park (7 hectares) connects all the sites via shaded trails winding between oaks and meadows. At the summit, the 17th-century Villa Savorelli overlooks the landscape, surrounded by an Italian garden featuring a boxwood labyrinth.

visits.text: Tagliacozzo - a medieval town of 7,000 inhabitants in the Marsica, near the border with Lazio. The Battle of Tagliacozzo in 1268 saw Charles of Anjou crush the forces of Conradin of Hohenstaufen, the last Swabian claimant to the throne of Sicily. Dante cites this confrontation in the Divine Comedy.

Piazza dell'Obelisco - the main 15th-century square, bordered by Renaissance palaces and arcades. The central obelisk, erected in 1770, commemorates the 1268 Angevin victory. The square is considered one of the region's most harmonious.
Chiesa e Chiostro di San Francesco - a 13th-century Franciscan complex with a double-gallery cloister and a church preserving 15th-century frescoes attributed to the school of Benozzo Gozzoli.

activities.text: Excursion to Lago del Salto - an artificial lake created in 1940 by the dam on the Salto river, 12 km from the center. Offers water activities and forest walks along its shores.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

visits.text: Mount Etna, at 3,357 meters, is Europe's highest active volcano. Its eruptive activity has been documented since 425 BC. Parco dell'Etna, created in 1987 across 59,000 hectares, encompasses over 300 secondary cones.

The Funivia dell'Etna cable car ascends from Rifugio Sapienza (1,923 m) to 2,500 meters in 15 minutes. From there, the summit craters are accessible on foot in 2 hours round-trip, with a guide mandatory above 2,900 meters.

Taormina's Greek Theatre, built in the 3rd century BC and remodeled by the Romans, is Sicily's second-largest ancient theatre. Its unique feature worldwide: the stage frames smoking Mount Etna 30 km away and the Bay of Naxos, Greece's first Sicilian colony.
Isola Bella, a rock connected to the coast by a natural sand bar, remained private property until 1990. Its botanical garden shelters rare Mediterranean species and its waters form a nature reserve.

Corso Umberto I, a 500-meter medieval artery, preserves 14th-century Gothic palaces. Piazza IX Aprile with its terrace overlooking the sea and Etna constitutes one of Sicily's most celebrated panoramas.

activities.text: Hike in the Valle del Bove, a collapsed caldera measuring 7 by 5 km at 1,800 meters altitude, ringed by 1,000-meter walls. Historic lava flows layered here read like geological strata.
Tasting of Etna DOC wines (red Nerello Mascalese, white Carricante) at cantine in Randazzo or Linguaglossa—vineyards at 800-1,000 meters on volcanic soil.
Swimming at Mazzarò beach, accessible by cable car from Taormina (5 minutes, ~€3 round-trip). Pebble beach nestled in a cove with views of Isola Bella.
Excursion to Giardini Naxos, 4 km downhill, site of Sicily's first Greek foundation (734 BC) with a museum of Corinthian ceramics.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Sicily

visits.text: The Ori di Taranto fit into a handful of display cases and justify the journey: gold jewelry crafted between the 4th and 1st centuries BC, excavated throughout the region. The MArTA, Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Taranto, on Via Cavour, covers everything else from the Palaeolithic to the Middle Ages, including the statue of Zis, a Messapian deity. Open daily, long hours. Minimum two hours.

The Castello Aragonese locks off the entrance to Mar Piccolo with its pentagonal footprint. First Byzantine nucleus around 780 AD, then Ferdinand II of Aragon had it reworked in the late 15th century by Francesco di Giorgio Martini, military engineer. Today it belongs to the Italian Navy and is open to visit free of charge, guide included. Book ahead: slots are limited despite the free entry.

Two columns still standing, and that's all that remains: the Doric temple in Piazza Castello, Taranto, is described as the oldest place of worship in Magna Graecia. It's embedded today in the convent of San Michele, now a music institute. The square also concentrates the Palazzo di Città and the Castello Aragonese. No admission, just look.

Founded around the mid-10th century, the Duomo di San Cataldo is considered the oldest cathedral in Puglia. Its facade was redone in the 18th century; inside, a dome with Byzantine overtones sits alongside Baroque excess, and the saint's relics are in the chapel at the back. It stands on Piazza Duomo in the heart of the Città Vecchia. Smart dress required.

Taranto's Città Vecchia occupies an island between two seas, and it hasn't been repainted for postcards: tired facades, drying laundry, craft workshops, Baroque churches at street corners. It's the oldest and most lived-in quarter of the city. Belvedere at Piazza Fontana at sunset. In the evening, stay on the well-frequented main streets.

The Ponte Girevole connects the old town to the new by pivoting on itself, above the canal joining Mar Grande and Mar Piccolo. The canal was dug in 1481 against the Turks; the first bridge dates from 1887, operated by a hydraulic system fed from a cistern in the castle. The current electric version has been running since 1958. Watch it open; it's the city's signature spectacle.

The Chiostro di San Domenico completes the Città Vecchia loop in Taranto, with the Chiesa di San Domenico Maggiore and the Chiesa del Carmine. Taranto has many centuries-old convents and cloisters, and they're the quietest spots on the island. Twenty minutes each, fitted in between alleyways.

activities.text: Legend has it that Taras founded the city on a dolphin's back, and dolphins are still here: the Jonian Dolphin Conservation takes visitors out on observation trips in the Gulf of Taranto alongside researchers. This isn't a dressed-up tourist cruise; it's data collection. Reservation required, trips cancelled in rough weather.

On May 8, Taranto sends its saint to sea: the statue of San Cataldo is loaded onto a boat and followed by a flotilla in procession, and as it enters the canal the castle releases a cascade of fireworks. This is the city's feast day, not a tourist reenactment. Out of season, it's a reason to plan a May visit.

places.name: Tarquinia

visits.text: Necropoli dei Monterozzi - Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004, this 130-hectare necropolis is the largest known in Etruria. It contains over 6,000 sepulchers carved into rock, of which approximately 200 are adorned with frescoes - the only major testimony of pre-Roman classical painting in the Mediterranean. Archaeologist Massimo Pallottino defined it as "the first chapter in the history of Italian painting." The oldest date back to the 7th century BC. Tombs are accessible through long dromoi (sloping corridors) and visible through climate-controlled glass doors that maintain constant temperature and humidity. Among the most famous: the Tomb of the Leopards (5th century BC, vividly colored banquet scene), the Tomb of Hunting and Fishing (hunting and diving scenes), the Tomb of the Augurs (funeral games scenes), the Tomb of the Lionesses (acrobatic dolphins, music and dance).

Museo Archeologico Nazionale - Palazzo Vitelleschi - Housed in this palace built between 1436 and 1439 for Cardinal Giovanni Vitelleschi, a blend of late Gothic and early Renaissance, this museum presents its collections on three levels. On the ground floor, stone sarcophagi from the Hellenistic period, including that of the Priest (Laris, head of the Partunu family). On the first floor, the famous Cavalli Alati (Winged Horses), a 4th-century BC terracotta high relief from the pediment of the Ara della Regina temple - one of the best-known works of Etruscan art. On the second floor, a panoramic loggiato and climate-controlled rooms reconstructing painted tombs whose frescoes have been detached for conservation: Tomb of the Triclinium, of the Chariots, of the Olympics, of the Ship.

Medieval historic center of Tarquinia - The perched medieval town overlooks the Tyrrhenian coast and the Maremma countryside. The Chiesa di Santa Maria in Castello (12th century), the most representative of the town's medieval architecture, stands near the cylindrical torrione known as "Matilde di Canossa's tower." The alleys contain Gothic palaces, Romanesque towers, and peperino façades.

activities.text: In-depth visit to the painted tombs - About twenty tombs are open to the public in rotation along a marked route on the grassy hillside. QR codes along the path enable 3D virtual tours of the interiors, to appreciate fresco details invisible from the glass doors. For enthusiasts, it's possible to request extraordinary opening of normally closed tombs (Tomb of the Ogre, of the Shields, of Typhon) - by advance written request to the superintendency.

visits.text: Cerreto Sannita resembles no other village in the region, and for good reason: on June 5, 1688, an earthquake completely destroyed it, and the bishop seized the reconstruction to impose a grid plan—perfectly parallel streets, geometric squares. It's one of the few Baroque urban plans built from scratch in Southern Italy. The specialty since the 17th century: Cerreto majolica, with workshops still active around the cathedral. The Museo della Civiltà Contadina exhibits the oldest pieces. Awarded the Touring Club's Orange Flag.

Cusano Mutri is the exact opposite of Cerreto: no urban planner, no plan. The medieval village coiled upon itself at the foot of Matese, at 450 m, and the lanes cross on steep slopes among blackened stone houses. In autumn, this is where people come for the Sagra dei Funghi, mushroom festival in late September—porcini, ovoli, around 80 stands, truckloads of pilgrims hunting for cèpes. The rest of the year, stop here to climb up to the Church of San Giovanni Battista, then descend via the belvedere overlooking the Lavello gorges.

At Pietraroja, in a small limestone quarry above the village, a Veronese amateur named Giovanni Todesco picked up a 38 by 26 cm slab in 1980 and stored it in his basement. Thirteen years later, he pulled it out and showed it to a Milan paleontologist: it's the first dinosaur ever found in Italy. Scipionyx samniticus, nicknamed Ciro by the press, made the cover of Nature in 1998—a 24 cm hatchling whose fossilized internal organs are visible: intestines, muscles, even its last meals (a half-digested lizard leg). The Parco Geopaleontologico displays a faithful replica. The original is kept at the Soprintendenza in Benevento.

activities.text: At the Grassano Springs in San Salvatore Telesino, water emerges from the rock at 10°C year-round and feeds a river of almost surreal transparency. The Romans had spotted it—the site adjoins the remains of Telesia's walls, a Samnite-Roman city taken by Hannibal then abandoned. Today it's a picnic spot crowded on Sundays, with a few restaurants by the water serving fresh trota all'acquasale. Go on a weekday—it's deserted and magical.

Telese Terme is the local thermal spa. Sulfurous waters burst forth after the 1349 earthquake and founded the village's fortune. Lake Telese, formed by the springs, stretches 800 meters: you can bike around it in 30 minutes, or head straight to the spa for a half-day of hot baths (38°C) and mud treatments. This is the real reason to sleep here rather than in Cerreto: tucked in at 10 PM in a thermal hotel after a day scrambling through villages is unbeatable.

days_plan.itin_title: Sannio, Irpinia & Daunia: 5 Days Through Italy's Interior from Naples to Foggia

visits.text: Tempio Pausania wears its nickname proudly: the "city of stone." Locals earned it through countless facades and pavements built from the omnipresent grey granite. Perched at 566 meters above sea level at the foot of Mount Limbara, it's the historic capital of the Gallura region, far removed from the hustle of Costa Smeralda. Piazza San Pietro is the heart: the San Pietro Apostolo cathedral with its austere late-Baroque granite facade, plus the neighboring oratories. Touristy, yes, but beautifully preserved. Pro tip: visit late afternoon when the granite turns copper under the slanting sun.

Nuraghe Majori hides 1.3 km from the center on the SS133 toward Palau. It's a single-tower nuraghe built from granite—a rarity, since most nuraghes use basalt—nestled in dense vegetation. It's one of 31 Sardinian sites on the UNESCO candidate list. Well preserved, with a central corridor and two lateral chambers still clearly legible. Allow 30 minutes on site, €2.50 entry, €3 with guide. Small refreshment area at the entrance, welcome after the winding Limbara roads.

Calangianus, 9 km from Tempio, is Italy's cork capital. The Cork Museum, housed in a former Franciscan convent, displays machines, tools, and panels tracing the entire chain from bark stripping to finished cork. The region supplies most Italian corks and a good chunk of French ones too. A short but instructive detour, especially for understanding why you pass so many stripped cork oaks on the road.

Aggius, 6 km from Tempio, is probably the prettiest village in inland Gallura. Italian Touring Club orange flag, deservedly so: granite houses, cobbled lanes, flowered windows contrasting with grey stone. D'Annunzio nicknamed its male choir "the Rooster of Gallura," alluding to its vocal power. Aggius was also one of the most active centers of Sardinian banditry in the 19th century. Park at the village entrance, the center is walkable in an hour. On Sunday mornings you might catch choirs rehearsing in some churches.

Two museums in Aggius are worth the stop. The MEOC (Oliva Carta Cannas Ethnographic Museum) is Sardinia's largest ethnographic museum: hand-woven carpets, antique looms, rural daily objects. The Banditry Museum, in the old courthouse, traces the stories of the island's most notorious bandits through period documents, photos, and seized weapons. €4 entry, €3 if combined with MEOC. Closed Mondays. If the ticket office is closed, ask the MEOC volunteers across the street.

Valle della Luna lies 3 km north of Aggius on the SP74. Picture a plain studded with massive granite boulders, eroded into smooth shapes by the Quaternary period, sometimes 10 meters high. Locals also call it Piana dei grandi sassi. Protected natural site since 1966. At the valley's heart stands Nuraghe Izzana, one of Gallura's largest. A road cuts through to a viewpoint offering the overview. Allow an hour on site.

activities.text: If you arrive early in Olbia, grab a coffee in the historic center before hitting the road. Otherwise, head straight for Gallura on the backroads: the SS127 between Olbia and Tempio cuts through landscapes of wind-sculpted granite and cork oaks, virtually traffic-free. Count on 1 hour driving, but budget two photo stops. In Tempio, spend your evening on Piazza Gallura or in a downtown trattoria: try the zuppa gallurese, the emblematic dish made with stale bread, cheese, and broth.

Vermentino di Gallura DOCG tasting—Sardinia's only DOCG wine. Cantina Gallura in Tempio Pausania offers afternoon visits with tastings. The local Vermentino stands out for its minerality, amplified by the granitic soils. Count on €10-15 for a tasting with cheese and charcuterie plates. Call ahead the day before in high season.

Hike in Valle della Luna: a marked trail starts from the viewpoint and gets you close to the granite blocks. Count on 1h30 round trip, easy level, 200m elevation gain. The low-angle morning or sunset light brings out the polished granite grain. Bring water, no services on site.

Shopping for traditional Sardinian carpets in Aggius. It's one of the last villages on the island still producing wool carpets on manual wooden looms. Several workshops are open to the public, where you can watch weavers at work and buy directly. Small models €50, large formats €300-500. More authentic than a Costa Smeralda souvenir.

places.name: Termoli

visits.text: First real highlight of the route: the Costa dei Trabocchi between Francavilla al Mare and Vasto. These wooden fishing machines on stilts, with their articulated arms and large square nets, are a medieval invention found nowhere else in Italy so well preserved. The Via Verde, a former railway line converted to bike path, follows the coast for 42 km—you'll cross it several times by car. Recommended photo stops at San Vito Chietino and Rocca San Giovanni. The Trabocco Punta Cavalluccio, the most photogenic, overlooks a turquoise-water cove.

Vasto, midway, merits a lunch stop. Old town on a promontory, plunging views of the Adriatic, 15th-century Castello Caldoresco, San Giuseppe cathedral, Palazzo Gargasanti. Main square Piazza Rossetti, dedicated to poet Gabriele Rossetti—father of Pre-Raphaelite Dante Gabriel. The center can be covered in 1 hour, and it's a chance for a last Abruzzese lunch before crossing into Molise. Park at the bottom; it's a steep climb.

If you have time to dip your toes before continuing to Termoli, this is the spot. Punta Aderci, just south of Vasto, is a 285-hectare regional nature reserve—limestone cliffs, pebble beach, crystalline waters—one of Abruzzo's most beautiful beaches, Blue Flag certified. Easy trail from the parking area, 20-minute walk. Loggerhead turtles occasionally nest on this stretch of coast.

Arrive in Termoli late afternoon via the Borgo Antico. The fortified promontory plunges into the sea, dominated by the square silhouette of the Castello Svevo. First glimpse: just park at Parcheggio Via Francesco de Sanctis, climb to the viewpoint, and savor the contrast with this morning's trabocchi. Tomorrow we'll tackle the town in detail. Tonight, just dinner facing the sea.

The Castello Svevo plunges straight into the sea. Frederick II had it rebuilt in 1240 atop a 12th-century Norman tower, after the Venetian fleet allied with the pope destroyed the walls. Spot the six-meter crack still visible on the left facade, souvenir of the 1627 earthquake. The fortress also weathered a Turkish assault on August 2, 1566. Small but sturdy, you can circle it in 30 minutes. The viewpoint at its base is where everyone takes their photo—come late afternoon when the light is better.

The Borgo Antico is the maze perched on the promontory behind the castle. Pastel-colored houses, alleys so narrow that Vico II Castello narrows to 34 cm at its tightest point—among Europe's narrowest. A large man can't pass. The borgo is surrounded by a wall that drops sheer into the sea. Follow the orange flags to Piazza Duomo and the Cathedral of Santa Maria della Purificazione, 12th-13th century Apulian Romanesque, built atop an ancient pagan temple. Allow two good hours to wander without missing anything.

Termoli's trabucchi line the waterfront especially toward Punta Penna. Rarer than in Abruzzo, but well preserved. Several have been converted to restaurants: you lunch with your feet practically in the water, fish caught that morning. Touristy, but genuine, and the formula costs no more than downtown. For sunset, it's unbeatable.

Today, a choice: day trip to the Tremiti Islands from Termoli port, or explore the Molise Costa Verde. Both options are solid; I'll describe the Tremiti first, more memorable. The archipelago is 1h15 by fast ferry. Five islands, only two inhabited: San Domino and San Nicola. Turquoise waters, white cliffs, coves accessible only by boat. Leave on the first morning ferry (around 9am), return around 5pm—doable as a day trip.

San Domino is the archipelago's green island: pine forests, hiking trails, spectacular cliffs. Island boat tour (45 min) recommended to see the Grotta del Bue Marino and rocky sea stacks. Cala delle Arene beach, coves with limpid waters, snorkeling practically mandatory. The village center is tiny; you'll eat simply, grilled fish.

Five minutes by boat, San Nicola is the historical island. Abbey of Santa Maria a Mare, founded by Benedictines in the 9th century, fortified in the 13th. 11th-century mosaic pavement, one of the oldest in neighboring Puglia. Homeric legend: Diomedes, hero of the Iliad, is said to be buried here. Under Mussolini, the archipelago served as an internment site (confino) for political opponents—several hundred to over a thousand anti-fascists were detained here according to sources. 1.5 hours on San Nicola passes quickly.

activities.text: Lunch on a trabocco. This is the signature experience of the Abruzzo Adriatic coast: raw fish, fritto misto, squid-ink pasta, local white wine, all on a wooden platform suspended above the waves. Trabocco Punta Cavalluccio or Trabocco di Mucchiola are among the best rated. Expect €50-70 per person, booking essential in season. It's a unique sensation, memorable.

First dinner in Termoli at the foot of Castello Svevo. Brodetto alla termolese (taste tomorrow at a proper address; tonight keep it simple), fish fritto misto, or a seafood pasta dish. Plenty of waterfront restaurants, variable quality—prefer those on the Marina harbor side. Tintilia or Trebbiano molisano to accompany.

Head to the port to taste brodetto alla termolese, the local fish soup eaten with a slice of grilled bread rubbed with garlic. Each fisherman has his version, with seven or nine species according to tradition. Port restaurants (Marina side) serve the most authentic version, those in the borgo a more polished one. It's a meal in itself, hearty—plan nothing else after.

Late afternoon, walk on Sant'Antonio beach, north of the promontory. Fine sand, shallow waters, views of the castle silhouette rising above the ramparts. Here every August 15 at midnight unfolds the Incendio del Castello, reenactment of the 1566 Turkish attack with fireworks launched from the fortress. If you're there for Ferragosto, it's the event not to miss.

Evening in Termoli with aperitivo on the borgo ramparts, then dinner at a downtown trattoria. Ask for ventricina, spicy local sausage aged minimum 90 days, and taste Sant'Angelo caciocavallo, pear-shaped cheese aged in caves. These two products are pillars of Molise cuisine you'll encounter throughout the journey.

Boat tour around the five islands from San Domino. This is the signature activity: 45 min to 1 hour, skirting cliffs, sea caves, viewpoints inaccessible on foot. Several operators at the port, expect €15-20. Some include a swim stop in a hidden cove. If you have snorkel gear, bring it: water transparency is exceptional, you can see the seabed at 15 meters.

Alternative to Tremiti day: Molise Costa Verde (Petacciato, Campomarino Lido, Marina di Montenero). Sandy beaches with few crowds, shallow waters, ideal for families. Marina di Montenero has earned multiple Blue Flags. Quieter, less spectacular than the Tremiti, but authentic—this is where local Italians spend their summers. Half-day beach plus lunch at the port suffices.

Return to Termoli port late afternoon. Last evening on the coast before heading inland tomorrow morning. Molise olive oil tasting—the region produces PDO oils like Olio Molise DOP, based on Aurina, Gentile di Larino and other local cultivars. Several cellars and specialty shops downtown offer tastings and sales.

visits.text: Terricciola developed around a hill inhabited since Etruscan times, as evidenced by 4th-century BC hypogea (underground chamber tombs) discovered beneath Via della Fonte. These underground vaults still served as wine cellars last century. Several are being reopened to the public thanks to European funds. The clayey, sandy soil, rich in Pliocene marine fossils, is ideal for Sangiovese, Trebbiano, and Merlot.

The Pieve di San Verano is the main parish church of the Terricciola territory, a few kilometers from the borgo. A sober Romanesque building whose interior houses medieval decorative elements. The hamlet of Morrona, in the municipality, contains a Hellenistic-era necropolis with hypogeal chamber tombs among the best documented in the Pisan hills.

activities.text: Terricciola has about 25 independent wineries and is a member of the National Association of Wine Cities. The municipality is part of the Pisan Hills Wine Route. Several estates offer year-round tastings: red Sangiovese, white Vermentino and Trebbiano, with a mineral signature linked to sea breezes rising up the valley. The White Night of Wine takes place every first weekend in July.
Panorama over the Pisan hills and Valdera from the heights of the medieval borgo, whose alleyways and Renaissance houses have retained their original appearance.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Pisa Province

visits.text: Villa d'Este - Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001, this villa was commissioned by Cardinal Ippolito II d'Este, appointed Governor of Tivoli in 1550. Frustrated at not being elected pope, he hired architect Pirro Ligorio to transform a former Benedictine convent into a prestigious residence. The 4.5-hectare terraced gardens house over 500 fountains, 300 water jets, and some sixty cascades - all powered solely by gravity, without a single pump, thanks to water channeled from the Aniene River through an underground conduit dug in 1564-1565. The Fontana dell'Organo (1568), a hydraulic organ built by Frenchmen Luc Leclerc and Claude Venard, still plays melodies every two hours. Franz Liszt lived here for twenty years and composed "Fountains of the Villa d'Este."

Villa Adriana - A UNESCO site since 1999, this imperial residence was built between 118 and 138 AD by Emperor Hadrian on a 120-hectare plateau (40 hectares visitable), 28 km from Rome. A great traveler and amateur architect, Hadrian recreated monuments that had impressed him across the Empire: the Pecile recalls Athens' Stoa, the Canopus evokes an Egyptian canal lined with statues, and the Teatro Marittimo is an artificial island encircled by a canal where the emperor withdrew to meditate. A network of underground carriage-accessible galleries allowed servants to move about without disturbing the imperial spaces. After centuries of pillaging (marble, mosaics, and sculptures scattered across European museums), the villa inspired the greatest Renaissance architects from Bramante to Palladio.

Villa Gregoriana - This nature park, landscaped in 1835 by Pope Gregory XVI, occupies the gorge of the Aniene River, where the river plunges in a Grande Cascata with a 120-meter drop. Steep paths wind through dense vegetation to reach caves (including Neptune's Cave and the Sirens' Cave) and the ruins of the Roman villa of Manlio Vopisco. On the ancient acropolis overlooking the gorge stand the Temple of Vesta (1st century BC), a tholos with Corinthian columns, and the more austere rectangular Temple of the Sibyl.

activities.text: Stroll on the acropolis of ancient Tibur - From the esplanade of the temples of Vesta and the Sibyl, panoramic views embrace the entire valley of waterfalls and the wooded gorges of the Aniene. Below, the Ponte Gregoriano and ruins of Roman villas complete the scene.

places.name: Torino

visits.text: Land at Caselle, 16 km north of the city center, and take the shuttle or taxi straight to the Quadrilatero Romano (old town district, €100-160). This is the ancient layout of Augusta Taurinorum, founded by Augustus around 28 BC, and the current street grid still follows the Roman decumanus and cardo to the meter. Drop your bags on Via Sant'Agostino or Via delle Orfane. Useful tip: Turin is flat, everything is 15-20 minutes on foot, save the car for Lucedio and the Sacra from D4 onwards.

At nightfall, walk due west to Piazza Statuto. For Turin's esotericists, you're standing at the apex of the worldwide triangle of black magic—the other two points being London and San Francisco. The square was laid out in 1864 on the site of an ancient Roman necropolis and medieval gallows. At its center, the Monumento al Traforo del Fréjus erected in 1879 celebrates the piercing of the railway tunnel. Look up at the statue crowning the rocky pyramid: an angel with an inverted pentacle on its forehead, wings spread, identified with Lucifer by the city's esoteric guides. It's a bit Turin's hermetic quirk—unofficial capital of Italian occultism since the nineteenth century.

Slip two streets over to spot the Portone del Diavolo—the 'devil's door'—at Via XX Settembre 40, on the facade of Palazzo Trucchi di Levaldigi. The carved black wooden door dates from the late seventeenth century, adorned with grimacing heads and a knocker shaped like a gaping maw. According to legend reported as early as 1790, it appeared one stormy night in place of an ordinary door, following a botched alchemical pact between the master of the house and a visiting mage. More prosaically, the Mannerist iconography fits the fashions of the era in noble townhouses. The rumor, though, persists: don't touch the knocker.

Pivot this morning toward the opposite pole. If Piazza Statuto is the black epicenter, Piazza Castello embodies white magic according to the same Turin esoteric corpus. The contrast is physical: here the square is rectangular, axial, dominated by Palazzo Madama and enclosed by the royal facade of Palazzo Reale. At the palace entrance, flanking the gate since 1846, two equestrian statues of the Dioscuri Castor and Pollux—the divine twins of the Greco-Roman pantheon. According to local occult reading, Pollux bears an inverted pentacle on his chest and guards the threshold between the two worlds. Look for the detail yourself in the morning light and form your own opinion.

Visit the Palazzo Reale, residence of the Dukes then Kings of Savoy from 1646 to 1865, UNESCO-listed since 1997. Beneath the palace and its gardens, Turin esotericists locate the famous 'alchemical grottoes' where Michel de Nostredame—known as Nostradamus—supposedly manufactured gold for Duke Emmanuel Philibert around 1556, according to legend. No archival documents confirm the episode, but historian Marziano Bernardi identified in 1959 unidentified vaulted underground rooms beneath the eastern wing. Not open to visitors today. On the piano nobile, pass through the Armeria Reale, one of Europe's finest collections of antique arms: 5,000 pieces including the sword of Saint Maurice. Combined ticket €15, 2 hours.

Walk 600 m east to the Mole Antonelliana, Turin's graphic signature. Conceived in 1863 by architect Alessandro Antonelli as a synagogue (the Turin Jewish community had just obtained civil emancipation), it was abandoned mid-construction by the community who found the ambition disproportionate. The city took it over and completed it in 1889 at 167.5 m—Europe's tallest masonry building at the time. For Turin esotericists, it's the city's energy antenna, planted precisely at the intersection of the two triangles. For visitors, it's above all the setting for the Museo Nazionale del Cinema, stretched over 30 m in height in the spiral-ascending central hall.

Dive two hours into the Museo del Cinema, one of the world's most creative in its scenography: immersive projections, original costumes (from Maciste 1914 to Avengers), tributes to Dario Argento and the Italian giallo born in Turin. Argento shot Profondo Rosso here in 1975, Suspiria in 1977. Then take the transparent panoramic elevator that pierces the dome in 59 seconds to climb to the terrace at 85 m—360° view over Turin, the Po, and on clear days the Western Alps from Monte Viso to Monte Rosa. Combined Museo + elevator ticket €17.

Push through the door of the Cattedrale di San Giovanni Battista at 8:30am, quiet early opening. It's here, in the Cappella della Sacra Sindone restored by Guarino Guarini from 1668 to 1694 and reopened in 2018 after twenty-two years of work following the 1997 fire, that the Holy Shroud rests—linen cloth measuring 4.42 × 1.13 m bearing the imprint of a crucified man, property of the Vatican since 1983. Between ostensions, you see the armored reliquary but not the cloth itself. A full-size copy is permanently displayed in the left side nave, faithful facsimile of the flagellation marks, blood stains and dorsal facial image. The scientific debate on authenticity remains open since the disputed carbon-14 dating of 1988. Free entry, 30 minutes.

Five minutes on foot, at Palazzo dell'Accademia delle Scienze, descend two levels into the Museo Egizio. Founded in 1824 by Carlo Felice with the purchase of the Drovetti collection, it's the world's second-largest collection of Egyptian antiquities after Cairo—ahead of London, ahead of Paris. 6,500 pieces displayed out of 12,000 conserved: papyri, sarcophagi, mummies, sphinxes, complete funerary furnishings of Kha and Merit (royal architect of the 18th dynasty, circa 1450 BC, rediscovered intact in 1906). Look for the gallery of Sekhmet statues, lion-headed goddess of war and plague: 21 effigies in black granodiorite aligned, dated to Thutmose III. Turin guides say you must never look in the eyes of the third from the left. Ticket €18, allow 3 hours.

Stretch your legs via Garibaldi, pedestrian axis toward Piazza Castello, and stop at Via Stampatori 4 in front of the house where Erasmus of Rotterdam lodged in 1506. Further on, Via Lagrange, before the statue of Joseph-Louis Lagrange born here in 1736—the mathematician whose analysis founded modern celestial mechanics, pupil of Turin before Berlin and Paris. The city accumulates intellectual figures on every street corner, without trumpeting it.

Take off early heading east, A4 motorway then Vercelli exit, 75 km in 1 hour to Trino. At dawn, cross the Vercellese rice fields: over 80,000 hectares, water reflecting the sky in perfect checkerboards—this is where 50% of Italian rice is cultivated, direct heritage of the Lucedio Cistercians. Ground mist, grey herons, factory silence in the open air. The Abbey of Lucedio surges at the end of a straight road: fortified Cistercian complex, red bricks, pentagonal tower, arcaded cloister. Founded in 1123 by monks from La Ferté in Burgundy, they drained the marshes of the lower Po plain and invented Italian rice cultivation in the fourteenth century.

Visits are only possible by guided reservation (€15, 1.5 hours, weekends and certain weekday afternoons). The guide opens the nave of the Chiesa del Popolo, descends to the crypt of the mummies (two monks naturally mummified by the dry climate), shows the 'weeping column'—pillar of the chapter house that oozes reddish moisture that analysis has never definitively explained. The dark legend tells that in 1684, witches from the nearby Darola cemetery invoked the devil, who possessed the monks for a full century: orgies, ritual rapes, torture. Pius VI secularized the abbey in 1784, exactly one hundred years later. The timing is troubling. The diocesan archives neither confirm nor deny.

800 m from the abbey, follow the path to the abandoned chapel Madonna delle Vigne, in the hamlet of Darola. On the interior west wall, a musical score painted in the eighteenth century, notes in bass clef, which appears innocuous. Read backwards from the mirror, it would compose a Luciferian invocation chant—at least that's the reading by Italian occultism writer Renato del Ponte in 1995. No academic musicologist has confirmed. The chapel is open to drafts, partially ruined. Go in daylight, the ground is treacherous after rain.

Depending on your flight, two options to close the loop. If takeoff in late afternoon: leisurely morning in Cogne or detour via Pont d'Aël (45.7011, 7.2261), 8 km from Aosta, spectacular Roman aqueduct in dry stone, built in 3 BC over 56 m long and 66 m high above the torrent, which supplied Aosta from the Grand-Nomenon springs. Still standing at 2,020 years, it's one of the finest intact Roman works in the Italian Alps. Free access, marked trail from the parking.

If early departure from Caselle: direct route to Turin, 110 km, 1h45 motorway. If you have two hours margin, signposted stop at Castello di Issogne (45.6588, 7.6864), 30 km south of Aosta on the motorway, unique castle of its kind—sober exterior, interior entirely painted in fresco around 1490 by the so-called Pseudo-Fra' Antonio Mazzucchini on commission from Georges de Challant. Market scenes, baker and tailor shops, soldiers in armor, kitchen with its utensils: exceptional iconographic testimony on daily life at the turn of the fifteenth century. Ticket €6, 45 minutes visit.

Turin Caselle Airport, 16 km north of Turin center, allow 35 minutes by taxi (€35-45) or shuttle (€8, departures every 30 minutes from Porta Susa). Arrive 2 hours before for Schengen flights, 3 hours for non-Schengen flights.

activities.text: Dinner at Tre Galline, Via Bellezia 37, Turin's oldest trattoria attested since 1832. The vaulted hall, white tablecloths, waiters in vests—nothing has budged in 190 years. The menu is 100% Piedmontese without compromise: carne cruda all'albese (hand-cut Albe tartare, Parmesan, truffle in season), agnolotti del plin in melted butter and sage, brasato al Barolo (beef braised 6 hours in grand cru wine). Book ahead without fail, twenty covers in the dining room, two seatings at 7:30pm and 9:30pm.

Before heading back, drink a bicerin in one of the historic cafés downtown. The bicerin (literally 'little glass' in Piedmontese) is an eighteenth-century Turin invention: black coffee, melted chocolate, whipped cream, served layered in a thick glass. At Caffè Al Bicerin, Piazza della Consolata 5, open since 1763, they serve it exactly as in the days when Cavour, Dumas and Nietzsche ordered it at the counter. €6, worth the cultural detour.

Cross the Po at dusk via Ponte Vittorio Emanuele I and climb up to the Chiesa Gran Madre di Dio. Built 1818-1831 in neoclassical style as homage to the return of the Kings of Savoy after Napoleonic occupation, it openly imitates Rome's Pantheon—dome, hexastyle pronaos, monumental staircase. Turin esotericists claim the Holy Grail is buried beneath the central altar, guarded by the statues of Faith (staring fixedly at the cathedral, hence the Holy Shroud) and Religion (pointing at the ground, hence the Grail). No excavation has confirmed it. The view from the parvis over Turin and its Mole alone justifies the crossing.

Dinner in the Quadrilatero, more contemporary vibe tonight. Vintage 1997, Piazza Solferino 16, serves refined Piedmontese cuisine without veering into stuffy gastronomy: egg cooked at 63°C with truffles (in season), risotto with Castelmagno, supreme brasato. Impressive Piedmont wine list with Barolo and Barbaresco by the glass. Booking essential.

Try the Turin ritual of merenda sinoira, hearty snack that appeared in nineteenth-century workshops, still alive. Spread of antipasti around 5-7pm in any vinaiola: vitello tonnato, peperoni con bagna cauda, frittata di erbe, Piedmontese salumi, Castelmagno and Bra cheeses accompanied by a glass of Dolcetto or Barbera. At Tre Galli, Via Sant'Agostino 25, the atmosphere remains that of a local circle, not a tourist trap.

Dinner at Consorzio, Via Monte di Pietà 23, restaurant founded in 2008 by five sommelier friends determined to serve contemporary Piedmontese cuisine, entirely organic and local, with a list of rare natural wines hard to find elsewhere. Revisited bagna cauda, house-made plin with Fassona beef, panna cotta with Moscato d'Asti. Noisy dining room, young vibe. Book two weeks ahead.

Before leaving Lucedio, buy rice at the estate shop, to the right after the entrance gate. Riso Lucedio is still today a family rice farm (the Salvadori di Wiesenhoff family bought back the lands in 1937). Carnaroli, Arborio, Vialone Nano varieties, sold directly, €6-9 per kilo. It's the Carnaroli PDO that makes Italy's best risottos according to Piedmontese chefs. You leave home with a 1 kg bag and a story to tell while cooking.

Return to Turin for the night, dinner at Da Mauro, Via Maria Vittoria 21. Historic Sicilian cuisine installed in Turin since 1968—nod to the twentieth-century south-north Italian migrations. Pasta alla Norma, parmigiana, house-made cannoli. Thirty covers in a vaulted room, family atmosphere, reasonable prices. Open for three generations, always full.

Before the airport, final tasting of Turin pastries at Stratta, Piazza San Carlo 191, open since 1836. The cri-cri (chocolates filled with Piedmont hazelnut coated in crystallized sugar), marrons glacés (invented in Turin in the seventeenth century, PDO from Cuneo chestnuts), gianduja in bars. Bring back a box, lasts two weeks, impresses more than a bottle.

If you're passing through Turin without cumbersome luggage, final coffee at Mulassano, Piazza Castello 15, tiny 1907 Art Nouveau bar opening onto the royal square. The tramezzino (triangle sandwich of crustless white bread) was invented here in 1925—it became an Italian classic served in bars across the country. Eat two tramezzini standing at the counter, watch the green marble and original silver decor, and end the journey where Turin shows itself best: in the details of daily life, not in the attractions.

visits.text: A 16th-century watchtower watches over Torre Colimena, a hamlet of Manduria set between beach and lagoon. Built under Spanish rule against Turkish raids, it now houses a small ceramics museum. The sand gives way to rock near the tower.

activities.text: If you love birds, the Salina dei Monaci, a former Roman salt pan of some 25 hectares near Torre Colimena, welcomes flamingos from April to October, along with herons and stilts. A trail crosses the reserve. Bring binoculars and stay on marked paths.

places.name: Torre Dell Orso

visits.text: Locals simply call them the Due Sorelle: twin faraglioni standing a few metres off the shore, at the southern end of the bay at Torre dell'Orso. Local legend has them as two sisters who drowned and were turned to stone by the gods. The path through the pine wood leads to the headland above them.

The 16th-century tower that gives Torre dell'Orso its name commands the southern headland of the bay. It formed part of the coastal warning system against Ottoman ships. Below it runs nearly a kilometre of pale sand, backed by low dunes and a wood of Aleppo pines.

activities.text: To get a spot on the beach at Torre dell'Orso in July or August, arrive before 8.30am. After that the free stretch is taken and the lidos are full. Reckon on around 15 EUR for a parasol with two loungers in June, considerably more at the height of summer.

visits.text: The Torre Guaceto headland closes the reserve on the seaward side, and it's the only spot where the full sequence makes sense: fields and olive groves, then scrubland, then wetlands, then dunes, then the Adriatic. The Aragonese tower gives its name to the entire marine protected area. Some zones are closed to swimming to protect the habitat, and that's not for show. Read the signs before laying down your towel.

Sand, dunes, nothing else: the Spiaggia delle Conchiglie is the main beach of Torre Guaceto, and a 2019 excavation campaign uncovered a Bronze Age necropolis here. People swim here in summer, directly above tombs three thousand years old. Private vehicles are prohibited up to the beach: shuttle or bicycle, no exceptions.

activities.text: Mask, fins, snorkel: snorkeling at Torre Guaceto is done with marine biologists, above posidonia seagrass beds. Salema, mullet, sea urchins, sea turtles, a seabed left intact by protection. Commercial fishing is permitted just once a year within the marine area, which explains the rest. Book through the consortium, not on the spot.

Rent a bike rather than a parking spot: the interior trails of Torre Guaceto are designed for two wheels or feet, with boardwalks and marked paths through wetlands and olive groves. Birdwatching is a bonus during migration seasons. Bring a light layer in spring and autumn; the sea wind can drop quickly.

A tomato that nearly vanished: the Fiaschetto tomato of Torre Guaceto, a Slow Food Presidium, now grows only here, organically, with a tangy, faintly salty taste. Found fresh or as passata, alongside the brindisino artichoke, Castel Serranova wine, and olive oil from the reserve's own trees. Restaurants from Carovigno to Ostuni serve it, or buy direct at the reserve.

visits.text: Marvel at the Castle of Torrechiara, one of the most beautiful and best-preserved castles in Italy, rising majestically above the Parma hills. Built in the 15th century by Pier Maria Rossi for his beloved mistress Bianca Pellegrini, the fortress combines military strength with Renaissance elegance, its four corner towers connected by crenellated walls creating a fairytale silhouette against the sky.

Explore the castle's famous Camera d'Oro (Golden Chamber), decorated with frescoes depicting the love story of Pier Maria and Bianca, making this fortress a rare example of a castle built for love rather than war. The interior preserves remarkable Renaissance decorations while the exterior walls have defended the hilltop for over five centuries.

activities.text: Admire the castle illuminated at night, when carefully placed lighting transforms this romantic fortress into a magical spectacle visible from the valley below. The strategic position on the road to the mountains makes Torrechiara the perfect castle to visit when combining a mountain excursion with cultural heritage.

visits.text: Torriglia is 45 minutes from Genoa and feels like another world - meadows, beech forests, silence. The ruined castle overlooking the town changed hands three times: Malaspina, Fieschi, Doria. Every ambitious Ligurian family passed through here. Today enough remains to grasp the site's importance, and the view over the Scrivia valley alone justifies the climb.

Lake Brugneto hides a secret the local fishermen love to tell: two villages were drowned beneath its waters in 1959 when the city of Genoa built the dam for its water supply. During droughts, when the level drops, the bell tower of Frinti reappears at the surface - and some say they can hear its bell ringing. It's Liguria's largest lake, at 776 m altitude. A flat trail circles it in 3 hours.

Monte Antola peaks at 1,597 m - the Genoese call it 'their mountain' and have been climbing it for generations. On clear days, you can see Corsica from the summit. The regional natural park surrounding it marks the meeting point of four provinces: Genoa, Alessandria, Pavia, Piacenza. More than a dozen trails of varying difficulty converge toward the summit from the Scrivia and Trebbia valleys.

activities.text: Hike around Lake Brugneto on the circular trail - 12 km, flat, family-friendly. You'll follow the wooded shoreline, cross a few hamlets, and if it's a dry year, watch for the bell tower that resurfaces. Start from the dam parking lot.

Dinner of canestrelli and local cheeses at a trattoria in Torriglia. Torriglia's canestrelli - flower-shaped shortbread cookies - have been the village specialty for centuries. Here they're served with wine from the Genoese hills.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand tour of the four provinces in 5 days

visits.text: Cala Goloritzé was born from a landslide in 1962—the beach is younger than your parents. Composed of polished white pebbles and fine sand, dominated by the limestone needle of Monte Caroddi peaking at 143 meters. It's on this needle that Manolo and Alessandro Gogna opened the route "Sinfonia dei Mulini a Vento" in 1981, now legendary among climbers. A natural arch closes the bay to the north. A freshwater spring gushes under the pebbles and mingles with the sea. Natural monument since 1995, access limited to 250 people per day in high season, trail closed at 2pm, beach to be vacated by 4pm. €7 entry via the Heart of Sardinia app, reservation mandatory May to October.

Pedra Longa, a 128-meter limestone monolith planted in the sea north of Santa Maria Navarrese, is the official starting point of the Selvaggio Blu. Accessible in 20 minutes walk from parking, easy trail. The rock takes on a pink hue at sunset. Small pebble beach at its feet, snorkeling possible.

Tortolì-Arbatax, your evening stop, is twin: Tortolì the town (11,000 inhabitants), Arbatax the port. Cea beach, 5 km south, is worth the detour for its two red sea stacks planted in the water, remnants of an eroded cliff. Arbatax's Rocce Rosse, in the port, are of the same red porphyry—a color you won't see anywhere else in Sardinia. Orange sunsets guaranteed. Tortolì is also a good spot for artisan gelato at Lara, one of the island's references.

activities.text: Hike to Cala Goloritzé from the Golgo plateau (Su Porteddu): 3.5 km, 500m elevation gain, 1h30 descent, 2h climb. Trail partly shaded, but climb back demanding in full sun. Download the Heart of Sardinia app BEFORE, network at the starting point is weak. The kiosk opens at 7:30am—leaving at dawn is the strategy: quiet beach before 10am, return before the heat. Closed shoes mandatory (checked at kiosk).

Trenino Verde de Sardegna: the Arbatax-Gairo section is one of Europe's most spectacular, narrow-gauge train built in the late 19th century snaking through the Ogliastra mountains. 4h30 round trip, €25-35. Reduced service off-season, check schedule at treninoverde.com. If you do it, plan a dedicated day—it's slow, but worth it.

days_plan.itin_title: Sardinia's Wild Interior and Eastern Coast: 6 Days from Olbia to Cagliari

visits.text: The Cathedral of San Nicola Pellegrino is, without detour, the most beautiful of Puglia's Romanesque cathedrals. Started in 1099 on a 4th-century paleo-Christian church, completed in the 13th century, it stands alone on its square, ten meters from the sea—a placement unique in Italy. The stone, called "Trani stone," is a pinkish-white limestone tuff almost unreal that changes color through the day: golden in the morning, pink at sunset. The 59-meter bell tower rests on a broken arch crossed by the street, a rare feat in Romanesque architecture. Bronze portal by Barisano (1180). Don't miss the triple crypt, one above the other, descending to the 4th-century vestiges.

200 meters from the cathedral, the Castello Svevo completes Trani's medieval trilogy. Built between 1233 and 1249 by Frederick II—the emperor really left his mark everywhere in the region—it controlled the harbor. Square plan, four corner towers, moats on three sides, the fourth opening directly onto the sea. Restored, it now houses a museum and temporary exhibitions. The terrace offers the best view of the cathedral and harbor. 5-euro entry, closed Monday mornings.

Trani's semicircular harbor, one of the most photographed in Puglia: blue and white fishing boats lined up, ochre facades, the pinkish-white stone cathedral reflecting in the water. The evening passeggiata starts around 7pm on Via Statuti Marittimi, and everyone ends their round in front of the illuminated cathedral. Several wine bars on the quay for an Aperol at sunset.

The church of Ognissanti, called "church of the Templars," dates from the 12th century. Small Romanesque church with three naves and three apses, built by the Templars to bless crusaders before their embarkation toward the Holy Land from Trani's harbor. Sober atmosphere, off the main tourist circuit. Open by request, contact the parish.

Behind the harbor, narrower, quieter alleys: you're entering the Giudecca. Trani was in the Middle Ages one of the largest Jewish centers in Southern Italy. In 1231, Frederick II granted the local community the monopoly on raw silk production, in exchange for a third of the profits. Four synagogues were built in the 13th century. The Scolanova, one of four medieval synagogues still standing in Italy, was confiscated by the Church in 1380 during a wave of antisemitism and converted into a church; it was returned to the Jewish community in 2006.

Two steps from the Scolanova, the Sant'Anna Museum occupies another former medieval synagogue, also transformed into a church in the 14th century. It tells today a thousand years of Jewish presence in Trani: silk trade, persecutions, forced conversions, exile, and the recent return of a small community. Small museum, but dense. Budget an hour.

A strange anomaly in the heart of Trani: Palazzo Caccetta, 15th-century Venetian Gothic facade, carved balconies, mullioned windows. One of the very rare examples of civil Gothic in Puglia, a sign that Trani then traded directly with Venice. Exterior visit only, but the facade is worth a photo stop.

The historic center on the land side, less photographed than the harbor, deserves a morning. Small Romanesque churches (San Francesco, San Giacomo), degraded but inhabited noble palaces, morning market at Piazza della Repubblica. This is where you see the real Trani, not the postcard version.

activities.text: Fish dinner at Trani's harbor. Recommended addresses: Corteinfiore (Michelin-starred, pricier) or Osteria Frangipane (simple, excellent value). Local specialty: troccoli ai frutti di mare, fresh long pasta with square cross-section.

Walk along Molo Sant'Antuono, the jetty that closes the harbor on the east side. Panoramic view of the cathedral, a chance to understand why this town seduced all the Romantic painters of the 19th century. Very popular late in the day with locals.

Tasting of Moscato di Trani, a sweet DOC wine produced only in the municipality. Several wine bars downtown offer a selection from small producers. Reliable address: Enoteca Beverbar, Piazza Repubblica.
Swim at Spiaggia di Colonna, just south of the cathedral. Small pebble and flat-rock beach, transparent water, cathedral in the background. Iconic Trani photo at sunset.
