visits.text: Trapani stretches along a sickle-shaped promontory—its name derives from the Greek Drepanon (sickle). Its old town preserves Arab streets aligned parallel to the prevailing wind and 17th-century Baroque palaces. The port, 160 km from North Africa, served for centuries as the maritime gateway to Tunisia.

Trapani's salt pans have operated continuously since Phoenician antiquity. The 18th-century windmills, now national monuments, pumped seawater through the evaporation basins. Trapani salt has been protected by European PGI status since 2018.

Erice, a medieval town perched at 751 meters, was founded by the Elymians—a pre-Greek people of Anatolian origin according to Thucydides—then successively occupied by Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, Normans, and Spanish. Its 70 churches for 700 inhabitants make it Sicily's most church-dense town.

Marsala, 30 km south, is renowned for its fortified wine discovered by Englishman John Woodhouse in 1773. It's also where Garibaldi landed on May 11, 1860 with his Thousand to conquer the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

activities.text: Marsala DOC wine tasting at Florio or Pellegrino cellars, the two historic producers founded in the 19th century—available in dry, semi-dry, or sweet styles.
Sunset over the salt pans from Nubia's viewpoint: the low-angle light turns the basins pink and orange, with windmills silhouetted against the sky.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Sicily

places.name: Trastevere

visits.text: Trastevere ('beyond the Tiber') is one of Rome's oldest neighborhoods: from the Republican era, it welcomed foreigners, merchants, sailors, and the city's first Jews. Julius Caesar owned a villa here with his famous gardens (horti Caesaris). Its medieval urban fabric—cobbled alleys, ochre and brick façades, arches between houses—formed between the 10th and 13th centuries. The inhabitants, the Trasteverini, still spoke a dialect close to Corsican as late as the 19th century, a legacy of the Corsican and Sardinian presence in the quarter. Piazza di Santa Maria in Trastevere is the neighborhood's heart: in the evening, musicians, neighbors, and travelers occupy the church steps.

The basilica of Santa Maria in Trastevere is one of Rome's oldest churches dedicated to Mary, founded in the 3rd century. Its 12th-century reconstruction gave it its golden mosaic façade—visible from the square—and its Romanesque bell tower. The interior preserves granite columns salvaged from Roman baths and extraordinary apse mosaics by Pietro Cavallini (13th century).

activities.text: Dine in the alleys behind the piazza rather than facing it: Via della Paglia, Via dei Vascellari. Neighborhood trattorias serve classic Roman cuisine—cacio e pepe, coda alla vaccinara—in a persistent village atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Rome: Historic Center, Ancient Ruins & Vatican Treasures

map_keywords: Piazza di Santa Maria in Trastevere Roma
Basilica di Santa Maria in Trastevere Roma

visits.text: Piazza della Repubblica — Treia's finest square and one of the most theatrical in all of Le Marche. Its horseshoe shape opens eastward onto a wide panoramic terrace behind a late 18th-century balustrade. On clear days the view reaches Monte Conero and the Adriatic. The square is framed by three remarkable buildings: the Palazzina dell'Accademia Georgica (designed by Valadier, 19th century), which holds 15,000 volumes and the 1,196 parchments of the municipal historical archive; the Palazzo Comunale (the result of merging two medieval palaces, restructured in the Renaissance), which houses the Pinacoteca with portraits of Treia's nobility and paintings by Pietro Tedeschi, Antonio Balestra and Agostino Bonisoli; and the Cattedrale della SS. Annunziata, designed by Andrea Vici, a pupil of Vanvitelli — one of the largest churches in Le Marche by floor area. In the sacristy: a lunette by Vincenzo Pagani (Deposition of Christ) and a panel by Giacomo da Recanati.

Porta Vallesacco and Teatro Condominiale — Porta Vallesacco is the most celebrated of Treia's seven medieval gates — declared a national monument because it was here in 1263 that the Montecchiesi (the inhabitants of what is now Treia) repelled the troops of Corrado d'Antiochia. Just beyond it, the Teatro Condominiale (1801, architect Lucatelli) is a rare example of a theatre with entirely wooden balconies. Its stage curtain, painted by Silverio Copparroni in 1865, depicts exactly this Battle of Vallesacco. The theatre also houses the Dolores Prato Study Centre, dedicated to the great novelist born here — her autobiographical novel Giù la piazza non c'è nessuno, published when she was 87, is considered a masterwork of 20th-century Italian literature.

Museo Civico Archeologico (Convento San Francesco) — housed in the former San Francesco convent, this museum holds sculptural and architectural fragments from Roman Treia, along with an exceptional collection of statuettes and cult objects of Isis and other Egyptian deities of the Ptolemaic period — unearthed in the early 20th century on the site of the ancient Roman city, where the Santuario del SS. Crocifisso now stands. The outline of an amphitheatre is still visible in the vegetation of a nearby field. Key pieces include two portrait heads, a headless togated statue and a small head of Mercury.

Torre Onglavina — a 12th-century tower on a polygonal plan, the only surviving remnant of one of the three castles that once formed Treia under the name Montecchio (del Cassero, dell'Elce and dell'Onglavina). Restored in the 1950s, it offers the best view in the village: the Sibillini, the Majella, the Gran Sasso, the Conero and the Adriatic all in one sweep. Not to be confused with the Torre San Marco, another crenellated 12th-century torrette still standing near Porta Palestro.

activities.text: Disfida del Bracciale (event, first Sunday of August) — Treia is the Italian capital of the Pallone col Bracciale — a team sport once as popular as football, with neighbourhood sides competing in an annual tournament dating back to 1978. Carlo Didimi, the greatest player of the 19th century, was born here. For ten days before the event, the village transforms: taverns, costumed craftsmen, street performances. A Museo del Gioco del Pallone col Bracciale presents trophies, bracelets and 19th-century balls.

Calcione and Treia specialities — the calcione is Treia's savoury-sweet speciality: a flaky pastry filled with eggs, pecorino, sugar and olive oil. Eaten as a snack or dessert. Annual festival in May (Sagra del Calcione). Best paired with the quintessential vincisgrassi and ciauscolo from the Macerata province.

days_plan.itin_title: The Hidden Villages of Le Marche

visits.text: The silence of the rectilinear streets, the pastel facades, and the oversized volumes: Tresigallo resembles a De Chirico painting in three dimensions. Rebuilt in the 1930s by minister Edmondo Rossoni, a native of the town, it's the only rationalist foundation town recognized as a Città d'Arte in Italy. Free self-guided visit, on foot in 2 hours.

On Viale Roma, the Casa del Fascio dominates with its clean geometries, marble, and absolute symmetry. Right next door, the Bar Roma, abandoned and weathered, adds a layer of melancholy. The entire boulevard can be walked in 15 minutes, but you stop at every facade.
Tresigallo's rationalist cemetery is a monument in its own right: three-arched portal, enclosing walls, and Edmondo Rossoni's tomb at the center. Austere, geometric, strangely beautiful. Free access.

activities.text: Walk Viale Roma looking for details: the large SOGNI inscription on the Urban Center (former public baths), the church portico, the monumental stadium entrance. Each building tells a chapter of the corporatist utopia of the 1930s.

days_plan.itin_title: From Ferrara to the Delta in 5 Days: Delizie, Ravenna, and Bertinoro

visits.text: Explore Treviso, the birthplace of tiramisu, radicchio rosso, and prosecco - three delights that make life more delicious. This beautiful Northern Italian city features breathtaking frescoed buildings, mighty defensive walls, and narrow curving streets often overlooked by travelers heading straight to Venice.

Visit the Church of St. Francis (Chiesa di San Francesco), a late Romanesque/early Gothic masterpiece with important 13th-century frescoes. Inside are the tombs of Petrarch's daughter Francesca and Dante's son Pietro - remarkable literary connections.

Discover Piazza dei Signori, the main square surrounded by Palazzo del Podesta with its 13th-century Civic Tower, the Gothic Palazzo dei Trecento, and Palazzo Pretorio. The Loggia dei Cavalieri, a 13th-century structure with faded frescoes, served nobility for meetings and games.

activities.text: Explore La Pescheria, a small island where the fresh fish market has operated for centuries, and the Church of San Nicolo for its frescoes including the earliest known depiction of spectacles in Europe.
Visit the Duomo San Pietro, Treviso's seven-domed cathedral housing a Titian and an atmospheric crypt, plus the Civic Museums of Santa Caterina and Luigi Bailo for fine art and exhibitions.

days_plan.itin_title: Veneto's Palladian Villas: Day Trips from Padova to Brenta Canal & Lakes

visits.text: Built around the Turris Magna Orsiniana, raised between 1401 and 1406, the Palazzo Gallone became the residence of the Gallone princes after they bought Tricase in 1588. Its size fed the legend of 365 rooms. It now houses the town hall and can be walked through freely on weekdays.

Piazza Don Tonino Bello, the old village square, faces the 18th-century Chiesa Matrice, rebuilt after successive destructions including that of 1480. It is named after the pacifist bishop who served as parish priest of Tricase. You reach it through a passage from Piazza Pisanelli.

activities.text: If you are there in early September, the Salento International Film Festival takes over the throne room of Palazzo Gallone. The rest of the year, the Chiesa dei Domenicani and Piazza Pisanelli are enough to fill an hour. Parking is free a few minutes from the centre.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

places.name: Tricase Porto

visits.text: Tiny, but a working port all the same: Tricase Porto lines up a handful of fishing boats, a beach of sand and pebbles the size of a handkerchief, and the Passeggio degli Dei along the cliff. The rest of the coast is rock. Water shoes are essential if you swim.

The borgo dei pescatori at Tricase Porto lines its low houses above the quay, inside the boundary of the Costa Otranto-Santa Maria di Leuca regional park. No large beach club is allowed here. The taverns on the quay mainly open in the evening, and you should book in August.

activities.text: When the sea is calm, a few strokes are enough to reach the Isola, the rocky islet visible from the shore at Tricase Porto. The inlet stays sheltered in a westerly. Avoid days of tramontana, when the swell rolls straight into the cove.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

map_keywords: Passeggio degli Dei cliff walk Tricase Porto

visits.text: Start at the end of Corso Vittorio Emanuele. The tufa cliff plunges 50 meters to the sea, and in front of you lies the postcard view: the islet of Santa Maria dell'Isola with its monastery perched on top. On clear days, Stromboli smokes on the horizon. Perfect light at sunset.

Descend to the sanctuary via the staircase carved into the rock. From the top, the terrace overlooks the beach and olive gardens. The church dates from the 7th century, rebuilt after the 1783 earthquake. Go in late afternoon when the tour groups have left.

Push open the door of the Norman cathedral (12th century). It houses two unexploded bombs from World War II, suspended as ex-votos. The Madonna di Romania, a blackened Byzantine Virgin, has watched over the nave since the 9th century.

Get lost in the old-town lanes, among the Cesareo, Toraldo and d'Aquino palaces. The 17th-18th century facades are decorated with carved coats of arms. Head to Piazza Ercole for the locals' aperitivo—not the crowded terraces of the corso.

Drive 15 minutes south to Capo Vaticano. The 1863 lighthouse marks the headland, and white cliffs plunge into turquoise water that the Touring Club ranked among the world's 100 most beautiful beaches. Free viewpoint, €3 parking.

Descend to Grotticelle beach via the 180-step staircase (sign at top). Golden sand, crystal-clear water, sandy bottom turning sapphire blue 10 meters from shore. You can wade out a long way. Arrive before 11am to get a spot.

activities.text: Taste Tropea's IGP red onion in sweet form: ice cream at Gelateria Tonino (Via Liberta). Paradoxical but delicious. €3 per scoop. Purists ask for 'nduja instead.

Dine with your feet in the water at a marina restaurant. Order spaghetti alla Tropeana: pasta, red onion, pecorino, olive oil, anchovies. Around €14. Wine: a white Cirò, Calabria's historic appellation.

Embark on a 4-hour boat excursion along the Costa degli Dei. Departs from Tropea port, €35-50 per person. Swimming stops at Grotta del Palombaro (sea cave beneath the sanctuary) and Cala dell'Acquacalda. Aperitif on board on the way back.
Alternatively, rent a boat without license (40 HP max motor) for the day. Around €150-200 for 6 people, fuel extra. More expensive but you choose your coves. Coastal license not required.

In the evening, try 'nduja at a local producer's. Spicy spreadable sausage made from pork and Calabrian peppers, originating from Spilinga (15 km away). Served with pane casereccio and a glass of red Magliocco.

places.name: Tuscania

visits.text: Basilica di San Pietro - On the colle di San Pietro, probably the ancient Etruscan acropolis, this Romanesque-Lombard basilica (8th-13th century) stands among three watchtowers and the Palazzo dei Canonici, on a vast meadow dotted with Etruscan sarcophagi. The grey tufa façade is pierced by a Cosmatesque portal with mosaics and surmounted by a large white marble rose window with three concentric circles (symbol of the Trinity), flanked by sculptures of the four Evangelists and two dragons. Inside, the central nave preserves a rare Cosmatesque pavement with geometric motifs. The crypt, supported by 28 reused columns (Roman and early medieval), forms a stone forest beneath groin vaults. Orson Welles shot scenes of his Othello here, Monicelli filmed L'Armata Brancaleone, and Pasolini his Gospel According to St. Matthew.

Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore - At the foot of the colle di San Pietro, this former cathedral of the Diocese of Tuscania (consecrated October 6, 1206) combines Romanesque and pre-Gothic styles. The façade associates a superb rose window, mosaics, and reused carved fragments. The interior houses a monumental 14th-century Last Judgment attributed to Tuscan painters Gregorio and Donato d'Arezzo, painted columns, and a very rare 13th-century immersion baptismal font. The massive, squat bell tower stands detached from the church body.

Museo Archeologico Nazionale - Installed in the former Franciscan convent of Santa Maria del Riposo, this free museum assembles dozens of sarcophagi in nenfro (local volcanic tufa) and terracotta from surrounding necropolises, notably those of the aristocratic Curunas and Vipinana families (4th-2nd century BC). The Amazons' Sarcophagus, decorated in relief with scenes of Amazonomachy on three sides, is one of the major pieces. In the early 19th century, the Campanari family exported sarcophagi to London (1837), arousing the enthusiasm of archaeologist George Dennis who baptized Tuscania "the city of Etruscan sarcophagi."

Medieval historic center - Tuscania's walls, erected by the Etruscans then expanded in the 13th century to a perimeter of 4,700 meters, encircle a town of plastered palaces and tufa houses. Etruscan sarcophagi are scattered everywhere: in streets, squares, embedded in church walls, used as street furniture. Piazza Basile lines semi-recumbent figures from sarcophagus lids along a low wall. The Parco Torre di Lavello, on the ancient walls, offers a panorama over the valley and the Colle di San Pietro.

activities.text: Excursion to the Necropoli Madonna dell'Olivo - 2 km southwest of town, this Etruscan necropolis arranges its tombs on three rocky terraces in the Marta valley. On the upper level, the Grotta della Regina, a vast L-shaped hypogeum with a network of underground corridors on several levels, is one of the most important in central-northern Etruria. Visit by reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Lazio: Etruscan Sites and Volcanic Lakes

map_keywords: Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore Tuscania

visits.text: Five kilometres of walls once ringed the Messapian town of Ugento, enclosing around 145 hectares: one of the largest in Messapia. Stretches of megalithic blocks are still visible around town. Ancient coins carry the city's Messapian name, Ozan. Follow the Sistema Museale signs so you miss nothing.

Ugento's most famous bronze is not in Ugento: the Zeus Stilita, a statuette dated to around 530 BC and found by chance during building work in 1961, is kept at the Taranto museum. The Nuovo Museo Archeologico, housed in a Franciscan convent, displays a copy of it along with the Tomba dell'Atleta.

The Cripta del Crocifisso opens away from the centre, near the old walls: a rock-cut church where Latin and Byzantine frescoes sit side by side, spanning the 13th to the 17th century. An immersive installation at the museum lets you take it in even when the doors are shut. The combined Sistema Museale ticket costs a few euros.

activities.text: Round it off with the Collezione Archeologica Adolfo Colosso, set up in the stables of Palazzo Colosso: close to 800 pieces gathered in the 19th century by a local family. Messapian inscriptions, ceramics, armour. A single ticket opens several sites, so ask for it at the first museum.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce
Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: Before Urbania, mandatory stop at Urbino—30 km north, birthplace of Raphael in 1483. The Ducal Palace of Federico da Montefeltro, the Renaissance's "ideal condottiere," houses one of Italy's most mysterious masterpieces: the Studiolo, a small private study lined with trompe-l'oeil marquetry by the finest Florentine craftsmen. False half-open cabinets, false shelves with books and scientific instruments, a false parrot—everything creates perfect illusion. Federico, blind in one eye (he only ever allowed himself to be painted in left profile), would meditate here on philosophy and alchemy. Budget 2 hours.

The stop that justifies the entire detour: the Chiesa dei Morti in Urbania, 30 km south of Urbino in the Montefeltro. Eighteen 16th-century mummies lined up behind the altar, preserved not by embalming but by a fungus (Hyphae bombicina pers.) present in the soil of the old San Bartolo church cemetery. When the bodies were exhumed in 1804 on Napoleon's orders (Edict of Saint-Cloud banning burials within city walls), they discovered the corpses hadn't decomposed. Each has its story: a woman who died in childbirth, a hanged man, a murder victim, a drowned man identifiable by his mud-filled hair, and a young man buried alive during a cataleptic seizure. Touching and chilling at once.

Urbania's centro storico deserves half an hour: former capital of the Duchy of Casteldurante, famous for its Renaissance majolica (the celebrated "casteldurante" pieces found in every European museum). The Palazzo Ducale dei Montefeltro houses a small ceramics museum. A walk along the Metauro completes the visit.

activities.text: Dinner at Big Ben (yes, really), local Urbania trattoria specializing in regional cuisine: crescia sfogliata (puff pastry flatbread), black truffle tagliatelle from Acqualagna (the neighboring town is Italy's black truffle capital), Apennine game. Easy prices, family atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Umbria: 8 days Among Mummies, Mystics & Caves

visits.text: First stop at Gradara, 25 minutes south of Rimini: a Renaissance castle perched on a hilltop, with its double ring of walls and 30-meter keep. The Malatesta family held the fortress from the 13th century onward. Legend has it that the chamber where Paolo and Francesca—Dante's famous lovers—were discovered by Gianciotto stands here. True or not, it's one of the best-preserved medieval castles on the Adriatic coast. Allow a good hour for the rampart walk and interior visit.

Next, head to Pesaro on the Adriatic shore, birthplace of Rossini in 1792. His house-museum on Via Rossini takes less than an hour to visit: original scores, letters, and the Pleyel piano on which he supposedly composed. The compact historic center revolves around Piazza del Popolo and the Ducal Palace. If you're here in August, the Rossini Opera Festival showcases the world's finest tenors in full productions—it's a major event, not a minor detour.

Arrive in Urbino late afternoon. The city cuts against the sky like a ship's prow between two valleys, at 460 meters elevation. First glimpse of the Ducal Palace and neoclassical cathedral, within the Renaissance ramparts. The historic center has been economically stagnant since the 16th century—which saved its nearly intact quattrocento appearance and earned it UNESCO status in 1998.

The Ducal Palace, full day. Federico da Montefeltro, condottiere and humanist prince, launched its construction in 1454 to 'surpass in beauty all other princely residences in Italy.' Mission accomplished: Castiglione, who spent ten years there between 1503 and 1513, called it 'the most beautiful in Italy' in The Courtier. Reddish bricks outside, luminous courtyard of honor by Luciano Laurana, 1,000 illuminated manuscripts in the library (one of Europe's richest at the time). Upstairs, the National Gallery of the Marche displays Piero della Francesca's Flagellation and Madonna of Senigallia, Raphael's La Muta, The Ideal City, and two Titians. Look for Federico's Studiolo, a 3.60 × 3.35-meter room of trompe-l'oeil marquetry—the only room that has remained completely intact since the 15th century.

Then Raphael's birthplace on Via Raffaello, climbing northward. He was born here in 1483, a year after Federico's death, and spent his childhood in his father Giovanni Santi's workshop. The house contains an early fresco—Madonna and Child—attributed to the teenage Raphael. Modest but moving; you're standing where the painter learned his craft.

To finish: the Oratory of San Giovanni Battista, a tiny chapel from the outside, but inside, a 1416 fresco cycle by brothers Lorenzo and Jacopo Salimbeni. A Crucifixion saturated with figures, colors still vivid after six centuries. Barely frequented, it's one of Urbino's lovely surprises.

activities.text: Dinner on the heights: crescia sfogliata stuffed with prosciutto and formaggio di fossa, cappelletti in brodo, and a glass of Bianchello del Metauro. Several trattorias around Piazza della Repubblica.
Walk on the ramparts late afternoon: the partial tour of the Renaissance walls offers the best views over the city and the Montefeltro hills. At sunset, the palace's bricks turn copper.
Formaggio di fossa tasting at a shop in the center. Aged underground in pits dug into tuff, it develops an intense flavor and crumbly texture. Local specialty, very different from classic pecorino.

days_plan.itin_title: Marche & Abruzzo in 8 Days: From Rimini to Pescara, Hills to Wild Nature

places.name: Vada

visits.text: Castagneto Carducci - Medieval village - Perched on a hill overlooking the Etruscan Coast, Castagneto Carducci bears the name of poet Giosuè Carducci (1835-1907), Italy's first Nobel Prize winner in Literature in 1906, who spent his childhood here from 1838 to 1848. The medieval village preserves its ramparts and stone alleyways. The municipality is surrounded by vineyards producing Bolgheri and Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC wines.

Bolgheri - Viale dei Cipressi and medieval borgo - The avenue of cypress trees leading to Bolgheri from San Guido, planted in 1831, was immortalized by Giosuè Carducci in his poem 'Davanti San Guido' (1874). The cypresses, now centuries old, form a vegetal corridor nearly 5 kilometers long. Inside the medieval village, small shops sell Bolgheri DOC wines including Sassicaia, created in 1948 and which became the first Super Tuscan classified in an individual appellation in 1994.

Vada and beaches of the Etruscan Coast - Vada was the ancient port of Volterra from the 4th century BC and was mentioned in Cicero's writings. Amphorae discovered on the seabed testify to the intense commercial activity of this port. The beach of Vada, stretching 5 kilometers of fine sand, has regularly received the Blue Flag certification.

Populonia - Medieval village and Etruscan acropolis - Populonia is the only one of the twelve great Etruscan cities built directly on the sea, on the Piombino promontory overlooking the Gulf of Baratti. Founded around the 6th century BC, it became the wealthiest mining city in the ancient Mediterranean thanks to iron processing extracted from Elba Island. The medieval village built on the Etruscan acropolis offers a 180° view over the gulf and the islands of the Tuscan Archipelago.

Archaeological Park of Baratti and Populonia - This 80-hectare park preserves Etruscan and Roman remains, accessible via developed trails. The necropolis of San Cerbone is the only Etruscan necropolis built by the sea. The 7th-century BC Tumulo dei Carri with its bronze chariot is particularly well preserved. Iron slag accumulated during centuries of metallurgical activity still forms black dunes on the beach.

Gulf of Baratti - The beach of the Gulf of Baratti, nestled between wooded hills and the sea, is one of the most preserved beach sites on the Etruscan coast. Submerged remains from the Roman era have been discovered offshore.

Castiglioncello - Baia del Quercetano and Castello Pasquini - Originally an Etruscan village (4th-3rd century BC), Castiglioncello owes its modern fame to patron Diego Martelli, who established his residence here (Castello Pasquini, 1889) and hosted the Macchiaioli painters (Giovanni Fattori, Odoardo Borrani, Telemaco Signorini), Italian precursors of French Impressionism. These artists depicted the coves, pine forest, and red cliffs of Castiglioncello in hundreds of paintings.
Coastal path Punta Righini and coves - The coastal path follows the characteristic red limestone cliffs, overlooking turquoise, shallow coves. Some coves are accessible only on foot or by swimming.

Archaeological Museum of Castiglioncello - Installed in the Palazzo Bombardieri of Rosignano Marittimo since 1996, this museum preserves collections from a necropolis of over 350 Etruscan and Roman tombs discovered in Castiglioncello, testifying to connections with the city of Volterra in the 3rd-2nd centuries BC.

activities.text: Walk on the Viale dei Cipressi of Bolgheri - The 4.7 km cypress avenue between San Guido and Bolgheri can be walked or cycled in both directions. The road is lightly trafficked and shaded.
Swimming at Vada - The beaches of Vada offer accessible swimming areas. The northern zones (Secche di Vada) are rockier and appreciated by divers; the southern zones are sandy.

Hiking in the archaeological park of Baratti and Populonia - The main trail (necropolis circuit) covers about 3 km through the necropolis, ancient quarries, and Mediterranean forests of the promontory.
Swimming in the Gulf of Baratti - Fine sand and crystalline water protected by the promontory. Free access from the park parking lot.

Swimming in the coves of Castiglioncello - The coves between Punta Righini and Porticciolo offer clear waters appreciated for snorkeling. Baia del Quercetano and Cala delle Morelle are accessible on foot from the village center.
Coastal hike Castiglioncello - The panoramic trail along the cliffs from Punta Righini offers views of the islands of the Tuscan Archipelago. About 5 km round trip.

visits.text: The Abbey of Vallombrosa (Santa Maria di Vallombrosa) was founded in 1036 by Giovanni Gualberto—a Florentine nobleman who had renounced his court life after granting forgiveness to his brother's murderer before the Crucifix of San Miniato al Monte, seeing Christ bow his head in approval. He retreated to these Apennine forests at 1,000 meters altitude to found the Vallombrosian Congregation, recognized by Pope Urban II in 1090. The abbey took its current form in the 15th century, with expansions in the 16th and 17th centuries. The church preserves Lorenzo Lippi's Trinity, a glazed terracotta altarpiece from Andrea della Robbia's workshop, and the reliquary of the arm of Saint John Gualberto by Florentine goldsmith Paolo Sogliano (1500). Perugino's Assumption (1498-1500), once on the altar, is now in Florence's Accademia Gallery. John Milton visited the abbey in 1638 and evoked its forests in Paradise Lost. Lamartine dedicated a poem to it in his Harmonies (1830).

activities.text: Forest walk in Vallombrosa forest, a biogenetic nature reserve since 1973: centuries-old beeches, white firs, and Scots pines in a dense, silent undergrowth. The Sentiero del Calvario climbs from the abbey toward the Hermitage of Paradisino (11th century), where anchorite monks retreated to isolated cells—panoramic view over the Arno valley.

days_plan.itin_title: The Finest Stops Around Florence in 7 days

visits.text: The Sacro Monte of Varallo is the oldest and most important of Piedmont's Sacred Mountains, inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage in 2003. Founded in 1491 by Franciscan friar Bernardino Caimi, who had lived in the Holy Land, it recreates Jerusalem's Holy Places on the hillside for pilgrims who couldn't travel there. Over 40 chapels spread across the cliff, decorated with frescoes and polychrome terracotta sculpture groups depicting scenes from Christ's life, were created between the 15th and 19th centuries. Gaudenzio Ferrari, who executed his major works here between 1517 and 1530, developed a narrative and expressive style that prefigures baroque.

Varallo, founded in the 13th century, is the main town of Valsesia. Its historic center preserves arcaded medieval houses, the Pinacoteca del Sacco (15th to 18th-century paintings including several works by Gaudenzio Ferrari), and the Collegiata di San Gaudenzio. Valsesia climbs about 80 km from the plain to the foot of Monte Rosa (4,634 m), second highest summit in the Alps.

Upper Valsesia opens onto Alagna Valsesia, a Walser village at the foot of Monte Rosa at 1,191 meters altitude. As in Valle del Lys, the Walser built their typical stadel here from the 13th century. The local Walser museum traces the history of these pioneers from Valais. Alagna is the starting point for Monte Rosa ascents and the Monterosa Ski domain.

activities.text: Rafting or kayaking on the Sesia torrent from Varallo or Borgosesia: the rapids of the Sesia (class III to IV depending on season and sector) are among Piedmont's most popular. Providers offer guided 2 to 4-hour runs.
Canyoning in gorges of a Sesia tributary (several equipped sectors in the valley, beginner to intermediate level, wetsuit and helmet provided by outfitters).
Catch-and-release sport fishing on authorized Sesia stretches (salmonids in alpine setting, daily permit required, available from local fishing associations).

places.name: Varano De Melegari

visits.text: Visit the Castle of Varano de' Melegari, a fortress of significant importance in the regional history of the Parma province. This medieval stronghold, strategically positioned at the entrance to the Ceno Valley, played a crucial role in controlling the mountain passes and trade routes through the Apennines for centuries.

Explore the village nestled below the castle walls, where traditional stone architecture reflects centuries of mountain community life. The settlement marks the gateway to the more dramatic castle landscapes of the upper valleys, serving as a perfect transition point between the plains and the Apennine mountains.

activities.text: Take in views of the surrounding valley from the castle grounds, where the landscape begins its dramatic rise toward the Apennine peaks. The area offers the first taste of the mountain scenery that characterizes the famous castles further up the valley.

visits.text: Varese Ligure's Borgo Rotondo is a stroke of medieval genius: in the 13th century, the Fieschi counts designed an elliptical urban core where the houses themselves serve as ramparts - no outward-facing windows, blind facades. Inside, arcades sheltered merchants and artisans; the central square served as marketplace. The result is a fortress-village with no equivalent in Liguria. Ochre, orange, and green houses - Ligurian colors in an Alpine setting.

The Fieschi castle dominates the northern entrance to Borgo Rotondo. Its high tower - called 'del Piccinino,' built in 1435 by the Milanese condottiero Niccolò Piccinino who had just besieged the village - was one of the most technically advanced of its era. The castle remained with the Fieschi until 1547, when Gian Luigi Fieschi's conspiracy against the Doria failed and Charles V distributed their fiefs to the victors.

Varese Ligure was the first village in Italy to obtain the 100% organic production label - 95% of its agricultural activity is certified organic. This is no accident: the Vara valley, between Liguria and Emilia, has remained outside intensive farming. The local dairies, farms, and vineyards bear witness to a rural economy that still operates the old way.

activities.text: Hike in the Vara valley from Varese Ligure - marked trails through meadows and mixed forests, with views of the ridges separating Liguria and Emilia. 2 hours round trip for the most accessible circuits.
Tasting of local organic products in Borgo Rotondo shops - goat and sheep cheeses, valley salami, Apennine honey, and Ligurian olive oil. Direct purchase from producers, not a souvenir shop.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand tour of the four provinces in 5 days

visits.text: An ancient Messapian city, Vaste, a hamlet of Poggiardo, preserves in the Parco dei Guerrieri an open-air museum of some 20 hectares: ancient walls, necropolises, and the Byzantine crypt of Santi Stefani covered with frescoes. Booking is absolutely essential: the site opens very limited hours.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Tour of Salento: 10 Days from Lecce

visits.text: Vasto - a medieval town perched on a 144-meter promontory overlooking the Adriatic Sea, founded by the Romans as Histonium. The historic center preserves its medieval street layout with Renaissance palaces and cobblestone lanes paved with river stones.

Castello Caldoresco - a 15th-century fortress built by Giacomo Caldora, Lord of Abruzzo, on the ruins of a Norman tower. Four corner towers and a central keep dominate the town. Now houses the Museo Civico and its Roman archaeological collection.

Loggia Amblingh - a 16th-century Renaissance gallery, the sole surviving remnant of the D'Avalos palace. This Spanish-origin family ruled Vasto for two centuries. The poet Gabriele D'Annunzio, a native of Abruzzo, used to stroll here as a child during visits to the town.

Punta Penna and lighthouse - a rocky point at the southern tip of the promontory, offering views of the Trabocchi Coast to the north and the Tremiti Islands on clear days. The lighthouse dates from 1905.

activities.text: Stroll along the Lungomare di Vasto - the seafront promenade below the promontory, with Vasto Marina beach and its 8 km of fine sand.

Explore the Costa dei Trabocchi heading north - this coastline, designated a nature reserve, is famous for the trabocchi, ancient fishing machines on stilts planted in the sea, some dating back to the 17th century.

days_plan.itin_title: Italy's Most Beautiful Villages in Abruzzo

visits.text: Velia, founded around 540 BCE by Greek colonists from Phocaea fleeing the Persian invasion, is Paestum's lesser-known little sister. It housed the Eleatic school of philosophy—Parmenides, Zeno (of the paradoxes)—which laid the foundations of Western metaphysics. The site, in a swampy area abandoned in the Middle Ages, preserves the acropolis, theater, and above all the Porta Rosa: the only 4th-century BCE Greek rounded arch to reach us, and the oldest preserved rounded arch in Italy. More modest than Paestum, but far quieter—rarely more than 50 visitors per day.

Velia's acropolis, atop the hill, retains vestiges of Athena's temple and offers a clear view over the Tyrrhenian coast. The climb is short but steep. Nice picnic area under umbrella pines at mid-slope.

activities.text: Picnic on site with Cilento products: goat cheese, white figs IGP, olive oil, Aglianico red wine. Buy at the local cooperative in Ascea Marina before heading up.

days_plan.itin_title: Naples to Matera Road Trip: 16 Days Through Southern Italy

visits.text: You arrive at Capracotta via a steep road from Agnone, and at 1,421 meters you reach the highest village in central-southern Italy. Nicknamed the 'queen of snows': on March 5-6, 2015, 256 cm reportedly fell in 24 hours—record announced locally, never certified by Guinness, but legendary in all Italian snow conversations. Etymology uncertain: perhaps from Latin Castra Cocta (burnt camp), perhaps from Lombard tradition of sacrificing a goat before settling new territory. Santa Maria Assunta church, baroque facade, view over Sangro valley. And an odd tradition: over 1,000 tailors left Capracotta in the 20th century, including two successive presidents of the Italian National Tailors' Academy. A village of shepherds who made careers in couture—that pretty much sums up Molise.

One kilometer above the center, the Giardino della Flora Appenninica is one of Italy's highest botanical gardens—around 1,500 meters. Nine hectares of endemic central-southern Apennine flora: medicinal plants, marsh species, themed trails. Odd peculiarity: at 41° latitude (same as Madrid or New York), Capracotta maintains an alpine climate thanks to altitude. The garden showcases this anomaly. Open only June-September, check before climbing. It's small, doable in 1 hour, but it changes how you see vegetation on trails you'll take afterward.

First UNESCO Biosphere Reserve established in Italy, in 1977: the MAB Collemeluccio-Montedimezzo was inscribed before Cilento National Park, before Vesuvius, before Stelvio. And nobody talks about it. Two cores 15 km apart: Collemeluccio (Pescolanciano municipality) and Montedimezzo (Vastogirardi), 654 total hectares. Peculiarity: Abies alba (silver fir) forest, vestige of vanished Apennine fir forests—you won't find stands this well-preserved except here, in Tuscany and Calabria. Marked trails, visitor center at Montedimezzo (aviaries for injured fauna, screening room). The 'Colle Gendarme' viewpoint overlooks the Trigno valley: here you understand why this forest survived—rugged terrain, late access, inaccessible to major industrial logging.

On the descent road, make a quick stop at Pescolanciano. Ducal d'Alessandro castle (13th century, remodeled 16th), compact historic center, Oscan Samnite inscriptions found in the surroundings. Little-known anecdote: in the 18th century, Duke Pasquale d'Alessandro founded a renowned ceramic factory here, whose pieces are now scattered across several Italian museums. The borgo itself can be covered in 30 minutes—no more, but the detour is worthwhile for the perched castle and view over the fir forest just left behind.

Wild story: Castello Pandone dominates Venafro from its hill. Lombard origin, enlarged by the Pandone in the 15th century, transformed into a Renaissance residence by Count Enrico Pandone in early 16th century. He commissioned, between 1522 and 1527, the fresco cycle unique in Italy: his breeding horses, life-size, in slight relief on first-floor walls. Each equestrian portrait bears the horse's name, breed, coat—it's a ducal catalog in paint. Stunning effect, almost 3D. Enrico was beheaded for treason against Charles V, but his equine obsession survives him. Since 2013 the castle houses the Museo Nazionale del Molise—medieval frescoes, 15th-century Nottingham alabaster polyptych. 1.5 hours.

Rare urban curiosity in Italy: Venafro's Roman amphitheater, the Verlasce, has become an urban square. Its elliptical form still reads in the street layout, and some medieval houses are literally built into reused Roman arches. It's one of the most striking cases of urban continuity between antiquity and Middle Ages. Walk slowly, look up, spot Roman stones reemployed in foundations.

Outside the center, Venafro's Roman theater is more modest than Saepinum but preserved. Dated to 1st century BC, it was pillaged for stones during the Middle Ages. What remains: orchestra, part of cavea, stage wall. Countryside setting, olives all around. Combined with Verlasce, it gives a good sense of Roman Venafrum—Venafro oil was at the time one of the Empire's most renowned. Cicero and Horace mention it in their texts.

The Romans considered Venafro oil the best in the ancient world. The Parco Regionale dell'Olivo today protects historical olive groves on Monte Santa Croce slopes. The local cultivar, aurina, is ancestral—Slow Food made it a Presidio. Some plants are several centuries old. Marked trail, educational panels. 1 hour for a short loop, more if you extend.

activities.text: Reserve key trail: the Collemeluccio fir forest crossing to the abandoned water mill on the Trigno. 2-hour round trip, gentle elevation, boreal forest atmosphere planted in the southern Apennines—surreal. Furtive fauna: roe deer, wild boar, sometimes wolf in winter (tracks in snow rather than encounters). In spring, the understory carpets with squill, Neapolitan crocus, snowdrops. Good shoes suffice.

At noon, ask for pezzata di pecora in Capracotta: mutton boiled long with aromatics and tomato, served with country bread. Village signature dish, direct transhumance heritage—it's what shepherds ate leaving summer pastures, culled meat cooked until melting. Festive, filling, dated. Several downtown trattorias serve it in winter. Summer, lighter version, or polenta alla pecorara.

Aurina oil tasting at Colonia Julia, historic Venafro producer. Endemic cultivar, nearly extinct, saved by a few stubborn families. Herbaceous notes, green almond, peppery finish. Slow Food Presidio. Visit to Monte Santa Croce olive groves plus comparative tasting with other Molise oils (Gentile di Larino, etc.). By reservation, allow 1.5 hours.

Dinner in Venafro at a producer's or downtown trattoria. Specialties: caciocavallo and buffalo latticini (Caseificio Angiolillo, renowned locally), pasta with aurina oil, lamb from Volturno valley. If you've tasted Tintilia, try tonight Falanghina del Molise (white, fresh, little-known) or Pentro DOC.

places.name: Venezia

visits.text: The Grand Canal is Venice's main artery: 3.8 km long, 50 to 70 m wide, 5 to 10 m deep, in an inverted S-shape. It's lined by more than 170 remarkable buildings constructed between the 13th and 18th centuries. Four bridges span it: the Rialto (1591, resting on 12,000 elm piles), the Accademia (1854), the Scalzi (1934), and the Constitution (2008). Vaporetto line 1 goes up the canal from the station to San Marco, stopping at every stop—the slowest and most beautiful way to discover the city.

St. Mark's Basilica was founded in 828 to house the relics of Saint Mark, stolen from Alexandria by Venetian merchants that same year. Rebuilt after a fire in 976, it was consecrated in 1094 in its current form. Its interior decoration covers 4,240 m² of mosaics. The Pala d'Oro, a Byzantine gold altar retable, is set with 1,300 pearls, 300 emeralds, 300 sapphires, and 400 garnets. The four bronze horses on the façade are copies—the originals, dating from the 2nd-3rd century AD, are preserved in the interior museum to protect them from pollution.

The Doge's Palace (Palazzo Ducale) was the seat of the Venetian Republic's government for nearly a thousand years. Its Venetian Gothic style—arcades in white and pink marble lace, openwork loggia—is one of the most accomplished examples of this style in the world. The Hall of the Great Council (1,300 m²), the largest room in Europe at the time of its construction, could accommodate up to 1,800 patricians. The Bridge of Sighs (1600) connects the palace to the prisons and owes its name to the supposed sighs of condemned prisoners glimpsing the lagoon for the last time.

The sestiere Dorsoduro (hard back) takes its name from the rockier nature of its soil, making it less subject to acqua alta than other districts. It concentrates three major cultural institutions: the Gallerie dell'Accademia (Venetian painting from the 14th to 18th century, including Bellini, Giorgione, Titian, and Veronese), the Peggy Guggenheim Collection installed in her unfinished palace on the Grand Canal, and the Basilica of Santa Maria della Salute—a Baroque dome built between 1631 and 1687 in thanksgiving for the end of the 1630 plague, resting on more than one million alder wood piles.

Murano is an island 1.5 km north of Venice, famous for its glassmaking since 1291—the year the Venetian Republic ordered the transfer of all the city's furnaces to the island to reduce fire risks. Master glassmakers there enjoyed exceptional privileges: their daughters could marry Venetian nobles. The Museo del Vetro traces the evolution of the technique since Antiquity. The Basilica of Santi Maria e Donato (12th century) preserves a Byzantine floor mosaic among the best preserved in Italy.

Burano is an island 7 km from Venice, recognizable by its brightly painted houses—red, yellow, blue, green. Tradition has it that fishermen chose these colors to find their own house in the lagoon fog. The island is also known for its needle lace, inherited from the 16th century, displayed at the Scuola dei Merletti (lace school). Its bell tower leans noticeably—visible from anywhere on the island.

Torcello is the first inhabited island of the Venetian lagoon, settled as early as the 5th-6th century by refugees fleeing barbarian invasions. Today almost deserted (about ten inhabitants), it preserves the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta—founded in 639, the oldest in the lagoon—with its 11th-12th century Byzantine mosaics including a Last Judgment on the counter-façade. The cathedral also contains Attila's Throne, a carved stone block that tradition says served the Hun chief—actually a seat reserved for medieval judges.

The Rialto Bridge was built between 1588 and 1591 by architect Antonio Da Ponte, after a long debate between a single arch (simpler for boats) and three arches (more stable). The single arch won—48 m span, without joints, the bridge has stood for over four centuries. It rests on 12,000 elm piles. It's the first stone bridge over the Grand Canal, preceded by wooden bridges that regularly collapsed from the 12th century onward. Two rows of shops frame the central passage.

The Rialto market is divided into two side-by-side parts: the Pescheria (fish market) in a neo-Gothic building from 1907, and the Erberia (vegetables and fruits). Commercial activity at Rialto dates back to the 10th century, when this slightly elevated district was the first colonized—Venice was actually called Rialto (from Rivus Altus, high shore) in its early centuries. The market is active Tuesday to Saturday, early morning until noon.

The sestiere of Cannaregio, in northern Venice, houses the world's oldest Jewish ghetto—founded in 1516 when the Venetian Republic concentrated the Jewish population in an area isolated by gates locked at night. The word ghetto comes from the Venetian term for foundry (geto), as the area previously housed a foundry. Five synagogues dating from the 16th and 17th centuries still stand and some remain active.

The sestiere of Castello, in the eastern part of Venice, houses the Arsenal—a military shipyard founded in the 12th century that enabled Venice to dominate the Mediterranean. At its peak in the 15th century, it employed 16,000 workers (the arsenalotti) capable of assembling a complete warship in a single day. Dante drew inspiration from it to describe Hell in the Divine Comedy. The Arsenal buildings are undergoing cultural reconversion.

activities.text: Cross the Grand Canal by traghetto: a large gondola with two oarsmen that connects the two banks for €2, in 3 minutes. You travel standing, like the Venetians. Several crossing points exist between Santa Sofia and San Tomà. It's the only way to cross the canal without using one of the four bridges.

Visit St. Mark's Basilica early in the morning (opening 9:45am) or book a slot online to avoid lines. Basic entry is free but access to the museum, Pala d'Oro, and horses is paid separately. No entry with luggage—paid lockers are available nearby.

Attend a glass-blowing demonstration in one of the workshops open to the public in Murano. Most workshops offer free demonstrations, with an attached shop. Master glassmakers work glass molten at 1,400°C—a technique whose secrets were so jealously guarded that artisans who fled Murano risked the death penalty under the Venetian Republic.

Organize your day by vaporetto from Fondamente Nove: Murano in the morning (line 4.1), then Burano (line 12 from Murano or Fondamente Nove), then Torcello 5 minutes from Burano by shuttle boat. The return is via Burano and Fondamente Nove. Plan a full day—boats are not very frequent to Torcello.

Get lost in the calli (alleyways) and campi (small squares) of San Polo and Dorsoduro, far from the main tourist arteries. Venice has about 3,000 streets, most less than 2 m wide. Moving away from San Marco and the Rialto, the city becomes a village again: children play on the campi, residents do their shopping, delivery boats supply grocery stores. It's the Venice that tourists who stick to the main routes never see.

Head to Piazzale Roma (bus and car terminal) or Santa Lucia station by vaporetto or on foot. From Piazzale Roma, trains connect Venice to Milan (2h20), Bologna (1h40), or Rome (4h). For Marco Polo airport, the Alilaguna water bus directly connects St. Mark's Square in 1h15, or an ACTV bus from Piazzale Roma in 25 minutes.

visits.text: Thirty minutes east and you're in Venosa, ranked among Italy's most beautiful towns. Founded as a Roman colony (Venusia) in 291 BC, it's the birthplace of the poet Horace (65-8 BC)—a statue depicts him in the central square. The "House of Horace," reconstructed using experimental archaeological techniques on the foundations of a 2nd-century AD domus, can be visited. This is also where Hannibal ambushed two Roman consuls in 208 BC.

The Archaeological Park of Venosa comprises the remains of ancient Venusia: a Roman amphitheater, baths, a domus with mosaic fragments, and sections of the Via Appia that crossed the city. But the crown jewel is the Abbey of the Trinity complex. The old church (5th-6th century) is built on the ruins of a Roman temple and houses the tombs of the Hautevilles—the Norman conquerors of southern Italy, including Robert Guiscard. The church is still active, run by the Trinitarian Order.

Just behind it, the Incompiuta (the Unfinished) is a striking sight. Begun in the late 11th century to replace the old church that had become too small, this basilica was never completed. You walk between massive stone walls and pillars that support nothing—the sky is the ceiling, grass the floor. The columns and capitals recycled from Roman, Lombard, and Norman monuments create a unique architectural blend. It's one of the most moving sites in all of Basilicata.

In central Venosa, the Castello Pirro del Balzo (1470) imposes itself with its square plan flanked by four cylindrical towers and its drawbridge over the moat. It houses the National Archaeological Museum with coins, pottery, and funerary elements. If you have time, visit the Jewish catacombs (3rd-7th century), testimony to one of Italy's oldest Jewish communities.

activities.text: Enjoy the evening tasting Aglianico del Vulture, Basilicata's great red wine. This grape variety grown on Vulture's volcanic soils produces tannic, deep wines often compared to Piedmont's Barolo. Several wineries around Venosa and Rionero in Vulture offer tastings. Pair your glass with soppressata, caciocavallo podolico, and taralli with fennel seeds.

places.name: Ventimiglia

visits.text: First shock: Ventimiglia Alta, the medieval upper town, perched above the Roia River. You climb narrow lanes smelling of fresh laundry and tomato sauce up to the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, Romanesque, built atop an 11th-century baptistery. The town still follows the Roman grid of ancient Albintimilium. Little-known fact: this is where Sant'Ampelio, patron saint of Riviera sailors, once lived. Avoid Friday mornings, market day: everything's parked below, the lanes stay quiet but car access is a nightmare.

Picture this: 1867, an Englishman who made his fortune in China trading tea and silk sails along the Ligurian coast from Menton. He spots the Mortola headland, goes ashore, buys the property three months later. That's how the Hanbury Gardens were born. Today: 18 hectares of terraces tumbling toward the sea, 5,800 species from around the world—a miniature Australian forest, Mexican garden, Far Eastern cycads. Queen Victoria visited in 1882. No parking at the gate: take bus line 1 or a taxi from Menton. And buy your ticket online—the July queue at the gate is brutal.

The Balzi Rossi caves, on the French border, rank among Europe's major prehistoric sites. Not for their raw beauty: for what's been found there. Excavations began in 1846 under Prince Florestan I of Monaco, uncovering 25,000-year-old burials, Paleolithic Venus figurines, and a bone fragment from a Heidelbergensis-type woman (roughly 200,000 years old). The museum, founded by Thomas Hanbury in 1898, displays casts and flint tools. The caves themselves aren't always open to visitors: call ahead.

activities.text: Ventimiglia's Friday market is an institution at the border. Several hundred stalls set up at dawn along the seafront and via della Repubblica: fabrics, bags, charcuterie, cheese, basil and Taggiasca olives by the kilo. Locals from Menton descend in droves. Tip: park on the French side in Menton and cross on foot—Italian parking lots explode by 9 a.m.

Aperitivo at sunset on the Ventimiglia marina, facing the old town clinging to its hill. Order a local Vermentino from the Riviera Ligure DOC and a plate of panissa (fried chickpea flour cakes): it's the Ligurian version of Nice's socca, and arguably better here than in Nice—Italians will tell you they invented it.

places.name: Verbania

visits.text: Lose yourself in the magnificent Botanical Gardens of Villa Taranto, twenty hectares of pure wonder on the shores of Lake Maggiore. Created by Scottish Captain McEacharn from 1931, these enchanting English-style gardens feature labyrinths of dahlias, water lily pools, valleys of rhododendrons, waterfalls and fountains in a place where care and love for nature are palpable at every turn.

Visit Villa San Remigio on the Colle della Castagnola, built in the early twentieth century by the poet and musician Marquis Silvio della Valle di Casanova and the painter Sofia Browne. Their dream garden is a true hymn to love, composed of several themed gardens overlooking the lake in a romantic atmosphere suspended in time.

Discover Villa Giulia and its park in the heart of Pallanza, built in the mid-nineteenth century by the Branca family, inventors of the famous Fernet. Now municipal property, it hosts temporary exhibitions while the park, always open and free, offers a privileged view of the lake and the picturesque village of Pallanza.

activities.text: Walk the lakeside promenade from Verbania to Pallanza, a pedestrian and cycle path of about 2 km offering breathtaking panoramas, ancient villas and dream palaces. An itinerary for daydreaming of a less hectic life on the lakefront, imagining yourself in an age of noble titles and grand balls.

Venture along the path to the Church of Buon Rimedio, an ancient mule track through jasmine-scented woods to a small eighteenth-century church. From this natural balcony overlooking Lake Maggiore you can enjoy breathtaking panoramic views and picnic at the equipped area with lakeside tables.

Explore the historic village of Pallanza with the Museo del Paesaggio housed in the Palazzo Viani Dugnani, rich in paintings, sculptures and archaeological finds. Then treat yourself to a stop at one of the lakeside terraces on the main square to savour the relaxed atmosphere of this enchanting corner of Piedmont.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of the Italian Lakes: Milan, Lakes Maggiore, Como and Verona

map_keywords: Santuario Madonna del Buon Rimedio Verbania

visits.text: Vernole is nobody's postcard village, and that comes as a relief: a farming market town, a few courtyard palaces, not a fridge magnet in sight. It administers Acaya and Le Cesine, which makes it a practical base rather than a headline stop. Allow twenty minutes and park on piazza Vittorio Veneto.

Under piazza Vittorio Veneto in Vernole, the trappeto Caffa is an oil press cut into the rock, in use for a long time before it was abandoned and later restored by the town. The Chiesa Madre, dedicated to Maria Santissima Assunta, closes the same square with its bell tower. Ask at the town hall about opening the trappeto, as it is not a given.

activities.text: If you are heading for the coast, fill up in Vernole: filling stations thin out beyond here and many close on Sundays. The town also holds the last food shops before San Foca. Ten minutes is all the stop needs.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Salento in 11 days: Griko Villages and Otranto

visits.text: The Abbey of Casamari, 10 km east of Veroli, was founded in 1053 on the site of Cereatae Marianae, a Roman municipium dedicated to the goddess Ceres and birthplace of Caius Marius—the Roman general who was consul seven times. Originally Benedictine, it passed to the Cistercians in 1144 after Bernard of Clairvaux advocated for this affiliation during the schism of Anacletus II. Reconstruction in Burgundian Cistercian Gothic was carried out between 1203 and 1217. A national monument since 1874.

The cloister of Casamari is a square of galleries with pointed arches typical of Cistercian architecture: alabaster windows diffuse golden light, sober capitals without figurative decoration (Cistercian rule), and a central fountain in the courtyard. The abbey church with three naves reproduces identically the plan of Fossanova Abbey—the only other preserved example in Italy.

On May 13, 1799, French soldiers pillaged the abbey and killed six monks, known since their beatification on April 17, 2021 as the Martyrs of Casamari. Napoleon definitively closed the monastery in 1811; it only reopened in 1929 and today houses the headquarters of the Congregation of Casamari, which manages a dozen abbeys and, since 1930, a mission in Ethiopia.

Veroli's historic center preserves several witnesses to Roman antiquity: polygonal walls supporting the acropolis, remains of the ancient forum beneath the cathedral, and Latin inscriptions reused in medieval palace facades.

activities.text: The monastic pharmacy of Casamari and its liqueur laboratory are open for visits. The monks have distilled several preparations from Ernici Mountain herbs for generations; products are sold at the abbey shop.

days_plan.itin_title: Ciociaria Circuit: Abbeys and Medieval Hilltop Villages

visits.text: The Arena di Verona is a Roman amphitheater built around 30 AD in pink marble from Valpolicella, the third largest in Italy after the Colosseum and the amphitheater of Capua. Its exterior dimensions reach 152 × 128 m and 32 m in height, with a cavea that could accommodate 30,000 spectators in Roman times. An earthquake in 1117 destroyed almost the entire outer ring—only a fragment of four arches survives, visible from Piazza Bra. The interior, remarkably well-preserved, has hosted an open-air opera festival since 1913 that welcomes up to 22,000 spectators per evening.

Piazza delle Erbe occupies the site of the ancient Roman forum and constitutes Verona's oldest square. It's bordered by 16th-century frescoes of Casa Mazzanti, Palazzo Maffei and its 17th-century Baroque façade, and the Torre dei Lamberti (accessible by 368 steps or elevator, panoramic view over the rooftops). At the center, the Madonna Verona Fountain dates from 380 AD. Under the arch leading to Piazza dei Signori, a suspended whale rib has served as a talisman since the Middle Ages—according to tradition, anyone who lies while touching it will have it fall on them.

Piazza dei Signori, called Dante Square due to the poet's statue at its center, was the seat of power for the Scaligeri (della Scala), lords of Verona from 1262 to 1387. On its eastern side open the Arche Scaligere, an ensemble of Gothic sarcophagi suspended among spires and pinnacles—funeral monuments of the della Scala lords, considered among the masterpieces of 14th-century Italian Gothic sculpture.

The Casa di Giulietta at 23 Via Cappello is a 13th-century medieval palace that belonged to the Dal Cappello family—Shakespeare's Capulets. The famous balcony was added in the 1930s to meet the influx of visitors. In the courtyard, the bronze statue of Juliet has been replaced by a copy: the original was too worn from the tradition of touching her right breast, supposedly bringing good luck in love. The entrance walls are covered with love messages left by visitors from around the world.

Castelvecchio is a fortress built between 1354 and 1356 by Cangrande II della Scala on the north bank of the Adige. It now houses the Civic Museum of Verona, one of the most important art collections in Veneto with works by Mantegna, Giovanni Bellini, Pisanello, Veronese, and Tintoretto. The Ponte Scaligero (1356), reconstructed identically in 1951 after its destruction during World War II, connects the fortress to the opposite bank and offers one of the city's most photographed panoramas.

activities.text: Attend an open-air opera at the Arena: the Verona Festival runs from June to early September with productions of Aida, Carmen, or Turandot staged in this Roman setting. The performance begins at sunset and spectators traditionally bring candles to illuminate the tiers at the beginning of the evening—a truly unique atmosphere.

Stroll through the historic center between Piazza Bra, Piazza delle Erbe, and Piazza dei Signori in the evening. The three squares are connected by pedestrian streets animated by shops and restaurants—Verona has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000 for the exceptional density of its Roman, medieval, and Renaissance heritage in such a compact space.

visits.text: Rocca Malatestiana di Verucchio - Perched on a rocky spur at 330 meters above sea level commanding the entire Marecchia valley to the sea, this fortress is known as the 'Rocca del Sasso' (Rock Fortress). This is where the Malatesta dynasty was born—Dante cites in the Inferno the 'Mastin Vecchio' of Verucchio, father of Gianciotto and Paolo, protagonists of the tragedy of Paolo and Francesca. Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta renovated the rocca between 1442 and 1449, turning it into a defensive stronghold facing the Montefeltro of Urbino.

Castle of Montebello (Poggio Torriana) - A ten-minute drive from Verucchio, this rocca perched at 436 meters dominates the valleys of the Marecchia and Uso rivers. Built in the 12th century around a 3rd-century BC Roman tower (the Latin name Mons Belli means 'mountain of war'), the fortress passed from the Malatesta to the Guidi di Bagno and then to the Montefeltro. It owes its fame to the legend of Azzurrina: on June 21, 1375, the summer solstice, little Guendalina, daughter of lord Uguccione, born albino with bluish reflections, disappeared into the castle's icehouse and was never found. A 17th-century account recorded the story and gave her the nickname 'Azzurrina' (Little Azure). Tradition holds that her ghost manifests every five years on the summer solstice. Period furnishings (14th–18th century) and nighttime ghost tours make this one of Italy's most famous haunted castles.

Civic Archaeological Museum - Installed since 1985 in the former Augustinian monastery (13th century), this museum displays across three floors and eight rooms the treasures from the Villanovan necropolises excavated at the foot of Verucchio. Over 600 burials dating from the 10th to the 7th century BC yielded objects of exceptional preservation: a wooden throne carved with human figures (a unique piece in the world), textiles, baskets of plant fibers, jewelry in gold and Baltic amber. Verucchio controlled the Adriatic trade routes for amber between Greece, the Orient, and northern Europe.

Convent of San Francesco at Villa Verucchio - At the foot of the village, this convent houses in its cloister a monumental cypress tree estimated to be about 700 years old, planted according to tradition by Saint Francis of Assisi himself. The church preserves a 14th-century Crucifix.

activities.text: Walk through the medieval village - Stone lanes climbing toward the rocca offer views over the valley and, on clear days, to the nearby Republic of San Marino. The route passes the church of Sant'Agostino, the monastery of the Poor Clares, and several 15th–16th-century palaces.

days_plan.itin_title: Romagna Circuit: Medieval Fortresses and Hilltop Villages

places.name: Vetralla

visits.text: Historic center of Vetralla - A major stop on the Via Francigena, Vetralla occupies a hill inhabited since the 6th century BC. Enter through Piazza Marconi and its medieval fountain, then follow Via Cassia Interna: Palazzo Franciosoni (Vignola school), the 18th-century Duomo, and two baroque fountains on Piazza Umberto I punctuate the walk.

Church of San Francesco - Vetralla's oldest, erected in the 7th century then rebuilt in Romanesque style in 1207. The peperino stone facade incorporates Roman fragments from the nearby Forum Cassii. Inside: a Cosmatesque pavement, a marble tabernacle from Andrea Bregno's workshop (15th century), and the sarcophagus of condottiere Briobris, who died in 1353 at age 33.

Etruscan Necropolis of Norchia - 15 km from Vetralla, one of Etruria's most spectacular necropolises. The tombs (4th–2nd centuries BC) are carved into tufa cliffs: some reproduce Doric temple facades with pediments, friezes, and busts. The Lattanzi tomb, dated around 320 BC, featured a facade nearly 18 meters high with two levels of columns. The Via Cava Buia, a 400-meter gallery cut through rock with 10-meter-high walls, once led to the city. A semi-abandoned site—bring sturdy shoes.

activities.text: Forum Cassii and Santa Maria di Forcassi - 2 km from Vetralla, the ruins of the ancient Roman mansio (relay station on the Via Cassia) appear on the Tabula Peutingeriana, Europe's oldest road atlas. The medieval chapel preserves 14th-century frescoes beneath a partially collapsed roof. The Order of Hospitallers cared for pilgrims here during the Middle Ages.

places.name: Vetulonia

visits.text: Vetulonia—Vatluna in Etruscan—was one of the twelve cities of the Etruscan League, prospering from the 9th to 3rd centuries BC through metalwork and maritime trade via Lake Prile, now silted by alluvium. The city was rediscovered in 1880 by physician Isidoro Falchi, who identified the site beneath the medieval village of Colonna di Buriano. The archaeological zone of Poggiarello Renzetti, below the village, reveals the remains of the main street and Etruscan shops. The cyclopean walls of the Mura dell'Arce, which encircled a living space of about 16 hectares, are partially visible in the village center.

The necropolis spreads across the hills at the village's foot along the Via dei Sepolcri. The Tomba della Pietrera is the site's largest funerary monument: two tholoi stacked one atop the other, surrounded by a tumulus 60 meters in diameter, dating from the 7th century BC. One of the eight statues that once decorated it—a mourning figure—is now visible in Florence. The Tomba del Diavolino II, accessible through a long partially uncovered corridor, is another major tumulus from the same period. The panorama from the tombs embraces the Grosseto plain, the opposite hill of Roselle, and the sea in the distance.

The Civic Archaeological Museum Isidoro Falchi, dedicated to the archaeologist who rediscovered the city, houses a remarkable collection of objects from excavations: bronze banquet ware, jewelry, helmets, Greek and Phoenician imports testifying to Vetulonia's commercial openness across the entire Mediterranean.

activities.text: Walk along the Mura dell'Arce walls and through the medieval village's narrow streets perched on its hill, with views over the Maremma plain and the Tyrrhenian Sea. The village retains a preserved atmosphere, far removed from the usual tourist circuits.

places.name: Via Dei Condotti

visits.text: Via dei Condotti takes its name from the condotti—the conduits of the Aqua Virgo aqueduct, built in 19 BC by Agrippa to supply the thermal baths in the area. Transformed into a fashion artery in the 18th century following the construction of the nearby scalinata, it became one of the three 'Trident streets' converging on Piazza di Spagna. In 1905, Bulgari opened its first workshop at number 10; in 1921, Guccio Gucci inaugurated his first boutique at number 8. The apartment where Guglielmo Marconi, inventor of the radio, lived for several years sits on this same street.

activities.text: Stroll through the Trident: beyond Via dei Condotti, the parallel streets Via Borgognona and Via Frattina extend the neighborhood experience toward Via del Corso with its 18th-century palaces and balustrade façades.

places.name: Vicchio

visits.text: Vicchio is the birthplace of two painting giants: Giotto di Bondone (born around 1267 in Vespignano) and Fra Angelico (born around 1395 in Vicchio). The Giotto House-Museum in Vespignano—a medieval farmhouse on the hill where, according to tradition, Cimabue discovered him drawing his sheep on stones—is now a cultural space open on weekends and during events. Vasari recounts this tradition and turned it into an emblematic story of artistic transmission. A bronze statue of Giotto with palette and brushes stands in Vicchio's main square.

The Museum of Sacred Art and Popular Religiosity Beato Angelico, inaugurated in 2000, was created in the 1960s to save artworks from rural churches abandoned during agricultural exodus. It preserves paintings and sculptures from the Middle Ages to the 18th century: a glazed terracotta Madonna and Child attributed to Andrea della Robbia, a Saint John the Baptist from the same workshop, and Gothic altarpieces from about fifteen Mugello churches. Of note: the former house of Benvenuto Cellini, who stayed in Vicchio between 1559 and 1571, now houses a goldsmithing school.

activities.text: Painters' Trail: a marked hiking route linking Vespignano to the Cimabue Bridge, a late 13th-century medieval bridge over the Sieve River, symbolic site of the legendary meeting between Cimabue and the young Giotto. The route crosses the same landscapes of cultivated hills that inspired the painters of Mugello.

map_keywords: Pieve di San Giovanni Battista Vicchio

visits.text: Teatro Olimpico - Climb the steps from Piazza Matteotti and step into one of the world's last surviving Renaissance theaters. Palladio designed it in 1580 for the Accademia Olimpica within the walls of the old medieval castle prison, but died just three months after construction began. His son Silla and then Vincenzo Scamozzi completed the building, inaugurated on March 3, 1585 with a performance of Sophocles' Oedipus Rex. The stage is the highlight: seven wooden and stucco corridors painted in trompe-l'oeil recreate the seven streets of Thebes in just 12 meters of actual depth, creating the illusion of perspectives stretching to infinity. This set, installed for the opening performance, is the world's oldest surviving stage scenery still in its original location. The elliptical cavea with tiered seating draws inspiration from ancient Roman theaters like those described by Vitruvius in his treatise De Architectura. The building still hosts performances and concerts today.

Basilica Palladiana - On Piazza dei Signori, this building marks Palladio's consecration as the city's architect. In 1546, the Council of One Hundred chose the 38-year-old architect to save the old Gothic Palazzo della Ragione, one corner of which had collapsed. His solution—a double marble loggia in white Istrian stone punctuated by the serliana, an arched central opening flanked by two rectangular bays—wraps the medieval building without destroying it. It took 60,000 ducats and sixty-five years of construction to complete the ensemble in 1614, thirty years after Palladio's death. The great Salone on the first floor measures 52 meters long by 22 wide, covered by an inverted ship's hull wooden ceiling. Climb to the upper loggia for views over the rooftops and the 12th-century bell tower. The ground floor houses the Jewelry Museum across 410 square meters.

Loggia del Capitaniato - Facing the Basilica across Piazza dei Signori stands this loggia that Palladio designed in 1571 to serve as residence for Venice's governor of the city. Only three of the planned five bays were built, but the facade is one of the architect's most expressive: colossal composite half-columns, projecting balconies, reliefs celebrating the victory at the Battle of Lepanto (1571) against the Ottomans. The broken entablature and sculptural details anticipate the Baroque. Palladio himself never saw it completed.

Palazzo Barbaran da Porto (Museo Palladio) - Walk down Corso Palladio to this palace built between 1569 and 1575 for Montano Barbarano, one of the few Palladian buildings that Palladio personally supervised to an advanced stage. The facade creates a dialogue between two superimposed orders—Ionic below, Corinthian above—with reliefs of exceptional precision. The interior now houses the Museo Palladio: models, original drawings and videos connect the architect's work with his heirs from the White House to the University of Virginia.

Palazzo Chiericati - At the far end of Piazza Matteotti, this palace commissioned by Count Girolamo Chiericati in 1550 stands as a masterpiece of Palladian civic architecture. Its two-level facade of colonnaded loggias was originally built at the edge of a river port. On the ground floor, Doric columns support an open colonnade; on the upper floor, the central rooms advance onto a covered Ionic terrace. The building houses Vicenza's Civic Museums with works by Memling, Tintoretto, Veronese and Giambattista Tiepolo.

Chiesa di Santa Corona - Walk up Corso Palladio to this Dominican church founded in 1261 by Bishop Bartolomeo da Breganze to house a thorn from Christ's crown, brought from Paris as a gift from Saint Louis. Its Gothic naves conceal two treasures: the Baptism of Christ by Giovanni Bellini (1502), painted when the master was over seventy, and the Adoration of the Magi by Paolo Veronese (1573). Both works remain in the chapels for which they were commissioned.

Villa Rotonda (Villa Almerico Capra) - Take the road climbing south from the city to reach this villa commissioned in 1566 by Paolo Almerico, a retired Vatican ecclesiastic, on a hill overlooking the Vicentine countryside. Palladio himself classified it as a palazzo rather than a villa: no agricultural outbuildings, no utilitarian function, only beauty. The plan is unique in architectural history: a perfect square with four identical facades, each featuring a six-column Ionic portico, all converging on a circular central hall topped by a dome. The villa is oriented 45 degrees from the cardinal points to capture sunlight at every hour. Its influence is immense: Thomas Jefferson drew on it for his own home at Monticello in Virginia, and five copies exist in England alone, including Chiswick House in London.

Villa Valmarana ai Nani - A few hundred meters from La Rotonda, this 17th-century villa is famous for its frescoes, painted in 1757 by Giambattista Tiepolo in the main palazzina and by his son Giandomenico in the foresteria (guest quarters). Giambattista's frescoes depict scenes from the Iliad, the Aeneid, Jerusalem Delivered and Orlando Furioso with the luminous palette characteristic of Venetian Rococo. Giandomenico's in the foresteria show scenes of peasant life and commedia dell'arte characters—a radical break from his father's heroic register. The name 'ai Nani' comes from twenty-one stone dwarf statues lined along the perimeter wall, protagonists of a local legend.

Santuario della Madonna di Monte Berico - Climb on foot or by car to this sanctuary perched on Monte Berico hill, accessible from the center via a long covered portico of 150 arches built in the 18th century. The current church dates from 1703 and replaces a 15th-century Gothic building constructed following a Marian apparition in 1426, during a plague epidemic. The interior preserves a Pietà by Bartolomeo Montagna (1500) and a painting by Paolo Veronese depicting the Feast of St. Gregory (1572). The terrace offers panoramic views of Vicenza, the Venetian plain and the Prealps.

activities.text: Stroll along Corso Palladio - The historic center's main artery connects Piazza del Castello to Piazza Matteotti over roughly 600 meters. Lined with Renaissance and medieval palaces, it's the city's pedestrian heart. Note Palazzo Porto-Colleoni at No. 19 (late 15th-century facade), Palazzo Pojana, and at the street's end, the unfinished fragment of Palazzo Porto-Breganze, Palladio's last project, of which only two of seven bays were built by Scamozzi.

Piazza dei Signori at dusk - The square was the Roman forum of the city founded in the 2nd century BC. At sunset, the two Venetian columns—one topped by the winged lion of St. Mark, the other by Christ the Redeemer—catch a golden light. Locals fill the terraces beneath the Basilica's arcades for aperitivo, following a habit that dates back centuries: the shops under the loggias were already active in Palladio's time.

Ponte di San Michele and the Retrone river - Walk down to this bridge built between 1621 and 1623 to span the Retrone River. The view from the banks reveals the rear facades of medieval palaces lining the waterway: a rarely photographed image of Vicenza, quite different from that of the grand squares.

Giardini Salvi - These historic gardens, 500 meters from the train station, are laid out around a canal and a Palladian loggia built by Lorenzo Rubini in the 16th century. The adjacent English garden dates from the 19th century. Ideal for a break after morning visits before heading out to the villas.

Cycling excursion in the Colli Berici - The hills bordering Vicenza to the south, between 100 and 400 meters altitude, are crossed by quiet roads passing through medieval villages and vineyards producing DOC Colli Berici (Garganega, Tai Rosso, Cabernet). Local outfitters offer road bikes or mountain bikes with marked routes. The climb to Brendola or Barbarano offers views over the Po plain.

Parco Querini - This vast 13-hectare park in the heart of the city is laid out as an English garden around a small artificial lake, with wooded hills, canals and two small neoclassical temples. Locals use it for daily walks. A rosarium and several rare shrub species also make it a botanical site.
